### The test that could not use the debug action

Writing the tests turned up one thing worth recording: `life:adjust` — the manual-table action that
moves a life total, and the quickest way to set up a board in a test — **records nothing**. It
writes the new total straight onto the seat without going through `loseLife`, which is right for
what it is (somebody at a manual table correcting a number, not an event in a game) and means it
does not turn a spectacle cost on. The test that needed an opponent to have lost life had to make
them lose it for real, with a Lightning Bolt pointed at them. That is the right shape: the fact is
recorded by the rules, and a test that could fake it would not be testing the rules.

## D198 — Overload: the first alternative cost that changes what the spell does

Four alternative costs in, the family had a shape: evoke and dash change what becomes of the
permanent (D194, D195), bestow changes what kind of object the spell is (D196), spectacle changes
only the price (D197). Overload (CR 702.96) breaks it in the one direction left — it rewrites the
**text**: "change each instance of 'target' to 'each'".

A Mizzium Mortars for {1}{R} deals four damage to one creature you don't control. The same card for
{3}{R}{R}{R} deals four damage to **every** creature you don't control, and points at nothing while
it does it.

### Two effects on one card, rather than one effect with a flag in it

`CardScript.overload` holds a cost **and an `onResolve` of its own**, and `completeResolution` picks
between the two on the stack object's `overloaded`. That was a choice, and the alternative — one
effect branching on `c.overloaded` — is worse for a reason worth writing down: the printed half
reads `cardTargets`, which is empty on an overloaded cast, so every line of it would have to guard
against a target it will never have, and the sweep would have to ignore a target it was never
given. The two halves are two different spells with one name, and two functions is what that is.

It is also the only one of the five where the *resolution* reads the flag at all. The other four
are spent by the time the spell resolves: evoke's sacrifice is a card trigger, dash's return is
scheduled as the permanent arrives, bestow's difference is on the card itself, and spectacle's is
over once the mana is paid. This one has to be asked at the moment the effect runs.

### Targeting nothing is the point, not a detail

The overloaded entry in `legalActions` carries `specs: []`, and `castSpell` sets `specs` to the
empty list when the flag is set — which refuses a target sent with it through the same
`checkTargets` every other cast goes through. That empty list is most of what the keyword is worth
at a table:

- a ward (CR 702.21) never triggers, because nothing becomes the target of anything — the printed
  Mortars at a Sedgemoor Witch has to pay {3} on top of its {1}{R} or be countered, and the
  overloaded one walks through;
- a Willbender has nothing to redirect and a Swerve nothing to point elsewhere;
- protection, hexproof and a Dive Down save nothing;
- and the spell cannot fizzle, so answering the one creature worth killing no longer answers the
  card.

The only answer left is a counterspell, which is why the stack says `(overloaded)`: the player
holding a Counterspell is deciding about a sweeper rather than a removal spell, and both players can
read which it is.

It is also four damage rather than "destroy", which a test says out loud with a Wall of Frost: a 0/7
takes the four and stands. That is the difference between this card and the Day of Judgment in the
same pool, and the reason it is not simply better.

### Dearer, and still an alternative cost

Overload is the first of the five that costs *more* than printed, which makes it the kicker's
neighbour on price and its opposite in mechanics: a kicker is paid **on top of** the printed cost,
an overload cost **replaces** it. So it goes in the alternatives list with the other four rather
than beside the kicker, and being dearer costs nothing there — the loop asks `canAfford` per
alternative, so the row is simply absent on a turn six mana is out of reach. That is the same answer
the printed cast gets when it cannot be paid, rather than a greyed-out row.

### One loop instead of eleven spreads, because TypeScript said so

`apps/web`'s `playAction` had grown one `const withX = play.flag === true ? { flag: true } : {}` per
alternative cost, each spread into the action it builds. The eleventh — this one — made the web
typecheck fail with **TS2590, "expression produces a union type that is too complex to represent"**:
eleven spreads of `{} | { flag: true }` is a union of 2,048 object types, and TypeScript stops
before it gets there.

So the eleven are now one `COST_FLAGS` list and one loop into a single object, and the eleven
comments are one comment that says what the family is: the engine offers a card as two or three
separate plays, one per price, and the flag is what tells it which row the player tapped. A cast
sent without the flag is not a validation error — it is quietly the *other* play, refused for want
of mana or for being in the wrong zone, about a card the table had just offered. Most of the eleven
were found that way in a browser suite rather than by reasoning, because the engine's own tests
build the action by hand.

A type error is not usually a design note, but this one is: it was counting the shape the code had
drifted into.

### Mizzium Mortars, and the slot it takes

**Mizzium Mortars into Ember Rush**, for the second Raging Goblin. Ember Rush is the deck that can
pay either half — eighteen Mountains and a Mutavault, so six lands is six red — and the one that
wants both: the cheap half is the answer a burn deck never had for a 4/4 blocker, and the dear half
wins the game this deck has otherwise already lost, the one where it is out of cards against a board
it cannot attack into. The cut is the second copy of the weakest card in the list, which is this
list's own rule; one Raging Goblin stays, so the three test files that use it by name are untouched.

### Measured: level again, and the first alternative cost the bot pays without being told to

Two seed sets of 288 paired duels, probing the revert:

```
3300   with Mizzium Mortars 210-78   with a 2nd Raging Goblin 208-80   +2
5100   with Mizzium Mortars 208-79   with a 2nd Raging Goblin 203-85   +5
```

Level — the fifth slot in a row inside the ±20 floor. Worth one honest note: this is the first of
the five where both arms lean the *same* way, and the lean is positive. Two and five are still
noise, so the entry is "level" and not "worth four games"; a card that is actually worth something
to this instrument looks like D139's clock, not like this.

`cast-counts.mjs` over the same 288 games:

```
 63%  cast   62 + used    0 / in hand   98 games  x1  Mizzium Mortars
    11  Mizzium Mortars (overloaded)
```

**Eleven of sixty-two castings were the sweep** — 18%, against spectacle's 27%, dash's 23%, evoke's
one in thirty-three and bestow's nought in sixty-three. And this one is the interesting number of
the five, because it is the first that is a *judgement* rather than an arithmetic consequence.
Spectacle and dash are cheaper and give up nothing the bot values, so taking them is not a decision;
bestow and evoke cost a body, so a greedy evaluation never takes them. Overload costs **four more
mana** and the bot still pays it almost one time in five — which it can only be doing because the
one-ply search can see the board it clears.

And `wasted-plays.mjs` says it is not paying it into nothing: over 72 games and 576 plays, the
suspects are a Goblin Arsonist (1 of 27) and a Flame Slash (1 of 22), and **Mizzium Mortars is not
in the list at all**. The sixteenth member of the "spent on nothing" family did not need writing,
because the search already prices a sweeper against an empty board correctly. That is the first time
one of these keywords has needed no bot work for a reason better than "it never presses it".

## D199 — The two rows that behave unlike the others, driven in a browser, and four tries at one deck

`LIST=costs` (D196) asks whether a second row on a card in hand can be pressed at all. Spectacle
and overload each add something no other row has, and neither could be reached by the existing
scenarios:

- **Spectacle's row appears mid-turn.** It is not on the card until an opponent has lost life this
  turn, and it is gone when the turn ends. Pressing it is a claim about a table that redraws its own
  sheet while the player is looking at it.
- **Overload's row has no targets at all.** The table has to send it the moment it is chosen; one
  that walked the player through picking a creature would hang on a question the engine refuses.

So `LIST=earned`: a mono-red sixty pasted in as text, and both rows required. What it cost to get
the deck right is the interesting part, because every attempt failed for a reason about the *game*
rather than about the harness.

**Try one — twelve Swiftspears, nothing else to earn it.** Three games, spectacle row reached in
none of them. An attack lands in *combat*, so the row only exists in that turn's postcombat main
phase, which is not where most casting happens. Six Lightning Bolts earn it precombat instead, and
a Skewer in the same hand then shows both of its rows at once.

**Try two — twenty-four burn spells and no bodies.** Against Tidal Mind's Wall of Frost that is two
decks that cannot close: one run went **450 moves of nothing but Pass** without reaching a winner,
and a second had to be killed. The list needed a clock, and prowess creatures are the clock a list
of twenty-four spells wants.

**Try three — the clock, plus Ember Rush as the opponent.** Both at once, and the second half was
wrong. Games came down to about **six moves**, three of them inside twenty-nine, and never saw a
sixth land: three runs pressed the spectacle row five times between them and the overload row not
once. One row wants a turn of combat behind it and the other wants six mana; a game short enough
for the first is too short for the second.

**Try four — Sol Rings, and the opponent back to Tidal Mind.** Eight mana rocks are what a player
would add to a deck that means to overload on time: three Mountains and two rocks is {3}{R}{R}{R} on
turn four, and an artifact spell is a noncreature spell, so each rock is a prowess trigger too. And
with the clock in the list, Tidal Mind is the right opponent after all — games of 36 to 59 moves,
**three runs out of three**, where Ember Rush managed three out of four. The stall was the missing
clock rather than the matchup, which is only visible in hindsight and is why the Ember Rush attempt
is written up in the file where it was made rather than deleted.

The deal budget is **five games** rather than `LIST=costs`'s three, for the reason the runs showed:
whichever row a shuffle offers, the other is usually one deal away, and a game under this list is
short enough that a re-deal costs nothing. A required check that fails one run in four is not a
check.

## D200 — A finished game stops asking: the one outstanding question that was not a field

CI failed once, on a commit that changed nothing but a browser script:
`apps/realtime`'s whole-game test got `awaiting: { kind: 'attackers', seats: [ 1 ] }` where it
expects null. The next commit was green and fifteen local repeats of that suite passed, so it was
intermittent and never reproduced — but looking for a mechanism that could produce exactly that
symptom found one, and it is a real bug that had been there since the automation layer.

`engine.ts`'s game-over block is careful about this already, and says so: a resolution can be
halfway through asking somebody a question when the last opponent dies, so ending the game sets
`pendingDecision`, `pendingChoice`, `pendingPayment`, `pendingOfferedCast` and `pendingDiscard` to
null and takes priority away (CR 104.1). It was found by a playout — a game that ended on a Magma
Jet left its scry standing.

Every one of those is a **field**. A combat declaration is not: `pendingDeclaration` derives it from
the step and the combat record. So a game that ended while attackers or blockers were owed went on
asking for them forever, and because `legalActions` withholds priority while a declaration stands,
the table had nothing else to offer either — a game-over screen that is also demanding attackers,
with no way out of it.

One line, where the other five are set: `pendingDeclaration` returns null on a finished game. The
test owes a declaration and then ends the game.

**And the fix is a candidate rather than a confirmed cause**, which is worth keeping straight. The
failure was never tied to either of that test's two `awaiting` assertions — they produce the
identical CI line and mean opposite things, one being the server not having finished the turn the
roll gave it and the other a finished table still asking — so both now carry a message naming
themselves, and the hunt stays open with the other suspect written down: a race between `runBots`
taking the bot's first turn and the view the test reads straight after `auto:keep`.

The general lesson is the one the game-over block had already half-learned. A rule that clears
outstanding questions has to enumerate them, and a derived question is the one that escapes the
list — because nothing in it looks like a field to set to null.

## D201 — The table's own atmosphere, and the test that had to be a browser

The engine had got a long way ahead of the table. Thirteen decks, two hundred scripted cards, five
alternative costs — played on a board that looked like a well-organised form. Two of the pieces
CLAUDE.md specifies for the Play Realm were simply not built, and they are the two that make a board
feel like a game: the mana embers behind it, and cards that move under the cursor.

### A second canvas, because it belongs to the game rather than the app

`AmbientCanvas` already exists and is the wrong thing to reuse. It is the *app's* backdrop — violet
runes and sigil rings, `position: fixed`, the same on the deck builder and the login page. What a
table wants is the opposite of shared: WUBRG embers at the board's own layer, moving with it, and
reacting to the cursor the way the spec asks (a 160px aura, embers pulled towards the pointer).

So `ArenaEmbers` is its own component, and four rules keep it from costing anything:

- **Reduced motion allocates nothing**, returning before the first array is built.
- **A hidden tab stops it.** `visibilitychange` cancels the loop; a table left open in a background
  tab should not be drawing.
- **The count is capped by width**, because a four-seat pod on a phone is the smallest screen with
  the most on it.
- **Two arcs per ember, not `shadowBlur`.** A core inside a dim halo is what makes an ember read as
  glowing rather than as a speck of dust, and the obvious way to get the same look is the one canvas
  property that reliably costs a frame on a phone. The first version drew one dot per ember and
  looked like dust in the screenshot, which is how this was found.

`isolate` on the table root is the line that makes `-z-10` safe. Without a stacking context there, a
negative index puts the canvas behind the page's own background and nothing is visible at all.

### One transform, three jobs

A card at this table is already carrying two transforms: it is centred on a slot that is bigger than
it, and it turns a quarter when tapped. The tilt is a third, and Tailwind's utilities cannot be
ordered against each other — so the three are written as one arbitrary transform in the order that
reads correctly (centre, turn, lean), with the tapped rotation travelling as `--card-rot` so the
tilt never has to know whether the card is tapped.

The pointer handler writes custom properties **straight onto the node**, not through React state.
Forty cards times a pointermove each is the one place in this app where a re-render per frame would
be felt, and none of what changes is state any component reads: it is four numbers that only CSS
looks at. The same argument `CombatArrows` makes for drawing itself.

Mouse only. A touch "hover" is a tap in progress, and tilting the card somebody is pressing is the
opposite of helpful.

### Reduced motion needed its own rule

`index.css` already kills every transition under `prefers-reduced-motion`, and that is not enough
here: a tilt with no transition is not an absent tilt, it is an **instant** one, and a board of
cards snapping between angles under the cursor is worse for somebody who asked for less movement
than a smooth lean. So the tilt variables are pinned flat, and the handler's work lands on nothing.

### The test had to be a browser, and that is the general lesson

Neither of these can be seen by any test that does not move a real pointer. The web package's tests
are reducer tests that never touch the DOM; a component test for the card would be asserting that a
handler it called by hand did what it says it does. Playwright's `hover` dispatches a genuine
`pointermove`, so the solo suite hovers a card — off centre, because both tilt variables are zero at
the middle — and reads the variables back off the element.

An effect that lives entirely in the browser is one only a browser can be asked about. That is the
same argument `LIST=cascade`, `LIST=costs` and `LIST=earned` each made about a *row* the engine
offers, arriving from the other direction: there the engine knew the answer and the table was
untested, here nothing but the table knows anything at all.

## D202 — Energy: a resource that is saved, and an instrument that found a bug by its absence

Every cost this engine could pay came out of one of five pots: mana, life, tapping something, cards
in a graveyard, or counters on a permanent. Energy (CR 122) is none of them. It is a counter on the
**player**, it is never emptied, and it is the first resource here that a deck *saves up* over
several turns and spends at once.

### It needed no new state, which is the part worth noticing

`Seat.counters` has read "arbitrary named counters (energy, experience, rad, tickets, ...)" since
the first week and nothing had ever used it. So the work is not in the state at all — it is in the
cost (`AbilityCost.energy`), in the offer (`legalActions` skips an ability whose energy the seat
does not have, the same CR 118.4 rule life and `removeCounter` already follow), in the payment and
its refusal (`autoActions`), and in one place for the arithmetic: `addEnergy` / `spendEnergy` /
`energyOf` in `effects.ts`, which is `recordLifeLost`'s discipline for the same reason — a resource
whose arithmetic is written out at each call site is one that eventually goes negative somewhere.

Nothing in `endTurnCleanup` touches it. That absence is the whole character of the resource, so it
is said out loud there and has a test of its own: a Longtusk Cub that connects on turn five has its
counters on turn six, which is the only reason a three-energy card is ever castable.

### Four cards, which are the whole mechanic

**Aether Hub** ties energy to mana: a land that arrives with one and spends it for a colour.
**Longtusk Cub** makes it — two every time it connects, and two of them for a +1/+1 counter.
**Bristling Hydra** is the payoff: three on arrival, three to grow *and* gain hexproof until end of
turn, which is the one answer in that deck to a removal spell already on the stack. And **Harnessed
Lightning** is the first spell here whose effect asks **how much of a resource to spend** — D130's
number-decision shape, built for Toxic Deluge's life, pointed at a different pot. Its `best` is the
cheapest kill rather than the whole pool, because energy kept is a Hydra protected later.

All four into Kindle Grove, which can cast them and already wants creatures to connect: a Mountain
becomes the Hub, and one each of Borderland Marauder, Ambush Viper and Lightning Strike makes room.

### The instrument, and the bug it found by looking for an absence

No existing harness could see this mechanic. `cast-counts.mjs` counts **casts** and three of the
four cards spend through an *activated ability*; `deck-probe.mjs` answers whether the deck won more;
`wasted-plays.mjs` never flags spending energy because spending it always moves something. So
`scripts/measure/energy.mjs` watches the pot itself: in, out, the high-water mark, and what was left
unspent when the game ended.

Its first full run reported that the Aether Hub had given out thirty-six energy and **none of it was
ever spent** — and that absence was a real bug, one zone away from the cards. `manaSources`, the
list the engine auto-taps from, read the mana, the tap, the sacrifice and the life on an ability and
nothing else. A Hub's coloured rows cost `{T}` and one energy, so the auto-tapper saw five free rows
and would tap the Hub for any colour with no energy at all. A land that quietly makes any colour for
nothing is not the card.

Two halves to the fix, and the second is a judgement rather than a rule. A row whose energy the seat
does not have is not a source. And where a permanent offers both a free tap and a paid one — the Hub
is the pool's first card actually shaped that way — the auto-tapper takes the free one, the same
conservative rule that stops it charging life for a tap that did not need it. Spending a saved
resource to fix a colour is a judgement about the next three turns, and a solver that knows about
one cost is not in a position to make it; the player still sees all six rows.

### Measured: level, and a bot that does not hoard

Two seed sets of 288 paired duels, probing the revert of all four cards at once:

```
3300   with the energy four 157-131   without 164-122   -7
5100   with the energy four 165-123   without 168-119   -3
```

Level and faintly negative — both arms the same way for the second time in the session, from a
**four-card** swap rather than a one-card slot, and still inside the ±20 floor.

And the question this piece was written around, which was whether the bot would simply sit on the
counters:

```
energy in: 401        out: 326        81% of it spent
  225  Bristling Hydra            222  Hydra — grow and gain hexproof
  113  (a chain not attributed)   104  Longtusk Cub — a +1/+1 counter
   36  Aether Hub
   18  Harnessed Lightning
    9  Longtusk Cub
111 seat-games of 576 had any; mean peak 2.6, most ever 6; 0.6 unspent at the end
28 of those 111 spent none of it
```

**It spends it**, which is the opposite of the worry. Four fifths of everything handed out, with
little more than half a counter left over at the end of an average game.

The honest surprise is elsewhere in that table. **Longtusk Cub gave nine energy in 288 games** — the
card whose job is to *make* the resource makes almost none of it, because a 2/2 that has to connect
rarely connects in a format full of blockers. The mechanic in this deck runs on the payoff card's
own arrival trigger: the Hydra is its own enabler. That is worth knowing before anybody designs a
second energy deck around a creature that has to get through.

## D203 — Embalm and eternalize: a copy with exceptions, and the cheap ability the bot never sees

Embalm (CR 702.89) and eternalize (CR 702.100) are the fourth and fifth things this engine can pay
for out of a graveyard, and the first two whose product is **not the card**. Flashback and escape
cast it, delve feeds another spell with it, unearth puts the creature itself back for one turn.
These exile the card for good and hand over a *token copy of it* — "except it's a white Zombie with
no mana cost", or a black Zombie with base power and toughness 4/4.

### The exception clause was the only thing missing

`copyAsToken` already built a token from the copied card's own definition, which is what a copy is
(CR 707.2). A copy with *different* characteristics needs a different definition — and `defKey` is a
card's lowercased **name**, so an altered definition registered under its own name would have
rewritten the printed card every other copy reads. The Sacred Cat still in the library would have
become a Zombie with no mana cost too; or, because `createToken` keeps whatever is already
registered, the alteration would have been silently dropped. Either way nothing would have thrown.

So `TokenCopyProfile` is a short list of printed fields to replace, registered under the card's key
plus a suffix (`sacred cat#embalmed`), with the token's `name` left alone. That last part is not
cosmetic: `scriptFor` looks a script up by **name**, so leaving the name alone is exactly what gives
the token the copied card's abilities — which is the whole reason these keywords are printed on
cards with text rather than on bears. An Angel of Sanctions token exiles another permanent when it
arrives and hands it back when the token dies, and a token built as a plain 3/4 flier would have
been a strictly worse card with no error anywhere to find it. There is a test for that, and one for
the printed card in the library being untouched.

`oracleText` is deliberately left alone, embalm reminder text and all: the ability is gated on
`fromGraveyard`, so a permanent on the battlefield is never offered it, and a token never reaches a
graveyard to be offered it there. Printing the card's own text on the token is also what a player
wants to read.

### The cost is paid at activation, which is the half that is not bookkeeping

`AbilityCost.exileSelf` is `discardSelf` one zone along, and it is a cost rather than an effect for
one reason: embalm exiles the card **as the cost**. Done on resolution instead, the same Sacred Cat
could be embalmed again while the first ability was still on the stack — two Cats for one card,
which is the kind of bug that never gets reported as one because the deck just quietly plays better
than it should. There is a test that activates it twice and reads the refusal.

### Four cards into Dawn Tithe, and the Rest in Peace that could not come with them

**Sacred Cat** ({W} 1/1 lifelink, *Embalm {W}*) is the keyword at its clearest: a one-drop that
blocks, gains a life, dies, and is a one-drop again. **Adorned Pouncer** ({1}{W} 1/1 double strike,
*Eternalize {4}{W}{W}*) is eternalize's size clause as the whole card — two damage becomes eight.
**Sunscourge Champion** ({2}{W} 2/2, gain 2 life, *Eternalize {5}{W}{W}*) makes the keyword an
*input* in the deck whose archetype is that gaining life is something other cards read. And **Angel
of Sanctions** ({3}{W}{W} 3/4 flying, *Embalm {3}{W}{W}*) is the one that proves the token is a copy.

Dawn Tithe rather than Skyward Writ, which was the first choice and the wrong one. Skyward Writ runs
the pool's only **Rest in Peace**, and a symmetric graveyard hoser cannot sensibly share a sixty
with four cards that need a graveyard. Moving the hoser was worse than moving the cards: it is the
pool's only copy of itself, three tests build boards out of it, and the decks that have no graveyard
of their own all have *death* triggers that a graveyard replacement would switch off as well. So the
four went to the deck that wants them and the hoser stayed where it was.

### Measured: the slot is not level, and the measurement needed fixing first

Probing the revert of all six cards, two seed sets of 288 paired duels:

```
seeds 3300   with: 206-81    without: 159-129    +47
seeds 4400   with: 198-90    without: 179-108    +19
```

Two answers 28 games apart, which is the first thing to say about them: the same *old* list measures
55% on one seed set and 62% on the other, so this deck's own noise is wider than the ±20 the
measurement README quotes. What both runs agree on is the sign and roughly the size — the new list
is somewhere around seven to ten points up, against a recorded table standing of 62%. Isolating the
one swap that looked like a clear upgrade on card quality alone, Angel of Sanctions over Serra Angel,
came back at **+11 of 287** — inside the floor and unresolvable — so the gain is spread across the
six cards rather than carried by one of them.

**And then the field table said the probe was reading far too much into it.** Run on the same seeds
as the table already published (`SEEDS=12 SEED0=4400`), Dawn Tithe goes from **187-101 (65%, joint
second)** to **198-90 (69%, clear second)** — eleven games and four points, against a probe that
wanted to call it forty-seven. The pool's whole spread is unchanged: 41 points before, 42 now, with
Ember Rush still alone at the top on 76% and Blight Vector still last on 34%. Verdant Guard dropped
four points without changing a card, which is the field effect this table has shown five times now.

So the slot is **+4 points on the instrument that answers this question**, and the deck does not need
trimming: it has two losing matchups (Kindle Grove 10-14, Verdant Guard 11-13), nothing in the
pool's bottom half that it beats worse than Ember Rush does, and its arrival in second place
*narrows* the gap at the top from twelve points to seven.

The lesson is the one the measurement README already warns about, pointing the other way this time.
D183's planeswalker run found the **table** larger than the paired probes; here the probe was three
to ten times the table. A paired probe swaps cards inside one deck and amplifies whatever the seeds
gave it; the table re-measures the whole field and lets the field move too. Where the two disagree,
believe the table — and never publish the probe alone.

**That lesson is withdrawn by D258, and this entry's number with it.** Neither comparison above had
paired arms (D257), and the mechanism the paragraph proposes does not exist for the row it was read
off: `deck-table` plays the subject's own 288 games over the same pairings the probe does, so
letting the field move changes the other twelve rows and not this one. Re-asked with canonical
lists, these six cards are worth **about +20 of 288** on the table and +18 to +30 on the probe —
two to three times the +11 this entry believed, and the probe it dismissed was the closer of the
two. The slot stands; the lesson drawn from it was backwards.

```
 76%  218-70   ember-rush        (was 75%, 215-73)
 69%  198-90   dawn-tithe        (was 65%, 187-101)   <- the six cards
 61%  176-112  verdant-guard     (was 65%, 187-101)
 56%  162-126  kindle-grove      (was 55%)
 53%  154-134  forge-alliance    (was 56%)
 50%  144-144  skyward-writ      (was 49%)
 45%  130-158  rot-harvest       (was 45%)
 43%  124-164  ashen-rite        (was 46%)
 42%  121-167  arc-tempest       (was 39%)
 41%  119-169  hollow-tide       (was 42%)
 41%  119-169  delta-bloom       (was 44%)
 37%  107-181  tidal-mind        (was 34%)
 34%  97-191   blight-vector     (was 34%)
```

### And a correction worth more than the finding it replaced

The first version of this entry said the bot would not press the button: the new block in
`graveyard-costs.mjs` reported a Sacred Cat embalmed **12 times** across 288 games against 144 turns
on which the engine offered it, and the cause looked like `candidateActions` in `bot.ts`, which
sorts the legal plays by mana cost and keeps the top eight — descending, so the cheapest plays are
the first dropped. A tidy story about a one-mana ability never reaching the search.

It was wrong, and `cast-counts.mjs` is what said so: the same games, the same seeds, **125 embalms**.
At two seeds the two harnesses agree to the game (44 and 44), so the disagreement was never about
the decks or the bot. It was about where the two instruments look. `cast-counts` counts the
**action** a seat took; this block was reading the **stack** between actions — and with
`autoPass: true` an object nobody wants to respond to is put on the stack and resolved *inside the
same `applyAction`*, so a harness that looks between actions sees only the few that somebody held
priority over. Roughly one in eight.

Which also means every escape and delve number this harness has ever printed was that fraction. It
reported **17 escaped Woe Striders** across 288 games; `cast-counts` reads **23 in 48**. So the whole
block now counts actions, and the cards a cost spent are read as the cards that left the seat's
graveyard for exile while the action was applied — which keeps the per-cast spread without the
stack. One more trap on the way: counting every cast of a watched card read **97 "escapes"** of a
Phoenix of Ash in 144 games, of which 72 exiled nothing at all, because a Phoenix cast from *hand*
is the same card and the same action type. Escape says so on the action; for delve the test is
whether any card was actually exiled.

The lesson is the general one: an instrument that watches a *place* sees what happens to be sitting
there, and an instrument that watches an *action* sees the action. Prefer the action, and then check
that the action paid the cost you are counting.

**D171's three numbers, re-measured on its own seeds and 144 games each:**

| | D171 said | it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phoenix of Ash escapes (Arc Tempest) | 5 | **25**, every one of them 3 cards |
| Gurmag Angler delved casts (Hollow Tide) | 11, 30 cards | **29**, 98 cards — one to six deep |
| Treasure Cruise delved casts | 10, 48 cards | **51**, 204 cards — most of them four deep |
| Woe Strider escapes (Ashen Rite) | not measured | **52**, and 11 of 144 games saw two |

So escape is not rare, Arc Tempest's reservation rule was never suppressing it, and the "pool's
first escape card lives in the deck least able to use it" line in D171 and in the arena-engine doc
was an instrument artefact. The *shape* of the delve spread survives, because that was never about
the count. (One deck note that changed underneath this: Treasure Cruise is in Hollow Tide now, not
Tidal Mind, which runs neither delve card.)

With that fixed the two harnesses agree to the game, and the real answer is the opposite of the
first one. **The bot takes very nearly every chance it is given**, counted against the turns on
which the engine actually offered the ability:

```
125  Sacred Cat (embalm)           offered on 144 turns   87%
 80  Adorned Pouncer (eternalize)  offered on  89 turns   90%
 32  Angel of Sanctions (embalm)   offered on  32 turns  100%
 18  Sunscourge Champion           offered on  20 turns   90%
```

`cast-counts` says the same thing from the other end: all four are among the deck's most-used cards,
each worth well over one use per game it is drawn — Sacred Cat at **202%** (192 casts and 125
embalms across 157 games it was in hand), Adorned Pouncer 155%, Angel of Sanctions 110%, Sunscourge
Champion 106%. A card used twice as often as it is drawn is a card that really is two cards.

A card that is used twice as often as it is drawn is a card that really is two cards, which is what
the keyword promises and the first measurement hid. The honest unearth comparison sits beside it: in
Ashen Rite's 288 games a Dregscape Zombie reached the graveyard in 64 of them, and the same block —
before the fix — read 10 unearths where `cast-counts` reads 6 in 48 games. Both numbers in that pair
are now worth re-reading.

### And the browser, which found something the engine could not

`LIST=graveyard` in `scripts/e2e-solo.mjs` is the first browser scenario that presses a button on a
card **in the graveyard**. Flashback and escape made that row a place with casts in it and the driver
has walked it since; these are *abilities*, so the claim is different — the table badged a card in the
graveyard as playable for an ability, put the ability's printed text on the button, sent it with no
targets to pick, and then drew the token. Three runs, 27 to 28 checks each, both rows pressed in every
one of them.

**And the one check it cannot make honestly is the 4/4.** Three runs pressed the eternalize row every
time and not one of them ever had a 4/4 Zombie on the board when the driver looked: 32 token faces
across the three, all of them 1/1 Cats and 3/4 Angels. The cause is not the keyword. The opponent's
whole turn runs inside the same write as the pass that resolved the ability, a 4/4 is the biggest
thing on the board, Tidal Mind holds two Doom Blades and a Man-o'-War, and a token that is **bounced
ceases to exist** rather than going to a hand — so the board between two of the driver's moves is
simply not a place an eternalized token reliably sits. The first version of the sampler read the
board on the move the row was pressed, which was worse and for a different reason: the ability was
still on the stack, so the token did not exist yet at all.

What proves the size instead is a test one layer in, and it is the better test: the altered definition
survives `viewFor` and `packView` with its 4/4 and its empty mana cost intact, **beside the printed
card in the same payload**. That is the collision `TokenCopyProfile.as` exists to prevent, asked of
the wire format rather than of the engine — because `packView` deduplicates the definitions it sends,
and two definitions that share a name is exactly the case it had never been handed. So the browser
proves the button and the Zombie, and the view test proves the size.

## D204 — Miracle: the cast offered as the card is drawn, and the two slots that disagreed

**The keyword.** Miracle is an offer rather than a cost: the engine stops the table the moment a
card is drawn, says it was the first card drawn this turn, and names a cost that is not the card's
own (CR 702.94a). Three keywords now share `pendingOfferedCast` — cascade, madness and miracle —
and miracle added the one disposition the other two have no use for: **declining leaves the card
exactly where it is**, in the hand it has just arrived in. Cascade's hit goes back to the library
and madness's goes to the graveyard; `pendingOfferedCast.stays` is the flag that says "do not move
it", and `settleOffer` and the decline path both read it.

What the engine needed beside it was a fact it had never kept: **which draw of the turn a card
was**. `spellsCastThisTurn` and `lifeLostThisTurn` are counts, and a count cannot tell the first
card of a `draw(2)` from the second — so `drew` now carries `{ seat, card, nth }` and
`cardsDrawnThisTurn` is reset in cleanup beside the other two. The printed *reveal* from hand is
deliberately not modelled: a hidden-information gesture whose only effect is to let the offer
happen is an interaction the table would have to stop for twice.

Two cards, both put in decks that would never play them at the printed cost, which is the honest
test of the keyword rather than of the cards: **Thunderous Wrath** ({4}{R}{R}, miracle {R}) in Arc
Tempest and **Terminus** ({3}{W}{W}, miracle {W}) in Skyward Writ.

### How narrow the window actually is

`offers.mjs` over 288 games per deck, seeds 12 from 3300:

| | offers | off the keyword's own card | first draws in the games | taken back, cost unpayable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Arc Tempest | 65 | 59 Thunderous Wrath | 4829 | 2 |
| Skyward Writ | 61 | 52 Terminus | 6519 | 12 |

So one copy in sixty is offered about **once every ninety first draws**, and twelve of Skyward
Writ's offers were taken back because {W} was not up when the card arrived — a miracle drawn on a
turn whose mana is spent is a card you simply drew. That is the keyword, not a defect: the offer is
made in the draw step, before the land drop.

### Two slots, three instruments, and only one of them agreed with itself

The thirteen-deck table at `SEEDS=12 SEED0=4400`, against the same table before these two cards
went in, moved **exactly two rows outside the instrument's own ±20-game floor, and they are the two
decks that got a card**:

| deck | before | after | move |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| arc-tempest | 121-167 (42%) | 144-144 (50%) | **+23** |
| skyward-writ | 144-144 (50%) | 112-176 (39%) | **−32** |

Every other row moved five games or fewer. The paired probes, each swapping the one card for a
filler inside the deck's own sixty, say:

| card | seed set 3300 | seed set 4400 | the table |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Thunderous Wrath | costs 26 | gains 14 | gains 23 |
| Terminus | costs 32 | costs 29 | costs 32 |

**Terminus is a real loss and the Wrath is not readable.** Three measurements agree on Terminus to
within three games; the Wrath's own probe disagrees with itself in *sign* across two seed sets and
with the table on one of them. Published both ways round rather than picking the flattering one,
and the rule it confirms is D203's: where a paired probe and the table disagree, the table is the
one to publish, and a one-card slot is at the edge of what either can resolve.

The one cross-check worth keeping: the probe's stock arm for Skyward Writ at seed 4400 reads
112-176, which is the table's row for that deck to the game. Two harnesses that share no code
agreeing exactly is the best evidence either of them is measuring what it claims.

### Why Terminus loses, which is a fact rather than a theory

The same instrument was taught to count what an offered cast actually *cleared*, per card: how many
creatures left each side on the action that cast it, and how often the caster was the one ahead on
board when it was offered.

```
    52  Terminus: 32 of the caster's creatures gone, 41 of the opponent's, 9 cast while ahead on board
    59  Thunderous Wrath: 0 of the caster's creatures gone, 4 of the opponent's, 12 cast while ahead
```

A symmetric sweeper in a deck of small white creatures spends a card to break roughly even on
board — and **nine of the fifty-two were fired by the seat that was winning the board**, in its own
draw step, before the turn those creatures were for. That half is the bot's, and it is D205. The
other three-quarters is the card in that deck.

### And an instrument that was six times out, one measurement after the last one

`offers.mjs` reported "62 cascade cards were cast, so 60 of those found nothing at all" for Arc
Tempest — a deck that holds no cascade card. Its `hasCascade` asked the script for a trigger that
fires on its controller casting it, which is the shape **cascade, storm, replicate and conspire all
share**: every Grapeshot in the deck counted as a cascade. The pool has exactly two cards with that
trigger, one of each keyword, and the only thing that tells them apart is the card's own text, so
the check reads the oracle text now. Same lesson as D203 one instrument later, and worth saying
plainly: a measurement that is six times out looks exactly like a measurement.

### The browser

`LIST=miracle` in `scripts/e2e-solo.mjs` is sixty cards built so the turn's first draw is often a
Thunderous Wrath — eight copies, mono-red, for the reason `LIST=costs` paid for twice. Three runs,
**26 of 26 checks each**, and what they collected off the bar is the whole claim in one string:

```
took a free cast: Thunderous Wrath is the first card you drew this turn: you may cast it for {R} (miracle)
```

Cascade and madness make their offer on a card in **exile**; miracle makes it on a card in **hand**,
in the draw step, before anything else can happen on the turn. That difference is invisible in the
engine's own tests and is the sentence a player reads, which is why the check is the sentence. Two
driver fixes came out of it: the prompt was being cut at eighty characters, which threw away the
keyword's name at the end of it (the sentence is 88), and the fallback for a hit with modes only
ever looked in exile, where a miracle card never is.

## D205 — The bot never declined an offered cast, and the sweep it fired at its own board

**The finding, from the instrument rather than from a suspicion.** Across 576 games on two decks,
the engine made 126 offered casts and the bot took **every single one**: 65 of 65 in Arc Tempest's
field, 61 of 61 in Skyward Writ's, nothing declined. An earlier run of the same instrument, with
more than one copy of each card in those decks, read 99 of 99 — the ratio is what is stable. `botAction`'s own comment explains why, and it
was written before anything had measured it: in the offer window `legalActions` narrows `plays` to
the casts of the one card on offer, so the search picks the best of a one-element list however the
position scores. There is no "pass" among the options.

A free spell is nearly always worth casting, so for most of what gets offered this costs nothing.
The exception is the card whose value is entirely about who is ahead when it resolves, and miracle
is where the pool has one: **Terminus, offered in its controller's own draw step**, which is the
one moment in the game when the board in front of it is the board that seat built.

**The rule is a fact, not a weight**, which is the sixteenth member of the family that starts at
`ritualBoughtSomething`: drop the option when a sweep that hits every creature would take more of
this seat's creatures **and** more of its power than the opponents'. Both halves are required, and
that is what keeps it conservative — losing a 1/1 to take a 5/5 reads as "more bodies of mine", and
losing a 5/5 to take two 1/1s reads as "more power of mine", so only a sweep that is worse for this
seat on both counts has no reading of the board that justifies it. Detected from the card's own
words (`/destroy|exile|put all creatures/`) for the reason `destroysOneOfItsOwn` gives; Toxic Deluge
is deliberately outside it, because "each creature gets -X/-X" is a sweep whose size is chosen while
it resolves and so is not knowable from the cast.

**What it is worth, measured four ways.** It changes **16 of 7192 casts** (`disagree.mjs`, 0.2% of
casts and 0.04% of all decisions) and is level bot against bot: **470-464 of 936**. Where it is
worth something is to the deck that holds the card — Skyward Writ's own record, same list, rule on
against rule off:

| seed set | without the rule | with it | move |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3300 | 93-195 | 101-187 | **+8** |
| 4400 | 112-176 | 129-158 | **+17** |

And the probe's other arm, the same list with Terminus cut for a Leonin Skyhunter, comes back
**byte-identical with the rule on and off** (125-163 and 141-147 on the two seed sets). A rule this
narrow should look exactly like that: nothing at all happens in a deck with no sweeper in it, and
the one deck with a sweeper gains.

**And then the table said more than the duel did.** Re-run at the same seeds with the rule on, the
thirteen-deck standings move **two** rows outside four games, and they are the two decks in the pool
that hold a card it can fire on: **Skyward Writ +17** (112-176 to 129-159, which is its own probe's
+17 at those seeds to the game) and **Verdant Guard +9** (176-112 to 185-103) — Day of Judgment,
in a deck that never had a miracle card and did not change a line. Nothing else moved more than
four. A rule that is level bot-against-bot and worth twenty-six games to the two decks that can use
it is not a wash; it is a rule about two cards, measured on a pool where eleven decks do not hold
them.

**On by default, and not because of the record.** Level is level; what it buys is the play. A bot
that puts its own board on the bottom of its library in its own draw step looks broken to the person
sitting opposite, which is the same reason `ritualBoughtSomething` is kept at three games. Off is
the control it was measured against.

**What it does not fix, said plainly.** With the rule on, the Terminus slot still costs Skyward Writ
24 games on one seed set and 12 on the other — one of those is inside the floor, the other is not.
So the bot's share of D204's −32 is about a third of it, and the rest is a symmetric sweeper in a
deck of small creatures. The slot is kept, with the deck at 45% rather than the 50% it had before
miracle, and that is the first place to look if Skyward Writ needs those games back.

## D206 — Rebound, and the drop-this-option rule that would have declined it every time

**The keyword.** Rebound is the fourth way a card in this engine gets cast twice, and the first
that pays for the second casting with **time**: cast it from your hand and it goes to exile as it
resolves, and at the beginning of your next upkeep you may cast it from there for nothing
(CR 702.88). Flashback charges a second price, escape charges mana and a graveyard, madness and
miracle charge less than the printed cost once. Rebound charges nothing at all, and what makes it
fair is that the opponent gets a whole turn in between.

Almost all of it is machinery that already existed. The promise is a **delayed trigger** (CR 603.7),
the same arrangement dash's return and unearth's exile use — `reboundCast()` builds it, the card
carries it, and `completeResolution` schedules it as the spell leaves the stack. The offer is
`pendingOfferedCast` for the fourth time, and declining reuses miracle's `stays`: "do not move the
card" is the same disposition whether the card is sitting in a hand or in an exile.

Two halves of the rule are load-bearing, and both are about the *second* casting:

- It only rebounds if it was cast **from a hand**, which is `StackObject.rebounding`, read as the
  spell is announced because by then nothing else knows where the card came from. The rebound cast
  comes out of exile, so it is not flagged, so it does not rebound again — a card that remembered
  nothing would be two damage every upkeep for the rest of the game.
- A spell that never **resolved** never got there. A countered Staggershock goes to the graveyard
  like any other countered spell, which is why `spellLeavesStack` takes `resolved` as a parameter
  and why the branch is at the one call site that knows.

Two cards, both cheap, both in decks that read "whenever you cast" or "whenever this deals damage",
so the second casting is a second *trigger* on a different turn: **Staggershock** ({1}{R}, 2 damage,
in Arc Tempest for a Monastery Swiftspear) and **Distortion Strike** ({U}, +1/+0 and unblockable, in
Tidal Mind for a Doom Blade — a closer in the deck that has never been short of answers).

### The rule that would have killed the keyword, found by reading rather than by measuring

`expiringPumpCanMatter` drops a pump cast outside a combat, and its comment says exactly why: "an
upkeep, a draw step, a main phase with an instant in hand — a card spent two steps before the
question it answers", with 59 of 95 measured casts in an upkeep or a draw step. That argument is
right about a card in hand and **false about an offered cast**: the offer is the only moment there
is, and declining it strands the card in exile for good. Distortion Strike's rebound cast would have
been declined every single time, in the one step the keyword happens in.

The fix is `offerCannotWait`, and the thing worth keeping about it is that the distinction is a fact
on the board rather than a new flag: a declined offer leaves the card where it is, so the card's
**zone** says what declining costs. A miracle card sits in the hand it was drawn into and can be
cast later for its printed cost; a cascade hit, a madness card and a rebound card sit in exile,
where declining is final. So the "a better moment is coming" drop stands for everything in a hand
and steps aside for an offer the player cannot come back to.

The other members of the family were checked and deliberately left alone. A Fog with nothing
attacking, a protection trick with nothing threatened and a ritual that buys nothing do nothing
*now* whether or not they are offered — those are facts about the board, not claims about timing,
and they are right under every disposition.

### What the slots are worth, which is "nothing much", said properly

Paired probes, each swapping the one card for the card it replaced, 288 games per arm, two seed
sets:

| card | seed set 3300 | seed set 4400 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Staggershock | gains 3 | gains 1 |
| Distortion Strike | gains 4 | costs 14 |

Every one of those is inside the instrument's own ±20-game floor, and the Distortion Strike pair
disagrees in sign — which is the D204 lesson again rather than a finding about the card. Worth
putting beside it: **Tidal Mind's own record for the unchanged list reads 123-165 on one seed set
and 94-191 on the other**, a 29-game spread with nothing changed at all, so the deck's noise is
larger than either reading. The slots are kept because they cost nothing measurable, the keyword is
exercised, and the Doom Blade the Strike replaced was the deck's eighth answer in a deck that has
never been short of them.

**And the keyword does happen.** `offers.mjs` over 192 games: **39** Staggershock rebound offers in
Arc Tempest's field and **24** Distortion Strike offers in Tidal Mind's, one copy each — so a single
rebound card is cast and resolved in about a fifth of the games it is in, and every one of those is
a second spell a turn later. The same runs recorded the instrument's **first declined offer ever**,
one in each: the bot now has two reasons to pass on a free cast (D205's sweep, and a pump with
nothing to pump) where before it had none.

### The browser

`LIST=rebound` is the first browser scenario whose claim spans **two turns**: the spell resolves, the
card goes somewhere no other spell goes, the opponent takes a whole turn, and the bar comes back in
the player's own upkeep offering a free cast of a card they no longer have. Three runs, 26 to 27
checks each, all passing, and the sentence they collect is the whole claim:

```
took a free cast: Staggershock rebounds: you may cast it from exile without paying its mana cost
```

## D207 — Replicate, the cost paid several times over, and the slot that was worth −19 or +1

**The keyword.** Replicate is the engine's first cost that can be paid **more than once on one
casting**, and the first announced number that is not {X}: "pay this cost as many times as you like,
and copy the spell for each" (CR 702.56). Everything else in the cost family is a yes or a no — a
kicker is paid or not, an alternative cost replaces the printed one or does not.

Two pieces already existed and this is the first card to put them together. The copies are a **self
spell-cast trigger**, which is storm's shape with the count read from the casting rather than from
the turn, and `copySpellOnStack` already carried the original's targets *and* its division (D131) —
so a replicated Pyromatics divided one damage each between two creatures really is two damage each.

The count is offered as **one play per affordable number**, which is the kicker's arrangement rather
than {X}'s picker, and that was a deliberate choice about the client: the table already draws a
second play on the same card at a different price, so a count whose ceiling is the mana available is
exactly that list and needs nothing new. {X} has a picker because X ranges to twenty; replicate in
this pool ranges to four, and four is the cap for the same reason — an eleventh near-identical row
is not a play anybody is choosing between.

### The bot cast it 49 times and paid the cost not once

`legalActions` offered the rows, the search chose between them, and **the action the bot sent
dropped the count**: `candidateActions` builds a cast from the play and carries eleven cost flags,
and a twelfth that is a number was not one of them. So a chosen "replicate x2" became the printed
cast, the engine charged {1}{R}, resolved it, and nothing anywhere looked wrong — no refusal, no
failing test, no stuck game. 49 Pyromatics casts in 96 games, zero replicate payments.

It was found by **counting what the bot paid**, which is a five-minute script rather than a test, and
the same comment block in `candidateActions` had already said why that bug keeps happening: "a cast
sent without the flag is quietly the *other* play". It is the twelfth time; the web client needed
the same line, and a reducer test now holds it.

With the count carried through, the bot uses the keyword like a player would:

| | casts | x1 | x2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pyromatics, Arc Tempest's field, 96 games | 49 | 9 | 1 |
| Train of Thought, Hollow Tide's field, 96 games | 33 | 16 | 1 |

Half of every Train of Thought is cast for two cards or more, which is the keyword doing exactly
what it is printed for: a bad card early, a refill late.

### The same card in the same deck, worth −19 and +1

Pyromatics first went into Arc Tempest in the **Firebolt's** slot. Paired probes, 288 games per arm:

| what Pyromatics replaced | seed set 3300 | seed set 4400 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a Firebolt (2 damage for {R}, and again from the graveyard for {4}{R}) | **costs 10** | **costs 19** |
| the second Think Twice (a cantrip the deck has six other ways to do) | gains 1 | gains 1 |

**That is the finding, and it is not about replicate.** What a slot is worth is a fact about the card
that *pays* for it: the same card, in the same deck, measured on the same two seed sets, is a
ten-to-nineteen-game loss against a Firebolt and dead level against a redundant cantrip. Both
readings are right. A probe that had only been run once would have concluded something about the
keyword, and it would have been wrong either way round.

Train of Thought, in Hollow Tide for the third Fog Bank, reads **costs 7 and costs 2** — inside the
floor on both seed sets, which for a card that is a bad draw-one most of the time and a four-card
refill occasionally is the answer the keyword deserves.

**One thing left open, and it is the bot's rather than the card's.** With eight mana up, a single
Pyromatics offers *five* plays, and `candidateActions` keeps the eight most expensive plays before
the search sees them — so one card with replicate can take five of those eight slots away from the
rest of the hand. It has not been measured and the cheap slot's +1 suggests it costs little, but a
hand of five spells and a Pyromatics is a position where the search may be looking at one card.

### The browser

`LIST=replicate` plays twenty-eight Mountains and eight Pyromatics — a deck with no curve, so there
is spare mana by turn five and the table has three rows to offer on one card. Three runs, 25 of 25
checks each, with `x1` and `x3` rows pressed across them. What it proves is the half that was broken
in the bot and would have been broken the same way here: the row's own price was charged, rather than
the printed cost on a card the table had drawn an expensive row for.

## D208 — Extort, and the first optional mana cost paid in the middle of a resolution

**The capability, which is the point of the piece.** This engine could already ask for mana in three
places: as a spell is cast (a kicker, a replicate count, every alternative cost), as an ability is
activated, and from an *opponent* answering a ward. What it could not do is let a card ask **its own
controller** for mana while the card's ability is resolving — which is what extort is: "whenever you
cast a spell, you may pay {W/B}; if you do, each opponent loses 1 life and you gain that much"
(CR 702.100).

The card cannot do it itself, and that is the whole design constraint: paying means **tapping
lands**, and the only thing in this engine that taps lands is `payFrom`, which lives in the
automation layer. A script cannot reach it (the import would be a cycle, and a card deciding which
lands to tap would be a card doing the engine's job). So the price goes on the **answer**:
`ChoiceDecisionSpec.payIfChosen` names an option and a cost, and the engine pays it between the
question being answered and the effect being run.

Two rules make it behave, and both are the discipline the rest of the engine already keeps:

- **The priced option is not offered to a seat that cannot pay it.** Same rule `legalActions` keeps
  about plays, and it gives the quiet case for free: filtering leaves one word, a question with one
  answer is answered by the engine rather than drawn as a prompt with one button, and an extort
  trigger with no mana up resolves without stopping the table at all.
- **The payment happens before the effect**, so an effect reading `chosenOption` is reading an
  answer that has already been paid for. It is also re-checked there rather than trusted: nothing
  can spend the seat's mana between the two moments, but a client is free to send an `auto:decide`
  naming a word that was never offered, and an unpaid extort that drained an opponent anyway would
  be the engine lying about a cost.

Nothing in the client needed changing. The question is the same word question Obelisk of Urd and
Voice of All already ask, so the bar draws it, the socket carries it and the browser driver answers
it — which is the argument for reusing the shape rather than adding a fourth pending state.

**Two cards, both bought for their text.** Basilica Screecher (a 1/2 flier) in Hollow Tide and
Basilica Guards (a 0/4 that cannot attack) in Skyward Writ — the two decks whose problem has always
been finishing a game they are not losing. Extort is a clock that costs no cards at all.

### What it is worth, and how often it even happens

| | the extort creature reached the board | questions asked | paid | life drained |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hollow Tide, 96 games | 40 | 101 | 101 | 101 |
| Skyward Writ, 96 games | 30 | 121 | 121 | 120 |

So about **four payments in a game the creature lands in**, and one life each in a duel. The bot pays
every time, which is its whole policy and is deliberate: extort fires *after* the spell that
triggered it has been paid for, so the mana it spends is mana the turn did not use, and "hold a land
in case I draw something" is the two-step plan this bot has never been able to price (D108, D110).

The slots, 288 games per arm on two seed sets: **Basilica Screecher costs 4 and 3**, **Basilica
Guards gains 1 and 5**. All four inside the instrument's floor, which for a keyword that drains one
life a spell is the honest answer rather than a disappointing one — one copy in sixty cards, landing
in 40% of games, draining about one life a game. What the piece bought is the *capability*; the card
is the smallest honest demonstration of it.

### The browser, and a check that was wrong the first time

`LIST=extort` plays eight Screechers behind twenty-four Swamps and cheap removal, so the question is
asked often. Three runs, 25 of 25 checks each.

Two things the browser forced, and the second is the better lesson:

- **The driver always pressed the first word**, which for extort is `Decline` — so a scenario about
  paying an optional cost could never once have paid one. It picks a random word now, which is the
  same argument the play-row picker already made in its own comment: a driver that always takes
  option one would look identical to a table that could not offer the others.
- **The first version of the check passed on a run that declined every time.** It matched
  `Pay {W/B}` anywhere in the line, and the prompt's own text carries *both* button labels — so the
  paying word was in the string either way round. The driver reports the chosen word first for
  exactly this reason, and the check anchors on it. A check that cannot tell the two answers apart
  is not a check, and it passed before it was right.

## D209 — Suspend, the only mechanic here that spends turns, and the offer that cannot be declined

**The keyword.** Suspend is a special action from the hand: pay the card's own suspend cost, exile
it with time counters, and remove one at the beginning of each of your upkeeps. When the last comes
off, you cast it without paying its mana cost (CR 702.62). It is the only thing in this engine that
spends **turns** as a resource — a {R} sorcery on turn one that deals three damage on turn two.

Three joints, and two of them already existed:

- **The special action is foretell's.** A play from hand that is not a cast, pays a cost of its own
  and ends with the card in exile — a row in the play sheet, an action, a path through the client.
  Two differences: the cost is the card's rather than a fixed {2}, and the card is **public**, which
  is half of what the mechanic costs you. Everyone can see it coming and count the turns.
- **The counters are ordinary counters.** They work on a card in exile because counters have always
  been a field on the *instance* rather than a thing about the battlefield, so the whole of
  "suspended" is `TIME` counters and the upkeep taking one off. The counter reaching nothing is also
  what stops the card being suspended: `addCounters` deletes a counter that hits zero, so a card
  whose cast is impossible is left in exile with no counters and is never offered again — which is
  the rule ("it remains exiled") for free.
- **The cast is the offer family for the fourth time**, with the one thing it had never needed.

### The offer that is not a question

Cascade, madness and miracle all say "you may", and declining each of them is a real answer. Suspend
does not: the rules say you cast it. So `pendingOfferedCast` carries `mandatory`, and three things
follow from it.

`legalActions` gives that seat the casts and **no pass** — which is the whole of the rule enforced in
one line. `settleOffer` answers the question itself when there is no legal cast at all, because an
offer with no pass and no play would be a table stopped for good; the card stays exiled and the
engine says so through the replacement channel. And the bar draws no **Decline**.

That last one is a browser finding rather than a design decision. The first run of `LIST=suspend`
passed its checks and printed this:

```
took a free cast: Rift Bolt's last time counter is gone: cast it without paying its mana cost Cast it Decline
```

The engine was right and the table was wrong: a Decline button whose only outcome is a refused
action. `mustCastOffered.mandatory` carries the fact to the client now, the bar omits the button, and
the browser driver reports rather than presses when the button it expects is missing — because a run
that reaches that branch on a mandatory offer has found a real problem.

### Two cards chosen so the measurement is about the keyword

Both are a card Kindle Grove already plays with suspend bolted on, which is the point: **Rift Bolt**
for the Lightning Strike (three damage for {1}{R} now against three for {R} and a wait) and **Search
for Tomorrow** for the second Rampant Growth (a basic land tapped for {1}{G} on turn two against one
untapped for {G} on turn three). So what the probe reads is a turn of waiting against two mana,
twice over.

| | seed set 3300 | seed set 4400 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| both suspend cards against the two they replaced | gains 2 | costs 6 |

Level, twice, inside the floor — which for this comparison is the interesting answer rather than a
dull one: **a turn is worth about the two mana it saves** in this pool, and the keyword is a fair
trade rather than a bargain or a trap.

And it is used. Over 96 games of Kindle Grove against the field: **21 Search for Tomorrow and 6 Rift
Bolt suspended, 24 of those 27 cast off their last counter**, and two still waiting in exile when the
game ended. The bot suspends under the same rule it foretells under — spend it when the mana had no
better home — because `simulate` sees a card leave the hand and nothing happen, which is foretell's
problem with a longer wait. `foretellIsSpareMana` is `specialIsSpareMana` now and answers for both.

### The browser

`LIST=suspend` plays eight Rift Bolts behind twenty-four Mountains. Three runs, 26 of 26 checks each,
both halves required: the suspend row pressed on a card in hand, and the cast arriving in a later
upkeep off the last counter. It is the first scenario here whose two required checks are *two turns
apart* in the same game.


## D210 — Dredge, the replacement effect on a draw, and the rule that followed from deferring it

**The keyword.** "If you would draw a card, you may instead mill N cards and return this card from
your graveyard to your hand" (CR 702.52a). Every replacement effect in this engine before it was a
**zone change** — dies, to-graveyard, leaves-battlefield — and those are easy here because the card
is already moving: `relocate` records it, `settle` finds it in one of three lists, and whatever
replaces it is handed the card. A draw is not a zone change the engine can catch after the fact. By
the time the card has moved, the answer is moot.

### Why the draw is deferred rather than paused

Two walls, and they are both about where `draw` lives.

It is in `effects.ts`, which sits **below** the layer that knows what a card's script is. Madness
gets installed by `automation.ts` because that module can ask `scriptOf(next, id)?.madness`;
`effects.ts` cannot, and a module cycle is the reason. So `draw` cannot look up a dredge card even
if it wanted to.

And a resolution cannot stop anywhere except a **decision spec** — a question the card declares,
asked before its effect runs, answered into `ctx.decisions`. Dredge is not on the card that draws;
it is on a card in a graveyard, and the engine does not know how many cards an effect will draw
before running it.

So the draw is **deferred**. `drawLater(state, seat, n)` adds n entries to `GameState.drawsOwed`,
the surrounding effect finishes, and the first thing the next `settle` does is `drainOwedDraws`:
take the head, and either raise `pendingDredge` or just draw it. A queue of one entry per card
rather than a count per seat, because it has to survive a dredge taken in the middle of it — "each
player draws" owes two draws to two seats, and a `draw 3` whose first card is dredged still owes
two.

Putting the drain at the **top** of `settle`, before the deaths and the draws are announced, is what
makes the deferral invisible to everything else: a card deferred by `drawLater` reaches its `draws`
trigger and its miracle offer in the same settle pass an immediate draw would have.

### The rule the deferral imposes, written at the function

**Only a draw that is the last thing a card does may be deferred.** Dark Confidant reads the hand to
find what it drew and charges for its mana value; Faithless Looting draws two and then offers the
hand to discard from. Both would see a hand without the cards if the draw were deferred past them,
so both call `draw` and neither is ever offered a dredge. Nothing in the type system can tell those
apart from a terminal draw, which is why the rule is documented at `drawLater` and the pool opts in
one call site at a time: the eighteen places where `draw(c.state, c.controller, n)` *is* the whole
effect, plus the draw step. All 1063 tests passed unchanged across that conversion, which is the
claim about it being invisible, tested.

The documented consequence: **a draw a card performs inside its own effect cannot be dredged.** That
is a real gap in the rules, and the honest version of it is a sentence rather than a half-working
mechanism — the same shape as `becomes-tapped` being the one trigger with no card behind it.

### The sixth stopped table, and a decline with a job

`pendingDredge` is the sixth thing that stops this table dead and the first about nothing on the
stack: no spell, no target, nothing cast. Two buttons like a ward, because declining is the other
half of a question rather than a gesture the table already has a meaning for.

The decline has a job no other decline in this engine has: **it takes the draw.** The first version
cleared `pendingDredge`, sliced the owed draw off the queue and drew nothing — because handing the
draw back to the drain would offer the same dredge again, forever, with the card still sitting in the
graveyard. One test caught it (`library - 1` read `library`). `auto:dredge` with `dredge: false`
draws the card itself, which is also the only way "no" means the ordinary card off the top rather
than no card at all.

The library's length is the other half of the rule and it is not decoration: a dredge the library
cannot pay for **is not offered**, so there is no unaffordable button and no way to deck yourself for
free. A graveyard holding two dredge cards offers the cheaper one — the same "one at a time"
concession `tickSuspended` makes, because the alternative is a third kind of prompt for a case this
pool cannot build.

### The bot reads the library's size and never its contents

A dredge is the only decision here that trades a card the bot **cannot see** for one it can, which
makes it the one place a confident rule could be badly wrong and still look fine: a line that
dredged its library away wins the simulation it was scored in and loses the game. So it is a fact
about the board rather than a search — `dredgeIsWorthIt` — and it is two facts.

The library has to afford the mill **four times over**, because the question is asked again every
turn and a library that can pay once can pay only once. And the card's **mana value has to be no
more than the lands standing**: "a card I could pay for", not "a card I could pay for this instant
with these colours". The looser form on purpose — a dredge taken in the draw step is for a turn that
has not happened yet, and the tight form declined a three-drop all the way through the turns when
filling a graveyard is the whole plan. Both read the library's *size* and never its contents, which
is the D164 discipline: a rule that looked at the top card would be exactly the violation that audit
went looking for.

### What it measures, and the question that has to be asked first

| of 288, the deck **without** the card | seed set 3300 | seed set 4400 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rot Harvest without Shambling Shell | 142 wins against 134 | 128 against 114 |
| Blight Vector without Darkblast | 110 against 104 | 98 against 85 |

Four readings, all the same sign: **both dredge cards cost their decks** — 8 and 14 games for the
Shell, 6 and 13 for the Darkblast. Each is inside the ±20 floor on its own, and four readings landing
on the same side of it is a different thing from one.

Which raises the question D205 put into this project's method: is that a bad card or a badly played
one? The bot takes a dredge whenever `dredgeIsWorthIt` says yes, and it says yes a great deal — 130
of 137 offers. A dredge **skips a draw**: the card it hands back is one you have already seen, the
card it skipped was new, and three more go into the graveyard unseen. A rule that always takes that
trade is exactly the kind of rule a slot probe mistakes for a card. So the same four probes were run
again with `BOT={"dredgesForValue":false}` — the bot never dredging — which is the control the flag
exists for.

| the same slot, with the bot **never** dredging | seed set 3300 | seed set 4400 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rot Harvest without Shambling Shell | 142 against 137 | 126 against 116 |
| Blight Vector without Darkblast | 109 against 106 | 99 against 92 |

**Both halves of the loss are real, and they are different sizes.** With the keyword switched off the
cards still cost 5, 10, 3 and 7 — they are simply worse than the Endless One and the Doom Blade they
replaced, which is a fact about two cards and not about dredge. The rest, **3, 4, 3 and 6 games of
288, four times out of four**, is the bot taking every dredge it is offered.

That reading looked solid — four pairs of numbers, all the same sign — and **it was wrong**. See
D212: measured head to head with `bot-duel`, which varies the rule and holds everything else, the
same two configurations are level to within two games of 624. The 3-to-6 was the difference of two
*noisy* numbers, each of them a slot probe with a ±20 floor, and differencing two of those is a
noisier thing than either. The instrument was the mistake, not the arithmetic.

The default stays **on** regardless, for the reason the Dark Ritual rule stayed: a bot that is
offered a mechanic every turn and never takes it looks broken to the person sitting opposite.

One other thing the runs printed and it is worth not hiding: one arm of one probe reported **1
unfinished game of 288** — a game that ran out of move budget. It was in the *rule-off* arm, where
no dredge is ever taken, so it is not a dredge loop; the engine's own playout tests still play every
deck pairing to a winner.

### The card was wrong before the keyword was, and only an instrument could say so

Dredge went on a dredge **land** first: a Swamp that enters tapped, taps for {B}, dredge 2 — minimal,
readable, and the one card whose value is flat enough to make the keyword the only variable.
`dredge.mjs` then reported it **offered three times in 96 games**. A dredge card does nothing except
from a graveyard, and nothing in this pool destroys a land.

The same keyword on **Shambling Shell** — {1}{B}{G} for a 2/2 that sacrifices itself to grow
something — in Rot Harvest, which already runs two sacrifice outlets, a Blood Artist and a Zulaport
Cutthroat: **137 offers, 130 taken, 7 declined, 390 cards milled** over the same 96 games, with the
subject's library bottoming out at a median of 43. Darkblast, {B} for -1/-1 in Blight Vector, reads
**63 offers, 62 taken, 1 declined, 186 milled**. Before asking what a keyword is worth, ask how often
the card gets to use it — and the general form of that is now written up in
`scripts/measure/README.md`.

### The browser

`LIST=dredge` plays eight Darkblasts and twenty bodies behind twenty-four Swamps: the spell is cast
at a creature, lands in the graveyard, and from then on every draw step stops the table. Both halves
required — the dredge pressed, and a Darkblast cast *after* one was taken, because a prompt that
hands back a card nobody then plays has proved the question and not the keyword. Three runs, 26 of 26
checks each.

One thing it did not fall for, because the extort run already had. The prompt's own sentence carries
both button labels ("… instead of drawing? Mill 3 Draw instead"), so a check matching the text would
pass on a run that declined every time. The check is anchored on the **driver's** report of which
button it pressed.

### The question it asks every turn, and the answer you can give once

A dredge card sits in a graveyard for the rest of the game, so the table stops in **every** draw
step for as long as it is there. That is correct Magic and it is also twenty taps a game for an
answer most players give the same way every time — which is the shape `autoPassOff` already had an
answer for (#79): being asked is a *preference*, not a rule, and two people at one table can
reasonably want different ones.

So `GameState.dredgeStops` holds a standing answer per seat, set by `auto:dredgeStops` with `ask`,
`always` or `never`. `drainOwedDraws` reads it before raising the question: `never` takes the draw,
`always` takes the dredge, and absent asks. Three things about the shape are deliberate.

**Absent is "ask", and that is the default.** A mechanic that answers itself without being told to
is the bug the whole offer family exists to avoid, and the bot numbers in the table above are
numbers about a bot that is asked — a default of `always` would have quietly changed what they mean.

**It is said out loud.** This is the one path in the engine where cards move — three off a library,
one out of a graveyard — with nobody pressing anything, so both branches write a line through the
replacement channel. A player who set `always` four turns ago should still be able to read what it
did.

**And the control does not disappear.** It is drawn beside the question, which is where a player
is when they get tired of it — but also whenever a standing answer is set, because a seat that
chose `always` is never asked again and a control that only appeared with the prompt would be a
one-way door. The engine's half of that is `AutomationView.dredgeStanding`, which travels so the
table can show the setting back.

The move itself is `takeDredge`, shared by the button and the standing answer, because "what a
dredge does" should not be written twice.

## D211 — Buyback, and what is left when a cost buys neither a better spell nor a cheaper one

**The keyword.** "You may pay an additional cost as you cast this spell. If you do, put this card
