into its owner's hand instead of into your graveyard as it resolves" (CR 702.26a). Every optional
cost in this pool before it changed *what the spell does* — kicker branches the effect, replicate
multiplies it, and the five alternative costs replace the price and sometimes the result. Buyback
changes none of that. The spell is the same spell with the same targets; what the extra mana buys
is **the card**.

### Why it was two days' design and twenty minutes' code

Both joints already existed, and finding that out was the whole of the design.

The **second row** is the kicker's arrangement. `legalActions` already offers one card twice at two
prices — that is how a kicker, a morph, a split card and five alternative costs all reach the table
— so a player sees `Cast Capsize` and `Cast Capsize with buyback {3}` and the row's own words say
what the three mana is for. Nothing in the client changed.

The **destination** is flashback's. `spellLeavesStack` already decided where a spell's card goes as
it leaves the stack, already knew about two dispositions that are not the graveyard, and already
took a `resolved` flag — because the adventure's exile depends on the spell having finished and
flashback's does not. Buyback is a third disposition on that same switch, and it is on the
`resolved` side.

So the effect never reads the keyword. There is a `ctx.kicked` because a kicked spell is a
different spell; there is no `ctx.boughtBack`, because a bought-back spell is the same spell you
happen to keep.

### The test that was useful because it failed for the wrong reason

"A countered buyback spell goes to the graveyard" is the claim the `resolved` flag exists for, and
the first version of that test failed — but not over buyback. It aimed the counterspell with
`{ kind: 'spell', id }`, which reads correctly and is not how this engine targets a spell on the
stack: the convention everywhere else is `{ kind: 'card', id }`, the Cancel resolved countering
nothing, and the Capsize resolved afterwards and went home. The assertion that caught it was about
the card's zone, so the failure looked exactly like the bug it was written to prevent.

Worth keeping as a general note: **a test that fails for the wrong reason is cheaper than one
written to pass.** Had the target been right first time, the test would have been green either way
and the `resolved` flag untested.

### Two refusals, both two-sided

The row is offered only on an **instant or a sorcery**. A permanent spell that resolves becomes a
permanent and never leaves the stack for a graveyard at all, so "instead of into your graveyard" has
nothing to replace and the extra mana would buy nothing. `legalActions` does not draw the row and
`auto:cast` refuses the flag — the same two-sided discipline every cost flag here keeps, because a
table offering a play the engine then refuses is the one bug that file exists to prevent. And
buyback is not paid beside an alternative cost, which replaces the printed cost it is added to.

### The bot pays it, and this time that was checked rather than assumed

**25 of 54 Capsize casts and 5 of 44 Whispers of the Muse casts**, over 96 games each, counted off
`action.buyback` on the action the bot actually sent. That check is D207's lesson made routine: the
replicate count was dropped between the chosen play and the action for a whole piece, with no
refusal and no failing test, because a cast missing a cost flag is quietly the cheaper play. Every
new flag gets the twenty-line script now.

The split between the two cards is the cards rather than the bot. Capsize's buyback is {3} on a
three-mana spell, so six lands pays both halves and a control deck has six lands; Whispers' is {5}
on a one-mana spell, which is a mana sink by design and only reached in the long games.

### What it measures, and the slot that had to be moved after it was measured

| of 288, the deck **without** the card | seed set 3300 | seed set 4400 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hollow Tide without Whispers of the Muse | 96 against 93 | 120 against 125 |
| Tidal Mind without Capsize, paid for by a **Man-o'-War** | 125 against 102 | 99 against 87 |
| Tidal Mind without Capsize, paid for by a **Thieving Magpie** | 114 against 102 | 91 against 87 |

Whispers is level: +3 and −5, which is the honest answer for a one-mana cantrip whose buyback is
reached in about one game in five.

Capsize is not, and the two rows for it are the point. Against the second Man-o'-War it costs Tidal
Mind **23 and 12 games of 288** — the first of those is outside the ±20 floor, which almost nothing
in this pool is. Re-priced against the second Thieving Magpie, the same card in the same deck on the
same seeds costs **12 and 4**. Half the loss was the *payer*: a Man-o'-War bounces a creature **and
leaves a 2/2 behind**, so "a bounce for a bounce" was never the fair comparison it reads as.

That is D207's rule applying for the second time — what a slot is worth is a fact about the card
that pays for it — and it is written into this project's method precisely so a 23 does not get
published as a fact about a keyword. **The committed slot was moved to the arrangement that
measured better**, which is the Magpie's.

### Why a famous card costs this deck games, and what it is not

The first thing to rule out was the bot casting it into nothing, because a six-mana play that buys
nothing is the failure mode `wasted-plays.mjs` exists for. **Capsize does not appear in that
instrument's list at all** across 312 games — it is cast on real targets. So the loss is not a
wasted play; it is a slow one. Six mana to bounce a single permanent is a tempo loss against an
aggressive field, and what the extra three mana buys — never running out of the answer — is a long
game this pool rarely reaches.

Kept anyway, inside the floor on the arrangement that stands. The keyword works, the table draws it,
the bot pays it 25 times in 96 games, and a card that is famous for a reason the simulation cannot
reach is worth more to a person sitting at the table than four games of 288. What this is not is a
claim that buyback is bad: the keyword is one card's price list, and the one card that priced badly
here is slow for reasons that have nothing to do with keeping it.

## D212 — The dredge rule, measured on the right instrument, and a claim withdrawn

**D210 published a number that does not survive the instrument built for the question.** It said
taking every dredge costs the deck 3 to 6 games of 288, four times out of four. It does not.

### What the two instruments actually compare

`deck-probe` prices a **slot**: the deck with a card against the deck without it, both bots the same.
To ask what a *rule* costs, D210 ran that probe twice — once with the rule on and once with it off —
and subtracted. Each probe is a number with a ±20 floor on it. The difference of two such numbers is
noisier than either, and four same-sign readings of a small difference is exactly what noise looks
like when you go looking for a sign.

`bot-duel` prices a **rule**: both bots play every deck pairing in both seats on identical seeds, so
the deck, the matchup and the seat all cancel and what is left is the setting. It is the instrument
this project already wrote down as the right shape for a change to the opponent, and its negative
control is not approximately level — two identical bots score **exactly 312-312 of 624**.

### The four runs

| | of 624 |
| --- | --- |
| control: identical bots | 312-312 |
| the tighter rule against the first one | 313-311 |
| the tighter rule against **never dredging** | 312-312 |
| the first rule against never dredging | 311-313 |

Every configuration is level within two games. Always-dredging, never-dredging and the tighter rule
are the same bot as far as 624 games can tell. **The 3-to-6 is withdrawn.**

### The rule that was built to beat it, and why it is kept anyway

The tighter rule reads four facts instead of two, each one a reason *this* card is worth three off
the library: a copy is not already in hand, the cost is payable now (the question is asked in the
draw step, after the untap, so "payable" reads as "usable this turn"), the card has something legal
to point at, and the library still holds **twenty cards** — a flat floor rather than a multiple of
the dredge cost, because a seat down to twelve cards has already milled its deck away.

Two of those four barely fire in this pool. A copy in hand is impossible when each deck runs one of
the card, and "payable now" is true of a {B} instant from turn one. What does fire is the floor
(11 and 5 declines per 96 games) and the empty board (a Darkblast with no creature to shrink).
Measured: nothing.

Kept anyway, and the reason is the one `ritualBoughtSomething` was kept for. A bot that dredges
itself down to twelve cards, or buys back a removal spell with nothing to remove, looks broken to
the person sitting opposite — and that is worth more here than a win rate that cannot tell the
difference. The flags stay so the next person can re-ask: `dredgesForValue` turns it off entirely,
`dredgesTightly: false` is the first rule, kept as the control this one was measured against.

### The lesson, which is the part worth keeping

**Measure a bot rule with the bot instrument.** A slot probe answers "is this card worth its place",
and no amount of running it twice turns it into an answer about the opponent. The giveaway was
available before the run: `bot-duel`'s own header says so, and its control scores *exactly* level,
which is the property that makes two games readable and 3-of-288 arguable.

And the smaller one: **a difference of two noisy measurements needs its own error bar.** Four
readings agreeing in sign is not four readings of the same thing — it is two subtractions, each
carrying both probes' noise.

## D213 — Proliferate, the first question whose answer can be a player

Every question this table has ever asked is answered with **cards**. A sacrifice, a scry, a search, a
discard, a damage order, a copy's new target: all of them are "tap the lit cards and confirm", and
the whole chain — the engine's `candidates`, the client's lit ring, the driver's tap loop — is built
on that. Proliferate chooses "any number of permanents and/or players with counters on them"
(CR 701.27a), and poison lives on a **seat**. So this is the first answer in the game with no card in
it.

### The shape: one more decision flag, not a sixth question type

`CountersDecisionSpec` is an ordinary `DecisionSpec` with `counters: true` on it, and that flag does
two things and nothing else: `decisionCandidates` is replaced by `proliferateCandidates`, which
returns battlefield permanents carrying a counter **plus** `seat:N` for every player carrying one;
and the client reads the same flag to light a seat strip and to word the instruction as "tap the
permanents and players".

A `seat:` prefix inside the same `candidates: string[]` rather than a second list. Two lists would
have meant every consumer of a decision — the reducer, the bot, the view, the driver — learning that
a decision can have two kinds of answer, for one keyword. One list means the id namespace grows by a
prefix and the machinery above it does not change at all: `min`/`max` still count the answer,
`chosen` still holds it, and `auto:decide` still carries it.

That bought something immediately: half of the client work was already done. The table's lit-cards
set takes `ask.candidates` wholesale, so the permanents lit themselves; all that was left was the
seat strip, which has no card to light and borrows the targetable ring it already had for spells.

Two places had to learn the prefix, and both are about **naming**: the log line (`auto:decide` asked
an instance for its name and threw `no card with id seat:1` — the one crash this piece produced), and
the strip's own button, which now says **Choose Nick** rather than *Target* Nick, because a
proliferate does not target (CR 701.27a) and a button that said so would be describing a different
game.

### The rule: one more of each kind already there

`proliferate(state, chosen)` adds one of **every** counter kind already on a thing, which is the
keyword's whole subtlety. A permanent with a +1/+1 and a -1/-1 on it gets one of each. A permanent
with nothing gets nothing — and is not a candidate, so "nothing to proliferate" is not a refusal but
an absence. Poison is read off the seat's own `poison` field rather than its counters record, because
that is where this engine keeps it.

And the thing people expect of it that it does not do: **a suspended card is not proliferated.** Time
counters sit on a card in **exile**, and exile holds no permanents — so proliferate cannot hurry a
Rift Bolt along. That is the answer paper gives, and it is a test rather than a comment: the
suspended card is not in `proliferateCandidates`, and `proliferate` called on it by hand changes
nothing.

### Two cards, both measured level

Contagion Clasp (`{2}` artifact; a `-1/-1` on arrival, then `{4}, {T}: Proliferate`) went into Blight
Vector for the second Tainted Strike; Steady Progress (`{2}{U}` instant; proliferate, draw a card)
into Hollow Tide for the third Mind Sculpt. Both priced on two seed sets of 288 paired games:

| | seeds 3300 | seeds 5100 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contagion Clasp, in Blight Vector | −8 | +4 |
| Steady Progress, in Hollow Tide | −11 | +4 |

Both cards are level: each pair disagrees in **sign** and every reading is well inside the ±20 floor
a 288-game paired probe has (D96, D211). That is the honest read and it is the expected one — a
two-mana artifact whose ability costs four is a slow card in a format these decks usually finish
before turn eight. Neither slot is moved, because nothing says to move it.

### The browser row cost two things the table was missing

`LIST=proliferate` plays a deck built for the question — sixteen infect creatures to put poison on
the computer, eight Clasps to ask, four Sol Rings so the `{4}` is affordable before the game ends —
and requires that a **player** was chosen by tapping their own strip. Getting there found two
defects that had nothing to do with this keyword:

**The board never said a permanent had something to do.** Hand, graveyard, exile and the command zone
all badge a card `playable`; the battlefield did not. So an Equipment that could move, a Vehicle that
could be crewed, a monstrosity, a regenerate and the Clasp's own ability were all invisible — the
plays were on the card's sheet the whole time, and nothing told a player to open it. `cardBadges` now
badges a permanent with any play that is **not a mana ability**; mana abilities are excluded because
every untapped land has one, and a badge on half the board says nothing.

**No browser suite had ever activated an ability of a permanent**, for exactly that reason: the
driver only taps what carries the badge. It can now, and that is **off by default** — which is the
part worth writing down. The first version turned it on for every caller and `LIST=cascade`
immediately stopped casting Bloodbraid Elves: that deck runs three River Boas, regenerating one costs
`{G}`, and a Forest spent on a shield nobody needed is a Forest the four-mana Elf wanted. Pressing an
arbitrary activated ability is not "the simplest legal thing" — it is a scenario, so the scenario
asks for it and the other fifteen runs keep playing the way they did.

### The lesson

**A new kind of answer is cheaper as a new kind of id than as a new kind of question.** The six
stopped-table states each cost a reducer branch, a view field, a client mode and a driver branch.
This one cost a prefix, because it kept the answer's *shape* — a list of ids with a count on it — and
only widened what an id may name.

## D214 — Echo, the first cost the game asks for, and the question whose "no" kills the asker

Every cost this engine has implemented is one a player **reaches for**: a cast, an activation, a
kicker, a replicate count, a ward an opponent may decline, an extort paid mid-resolution. Echo
(CR 702.29) is the first the *game* asks for. It arrives in the controller's upkeep, before anybody
has done anything, and declining does not mean missing out on something — it means the permanent
goes to the graveyard. **This is the first question in this engine whose "no" destroys the thing that
asked it.**

### It needed no new machinery, which is the interesting part

Three pieces, all already present, and the piece is the demonstration that they compose:

- **When.** `{ kind: 'step', step: 'upkeep' }` already defaults to `of: 'you'`, so the trigger fires
  in the controller's own upkeep and nobody else's.
- **Once.** `TriggerDef.condition` is the intervening-if clause (checked before the trigger goes on
  the stack and again as it resolves, CR 603.4). It reads a new instance flag, `echoDue`.
- **The price.** `ChoiceDecisionSpec.payIfChosen` — extort's shape — is a question with a cost on one
  of its answers, paid by the engine before the effect runs.

What that composition buys for free is the half that would otherwise have been a rule: **a cost the
seat cannot pay is not offered**, because `payIfChosen` filters the priced option out. So a player
who cannot pay is never shown a question with one button. The permanent goes, and the engine says so
through the same channel every other unaskable question uses. One line of card script, no new state.

### The flag, and why it is a flag

`CardInstance.echoDue` is set **wherever a permanent comes under a controller's control** — the
arrivals pass, and `gainControl` — and cleared by the trigger that read it, whichever way the
question went.

Arithmetic on `enteredTurn` was the obvious alternative and it is wrong. Echo's clause is "since your
last upkeep", and at a four-seat table that is not "this turn or last turn": a creature that entered
during an opponent's turn has had no upkeep of its controller's in between, and one that entered
three opponents ago has had none either. A flag says the thing the rule says.

`gainControl` sets it without asking whether the card has echo, because asking would mean reading a
script and that module sits below the one holding them. A flag on a permanent with no echo trigger is
inert — the only reader is an echo trigger's own condition.

### A test that could not be written the obvious way

"Tapped out in your own upkeep" turns out to be **impossible for a creature you cast**: lands untap
before the upkeep, so a seat with enough lands to have cast the creature can always pay for it. The
first version of that test tapped the lands by hand during the opponent's turn and proved nothing —
the untap step undid it.

The honest scenario is a permanent that reached the battlefield **without being cast**: reanimated,
put there by an effect, or taken off somebody. So the test puts the Marshal onto the battlefield with
one Mountain up, and the echo is unpayable because the creature never cost anything. Which is also
the only way it happens in a real game.

### Two cards, four readings, all of them positive

| | seeds 3300 | seeds 5100 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mogg War Marshal, in Ember Rush (for the 2nd Goblin Arsonist) | +8 | +6 |
| Yavimaya Granger, in Kindle Grove (for the last Rampant Growth) | +7 | +2 |

Each is stock-minus-variant out of 288 paired games, so a positive number is the echo card winning
more than the card it replaced. Every reading is inside the ±20 floor, so none of them is a *result* —
but all four have the same sign, which is the most a slot probe can honestly say for a card this
small: **the slot is paid for.**

The pair was chosen so the two halves of the keyword are both in the pool. Mogg War Marshal is the
one you often **decline**: it makes a Goblin when it arrives and another when it dies, so refusing
costs the 1/1 that asked and leaves the board the same size. Yavimaya Granger is the one you **pay**:
its land is already on the battlefield by the time the question comes, so the three mana are spent
either way and the only question left is whether a 2/2 is worth two more.

### What is deliberately not measured, and what it would take

The bot's rule is "pay", written as `best: () => 'Pay {…}'` on the card. **It is not priced head to
head**, and D212's lesson says why that matters: a bot rule is measured with `bot-duel`, which varies
a `BotOptions` flag and cancels the deck, the matchup and the seat. `best` receives `(state, chooser)`
and cannot see `BotOptions`, so there is no switch to vary. Threading the options into that call is
the change that would make every card-authored bot answer measurable — the extort `best`, the
proliferate choice and this one — and it is a change to the decision machinery rather than a rider on
a keyword, so it is left as an open question rather than done badly here.

What *is* measured is the slot, above, and the table: `LIST=echo` plays eight Marshals through a real
browser and requires **both** answers to be pressed, because a run that paid every time has proved
the question and not the keyword.

### The browser row earns its place for a reason no other row does

Echo is the only question in this pool raised in a step a table normally passes straight through.
Every other prompt these runs press follows something the player did. This one arrives in the upkeep,
and the upkeep is where auto-pass lives — so a table that passed priority past its own question would
lose the creature silently, and no engine test can see that, because no engine test passes priority
the way a table does.

## D215 — Cumulative upkeep, a price that climbs, and the question a card works out when it is asked

Echo (D214) is a cost the game asks for, once. Cumulative upkeep (CR 702.24) is the same question
every upkeep with one thing echo did not have: **the price goes up**. An age counter goes on as the
ability resolves, and the cost is "its upkeep cost for each age counter on it" — so the first upkeep
asks {1}, the second {2}, the third {3}, and a card worth a mana a turn stops being worth it
somewhere around the fourth.

### The shape, and the one that was rejected

`ChoiceDecisionSpec.payIfChosen` is a static `{ option, cost }` pair, and here the cost, the words on
the buttons and the prompt are **facts about this resolution** rather than about the card. Two shapes
could carry that:

1. **Widen `pendingPayment`** — the ward-only stopped-table state — into a general "a cost the game
   demands", with the consequence named (counter that object, or sacrifice this permanent).
2. **Let a card compute its question when it is asked**, the way `NumberDecisionSpec.range` already
   computes its bounds.

**The second, and the reason is that echo already exists.** Echo asks its question through the
decision machinery; routing cumulative upkeep through `pendingPayment` would give the pool two
mechanisms for one question shape — "pay or lose it" — with two reducer paths, two client modes, two
bot branches and two places for the next keyword to be written wrongly. Widening the thing that was
already nearly right is cheaper than building its twin.

And it *was* nearly right. `DecisionSpecOf` is "a spec, or a function of the state and the source",
and it is resolved in exactly one place: `decisionSpecsFor`, which every reader of a card's questions
already went through — the plan, the asking, the payment for a priced answer, and the fallback when
that payment turns out to be impossible. Four readers, one funnel, no consumer downstream learns that
a question can be computed.

Two orderings make it correct, and both are written on the type:

- The age counter is added in **`beforeDecisions`**, which runs before any question is planned, so
  the counter is on the card by the time the price is read.
- The function must be **pure** and read nothing that can change between the question and its answer,
  because the engine resolves it more than once and the three resolutions must agree.

One place could not use it and says so: the bot's `chosenNumberIsNothing` rule reads a *spell's*
decisions before the cast, where there is no stack object and so no source to compute from. It skips
computed questions, which costs nothing — nothing with a computed question is a number question.

### The measurement, and a card with no fair payer

Mystic Remora ({U} enchantment, cumulative upkeep {1}, two cards whenever an opponent casts a
noncreature spell) went into Tidal Mind. **There is no card in that deck that does nearly what it
does at nearly its price**, so this slot cannot read the keyword the way the Rift Bolt and Search for
Tomorrow slots did. What it can do is **bracket** it, which is D207's remedy applied up front rather
than after a surprise:

| payer | seeds 3300 | seeds 5100 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the second Man-o'-War (a card this deck gets a lot out of) | −9 | −10 |
| Tormod's Crypt (the most marginal card in the list) | +2 | −8 |

Both pairs are inside the ±20 floor, so neither is a result. But the signs are informative: against a
good card the Remora is **consistently a little worse**, and against a marginal one it is level. The
honest summary is that this card is a wash in this deck, and the slot is justified by the pool
needing a card behind the keyword rather than by a win-rate gain — the same "kept anyway, and here is
why" D212 recorded for the dredge rule.

**The alternative, with its numbers, rather than a silent preference**: the Crypt's slot is the
better home by the readings above, and it is not taken only because the Crypt is the pool's single
copy and two tests plus the script-coverage test need it to exist somewhere. Moving it to another
deck to free that slot would mean an unmeasured change to a second deck, which is worth doing
deliberately or not at all.

### The browser row proves the one thing the engine tests cannot

`LIST=upkeep` plays eight Remoras and requires **two different prices** to have been pressed. The
engine's tests pin the arithmetic on a board built by hand; what they cannot see is the **button**.
The question is rebuilt on each asking, so a table that re-rendered the first one would offer
`Pay {1}` against a cost of `{2}`, the engine would refuse the payment, and the permanent would go
with the player unable to see why. Two prices in one run is that claim, and nothing weaker is worth
a row.

## D216 — Level up, a creature whose characteristics are a count on itself, and two zeros worth checking

Every permanent in this pool is what its card prints plus whatever has been layered on it. A leveler
(CR 702.87, CR 711.3) is the first whose **printed** characteristics depend on its own counters: a
Student of Warfare is a 1/1, a 3/3 first striker at two level counters, and a 4/4 double striker at
seven — one card, nothing layered on it, three creatures.

### Where the bands live, and why not in the script

On the **definition**, as `CardDef.levelBands`. The ability that adds a counter is script behaviour
and lives in `abilities`, built by `levelUpAbility`; what the creature *is* at each level is a
printed line on the card, exactly as its base 1/1 is.

That split is forced as well as tidy. The module that turns printed values into current ones is
`characteristics.ts`, and it **cannot read the script registry** — `scripts.ts` imports it, so the
dependency only runs one way. Putting the bands in the script would have meant either a cycle or a
second mechanism for "what is this permanent", which is the thing the layer system exists to be.

### The layer it sits in, and the two interactions that prove it

A band **sets** the size, which is layer 7b (CR 613.4). So:

- A **pump lands on top of it**: a level-two Student with a Giant Growth is a 6/6, not a 3/3 and not
  a 4/4. Written as a 7b base rather than a +2/+2 for exactly this.
- A **later setting effect beats it**: a Turn to Frog on a level-seven Student makes a 1/1 with no
  abilities, because the band's timestamp is the permanent's own arrival and every setting effect in
  the game is later than that.

The band's keywords are seeded alongside the printed ones, which gets "loses all abilities" right
without a line of its own: the loop that clears keywords when it meets `losesAllAbilities` clears the
band's first strike exactly as it clears a printed keyword.

And one interaction nobody planned, pinned because the two keywords were built two pieces apart:
**proliferate finds level counters.** A level counter is a kind of counter, so a Student at level two
proliferated is at level three, and the band reads that without being told.

### The field this slot found, and the bug it had already caused

`normaliseDef` is an **allow-list**: a caller-supplied deck reaches it, and a field it does not name
is dropped. `levelBands` was not named, so the first level-up card reached `cardDefs` with
`levelBands: undefined` and sat there as a 1/1 at level seven, with every engine test agreeing.

Printed **loyalty** was dropped the same way once — its comment is still in that function — which
makes two for two on fields this allow-list has quietly eaten. The fix is three lines and a
validation block: bands are checked for shape, capped at four, and clamped to ±99, all of them
payload limits rather than rules limits, because a caller-supplied card claiming a power of a billion
is a number that breaks every readout that prints it.

### Two zeros, a third seed set, and a control

| | seeds 3300 | seeds 5100 | seeds 7700 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Student of Warfare, in Dawn Tithe (for the 2nd Ajani's Pridemate) | 0 | 0 | +1 |
| Beastbreaker of Bala Ged, in Kindle Grove (for the 2nd Burning-Tree Emissary) | +4 | +4 | — |

**Exactly zero twice is not a measurement, it is a smell.** 208-80 against 208-80 and then 206-82
against 206-82 reads like a swap that never happened — a `CHANGE` that silently matched nothing, or a
variant built from the stock list. So two things were run before any of it was written down:

- A **third seed set**, which came back +1. Not zero, so the first two were a coincidence rather than
  a stuck arm.
- A **control that must move the number**: two Swords to Plowshares swapped for two Plains in the
  same deck, same seeds, which moved it by **23** (208 → 185). The harness can see changes in this
  deck; it simply has nothing to see in this one.

Which makes the honest reading: a one-mana 1/1 that eats spare white mana is **level** with a
two-mana 2/2 that grows on lifegain, in a deck that wins 72% of its games either way, and the
Beastbreaker is worth four games of 288 in the deck that ramps into it. Neither is a result; both are
inside the ±20 floor. The slots are paid for and the keyword is in the pool.

**The bot does level**: 19 Students cast and 60 level-ups across 48 games, counted off `auto:activate`
by card name rather than inferred — which is what ruled out the other explanation of a zero, that the
card was never played at all.

### The browser row is about the card face

`LIST=level` presses the row and then **reads the board**: a card face saying `3/3` beside
`Student of Warfare` is the only evidence that what the table draws is the creature the engine is
playing with. The engine's own tests read the bands off `characteristicsOf`, which is the right place
to pin the arithmetic and the wrong place to find out what a player sees — a table drawing the
printed 1/1 would have somebody blocking a 3/3 with a 2/2 and losing a creature to a number that was
on screen the whole time.

It also closes a loop from D213 without needing anything: the battlefield badges a permanent
`playable` when it has a non-mana play, so a Student with white mana up *says* it has something to
do. That badge was added for the Contagion Clasp and the first card to benefit from it was this one.

## D217 — Vanishing and fading, the same clock read one turn apart

Every cost in this pool is now accounted for, and the two keywords here are not costs at all. A
vanishing or fading permanent arrives with counters on it and spends one each of your upkeeps, and
when they run out it is sacrificed. Nobody is asked anything. The only decision either keyword
involves is the one made before it was cast.

### Two sentences in a different order, and a turn between them

Vanishing N (CR 702.63): remove a time counter, and **when the last one is removed**, sacrifice it.
Fading N (CR 702.32): remove a fade counter, and **if you cannot**, sacrifice it.

Read them twice and they look like the same rule. Count them and they are not:

| | upkeep 1 | upkeep 2 | upkeep 3 | upkeep 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Calciderm, vanishing 4 | 4 → 3 | 3 → 2 | 2 → 1 | 1 → 0, **gone** |
| Blastoderm, fading 3 | 3 → 2 | 2 → 1 | 1 → 0 | nothing to remove, **gone** |

Both give their controller **three** turns of a 5/5 with shroud, and only one of them says three on
the card. That is the whole history of the pair — fading was printed first, players kept counting the
printed number as the number of turns they were getting, and the keyword was reprinted under a name
whose number means what people thought it meant.

So the pool holds both, in the two colours that want a cheap enormous body: Calciderm into Forge
Alliance for the second Serra Angel, Blastoderm into Kindle Grove for the second Thragtusk.

### Where the asymmetry lives, and the one case it is visible in play

In the `condition`, which vanishing has and fading does not. Vanishing's printed intervening-if is
"if this permanent has a time counter on it"; fading has no such clause, because the absence of a
counter is its trigger.

That is a one-line difference with a real consequence for any permanent on the battlefield **with no
counters**. Entering gives it its counters by any route, a token copy included — "enters with four
time counters" is one of its own abilities, so a copy brings it along. What does not is a permanent
that reached the battlefield without entering: a card put there by hand in tabletop mode, or one that
*became* a copy of one of these while already on the battlefield. A clockless Calciderm sits there
indefinitely; a clockless Blastoderm is sacrificed on the next upkeep. Both are what the cards say,
and neither is a special case in the engine.

### It needed nothing new, which is now the third time running

`{ kind: 'step', step: 'upkeep' }` already defaults to the controller's own upkeep; `entersWith`
already puts counters on a permanent as it arrives; `TriggerDef.condition` is the intervening-if;
`moveToGraveyard` is the sacrifice, rather than `destroy`, because a sacrifice is not a destruction.
Echo, cumulative upkeep and now these two are four keywords built out of one trigger shape, and the
only new code is two small functions and a counter name.

`FADE` is its own counter rather than a second user of `TIME`. The two keywords are not the same
mechanic, the printed line says "fade counter", and the table draws the counter's name — so a
Blastoderm showing `time 3` would be wrong on the card face even where it was right in the
arithmetic. `TIME` stays shared with suspend, where sharing is harmless: a suspended card is in exile
and these are on the battlefield, so no object ever carries one for two reasons.

**Proliferate finds both clocks**, unplanned and correct: a time counter and a fade counter are
counters, so one more of each kind already there buys another turn of a 5/5. That is now the third
keyword proliferate has reached into without being told about it (level counters were the second),
which is the argument for `proliferateCandidates` reading the counters a permanent *has* rather than
a list of counters the engine knows about.

### The seven tests passed first time, so one of them was made to fail

An off-by-one that holds on the first run is either right or untested, and the two are
indistinguishable from the green tick. So `fadingTrigger` was temporarily rewritten with vanishing's
body — remove a counter, sacrifice when it hits zero — and the suite run again:

- The central test (**both leave on the fourth upkeep**) failed, as it must: the Blastoderm died on
  the third.
- The clockless test (**a Calciderm stays, a Blastoderm goes**) still passed, which is worth knowing
  about it: under vanishing's body a counter removed from nothing is still nothing, so it reads the
  same. It discriminates the condition, not the ordering.

One discriminating test is enough, and knowing which one it is was worth the two minutes.

### The two slots, and the zero that came with a control already in it

| | seeds 3300 | seeds 5100 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calciderm, in Forge Alliance (for the 2nd Serra Angel) | −3 | +1 |
| Blastoderm, in Kindle Grove (for the 2nd Thragtusk) | +2 | 0 |

Four readings of 288 games, every one inside the ±20 floor, and the pair for each card disagreeing in
sign. So neither is a result, which is what a four-mana body swapped for another four-or-five-mana
body ought to measure in decks that win around 56% and 60% of their games either way.

One of them is **exactly zero**, which D216 established is a smell rather than a reading. It needs no
separate control this time, because the other three readings are the control: the same harness, the
same two decks and the same two swaps moved the number by −3, +1 and +2, so it can plainly see
changes here and simply had nothing to see on that seeding.

**And the bot casts them more often than what they replaced**, which is the half that rules out the
other reading of a zero:

| | cast | of games holding it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calciderm | 31 | 55 (56%) |
| Serra Angel | 8 | 25 (32%) |
| Blastoderm | 18 | 29 (62%) |
| Thragtusk | 16 | 32 (50%) |

Both new cards are a mana cheaper than the card whose slot they took, and that is what the counts
show: a four-drop gets cast in a game a five-drop sits in hand for. The slots are paid for, the
keyword is in the pool, and neither card changed what the decks win.

### `LIST=vanish` reads the clock off the card, because the player has to

A 5/5 with shroud that disappears without warning is not the card either keyword prints. The counters
live on the instance and every engine test reads them straight out of state, where nobody playing the
game can see them — so the browser row reads `fade 3`, `fade 2`, `fade 1` off the **card face** in a
real game, and the check is not that a label exists but that the same clock was seen at more than one
number.

Two readings of one clock rather than two clocks at one reading, and that distinction is the whole
helper: a Calciderm and a Blastoderm on the board together give `time 4` and `fade 3` on the first
move of the game, and nothing has counted down at all. `hasACountdown` groups by clock before it
counts, for exactly that reason.

The counter comes off in the upkeep, which is the step the table passes straight through — so this
is also the second thing `LIST=echo` established the need for: a claim about a step nobody stops in
can only be made by watching a game play itself.

## D218 — Split second, the pool's first rule about the stack

Every rule in this engine about what a player may do reads the board, the step or the seat. A land
drop reads the step and the count; a sorcery-speed ability reads the step and the stack's emptiness;
a morph reads the hand. Split second (CR 702.19) reads **the stack itself**: while a spell with the
keyword is on it, nobody may cast a spell or activate anything that is not a mana ability.

Which makes it the first thing here whose answer to "may I?" depends on an object somebody else put
on the stack a moment ago.

### Where it goes, and why that is the whole implementation

In `legalActions`, in two places, because that function is the one place that decides what a seat may
do. `splitSecondHeld(state)` walks `stackOrder` for a **spell** whose script declares it; the cast
loop skips every card and the activation loop skips every ability whose `produces` is undefined.

Nothing else needed to know. The table reads `legalActions` and draws an empty list; the bot reads
the same list and passes; `auto:cast` and `auto:activate` refuse because they check the same
function. One gate, four readers, and the keyword cost about fifteen lines.

Two details in the rule rather than in the code:

- **Spells only.** The keyword says "while this **spell** is on the stack", so an ability on the
  stack stops nothing, even one from a permanent whose card has the word on it. `kind === 'spell'`
  is that sentence.
- **Mana abilities are exempt**, and the exemption earns its keep: a seat part-way through paying for
  something can finish. `ability.produces !== undefined` is the same flag `isManaAbility` is built
  from, so the gate and the label can never disagree about what a mana ability is.

### The hand is told why, which is where the one UI question went

A hand that goes grey with no explanation is the complaint `blocked` exists to answer, so the cast
gate records `a spell with split second is on the stack` for every card in the player's hand. It is
the only reason in that list which is about something **on the stack** rather than about the card the
player is holding.

And it needed no client work at all, which is worth recording as a result rather than an omission:
`reasonCannotPlay` in `apps/web` reads `blocked` straight off the view and hands it to the card
sheet, so a new reason is **data** rather than a new path. That pass-through already has its own test;
this keyword adds a string to a list it already renders. There is no browser row for split second for
the same reason — the claim is a legality rule, it is pinned where legality lives, and the only thing
the screen does with it is print a sentence it is already tested to print.

### Read off the seat holding priority, which cost a test rewrite

The first two tests asked `legalActions(state, 1)` while seat 0 still held priority and got an empty
`plays` and an empty `blocked` — and passed, for the wrong reason. `legalActions` answers "what may
you do **now**", so a seat that is not being asked is told nothing at all rather than told it is
blocked.

So the reason a player actually sees is the one on their own card in their own window, and the tests
say so: the caster's own Lightning Bolt carries the reason while the caster still holds priority, and
the opponent's Cancel carries it once priority has passed to them with the Shock still waiting —
which is the one window a Cancel was ever going to be used in.

### What the keyword is not, as a test rather than a comment

**It is not uncounterable.** Split second stops *casting*, and plenty of things that counter a spell
are not cast: a Chalice of the Void set to two is already on the battlefield, its trigger goes on the
stack above the Shock, and the Shock is countered by a permanent that could not care less about the
keyword. That is a test, because it is the thing the keyword is most often mistaken for.

In this pool the practical consequence is sharper than the rule: every *cast* answer to a spell here
is a counterspell, so against two Counterspells, a Cancel, a Disallow and a Saw It Coming, split
second is close to "this resolves". That is the card's whole selling point and it is still not what
the rule says.

### The two slots, and the first slot reading this project has had to act on

Sudden Shock against the **Lightning Strike** is as clean as a slot probe gets: same cost, same
colour, same card type, same deck, and the only differences are a damage and the keyword. So that
number is the keyword's price with everything else held still.

It came back **−22 and −17 of 288**. One reading outside the ±20 floor, both the same sign, on the
cleanest payer available — which is the first slot reading in this project that is a result rather
than noise, and what it says is plain: **in this pool the window is worth less than the third
damage.** A Lightning Bolt or a Magma Jet would say the same thing, so there is no burn slot in Arc
Tempest that split second wins.

So the slot moved, and finding where took two tries that the pool refused:

- **Lava Spike** looked right — three damage but *to a player only*, so it answers nothing on the
  board. It is **escape fodder** in several arc-tempest tests, which place it in that deck's
  graveyard by name for Phoenix of Ash. Removing it from the deck breaks them.
- **Lightning Strike** itself was the first choice and is the payer whose number said no.

The committed slot is the **second Preordain's**, and that reading is **−1 and −1**: dead level.
Both numbers are reported, because a slot's number is a fact about the payer (D207, D211) and quoting
only the flattering one is exactly the mistake. Krosan Grip against the second Golgari Charm is
**+2 and +9**, inside the floor.

**And the bot casts them**, which is what makes those numbers readings rather than silence:

| | cast | of games holding it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sudden Shock | 43 | 54 (80%) |
| Lightning Strike | 48 | 60 (80%) |
| Krosan Grip | 21 | 53 (40%) |
| Golgari Charm | 31 | 43 (72%) |

Sudden Shock is cast at exactly the rate the Lightning Strike is, so the −22 is not "the card sat in
hand" — it is two decks playing the same number of burn spells and one of them dealing less damage.
The Grip's 40% is the shape of a card that needs a target: it is cast when there is an artifact or
an enchantment to kill and held when there is not, which is the Naturalize's own behaviour (52%) on
a card that costs a mana more.

**The third pool-keeps-a-copy lesson, and the first where it was the *deck* keeping it.** Tormod's
Crypt and the second Sacred Cat taught that the pool needs a copy of what a test reads. Lava Spike
adds the sharper version: a test can name a card in a *particular deck's* graveyard, so a card can be
safe to reduce and still unsafe to remove from one list. Checking a payer now means grepping the
tests for the card **and** the deck before the probe runs, not after.

### What the bot does not know

Split second makes an opponent's held counterspell worthless, and the bot that holds it has no idea.
Its "keep mana up for an answer" rule (D148, D149) reads the board and its own hand; it cannot read
"the spell about to be cast at me will not let me cast this". Nothing here tries to teach it, and
nothing should until there is an instrument that would notice — the bot is not wrong to hold the mana,
it is simply holding it for a spell that will not get its window.

## D219 — Ninjutsu, a creature that arrives already attacking

Every creature in this pool reaches the battlefield one of four ways: cast, reanimated, made as a
token, or put there by an effect. All four happen outside combat, or at least outside a combat that
is already half-resolved. Ninjutsu (CR 702.49) is the first that happens **in the middle of one**: an
unblocked attacker goes back to its owner's hand and this card takes its place, tapped and attacking
the same player, after the defender has already decided not to block.

Two things the engine had never done, in one keyword.

### A cost paid with a permanent that is not destroyed

`AbilityCost.returnsUnblockedAttacker`, and it is a different thing from a sacrifice in the way that
matters: the creature goes to a **hand**. You keep both cards. A sacrifice cost's whole arithmetic —
is what I am feeding worth less than what I am getting — does not apply at all.

So it is its own cost field, its own candidate list (`returnOptions` on the play), and its own field
on the action (`returned`). One field for both would have made every reader guess which, and the two
are opposites. The bot's branch is separate for the same reason: the sacrifice branch declines plays
when the fodder has text on it, which would have it refusing a **free** swap because a Blood Artist
is a card.

And the timing is the candidate list rather than a step check, which is the shape every other cost
here has: the one fact the cost needs is the one fact that says when it may be paid. But it took a
correction — the first version filtered attacks on `blockers.length === 0` alone, which is true the
instant an attacker is declared, so a ninja could have been swapped in during the declare-attackers
step before the defender had any say. "Unblocked" means *the player who could have blocked it did
not*, so the filter also requires the defending seat to be in `blockersDeclaredBy`. The test that
caught it is the one asserting the ability is **not** offered yet.

### A creature put onto the battlefield already in combat

`enterAttacking`, which appends to `combat.attacks` directly. That is not a shortcut, it is the rule:
the creature was never **declared** as an attacker (CR 506.3c), so nothing that triggers on attacking
triggers — and the engine gets that for free, because `raise('attacks')` lives in the declaration
path this never goes through. A test pins it by checking the stack is empty afterwards.

The defender has to travel on the stack object. By the time the ability resolves, the attacker whose
place the ninja is taking is in a hand and its attack is gone from the board, so there is nothing left
to read — `StackObject.enteringAttack` carries it, for exactly the reason `attacked` and `answering`
do. Named for what it holds rather than for the keyword, because any effect that puts a permanent onto
the battlefield attacking wants that and nothing else.

### The UI needed one field and one sentence, because the gesture was already there

A cost paid by tapping one of your own permanents is the `feeding` mode, built for sacrifice outlets.
Ninjutsu reuses it with one addition: the mode now says **which** cost it is, so the bar reads "tap an
unblocked attacker to return to your hand" rather than "tap a creature to sacrifice" — which over a
ninjutsu swap would tell the player they are about to lose the creature they are in fact getting back.

One mode rather than two, because the gesture is identical and only the field and the wording differ.
That is D213's lesson in a third place: a new kind of answer is cheaper as a new *value* in the
machinery that already exists than as a new question.

### The slot is level, and the keyword does not happen in a bot game

Ninja of the Deep Hours went into Skyward Writ for the second Omenspeaker — same cost, same colour,
same two-drop slot — at **+2 and −1 of 288**. Level, inside the floor, and the deck is the right home
for the reason the keyword needs: Skyward Writ's whole plan is fliers nobody blocks.

But the keyword itself **never fires**, and the number says so rather than hinting at it: across 48
games, **zero** ninjutsu activations. The first instinct was that the bot would not take the play. It
takes it: asked directly on a board with a Ninja in hand and a Hawk through, `botAction` returns the
activation with the right attacker named. So the situation is what never happens, and counting the
windows says precisely which part:

| in 95 of its own declare-blockers steps, over 48 games | |
| --- | --- |
| an unblocked attacker it controls | 19 |
| a Ninja of the Deep Hours in hand | 2 |
| both at once (the window) | **0** |

Not mana, and not judgement. **The bot casts the Ninja as a 2/2 the moment it can** — 13 casts in 48
games — so it is never in hand when the swap exists. Which is the dredge-land lesson in a new shape:
a card that only works from one zone is worth nothing until something keeps it there, and here the
something is a bot rule rather than a sacrifice outlet.

So ninjutsu is implemented, tested, and **unmeasured in bot play**, and that is written down rather
than papered over with the slot's level reading. The rule it needs is a holding rule — "do not cast a
card with ninjutsu while an attacker could get through" — which belongs to the family of hand-taught
facts D148 and D152 are about and needs their treatment: a flag, a count of the windows before and
after, and `bot-duel` to price the rule rather than the slot. That is its own piece.

One more thing the window count says: even a perfect holding rule has thin ground to work with. Two
of 95 steps had the card in hand at all, because it is a one-of in a sixty-card deck. The rule is
worth building for the player's sake; expecting it to move a win rate would be the mistake D212 is
about.

## D220 — The bot holds the ninja, which is the half that makes D219 happen

D219 shipped ninjutsu and measured it firing **zero** times in 48 bot games, with the windows
counted to say why: in 95 of its own declare-blockers steps the deck had an unblocked attacker 19
times and a Ninja of the Deep Hours in hand 2 times, and never both, because the bot cast the ninja
as a 2/2 the moment it could. The card was never in the zone the keyword is used from.

This is the rule that fixes it, and it is a **holding** rule rather than a judgement.

### Where it goes, and why it is not a new kind of thing

Into the family of filters that already drop "a play that bought nothing" — the ritual with nothing
to spend it on, the Fog with nothing attacking, the protection trick with nothing to protect
against, the animated land with nothing to attack. One more line in the same loop.

But it is the family turned the other way up, and that is worth being precise about. The others drop
a play that bought **nothing**; this drops a play that bought something **small**, because the card
is about to buy something bigger. The protection trick's own comment already said the real reason
those filters work — "it leaves the card in hand for the moment it is for, which is the only moment
the search can tell cast it from pass" — and ninjutsu is that sentence with the moment named.

`aSwapIsComing` is one question about the board: **do I control a creature that could attack and that
nothing untapped could block?** Not a forecast. It does not ask whether the opponent will find a
blocker, or whether the attack is worth making — both are facts about a turn that has not happened.
It only has to be right often enough that the card stops being cast on turn two into an empty board,
and it must not hold the card **forever**, which is why the condition is about a creature that exists
rather than one that might. The second test is that half: with nothing of its own able to attack, the
bot casts the ninja rather than keeping it for a moment that never arrives.

### What it is worth: the play, and not the win rate

**It creates the windows it was built for.** Same 48 games, same seeds, the flag the only difference:

| | rule off (the old bot) | rule on (the default) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ninjutsu activations | **0** | **3** |
| steps with a ninja in hand | 2 | 4 |
| steps with both a ninja and an attacker through | 0 | 2 |

**And it costs nothing.** `bot-duel` across every deck pairing, both seatings, three seed sets:
**467-467 of 936** — identical to the identical-bots control, which is also 467-467.

That identical reading is exactly the smell D216 named, so it was checked rather than reported. A
**positive control** on the same harness — `lookahead: false`, a flag the record already says matters
— came back **90-221 of 312**. The instrument is emphatically live; it simply has nothing to see here,
which is what you would expect of a rule that changes three plays in 48 games of one deck in a field
of thirteen. (And most of those 936 games are mirrored: in a pairing where neither deck holds a
ninja, the two bots are identical and the two seatings cancel exactly, which is why the control sits
on a clean 467-467 at all.)

So the honest summary is `reserveForAnswers`'s, word for word: **level, and what it changes is the
play.** Kept on by default for the reason `ritualBoughtSomething` and `dredgesTightly` are kept — a
bot that holds a card with a keyword printed on it and never uses the keyword looks broken to the
person sitting opposite, and this is a solo play realm before it is a benchmark. Off is the bot as it
was, kept as the control.

### What is still thin, said plainly

Two of 95 declare-blockers steps had the card in hand at all, because it is a one-of in a sixty-card
deck. The rule is worth having for the player's sake and for the keyword's; expecting it to move a
win rate off that base would be D212's mistake, and the numbers above are reported so nobody tries.

## D221 — Modular, the pool's first 0/0, and a zero that means the opposite of the last one

Modular N (CR 702.43): the creature enters with N +1/+1 counters, and when it dies you may move its
counters to another artifact creature. Two cards, Arcbound Worker and Arcbound Ravager, both into
Forge Alliance, which is the deck where "another artifact creature" is a sentence with somewhere to
point.

### The first printed 0/0, which is the same fact as the keyword

A modular creature is alive only because of its own counters. That makes the Worker the pool's first
printed **0/0**, and it needed no special case: `entersWith` puts a +1/+1 on it as it arrives and the
layer system does the rest. Three consequences, all tests rather than comments:

- A **−1/−1 counter kills it**, because the two annihilate and a 0/0 is lethal to itself. A Contagion
  Clasp is removal for this card.
- A 0/0 **put onto the battlefield without entering** — the tabletop's "Move by hand", or a test
  board built by hand — never ran `entersWith`, so it is a literal 0/0 and the state-based actions
  take it immediately. The third keyword to find that fact, after echo and vanishing, and the
  sharpest: here it is the difference between a card and no card at all.
- And the state-based action that does it runs **when a player would receive priority** (CR 704.3),
  which is why a test that adds the counter with a bare effect call and then drains sees nothing
  happen: with an empty stack there is nothing to drain. The pass is part of the test.

### The counters move, and the number comes from the past

The first ability here that **moves** counters off a dying permanent rather than counting them. The
number cannot be read off the creature — a card leaving the battlefield loses its counters on the way
out, so by the time the trigger resolves it is in a graveyard with nothing on it. `subjectCounters`
carries what it had, and that field was built two keywords ago for the other shape of the same
problem. It needed nothing added.

`modular: { count: 1 }` is the printed number and deliberately **not** what moves. What moves is what
the creature actually had: a Worker that picked up a second counter passes two on, and a Ravager that
ate three artifacts passes four. That is why the trigger reads the board rather than the card.

Two details in the printed text that are easy to get wrong and are both tests:

- **"You may"**, so the target spec is `optional: true` — up to one. Forced would be actively bad,
  because the legal targets are *any* artifact creature including the opponent's: a dying Worker
  whose only companion is an enemy Juggernaut would have to grow it.
- And the trigger is **not asked at all** when there is nothing to move. The printed trigger fires
  either way and then moves zero, but a table that stops to ask which creature should receive nothing
  is asking a question whose every answer is identical — the same principle echo's unaffordable cost
  gets. An intervening-if on the counters it had.

### A cost that spends an artifact, which the pool has never had

The Ravager's ability needed `AbilityCost.sacrifice` widened to `'artifact'` — the fourth member of
that union and the first that is not about creatures. There are twenty-odd artifacts in this pool and
until now nothing could pay with one. An artifact **creature** satisfies it too, which is the rule
rather than a convenience, and it is read off `characteristicsOf` so an animated land counts and a
Mutavault does not. The source itself is a legal answer, because the card says "an artifact" and not
"another": refusing it here would be the engine inventing a restriction.

### The slots: two payers, four readings, all the same sign

| | seeds 3300 | seeds 5100 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arcbound Worker, for the 2nd Elite Vanguard | −1 | +3 |
| Arcbound Ravager, for the 2nd Loxodon Warhammer | −7 | −13 |
| Arcbound Ravager, for the 2nd Raise the Alarm | −9 | −7 |

The Worker is level — signs disagree, both inside the floor, which is what a 1/1 for one swapped for
a 2/1 for one ought to measure.

The **Ravager is a downgrade**, and it took two payers to say so honestly. The Warhammer reading is
the Capsize lesson again — that card is this deck's best and does two things at once (cast 24 times
and equipped **57** in 41 games), so "a two-mana artifact for a three-mana one" was never the fair
comparison. Re-priced against the second Raise the Alarm — two mana of board against two mana of
board — it still costs **9 and 7**. Four readings, one sign, all inside the ±20 floor: not a result by
this project's own standard, but the most a probe can say, and it says the card is worse than what it
replaced.

### And the reason is a zero that means the opposite of the last one

The Ravager is cast in essentially every game it is drawn — 10 casts, and `cast-counts` says 24 of 24
games holding it. It is not a stranded card. But its ability was **activated zero times**, and this is
where the instrument earns its place:

| across 48 games | |
| --- | --- |
| times the "Sacrifice an artifact" row was **offered** | **437** |
| times the bot took it | **0** |

Ninjutsu's zero was a **zone** problem: the situation never arose, 19 attackers and 2 ninjas and never
both. This zero is a **judgement** problem: the situation arises constantly and the bot declines every
time. Same instrument, opposite diagnosis, and the README lesson written one piece ago is exactly the
thing that told them apart.

The cause is identifiable and not mysterious: the bot's sacrifice branch refuses to feed anything with
its own text, which exists because feeding a Blood Artist to a Vampire Aristocrat is a disaster —
and every artifact in Forge Alliance has text on it. So a Bonesplitter that has done its job, a
Vehicle nobody is crewing and a spent Mind Stone are all refused, and the Ravager stays a 1/1 for the
whole game. A 1/1 for two that never grows is worse than two 1/1s for two, which is what the −9 and
−7 are measuring.

So modular is correct, tested and shipped; the Ravager's slot is honestly a loss while the bot will
not feed it; and the rule it needs — for an **artifact** cost, prefer an artifact that is not a
creature and is not currently attached — is its own piece, with its own before-and-after count and its
own duel. The alternative was to quietly drop the Ravager and lose the only card in the pool that can
pay an artifact cost, which would hide an engine gap behind a tidy number.

## D222 — Feeding the artifact cost, and the stall the scenario found on its way there

D221 shipped the Arcbound Ravager and measured its "Sacrifice an artifact" row **offered 437 times
across 48 bot games and activated 0 times**, and named the reason: the branch answering it was the
*creature* branch, whose first rule is "never feed anything with text of its own". Over an artifact
cost that rule is not merely unhelpful, it is backwards — nearly every artifact is only text, a
Loxodon Warhammer is a rules box with no body at all — so it refused the whole pool and the Ravager
sat there as a 1/1 for the length of every game it was drawn in. This is the rule that answers it.

### One fact, and the two readers that would otherwise each invent it

`LegalPlay.sacrificeKind` is set to `'artifact'` when the cost eats one, and absent otherwise. A
field rather than something each reader works out, because the candidate list cannot be read for it:
an artifact cost on a board whose only artifact is a Juggernaut offers one artifact creature, which
is indistinguishable from a creature cost — so a reader guessing from the candidates would guess
wrong exactly where the board is narrowest.

Two readers need it. The **bar**, which has to ask in the right words, and the **bot**, whose
judgement about what it minds losing is a different judgement for a Bonesplitter than for a Centaur
Courser. `sacrificeOptions`' own docblock was stale from the moment D221 shipped — it said
"creatures" — and is now "permanents", with the kind beside it.

### The rule: is this artifact doing anything?

`spentArtifact` replaces the creature branch's two rules, which are both arithmetic about losing a
body and neither of which is a sentence about an artifact. Three clauses, each a fact about the
board rather than about the card:

- **Not currently a creature**, read off `characteristicsOf` and not the printed type line, which is
  the whole difference between a Sky Skiff somebody crewed and the same card sitting idle. A crewed
  Vehicle is a body in a combat.
- **Not attached.** An equipped Darksteel Plate is the reason its holder is still alive; the same
  card unattached is a card.
- **Not a mana source**, which nothing in this pool exercises — the only artifact cost here is the
  Ravager's and Forge Alliance has no rocks. In anyway, because a bot that eats its own Sol Ring to
  grow a 1/1 is a bug waiting for the next deck, and the clause is one question about the card. It
  is tested with a deck the test builds for itself, which is what `deckSpecs` is for.

Cheapest by mana value among what is left, and that is the weak part, said out loud: mana value is a
fair proxy for what an artifact cost to get and a poor one for what it is worth now. The judgement it
misses is real — an unattached Warhammer with a creature to carry it is live, the same card on an
empty board is not — and it is a question about next turn.

`BotOptions.feedsArtifacts` is on by default, and it is the one flag in that family whose `false` is
the *old* behaviour rather than the new one: every other filter there drops a play the default takes,
this one adds a play the default makes. Hence an explicit `=== false` at the gate rather than
`?? true`, which would read as though not feeding were the rule.

### What it is worth, and the number that says why it is small

Activations across the same 48 games, same seeds, the flag the only difference: **0 → 4**.

Four, of 434 windows. The honest follow-up was to ask why — and the first answer to that was wrong,
which is worth more to this file than the rule is.

The candidate tally that produced it was read off the arm **with feeding on**, where the bot had
already eaten the idle artifacts before anything counted them; it reported one idle Equipment in the
whole run, and the conclusion drawn from that was "there is nothing here to eat". Run on the bot as
it actually ships, the same instrument says something else:

| across 48 games | feeding **on** | feeding **off** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| windows the row was offered in | 434 | **437** |
| of those, nothing but the Ravager itself on offer | 383 | **220** |
| other artifacts on offer, already **attached** | 89 | **191** |
| other artifacts on offer, **idle** | 1 | **104** |
| artifacts eaten | 4 | 0 |

So that was the instrument reading its own effect. **A filter changes the board it is measured on**,
and any tally of what a rule *could* have picked has to be read with the rule off or it describes the
aftermath rather than the choice. Idle Equipment is on offer in a good half of those windows; the
four eats are the search rarely preferring the activation, not a shortage of candidates.

What survives is narrower than first claimed and still worth having: in **220 of 437** windows the
only artifact on offer is the Ravager itself, which the engine offers because the card says "an
artifact" and not "another". A naive "eat the cheapest artifact" would bin the card for a counter on
nothing in every one of those, so refusing to let it eat itself is the commonest single thing the
rule does.

And the refinement that looks obvious is still dead, for the reason it always was. "Unattached **and**
nothing could carry it" collapses to *never*, because the Ravager is itself a creature that can carry
Equipment, so while it lives there is always somewhere for the Equipment to go.

### The stall the scenario found, which was not what it was built for

`LIST=artifact` exists for one sentence. The feeding bar now carries three costs through one mode —
sacrifice a creature, return an unblocked attacker to your hand, sacrifice an artifact — and the
words it prints are the only thing on screen that says which. Over an Arcbound Ravager the default
wording is actively wrong: half the cards it lights are not creatures, so "tap a creature to
sacrifice" sends the player looking for one and leaves the bar apparently unresponsive. An engine
test knows the cost and cannot know what was said about it, so the claim is pinned in a browser.

It caught the sentence on its first run. It also **stopped dead on turn three and sat there for two
thousand moves**: a prompt open, nothing lit, and nothing on screen able to answer it.

A dying Arcbound Worker's modular trigger asks for "up to one target artifact creature" (CR
702.43b). Zero is a legal answer, so the ability goes on the stack whether or not the board has
anything to point at — and the choosing prompt **had no control on it at all**. The reducer said why,
in a comment that was true when it was written: *"a trigger's targets are never optional: it was only
put on the stack because legal ones existed."* Modular is the first trigger here that says "you may",
and it falsified that sentence the moment D221 shipped. Three suites missed it, correctly: the
engine's tests answer with `auto:choose, targets: []` directly, which is a path the table never
offered, and no starter deck puts enough Arcbound creatures on one board to reach it.

The fix is three lines of arithmetic and a button. `specsWanted` and `specsRequired` were lifted out
of `targetsWanted`/`targetsRequired` so the two readings of "how many targets" cannot drift again —
the inlined copy in the choosing branch is exactly what drifted. A tap sends at the **most** the
specs can take; the button sends at the **fewest**, and reads "Choose nothing" with none chosen. The
hint under the description now says "choose a target, or none" when the trigger says you may.

This is the second defect in a row that a browser row found in code three suites had passed, and the
shape is the same both times: a claim about what the **player** can see or do, which every layer
below the browser is structurally unable to make.

### What the rule is worth, measured, and the control that says the instrument works

`bot-duel` across every deck pairing, both seatings, three seed sets, the flag the only difference:

| seed set | `feedsArtifacts: false` vs the default |
| --- | --- |
| 3300 | 467-467 (2 unfinished) of 936 |
| 8800 | 469-467 of 936 |
| 5500 | 466-468 (2 unfinished) of 936 |

Flat three times, which is the smell D216 named and the same reading D220 got for the ninja rule. So
it was checked rather than reported: the **positive** control on this build, `lookahead: false`, came
back **91-220 of 312**. The instrument is emphatically live; a rule that changes four plays in 48
games of one deck in a field of thirteen has nothing for it to see. That is the distinction the
README lesson draws — a negative control proves the harness is fair, a positive control proves it is
connected — and this is the second rule in a row where only the second control made the flat reading
mean anything.

### What the slot says, and the default the measurement sent back

`deck-probe` with `BOT=` — the same slot, same direction, same seeds, priced by two players, which is
what that argument exists for and is not two probes differenced (D212):

| seeds | feeding | deck with the Ravager | deck without it | taking it out is worth |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3300 | on | 135-153 | 151-137 | +16 |
| 3300 | **off** | **142**-146 | 151-137 | +9 |
| 5100 | on | 168-120 | 181-107 | +13 |
| 5100 | **off** | **174**-114 | 181-107 | +7 |

The "without it" column is identical inside each seed set, which is the control built into the
arrangement rather than one that had to be run: with no Ravager on the board the flag cannot change a
thing, and it did not. So the two readings that matter are paired on the same shuffles with the flag
the only difference, and **feeding cost the deck 7 games of 288 at one seed set and 6 at the other**.
Inside the ±20 floor, so not a result by this project's standard — but the same sign twice, and the
sign is the wrong way round for a rule that was meant to help.

The counting instrument says why in one line. Of the four artifacts the rule ate across those 48
games, **four of four** were eaten on a board where the seat controlled a creature that could have
carried them, and **two of the four were Loxodon Warhammers** — the deck's best card, and the one
D221 had already singled out for doing two things at once (cast 24 times and equipped 57 in 41
games). The other two were a Bonesplitter and an uncrewed Sky Skiff. Equips were 112 with the rule on
against 110 with it off, so it is not displacing the equip in the count; it is eating the card before
the equip happens. One +1/+1 counter on a 1/1 is not worth any of those four.

And that is exactly the weakness the rule's own docblock named when it shipped: *"an unattached
Warhammer with a creature to carry it is live, and the same card on an empty board is not."* The
measurement found the clause that had already been flagged as weak, which is the argument for writing
the weakness down rather than hoping.

### Why this is a default and not a patch

The obvious next clause is "unattached **and** nothing could carry it". It collapses to never, because
the Ravager is itself a creature that can hold Equipment, so while it lives there is always somewhere
for the Equipment to go. The next idea — a syntactic test for an inert artifact, "no activated ability
and no static" — was audited against every artifact in the pool and **fails**: it passes an Obelisk of
Urd, whose +2/+2 anthem lives in an enters-the-battlefield choice rather than in `statics`, so the bot
would eat a lord. The audit is the real answer and it is a fact about the pool rather than the code:

| every non-creature artifact in the pool is | and so |
| --- | --- |
| Equipment (Bonesplitter, Basilisk Collar, Darksteel Plate, Loxodon Warhammer) | you would rather equip it |
| a Vehicle (Sky Skiff, Renegade Freighter, Consulate Dreadnought) | you would rather crew it |
| a mana source (Sol Ring, Mind Stone) | you would rather tap it |
| a standing answer (Chalice of the Void, Tormod's Crypt, Icy Manipulator, Contagion Clasp, Strionic Resonator) | you would rather keep it |
| an anthem (Obelisk of Urd) | you would *certainly* rather keep it |

**There is no spent artifact in this pool.** A bot rule cannot conjure one, which makes this a deck
question and not a judgement question — and the only honest reading of "the keyword never fires" here
is that the pool has nothing worth feeding it.

So `feedsArtifacts` defaults to **off** and stays written, tested and switched on by its own flag, the
way `dredgesTightly`'s loose variant is kept as a control. What it is waiting for is a card that wants
to go: an Ichor Wellspring or Chromatic Star shape, cheap, with a trigger that fires when it *leaves*
rather than text it uses while it stays. That is #206, and it now has a specification instead of a
hunch. What the piece delivers unconditionally is the rest: `sacrificeKind`, the bar asking for an
artifact in the right words, the self-eating refusal, the browser row, and the unanswerable prompt it
found on the way.

## D224 — The bot was reading its own shuffle, and the check that should have caught it had not been run

A real fairness bug, found by accident while doing something else, and the way it was found is worth
as much as the fix.

### What it was

The search plays a candidate action out with `applyAction`, on the **real state**. So anything the
engine *reveals* inside that line, the search learns — and a Mirko Vosk, Mind Drinker attacking
reveals a lot: "whenever it deals damage to a player, that player reveals cards from the top of their
library until four land cards are revealed". How many cards that is depends entirely on the order of
a library nobody is entitled to read, and the bot was choosing its blocks on the answer.

A person in that seat knows their decklist and does not know the shuffle. The bot knew both.

### How it was found, which is the uncomfortable part

Not by the audit. #164 built exactly the right instrument — `scripts/measure/hidden-info.mjs`, which
sweeps all 156 deck pairings, asks 16,804 decisions three ways each, and reports how many answers
move when the hidden cards are permuted. Run on the shipping bot it reads **9**. Nobody had run it.

What stood in for it in the suite was a unit test over **three fixed pairings**, and that passed. It
passed because those three games never reached the position, not because the position was not there:
the leak is reachable on `hollow-tide` v `kindle-grove` at seed 4242, turn 19, and always was. Adding
one card to Forge Alliance for an unrelated piece (#206) changed which game the third pairing plays,
and the luck ran out. That is the whole mechanism by which this was discovered, and it is luck in the
other direction.

Then a wrong fix for the *check* was tried and measured: widen the three pairings so **every deck
appears**. It still passed against the leaking bot. The leak is about one decision in 1,900 and seven
games are about 800 decisions, so a bigger sample buys a coin flip rather than a check. Breadth is not
the fix — **naming the position is**. The regression case is now first in the list so a failure says
which game it was, and the exhaustive sweep stays as the release check.

### The fix, and the line it draws

`asTheySee(state, seat)` puts every hidden zone into **one canonical order** before the search looks
at it, and `simulate` and `bestPlan` each do it once per decision rather than once per candidate.

Two halves to the canonical order, and both are load-bearing:

- **Sort**, which is what makes it canonical: two permutations of the same cards sort identically, so
  the order carries no information and the audit's scramble cannot move the answer. This is the fix.
- **Then shuffle from a constant seed**, which stops the canonical order being a lie. Sorted by key,
  every Mountain sits in one block, and a Mirko Vosk revealing "until four lands" off an alphabetical
  library predicts a mill wrong by the length of the deck. A fixed shuffle of the real contents is a
  *typical* order instead — which is what a player's feel for their own deck actually is.

What it deliberately does **not** do is hide the cards' identities. The contents of each pool survive
and only the order is flattened, because that is the real line: you know your decklist, you do not
know the shuffle. It is also the line the audit itself draws, by permuting *within* a pool rather than
replacing cards with others — so the fix and the check agree about what hidden means without either
being written from the other.

It is applied **inside the search only**, which is `noAutoPass`'s argument word for word: the
simulated state is scored and thrown away, never applied to the real table, so this changes what the
bot *sees* and never how the game runs. The action it returns names instances, and those are untouched.

`hiddenFrom` is a second copy of the pool definition that `playout.test.ts` already had, on purpose.
A test that imported the implementation's idea of "hidden" would be auditing it against itself and
would pass for any pair of matching bugs.

### What it is worth, both ways

| across 156 pairings, 16,804 decisions asked three ways | |
| --- | --- |
| decisions that changed, bot reading the shuffle | **9** |
| decisions that changed, bot blind to it | **0** |
