`BotOptions.blindToShuffle` exists so that table has two rows. A test asserting "the answer does not
change" is worth exactly as much as the proof that it could have changed, so the audit is now **two**
tests: the sweep with the blinding on, and the named position with it off, asserting the bot *does*
change its mind. If the second ever goes green, the first has stopped checking anything. The flag is
a measurement control and nothing else — `false` is the bot reading the shuffle, and it must never
reach a real table.

### And what the cheat was worth: nothing

`bot-duel` across every deck pairing, both seatings, three seed sets, the cheating bot against the
fair one:

| seed set | `blindToShuffle: false` vs the default |
| --- | --- |
| 3300 | 467-467 (2 unfinished) of 936 |
| 8800 | 468-468 of 936 |
| 5500 | 472-462 (2 unfinished) of 936 |

Level, level, and +10 inside the ±20 floor. The positive control on this same build — `lookahead:
false` — reads **91-220 of 312**, and reads the same 91-220 on the build *before* the blinding, which
says something extra for free: the search lost no measurable strength by losing the shuffle.

So the bot was reading its own library and **getting nothing for it**, which makes this the best
shape a fairness fix can have — correctness with no price to argue about. It is worth saying that the
flat reading here needs no apology under D216's rule, because the connectedness of the flag is not in
question: `hidden-info` already showed it moving **9 decisions of 16,804**. A rule that changes nine
decisions in seventeen thousand cannot move a win rate over 936 games, and the duel saying so is the
two instruments agreeing rather than one of them being asleep.

## D223 — The card the pool was missing, and the question "is it idle" replaced with "is it a loss"

D222 ended with an artifact cost the deck could not pay well and a bot rule switched off because what
it fed the cost was wrong. This is the card that fixes the first and the narrowing that fixes the
second. It needed D224 shipped first: the deck change turns the hidden-information audit red, because
adding one card to Forge Alliance was what surfaced the shuffle leak.

### The rule: not "is it idle" but "is sacrificing it a loss"

D222's rule asked whether an artifact was **doing anything right now**, and the instrument said what
that was worth: four artifacts eaten across 48 games, four of four with a creature standing by that
could have carried them, two of them **Loxodon Warhammers**. Paired on the same seeds it cost 6 to 7
games of 288.

The question was wrong, not the implementation. An Equipment doing nothing this instant is a card you
equip next turn — "idle" and "spent" are different words. The right question is whether sacrificing it
is a **loss at all**, and the only artifact that honestly answers no is one whose own text fires when
it reaches a graveyard. `paysForLeaving` is that clause, and it replaced two others:

- the mana-source clause is **subsumed** — a Sol Ring has nothing to say about graveyards — so it was
  deleted rather than kept as a second way of saying the same thing;
- and the "no activated ability, no static" test that looked equivalent was **audited against the
  pool and rejected**: it passes an Obelisk of Urd, whose +2/+2 lives in an enters-the-battlefield
  choice rather than in `statics`, so that version eats a lord. The audit is one command
  (`AUDIT=1 node scripts/measure/artifact-cost.mjs`) and it is the reason this clause reads the way
  it does rather than the way it first looked like it should.

`isCreature` and `attachedTo` stay with no card behind either of them, which is the opposite of this
engine's usual rule about options nothing fires. The distinction: those are **refusals**, not offers.
A refusal that never fires costs nothing and stops the bot eating a body for a counter the day a card
exists with a `to-graveyard` trigger on a creature.

### The card, which is the sixth kind of artifact in the pool

Ichor Wellspring, {2}: "enters the battlefield **or** is put into a graveyard from the battlefield —
draw a card." Every other non-creature artifact here is Equipment, a Vehicle, a mana source, a
standing answer or an anthem. This is the only one whose whole text is about **going**.

Two triggers rather than one, because the engine has no "or" for two different events and does not
need one: that templating *means* two triggers, and the rules read them separately too (CR 603.2
raises each on its own). In printed order, so a log reads the way the card does. `who: 'self'` named
on both, which is load-bearing on the graveyard event — `who` defaults to **`another`** there and to
`self` on the five board events, so the default would have made this a card that draws whenever
anybody else's card is binned. `drawLater` for both, so a dredge can replace either.

### The slot, and the lesson that picked the payer

`cast-counts` named the deck's dead slot without ambiguity: **Disrupt Decorum, 0 casts in 144 games**,
in hand 45 of them. It is not the payer. Goad is a mechanic only a pod can use, and that card is the
pool's only one — a duel measurement is not a reason to delete the pod's card.

So the payer is the **second Leonin Skyhunter**, and paying from a two-of is the point rather than a
convenience. `arena()` places a card by finding it in that seat's library, so a test naming a card in
this deck breaks the moment the deck stops carrying it — and every one-of the usage instrument
offered is named by a test somewhere, the Angelic Gift and Firemane Avenger included. That cost one
wasted swap before the grep: the README lesson from D201 says to check the payer *and* the deck
before the probe runs, and it says nothing about checking a one-of against the whole suite. Cutting
one copy of a two-of leaves the card in the library and every test standing. It is also a hard payer
by this project's standard: same mana value, and the bot casts a Skyhunter in 96% of the games it
holds one.

### What it is worth

The rule now eats the Wellspring and nothing else. Across the same 48 games it ate **one** artifact,
and it was the right one — against D222's four, of which four were mistakes:

| across 48 games, feeding on | D222's rule | this one |
| --- | --- | --- |
| artifacts eaten | 4 | **1** |
| eaten with a carrier standing by | 4 | 1 |
| Loxodon Warhammers eaten | 2 | **0** |

One in 48 is not a per-game number, and the reason is arithmetic rather than judgement: one copy of a
two-mana artifact rarely shares a board with the Ravager. The eligibility is right and the frequency
is a fact about a 60-card deck with one of them in it.

### The slot, and the default set for the third time

`deck-probe` with `BOT=` on both arms — the same slot, same direction, same seeds, priced by both
players, which is what that argument is for and is not two probes differenced (D212):

| seeds | feeding | with the Wellspring | without it | taking it out is worth |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3300 | off | 143-145 | 142-146 | −1 |
| 3300 | **on** | **144**-144 | 142-146 | −2 |
| 5100 | off | 177-111 | 174-114 | −3 |
| 5100 | **on** | **180**-108 | 174-114 | −6 |

Two readings, one table. **The slot**: taking the Wellspring out costs 1 to 6 games of 288, same sign
in all four arms, so the card is level to slightly good against a Leonin Skyhunter the bot casts 96%
of the time it holds one. **Feeding**: the stock column with it on against the stock column with it
off is **+1** at one seed set and **+3** at the other — against D222's **−7 and −6** for the rule
before the narrowing.

So `feedsArtifacts` goes back **on**, and the default has now been set three times by three
measurements: on off D221's count of 437 offers and zero activations, off because of the two
Warhammers, and on again because the narrowing removed those and the sign flipped with them.

**The +1 and +3 is not the argument, and should not be read as one.** It is well inside the ±20 floor
and the rule fires once in 48 games, so the honest description is "no longer a loss" rather than "a
gain". The argument is D220's — the one that keeps `holdsNinjas` on: a cost printed on a card that
never fires looks broken to the person sitting opposite, and this is a solo play realm before it is a
benchmark. What the probe was for here was narrower and it did its job: it ruled out the harm that
sent the default back last time, which is what lets the judgement decide. `false` stays as the
control the probe is run against.

## D225 — The last zone change nothing could read, and the card that reads it

Exile was the hole in the family. `died` and `entered` were the first two events the engine ever
raised; `left` came with the Banisher Priest; `drew` with the draw watchers (D150); `toGraveyard`
with Planar Void and Rancor (D153, D157); `discarded` with madness (D171). That left one
destination a card could reach with nothing in the engine able to see it — and it is the one the
pool has been sending cards to since its first month. Journey to Nowhere, Banisher Priest, Flickerwisp
and Cloudshift have all been exiling creatures for two hundred decisions, and no card could tell.

### The event, and the one list in the family that is not a list of ids

`GameState.exiled` carries three fields per entry where every sibling carries a bare id, and the
reason is that the move destroys all three:

- an exile zone belongs to the card's **owner**, so the controller of the permanent is gone
  afterwards — and "a creature **you control**" is a question about the controller;
- a card in exile has lost its counters, so asking `characteristicsOf` after the move answers about
  a different object — an animated land reads as a land, a face-down 2/2 as nothing at all;
- a creature card exiled out of a **graveyard** to pay for escape is, once it is sitting in exile,
  indistinguishable from a creature that was on the battlefield a moment ago.

So `ExiledCard` has one field per word of the printed phrase it exists for — `wasCreature`,
`controller`, `from` — each computed in `relocate`, which is the one place a card changes zone and
therefore the one place that cannot forget. The trigger's filters (`what`, `whose`, `from`) are the
three questions asked of them, and there is no `who`: a card cannot watch its own exile, because a
watcher has to be somewhere, and nothing is printed that fires from exile.

### One move, even when the engine makes it in two

The interaction that paid for the design, and it was a failing test before it was a feature. **Rest
in Peace** is in Skyward Writ's sixty, and while it is out every creature you lose is exiled instead
of buried — which the printed rulings say is a creature of yours being exiled, and which Soulherder
counts. The first version of this said it did not.

The cause is a simplification three decisions older than this one: `replaceZoneChange` runs *after*
the physical move and corrects it from the graveyard the card has already reached, so the second hop
read `graveyard → exile` where the rules say there was one move, `battlefield → exile`, and the
graveyard was never touched (CR 614.1). `exileCameFrom` is the correction, and `left` is what makes
it safe rather than a guess: that list holds cards that have left a battlefield since the last
settle and is drained *before* any trigger is raised, so the only window in which it is non-empty is
the replacement pass itself. An escape cost, a Planar Void's trigger and a Tormod's Crypt all see an
empty list and are recorded as what they are.

### Soulherder, and why it is this card rather than a watcher

`{1}{U}` for a 1/1 that grows whenever a creature you control is exiled, and that exiles one itself
at the beginning of your end step. Two abilities that feed each other, which is the whole reason it
is this card: a watcher that needed another card to do anything would have been a slot waiting on a
draw, and D221's lesson is that an option nothing fires is worth nothing. This one grows every turn
on its own and takes a free counter from every other blink in the deck.

It came in for the **Disenchant**, which `cast-counts` named as Skyward Writ's worst conversion: in
hand in 64 of 144 games and cast 35 times, the signature of a card with no legal target half the
time. The copy in Dawn Tithe stays, so the pool keeps Disenchant and a pasted list can still play it
— which is the lesson D223 paid for twice (a card in **no** deck is unreachable by every path, and a
test that names a one-of breaks when the one-of goes).

### A prompt with nothing on it is not a question

Found by the card and fixed generally. `obviousTargets` returned null for *any* optional spec, so
the controller was asked even when the candidate list was empty — and a lone Soulherder would have
put a prompt with nothing to point at in front of a player at the end of every single turn. An
optional spec with no legal targets has exactly one legal answer, so the decision is skipped and the
ability still goes on the stack and does as much as it can, which is nothing (CR 608.2). The modular
trigger had been in the same position since D221 and had been papered over in the UI instead: the
"Choose nothing" button D222 added is still the right control for a *real* "up to one", and is no
longer the only thing standing between a player and a dead prompt.

### What the bot does with it, measured rather than assumed

`scripts/measure/blink-use.mjs`, 48 games of Skyward Writ against the field:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Soulherders cast | 18, in 15 games |
| end steps it was asked about | 34 (2.3 per game on board) |
| declined | 0 |
| blinked a token, which does not come back | 1 |
| blinked something carrying counters | 3 |
| blinked something with nothing to re-trigger | 22 |
| counters on it, best in a game | 2.5 average, 8 highest |

Two readings. The card **works**: it is cast when drawn, it fires twice a game, and it ends games as
a 3/3 or better with six of those counters coming from something other than its own blink. The bot
**plays it adequately and not well**: 22 of 34 blinks had no arrival to re-trigger, which is fine
(the counter is the point), but 4 of 34 were real losses — one token destroyed outright (CR 111.7)
and three creatures stripped of their counters (CR 400.7).

That is the next piece of work rather than this one's, and it is a *judgement* problem of a kind the
bot has not had before: every other optional target in the pool points at the enemy, where the worst
a bad answer does is waste the card. This one points at your own board, so a bad answer destroys a
creature. The shape of the fix is the one `TargetSpec.friendly` already has — a fact the card
declares and the bot's ranker reads — and the number to beat is 4 in 34.

## D226 — What a blink costs, and the first target the bot could harm by pointing at it

D225 shipped Soulherder and read what the bot did with it: of 34 blinks across 48 games, **one
destroyed a token outright** (CR 111.7) and **three stripped a creature of its +1/+1 counters**
(CR 400.7). This is that number taken seriously.

### Why it is a new kind of mistake

Every optional target in this pool before now aims at the enemy. A Doom Blade pointed at the wrong
creature, a shield on the wrong body, a modular counter given to the wrong artifact — the floor on
all of them is "the card was wasted", which is why `chooseTargets` has been allowed to be as simple
as "the enemy, biggest first" with one hint (`friendly`) for the handful of cards aimed the other
way. A blink is the first target where a bad answer **costs you a creature**, because the permanent
does not come back as itself: a token ceases to exist, and counters, Auras and marked damage are all
gone from what returns.

And the bot could not have worked that out. A target spec is a candidate list and a filter; nothing
in it says "and then it comes back". So the card declares it, exactly as `friendly` is declared:
`TargetSpec.blinks`, carried by Soulherder's end step, Cloudshift and Flickerwisp.

### A ranking for the deals and a refusal for the destruction

`blinkLoss` is what a permanent's controller loses, and `blinkAdjust` flips the sign for an
opponent's — one function for both readings, which is the whole reason this is an *adjustment* to
the ordinary ranking rather than a third ordering. Four terms, and they are the four the instrument
counted rather than four this engine thought of: a token (the whole permanent), counters (a +1/+1 is
a loss, a −1/−1 is a creature healed), an Aura (and *whose* it is decides the sign — your Pacifism
on their creature is freed by the blink, theirs on yours is shed), and an Equipment (which merely
falls off, so it is a smaller loss). Marked damage is deliberately left out, and so is untapping:
both are real and neither is worth anything at the moment this engine's blinks are chosen, since
Soulherder's is an end-step trigger. Untapping is the better of the two to add if a probe ever comes
back asking for a term.

The token needed a **refusal** rather than a weight, and the instrument is what proved it: with the
ranking alone the bot still blinked a token once in 48 games, because a ranking only decides which
candidate is best and a board whose only other creature is a token leaves the worst play as the best
one. `blinkDestroysMine` drops it from the list, and only where declining is legal — a mandatory
blink with nothing but a token to point at has to point somewhere, and that is the rules' answer
rather than the bot's. It is kept narrow on purpose: it refuses destruction, not a bad deal.

### What it is worth

The instrument, same 48 games, same seeds:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| blinks taken | 34 | 31 (one declined) |
| a token destroyed | 1 | **0** |
| counters stripped | 3 | **0** |
| blinks with nothing to re-trigger | 22 | 15 |
| Man-o'-Wars and Omenspeakers blinked | 6 | 11 |

Four bad blinks to none, and the useful ones nearly doubled — the bot now reaches for the arrival
trigger instead of the biggest creature.

`bot-duel` four ways, and all four say the same thing — nothing:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `SUBJECT=skyward-writ`, seeds 3300, 288 games | 146-142 (+4) |
| `SUBJECT=skyward-writ`, seeds 5100, 288 games | 145-143 (+2) |
| the whole field, seeds 3300, 624 games | 311-313 (−2) |
| the whole field, seeds 5100, 624 games | 312-310 (+2) |

Level four times over: every reading is well inside the ±20 floor and they do not even agree on the
sign. That is the expected shape rather than a disappointment — a rule that changes four choices in
forty-eight games cannot move a win rate, which is the same arithmetic D223's +1 and +3 ran into. The
duel's job here was to **rule out harm**, and it does: the bot is not worse for knowing what a blink
costs.

The argument is the instrument's, and it is the same one D220 and D223 made. A bot that destroys its
own token to put a +1/+1 counter on a 1/1 looks broken to the person sitting opposite, and this is a
solo play realm before it is a benchmark.

### A measurement lesson that cuts against the obvious one

`SUBJECT` is new on `bot-duel`, and the first version of its docblock said it was there to stop a
one-deck rule being "drowned six to one" in a 312-game field. **That was wrong, and this file had
already said why**: a pairing where the setting is inactive for both arms is the same game twice on
the same seed, so it credits one win to each arm and contributes nothing to the difference and
nothing to its variance. The full field is not diluted — only the percentage is, and the difference
is what gets read. So narrowing buys **time**, not signal: the same number, six times sooner.

It also costs something that is easy to miss, and the rule being measured is the example.
`blinksWell` fires off Soulherder in Skyward Writ *and* Cloudshift in Verdant Guard, so
`SUBJECT=skyward-writ` prices three quarters of it. The whole-field run is what prices all of it.

### And the browser, where the prompt lives

`LIST=blink` is the eighteenth scenario in `e2e-solo.mjs` and the first whose question is about the
player's **own** board. The two required checks are the ones no engine test can make: the question
asked in the ability's own words, and the counter its answer pays for arriving on the **card face**.
The decline — "Choose nothing" being the right answer because the only other creature is a token — is
reported when the shuffle produces it rather than required, the way the damage-assignment order is:
a board whose only other creature is a token is a fact about the shuffle and not something a deck
list can arrange. 26 of 26, with the prompt answered in the second game of three.

It also made the driver say what it answered. A choose-prompt came back as `aimed a trigger`, which
is true of every trigger in the pool and useless to a scenario checking that a *particular* one
reached the table — the same mistake the feed prompt's words were added to fix (D222). It now carries
the ability's own description.

## D227 — Who has been leaving you alone, which only the engine can tell from who could not

D189 gave every opponent's strip `hit you N` — all the damage that seat has dealt you this game —
and closed half a question. The other half has been in the "Next" list ever since, with the reason
it was hard written down beside it: *a player who attacked somebody else instead of you looks
identical to a player who could not attack you at all*. Both show up as no damage and no badge.

### Legality is the whole of it

The difference between those two players is a legality check, and the only thing at the table that
ran one is the engine: `legalDefenders` is asked at every declaration, and it already knows whether
a creature *could* have been aimed at a given seat. So `Seat.spared` records, per declaring seat,
the attacking **power that could legally have come at you and went somewhere else**.

A creature goaded away from you (CR 701.38a), one held off by a "can't attack you", one that is
tapped or summoning-sick — none of them leaves anything behind, because none of them could have
attacked you. A board full of creatures that could have and did not is a choice, and this is the
record of the choice.

Two details that are load-bearing rather than incidental:

- **Read from the pre-declaration state.** `tapAttackers` runs a few lines later and a tapped
  creature has no legal defenders at all, so computed after it the tally is empty every single
  time. The question is about the moment the attack was declared.
- **Power, not a count of attacks**, so it reads against `damageFrom` in the same unit. "Hit you
  12, spared you 5" is a seat coming at you and holding something back; "hit you 0, spared you 20"
  is a seat that has left you alone all game while it could have done otherwise. And power *as
  declared*, which the pump cast afterwards does not change — that pump is a fact about the combat
  that followed, not about the choice of where to send it.

### It fires, which is a thing to check rather than assume

Twelve four-seat bot pods: **12 of 12** ended with a sparing tally, the biggest single number 174,
and the per-seat totals land in the same tens as the damage ones — `38/0/65/30 spared` beside
`33/40/36/9 hit` in the first game. That matters for the badge rather than for the engine: two
numbers a player is meant to weigh against each other have to be in the same range, and a column
that read 0 or 400 would be noise either way.

### Information and never enforcement

The same line the deals draw and `damageFrom` draws: no rule reads this field, no state-based action
consults it, and the bot does not either. The pod already has a rule about ganging up on whoever is
ahead (D137's `chaseTheCrown`), and "attack whoever has spared you least" would be a different piece
of work with its own measurement — the badge is a thing for the *people* at the table, which is what
a pod's politics is made of.

The badge draws nothing at nought, like its sibling: on turn one everybody has spared everybody and
a row saying so on every strip is noise. It is drawn in the green the table uses for what is going
your way, beside the red of what is not.

### And the browser found the bug a new field always has

The first pod run after this shipped crashed the `<Board>` component: *Cannot read properties of
undefined (reading '0')*, from `sparedYouBy`. The cause was not the field — it was a **server that
had not restarted**, serving a view built before the field existed, and the new reader trusting it
to be there.

That is the shape of every field added to a long-lived state, and this repo already had the
convention written down: `autoPassFor` reads its list as `(state.autoPassOff ?? [])` with a comment
saying a game stored before the list existed comes back without it. So both of today's new fields
now read the same way — `seat.spared ?? {}` where it is written and in the view, `me?.spared?.[...]`
in the browser, and `next.exiled ?? []` in the two places `settle` and `relocate` touch the exile
list (D225's field has exactly the same exposure and nothing had tested it either).

Worth writing down because of *what* caught it. The engine's tests build their own state and always
have the field; the web unit test builds its own view and always has the field; only a real browser
against a real server that was started an hour earlier reads a view that does not. A full-stack run
is not a slower unit test — it is the only thing in this project that sees two versions of the
software at once, which is also exactly what a player who leaves a tab open across a deploy sees.

## D228 — Affinity: a cost the board decides, printed on the spell rather than on a permanent

D132 gave the engine cost modification and only one direction of it: a permanent on the battlefield
changing what *other* spells cost. A Goblin Electromancer is found by a pass over everybody's
battlefield and applies to whatever matches its own predicate; a Thalia is the same machinery with
the sign flipped. Affinity is the mirror — a reduction **printed on the card being cast**, reading
its own caster's board (CR 702.41a).

### One function, because it is one question

`costChangeFor` is where they meet, and that is the whole of the design. It already answered "what
does this cost *here*, for *this seat*", and it is called from every place a cast cost is computed:
the printed cost, an alternative cost, and the payment that has to agree with the offer. Folding
affinity in means the offer and the payment cannot disagree — a table that showed a Frogmite at {1}
and then charged {4} would be a table nobody could trust — and it means affinity works under an
alternative cost without a line of extra code.

Three details are the keyword rather than the implementation:

- **Counted as the cost is computed.** The number is however many artifacts the caster controls at
  the moment somebody looks, so a Frogmite offered at {1} goes back to {4} when the artifacts are
  answered. Nothing is stored anywhere, which is also why the test for it is two boards rather than
  one game.
- **Generic only** (CR 601.2f), like every other reduction here. An affinity card with a coloured
  requirement keeps it.
- **Floored, and the floor is reported honestly.** Eight artifacts against a printed {7} take
  **seven** off, not eight — what the play reports is what the board actually did to the cost, and
  a table saying "{8} less" over a {7} spell would be describing a cost that does not exist.

### The two cards, and the slot argument that took three tries

Frogmite ({4} 2/2) and Myr Enforcer ({7} 4/4), both artifact creatures as printed — which is the
half that makes the keyword snowball, since each one cast makes the next cheaper. Forge Alliance is
the only list in the pool that can pay it: sixteen of its sixty cards are artifacts.

The slots are the interesting part, and the first two answers were wrong:

1. **Both Monastery Swiftspears.** Rejected by the test suite: a mentor test places one out of this
   deck's library.
2. **The Serra Angel and a Swiftspear.** The Angel is what `cast-counts` actually points at — 45%,
   ten casts in the twenty-two games it was in hand, which is what five mana looks like in a deck
   whose curve stops at four. Rejected for the same reason one step along: two crew tests pay
   "crew 2" with the Angel's four power out of *this* deck. Elite Vanguard (49%) is protected the
   same way by the Angelic Gift tests.
3. **A Swiftspear and a Plains**, which is what shipped. The land is the honest half: a deck whose
   spells get cheaper as the board fills needs fewer lands to cast them, which is why affinity decks
   have always run twenty rather than twenty-four.

That is D223's lesson arriving from the other side. There it was "pay from a two-of so the tests
keep standing"; here the cheapest slot in the deck turned out to be the one card no test can name —
a land.

### What the slot is worth, measured, and the two wrong answers on the way

The keyword was finished and the deck slot was not, and they are worth separating because only one
of them is a rules question. **The slot as first written was wrong, and the measurement is what
said so** — which is the entry this section exists for.

`cast-counts`, 144 games of Forge Alliance, "cast, of the games it was in hand":

```
 94%  cast 34 / in hand 36 games   Frogmite
 32%  cast 16 / in hand 50 games   Myr Enforcer
```

That is castability and not value — see the lesson in `scripts/measure/README.md`, because the
Serra Angel the Enforcer did *not* displace reads 45% and is a perfectly good card. Reading 32% as
"this card is bad" is the mistake the lesson is about, and the probe below is what kept it from
being made here.

Then the paired slot probe, four shapes, 288 games per seed set against the same two sets. The
first arm is the one that started all of this: take both cards back out and restore the Plains and
the Swiftspear.

```
                                            seeds 3300   seeds 5100
both cards out, land and Swiftspear back          +1         +23
Myr Enforcer -> the 21st Plains                   -5         +19
Myr Enforcer -> a second Frogmite                  0          +4
Ajani's Pridemate -> the 21st Plains             -12         +10
```

Read by what was *cut*, that is four unrelated numbers. Read by **what the deck ends up being**, it
is one pattern: every arm holding twenty-one lands reads positive on seeds 5100 and negative on
3300, and inside each seed set the readings fall in the order of how many affinity cards survive —
+1, −5, −12 on one, +23, +19, +10 on the other. Steps of about six games per card kept, arrived at
twice independently. The arm that keeps twenty lands (two Frogmites, no land back) reads 0 and +4,
which is stock.

So:

- **The {7} body was not the problem.** Swapping it for a second Frogmite bought 0 and +4 — inside
  the floor, and four of the twenty-three games. An hour was spent suspecting it on the strength of
  a conversion rate.
- **The land was.** Restoring it recovered nineteen of the twenty-three on the arm that failed.
- **The claim that paid for it was wrong, and specifically so.** "A deck whose spells get cheaper as
  the board fills needs fewer lands, which is why affinity decks run twenty rather than
  twenty-four" is true of an affinity deck and false of this one. Forge Alliance has sixteen
  artifacts, but its curve is twelve one-drops and seven four-drops, and the cards affinity made
  cheaper were two of sixty. **An archetype's land count does not transfer to a deck that merely
  contains the keyword.**

What shipped in the end is the smallest shape that carries the keyword: **one Frogmite, for one
Monastery Swiftspear, land count untouched** — one card in, one card out. It is the best pooled
reading of the arms that keep affinity (+14 of 576) and the only one positive on the arm that
actually failed the floor. Myr Enforcer came back out of the pool entirely, because `poolIndex` is
built from `STARTER_DECKS` and a card in no deck is not a card the engine has.

Nothing about the keyword goes untested for its absence, which is worth saying because it is the
reason the cut was cheap: the floor is reachable with a Frogmite, where eight artifacts take **four**
off a printed {4} and report `{8} less` beside it — a bigger overshoot than the Enforcer's, so the
honesty of the report is tested harder than before. The browser scenario pastes sixteen Frogmites,
which a custom list may do for any name the pool knows.

**The honest shape of this entry is that the first two answers were measured and neither held.**
None of the four arms clears the ±20 floor on its own, so "six games a card" is a consistent sign
across four comparisons rather than a reading — the kind of thing to re-measure the next time this
deck is balanced, and the kind of thing that would have been written up as a win if the probe had
been skipped.

## D229 — Myriad: the first card in the pool whose rules text reads differently at four seats

Every keyword in this engine is worth something in a duel. Flying, deathtouch, infect, affinity,
prowess — all of them are facts about a board, and a two-player table shows every one. A pod has had
nothing of its own: the monarch is a rule rather than a card, goad points at somebody else but
functions with one opponent, and the deals and the two politics tallies are information rather than
text. **Myriad is the first card whose printed text does nothing at all at two seats and three
things at four** (CR 702.111a), which is the reason it was worth the engine work.

### The keyword the engine acts on

`KEYWORDS` held sixteen facts the rules consult. Myriad is the seventeenth entry and the only
**instruction** among them, and it is in that list rather than in a card's `triggers` for one
reason: **Blade of Selves grants it**. Granting is all `PumpOptions.keywords` can do, and this
engine has no machinery for handing another permanent a *triggered* ability — so the keyword is the
declaration and `declareAttackers` is the implementation. The card itself is four lines, exactly like
the Basilisk Collar handing out deathtouch.

The composition is the work, and it is three primitives that have existed separately for a while
and had never been put together:

- `copyAsToken`'s machinery — a token of a nontoken's **printed** card (CR 707.2), from embalm;
- `enterAttacking` — a permanent that arrives in a combat already in progress, tapped and attacking
  a named player, from ninjutsu;
- a marker on the token that the end-of-combat step reads, which is `DASHED`'s shape.

`addTokens` is new, and it is the whole of the refactor: `createToken` returns a `GameState` and
myriad is the one caller in the engine that needs the **ids** of what it made — to put each one into
combat against a particular player, and to mark it. Diffing the battlefield before and after would
be the alternative and it would be wrong the first time a token's arrival makes another one.

### Where it runs, which is the rules rather than a choice

`myriadCopies` is called **after** everything else in `declareAttackers`: after the attacks are
built, after the pacts it broke are recorded, after the sparing tally is read, and after
`tapAttackers`. That ordering is the rule. Every record this function keeps is about the
**declaration**, and a myriad token was never declared as an attacker (CR 508.4) — so it breaks no
promise, changes no sparing tally, counts towards no battalion, and raises no `attacks` event.

The last of those is load-bearing rather than tidy: a myriad token is a copy of a creature with
myriad, so a token that triggered the keyword would make tokens of its own and those would make
more. Nothing guards against that in the loop. The reason three Angels is three rather than nine is
that the declaration is the only thing that runs myriad at all.

### What is deliberately missing, and it is the half that matters

The printed text is "**you may** create a token", and the engine takes every copy, every time. There
is nowhere to ask: this engine's questions are asked while a stack object resolves, and this happens
inside a declaration. The planeswalker half of the clause ("or a planeswalker they control") is
missing for the same reason.

In a duel that is exactly right, because there is nothing to decline. In a pod it is a real
deviation, and it is the one the measurement immediately ran into.

### What it is worth, which needed an instrument that did not exist

`deck-probe` prices a slot against the field and **every one of its games is a duel**, so a card
whose text reads "for each opponent" measures as precisely the noise floor and the harness says
nothing. That is a structural hole and myriad is the first card to fall in it, so
`scripts/measure/pod-slot.mjs` is the sibling: the subject deck sits at every table with three
opponents chosen from the seed, and each table is played four times with the subject moved one seat
along, so it occupies every seat equally often and turn order cancels. Paired, like `deck-probe` —
both arms play the same seeds, the same opponents and the same seats — and its zero is arithmetic
rather than evidence for the same reason `pod-duel`'s is, so the floor has to come from re-running a
real arm on disjoint seeds.

Two readings, 52 pods each, Forge Alliance with the Blade against Forge Alliance with the Ajani's
Pridemate it displaced:

```
                       seeds 3300        seeds 5100
stock (Blade):            4-48              2-50
variant (Pridemate):     15-37              6-46
the change:              -11 of 52         -4 of 52
```

**The direction is the same on both arms and the magnitude is inside the instrument's own noise, and
the second fact is established by the instrument itself rather than assumed.** The harness's
docblock says to get the floor by running a real arm twice on disjoint seeds, and that is exactly
what the *variant* column is: the same sixty cards, played against the same field, reading **15 and
6**. A spread of nine on an unchanged deck is the floor, so −11 is barely outside it and −4 is well
inside. Fifty-two pods cannot resolve a one-card change.

So the honest conclusion is narrow and worth stating plainly: **the Blade is not an improvement, it
is probably a small cost, and how much is unmeasured.** It ships anyway, and the reasoning is a
judgement rather than a number — the keyword needs a card in a starter deck to exist at all
(`poolIndex` is built from `STARTER_DECKS`, so a card in no deck is not in the pool), and the
engine's ability to play myriad is worth more to this project than one slot's win rate in a format
whose baseline Forge Alliance already sits under. What is not claimed is that the card is good.

Also worth recording because it is a fact about the **format** rather than the card: Forge Alliance
wins 4%–29% of its pods across these four arms against a 25% baseline, which is a much wider band
than any duel reading in this project. A pod has three opponents and three chances to be attacked,
and the per-seat splits here are single digits. Any future pod slot question needs far more games
than a duel question, and `pod-slot`'s docblock now says so.

Two candidate explanations for the cost, and the honest position is that the instrument has not
separated them:

- **The politics story does not actually follow from this bot's rules.** "Myriad makes you the
  archenemy" is the natural reading and `foeOrder` contradicts it: these bots attack the opponent
  with the **lowest life**, and myriad pushes all three opponents down while its controller stays
  at forty. By that rule the copies should make somebody *else* the target.
- **The horizon story is likelier.** Blade of Selves is {3} for **no stats** and equip {3} on top,
  and its entire payoff happens in a combat the bot cannot see from the main phase where it decides
  to cast and equip it. That is the same one-ply horizon that hid the pumps, the ritual and goad
  (D68, D69), and the keyword with the closest shape to this one — goad — is in the pool precisely
  because its value is a fact about the table rather than something a search can find.

The repair, when it comes, is the "may": the choice belongs in the declaration, with a bot rule to
make it, because a cost past the search horizon is a thing this project teaches by hand rather than
by weight. That is a later entry, and it needs a bigger `pod-slot` sample to be able to show its own
effect at all.

## D230 — The realtime whole-game failure, closed on a hundred runs rather than on a cause

CI run 324 failed `apps/realtime`'s "plays a whole game on its own against the server" with
`expected { kind: 'attackers', seats: [ 1 ] } to be null`, on a commit that changed nothing but a
browser script. It has not recurred. #178 held it open with an explicit exit criterion — another
occurrence that names the assertion, or **a hundred runs of the suite with none** — and this is the
hundred: 100 consecutive runs, 0 failures, which is 4,300 test executions of a suite whose 43 tests
include the whole-game play-out twice over.

**What that does and does not establish is worth being exact about, because the two are easy to
blur.** A hundred clean runs is the weaker of the two kinds of evidence the task would accept. It
closes the task on the terms the task set, and it does not identify the cause. The failure is still
unreproduced.

What *is* established is narrower and came from reading rather than running, and both halves rule a
candidate out by construction:

- **The suspect #178 named is impossible.** It proposed a race between `runBots` taking the
  server's first turn and the view the test reads straight after `auto:keep`. `runBots` is called
  synchronously inside the same read-modify-write as the action, so the ack's `stateVersion` already
  carries every move the bots made, and the test waits for a state event at least that version
  before reading. There is no window.
- **The other candidate is not one either.** `seatsToAct` and the view's `awaiting` both derive from
  `pendingDeclaration`, so they cannot disagree about who is owed a move — which was the obvious way
  for `runBots` to think a person was on the clock while the table still showed the bot's question.

Which leaves **a bot stall**, and the reason a whole session went into guessing at it: `stalls` was
collected from the first action and asserted only at the *end* of the test, a hundred lines after the
assertion that fails. Every one of `runBots`' silent ways out — a refused move, `botAction` offering
none, the five-hundred-move guard running out with a server seat still owed — fires that callback and
leaves the table in exactly the state the failing assertion reports. So the CI line we saw is what a
stall in that window *looks like*, and the stall's own reason, which names the move and the step, was
never printed.

Both halves of that are closed now: the stalls are asserted immediately after `auto:keep`, before the
`awaiting` assertion, because a stall there is a real failure rather than a detail — a person at that
table is looking at a board waiting for an opponent that will never move. And both `awaiting`
assertions carry the stall list in their message.

**The lesson is about test ordering rather than about concurrency.** An assertion that can only fail
*downstream* of a condition another assertion checks has to come second, or the cheaper diagnosis is
the one nobody gets to read. One occurrence of a four-word mismatch cost more than the fix for it,
and the fix was moving three lines.

If it recurs, it names itself. That is the whole of what this entry claims.

## D231 — Magecraft's "or copy" half, wrong for eight entries, and the audit that found it

The suite asserts every castable face in every deck **has** a script. Nothing asserted that a script
carries everything its card's printed text **promises**, and that is the worst shape of bug this
project can have: a card that silently does less than it reads throws nothing, fails no test, and
costs a player a game they cannot tell they lost to the engine rather than to their own misreading.

So `scripts/measure/card-promises.mjs` reads every card's `oracleText`, derives what it promised,
and reports the cards whose script does not carry it.

### What it found

**Dragonsguard Elite and Sedgemoor Witch** are both printed "Magecraft — Whenever you cast **or
copy** an instant or sorcery spell", and the copy half did nothing. The comment above them said so
and said why:

> nothing in this pool copies an instant or a sorcery, so a `spell-cast` trigger is the whole of
> what these cards do at this table. Said out loud rather than silently approximated, because the
> day something does copy one this is the line that is wrong.

That was true when it was written. **Twincast arrived (D131) and nothing noticed for eight entries.**
A copy of a spell is not cast (CR 707.12) — nobody announces it and no cost is paid — so the cast
event could not see one, and two cards quietly did half of what they read. Reachable by a player,
not only in theory: the lobby takes a pasted list (D125) and `customDeck` resolves any name the pool
knows, so Twincast and either magecraft card can sit in one deck. Across the shipped decks the three
live apart, which is the other half of why nobody noticed.

### The fix: one event with a discriminator, not a second event

`spell-cast` gains `how?: 'cast' | 'copied' | 'any'`, and **the matcher defaults to `cast`**. That
default is the whole design: every watcher older than this clause keeps seeing exactly what it saw,
so storm still counts spells cast, cascade still fires on a cast, prowess still pumps on a cast and a
Chalice of the Void still answers one. Magecraft asks for `any`, which is the printed reading and the
only card shape in the pool that wants it. A second event kind would have meant teaching every
existing watcher to ignore something new, which is the same choice backwards.

The copy is recorded where it is made and raised by `settle`, which makes `GameState.copied` the
eighth member of the detect-rather-than-announce family — `entered`, `died`, `left`, `drew`,
`toGraveyard`, `discarded`, `exiled`. `copySpellOnStack` lives below the module that can `raise`, so
a caller that had to remember to announce it is a caller that eventually does not. What is recorded
is the copy's **types** and whose copy it is rather than an id, because a copy of a spell is not a
card: it is a stack object with a synthetic id that has resolved or been countered long before
anything reads it.

Four tests, and the arithmetic is the assertion: a Bolt cast, a Twincast cast, and the copy the
Twincast makes is **three** magecraft fires, so three Pests and six counters rather than two and
four. The negative control is prowess on the same board — a 1/2 Monastery Swiftspear ends that line
a 3/4 and not a 4/5, because it counted the casts and not the copy.

### What the instrument is worth, which is not what its gap count says

Its first run reported **172 gaps**, its second **25**, its third **0** — and only one of those three
numbers was ever about the pool. 172 was a bug in its own field lookup (a promise with no colon read
`script[undefined]`). 25 was a table of field names written from memory, when embalm, eternalize,
unearth, cycling, crew, undying, persist, extort, storm, cascade and ward are carried by `abilities`
or `triggers` rather than by a field of their own; the table is now **derived from the pool** by
asking which fields the cards printing each keyword actually use. Only then is 0 the pool's answer.

Which is a sharp instance of the lesson I wrote into the measure README earlier the same day — before
trusting a flat reading, ask whether the harness is capable of a non-flat one — so the instrument now
answers that question about itself on **every run**: two cards are planted, one promising flying with
no script to carry it and one promising nothing, and the run prints what each reported. If the
planted gap ever stops being flagged, every clean run after that point means nothing, and that line
is what says so.

**And the real find came through a comment rather than through the heuristic.** The audit put two
cards' ward and magecraft in front of a reader and the reader read the lines next to them. That is
worth knowing about what this kind of instrument is for: not a gate that passes or fails, but a way
of walking a reader past two hundred and forty-five cards' worth of text in the places most likely to
be stale.

## D232 — The bot asks for peace: the one deal it can price, and the only thing it ever says first

The pod's conversation was a monologue. Three preset deals and `answerPact` have been here since
D91, and `answerPact` only ever **answered** — so in a solo pod, one person against three bots and
the way this table is most often played, nothing had ever spoken to the player first. They offered,
the bots agreed, and the politics the `hit you N` and `spared you N` tallies record ran one way.

`answerPact`'s docblock explained why it never offered, and the reasoning was right: what a deal buys
is somebody else's **future** behaviour, nothing in the bot models that, and "a bot that offered
deals it had no way to value would be making noise at the table, which is worse than silence."

### The exception, and why it is one

There is exactly one offer whose value is entirely in the **present**: asking for peace from the
player whose open board can already kill you. That is not a guess about next turn, it is a fact about
the battlefield now — and it is the same fact, read from the other side, that `answerPact` already
uses to decline a deal from somebody who is dead on the board. One board reading, two directions.

It offers a **truce**, which binds both ways (`promises` in `pacts.ts`), and that is the point rather
than an accident: a bot that asked for protection and promised nothing would be begging, and a player
has no reason to take it. Giving up its own right to attack is what makes it a trade, and
`keepsItsWord` means the promise is worth something.

The noise objection is answered rather than ignored, because it was the real risk. Three conditions,
all needed: the seat must be able to kill this one, no live pact may already cover it, and **one
offer outstanding at a time**. A seat that has already said no this turn is not asked again, and the
record answers that rather than a counter — declined pacts are never swept, so the refused offer is
still there with the turn it was made on.

### The measurement, and the thing it cannot measure

**`pod-duel` cannot price this, and not for want of games.** Bot to bot, nearly every one of these
offers is refused *by construction*: `offerPact` asks when an opponent's open power is at least its
life, `answerPact` accepts when its own open power is **less** than the offerer's life. The same
number, compared the same way, from each side — so a bot asked in the position that prompts the ask
says no. Thirteen pods, the same seeds with the rule off and on:

```
26 offers, 25 declined, 1 accepted
winner and length identical in 12 of 13 pods
```

The one that differed is the machinery working end to end rather than an anomaly: the board moved
between the offer and the answer, the truce was taken, and `keepsItsWord` kept it.

So between bots the rule is **near-inert**, which is what makes turning it on safe, and the value is
all on the other side of the table. **It is on by default and the reason is not a win rate**, which
is worth saying plainly rather than dressing a play-experience change as a measured one. Every other
flag in `BotOptions` defaults to whatever a paired run preferred; this one defaults to on because a
computer that asks you for a truce when your board can kill it is a different table to sit at, and
because a flag nothing turns on is a feature no player ever sees.

One consequence a player will meet immediately: **the bots will almost always refuse your offers
too**, for the same mirrored reason. That is correct play rather than a defect — "I can kill you, so
no deal" is what a person at a table says — and it is now pinned by a test so nobody rediscovers it
as a bug.

### What this is not

No UI work: `pactAsked` keys on "an offer whose `to` is me" and does not care who made it, so a
bot's offer renders in the existing prompt with Agree / No deal and is already covered by
`arena.test.ts`. Claimed on that basis rather than on a browser run, which would only re-confirm the
same function.

And the rest of a pod's conversation is still missing, deliberately: asking for help, pointing at a
threat, making a threat, trading a target for a target. **None of those is priceable from the present
board**, which is the line `offerPact` draws and the reason it is one function rather than a
vocabulary. The day there is a model of what another player does next, that list is what to spend it
on.

## D233 — The Postgres flake that was never about Postgres: a test that invented a name the product refuses

Task #111 has sat open since 25 October. CI run 235 failed the `legacy-postgres` job with 25 of 26
passing, the next run of a superset of the same code passed, and the commit under test had touched
only the rules engine, `apps/web` and docs — not `server.js`, not `db.js`, not `test/`. Three
sessions of suspects came and went. The task's own standing instruction was the right one: **wait
for an occurrence and read the named failure, and do not add a retry.**

### It had already occurred, and the log was still there

The thing that closed this was not a new occurrence. It was reading the one we had — properly.

The earlier entry on this flake said the job log was "reachable only through the GitHub tool's
*tail*", that the signed blob URL for the whole file is blocked by this environment's egress proxy
(it is — `curl` gets a 403 from the proxy), and that switching every `node --test` script to the
**spec reporter** would therefore make "a tail enough next time". **The first part was true and the
conclusion was wrong, and that is why this stayed open for five days.**

Two things it got wrong. The reporter change came *after* run 235, so run 235's output is plain TAP,
which prints `not ok 15` and its error block **inline at the point of failure** rather than in a
summary at the end. And GitHub appends the service containers' own logs to the job log after the
step finishes — here ~300 lines of Postgres `initdb` chatter and `RETURNING id` retries. A 150-line
tail of this job is *entirely* container teardown. It would have been, with the spec reporter too.

What works is asking for the whole thing: `get_job_logs` with `return_content: true` and **no**
`tail_lines`. The file is 736 lines, it comes back in one call, and it says:

```
not ok 15 - the reset response is identical for an account that does not exist
  location: 'test/postgres-write-paths.test.js:863:1'
  error: |-
    register p: {"error":"Inappropriate content detected. Please choose a different name."}

    400 !== 200
  stack: newPlayer (test/postgres-write-paths.test.js:269:10)
```

Not a 500, not a schema race, not a connection drop. A 400, from the moderation filter, on the
registration the test helper performs before the test under test begins.

`newPlayer` built its username as ``wp_${tag}_${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 8)}`` — six
random base-36 characters. `server.js` runs every registration past `isProfane()`, which lowercases
the name, strips every non-alphanumeric character, and asks whether a word from its eleven-word list
is a **substring** of what is left. Sooner or later six random characters spell one.

Measured rather than estimated, over 20,000,000 draws of the exact generator against the exact
filter: **8.8 × 10⁻⁶ per registration, which over the suite's 32 registrations is once in 3,552
runs.** The branch has ~380 CI runs and the job has been green in all but this one, which is the
rate behaving itself. Expected count across everything this suite has ever run is well under one,
and we drew it once.

### Why three sessions of suspects missed it

Every ruled-out suspect was a thing visible in the **Postgres container's** log — the `RETURNING id`
retries, the `players_pkey` duplicate, the DDL refused by the double `initDb()`. The job is called
`legacy-postgres`, the container log is long and alarming, and the diff was in the rules engine, so
the search went looking for a database fault. The failing line was in neither the container log nor
the diff. It was in the test's own name generator, and it would flake the same way against SQLite.
**The job's name was the misdirection.** D187 had already written down one correction of this exact
shape (a container log *is* evidence, sometimes); this is the complementary one — the job's subject
is not necessarily the failure's subject.

Worth being blunt about the cost: one whole-log read would have closed this at any point in those
five days, and a tail had been tried and had come back looking like a Postgres problem, which fed
the misdirection rather than correcting it. Two rules out of that. **The next unexplained CI failure
gets its whole log read first, before any hypothesis is formed about it** — and **a log tail that
comes back with no test output in it has told you nothing**, so it must not be read as though the
test output were absent.

### The fix: arithmetic, not a smaller probability

A retry would have hidden it. Re-rolling the name until the filter accepts it would have hidden it
too, and both leave the same bug in place for anyone who copies the helper. So the suffix is a
counter, and its digits come from `j m q v w x z` — **the seven letters that appear in no word on
the filter's list**. A refused name is now impossible rather than rare.

The alphabet is letters and not digits deliberately. `packages/shared`'s filter — the one legacy is
expected to adopt — folds `1` to `i`, `5` to `s`, `4` to `a` and turns the remaining non-letters
into single-character wildcards, so a numeric suffix reads as a word there *more* readily, not less.
Measured, for the record: the shared filter rejects 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ of the old random usernames, 28 times
the legacy rate, and `9.4 × 10⁻⁴` of the random names in `apps/api/src/account-recovery.test.ts`.
That second one has never flaked for a reason worth knowing — `apps/api`'s `routes/auth.ts` does not
call the moderation filter on a username at all, so there is nothing there to trip. Left alone; it
is not a flake, and a change there would be noise.

The two direct registrations in "the password policy is enforced on register and on reset" moved to
the same generator. They were never exposed — `server.js` checks the password policy *before*
`isProfane`, and they send a deliberately weak password, so the policy error always won — but that
is immunity by statement ordering in a file neither test mentions, which is not a thing to rely on.

### The guard, with its own positive control

`SAFE_LETTERS` is only safe relative to a word list that lives somewhere else and can grow. So a
plain `test` in the same file reads `badWords` out of `server.js` rather than copying it,
reimplements the server's check, and runs it over the **whole** generated name — every tag
`newPlayer` is called with in the file, 400 suffixes each — so a word straddling the join between
tag and suffix is caught as well. Add `wanker` to the server's list and this fails loudly on the
next run instead of flaking a registration months later.

Verified by breaking it on purpose, which is the only thing that distinguishes a guard from a
comment. With `SAFE_LETTERS` set to `crapjmq`:

```
✖ no account name this suite can generate is one the server refuses
  AssertionError: wp_g_rcrap would be refused for "crap"
```

Restored, and the suite reads 28 of 28.

### And the assertion message

``register ${tag}: ${JSON.stringify(reg.body)}`` named the refusal but not what was refused. The one
time it fired, the missing word was the username. It carries it now. A message that prints the
server's answer and withholds the question is half a diagnosis, and this suite exists because half a
diagnosis cost months once already.

### The loose end, named rather than quietly dropped

Scanning runs 232–381 for anything unread turned up exactly one other failure: run 324
(`20eb22e`, 29 October), where the **`v2`** job failed at `pnpm test`. That commit is from the #178
hunt and #178 was closed on a hundred clean runs afterwards, so it is most likely that family — but
**I did not read its named failure**, and saying so is better than implying it was checked. Its log
is at
<https://github.com/Nickbuildsdecks/grimore/actions/runs/40803141013/job/123215709926>
until 27 January. Every other `legacy-postgres` job in those 150 runs passed.
