## D234 — Transform: the third way a card has two faces, and the one field all three move

The pool had two of the three double-faced shapes and the engine had the mechanism for all of them
without knowing it. A modal DFC points the instance's `defKey` at its back face as it is **played**;
a morph points `defKey` at the real card when it is **turned up**. Transform (CR 701.28, CR 712) is
the same pointer moved at a third moment: while the permanent sits on the battlefield, by an effect.

So `transformPermanent` is eleven lines, and that is the finding rather than a disappointment.
`defKey` is what every reader downstream looks a face up through — `characteristicsOf`, the script
registry, combat, the bot's evaluation, the definitions the table draws — so a 1/1 Human Wizard that
turns over **is** a 3/2 flying Insect to all of them, and not one of them had to be told that cards
have backs. `printedDefKey` already remembered the front face for Clone, and `relocate` already put
it back on the way off the battlefield, which is CR 712.4a for free: a transformed Delver in a
graveyard is a Delver, which is the card that could be reanimated.

Written **symmetric**, because the rule is: transform turns over whichever face is up. Nothing in
this pool transforms twice and the second half is therefore untested by any card, so it is tested by
itself. A one-way assumption built in here is the kind that is wrong years later and costs nothing
now.

### The ninth member of the detect-rather-than-announce family

`transformed` joins `entered`, `died`, `left`, `drew`, `toGraveyard`, `discarded`, `exiled` and
`copied`, and it is the simplest of them: a list of ids, because the only fact it has to carry is
*which permanent*.

**Which face it became needs no recording, and that is the design rather than a shortcut.** The flip
moves `defKey` before `settle` raises the event, so the script that receives the event is already
the face the permanent now is. "When this creature transforms into Awoken Horror" is therefore a
trigger written **on Awoken Horror** — put it on the front face instead and it fires on transforming
back. The printed wording is the name of the script it is written on.

It is recorded rather than raised at the flip for the family's usual reason: `transformPermanent`
lives below the module that can `raise`. The contrast with morph is worth keeping: `turned-face-up`
*is* raised at its own call site, because turning a morph up is a player action with the seat in
hand, and a transform is almost always an effect resolving, where there is no action to hang it on.

### Two cards, and the one that needed a new hook

**Thing in the Ice // Awoken Horror** needed nothing new. `entersWith` put the four ice counters on
as printed data; one trigger does both halves of "remove an ice counter. **Then** if it has no ice
counters on it, transform it", because the card prints them as one sentence and two triggers would
be two objects an opponent could answer between. Defender is on the front face's script and not on
the back's, so a 0/4 that cannot attack becomes a 7/8 that can with nothing removed from anything.

**Delver of Secrets** needed one, and the reason is about hidden information rather than about
transform.

The card reads "look at the top card of your library. You may reveal that card." A choice needs the
player to see the card, and the obvious shape — a `ChoiceDecisionSpec` whose prompt names it — is a
**leak**: `view.ts` builds `awaiting` once and puts its `prompt` in every seat's view. So Delver asks
a `library-top` *cards* question instead, which is the channel scry already uses and which `view.ts`
sends to the asked seat and to nobody else (`canIdentify`, and the cards-without-a-zone-list block).
The prompt stays generic and the card travels privately.

And the question is put **every** upkeep, over a land as readily as over an instant, with no
`filter`. A question asked only when the answer mattered would tell the opponent the top card is an
instant or a sorcery by the mere fact of being asked — the existence of the question leaks what the
prompt was careful not to.

That left the bot answering it exactly backwards. `library-top` had one standing answer and it was
scry's — *choose a land, so it goes to the bottom* — and here choosing a card **reveals** it, so the
bot would have hidden every instant and revealed the cards Delver does not care about. The fix is
`CardsDecisionSpec.pick`, the card twin of `ChoiceDecisionSpec.best`: the card answers its own
question because only the card knows what its question means, and `preferredCards` reaches the spec
the way `preferredOption` and `preferredAmount` already do.

**Named `pick` and not `best` for a concrete reason**, recorded so nobody tidies it: two members of
the `DecisionSpec` union carrying a field of the same name with different signatures leaves
TypeScript unable to infer the parameters of *either* inside a spec literal. Sharing the name would
have meant annotating every existing `best` in the pool to pay for one new field.

One deliberate small deviation: the revealed card is **not** marked `revealed` on its instance. That
flag is sticky, so a card shown here would still be public three turns later in a hand. What the
table needs to know — that the creature turned over — it gets from the transform itself.

### Insectile Aberration has no script, and the suite had to learn that was allowed

The back face's whole text is "Flying". `printedKeywords` reads a keyword-only line straight off the
oracle text, so the card works with nothing written — and the deck-coverage test flagged it, because
its exemption was "a creature whose text is *empty*".

Generalised to the real rule: a card needs no script when its whole printed text is keywords the
engine already grants. Every comma- and newline-separated piece has to be a keyword
`printedKeywords` returned, so "Flying, whenever this attacks, draw a card" is still a card that
needs one. That is a better rule than a transform-shaped exemption would have been, and `card-promises.mjs`
reads clean on all four faces (351 cards, 249 promising something, 0 gaps, control still firing).

### The deck slot, and a thing about this file rather than about the deck

Both cards went into **Arc Tempest**, which is not a close call: Delver wants a library that is
twenty-five instants and sorceries out of sixty and Thing in the Ice wants four of them cast, which
that deck does by turn five on an ordinary draw. It also ran seven creatures, fewer than anything
else in the pool.

The first attempt cut Burst Lightning and Lava Spike and **broke twenty-six existing tests**, which
is the finding worth keeping: nearly every one-of in that deck is either the pool's only copy of a
mechanic or the card a test reaches for by name. Every candidate cut was referenced somewhere —
Firebolt least at three mentions, Twincast most at forty. So the payment came from two **doubles**
instead, the second Lightning Bolt and the second Counterspell, which leaves every existing test a
copy to find.

### The slot, priced rather than asserted

`deck-probe` with the change reversed — the two transform cards out, the second Bolt and the second
Counterspell back — across all twelve opponents, 34 paired games each, 408 in total:

```
                          SEED0=3300        SEED0=5100
stock (transform pair):   196-212  48.0%    201-207  49.3%
variant (what it replaced): 168-240  41.2%    148-260  36.3%
the change for the old list:  -28 of 408       -53 of 408
```

**Two disjoint seed sets, and the floor measured rather than assumed.** The README's discipline is
to run a *real* arm twice on disjoint seeds and disbelieve anything smaller than the gap. The stock
arm read **196 and 201** across the two — a spread of five on 408 games — and the variant arm read
**168 and 148**, a spread of twenty. So the floor here is somewhere between five and twenty games,
and both effects (−28, −53) clear it.

Per matchup, across all twenty-four readings the old list is **worse in twenty-one, level in two and
better in one** (ashen-rite on the first seed set, +4; it read −6 on the second). That is not a noise
shape.

**What is and is not settled.** The direction is settled: the transform pair beats the second
Lightning Bolt and the second Counterspell in this deck, comfortably. The *size* is not pinned any
tighter than "between about 28 and 53 games of 408", roughly seven to thirteen points, because the
two measurements of the same change differ by more than the floor — which is the honest reading of
two samples rather than an average of them presented as one number.

And it prices **this swap** — two creatures against a Bolt and a Counterspell — not the cards in
the abstract. Reported because the alternative was shipping the slot on "no claim that this is
stronger", which turns out to have been too modest.

### And a hole in the bot that only showed up because the deck moved

Changing Arc Tempest turned `playout.test.ts`'s Squelch control red with `auto:foretell` where it
expected `auto:pass`. Not noise: `spendsAnAnswersMana` opens with a check for `auto:cast` or
`auto:activate`, so **a foretell walks straight past the one rule written to keep answer mana free**
— {2} off two Islands, and the Counterspell in hand is no longer castable. Filed as #218 with the
second half of it, which is that the rule's `canCounterASpell` exemption is right for casting an
answer and wrong for foretelling one. The test strips foretell cards out of that hand meanwhile, so
it keeps testing the reservation rather than the hole, and says so.

---

## D235 — The one play the mana-reservation rule could not see

`spendsAnAnswersMana` is the thirteenth of the drop-this-option family and the one with the most
numbers behind it: three decks, 598 answer windows, and a rule that took Tidal Mind from countering
4% of the spells it held an answer for to countering 48% of them. Its docblock is three paragraphs
of measurement.

It opened with this line:

```js
if (action.type !== 'auto:cast' && action.type !== 'auto:activate') return false;
```

**A foretell costs {2}, out of the same lands.** So a seat holding a Counterspell on two Islands
would hide a card for later and discover it could not answer anything now — spending the exact mana
this rule exists to keep free, through the one play it never looked at.

### How it was found, which is the part worth keeping

Not by this rule's own tests, which are thorough and all passed. By **moving a deck**: two transform
cards went into Arc Tempest for D234, which changed what the bot draws, which turned an unrelated
control assertion in `playout.test.ts` from `auto:pass` into `auto:foretell`.

A bot test that reads a drawn card has two reasons its answer can change — the deck order moved, or
the bot is wrong — and the whole value here was in asking which. "Which deck change broke this" would
have produced a test fix and left the bug. The question that found it was "**is the new answer
wrong**".

### Two halves, and the second is the subtle one

The gate now covers `auto:foretell`. That alone would not have closed the hole, because of the
rule's fourth narrowing condition — *never the answer itself*:

```js
if (def !== undefined && canCounterASpell(def)) return false;
```

That is **right for a cast and wrong for a foretell**. Casting an answer *is* answering, so refusing
it would be the rule eating the thing it exists to protect. Foretelling one is not: the card goes to
exile face down, the {2} is gone, and this turn's answer is gone with it. And the card that made this
concrete is Saw It Coming — a counterspell *with* foretell — so the exemption would have waved
through the exact play that prompted the task.

So the exemption is now conditioned on `action.type === 'auto:cast'`, and a foretell of a
counterspell is as much "spending the answer's mana" as a foretell of anything else.

### What it is worth, measured

Behind `BotOptions.reserveAgainstForetell` so the fix could be priced against the bot as it was —
a correctness fix to a *measured* rule still owes a measurement, and widening what the rule catches
without re-reading its numbers would be helping itself to their authority.

`bot-duel`, six seed sets, both decks that hold foretell cards:

```
negative control, {} vs {}:                              144-144 of 288
arc-tempest, {} vs {"reserveAgainstForetell": false}:    144-144 of 288
tidal-mind,  {} vs {"reserveAgainstForetell": false}:    144-144 of 288
```

**Level — and identical to the negative control, which is a warning rather than a result.** A rule
that fires should move *something*, even to no net effect. `disagree.mjs` exists for exactly this
ambiguity and its docblock says so in its first line: a flat scoreboard means either "it changes the
choices and they are worth nothing" or "it changes nothing", and only a decision count tells them
apart.

It is the first of the two, and the count is worth having exactly:

```
action            decisions   differed
auto:foretell           35        5   14%
...every other kind      -        0    0%
all                  54970        5    0%
```

**So the rule fires, and my stated expectation was wrong in its framing.** I put on record before
running it that "the coincidence is narrow" — the rarity was right, and the implication I was
reaching for, that this might change nothing, was not. It changes **14% of foretell decisions**. What
is rare is the decision itself: 35 foretells in 54,970 decisions is 0.06% of everything this bot is
ever asked, so five corrected plays across a full field cannot move 288 games, and `bot-duel`
reading 144-144 is the arithmetic of that rather than evidence of inertness.

The denominator deserves naming: 5 of 35 is one in seven of a sample of thirty-five, so "about one
foretell in seven" is the honest shape and 14% is a number with two significant figures it has not
earned.

So it ships as **correctness rather than as a win**, the same footing `asksForPeace` took (D232) —
but on a sharper claim than that one could make. Not "this is right and unmeasurable": *this changes
about one foretell in seven, and a foretell is one decision in sixteen hundred, which is too few
plays to move a scoreboard and exactly the plays a person would notice losing a Counterspell to.*

### The flag stays either way

Not because it might be turned off, but because **two of the three tests need it as their control**.
"The bot does not foretell here" is worth exactly as much as the proof that it *would* have —
`blindToShuffle` is in the codebase for the same reason, and the lesson is written in
`scripts/measure/README.md`: give a fairness fix a flag so the cheat can be priced.

### What also came out of writing the tests

The first draft of the exemption test failed, and not because the fix was wrong. `advanceTo` crosses
the draw step, so the seat holds one card the test did not choose — and Arc Tempest has three
foretell cards, so the draw can quietly add a **second** foretell option. Measured on the spot: with
two foretells on offer the bot passes *even with the rule off*, so a board that did not control for
it would have read as the rule firing when it was not.

Which is the same lesson as the one that found the bug, from the other side: a position that depends
on an uncontrolled draw is an instrument with two inputs. The helper now puts every foretellable card
except the named one back into the library, and says why.

---

## D236 — The transform cards turn over less than half the time, and the slot's gain is probably the bodies

D234 priced the Delver + Thing in the Ice slot at seven to thirteen points over the second Lightning
Bolt and second Counterspell, on two disjoint seed sets. **It could not say why**, and the candidate
stories wanted opposite follow-ups. `transform-use.mjs` (#219) asks the mechanic rather than the
slot. 936 games, six seed sets, every pairing in both seats:

```
card                 deck          cast  flipped  of casts  turn  board  first
Delver of Secrets    arc-tempest     85       38      45%   10.3    3.2   t4
Thing in the Ice     arc-tempest     49        2       4%   18.5    1.0   t14
```

Turns count every seat's turn, so 10.3 is a seat's fifth and t4 is a seat's second.

### The small sample would have been published as a wrong number

The first run was one seed set, 156 games, and read **Delver at 12 of 16 — 75%**. The full field
reads **38 of 85 — 45%**. Same instrument, same code, thirty points apart.

That is worth more than the measurement it qualifies. The commit that added the harness said, in so
many words, that 16 and 12 casts were too small to carry a conclusion and the write-up would wait.
Had it not waited, this entry would be claiming Delver flips three times in four, which is not true,
and the number would have gone into the player cheat sheet and been read by somebody deciding
whether to keep the card.

**The rule is not "take bigger samples".** It is that a denominator under about twenty earns a
direction and not a rate, and this file now has an example of exactly how far wrong the rate can be.

### What the cards actually do

**Delver of Secrets flips fewer than half the times it is cast**, on average around its controller's
fifth turn, earliest its second. So it is not the turn-two clock the card is famous for — in this
pool it is a {U} 1/1 that becomes a 3/2 flier about half the time, usually not early. Real, modest,
and nothing like the story the card's reputation tells.

**Thing in the Ice flipped twice in forty-nine casts.** Four percent. Around turn eighteen. And both
times the board held **one** creature, so the printed "return all non-Horror creatures to their
owners' hands" — the whole reason the back face is a 7/8 and not a 4/4 — has never once mattered in
936 games.

### Which means the slot gain is almost certainly not the mechanic

This is the deflating read and it is the one the numbers support. Arc Tempest gained seven to
thirteen points from a swap whose two cards are, in practice, **a 1/1 that sometimes grows wings and
a 0/4 that blocks**. A 0/4 defender for {1}{U} is genuinely good in a deck whose problem is living
long enough to cast its spells, and that is a different card from the one the slot was chosen for.

So D234's measurement stands and D234's *explanation* was never offered — which is the right way
round, because the probe measured a swap and the swap did win. What is now on record is that
crediting the win to transform would have been wrong, and nobody had yet.

**The cards stay.** D229's rule is the reason they are here at all: a keyword needs a card in a deck
to exist in the pool, and transform now has two with a mechanic the tests pin. Pulling Thing in the
Ice because its back face is unreachable would take the pool's only `transformed` trigger with it.

### The better question, filed rather than guessed at

"Replace it" is the lazy move. The interesting question is **how close it gets**: Thing in the Ice
needs four instants or sorceries cast after it lands, out of a library that is twenty-five of sixty,
so a 4% flip rate is either "the deck never gets there" or "it dies first", and those want different
answers. An instrument that read the ice counters remaining when the permanent left the battlefield
or the game ended would say which — one counter short is a card that needs one fewer, and four
counters left is a card that needs replacing. #220.

### And the instrument's own negative control held

`0 flips back to a front face` across 936 games, which is the standing check on D234's claim that
the symmetric half of `transformPermanent` is exercised by no card in this pool. It is still true,
and it is now true on evidence rather than on inspection.

---

## D237 — Thing in the Ice never reaches one counter, so there is nothing to reshape

#220 asked which of two diagnoses explained a 4% flip rate (D236): the deck never gets there, or the
permanent dies first. Those want opposite fixes — one counter short is a reshape, four left is a cut
— and `countdowns.mjs` reads the number that tells them apart. 936 games, six seed sets:

```
card                 clock  started  ran out   left  ended  turns held
Thing in the Ice     ice         21        2    10     9      2.9
    left the battlefield with — 4 counters ×6, 2 ×4
    game ended with          — 4 counters ×8, 3 ×1
```

**Fourteen of twenty-one clocks still had all four counters**, which means the controller cast *not
one* instant or sorcery while the permanent was alive. Four more got halfway. One reached three. It
**never once reached one counter left.**

So the answer is neither of the two the task proposed, and the third is sharper than both: the card
is not answered before it converts and it is not one spell short — **it arrives too late to start.**
Nine of the twenty-one were still sitting on the battlefield when the game finished, eight of those
with four counters, and it holds its clock for 2.9 turns, which in a duel is about one and a half of
its controller's. Half the time it is answered, half the time the game simply ends around it, and in
both cases it has usually seen nothing.

### Which means: change nothing, and that is the finding

A reshape has nothing to work with. "One fewer ice counter" converts the four cases that reached two
and none of the fourteen that reached four. Two fewer converts the same four. The clock is not the
problem and shortening it is not the fix.

And the slot does not want fixing. D236 already established that Arc Tempest's seven-to-thirteen
points come from the **bodies** — a 1/1 that sometimes grows wings and a 0/4 that blocks — and a 0/4
defender for {1}{U} is a good card in a deck whose problem is living long enough to cast its spells.
The measurement that priced the slot and the measurement that explains it now agree, and they agree
on a card doing something other than what its name suggests.

The card also stays for the reason D229 put it there: transform needs a card in the pool to exist at
all, and Thing in the Ice carries the only `transformed` trigger. Pulling it for an unreachable back
face would take the mechanic's only trigger with it, to fix a slot that is winning.

**This entry exists to record a no-change, which is the outcome an investigation is most likely to
talk itself out of.** Three measurements were spent on this slot and the honest conclusion is that
the deck is right and the card is misnamed. Inventing an edit to justify the spend is the failure
mode, and it is a quieter one than being wrong.

### What else the instrument said, incidentally

```
Search for Tomorrow  time        23       23     0     0      3.0
Rift Bolt            time         6        6     0     0      1.5
Calciderm            time        32        0    15    17      4.5
Blastoderm           fade        18        5     2    11      4.7
```

**Suspend resolves, 29 clocks out of 29.** The `?` caveat on `time` applies in principle — expiry
and being answered are the same observation — but in practice nothing in this pool answers a card in
exile, so there is no competing explanation for a suspended card's counters reaching zero. Both
suspend cards convert every time, Rift Bolt in 1.5 turns and Search for Tomorrow in 3.

Calciderm and Blastoderm are where the unmeasurable rows bite: 17 of Calciderm's 32 and 11 of
Blastoderm's 18 were still on the battlefield when the game ended, which is a vanishing creature
doing its job, and the rest cannot be split between "the clock ran out" and "somebody killed it on
its last counter". #221 is the engine change that would separate them.

**Forward note (D238).** Those rows are now split, and two of the three numbers above were wrong:
Calciderm's four expiries were hidden inside its "left with 1 counter" bucket, and Blastoderm's five
were really four. The suspend judgement in this entry — believe the `?` rows because nothing in this
pool answers a card in exile — held exactly, 29 of 29.

**Second forward note (D242).** Both of those numbers were measured on the old seeding, where a
whole pass over the field shared one shuffle (D240). Re-measured with a seed per game, over two
independent bases: Thing in the Ice's clock count is **10 and 11**, not 21, and its expiry rate
**20% and 18%**, not 10%. The entry's headline — that it never once reaches one counter left — was
true of its sample and is not a law: one of the eleven at the second base did. The conclusion
stands on the distribution (one in eleven), not on the word *never*.

---

## D238 — A clock running out is a fact in the log, and two of three inferences about it were wrong

#221 proposed a tenth member of the detect-rather-than-announce family, raised as a `TriggerEvent`
like the nine before it. **Both halves of that were wrong, and the task said to check the first
before building:** *"whether any card would want the event, or only the harness. Decide that first;
it changes the size of the work by a lot."*

### Nothing printed watches a clock expire, so it is not an event

Vanishing and fading have no payoff cards — the expiry *is* the drawback. Suspend's "cast it when
the last time counter is removed" is a rule the engine implements directly in `tickSuspended`, not a
trigger a card carries. Thing in the Ice's flip is written as its own ability counting its own
counters. So a `TriggerEvent` for expiry would be a kind **nothing fires**, which is the thing this
engine already declines to add on purpose: `becomes-tapped` is deliberately card-less and says so.

### And a list `settle` drains into `raise` would have been invisible to the one consumer

This is the same trap `transformed` sprang (D234): `settle` drains these lists and raises them
inside one action, so anything outside the engine reading state between actions never sees them.
`transform-use.mjs` has to watch the board for exactly that reason. An `expired` list drained the
same way would have been unreadable by `countdowns.mjs`, which is the only thing that wanted it.

So: `GameState.expired` is recorded at the four sites that spend a counter to nothing
(`vanishingTrigger`, `fadingTrigger`, `tickSuspended`, Thing in the Ice's trigger) and drained by
`applyAction` into the **persistent log** — `LogEntry.data.expired`, plus a line in the message. The
log is the record, so the fact outlives the action that caused it.

One detail worth the field it costs: `ExpiredClock` carries the object's **name as the clock ran
out**. Thing in the Ice is why — its last ice counter coming off is what transforms it, so a name
read at log time says *"Awoken Horror's last ice counter is gone"*, and the Horror never had ice
counters on it. Same reason `ExiledCard` carries its facts: the moment is gone by the time anything
asks.

### What it was worth: 936 games, six seed sets

```
card                     clock  started  ran out    left  ended  turns held
Calciderm                time        32     4  13%      11     17    4.5
    left with — 4:1 3:8 1:2
    game ended with — 4:5 3:6 2:3 1:3
Search for Tomorrow      time        23    23 100%       0      0    3.0
Thing in the Ice         ice         21     2  10%      10      9    2.9
    left with — 4:6 2:4
    game ended with — 4:8 3:1
Blastoderm               fade        18     4  22%       2     12    5.8
    left with — 3:1 2:1
    game ended with — 3:2 2:2 1:7 0:1
Rift Bolt                time         6     6 100%       0      0    1.5
```

**The measurement validates itself, and this is the part worth keeping.** Three of the five rows are
*identical* to D237's, to the game: Thing in the Ice (21/2/10/9/2.9), Search for Tomorrow (23/23) and
Rift Bolt (6/6). Those are the three where the old zone-comparison could be right — `ice`, whose
expiry leaves the permanent where it was, and the two suspend cards, where D237 argued the `?` could
be believed because nothing in this pool answers a card in exile. **The two rows that moved are
exactly the two that printed `?`.** A change that moved everything would have meant the engine was
now disagreeing with arithmetic; a change that moved nothing would have meant it was not being read.

And D237's judgement call is now evidence rather than an argument: suspend converts **29 of 29**.

### The two inferences that were wrong, in opposite directions

- **Vanishing was wholly wrong: 0 expiries recorded, 4 real.** The last counter comes off and the
  sacrifice happens inside the same trigger, so a poll between actions sees "1 counter" and then
  "gone" — indistinguishable from removal. All four expiries sat inside the "left with 1 counter"
  bucket, which drops from 6 to 2.
- **Fading was nearly right by accident: 5 recorded, 4 real.** Its counters reach zero a full turn
  before the sacrifice, so "no counters, still on the battlefield" looked like an expiry — and it is,
  four times out of five. The fifth was a Blastoderm that spent its clock and then the game ended
  (the new `game ended with — 0:1` row).

An inference that is right on three rows, wrong on one and accidentally nearly right on the fifth is
the worst kind to have shipped: it would have survived any amount of staring at it.

### The harness's own bug, caught by the same tell as the last two

The first full-field run with the engine change read **Blastoderm: 0 ran out, 0%** — impossible, for
a creature that is sacrificed if it survives four upkeeps. The cause was `countdowns.mjs`, not the
engine: it closed a clock the moment the counters were gone, and **fading's expiry is the upkeep
after that**, by which time the tag was deleted and the engine's word went unread. Fixed by keeping
a spent-but-present clock open until either the engine says it expired or the object leaves.

That is the third finding in a row from a **rate that could not be true** rather than a rate that
looked wrong: Calciderm's 0% found the shared-`time`-zone bug (D237), "2 flips back" in a pool where
nothing flips back found the `relocate` bug (D236), and now Blastoderm's 0%. An instrument cannot
check its own reasoning, but it can check its output against a fact about the game, and that keeps
working.

### What the cards say, filed rather than acted on

**The printed price is collected 8 times in 50.** Calciderm 4 of 32, Blastoderm 4 of 18 — so a
Calciderm or a Blastoderm pays its drawback about one time in six, and the other five it is a 5/5 for
four mana with shroud and no downside, because the game ends around it (29 of 50 were still on the
battlefield at the end) or something answers it first (13 of 50).

Blastoderm's clocks last **5.8 table turns**, about 2.9 of its controller's, which is the three turns
the player cheat sheet promises — so that claim is now measured and holds. Calciderm's 4.5 is shorter
for a reason that is not its clock: it is answered early 11 times in 32 against Blastoderm's 2 in 18,
and *what* answers it is `creature-fate.mjs`'s question rather than a guess for this entry.

Whether a 5/5 for four whose drawback fires one time in six is correctly priced is a real question
and a `deck-probe` one. It is **not** answered here and nothing is changed on the strength of it,
for D237's reason: three measurements on an adjacent slot ended in a no-change, and inventing an
edit to justify a measurement is the quieter failure mode than being wrong.

### Tests

Four, one per expiry site, and the second is the point of the whole change: **a Calciderm destroyed
while holding its last time counter records no expiry.** Board identical to the real expiry — no
counters, card in the graveyard — and the log is what tells them apart. Without that control
`expired` would be a field set whenever one of these dies, which is the ambiguity it exists to
remove.

**Forward note (D239).** The `becomes-tapped` precedent cited above does not exist: City of Brass
has carried that trigger since #69, and `mechanic-coverage.mjs` found it an hour after this entry
was written. The conclusion stands and is better supported than the argument given for it — **no
trigger kind in this engine has ever had no card behind it**, so `expired` as a trigger would have
been the first of its kind rather than the second.

**Second forward note (D242): every number in the table above was measured on the old seeding and
two of them were off by half.** The engine change this entry is about is unaffected — `expired` is a
fact in the log and the four tests still pass — but the rates it published are not. With a seed per
game, over two independent bases: Calciderm **26% and 30%** against the 13% above, Thing in the Ice
**20% and 18%** against 10%, Search for Tomorrow **93% and 82%** against a perfect 100%. Blastoderm
at 22% and 21% was the one that happened to be right.

So the entry's two headline sentences both need restating. "The printed price is collected 8 times
in 50" is really about **one in four** (15 of 62, then 13 of 49). And "suspend converts 29 of 29" —
offered above as a judgement call vindicated — converts about **nine times in ten**; the perfect
record was the shared shuffle, not the mechanic.

## D239 — Nineteen mechanics rest on one card, none on none, and one doc claim was false

#223 asked the question the suite cannot: `deck coverage` asserts every card has a script and every
script has a card, and nothing asked how many cards hold a **mechanic** up. #220 found out what that
costs by accident — two singletons cut from `arc-tempest` to pay for two new cards broke **26
tests**, because each was the only card in the pool exercising its mechanic, and nothing said which
one-ofs were load-bearing.

`mechanic-coverage.mjs` counts and sorts ascending. 78 mechanics: 41 `CardScript` fields that are
mechanics rather than plumbing, 19 `TriggerEvent` kinds, 18 keywords.

### The headline is the row that is empty

**Zero of 78 are declared with no card at all.** That is the better of the two findings, and it is
a claim about four years of discipline rather than about this run: D229's rule — a keyword needs a
card in a deck to exist in the pool — has been kept without a single exception, including through
every week where the engine work landed before the cards did.

It is now a test as well as a convention (`has a card behind every mechanic it declares`), because
a negative result nobody re-runs stops being true quietly. The realistic failure is a field added
for an engine change whose cards never arrive: it throws nothing, fails nothing, and leaves a
capability only the docs believe in. **With its own standing control**, to the measure README's
standard: a mechanic nothing could carry goes through the same filter every run and has to come
back, because "no orphans" and "cannot see orphans" otherwise read identically.

### And nineteen rest on exactly one card

```
  1  keyword hexproof            Sigarda, Host of Herons
  1  keyword indestructible      Darksteel Plate
  1  script affinity             Frogmite
  1  script bestow               Boon Satyr
  1  script copiesACreature      Clone
  1  script cumulativeUpkeep     Mystic Remora
  1  script dash                 Mardu Scout
  1  script evoke                Mulldrifter
  1  script fading               Blastoderm
  1  script goadsOpponents       Disrupt Decorum
  1  script madness              Fiery Temper
  1  script makesMana            Dark Ritual
  1  script ninjutsu             Ninja of the Deep Hours
  1  script overload             Mizzium Mortars
  1  script spectacle            Skewer the Critics
  1  script vanishing            Calciderm
  1  script xIsANumberToMatch    Chalice of the Void
  1  trigger attacks-unblocked   Ophidian
  1  trigger to-exile            Soulherder
```

Three more are at one **on purpose** and marked as such: myriad is granted by Blade of Selves rather
than printed (D228), `transformed` has only Awoken Horror by design (D234), and `becomes-tapped` has
City of Brass because every other card that would use it charges you for your own mana (#69).

**Hexproof and indestructible are the two worth a second card.** Both are evergreen with a large
rules surface — hexproof interacts with every targeting decision the bot makes, indestructible with
every destroy, every sweeper and every lethal-damage state-based action — and each is one cut away
from being untested by any game the pool can play. The rest are keyword mechanics whose single card
*is* the pool's whole use of them, which is a different and much cheaper kind of thin.

### The claim the first believable run falsified

The docs said in five places that `becomes-tapped` is the engine's one trigger with no card behind
it, and **D238 said it this morning** — as the precedent for not making `expired` a trigger. The run
printed `1 trigger becomes-tapped — City of Brass`. #69 gave that trigger a card and the claim has
been stale ever since; the entries that state it in the present tense were written after.

**The true version is stronger than the one I used.** No trigger kind in this engine has *ever* had
no card behind it, so `expired` as a trigger would have been the first of its kind rather than the
second. #221's conclusion is unchanged and better supported; what was wrong was the supporting
rhetoric, which is the part nobody checks. A forward note is on D238 and the two live claims — the
progress doc's `Next` list and its #221 section — are corrected in place.

**This is the fourth time in two days a finding came from a reading that could not be true**, and
the first time one of them was about a sentence rather than a number: Calciderm's 0% (D237), two
flips back in a pool where nothing flips back (D236), Blastoderm's 0% (D238), and now a precedent
cited for a decision that did not exist. The instrument that found it was written for a different
question entirely and took four hours.

### Two bugs before the first believable output, both found the same way

The declaration parse ended the `TriggerEvent` union at `/^\n/m`, which matches at offset **zero**
because `^` is also the start of the string — so the kind list came back empty. That one the
instrument's own guard caught, which is why the guard exists: an audit whose list is empty reports
that the engine can do nothing, and must exit non-zero rather than print it.

The second got past the guard. The counts read `TriggerDef.event` where the field is `on`, so every
trigger kind read zero *again*, with the parse working. An optional-chained read of a field that
does not exist throws nothing and logs nothing. What caught it was `0 trigger etb` in a pool with
**41** of them.

### What is not done here

Writing second cards for the nineteen is a separate call and is **not** made on this evidence.
D237's lesson applies directly: the instrument comes first, and "these are fine" is a legitimate
outcome for most of this list, because a keyword mechanic with one card is the pool's whole use of
that keyword rather than a gap. Hexproof and indestructible are the two where the thinness is about
*rules coverage* rather than about pool design, and those are filed.

### Forward note, written an hour later: the hexproof number above is wrong

Starting #224 — the second card for the two thin rows — meant reading the pool, and the pool said
hexproof already has four cards. **Sigarda has it printed; Blossoming Defense, Dive Down and
Bristling Hydra all hand it out while they resolve.** "Hexproof rests on one card" was wrong by a
factor of four, and it is published above and in a commit message.

The cause is a blind spot in the instrument rather than a typo. A keyword is readable three ways —
printed in the text, declared in `script.keywords`, granted by an `equipBonus` — and all three are
*data*. The fourth way is `pump(..., { keywords: ['hexproof'] })` inside an `onResolve`, which is a
**closure**: there is no property to read, so the count simply could not see it.

Fixed by reading what a closure will say about itself, which is its source. That makes it a
**reader's signal and not a count** — a function mentioning `'hexproof'` may be granting it or
checking for it — so effect grants are tallied and printed in their own column, never silently
added, and the thin filter uses the sum because for "could one cut take this out of the pool" an
over-count is the safe direction. Same posture as `card-promises.mjs`, declared false positives and
all.

What survives: **indestructible is genuinely on one card.** Darksteel Plate, and nothing grants it
in an effect either, which makes it the thinnest real mechanic in the pool and the one row of the
nineteen that is about rules coverage rather than pool design. #224 is now about that alone.

And the route to this one is worth noting because it is not the one the last four took. It did not
come from a number that could not be true — it came from **starting the follow-up work the finding
asked for**, and reading the pool properly in order to do it. The instrument was wrong in a
direction that made the pool look worse than it is, which is the direction that gets acted on.

### The settled numbers, after a third pass — and these supersede both of the above

Reading the pool to write the indestructible card found the *second* blind spot, and it is the same
shape as the first. Knight Exemplar grants indestructible from a `statics` entry whose effect is a
**plain object**, so stringifying functions said nothing about it; Fleecemane Lion grants both
hexproof and indestructible while monstrous, the same way. The scan now walks the whole script tree
for a string **equal to** a keyword as well as reading every closure's source.

And the line between the two columns moved to the one that is actually meaningful: **the keywords a
card has, and the ones it gives away.** `equipBonus` used to sit in the first column, which is how
the gap hid — a Darksteel Plate is not indestructible, it makes something else so.

```
78 mechanics declared, 0 with no card at all, 17 thin and unexplained

  keyword indestructible  3   gives it away: Darksteel Plate, Fleecemane Lion, Knight Exemplar
  keyword hexproof        5   has it: Sigarda — gives it away: Blossoming Defense, Bristling
                              Hydra, Dive Down, Fleecemane Lion
```

**So the conclusion is the opposite of the one this entry reached, and #224 is closed unwritten.**
No keyword in the pool is thin — myriad is at one by design (D228) and every other one of the
eighteen has two or more cards putting it on the board. Indestructible has three, by three different
routes: an Equipment's grant, a conditional static a creature puts on itself, and a static one
creature puts on others. That is better coverage than most of the list.

The seventeen thin rows are now **all** `script` fields and `trigger` kinds, and every one of them
is the cheap kind of thin: a keyword mechanic whose single card *is* the pool's whole use of it.
Ninjutsu has one card because the pool has one ninja. There is no gap there to close, and writing
cards to close it would be the failure mode D237 names.

### What the three passes are actually a lesson about

**A static audit of a dynamic engine undercounts, and it took three passes to stop** — properties,
then closure source, then the whole tree. Each pass was found by trying to *act* on the previous
one's output, not by re-reading it: the hexproof miss surfaced when #224's slot needed picking, the
indestructible miss when its card needed choosing. Re-reading the instrument found nothing both
times.

Which is the argument for the shape the file now has. It reports two columns rather than one and
calls the second a **reader's signal**, it over-counts rather than under-counts on purpose, and it
says in its own docblock which bound it is and in which direction. An audit that cannot be exactly
right should be wrong in the direction that makes you look, and both of the published errors here
were wrong in the direction that makes you act.

---

## D240 — One seed is one shuffle wearing 156 deck pairings

Found while building `eval-calibration.mjs` for #225, and it is worth more than the task that
produced it.

The harness reported that **seat 0 won 27% of the field**. Seat 0 is always on the play here, and
being on the play is an advantage, so that is a reading that cannot be true. Mirror matches — same
deck both sides, where the seat is the only asymmetry — came out 25-27 and 28-24, so the engine has
no seat bias. The harness did.

### What it is

Every file in `scripts/measure/` loops `for (let i = 0; i < SEEDS; i++)` and hands `SEED0 + i` to
every game in that pass over the field. One `seed` is one RNG stream. The stream shuffles seat 0's
deck and then seat 1's, and **the same stream produces the same index permutation however different
the deck list is**. Every starter deck is built the same way, so the permutation lands on the same
kind of card in all of them.

Measured directly, opening hands over 156 pairings at a fixed seed:

```
seed 3300: seat 0 opens on 4.00 lands, mean over 156 pairings — variance ZERO
seed 3301: 2.08
seed 3302: 3.00, again zero
seed 3303: 1.15, with 144 of the 156 opening on one land or none
```

Zero variance across 156 different decks is the whole finding in one number. **156 games at one seed
are one shuffle wearing 156 deck pairings.**

The field-level consequence is as large as that implies. Seat 0's share of the whole field, by seed:
**42-114, 63-93, 108-47, 115-41** — 27% to 74%, settling at 53% over the four, which is the play/draw
advantage and is the right answer. With a seed per game instead, two passes gave **79-76 and 82-74**,
seat 0 at 52%.

### Why nothing has broken on it

**Paired designs cancel it.** `deck-probe` and `bot-duel` run stock and variant over the same seeds,
so the shared shuffle is common to both arms and drops out of the difference they report. Every
slot and rule priced in this log was priced that way, and those conclusions stand.

And the thing that should have given it away was in the log already, read as a happy accident:
`bot-duel`'s negative control is **exactly 468-468** and `deck-probe`'s is **151-137 and 151-137**.
Two arms of a stochastic measurement agreeing to the game is not luck and was never luck — it is
the shared shuffle doing its job. The README called it "a control you get for free". It was free
because the games were the same games.

### What is not immune, and the part that is worse than noise

An **absolute rate** is not immune, and this directory is mostly absolute rates: `cast-counts`
conversion percentages, `killed-by`, `mill`, `poison`, `countdowns`, `transform-use`, `monarch`,
`infect-clock`, `creature-fate`. A rate quoted over "936 games, six seed sets" has the error bars of
**six** trials, not 936.

And the shared seed does not merely widen the bars, it **biases** them — which the one reading that
could be taken both ways shows directly. `eval-calibration`'s mid-game sign accuracy:

```
shared seed per pass:   54%  70%  77%  79%  77%  67%   (turn bands 1-4 … 25+)
one seed per game:      53%  62%  69%  73%  72%  79%
```

Correlated games make an outcome more predictable from a position than it really is, so the old
seeding **flattered the thing being measured** by seven to ten points in exactly the bands that
matter. An instrument that shares a random stream is not a noisy version of the right answer.

### The rule this leaves

**A sample that shares a random stream is smaller than its denominator, and the question to ask of
any reading here is whether it is a difference or a level** — only the difference is safe. #226
carries the one-line fix for the rest of the directory, with the pairing and the negative controls
as the check that nothing broke on the way.

This is the fifth finding in two days that came from a reading that could not be true rather than
from scrutinising a conclusion, and the largest of them. The previous four were about one card or
one instrument. This one is about the denominator on most of this log.

---

## D241 — The evaluation is honest but blunt, and the hand term points the wrong way

#225 asked the question the progress doc's `Next` has been asking in prose for months: *"what is
missing is not depth, it is an evaluation worth searching with."* Four terms have been deleted after
measurement (D116), two attempts at pricing an answer in hand failed (D68, D69), and the standing
conclusion was about the **shape** of the function rather than any weight in it — but nobody had
asked the testable version. `evaluate` is a sum of life, hand, library, lands and creature
power-plus-toughness. That is a theory about Magic, and a theory that says who is ahead can be read
against who won.

`eval-calibration.mjs`, 936 games with a seed each (D240), one position per round sampled at the
start of seat 0's turn and recorded from both seats' points of view, so the base rate is exactly 50%.

### It is well calibrated, and that is the first half of the answer

```
win rate by evaluation margin, turns 5-12          sign accuracy by turn band
       < -20      104 samples     7%               turn   total  life  board  lands  hand  library
  -20 .. -10      538            17%               1-4      53%   51%    52%    50%   50%     49%
   -10 .. -3     1544            33%               5-8      61%   58%    60%    51%   46%     50%
     -3 .. 3     2999            50%               9-12     70%   66%    67%    53%   42%     50%
     3 .. 10     1575            66%               13-16    73%   69%    70%    53%   44%     48%
    10 .. 20      550            83%               17-24    75%   70%    70%    52%   49%     52%
       >= 20      106            93%               25+      78%   74%    72%    55%   55%     59%
```

Monotonic, symmetric, crossing 50% exactly at a margin of zero. A +10 margin wins 83% and a -10
loses 83%. **There is no systematic bias in it** — which is the property that actually matters for a
search, because a biased evaluation makes a deeper search prefer worse lines with more confidence.
Depth was never being wasted on a function that lies about which side is ahead.

**And the sum beats every one of its parts, in every band.** 61% against board's 60% at turns 5-8,
70% against 67% at 9-12, 78% against life's 74% at 25+. That is a direct defence of the shape four
deleted terms left behind: life and board each carry most of the signal, and added together they
carry more than either. The thing the log has been suspicious of for a long time turns out to be the
best part of this function.

### What it is not, is sharp early

61% at turns 5-8 — a seat's third or fourth turn — is the number that bounds what depth can buy.
That is the band where a search can still change an outcome; by the 17-24 band the function is at
75% and the game is mostly decided without it. **An evaluation that is honest but blunt early cannot
be fixed by looking further ahead**, because every leaf it reaches is scored by the same blunt
function. That is the sharpest statement of the open problem anyone has had here, and it is not the
one the `Next` list was making: the trouble is discrimination, not bias.

### The one term that measurably points the wrong way

**Cards in hand: 46%, 42%, 44% across turns 5-16.** Worse than a coin, consistently, in exactly the
bands that matter — and `CARD_IN_HAND = 1.5` is the second-largest weight in the function, behind
only a creature's power plus toughness.

Lands (51-55%) and library (48-52%) carry no signal either, but they are merely inert. Hand is
*inverted*: a seat holding more cards than its opponent is losing more often than not, and the
evaluation scores it as ahead.

**What that licenses and what it does not.** It does not say the weight's sign should flip: cards in
hand are a resource, and a bot that scored them negatively would dump its hand to raise its own
score. The causal reading is the other way round — a seat with a big hand is a seat that *could not
cast* what it drew, so hand size is a **symptom** of being behind rather than a cause of it. What
the number does say is that a function scoring a position partly by hand size is scoring part of "I
am behind" as "I am ahead", and that is a testable claim about a weight rather than a theory about
Magic. #227 lowers it and measures.

This also explains D68 and D69 rather than contradicting them. Both tried pricing an answer in hand
**above** a generic card and both made the bot play worse — D69's table shows it casting *more*
counterspells as the price went up. If the hand term is already inverted against outcomes, raising
it moves the evaluation further in the wrong direction, which is exactly what those two measurements
found and could not explain at the time.

### Three bugs in the harness before any of this was readable, all caught the same way

1. **Turn parity.** Sampling once per `turn` lands on alternate seats, and at the start of seat 1's
   turn seat 0 has had one more land drop — every time, whoever is winning. The land row read
   **38% in every band**. Not a fact about Magic.
2. **The same bug wearing different clothes.** Fixed by sampling each seat on its own turn, which
   has the identical problem with the sign reversed: on its own turn a seat has had one more land
   drop than its opponent. The land row came back at **41%**. A parity bug fixed by changing which
   parity is not fixed.
3. **The seed**, which is D240 and the largest thing this task produced.

Each was caught by a number that could not be true, and the fix for the first two is the same
principle: there is exactly one moment in a round where both seats have had the same number of
turns, and a comparison between seats has to be taken there or not at all. The harness now samples
that moment and records both seats' views of it, which makes the base rate 50% by construction and
the ladder symmetric — so a lopsided ladder is a bug rather than a finding.

---

## D242 — The seeding fix applied, and the first re-measurement halves two published rates

#226, the one-line change D240 asked for, across all 29 harnesses that had it. Every one now derives
its seed from the loop indices rather than using `SEED0 + i` for a whole pass over the field.

### Three kinds of harness, and getting the difference wrong would have been silent

The change is not "a seed per game" everywhere, which is what makes it worth doing carefully rather
than with a regular expression.

- **Absolute readings** — twenty-two of them, from `countdowns` to `killed-by` to `cast-counts` —
  want a seed per game. They are the ones the bug actually hurt.
- **`deck-probe` and `pod-slot`** also want a seed per game, and get it safely for a reason worth
  stating: their two arms are two calls to the same `record(ctx)` function, which re-runs the
  identical loop, so a seed derived from the loop indices is the *same* seed in both arms.
- **`bot-duel` and `pod-duel` want the opposite.** Their two (or four) calls are not two games, they
  are the two **arms** — the same decks with the bots swapped, the same table with TESTED and
  CONTROL rotated round the seats. Those must keep sharing a seed, and giving them one each would
  have quietly destroyed the pairing the whole file is built on. So they get a seed per *pairing*
  and per *table* instead.

The negative control is what says it worked, and it is exact: **`bot-duel` with the same bot in both
arms reads 156-156**. Identical arms, identical score, which is only possible if both are still
playing the same games.

And the indices rather than a counter, everywhere. A counter works today and desynchronises the arms
of a paired harness the first time one of them skips a game — an early `break`, a guard, an
unfinished game — which is the kind of failure that produces a plausible number and no error.

### What it changed, on the first harness re-measured

`countdowns.mjs`, 936 games, two independent seed bases, against D238's numbers from the old seeding:

```
card                  D238 (shared)   base 3300   base 9000
Calciderm                 13%            26%         30%
Thing in the Ice          10%            20%         18%
Search for Tomorrow      100%            93%         82%
Blastoderm                22%            22%         21%
Rift Bolt                100%           100%        100%
```

**Two of the five were off by half**, and the two independent bases agree with each other to within
a few points — which is the result that matters, because it says the new numbers are measurements
and the old ones were a sample of one shuffle.

Thing in the Ice's *denominator* moved as much as its rate: 21 clocks under the old seeding, **10
and 11** under the new. A shared shuffle does not merely bias how often a thing happens, it changes
how often the thing is even drawn.

### Two published conclusions restated, and one word retracted

- D238's "the printed price is collected **8 times in 50**" is really about **one in four** — 15 of
  62, then 13 of 49.
- D238's "**suspend converts 29 of 29**", offered as a judgement call vindicated, converts about
  **nine times in ten**. The perfect record was the shared shuffle rather than the mechanic.
- D237's "Thing in the Ice **never once** reaches one counter left" was true of its sample and is
  not a law: one of the eleven at the second base did. The entry's conclusion survives on the
  distribution — one in eleven is still nothing for a reshape to work with — but not on the word.

**None of the paired conclusions in this log moves**, which is the point D240 made and this entry
confirms: every slot and rule here was priced by a difference between two arms over the same seeds,
and the shared shuffle cancelled out of all of them.

### What was not done

The other twenty-eight harnesses are **changed but not re-run**. Re-deriving every absolute rate in
this log is a much larger job than the fix, and the honest position is written into the README
instead: a rate published before this has the error bars of its seed count rather than its game
count, and the three above are the measured example of how far that can be off.

---

## D243 — The inverted term is inert, and a calibration measures positions while a search compares plays

D241 found the one component of `evaluate` that points the wrong way: the cards-in-hand margin
predicts the winner at 46%, 42% and 44% across turns 5-16, worse than a coin in the bands where a
search can still change anything. `CARD_IN_HAND` is 1.5, the second-largest weight in the function.
#227 lowered it and measured. `bot-duel`, 936 paired games per arm, against stock:

```
handCardValue   record vs 1.5 (stock)
   1.0             467-468
   0.6             467-468
   0.3             466-468
```

**Level, across a five-fold cut**, and two of the three records identical to the game.

### It is a wash and not a dead switch, which is the thing that had to be checked

Two identical records across different settings is a reading to be suspicious of, and the README's
standing rule covers exactly this: *run `disagree.mjs` before calling a flat `bot-duel` result a
wash*, because "the setting changes nothing" and "the setting changes things that are worth
nothing" produce the same scoreboard. At 0.3 against stock:

```
auto:cast       3103 decisions    65 differed   2%
auto:activate   1043              39            4%
auto:attack     1558               5            0%
auto:block       640               2            0%
auto:turnUp       17               1            6%
                                 ---
                   112 of 16,761 decisions, 0.67%
```

So the weight reaches the search, changes about one decision in a hundred and fifty, and those
changes are worth nothing at all.

### Why a badly calibrated term can be an irrelevant one

This is the part worth keeping, because it is a correction to the natural reading of D241 and it
changes how the open problem should be attacked.

**A calibration measures positions. A search compares plays.** Those are different questions, and a
term can be badly wrong about the first while being nearly silent on the second — because what
decides a choice is not the term's correlation with outcomes, it is the term's **variation across
the options on offer at one decision**. Hand size barely varies across them: almost every play under
comparison is a cast, every cast moves exactly one card out of the hand, so the term contributes a
near-constant `−handCardValue` to the whole slate and cancels out of the comparison. The options it
*can* separate are the few that differ in cards spent, which is why the differences show up in casts
and activations and essentially nowhere else.

So D241's finding stands as a fact about the function and does not imply what it looks like it
implies. **The right question for "an evaluation worth searching with" is not which terms predict
the winner, it is which terms discriminate between the plays actually offered** — and those can be
measured apart. That reframing is worth more than the weight.

It also finishes the story D68 and D69 started. They raised this price and the bot got slightly
worse; lowering it does nothing. A term that is nearly constant across a slate cannot help, and
pushing it far enough in either direction only starts to distort the few comparisons it does touch.

### So the weight stays at 1.5, and there is a floor under it that is not zero

No change. And removing the term is not the simplification it looks like, because of a second term:
`LIBRARY_CARD` is 0.3, so drawing a card is worth `handCardValue − 0.3`. **At 0.3 a draw is worth
exactly nothing, and below it drawing becomes a cost the bot would avoid.** The 0.3 arm is level,
which says even "a draw scores zero" does not move the needle — but it is the floor, and it is a
floor the `LAND_ON_BOARD` note in the docblock did not mention because nobody had looked down.

Recorded as a no-change with a mechanism, which is the second one of those in this log in two days
(D237 was the first). The measurement that produced it was worth running precisely because the
answer was not the one the previous entry pointed at.

**Forward note (#228).** The `handCardValue` option this entry was measured with has been
generalised into `BotOptions.weights`, a record with a key per term — `life`, `hand`, `library`,
`land`, `permanent`, `creature` — each defaulting to the constant it overrides. So the arms above
read `{"weights":{"hand":1.0}}` now. The reason is the reason this entry gives: hand is not special,
any of these terms could be in the same position, and zeroing each in turn is how you find out which
ones are not. The empty override is the shipping bot by construction and changes **0** of 16,761
decisions, which is the control the new `term-leverage.mjs` runs on every pass.

---

## D244 — The terms that decide are the terms that are right, and the dangerous cell is empty

#228, the question D243 said to ask instead of D241's. A calibration measures positions; a search
compares plays; so the useful question is not which terms predict the winner but which terms
**separate the plays on offer**. `term-leverage.mjs` answers it by ablation — each term removed, every
arm asked the same position the shipping bot played — which makes it exact rather than estimated:
the real search on the real positions, with no sampling argument to make.

156 games, 16,761 decisions, one pass over the field:

```
term          changed  of all     cast  activate   attack   block   turnUp
creature         1070    6.4%    23.7%      5.5%     6.4%   27.7%     5.9%
life              381    2.3%     4.5%      3.9%     4.3%   20.9%     0.0%
hand              150    0.9%     2.7%      5.4%     0.3%    0.5%     5.9%
permanent         140    0.8%     4.2%      0.1%     0.4%    0.5%     0.0%
library            31    0.2%     0.9%      0.3%     0.0%    0.0%     0.0%
land               21    0.1%     0.6%      0.0%     0.1%    0.0%     0.0%
(control)           0    0.0%        —         —        —       —        —
```

### Crossed with D241's calibration, the table sorts itself

```
term        leverage    sign accuracy (turns 9-12)
creature      6.4%          67%   decides most, predicts best
life          2.3%          66%   decides much, predicts well
hand          0.9%          42%   decides little, predicts worst
library       0.2%          50%   decides little, predicts nothing
land          0.1%          53%   decides least, predicts nothing
```

**The cell that would be a problem is empty.** High leverage *and* poor calibration is where a weight
costs games, and nothing is in it: the two terms that decide things are the two that predict well,
the term that predicts badly decides almost nothing, and the terms that predict nothing decide
nothing. The evaluation's weights are, in effect, already sorted.

That closes the retune-a-weight avenue on evidence rather than by exhaustion, which is what four
deleted terms (D116), two failed answer-in-hand attempts (D68, D69) and D243's wash had only managed
between them. **No weight in this function is costing games.** If the bot is to get better, the
change is a term that does not exist yet, not a number that does.

### Two rows that look like dead weight and are not

**`library` at 0.2% is a field average drowning a term that belongs to one deck**, which is a lesson
this directory already learned about `bot-duel` against the slot probe and which applied here before
anybody tripped over it. The term is in the evaluation *for* the mill deck, whose entire plan it is
the only term that can see. Measured where it acts — `SUBJECT=hollow-tide`, counting only that
deck's own decisions — it reads **1.0%, and 3.8% of its casts**: five times its field number. Added
`SUBJECT` to the harness for exactly this, and the general form is worth keeping: **before calling a
term inert, ask whether the instrument could see it being otherwise.**

**`land` at 0.1% is a constraint rather than a discriminator, and zero is success for that kind of
term.** The bot's docblock records that the land drop is taken as a *rule* before the search runs,
because with a card in hand worth more than a land in play a land drop lowered the score and the bot
stopped playing lands — 60 games out of 60. So `LAND_ON_BOARD` does not exist to choose between
plays; it exists to make an inequality hold. The table confirms it from the other side: **`playLand`
is 0.0% for every single term**, so the one decision the land weight is about is not a search
decision at all. A weight whose job is to satisfy an inequality should have no leverage, and this one
does not.

### And the map of what the evaluation touches at all

`playLand`, `pass`, `decide`, `choose`, `discard` and `order` are **0.0% for every term**. The
evaluation reaches casts, activations, attacks, blocks and turn-ups, and nothing else — every other
decision in this engine is made by a rule or a heuristic. That is worth knowing before anybody
proposes a term about one of them.

**Blocks are the most weight-sensitive decision in the game**: 27.7% of them change without
`creature` and 20.9% without `life`, against 23.7% and 4.5% of casts. A block is a question about
whether to take damage and what to trade, so it reads both of the terms that matter, and it is the
one decision type where life is nearly as decisive as the board.

### Where this leaves the open problem

D241 said the evaluation is honest but blunt early (61% sign accuracy at turns 5-8) and that depth
cannot repair bluntness. D243 said the one badly calibrated term is inert. This says no term is both
decisive and wrong. Together they rule out the whole family of fixes that consists of changing a
number, and they point at the same place: **the function needs a term that sees something it
currently cannot** — and the honest next step is to find out what a player reads off a turn-six board
that none of life, creatures, lands, hand or library can express.

## D245 — Derive the list of documented mechanics, and give the guard a control

The player cheat sheet in `claude/play-realm-setup.md` had fallen two keywords behind without
anything saying so, and the audit that found them (`regenerate`, `prowess`) was a hand pass over 80
mechanics — right the day it was run and stale the next time a card was scripted. Same reasoning
that turned #223's finding into a test: a check worth doing once is worth doing on every push.

So `scripts/guards.js` now requires every mechanic a player can **read on a card** to appear in that
sheet's table, and the decision is in how the list is obtained. **Derived, not written here.** The
candidates are the engine's own `KEYWORDS` and the `CardScript` field names, de-camelCased so
`splitSecond` becomes "split second"; the filter is whether the word appears in some card's printed
`oracleText`. Nobody maintains a list and nobody maintains an exception list either: a bot hint like
`removesACreature` names nothing on any card and drops out by itself, and a keyword a player can
read cannot. It parses source rather than `dist`, because guards run before the build in CI.

The filter is the whole design, and the first draft had it wrong in a way that announced itself: it
asked whether the word appeared anywhere in `starterDecks.ts`, and demanded a cheat-sheet row for
`decisions` — a `CardScript` field printed on no card in any game of Magic. It was matching the
file's own comments. "Printed on a card" means the quoted `oracleText` values and nothing else in
the file.

It found a third gap on the first honest run, and the shape of the gap is the argument for deriving
the list from *printed* names rather than from mechanics: a row for the mechanic already existed —
"Cast a spell that costs a creature" — and it never used the words on the card. A player holding
Bone Splinters or Village Rites reads "As an additional cost to cast this spell, sacrifice a
creature" and looks for that phrase. A guard keyed to what the engine calls things would have passed.

**And the guard carries its own control**, by the standard `scripts/measure/README.md` sets for any
instrument whose interesting result is a zero: a pass is a zero and a broken extraction is also a
zero, so both halves of the filter are asserted against `flying` — known to be printed, known to be
documented. If the `oracleText` extraction ever comes back empty, every candidate is filtered out
and the check passes by seeing nothing, which is the one way it could be silently useless. Verified
the other way too, by renaming the phrase in the doc and watching it fail on exactly one mechanic.

## D246 — The first change out of the closed avenue, and the search overruled it

#222, reframed. Its original premise was wrong — D242's per-game seeding re-measured the
vanishing/fading drawback at about one game in four rather than one in six — but the question it was
asking survived the correction and turned out to be the one D244 had pointed at: **is a clock priced
at all?** Read the code and the answer is flatly no. `creatureValue` is power, toughness and keyword
values; `seatValue` counts permanents and creatures; nothing anywhere reads a countdown. A Ball
Lightning scores as a creature you keep.

### Measured first, and the pool has exactly one mistake of this kind

`scripts/measure/leaving-creatures.mjs`, 936 games. It counts the four decisions a clock would change
the sign of, and three of them came back clean:

```
attacks declined by a creature on its last turn      18   <- the mistake
removal spent on an opponent's leaving creature       5   <- none of it waste (see below)
a card spent on your own                             12   <- none of it waste either
blocks declined by one                                0   <- structurally impossible
```

The 18 are **Hellspark Elemental 10 of 78 and Ball Lightning 8 of 56**, 13% and 14% of the attacks
they were offered, and these are the two cards in this pool whose entire function is one attack. A
Ball Lightning that stays home is six mana of card for nothing.

**Blocks cannot appear here at all**, which is worth saying because a zero that is structural is not
a zero that might change: a creature that is gone at the end of this turn is not around for the
opponent's combat, so it is never a legal blocker.

**And the removal column had the opposite sign to the one it first showed.** The first reading said
five cards were spent on an opponent's creature that was leaving anyway, which sounds like pure
waste. Adding the **step** to the table turned it over: every one was cast in `declare-attackers` or
earlier, so the Maze of Ith and the Darkblast pointed at an attacking Ball Lightning stopped six
damage, which is the whole job of both cards. Same for the own-creature column — a Rancor returns to
its owner's hand and a Bonesplitter stays on the battlefield, so neither is lost with the body. The
instrument would have published an accusation without that column.

### The rule is a dominance argument, not a weight

A creature that will not exist after this turn **cannot block in between and cannot attack again**,
so attacking with it risks nothing it was going to keep: the worst case of attacking is no damage,
and the certain case of staying home is no damage. There is nothing to tune, which is the first time
that has been true of a change to `bot.ts`.

Deliberately narrower than "has a clock", and the two near misses are the reason the rule is right:

 - **not a dashed creature**, which returns to its owner's **hand** — one that dies in combat is a
   card lost.
 - **not a vanishing or fading creature on its last counter**, which dies at the next *upkeep*,
   after the opponent's turn, so it is still there to block. Losing it costs a block.

So the three cases are `leavesAtEndOfTurn` (a new flag on `CardScript`, carried by Ball Lightning and
Hellspark Elemental, where the sacrifice is printed text rather than a keyword), `UNEARTHED` and
`MYRIAD`. A test holds the flag to the trigger in both directions.

### And then the search overruled it, which is the finding

The rule went into `worthAttacking`, and the field count moved from **18 to 16**. A reading that
small against a rule whose unit test proves it fires is the kind of impossibility this project has
learned to chase rather than explain. Asking both bots the same positions said why:

```
                       declined
Ball Lightning       heuristic   0 of 34      search   5 of 34
Hellspark Elemental  heuristic   0 of 45      search   5 of 45
Dregscape Zombie     heuristic   0 of 18      search   0 of 18
```

**The heuristic declined none of 97 and the search declined 10.** `evaluate` scores a board with the
creature still standing on it higher and has no way to see that it is going away, so `declareBySearch`
was picking the plan that held it back over the heuristic's own declaration.

The fix that worked is in the **plan set**: `attackPlans` folds a leaver into every plan, the way
`legalDeclaration` already folds in CR 508.1d's forced attackers and the way `keepsItsWord` applies a
pact to every plan rather than scoring it as one option. A dominated declaration is simply never
offered. All four end-of-turn rows then read **0**, and every row that should not have moved did not
— Calciderm, Blastoderm and Mardu Scout are unchanged at 1 apiece.

**Not in the evaluation, and this is the part worth remembering.** Zeroing a leaver in `creatureValue`
would reach the same declaration and break something worse: the position after casting a Ball
Lightning is scored *before* its damage lands, so a creature worth nothing on the board is a cast
worth nothing, and the bot would have stopped casting the card at all.

### What it is worth

```
the whole field          473-463 of 936
ember-rush's pairings    148-140 of 288
kindle-grove's pairings  145-143 of 288
dawn-tithe's pairings    146-142 of 288
```

Small, and **honestly** small: +8 of 288 is inside the noise of a 288-game paired probe on its own.
What is worth something is that four independent readings agree in sign and none of them lost, on a
change that touches about 158 declarations in 936 games. The reason to keep it is the dominance
argument; the win rate is a check that the argument did not cost anything, not the case for it.

## D247 — Soulbond, and the first link between two permanents that is not an attachment

#229. Every join this engine had between two permanents was an **attachment**: `attachedTo`, set on
the Aura or the Equipment, pointing one way, because one host can carry several Auras and each Aura
has exactly one host. A soulbond pair is the opposite shape — symmetric, exclusive, and it breaks by
state-based action rather than by anything moving — so it needed its own fact and its own scope.

### Three decisions, and the first is the one the rest follow from

**The pair lives on the instance** (`CardInstance.pairedWith`), written on **both** halves. Written on
both because either card is the one a player happens to tap, and a reader that had to know which of
the two carried the keyword is a reader that will forget. On the instance rather than in a register on
`GameState`, for the reason `MYRIAD` gives: a fact about an instance is already per-permanent, already
serialised to Redis and already visible on the card, and a list elsewhere is a list that can fall out
of step with the battlefield.

**The bonus is a static with a live scope.** `ContinuousEffect.scope` gained `{ kind: 'pair' }`, which
is the only scope here whose membership *changes* while the effect sits there. Every other static is
created as its permanent enters with the cards it reaches fixed at that moment; a pair is made and
broken turns later. So the effect is created once, with `duration: 'permanent'`, and asks
`source.pairedWith` every time it is read — unpaired, it reaches nobody, which is "as long as this
creature is paired with another creature" holding itself. The alternative was adding and removing an
`ids` effect from the three places a pair can break, and the third one would have been forgotten.

**The pairing is two triggers on the card, not one.** "You may pair this creature with another
unpaired creature you control when either enters the battlefield" is one printed line and two
questions: this creature arriving finds a board that may hold several candidates, so the question is
*which* — a declinable target; somebody else arriving leaves only the newcomer, so the question is
*whether* — a word, which is what `ChoiceDecisionSpec` is for. One trigger would have had to ask the
harder question in both cases, and a prompt offering a choice of one is noise the engine refuses to
generate anywhere else.

### Breaking it is a state-based action, and one case is why

`breakEndedPairs` is a pass over the board in `stateBasedActions` rather than a hook on each way a
pair can end, because the list is longer than it looks: a member can die, be exiled, be bounced, stop
being a creature because an effect set its type — or **change controller**, which moves nothing and
raises nothing. An Act of Treason on half a pair leaves both creatures alive on the battlefield and
ends the pair anyway (CR 702.95b), and a hook-based version would have missed exactly the case the
rules spell out. `relocate` also clears the field on a zone change, which is not a duplicate: it
stops a pointer into a graveyard existing between the move and the next check.

### The cards, and the bot uses them

**Wolfir Silverheart** ({4}{G}{G} 4/4, +4/+4 to each half) and **Trusted Forcemage** ({1}{G}{G} 2/2,
+1/+1), both into Verdant Guard — the only deck in this pool that plays four creatures, which is the
only deck a pair is worth anything in.

Checked rather than assumed, because this is where ninjutsu failed before D219: across 96 games of
Verdant Guard's pairings the two landed **37 times and paired 33 of them**. The four that did not
were boards whose only other creatures were already spoken for. It pairs with whatever is there —
