a Fleecemane Lion seven times, a Llanowar Elves three, a Beast token three.

### What the slots are worth: the probe said +16 and the table says −8

Both cuts followed this list's own rule: the Ambush Viper is still in the pool at Kindle Grove and
Secure the Wastes at Forge Alliance, so both cards, both scripts and the instant-speed X cost all
keep a home. Two tests had to move with them, which is the cost of that rule and is cheaper than the
alternative.

The slot was priced with `deck-probe` first, over Verdant Guard's pairings, 288 games an arm:

```
with soulbond                    191-97
Ambush Viper + Secure the Wastes 175-113      -16
```

**That number is wrong, and the way it is wrong is the entry.** Confirmed on the field table at the
canonical seeds — the same field, once with the two cards and once with them reverted — Verdant
Guard reads **60% (173-115) with soulbond and 63% (181-107) without**. Eight games the other way.
The probe did not merely overstate the gain, as D203's did; it got the **sign** wrong, which is the
first time that has happened here and is the strongest case yet for the rule D203 already wrote
down: *never publish the probe alone.*

**Corrected by D258, and then corrected again.** Neither arm of either reading was paired — D257 is
why — and re-asked with canonical lists the paired probe reads **−18, −1 and +4** on three seed sets
against the table's −2. The sign is not established, so what these two cards are worth to this deck
is **below what 288 games can resolve**: the eight games above, the −16 the probe first read and
every figure in between are readings from inside the floor. The rule the paragraph above leans on is also wrong: a probe and a table never
play the same games, so their disagreement was never evidence about either instrument. What
replaced it is in D258.

So the slot costs Verdant Guard about three points, and the cards ship anyway. The reason is the
mechanic rather than the record: D229's rule is that a keyword needs a card in a deck to exist at
all, Verdant Guard is the only deck in this pool a pair is worth anything in, and a deck sitting
fourth of thirteen at 60% can afford three points. What would not be worth doing is hunting for a
neutral slot here, because the pool's problem is at the **top** of the table and not at the fourth
row.

### The table this leaves, and what the two changes in it are actually worth

Measured on the canonical seeds (`SEEDS=12 SEED0=4400`, 288 games a deck), with each change
isolated by re-running the same field with just that one turned off:

```
 77%  223-65   ember-rush      (D246 is worth +4 of this; nothing else moved by more than 2)
 75%  216-72   dawn-tithe
 64%  185-103  kindle-grove
 60%  173-115  verdant-guard   (63% with D247's two cards reverted)
 50%  144-144  forge-alliance
 50%  144-144  ashen-rite
 45%  130-158  skyward-writ
 45%  131-157  delta-bloom
 44%  128-160  arc-tempest
 41%  117-171  rot-harvest
 38%  109-179  hollow-tide
 30%  85-203   blight-vector
 28%  82-206   tidal-mind
```

**D246 is worth +4 of 288 to Ember Rush and nothing to anybody else**, which is a quarter of what
`bot-duel` read for it (+8 on that deck's own pairings, +10 across the field) and in the same
direction. Three decks hold a creature that cannot be kept and only the one whose Ball Lightning is
a six-power attacker gained measurably.

**And almost none of the movement since D203's published table belongs to this session.** Dawn
Tithe is six points up, Kindle Grove eight, Ashen Rite seven, Tidal Mind nine down, Skyward Writ
five down — and the two isolations above account for four games in total. Whatever moved the rest
predates both changes, which is a thing worth knowing before anybody reads this table as a result.
The spread is **49 points**, wider than D203's 42, and the top two rows are the problem: Ember Rush
at 77% has never been below 74% in any table since D114, and Dawn Tithe is now beside it.

## D248 — The spread is the pilot as much as the decks, and no card in Ember Rush carries it

#231 set out to trim Ember Rush, which has read 74–82% in every field table since D114 and had never
had a card cut. It does not need a card cut, and the measurement that says so also says why four
balance passes aimed at the bottom of the table never moved it.

### Nine changes, 2,448 games, and the biggest moved seven

Ember Rush was screened with `deck-probe` over its own pairings — six single swaps at 144 games an
arm, then three multi-card shape changes at 288:

```
single swaps (stock 103-41)
  Lightning Bolt -> Shock              105-39    +2
  Monastery Swiftspear -> Hill Giant   103-41     0
  Bonesplitter -> Mountain             108-36    +5
  Thermo-Alchemist -> Mountain         108-35    +5
  Ball Lightning -> Hill Giant         106-38    +3
  Hellrider -> Hill Giant              106-38    +3

shape changes (stock 206-82)
  -2 Swiftspear -1 Marauder +2 Hill Giant +1 Mountain   206-82     0
  -2 Bolt -1 Lava Spike -1 Strike +2 Mountain +2 Giant  204-83    -2
  -1 Ball Lightning -1 Hellrider -1 Bolt +2 Giant +1 Mtn 199-89   -7
```

**Not one cut made the deck worse than the noise floor**, and four of the nine read as *improvements*
— which is what a probe does when nothing is happening. `cast-counts` says the same thing from the
other side: the deck casts everything. Lightning Bolt 135 times in 144 games, Monastery Swiftspear
126, Shock 73, Thermo-Alchemist 55 casts and 191 activations, and the weakest cards in the list are
a Lava Axe and a Hill Giant at 55% cast rates. There is no slot to take out, because the deck is
forty-one cards that each cost one or two mana and each do something.

### And then the pilot was measured, which nobody had done

The whole field, canonical seeds, 288 games a deck, run twice: once with the shipping bot and once
with `lookahead: false` on **both** seats — the same decks, a shallower pilot.

```
                deep   shallow   move
kindle-grove     64%      72%     +8
ember-rush       77%      66%    -11   (223 -> 191, thirty-two games)
dawn-tithe       75%      64%    -11
verdant-guard    60%      57%     -3
delta-bloom      45%      53%     +8
arc-tempest      44%      50%     +6
skyward-writ     45%      48%     +3
ashen-rite       50%      45%     -5
forge-alliance   50%      43%     -7
rot-harvest      41%      42%     +1
tidal-mind       28%      39%    +11   (82 -> 113, thirty-one games)
hollow-tide      38%      38%      0
blight-vector    30%      31%     +1
```

**The pilot is worth four to five times any card change I could find.** Thirty-two games to Ember
Rush and thirty-one away from Tidal Mind, where the best cut to Ember Rush's sixty cards was seven.

**But not "one move of lookahead", and the correction is D249.** `lookahead: false` returns the
first candidate *before* the filter loop runs, so it turns off the search **and** the twenty
board-reading "this play buys nothing" rules in one switch. Read with the third arm D249 adds —
search on, filters off — the shipping bot's thirty-two games to Ember Rush are **+37 from the
filters and −5 from the search**, and Tidal Mind's thirty-one are about half each. The paragraph
below is right about the pilot and wrong about which half of it; `wasteFilters` exists now so the
question has an answer.

The spread narrows from **49 points to 41**, and the standard deviation across the thirteen decks
from 14.8 to 11.6 — so **about two fifths of the pool's imbalance, measured as variance, is the
pilot rather than the decks**, where "the pilot" means the search and the filter family together
(D249 splits them: 14.8 shipping, 13.6 with the filters off, 11.6 with both off). The direction is the one the shape of the search predicts: its gain
is "do not throw creatures away, and point removal well", which is most of what an aggro deck and a
removal deck do, and almost none of what a control deck's value is — holding a card for the moment
it is for, which a one-move search cannot see at all.

### What this changes

**Three things, and the first is a caveat on everything already written here.** Every balance entry
in this log is a measurement of *deck × pilot*, and the pilot's share is large. A table saying Tidal
Mind wins 28% is not saying the deck wins 28% in a person's hands, and D194's "this deck needs a way
to win, not more time" survives that, but "Tidal Mind is the worst deck in the pool by eleven points"
does not: with a different pilot it is eleventh by one.

**Second, trimming the top is the wrong lever and is now closed on evidence** rather than on
exhaustion — nine changes, 2,448 games, nothing above the floor. #231 is finished without a change
to any deck list, which is the result and not a failure to find one.

**Third, the lever that is left is the one this project has been circling since D110**: the bot's
evaluation, which D244 showed has no mispriced weight and D246 showed can be improved by giving it a
fact it could not see. Every point of pilot skill that helps a slow deck narrows the table, and the
table is the thing a person picking a deck actually feels.

## D249 — The filter family is the largest pilot effect in the pool, and one of them was broken

D248's switch turned off two things at once, and taking them apart found a twelve-point bug.

### `lookahead: false` was never only about depth

`bestPlay` returns `options[0]` before the filter loop when lookahead is off, so that flag skips the
search **and** the twenty board-reading "this play buys nothing" rules: a ritual with nothing to
spend it on, a Fog with nothing attacking, removal with nothing to remove, a pump that wears off, a
Clone with nothing to copy, a goad with nowhere to send, a crew that costs more than it buys, and
the rest. D248 read the whole difference as the search. `BotOptions.wasteFilters` exists now so the
arms separate — shipping is search and filters, `wasteFilters: false` is search alone,
`lookahead: false` is neither — and it covers the four rules with flags of their own as well, so the
middle arm differs from the last by the search and by nothing else.

Three tables, canonical seeds, 288 games a deck:

```
                 search      search      neither     filters   search
                 + filters   only                    worth     worth
ember-rush          223        186         191         +37       -5
dawn-tithe          216        196         185         +20      +11
kindle-grove        185        220         207         -35      +13
verdant-guard       173        167         163          +6       +4
forge-alliance      144        131         124         +13       +7
ashen-rite          144        155         131         -11      +24
skyward-writ        130        133         137          -3       -4
delta-bloom         131        134         152          -3      -18
arc-tempest         128        144         145         -16       -1
rot-harvest         117        118         122          -1       -4
hollow-tide         109        101         110          +8       -9
blight-vector        85         81          88          +4       -7
tidal-mind           82         99         113         -17      -14
```

**The filters, not the search, are the largest pilot effect in this pool**: +37 games to the best
deck and −35 to the third. Deviation across the thirteen decks goes 14.8 shipping → 13.6 with the
filters off → 11.6 with both off, so each half narrows the table and the search narrows it more.

### And −35 to Kindle Grove was one filter being wrong

`cast-counts` with the family on and off says where it went, by card, and the two readings are not
subtle:

```
kindle-grove   Harnessed Lightning    7 casts on   ->   39 off
ember-rush     Mutavault            104 uses on   -> 1015 off
```

The Mutavault row is a filter earning its keep: `animationCouldMatter` stops nine hundred
pointless animations of a land into a 2/2. The Harnessed Lightning row is a filter being broken.

**The card brings its own number.** Harnessed Lightning asks "pay how much energy?" and its
`beforeDecisions` puts **three energy in the pool before the question**, so the range it offers is
three wide. `chosenNumberIsNothing` asked that question from the board *before* the cast, where the
seat usually has no energy at all: the range came back `{min: 0, max: 0}`, the card's own `best` had
nothing to spend and answered nought, and the rule read that as "the card itself says nought buys
this" and dropped the cast. In 82% of the games the deck drew its own removal spell.

Fixed by **narrowing the rule rather than simulating the card**: a script with a `beforeDecisions`
is not this rule's business, which is the same line the function already draws around a question the
card computes for itself (`typeof spec === 'function'`). Running `beforeDecisions` here would mean
building an `EffectContext` for a spell that has not been cast — no stack object, no source, no
targets. Two cards in the pool have a number question and only Harnessed Lightning has a
`beforeDecisions`, so the fix is exactly as wide as the bug.

The field, measured on the canonical seeds with the fix in:

```
 77%  222-66   ember-rush      (-1)
 75%  216-72   dawn-tithe       (0)
 68%  196-92   kindle-grove   (+11)
 60%  173-115  verdant-guard    (0)
 ... every other deck within three games, nine of them within one
```

**+11 games to the one deck that holds the card and nothing anywhere else**, which is what a
one-deck bug fix should look like. It widens the spread by a point, because the deck it fixes was
already third — worth saying rather than hiding, and not a reason to leave a bot refusing to cast a
deck's removal.

### Arc Tempest's sixteen are not a bug, and that is the methodological half

`arc-tempest −16` was read next (#233), with the same instrument, and it does **not** come apart the
same way. The whole diff, 144 games each arm:

```
Counterspell          31 casts with the filters   ->   21 without
Phoenix of Ash       178 pumps with them          ->  224 without
Saw It Coming         30 casts / 10 foretells     ->   24 / 21
Gelectrode           125 pings                    ->  142
```

Those are one rule's trade rather than a mistake, and the rule is `reserveForAnswers`, which is part
of the family: holding mana up buys **ten more Counterspells** and costs **forty-six firebreathing
pumps**. So the obvious next question was whether the reservation is what the deck is losing, and
the answer is the other way round. The field with it off:

```
hollow-tide   109 -> 96    (the rule is worth +13 to it)
arc-tempest   127 -> 122   (+5)
tidal-mind     79 -> 83    (-4)
... nothing else moves by more than four
```

**The reservation rule is worth +13 of 288 to Hollow Tide and +5 to Arc Tempest**, which nobody had
priced per deck before, and it is not the source of Arc Tempest's loss.

So the finding is a negative one with a lesson in it: **a cast-count diff between two pilots is
confounded by divergence.** The two arms play different games from move one, so a card's count
drifts for reasons that have nothing to do with the rule under test — and `castsAnExpiringPump` only
looks at casts, so the Phoenix row cannot be it. Only a signal far larger than drift is readable,
and the Harnessed Lightning row (7 against 39, with a mechanism confirmed by reading the code) was
that. Arc Tempest's rows are drift-sized, and reading them as causes would have produced a
confident wrong answer of exactly the kind D119 warns about.

`ashen-rite +24` and `delta-bloom −18` in the **search** column are still open, and they need a
different instrument: there is no "search off, filters on" arm, so the two cannot be separated the
way the filters were.

## D250 — Soulbond through a real browser, and a badge the instrument could not see

`LIST=soulbond node scripts/e2e-solo.mjs`, 27 of 27. Soulbond was the last mechanic with a prompt
that shipped without a browser drive — #229 closed saying so, because every other prompt-carrying
mechanic got one (#174, #177, #210) and this one had only unit coverage for the two prompt shapes.

Three claims, because soulbond asks two different questions and then draws a third thing: the
soulbonded creature arriving asks **which** of your unpaired creatures to pair with (a declinable
`optional/friendly` target); any other creature arriving beside an unpaired soulbond creature asks
**whether** to pair, answered with a word (the table drew it as a primary button reading
`Pair them?`); and the board names the partner on the card itself. The list is eight soulbond
creatures and sixteen cheap bodies, because both prompts need *two* creatures and a stock Verdant
Guard draws its two pair cards in a game or two out of five.

**The finding is in the third claim and it is about the instrument, not the engine.** The first run
caught both prompts and zero badges — which reads as a pair the engine made and the screen never
drew. It was the regex. The badge span carries `uppercase`; Chromium applies `text-transform`
*before* handing text to `innerText`; so `cardBadges` writes "paired with Grizzly Bears" and the
board reads `PAIRED WITH GRIZZLY BEARS`. Case-insensitive, three distinct partners appear at once
(`PAIRED WITH TRUSTED FORCEMAGE`, `PAIRED WITH CENTAUR COURSER`, `PAIRED WITH GIANT SPIDER`).

Worth a decision number because the error was invisible from both ends: `arena.test.ts` asserts the
exact lowercase string and passes, the browser draws the badge correctly, and only the scan between
them was wrong. Every other board scan in that suite matches a card name or a body like `3/3` —
neither of which a transform touches — which is why twenty-odd checks' worth of `innerText` reading
has never met this. The rule it leaves behind: **`innerText` is what the element looks like, not
what the code wrote**, so a scan for prose that a stylesheet might transform is case-insensitive or
it is not a scan. The only reason this was caught rather than filed as an engine bug is that the
claim was narrow enough — *this* badge, naming *that* card — to be worth one look at the regex
before believing it.

## D251 — A static that hands another permanent a triggered ability, and two cards that cost six points

The structural gap the myriad docblock named in as many words: *"there is no machinery in this
engine for handing another permanent a triggered ability."* A continuous effect could change what a
creature **is** — bigger, flying, unable to block, a different colour, a different type — and
nothing anywhere could give it something it **does**. That is why Blade of Selves' myriad had to be
a keyword `declareAttackers` reads rather than an ability the Equipment hands out, and it is why
a whole class of printed cards was unscriptable.

**The design, and the one constraint that decided it.** A `TriggerDef` is a bag of functions and
`GameState` is data that gets cloned, serialised and handed to a bot search, so the ability itself
cannot live on an effect. So a grant is declared in two halves: the ability goes in
`CardScript.grantedTriggers`, and `PumpOptions.grants` carries *indices into it*. The effect holds
the indices; the grantor is its `source`; `scriptFor(name).grantedTriggers[i]` is the ability.

Putting it on `PumpOptions` rather than in a declaration of its own is the whole of why this was a
day's work instead of a week's. `modsFrom` is the single translation from "what a card says" to
"what an effect holds", and the five builders that read it — an Aura's bonus, a bestowed one, an
Equipment's, a `statics` entry and soulbond's pair — happen to be the complete list of ways a
printed card grants anything. One field, and every scope the engine has already answers "who gets
it": one card, a team, a creature type, or a soulbond `pair`, whose membership changes under the
effect while it sits there. Duration and removal come free too: the grant goes away with the
permanent that made it, by the same pass that takes away an anthem.

**The ability belongs to the holder, not to the grantor** (CR 113.6). `source` on the stack object
is the creature whose event fired it, so "whenever **this creature** deals damage" reads correctly
when the thing saying it is an Aura on somebody else, and the controller is the creature's
controller. The one thing that travels separately is `StackObject.grantedBy`, which carries the
granting card's **name** rather than its instance — because an ability is independent of its source
once it is on the stack (CR 608.2), so an Aura destroyed in the window before the trigger resolves
still draws the card. A test holds that window open in the combat damage step and kills the Aura in
it.

**Collection is one function now, not two.** `fireTrigger` was pulled out of `raise`'s watcher loop
so the printed and the granted case share everything after "does this match" — the intervening-if
clause asked its first time, the five fields saying what the event was about, the obvious targets
and the prompt when they are not obvious. A granted path that duplicated that would have been two
copies drifting apart, which is the bug `modsFrom`'s own docblock is about. `abilityTargetSpecs` is
the same move on the other side: three places looked a trigger's target specs up out of the
holder's script, and all three now ask one function that knows about grants.

Layer 6 comes out of the same loop shape the keyword clearing uses, so the timestamps are right
(CR 613.1f): a Turn to Frog cast *after* an Ophidian Eye takes the draw trigger away, and an Eye
cast after the Frog gives it back. Both halves are asserted on one board, because a version that
cleared everything would pass the first and fail the second.

**Two cards, two routes in.** Tandem Lookout ({2}{U} 1/1, soulbond) hands the ability to a pair;
Ophidian Eye ({1}{U} Aura, flash) hands the same ability to one creature. Two rather than one for
D239's reason, but the second one is doing more than making a count: the two reach `grants` by
different builders — `applyStatics` and `addAuraEffect` — which is the only evidence that the
`PumpOptions` decision carried to every builder rather than to the one written first.

**And the slot is a negative result, measured rather than hoped** — and it survived D257's audit,
which is worth saying because the sibling claim in D255 did not. Re-priced with `deck-probe`'s
paired arms the two cards cost **14 games of 288** (116-170 with them, 130-158 without) against the
−18 read here: same sign, same size, same conclusion. **Confirmed on three seed sets in D258** —
−14, −19 and −29 — which makes this the one slot claim of the four re-asked there that clears the
instrument's floor in direction and in rough size. The number here is a range rather than a figure.

Skyward Writ over 288 games at
the canonical seeds: **139-149 stock, 121-167 with the two cards in** for a Raise the Alarm and the
second Man-o'-War. That is eighteen games, about six points, and it drops the deck from 48% to 42%.

Two things worth having asked. A second arm cut a Pacifism and a Rest in Peace instead and read
**124-164** — three games of 288, which is noise — so *which* slots the cards take is not the cost,
the cards are. That arm was also illegal, which only the suite knew: Skyward Writ is the only deck
holding either card, and the deck-coverage test will not let a scripted card leave the pool
altogether. `mechanic-coverage` did not catch it because it reads scripts; the test reads decks.
Worth remembering as a rule — **a cut is not free just because the mechanic it serves has another
card.**

And `cast-counts` says the bot *casts* both of them, 70% and 101% of the games it draws them. So
this is a card being bad rather than a card being dead, and the 101% is the suspected reason: the
bot spends the Aura at the first opportunity, on whatever creature is there, and an Aura on a
creature an opponent can kill is a two-for-one. That is the same family as the blink pricing #209
fixed from the other side, it is a bot rule rather than a card problem, and it has a task of its
own rather than a guess folded in here.

The cards ship anyway, for the mechanic rather than for the record: a keyword needs a card in a
deck to exist (D229), this is the pool's only home for a blue three-drop that wants a flier, and
the machinery is the deliverable. But unlike D247, where a probe had the sign wrong and the table
said −8, this number is not noise and is not being rounded away: six points, in the open, with the
suspected cause named and the next instrument identified.

**Still open, deliberately.** A permanent that loses all abilities keeps firing its *printed*
triggers — the collection loop checks only for a face-down permanent (CR 707.2). Granted abilities
now honour layer 6 properly, which makes the two inconsistent; the printed half is a pre-existing
gap and is a task rather than a half-fix folded in here. And the bot's three readers of
`script.triggers` (`hasOwnText`, `paysForLeaving`, `arrivesAgain`) still see printed text only, so
a Grizzly Bears carrying an Ophidian Eye reads to the sacrifice-fodder filter as a body.

## D252 — The bot was enchanting the opponent's creature, which is a gift rather than a waste

D251 left Skyward Writ eighteen games of 288 worse and named the Aura as the suspect, with the
bot's eagerness as the guess. The guess was wrong in the right direction, and the instrument that
settled it is new.

**`granted-abilities.mjs`** asks the question whose answer separates "the effect is weak" from "the
bot misplays it": per grant that reaches the battlefield, how many times did the granted ability
trigger, and how often was everything holding it gone before it fired once. It counts triggers by
reading `StackObject.grantedBy`, which is the engine's own record of a granted ability, so it cannot
drift from what the rules did; and it reads the host off the state every move rather than off the
cast, because an Aura's host is only known once the spell resolves and a pair is made by a trigger
later still. A run where nothing was granted exits non-zero, for the reason `leaving-creatures` does.

Its first output, 48 games:

```
Ophidian Eye
    10 grants reached the battlefield
     0 times the granted ability triggered
  handed to: Warrior, Hidden Dragonslayer, Youthful Knight, Gurmag Angler,
             Impassioned Orator, Llanowar Elves, Kiora's Follower, Hellrider
```

**Six of those eight creatures belong to the opponent.** A granted ability belongs to the creature
holding it (CR 113.6), so an Ophidian Eye on their Gurmag Angler draws cards *for them*. That is not
a wasted card, it is a card given away — strictly worse than not casting it, and the whole of the
deck's lost games is a plausible size for it.

**The cause was a hint that was never applied.** `TargetSpec.friendly` has existed since the
prevention shields: not a restriction, just advice to the bot, whose default is "the enemy and the
enemy's creatures" — right for the removal and the burn that are most of what targets anything in
this pool and exactly backwards for a bonus. Seven specs carried it. `chooseTargets`' own docblock
named the gap in as many words — *"a pump spell gets aimed at an enemy creature — legal, and
wasteful. Fixing that in general needs the bot to read the script's intent, which is a different
piece of work"* — and `TargetSpec.friendly` repeated it: *"the pump spells do not carry this yet …
fixing it there is a change to five cards' measured behaviour rather than a flag."*

Both were right about the cost and wrong about the stakes: the word for an Ophidian Eye on their
creature is not *wasteful*. So the hint is applied now, on eleven specs: a shared
`TARGET_CREATURE_HELPED` for Giant Growth, Titanic Growth, Shield's Might, Crimson Wisps,
Distortion Strike, Tainted Strike, Wax and Selesnya Charm's pump mode; `friendly: true` on the Aura
targets of Angelic Gift, Robe of Mirrors and Ophidian Eye; and on `BESTOW_TARGET`, which is a fact
about the keyword rather than about Boon Satyr — bestow is only ever printed as a bonus.

A derived test holds it: every Aura whose effect only helps must be aimed friendly, read off the
scripts rather than from a list, with Pacifism as the control in the other direction so the check is
about *bonuses* rather than about Auras.

**And the win rate does not move.** The field at the canonical seeds, before and after, 288 games a
deck: verdant-guard +3, skyward-writ +2, dawn-tithe +1, five decks −1, four unchanged. Biggest move
three games, which is inside the noise floor of this instrument.

That is worth stating plainly rather than dressing up: **this is a correctness fix worth nothing
measurable.** The reason is arithmetic rather than mysterious — the eleven cards are one-ofs and
two-ofs cast a handful of times per 288 games, and even a play that is strictly a gift cannot move a
rate it only gets to make three times a game set. It does *not* recover D251's eighteen games, and
anyone reading that entry should not expect it to.

What it does buy is a bot that no longer makes a play a person would call a misclick, which matters
for the thing this engine is for — somebody sitting opposite it — and a hint that is now applied
everywhere it belongs rather than in the seven places somebody remembered.

**Still open.** With the aim corrected, the Eye now lands on its own side and *still* fires zero
times in 48 games: the hosts are a Wall of Air, an Omenspeaker, a Healer's Hawk. `friendly` says
which side, not which creature, and a combat-damage trigger on a 0/4 defender is worth nothing. The
next rule is "aim a combat-damage bonus at a creature that can attack", which is a board reading
rather than a flag, and `granted-abilities` is now the instrument that would price it.

## D253 — Which creature, not which side: a rule that works and is worth nothing

D252 taught the bot which *side* to put a bonus on. The Ophidian Eye immediately started landing on
a Wall of Air, which is the next question and a different one: `creatureValue` is power plus
toughness plus keywords, so a 0/4 flying Wall scores 5.5 and a 1/1 flying lifelink Healer's Hawk
scores 4. The Wall is the better creature by that measure, for every purpose except a trigger that
reads "whenever this creature deals damage to a player".

So `TargetSpec.helpsInCombat` is the third hint of its family, after `friendly` and `blinks`: this
bonus is only paid off by the creature dealing combat damage, so rank the creatures that can
**never** attack below the ones that can. A fact rather than a weight, which is the shape D246
settled on — `defender` and a blanket `cantAttack` are permanent, where tapped and summoning-sick
wear off and a bonus that lasts outlives them. Four specs carry it: Ophidian Eye's Aura, Distortion
Strike, Tainted Strike and Crimson Wisps. A Giant Growth deliberately does not — pumping a blocker
to win a fight is half of what that card is for, and a Wall is often the right answer.

**It does exactly what it says.** `granted-abilities` over 144 games, the rule on and off via
`BotOptions.helpsAnAttacker`:

```
 on: Healer's Hawk x6, Hanna x5, Hidden Dragonslayer x4, Paladin en-Vec x4, Omenspeaker x3, Wall x2
off: Wall of Air x5, Healer's Hawk x4, Wall x3, Serra Angel x3, Paladin en-Vec x3, Basilica Guards x3
```

**And it is worth nothing.** The same runs: the granted ability fired **6 times with the rule on and
6 times with it off**, 0.12 against 0.13 per grant. The field table at the canonical seeds moves by
one game in each direction and leaves ten of thirteen decks untouched.

The reason is in the same output rather than mysterious: **28 of 49 grants lost every creature
holding them before firing once.** Skyward Writ's creatures die; which of them is wearing the Aura
when they die does not matter. A rule about choosing between two creatures cannot help a deck whose
problem is that both of them are dead.

**Kept anyway, on D216's terms rather than on a win rate.** That entry shipped a bot rule that was
near-inert bot-to-bot — 26 truce offers, 25 refusals, the winner identical in 12 of 13 pods — and
said so: *"it is on by default because the value is the table a person sits at rather than a win
rate, which is a claim made on its own terms."* This is the same claim. A person playing against
this engine will see the Aura go onto a wall and draw the obvious conclusion about their opponent,
and no measurement here can price that. The rule is declarative, has no number in it, and comes with
the flag that proves it is inert; a unit test asserts both arms on a two-creature board, so the
claim stays honest if somebody later wonders whether it does anything.

What it must not be read as: a recovery of D251's eighteen games. Two rules in a row (D252, D253)
have now measured flat on that deck, and the instrument says why — the cards are weak in that list
and the bot was never the whole of it.

## D254 — Layer 6 reaches further than the keywords: a Frogged Blood Artist was still draining

Found while building D251, left out of it on purpose, and it is a rules bug rather than a bot one.

"Loses all abilities" is layer 6 (CR 613.1f), and `characteristicsOf` has honoured it since #88 —
for **keywords**, and for the statics the layer system reads. Nothing honoured it for the two kinds
of ability the layers never see:

- the **triggers** `raise` collects, which come off the card's script. The watcher loop asked only
  whether the permanent was face down (CR 707.2), so a Frogged Blood Artist went on draining every
  time something died.
- the **activations** `legalActions` offers, in all three places it offers them —`manaSources`,
  `potentialMana` and the play list. So a Frogged Llanowar Elves went on tapping for green.

Both are a 1/1 with no text doing something its text box no longer says, and the second one is worse
than it looks: `manaSources` is the single answer to "what can this seat pay", so the engine was
*offering* plays it should not have been able to afford.

`allAbilitiesLost(state, instance)` is the one question, asked in those four places. No timestamp
reading, unlike `grantedTriggersOn`, and that is a fact rather than a shortcut: a card's own text is
there from the moment it is on the battlefield, so every "loses all abilities" is later than it and
takes it. Only a *granted* ability can arrive after the Frog, which is why that function walks the
list and this one does not — and the two together are now the whole of layer 6 for abilities.

In the collection loop it clears the **script** rather than skipping the watcher, which is the
ordering: a Frogged creature still gets the abilities something else is granting it afterwards.

Held by a test with both directions on one board: the Elves is offered as a mana source before the
Frog and not after; a death raises the Artist's trigger before and raises nothing after. Read off
the **stack** rather than off a life total, because the Artist's trigger targets a player and the
engine stops to ask which — so the life total is the same either way and the question is whether the
trigger happens at all. The first version of that test asserted the life total and failed on the
control, which is the control doing its job.

**And it is worth nothing on the field**: the table at the canonical seeds is identical, all
thirteen decks, to the game before the fix. Turn to Frog is one card in one deck and the bot points
it at whatever is biggest, which is rarely something whose ability was doing the work.

That is three flat results in a row (D252, D253, D254) and the pattern is worth naming rather than
repeating: **a change that corrects what one card does to one permanent cannot move a thirteen-deck
field, and measuring it is still the right thing to do** — because the alternative is a changelog
full of improvements nobody priced, and because the two that turned out to matter this session
(D249's filter bug at twelve points, D251's slot at six) were found by the same instruments.

## D255 — Redirection, the last named gap in the replacement-effect family

The progress doc has carried this line since #85: *"what is left is redirection ('the next time ~
would deal damage, it deals it to ~ instead'), which nothing in the pool needs and which is not
approximated."* It is in now, and it turned out to be the shield plus one field rather than a
subsystem.

**The design.** `ContinuousEffect.preventsDamageAmount` is already a quantity spent by the damage it
absorbs; `redirectTo` says where the absorbed points go. `spendShields` reports what each
redirecting shield took and `dealDamage` deals it — by **calling itself**, which is what makes the
redirected damage a real damage event rather than a number written onto a life total: protection on
the destination stops it, infect on the source poisons with it, a lifelink source gains the life, and
a shield on the destination takes its share. `MAX_REDIRECTS` bounds the chain at four, because two
redirects pointed at each other's protectees is a legal board and a real loop; past the limit the
points are prevented, which is the safe direction to be wrong in.

**And one scope, which is the part that is not obvious.** Both printed cards say "you and/or
permanents you control", which is a *single* quantity over a player and everything they have — and
no existing scope could say it. `seat` is the player alone, `controller-creatures` is the creatures
alone, and two effects would have prevented twice as much. So `{ kind: 'seat-side', seat }` is the
pool's second scope `characteristicsOf` can never match, read live so a creature that arrives after
the shield is under it too. A test asserts the one-quantity reading directly: four points of attack
take two from a Harm's Way in total, not two apiece.

**Two cards.** Harm's Way ({W}, two points, into Forge Alliance for the second Secluded Steppe) and
Divine Deflection ({X}{W}, into Skyward Writ for the second Paladin en-Vec). The second is the
pool's eighth {X} spell and the first whose X is spent *twice* — once on what it stops and once on
what it deals. Tests hold the three claims that are new: the points land on the chosen target, the
card pays out **what it absorbed** rather than what it printed (X of four against four damage deals
four; X of one deals one; X of nothing does nothing at all), and the side scope is one shield.

**The slot cost ten games, and the slot is not why.** — **corrected: Harm's Way is worth +12, and
everything in the next two paragraphs was shuffle noise read as signal. D257 has the control and
the paired measurement.** The original text is kept because the mistake is the useful part of it.

Forge Alliance over 288 games at the canonical seeds: 148-140 stock, **138-150** with Harm's Way in
for the second Loxodon Warhammer, **137-151** with it in for a Secluded Steppe instead. One game
apart. That is D251's finding reproduced on a different deck and a different card: **where a new
card goes is not the cost, the card is.** It ships on the same terms (D229: a keyword needs a card
in a deck to exist), the land version is the one in the repository because it reads as the more
defensible list and measures the same, and Skyward Writ's half is noise either way (−2).

Worth naming as a method rather than a coincidence: two cut-set comparisons, on two decks, have now
both come back within three games of each other. **Trying a second slot is cheap and has twice told
us the same thing, so the next time a new card measures negative the question to ask is about the
card** — what the bot does with it, as D252 did — rather than about which slot it took.

**Both paragraphs are wrong, and instructively.** All three numbers are *unpaired* comparisons — a
stock table against a variant table — and D257 then measured two honest tables of the same deck
differing by up to thirty games for reasons that have nothing to do with its list. Two unpaired
readings agreeing to within three games is not evidence that the slot does not matter; it is two
draws from a wide distribution landing near each other.

Re-priced with `deck-probe`, whose arms share their seeds and (since D257) their pre-shuffle order,
so the shuffle cancels: **Harm's Way is +12 of 288 to Forge Alliance** — 147-141 with it, 135-153
without. The card is good for the deck. The method that survives is the opposite of the one this
entry proposed: **pair the arms**.

**And the paragraph above is withdrawn too, by D258.** Three paired seed sets read this card at
**+12, +5 and −13**, so its sign is not established and "one run answers the question" was the same
mistake one layer up. The honest entry is that Harm's Way's effect on Forge Alliance is **below what
288 games can resolve** — the unpaired −10, the paired +12 and the sign reversal between them were
all readings from inside the floor. The card stays on D229's terms, which is how it shipped.

What the sequence is worth keeping for: this slot has now been priced four times, by three
different methods, and each new method reversed the previous answer while the true value stayed
smaller than any of the instruments could see.

**Known limit, written down rather than discovered.** The table shows a redirect as prevention: a
`shielded: 2` on the seat and on each of its permanents, with nothing saying where the points will
go. That is true as far as it goes and it is what the opponent is entitled to know; what it does not
show is the destination, which the caster chose and can see on their own card. A view field for it
would be plumbing for one line of text on two cards, and the honest place for the complaint is here.

## D256 — The instrument could not see a shield, so every prevention spell read as waste

Found by running `wasted-plays` on the deck that had just been given a redirection card, and reading
the row rather than filing it:

```
    3 of    3 100%  Harm's Way  [forge-alliance]
```

A card that bought nothing every single time it was cast. It is not a card problem and it is not a
bot problem: the fingerprint `wasted-plays` compares either side of a play is counts of **cards,
bodies and life** — life and poison, permanents per seat, power, toughness, keywords, counters,
untapped permanents, and the four zone sizes. A prevention shield changes none of them. So a shield
cast with a Lightning Bolt in the air and a shield cast into an empty board produce the identical
fingerprint, and the instrument reported both as waste.

The fingerprint now sums the prevention on the table — `preventsDamageAmount` as a quantity, plus
one for each blanket `preventsCombatDamage` — which makes a shield cast a change like any other.
Before and after on two decks, 48 games each:

```
forge-alliance   Harm's Way  3 of 3  ->  1 of 3
skyward-writ     Holy Day    3 of 7  ->  gone
                 Divine Deflection 3 of 4  ->  gone
                 total  9 of 543 (2%)  ->  3 of 543 (1%)
```

Six false positives removed and one real suspect left standing, which is the right outcome: a Harm's
Way that genuinely absorbed nothing is a play that bought nothing, and that is what the row is
supposed to mean.

**Why it went unnoticed for eleven increments is the part worth keeping.** `wasted-plays` has been
read a dozen times since #162 and prevention was never near the top of its list, because until the
redirection cards nothing in the pool had a shield as its *whole* effect: Healing Salve's other mode
gains life, a Samite Healer's tap is an activation among many, and Holy Day sat at 3 of 7 in a list
whose top row was 79%. A new card put a 100% row in front of the question and the blind spot became
visible — which is the argument for adding cards to a pool with instruments pointed at it, and for
reading an instrument's whole output rather than its top line.

The header of the instrument now tells that story beside its other blind spots, because the next
person to meet a 100% row deserves to know which of them have been fixed.

## D257 — Two tables of the same thirteen decks disagree by thirty games, and one published sign was wrong

This is the most consequential entry in a while and it is about the measurement rather than the
engine. Three things were measured, in this order, each because the one before it did not add up.

**1. The order a deck's list is written in changes the games it plays.** `deck:load` builds the
library in entry order and then shuffles it, and a shuffle is a permutation of *indices*: the same
seed applied to two arrays holding the same sixty cards in a different order gives two different
libraries. `deck-order.mjs` is the experiment — Forge Alliance against Ember Rush, forty seeds, the
same sixty cards with the first entry rotated to the end — and it reads **9 of 40 games reached a
different winner**.

That is harmless at a real table and not harmless here. Every instrument that prices a slot runs the
same field twice and reads the difference, and the two arms were getting their lists by different
routes: `deck-table`'s and `deck-probe`'s `CHANGE` **append** a card the deck did not already hold
at the end of the list, while the same change typed into `starterDecks.ts` sits beside the cards it
is like. Two arms meant to differ by one card differed by one card *and* a reshuffle of the other
fifty-nine.

`canonicalDecks` fixes it in the harnesses rather than in the engine: every deck is sorted by card
name before it is handed over, so both arms share a pre-shuffle order and a shared seed means a
shared library. In the harness because a deck's pre-shuffle order is arbitrary either way — the
engine is not wrong — and because sorting inside `deck:load` re-shuffles every seed in the project
at once, which broke twelve tests pinned to boards they were written against. `deck-order.mjs`
reports both arms and is the regression check: `9 of 40` as written, `0 of 40` canonical.

**2. And then the control that matters more.** Two canonical tables of the same thirteen decks,
differing only in which seeds they used (288 games a deck each):

```
                 4400     7000    diff
blight-vector   117-171   87-201   -30
ember-rush      216-72   192-96    -24
verdant-guard   195-93   176-112   -19
forge-alliance  131-157  149-139   +18
rot-harvest     115-173  133-155   +18
hollow-tide     105-183  119-169   +14
delta-bloom     121-167  112-176    -9
...five more within eight
```

**Up to thirty games, ten points, between two honest measurements of the same deck.** That is the
error bar on a 288-game table, and it is wider than almost every per-deck effect this project has
published. The order finding above is a special case of it: a reshuffle is a reshuffle however it
is caused.

**3. So the two slot claims from today were re-priced with arms that are actually paired**, and one
of them had the sign wrong. `deck-probe` runs stock and variant over the same seeds, which with
canonical ordering now means the same libraries, so the shuffle cancels instead of being sampled
twice:

- **#230's two granting cards** cost Skyward Writ **14 games of 288** (116-170 with them, 130-158
  without). The unpaired reading was −18; same sign, same size, and D251's conclusion stands.
- **#239's Harm's Way is worth +12 games of 288 to Forge Alliance** (147-141 with it, 135-153
  without). The unpaired reading was **−10**. That is a sign reversal, and D255 is corrected in
  place.

**What follows, and it is a rule rather than an observation.** An unpaired comparison at 288 games —
today's table against a table from a previous commit, or a stock table against a variant table —
cannot resolve a one-card change, because its noise floor is wider than the change. A **paired**
comparison can: the same instrument, the same seeds, the same canonical lists, differing only by the
change. `deck-probe` was always built that way and this is the first time its arms have genuinely
been paired.

**Half of that is wrong, and D258 has the measurement.** Pairing is necessary and it is not
sufficient: the same paired probe run on two seed sets reads +30 and +18 on one change and −18 and
−1 on another, so a paired 288-game comparison has an error bar of its own of about **fifteen
games**. Both re-prices below rest on a single paired reading and neither was entitled to the
confidence it was given — see D258 for what each is worth on two.

Which re-opens something. D203 and D247 both found the probe disagreeing with the table and both
wrote down the rule "believe the table"; D203's probe said +47 where the table said +4, and D247's
said +16 where the table said −8. The probe's arms were not paired then and the table comparisons
were not paired either, so **neither of those disagreements is evidence about which instrument to
trust** — they are two noisy readings disagreeing. The rule those entries wrote down should not be
leaned on until it is re-asked with the paired probe, and the entries are marked accordingly.
**Re-asked in D258**, which replaces it: pair the arms, then either instrument answers, and never
set a probe reading against a table reading at all.

**The new baseline**, canonical lists, SEEDS=12 SEED0=4400, 288 games a deck, with ±10 points of
error bar on every row and the two-sample spread above as the evidence for it:

```
75% ember-rush   73% dawn-tithe   68% verdant-guard  67% kindle-grove
50% ashen-rite   45% forge-alliance  44% arc-tempest  42% delta-bloom
41% blight-vector  40% rot-harvest  39% skyward-writ  36% hollow-tide
30% tidal-mind
```

Published with the error bar attached rather than as thirteen numbers, because the honest reading of
this table is "four decks clearly ahead, one clearly behind, and eight that this instrument cannot
order".

## D258 — Pairing the arms is necessary and not sufficient, and the probe-against-table comparison was never a comparison at all

#240. D257 re-opened two entries and this closes them, then re-opens D257 itself. Both of the
re-asked entries had found `deck-probe` disagreeing with `deck-table` about a slot, both wrote down
the rule *believe the table*, and D257 pointed out that neither instrument's arms had been paired at
the time. Re-asked here with canonical lists on both sides — and the answer is that the rule was
never testable, and that the rule D257 put in its place is half right.

**First, the citation, because it has been wrong in five places.** The rule belongs to **D203**
(embalm and eternalize, six cards into Dawn Tithe). D194 is evoke, whose probe read +10 and −14 on
two seed sets and whose slot shipped as level — it never found a probe overstating anything. D247,
D257, `scripts/measure/README.md` and `deck-table.mjs`'s own docblock all attributed the rule to
D194, and D247 attributed D203's published table to it as well. Corrected in all of them. A rule
cited to the wrong entry is a rule nobody can check, and this one went unchecked for four entries.

### The two re-asks

`deck-probe` runs stock and variant over one seed set; the table was run three times — stock, then
once per change — at the canonical `SEEDS=12 SEED0=4400`, 288 games a deck.

```
dawn-tithe     209-79 with the six cards   189-99 reverted     +20
verdant-guard  195-93 with soulbond        193-95 reverted      -2
```

| | old probe | old table | paired probe | paired table |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| D203, six cards into Dawn Tithe | +47 / +19 | +11 | **+30** | **+20** |
| D247, two cards into Verdant Guard | +16 | −8 | **−18** | **−2** |

Paired, the two instruments agree on the **sign** in both cases. D247's recorded sign disagreement
was the unpaired probe being wrong, not a difference between instruments.

### Why that comparison could never have settled anything

Each table run prints the subject's own row and each probe prints its stock arm, so every run above
also measured the same deck twice with **no change at all**:

```
dawn-tithe      209-79 table   206-82 probe     3 games apart
verdant-guard   195-93 table   178-109 probe   17 games apart
```

Because the two harnesses derive their seeds differently, and a seed is a shuffle:

```
deck-probe:  SEED0 + ((pass * FIELD.length + j) * 2) + order
deck-table:  SEED0 + (((pass * ALL.length + a) * ALL.length + b) * 2) + order
```

A probe reading and a table reading are therefore **two different samples**, carrying the whole of
D257's thirty-game error bar before either arm has changed a card. Today's gaps between the paired
readings — ten games on D203, sixteen on D247 — are the size of the gaps on the unchanged decks.
Nothing is left over for an instrument-class effect to explain.

**And the mechanism the old rule rested on does not apply to the row it was read off.** D203's
argument was that "a paired probe swaps cards inside one deck and amplifies whatever the seeds gave
it, while the table re-measures every pairing and lets the field move too". The second half is true
and is the table's whole value. The first half is not true of the number both entries compared:
`deck-table` plays each pairing once per seed per order and credits both decks, so the subject's row
is twelve opponents × twelve seeds × two orders = **288 games over the same pairings the probe
plays**. For the subject's own win count the two instruments measure the *same quantity*. Letting
the field move changes the other twelve rows, not the one being read.

Two entries explained a difference by a mechanism that cannot produce it, and the simpler
explanation — two samples from a distribution ten points wide — has been available since D240 gave
every game its own seed.

### The finding that matters more: at 288 games this instrument cannot resolve a small change at all

D257's replacement rule was that a paired comparison *can* resolve a one-card change. It cannot, and
the way it cannot is worth the whole entry. Four changes through the same paired probe, three
disjoint seed sets each, 288 games an arm — every number the value of the **change**, so a revert's
delta is sign-flipped here:

```
                                        4400    7000    4688   spread
D203  six cards into Dawn Tithe          +30     +18     +21      12
D251  granting cards into Skyward Writ   -14     -19     -29      15
D247  two cards into Verdant Guard       -18      -1      +4      22
D255  Harm's Way into Forge Alliance     +12      +5     -13      25
```

**The first version of this entry had the first two columns and said "the sign agreed in all eight
readings", and the third set flipped two of them.** That was published, in `4c3ac93`, and it was
wrong — caught by the instrument this entry added, on its first real use, which is the one piece of
luck in the story. Four changes agreeing on two sets each is exactly what a floor wider than the
effects looks like from underneath.

What survives is narrower and more useful. **The two changes that held are the large ones**, around
±20 games, and the two that flipped each had a reading near zero. So the floor on this harness at
288 games a set is roughly **±20 games in direction, not merely in size**: a change smaller than
that is not measured here however many times it is run, and the failure mode is two sets agreeing by
luck. Pairing gives both arms the same libraries, which removes the reshuffle D257 found; it cannot
remove the game, because a changed card diverges the play from the turn it is drawn by an amount
that is itself a function of the seed.

**So one of D257's two re-prices stands and the other is withdrawn.**

- `#230`'s granting cards cost Skyward Writ **14 to 29 of 288**, negative on all three sets. D251's
  −18 stands in direction and in rough size.
- `#239`'s **Harm's Way is not measured**: +12, +5, −13. D257 read the first of those as a sign
  reversal against an unpaired −10 and D255 was corrected in place to +12. Neither figure was
  earned. The honest entry is that this card's effect on Forge Alliance is below what 288 games can
  see, and D255 now says that.

And D247's two soulbond cards are in the same position: −18, −1, +4. The eight games that entry
published, the −18 the probe first read and the −2 the paired table read are all inside a floor
wider than any of them.

### What the two slots are worth, and the practice that replaces the rule

- **D203's six cards are worth about +20 of 288 to Dawn Tithe**: +30, +18, +21 on three sets, plus
  +20 on the paired table. Four readings, one sign, and the only change here that clears the floor
  in both directions. That entry published +11 and called the probe a threefold overstatement; the
  probe was the closer of the two instruments and the slot is worth roughly twice what was recorded.
- **D247's two soulbond cards are not measured**: −18, −1, +4 on the probe and −2 on the table. The
  entry published −8 and the first version of this one published "between 2 and 18". Both are
  readings from inside a floor wider than either. The cards ship on D229's terms, which never
  depended on a number, and that reasoning is untouched.

So *believe the table* becomes three rules, none of which is about which instrument to trust:

1. **Pair the arms.** One instrument, one seed set, canonical lists, the two arms differing only by
   the change. Necessary, and this entry is why it is nowhere near sufficient.
2. **Read three seed sets and require them to agree on the sign.** `deck-probe` does this itself
   now: `SETS` defaults to 3, every set's delta prints with the spread and the mean, and the verdict
   says either "every set agrees, the change is worth the mean, in this range" or "the sets disagree,
   so this change is NOT measured at this sample count". Two sets agreeing is called out as the
   **weak** case, because that is the shape of the mistake made here. The blocks are sized off the
   loop's own bound (`SEEDS * opponents * 2`) so they cannot overlap — a hand-picked offset that did
   would make a later set a partial re-run and the spread would read smaller than it is.
3. **Never set a probe reading against a table reading.** They are different samples and will differ
   by up to thirty games with nothing wrong at all. That comparison has produced two published
   conclusions and both were wrong. Run the table for the question only it answers: what the change
   did to **everybody else** — in table A every other deck gained a game or three off Dawn Tithe's
   weaker list without changing a card, and in table B the field barely moved.

And a fourth that is about this project rather than the harness: **a slot change worth less than
about twenty games of 288 cannot be priced by anything here.** Four of the entries in this log rest
on numbers smaller than that. The answer is not a bigger run every time — it is to stop asking for a
number where the honest output is a direction, and to decide those slots the way D229 and D216
already do, on the mechanic and on what a person sees at the table.

Deliberately not done: the two harnesses are not given a shared seed formula. It would make the
comparison in rule 3 meaningful, and rule 3 is that nobody should be making it.

The negative control for the multi-set path is the old one per set: an empty `CHANGE` builds a
variant identical to stock, so every set must read exactly zero, and the summary says that in those
words rather than falling through to "the sets disagree". Checked at `SETS=3 SEEDS=1`: `+0, +0, +0`,
spread 0, on three sets that each played different games (12-12, 13-11, 15-9 stock).


## D259 — Treasure and Clue, and the mana source that is spent rather than tapped

The pool had no Treasure, no Clue and no Food — the artifact tokens a modern casual game is largely
made of — and the reason was not that nobody had got round to them. `manaSources` held this line:

```ts
if (ability.cost.sacrificeSelf) continue;
```

A mana ability that sacrifices its own permanent was refused, so a Treasure was a token the engine
could **create and never spend**: the auto-tapper would not count its mana, `canAfford` would say
no, and the spell the Treasure was made for would sit in hand beside it with nothing anywhere to say
why. Nothing would have thrown. That is the shape of bug this project keeps finding — a card that is
quietly worse than its text — and it is why the pool's token list was all bodies.

### The fix is a flag carried three hops, and the ordering was already right

`ManaSource.sacrifices` says the source is **consumed** by using it; `solveTap` carries it onto the
pick beside `life`; `tapSources` sacrifices the permanent instead of leaving it tapped. Tapped *and*
sacrificed, in that order, because `{T}` is part of the printed cost — a tapped Treasure cannot pay
it, and anything watching a tap sees one.

**What needed no code is the part worth recording.** A Treasure makes one of five colours, and the
solver's colour branch already reaches for the *least* flexible source that can pay a pip — so a
Swamp is spent before a Treasure that could also have made black, with no preference written
anywhere. For a generic pip a `choose` source sizes at one mana and ties with a basic land, and that
tie is broken by list order, so `manaSources` queues the consumed sources behind the free ones and
the existing machinery does the rest. The one judgement is that they go **ahead** of the painful
ones: a Treasure exists to be spent and a life total cannot be rebuilt, and the painful sources
already drop out of the list once the life is nearly gone, so the low-life case was never at risk.

One guard is speculative and says so in its comment: a permanent offering both a free tap for mana
and a free sacrifice for mana keeps the tap. No card in the pool has that shape — Mind Stone's
sacrifice row costs mana and is filtered out earlier — so the branch is untested and is there
because the next rock printed that way would otherwise be eaten for one mana on turn three.

### Two tokens, and the Clue is the control

**Clue** (`{2}, Sacrifice this artifact: Draw a card`) needed **no engine change at all**: it is Mind
Stone's second row with a different payoff, and `sacrificeSelf` has been a payable activation cost
since that card was written. It is in here precisely for that — if the Clue cashes in and the
Treasure does not, the fault is in the mana path and nowhere else.

**Thraben Inspector** ({W} 1/2, "when this enters, investigate") into Skyward Writ, for the second
Secluded Steppe: a one-drop blocker that becomes a card, which is two of that deck's jobs in a slot,
and a second body for its own Tandem Lookout to pair with. "Investigate" is written as the token
rather than as a keyword, on the same test myriad passes and this fails: a keyword earns its place
when the rules have to *consult* it, and nothing ever asks whether an effect was an investigation.

**Pirate's Prize** ({3}{U}, draw two and make a Treasure) into Tidal Mind, for the second Lonely
Sandbar. The slot argument is not ramp — that deck's late turns have always had mana and nothing to
spend it on — it is the turn the card is cast: four mana for two cards leaves one mana behind, so the
Prize and a Cancel fit under five lands where the Prize alone would end the turn.

### Measured: the position comes up, and the bot takes it

`spent-permanents.mjs` is new and asks the question a unit test cannot, because a unit test puts the
Treasure on the board and the spell in hand on purpose: **per game, how many were created, how many
were spent by their own controller, and how many were still sitting there at the end.** Telling a
spend from a removal is the only part that needed thought — a token that leaves the battlefield is
deleted outright, and this pool holds a Disenchant — so a disappearance is attributed to the action
it happened during: spending happens inside the controller's own cast, where a Disenchant is
somebody else's.

Tidal Mind, 96 games:

```
Treasure
    16 created
    13 spent by their own controller  (81%)
     0 taken away by somebody else
     3 still on the battlefield when the game ended
```

Four in five are spent, and the three left over are games that ended before the mana was wanted.
Against the `continue` this entry deletes that number is zero by construction — the engine could not
see the mana — which makes this the first slot in a while whose value is a behaviour rather than a
win rate, and the right way round: the card does what it says, and `deck-probe` could not have
resolved its handful of games anyway (D258).

And Skyward Writ's Clues, 96 games, which is the contrast worth having:

```
Clue
    35 created
    35 spent by their own controller  (100%)
     0 taken away by somebody else
     0 still on the battlefield when the game ended
```

**Every Clue is cashed and four Treasures in five are**, which is the right way round for what the
two cards are. A Clue is two mana for a card at a moment of your choosing, and in a deck that holds
mana up and passes there is almost always a turn with two spare; a Treasure is mana for a turn that
may never come, so the three left standing are games that ended before the deck needed them. Neither
number is a judgement about the slot — it is the mechanic working, which is what these runs are
for.

`cast-counts` says Pirate's Prize is cast in 35% of the games it reaches hand, the lowest row in
that deck and about right for a four-mana sorcery in a deck of answers.

### A second carrier, because one is how a path stops being exercised

**Lotus Petal** ({0} artifact, `{T}, Sacrifice: Add one mana of any color`) into Forge Alliance, for
the second Loxodon Warhammer. It is the Treasure as a printed card, and it is here because a path
with one carrier is a path that goes unexercised the day that card is cut — which this pool's own
coverage instrument has been saying about seventeen other rows for a while.

The slot argument is the artifact count. That deck reads its artifacts three times over — the
Frogmite's affinity, the Etched Champion's metalcraft, and the Ravager's "sacrifice an artifact"
cost — so the only swap worth making was one that kept the count level, and the second Warhammer is
the duplicate D255 had already named as the list's most expendable. One artifact out, one artifact
in, all three counts unchanged, and the Petal is a free artifact on turn one for a deck that wants
exactly that. Not priced, and said plainly: a one-card change is below what any instrument here can
resolve (D258), so it ships on the mechanic and on the count.

It is also **the pool's first spell that costs nothing at all**, which is a path of its own: a test
casts it off a board with no lands and then spends it on a Lightning Bolt, so "a free spell is
offered" and "a free spell is castable" are both held.

### And the instrument grew to the family, which is what caught the omission

`spent-permanents` first derived its set from the token defs' oracle text, which caught exactly the
two tokens it was written for — and would have missed Lotus Petal silently, because a printed card
is not a token. It now asks the **scripts** instead: every script with a `sacrificeSelf` cost
anywhere in its abilities. Same rule every instrument here follows, and the same failure it keeps
preventing.

That widened the question from "are Treasures spent" to "does the bot ever press a button that eats
the permanent", and the answer is yes, across the whole family:

```
forge-alliance  Lotus Petal   21 created   16 spent (76%)   5 left standing
skyward-writ    Clue          35 created   35 spent (100%)  0 left standing
tidal-mind      Treasure      16 created   13 spent (81%)   3 left standing
ashen-rite      Mind Stone    11 created   11 spent (100%)  0 left standing
```

Mind Stone's row had never been measured and is the one worth noting: that card has been in the pool
since #49 and "a rock early, a card late" was a claim about what it is *for*. Eleven of eleven says
the late half happens every game it is drawn. The two at 100% are the ones whose cost is mana the
deck has spare; the two in the seventies are the ones whose cost is a colour the deck may not need
before the game ends.

Two carriers also needed widening in the other direction: the "gone" test was `instances[id] ===
undefined`, which is true of a token and never of a card, so a Petal would have read as still on the
battlefield for the rest of every game. It now reads the zone.

### Food is deliberately absent

The third member of the family needs a card, D229's rule is that a mechanic without one does not
exist, and I cannot verify a Food card's printed text from this container — Scryfall is unreachable.
Inventing the text of a real card is worse than leaving the mechanic out, so it is out, and the
engine work above is what Food will need when the data is there: nothing.


## D260 — Seven readers of one field, and a guard for the class rather than the instance

D251 gave a card two ways to carry a triggered ability: printed on itself, or handed to it by
something else. Everything written before that reads only the first, and the failure mode is the
worst kind — **it goes quiet rather than wrong**. Nothing errors. A number comes back smaller than
the truth and looks like a finding.

This session had already found two of them separately — the bot's three readers in #236, and
`card-promises` calling Ophidian Eye an unscripted card because its whole text is an ability it
gives away — so the question worth asking was not "where is the next one" but **how many are
there**. Grepping for files that read `script.triggers` and never mention `grantedTriggers` found
four more; writing the grep into a guard found **two more again**, because they reach the field by a
different spelling (`triggers ?? []`) that the hand-grep missed. Seven readers, one field.

### The four that were real, and the measurement that says they were inert

- **`mechanic-coverage`** is the one that matters. Its entire job is "which mechanics are held up by
  too few cards", and it counted trigger kinds off printed triggers only — so a kind that no printed
  card carries would have read as **absent from the pool** by the instrument built to notice exactly
  that. Fixed by noting granted kinds into the grants column rather than the carriers column, which
  is the correct model and the one the keyword rows already use: an Ophidian Eye does not *have* a
  combat-damage trigger, it gives one away.
- **`draw-triggers`** watches `draws` triggers by name; a granted one was invisible.
- **`graveyard-costs`** tested for a `to-graveyard` trigger the same way.
- **`artifact-cost`**'s audit column printed `triggers 0` for an artifact that grants one.

**All four were inert, and that is measured rather than assumed**: the only granted trigger kind in
this pool is `combat-damage`, which five printed cards already carry, so `mechanic-coverage` reads
the same 17 thin rows before and after. The fix is correctness with no number attached — which is
the honest description, and the reason to make it anyway is that the instrument's job is to report
an absence, and it was the one thing it could not see.

### The two that were out of scope, with reasons rather than silence

- **`leaving-creatures`** asks whether a card's *printed* text gives it a clock, by name and with no
  board. A granted trigger is a fact about an **instance** — which permanent holds it right now —
  so reading it off a name would answer a different question. If a card is ever printed that hands
  another permanent a self-sacrifice clock, the fix is `grantedTriggersOn(state, instance)` and a
  board, not that predicate.
- **`storm`** reads `on.self === true`: a trigger about the card being cast. Storm is printed on a
  spell, nothing hands it out, and a permanent cannot be given a trigger that fires for another
  card's cast.

Both are exemptions in the guard with those sentences attached, the way `card-promises`'s `KNOWN`
and `mechanic-coverage`'s `EXPECTED_THIN` carry theirs. An exemption is a claim about the file.

### Why a guard and not a control

`card-promises` has a planted-card control, and the obvious move was to give every instrument one.
**It would not have caught any of the seven.** A planted positive is written by the same author at
the same moment as the predicate, so it encodes the same blind spot: a control written before D251
would have planted a card with a printed trigger, passed, and proved nothing about granted ones. No
self-test catches an unknown unknown.

What a grep *can* do is notice the **pairing** — the shape all seven shared — and fail on the PR
that adds the eighth. So `guards.js` now refuses a file that reads a card's triggers without
mentioning that the second list exists.

**And its own limit, found by trying to break it.** The first attempt deleted the granted read out of
`mechanic-coverage` and the guard still passed, because the docblock above the read still named the
field. A file passes by *mentioning* `grantedTriggers` anywhere, comment included. So this is a
tripwire for "did the author know the second list exists" — which is exactly the mistake all seven
made — and not a proof that the reading is correct. The proof of the reading is the instrument's own
output and its control. Written down rather than quietly tightened, because a guard that is believed
to check more than it does is the same failure one level up.

Verified both ways: a temporary file reading `triggers` with no mention of grants fails the guard,
and the guard passes again when it is removed.

### The rule this leaves

**When a card gains a new way to carry something, every reader of the old way is a blind spot until
it is checked, and none of them will tell you.** Three instruments in this session reported numbers
that were wrong in this exact shape — `wasted-plays` could not see a shield (D256), `card-promises`
could not see a granted trigger, `spent-permanents` could not see a printed card (D259) — and all
three were found by a human reading a whole output, never by a failing test. The guard turns one
instance of that class into a CI failure. The class itself is still caught by reading output, which
is the discipline the measurement README now carries as a rule rather than an anecdote.


## D261 — The exception thirty-five harnesses swallow, and the clean sheet it turns out to be

Every game-playing instrument in `scripts/measure` ends its move loop the same way:

```js
try { s = applyAction(s, action); } catch { break; }
```

**Thirty-five files, and not one reports that it caught anything.** If the engine throws during a
bot's own legal action the game stops, the harness counts it as a game it played, and the number it
prints is computed from a truncated game with no signal anywhere. `deck-probe` says
`(1 unfinished)` and that is the whole of what this project knew about it — and "unfinished" is four
different things wearing one word: the 4000-move cap, `botAction` returning null, `stateVersion` not
advancing, and a throw.

The last one is not a curiosity. `playout.test.ts` asserts the engine never refuses what it offered,
so a throw there would violate an invariant the suite already claims to hold — and it would mean
every number this directory has published, including today's, is short by the games it ate. That is
the widest version of the quiet-failure class this session kept finding (#236, D256, D259, D260),
and the only one that touches all of them at once.

### The answer: no throws, and the four causes separated

`unfinished.mjs` keeps every fault's message and action type, prints them deduplicated with the
decks and the first seed, turn and step, and **exits non-zero on any throw**. Four runs on the
current engine:

```
field, 1 seed            156 games    156 won    no throws, no stalls, no move caps
field, 8 seeds          1248 games   1248 won    ditto
field, 8 seeds, ctx     1248 games   1248 won    ditto  (the other arm, below)
deck-probe's own 288     288 games    288 won    ditto  (SCHEME=probe, verdant-guard)
```

So the `catch` in thirty-five harnesses is swallowing nothing on this build, and their numbers are
not truncated by faults they never reported. That is a claim about all of them, which is why the
instrument plays the whole field rather than one deck, and it is worth having written down whichever
way it came out.

### Two things the hunt found that the clean sheet does not say

**The instrument was not reproducing the harness it audits, and its own first real use caught it.**
Replaying `deck-probe`'s 288 games came back 288 clean where the probe itself had reported one
unfinished. The difference is one argument: every file here hands its `ActionContext` to
`deck:load`, `game:start` and `auto:start` and then **drops it** in the loop, and this file was
passing it. An audit that does not reproduce its subject cannot certify it, so the default now
matches the harnesses exactly and `CTX_IN_LOOP=1` is the comparison arm — which answers a question
nobody here had asked: **dropping the context mid-game changes nothing**, 1248 games to 1248 games,
identical outcomes on both arms.

**And the probe's unfinished game cannot be replayed at all, for a reason worth more than the
game.** That reading predates D259: Lotus Petal, Pirate's Prize and Thraben Inspector changed three
decks in the field and the consumed-mana-source rule changed what is affordable, so today's engine
plays *different games* from the ones that `(1 unfinished)` came out of. A historical reading from a
harness is not a reproducible observation once the engine has moved — which is the same lesson D258
reached about comparing two harnesses' *numbers*, arriving from the other direction. A clean sheet
from this instrument is a claim about the **current build**, and the only kind of claim it can be.

### What this leaves

The `catch { break; }` stays in all thirty-five, because the alternative — a throw taking down a
1248-game run at game 900 — is worse than a game ending early, and the instrument that can tell you
whether it ever happens now exists. **Run `unfinished.mjs` after any change to the engine's action
handling**, which is where a throw would come from, and the swallowing goes back to being harmless
rather than unexamined. It is cheap: 156 games on one seed takes under a minute.

## D262 — The four browser suites run in no gate at all, and one of them named a card by hand

The question that started this was small: three decks changed in D259 (a Thraben Inspector into
Skyward Writ, a Pirate's Prize into Tidal Mind, a Lotus Petal into Forge Alliance), and the browser
suites are not in `pnpm v2:test`. Did any of them break?

No. `e2e-table.mjs` 73/73, `e2e-solo.mjs` 24/24 against the changed Tidal Mind. But the answer took
two Playwright runs to get and **could not have been got any other way**, which is the finding:

- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` has three jobs and **no browser job**. Nothing in it mentions
  playwright, chromium or `e2e`.
- `pnpm v2:test` is `turbo run test --filter=./packages/* --filter=./apps/*`. `scripts/` is not a
  workspace package, so the four suites are outside the filter by construction.

Four suites, 24 to 73 checks each, covering the joints no unit test can reach — two isolated
browser contexts, a socket each, a hidden hand that has to genuinely not be in the other browser —
and they run **when somebody remembers to run them**. That is a reasonable place to be (a browser
job needs a browser, servers, Redis and a minute a suite, and these take 30-90s each locally), but
it is only reasonable if nothing silently *rots* between runs. Two things could.

### The assertion that named a card, which had already failed once

`e2e-table.mjs` asserted `peeked.includes('Vampire Nighthawk')` on Tidal Mind's deck-peek panel. Its
own comment records the history: it asked for Tidal Mind's single Counterspell first, a balance pass
cut that card, and the check went red while the panel was working perfectly. The repair at the time
was to name the three-of instead — which **moved the trap rather than removing it**. A deck list is
