nearly four in the other does not get a global default, and no judgement call is needed to say so.

### And the measurements say what the term actually is

This is the useful part, and it is a statement about the pod rather than about clocks.

**"Am I racing?" has one answer in a duel and three in a pod, and this term computes one number.**
Both scalings get that number wrong, in opposite directions:

 - **Undivided**, it is the *sum* — what the whole table could send if everyone attacked me every
   turn. True of one opponent with nine power, and also true of three with three each, which is a
   much slower death because they are not all pointed at me. It over-fears, and the 2.06x length was
   the bot flinching from an attack nobody was making.
 - **Divided**, it is the *mean*. Nine power on one seat and nothing on the others reads three, which
   under-fears the one opponent who can actually kill me — and that is the only one a clock is about.

The object a player reads in a pod is neither: it is **the shortest of the per-opponent clocks**, who
kills me first and in how many turns. In a duel those three objects coincide, which is exactly why
the duel measurement is clean and could never have exposed this. That is the fifth instance today of
a premise wider than its fixture, and the follow-up it names is concrete: compute `exposedPower` per
foe rather than table-wide and take the minimum clock. It is a different term, not a rescaling, so it
gets its own three seed sets.

Everything stays: the computation, ten tests, both candidate shapes, two `term-leverage` rows, and
both halves of the measurement. The duel result is real and is the strongest evidence yet for the
shape-over-weight thesis; the pod result is real and is why the thesis is not yet a shipped default.

## D277 — A bot change belongs on the list of things that wants a browser run

D262 left the four browser suites outside every gate on purpose, and said so plainly: *"a browser job
needs a browser, servers, Redis and a minute a suite"*, so **running the four suites after any change
to the table UI or the lobby remains a manual step.**

That list is one item short. Today's change was to the **bot's evaluation** — `castable` shipped at 1,
which moves 4.3% of its cast decisions and 1.0% of all of them — and a bot that plays differently
walks the browser suites down different paths: different cards cast, different prompts raised,
different boards to lay out. The gates that passed (guards, two typechecks, 2061 unit and integration
tests) do not drive a browser. So the real player path had not been exercised since the engine's
judgement changed, and nothing would have said so.

Run against the live stack, with the shipped default:

```
e2e-solo    28/28     e2e-table   73/73
e2e-arena   54/54     e2e-pod     42/42        197 checks, exit 0
```

Clean, which is the answer worth having rather than the interesting one: solo play, a two-browser
duel, the arena table and a four-browser pod all still work with the new evaluation, including the
control-bar and overflow checks #251 added. **A bot change is now on the list with UI and lobby
changes**, and the reason is in one line: the bot chooses which paths these suites walk.

Nothing in the code changed for this entry. It is a practice correction with a run behind it, which
is the only kind worth writing down.

## D278 — A pod clock is not a scaling problem, it is a missing attack model

D276 closed the clock as a duel term and named a follow-up: compute `exposedPower` per foe and take
the **shortest** clock, since the sum over-fears and the mean under-fears. Before building it, the
arithmetic was checked — and it refutes the follow-up.

A pod seat with one 3/3 blocker, against three opponents holding one 2/2 each:

| reading | unanswerable power |
| --- | --- |
| table-wide (the sum) | **4** |
| two opponents | 2 |
| **one opponent alone** | **0** |

The per-foe reading is zero because `exposedPower` spends my blockers against whatever attackers it
is shown, and shown one opponent's board it has the whole blocker pool for it. So **every**
per-opponent clock on that board says "nothing can touch me", and the minimum of them says it too —
on a board where four damage lands every turn. That is not an improvement on the mean; it is the
worst of the three.

So all three candidate objects are wrong in identifiable ways:

| | what it computes | how it fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sum (undivided) | everyone attacks me every turn | over-fears diffuse threats; measured: pod −4, 0 and **2.06x** length |
| mean (divided) | the threat is spread evenly | under-fears the one opponent who can kill me; measured: pod −8, 0, −4 at 1.29x |
| min of per-foe clocks | each opponent attacks alone | reads **0** where 4 lands a turn, as above |

### What the pod actually needs, and why the duel never needed it

The quantity a player reads in a pod depends on **how many opponents point at them**, and that is
not a property of the board — it is a property of what the other seats decide. My blockers are
shared: the same 3/3 answers any one of those three 2/2s and cannot answer two. So the incoming
damage is a function of the attack pattern, and no scaling of a board-wide sum recovers it.

**That is why the duel measurement is so clean and could never have pointed at this.** With one
opponent there is nothing to model: they attack or they do not, and the sum, the mean and the min are
the same number. +1.5 points over 2808 duels is a real result about a term whose object is
well-defined in that format and ill-defined in the other.

The project does have the raw material for an attack model elsewhere — `chaseTheCrown`, the threat
read on each opponent's strip, `offerPact`'s board reading, the `hit you N` / `spared you N` history
(D189, D227) — and none of it is wired into `evaluate`. That is a much larger piece of work than a
term, and naming it is the useful output here rather than attempting it.

### What this closes

`CLOCK_RATE` stays at zero with the duel result and both candidate shapes kept, and #259 is closed as
**refuted by arithmetic rather than by a measurement** — thirty seconds of checking instead of three
more seed sets in two formats. Worth noticing that the cheap check came last: the instinct after a
negative pod result was to build the next variant, and the thing that was actually missing was one
question asked of a three-creature board.

## D279 — The table does not ask questions it already knows the answer to, and the number says don't fix it

A premium table asks a player things worth asking. Nobody had counted how often this one asks
something with exactly one legal answer — a drawer that opens, interrupts the game, and offers the
only move available.

**The project already knew this mattered, one card at a time.** `LegalActions.mustCastOffered`
carries a `mandatory` flag whose comment is the whole thesis:

> a button that cannot be pressed is worse than no button — which is what the first run of
> `LIST=suspend` showed, with "Cast it Decline" on a question that has one answer.

That is written **at a card**. Nothing asked it of the whole set, which is D269's shape for the
fourth time: the answer existed in the codebase and no instrument could see it.

### The count

`one-answer.mjs` replays bot games and asks `legalActions` of the seat about to act at every state,
classifying whatever question is pending — so what it counts is what a *person* would have been
asked, because bots answer these silently. 78 games on the deck that holds suspend:

| question | asked | one answer | per game |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| declare attackers | 561 | 13 (2%) | 7.2 |
| `mustCastOffered` | 23 | **11 (48%)** | 0.3 |
| `mustSettleHand` | 194 | 0 | 2.5 |
| declare blockers | 165 | 0 | 2.1 |
| `mustDecide` | 65 | 0 | 0.8 |
| `mustChoose` | 50 | 0 | 0.6 |

1062 questions, **13.6 a game, and 24 of them (2%) had one answer.**

### Why that is a decision not to change anything

The two forced cases are real and both are rare: suspend's mandatory cast (11) and a declaration
where every able creature must attack and there is one seat to aim at (13). Across 78 games that is
**0.3 forced prompts a game** out of 13.6 questions. Auto-resolving them means an engine change on a
rules path, its tests, a browser run (D277) and the full suite — to save a third of one button press
a game. That is a worse trade than leaving it, and the arithmetic is the argument rather than taste.

Worth reading the rest of the table the same way. Of 13.6 questions a game, **9.3 are declaring
attackers and blockers** — that is Magic, every combat, not friction — and 2.5 are the opening hand.
The questions a *card* asks come to about 1.5 a game. **The table is not over-asking**, which is the
answer this was built to get and a better one than a list of things to fix.

The instrument stays as a standing check: a future card whose prompt has one answer lights up a row
that is currently zero outside those two cases.

### Two corrections in one file, and the pattern behind them

**Its first run reported 26 of 26 opening hands as forced — 81% of everything counted — and was
wrong.** The test read `bottomOwed === 0` as "nothing left to decide"; it means *nothing goes under
if you keep*, and the player may mulligan instead. The number was an artefact of my classifier, not
a fact about the table, and it was one paragraph away from being written up as a finding.

The reason the mistake was available is worth more than the mistake: `LegalActions` has **no "may
mulligan" field**, because the mulligan is an ordinary card action rather than an `auto:` one. So
nothing in the shape the instrument reads says whether a mulligan is on offer, and `bottomOwed` was
a guess standing in for it. It now asks the engine — `applyAction` is pure, so offering a mulligan on
a throwaway state costs one call and answers exactly the question. One answer per rule, from the
thing that owns the rule (D260).

**And then a zero from a freshly corrected classifier is worth nothing until it has been seen to
report something.** `DECKS` seats named decks at every table, and on Kindle Grove — Rift Bolt and
Search for Tomorrow — the `mustCastOffered` row reads 11 of 23. If it ever reads zero on a table
holding Rift Bolt, the file is broken rather than the table clean. That is D263's trap, caught for
the third time in this project and the second time today.

Both corrections are the same shape as everything else this week: **a check that asserted something
it had not established.** The classifier was not wrong about arithmetic, it was wrong about what the
answer space was — and it had never asked. The habit that catches it is cheap and keeps paying: before
believing a number, make the instrument produce the opposite number on purpose.

## D280 — Why the clock loses a pod: shared blockers make the reading superlinear, and the bot flinches

D276 said the clock's pod problem was units, and the per-opponent division fixed the **length**
(2.06x moves to 1.29x) without fixing the **record** (−8, 0, −4 over three seed sets). Something else
was going on, and "the games got longer" was a symptom rather than a cause. `aggression.mjs` names
it, on an ablation rather than an argument: the stock bot drives and both arms are asked the *same*
declaration, so there is no sampling to dispute.

### The measurement

| arm | declarations | creatures sent | per declaration | sent nothing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **pod**, shipping | 851 | 2088 | 2.45 | 202 (24%) |
| **pod**, clock at 1 | 851 | 1693 | 1.99 | **358 (42%)** |
| **duel**, shipping | 406 | 649 | 1.60 | 53 (13%) |
| **duel**, clock at 1 | 406 | 599 | 1.48 | **89 (22%)** |

The clock makes the bot cautious in **both** formats — and two and a half times more so in a pod:
**−18.9%** of creatures sent against **−7.7%** in a duel, and declining 42% of declarations where
the shipping bot declines 24%.

The duel row is the control that makes the pod row mean anything. Had the arm declined equally in
both, the finding would be "this term is passive" and the format explanation would be dead. It is
not equal, and the gap is the finding.

### And it is still the divided term, which is the part that matters

This was measured on the build that **already divides by the opponents the table started with**. So
the division did not make the caution comparable across formats, and the reason is structural rather
than a scale factor:

**`exposedPower` pools every opponent's attackers against one shared blocker pool, so unanswerable
power is superlinear in the number of opponents.** Three opponents holding two 2/2s each, against my
two blockers: six attackers, two get blocked, **four unanswerable**. One opponent holding two 2/2s
against the same two blockers: **zero**. Divide the first by three and it is still 1.33 against 0.
No single divisor undoes a superlinearity — which is the same arithmetic D278 demonstrated from the
other side, and this is what it costs in play.

### What that settles

The chain is now measured end to end:

1. The clock makes a seat fear the attack coming back, in proportion to the unanswerable power it
   reads, so it holds its blockers rather than swinging.
2. `exposedPower` reads *superlinearly* more at four seats, because blockers are shared, so the
   caution is 2.5x stronger there and no scaling fixes it.
3. **Mild caution wins a duel** (+1.5 points, −7.7% aggression) and **heavy caution loses a pod**
   (−3.8 points, −18.9%). In a duel, surviving the swing and winning the attrition are the same
   thing. At four seats they are not: a seat that never pressures anybody never wins, however long
   it lives.

So the clock cannot be made pod-safe by any weight or divisor, and **#262 is answered without
building the attack model it was going to scope.** The question "how concentrated are pod attacks"
was the wrong next question: the defect is not in how the term estimates who attacks, it is that the
quantity it is built on does not scale with the table at all.

An attack model would still be the thing that makes a pod clock possible, and it is now a bigger
piece than D278 implied — it would have to replace `exposedPower`'s pooled greedy assignment with a
per-opponent one that shares blockers honestly, which is the hard part D259 was closed on. Not
tonight, and not as a term.

### The method note

This is the second time in two days that the cheap question beat the expensive one, and the same
cheap question both times: **ask what the thing actually does before modelling why.** #259 was
refuted by one three-creature board; this was answered by counting what the bot sends. The
expensive plan — build an attack model, measure it in two formats over six seed sets — was queued
and would have been wasted, because it was aimed at the wrong defect.

## D281 — pod-duel's noise floor is ±16 of 104, and it retracts a claim I published twice today

The symmetric prediction from D280 — if caution loses a pod, aggression should win one — was tested
with the lever already to hand, `clockRate` at **−1**, which makes a seat value being attacked and
so swing more. `aggression.mjs` confirmed the lever is monotone before any win rate was spent:

| weight | creatures sent | declines a declaration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| −1 | 2343 (+12.2%) | 19% |
| 0 (shipping) | 2088 | 24% |
| +1 | 1693 (−18.9%) | 42% |

### The duel half confirms the mechanism emphatically

Three disjoint seed sets, 936 paired games each: **408-527, 416-519, 406-530.** About **−12 points**,
every set, which against the +1.5 the term earns at `+1` makes the duel response strongly monotone
in the weight. Ignoring the crack-back is a disaster in a duel, and that is the clearest confirmation
D280's mechanism could have: the term's whole effect is caution, and caution is worth real points at
two seats.

### The pod half retracts something instead

Three disjoint seed sets of 104 pods, one unchanged arm: **60-44 (+16), 50-54 (−4), 44-60 (−16).**

A range of **32 for a setting that did not change between runs.** That is `pod-duel`'s noise floor,
and it is the first time anybody has measured it — which matters because **the file says to measure
it before believing a difference, and I did not**:

> **Get the floor by re-running a real arm on a different seed set instead.** Two runs of the same
> setting on disjoint seeds differ by however much this harness wobbles, and that spread is the
> number to disbelieve smaller results than. A pod is noisier than a duel by construction — three
> opponents, three chances to be attacked — so expect it to be wide.

I quoted that docblock earlier today, for its *other* warning about the arithmetic control, and did
not do what this half of it says.

**So the pod readings for the clock at `+1` — 48-56, 52-52, 50-54 — are retracted as a result.** I
wrote them up as "−3.8 points, never once above zero" in D276, and repeated the figure in D280 and at
`CLOCK_RATE`. They sit well inside ±16. Three draws landing at −8, 0 and −4 from a distribution
centred near zero is unremarkable, and "never once above zero" is three coin flips, not evidence.
**D242's three-disjoint-sets rule was applied without its precondition**: the rule tells you a sign
that holds is believable, and it only means that once you know what a single reading wobbles by.

### What survives, and it is most of it

- **The duel result.** +1.5 points over 2808 games at `+1`, −12 over 2808 at `−1`, on a harness whose
  floor *is* established (±6 observed) with 936 games a reading. Monotone and solid.
- **The aggression figures.** 42% of declarations declined against 24%, −18.9% of creatures sent in a
  pod against −7.7% in a duel. An **ablation on identical positions**, exact, no sampling argument.
- **The length figures.** 2.06x moves undivided, 1.29x divided, paired on the same eight seeds.
- **The superlinearity.** 4 unanswerable table-wide against 0 per-opponent, arithmetic, certain.

What does *not* survive is one number: the clock's effect on who wins a pod. It is **unknown**, not
negative.

### The decision does not change, and is now better founded

`CLOCK_RATE` stays at **zero**. The retracted reason was "it loses pods". The real reason is stronger:
the pod win rate is unmeasured, and the pod *behaviour* change is large and exactly measured — a seat
declining 42% of its attacks where the shipping bot declines 24%, in games running 1.29x the moves.
Shipping a large unmeasured behavioural change to the format this project cares most about is the
thing not to do, and that holds whichever way the win rate would have gone.

### What a real pod reading costs

At ±16 of 104, resolving a 4-point effect needs roughly ten times the games — about **1000 pods an
arm, ninety minutes a reading**, three disjoint sets, so four to five hours for one question. Nothing
in this project has ever spent that on a pod.

**And a correction to the first version of this entry, which overreached.** It said every pod
win-rate number here is weaker than it reads. That is unfair to the work it tars, and checking took
one grep:

 - The myriad measurement (`pod-slot`) says its zero *"is arithmetic rather than evidence for the
   same reason `pod-duel`'s is, so the floor has to come from re-running a real arm on disjoint
   seeds"* — **and then does exactly that**, two readings of 52 pods on seeds 3300 and 5100 reading
   4-48 and 2-50. Same procedure I skipped, carried out, on an effect far outside any plausible
   floor.
 - `offerPact` opens with *"`pod-duel` cannot price this, and not for want of games"*, explains why
   bot-to-bot offers are refused by construction, and says outright **"it is on by default and the
   reason is not a win rate."**

So the practice was already right and already written down. **The only pod win rate ever published
as a result in this project is the one retracted above, and it is mine.** The gap was not a
systemic blind spot; it was that the floor existed as an instruction rather than as a number, and I
read the instruction and did not follow it. Writing a blanket warning about everyone else's numbers
was the same move as the error it was apologising for: a claim wider than what had been checked.

`pod-duel` should carry the floor in its docblock rather than an instruction to find it, so the next
person reads ±16 instead of being told to go and measure it. Doing that now.

## D282 — A blocker is not spent by blocking: the pooled-blocker bug, and fixing it rescues nothing

`exposedPower` kept **one** spent-blocker set across the whole table, so a blocker that answered
seat 1's creature was unavailable against seat 2's. That is not the rules. **Nothing taps a creature
for blocking**, and a creature untaps only in its own controller's untap step (CR 502.1) — which for
me comes after *all three* of their turns. My untapped 3/3 blocks seat 1's Bear on seat 1's turn,
seat 2's on seat 2's, and seat 3's on seat 3's.

The fix is structural rather than a constant: gather the blockers once, then run the greedy
assignment **per opponent**, each with its own spent set, and sum the unanswered power. At two seats
it is arithmetically the same function — one opponent, one set — so every duel measurement in the
project still reads on it.

### What the old function said, and what the board actually costs

Three opponents fielding a Bear each, against my one untapped 3/3:

| | reading |
| --- | --- |
| pooled | 4 — the Giant answers one Bear, the other two "get through" |
| per opponent | **0** |
| what the board actually costs in life | **0** |

Four points of pressure on a board that loses no life, and the error grows with the opponent count,
so no divisor undoes it. Three new tests pin the arithmetic: the shared blocker across opponents,
the blocker still spent once *within* one of their turns (the half a careless fix breaks), and the
sum over opponents rather than the max.

### D278's refuting example was wrong; its conclusion survives

D278 rejected a **minimum** per-opponent clock with this: a seat with one 3/3 against three
opponents holding a 2/2 each reads 4 table-wide and 0 against any one of them, "on a board where
four damage lands every turn". No damage lands on that board at all — each 2/2 attacks alone into an
untapped 3/3 that is untapped again on the next opponent's turn. The 4 *was* the pooling bug, and
the honest reading is 0 everywhere, so the min agrees because everything agrees.

The min is still the wrong object on arithmetic that holds: three opponents each with an
**unblockable** 2/2 cost six life a cycle and the min reads two. That is now the test, rather than
the refuted board.

### And D280's central claim is withdrawn, narrowly

D280 explained the clock's pod passivity as *"my blockers are shared, and the same 3/3 answers any
one of those 2/2s and cannot answer two"*, and concluded the term needs an attack model `evaluate`
does not have. The second half of that sentence is false: the same 3/3 answers **all three**, on
three different turns. Blockers are not shared across opponents. The object the term computes — the
sum over opponents of what each cannot be stopped from doing — is the right one, and is now what the
code computes.

**What that predicted did not happen, and this is the result worth having.** If pooled blockers were
why the term made a pod bot passive, fixing them should have brought the caution down toward the
duel's. Re-run on the fixed build, `aggression.mjs` on the same 851 pod declarations:

| build | declarations | sent | sent nothing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| shipping (both runs) | 851 | 2088 | 202 (24%) |
| clock at 1, pooled (D280) | 851 | 1693 | 358 (42%) |
| clock at 1, **fixed** | 851 | 1692 | **351 (41%)** |

Seven declarations of 851. The duel control reproduces D280 to the digit — 406, 599, 89 (22%) —
which is exactly what a fix that is arithmetically nothing at two seats should do, measured end to
end rather than argued. **The shipping rows being identical to the count is what makes this a paired
comparison**: the shipping bot has all three pressure weights at 0, so it never calls
`exposedPower`, the games are the same games, and the 851 positions are the same positions.

### Why it rescued nothing: a gradient, not a level

An attack declaration is decided by what the term **charges for tapping a blocker**, not by what it
reads at rest, and the fix moves those two in opposite directions. D280's own board — three
opponents holding two 2/2s each against my two blockers:

| | blockers untapped | blockers tapped (I swung) | charged for attacking |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| pooled | 8 | 12 | 4 |
| per opponent | **0** | 12 | **12** |

The level falls to the honest 0. The price of swinging **triples**, because each of those blockers
was answering an attacker on every one of their turns, and tapping them lets all six through. The
two effects roughly cancel in play, which is the 41% against 42%.

So the passivity is the term's **shape**, not this bug: tapping a blocker is priced as incoming
damage, which is true in a duel too (declines 22% against 13%) and simply has three opponents' power
to multiply at four seats. Both clock weights stay at 0.

**The 8 in that table was measured, not reasoned.** The first draft of it guessed 4; hoisting the
spent set back out of the loop for one run said 8 — six 2/2s against two blockers is two blocked and
four unanswered, four creatures and eight power, and D280's "four unanswerable" was four creatures.
A one-minute measurement against a confident guess, on the same afternoon a confident guess had to
be retracted (D281).

### What is still unmodelled, named narrowly this time

 - **Who points at me.** The term prices every opponent as attacking me with everything every turn.
   In a pod they have three choices of victim, and this file's politics readers (`chaseTheCrown`,
   the threat read, `offerPact`'s board reading) know something about which, and are not wired in.
 - **Blocker attrition.** A chump blocker dies and is not there next turn, where this model has it
   blocking forever. That is the function's existing deliberate omission — it declines to price what
   a block costs, because the creature terms and the combat heuristics already do — but across a
   *cycle* of turns it is the one place a per-turn reading leaks.

### The divisor it leaves behind

`clockRate` divides by the opponents the table started with, and D276 justified that as a units fix
for the superlinearity. Most of that superlinearity was this bug. What is left is real and is not a
bug: a pod seat is attacked three times before its own next turn, so `exposedPower` is honestly
three times a duel's number at the same per-opponent board, and dividing turns the term from *damage
per cycle* into *damage per opponent-turn* — the scale a duel-calibrated weight was calibrated in.

So it is a scale choice now rather than a units fix, and it is the open question if either clock is
ever turned on. Left alone: changing it would be a second behavioural change with nothing to pick
between the two, and a pod win rate still costs ~1000 pods an arm at the ±16 floor.

### The lesson that is not about blockers

The bug survived three measurements, two instruments and a long docblock **because it was written
down as a fact about the game rather than as a question about the code**. "My blockers are shared"
reads like domain knowledge; it was a description of a loop. Every number D276 through D280 took was
correctly measured on a function that answered the wrong question, and no amount of pairing, seed
discipline or ablation discipline could have caught it — only reading the loop against the rules.

## D283 — The player documentation had been counting by hand, and was two decks and fifteen cards out

`claude/play-realm-setup.md` is the thing a person reads before sitting down at the table. Its deck
section was headed **"Eleven starter decks"** and the registry holds thirteen; three separate places
said the engine knows **"three hundred and thirty-three"** cards and the pool index holds **348**;
`customDeck.ts` — the docblock on the feature that resolves a pasted decklist — opened by saying the
names are looked up in "the eleven starter decks".

Nobody wrote a wrong number. Each was right when it was written and nothing connected it to the
registry, so two decks and fifteen cards arrived and the prose did not move. The deck *bodies* were
all written: all thirteen decks are described at length a few lines under a heading that says eleven.

### Fixed, and then made unable to recur

 - The heading, the three card figures, and `customDeck.ts` — which now says "the starter decks" and
   carries no count at all, because that docblock has no reason to know how many there are.
 - **"The ten castable faces of the seven cards printed with more than one"** is now the nine such
   cards the registry holds: three splits (Wax // Wane, Fire // Ice, Assault // Battery), two
   adventures (Merfolk Secretkeeper, Garenbrig Carver), two modal double-faced lands (Hagra Mauling,
   Vastwood Fortification) and two that transform (Delver of Secrets, Thing in the Ice), with twelve
   extra faces between them. The old clause was the one I nearly refreshed without checking: it is a
   second count in the same sentence and it was wrong in a different direction.
 - `mechanic-coverage.mjs` prints the pool in one line — decks, distinct cards, multi-face cards and
   their extra faces, tokens — and the doc cites that command next to the figures. One command
   rechecks every number in the sentence.
 - A guard in `scripts/guards.js` reads the registry out of `starterDecks.ts` statically (it runs
   before anything is built) and fails when the doc omits a registered deck's name, or heads its
   deck section with the wrong spelled-out count.

### What the guard deliberately does not check

Prose elsewhere. "A full table with two starter decks" is a sentence about two of them, and a guard
that failed on it is a guard somebody switches off — so only the one heading, which is a pool-size
claim by construction. And not the card count: that needs the pool index, which needs the build,
which is why the doc cites the command instead.

**Four negative controls, because a guard that cannot fail is D263's trap in a new place.** The
heading set back to "Eleven" fails; a deck's name removed from the doc fails and names the deck; the
heading deleted fails; and renaming `STARTER_DECKS` so the parse finds nothing fails loudly with
*"the parse in this guard is broken and a pass would mean nothing"* rather than passing an empty
check — the rule `mechanic-coverage.mjs` states for reading a declaration out of source.

### The shape, which is the same one as D282 a few hours earlier

A fact the code knows, retyped into prose, and then diverging silently. D282's version was a loop
described as a rule of the game; this one is a registry described as a number. The fix is the same
both times and it is not "be more careful": make the prose cite the thing that knows, or put a check
on it. Two decks were added with a write-up each and neither touched the count above them, which is
exactly how careful people produce a stale document.

## D284 — The table that was never going to connect said "connecting" for ever

`apps/web/src/lib/table.ts` had no `connect_error` handler. The realtime server is WebSocket-only
(`transports: ['websocket']`, `allowUpgrades: false`) and the client matches it, so a network that
blocks WebSockets cannot play — and what a player saw was socket.io retrying silently behind a pill
reading `connecting`. The same screen for a server that is not running, a wrong
`VITE_REALTIME_URL`, and an origin the server refuses. The setup notes have listed this under *what
is not done* for months, ending "it would look like a table that never connects", and that was
exactly right.

The lobby now says, after three failed attempts:

> Cannot reach the table at *&lt;address&gt;*. Either it is not running, or this network is blocking
> WebSockets — the table needs them and has no fallback.

### Three decisions in that sentence, and one of them is measured

**It does not say which cause it is.** The temptation was to branch on the error's message and name
the origin case separately. Pointed at a closed port in a real browser, every `connect_error`
carries the message **`websocket error`** and nothing else — no status, no server text. So a branch
could not have told a blocked network from a refused origin, and naming one would have been a guess
dressed as a diagnosis. The raw error goes to the console for whoever runs the server; the player
gets what is true in every case.

**It waits three attempts.** One failure is ordinary — a reload racing its own teardown, a laptop
waking, a phone changing network — and socket.io retries in about a second, so a banner on the first
error would flash on tables that connect fine.

**It is a sentence, not a blocked screen.** The lobby's inputs stay enabled: a handshake can
recover, and a player who is told the table is unreachable is owed the attempt anyway.

### What was checked, and where

The sentence is four tests on a pure `connectionTrouble(attempts, url)` — silent on attempts one and
two, names WebSockets and "no fallback" on three, names the address including the same-origin default
(`VITE_REALTIME_URL` unset is the normal deployment, and "cannot reach the table at " with nothing
after it is how this change would have sent somebody hunting a missing variable), and keeps saying it
rather than going quiet on a long outage.

Then in a real browser against a closed port: the banner appears about three seconds in — 2.8s and
3.8s over two runs, which is three attempts at socket.io's randomised backoff — the lobby stays
usable, and the console carries the raw error. The **console** needed its own decision once that run
showed nine lines in four seconds: logged for the first few attempts and then one in ten, because an
outage left open overnight would otherwise be the only thing in there.

### And it does not break a phone, which #251 is the reason to check rather than assume

A sentence is a layout change, and the last one of those presented as four gameplay failures because
a control bar pushed the table sideways on a phone and no check could see it. Measured on the lobby
with the connection failing: **375x812 reads scrollWidth 375 against innerWidth 375, and 320x568
reads 320 against 320** — no sideways scroll at either, with the banner wrapping to 66px and 82px of
height inside the column. Nothing to fix, which is the result rather than the absence of one.

### What is still not done

The fallback itself. Polling stays off, which is a server change with deployment consequences (long
polling behind the Redis adapter wants sticky routing) and not one to make as a side effect of
putting a sentence on screen. The gap is now **legible** rather than closed, and the setup notes say
so in those terms.

## D285 — The seat that could not be reclaimed, and two things found by looking at the screen

A seat is remembered in `localStorage` and reclaimed on every connect, which is what makes a reload
or a dropped phone rejoin the same game. When the reclaim was refused the client called
`writeStored(null)` and **said nothing**. A player who reloaded after the grace window closed, or
whose table had ended while their laptop was shut, landed in the lobby with no seat and no
explanation — the same screen as somebody who had never joined a table at all. Same family as D284,
found by looking for the rest of it.

It now says, in the dismissible banner the lobby already has:

> Table BRAVE-OTTER-42 has ended, so there was no seat to get back to.

`rejoinTrouble(code, table)` classifies on the error **code**, which is an enumerated contract
(`PodErrorCode`), so unlike D284's handshake this *is* reading rather than guessing. Four sentences:
the table ended, the table started without this seat, the table is full, and a seat already held
somewhere. The last stays neutral — `already_in_pod` covers both "this socket is in a table" and
"this player is seated at the one being reclaimed", and naming either would be wrong half the time,
while the remedy is the same.

### And then the browser said two things the unit tests could not

**One: the server's prose won.** The first browser run put *"pod BRAVE-OTTER-42 does not exist"* on
screen — the server's own message, arriving as a `pod:error` broadcast *after* the ack whose sentence
it replaced. `state.error` holds one string, so the duplicate is not additive.

That reverses a documented choice. `showsBroadcastError` said of `not_found`: *"Nothing on this
client sends an event without an ack, so these reach the player twice over rather than not at all.
Shown, because a banner the player can act on is worth a duplicate."* The premise is right and the
conclusion does not follow — the second banner replaces the first rather than adding to it, and the
one it replaces is the better written of the two. `not_found` is now suppressed in the broadcast,
and only `not_found`: all three paths that can raise it (join, watch, reclaim) answer it on their
ack, where `bad_payload` and `internal` have no better sentence anywhere. The test that asserted the
old answer now asserts the new one, next to the reasoning.

**Two: a malformed stored seat showed zod.** Seeding storage with a made-up code to reproduce "the
table has ended" produced, instead:

> code: Pod code must look like WORD-WORD-NN; seatToken: String must contain at least 16 character(s)

`readStored` checked that the three fields were strings and nothing else, so a seat left by an older
build, a truncated write or a hand-edited value was sent anyway and the server's validator answered
the player. It now validates against **`PodJoinInput`** — the schema the server will apply to that
exact reclaim, exported from `@grimore/shared`, so this is the same answer rather than a second copy
of the rules (D260). A stored seat that cannot be a valid request is not a seat, and starting at the
lobby is what the existing catch already did for storage that will not parse. Reading `ok.data`
rather than the raw fields also normalises: `PodCode` trims and upper-cases, so a seat stored in the
wrong case comes back in the form the server indexes by.

Verified in a browser both ways: the sentence survives the broadcast (banner at 1.9s, lobby usable,
seat forgotten), and the malformed seat now produces no banner at all.

### The pattern across D284 and D285

Both silences were in the same forty lines, and neither was found by a test — they were found by
asking *what does a player see when this fails?* and then making it fail. The unit tests pin the
sentences; the browser is what found the server's prose overwriting one of them and zod text in
place of the other. **A failure path with no screen attached to it is not covered by a test that
asserts the state field.**

### The watcher, which is the third screen

A spectator has no connection pill at all — nothing on that screen has ever said anything about the
socket — so a dropped watcher sat in front of a frozen board with no way to tell it from a slow one,
and before the table deals, *"waiting for the table to deal"* is also what an unreachable server
looks like to one. Both branches of the watching view now carry the same sentence. `e2e-table`, which
drives a third browser as a watcher, is 73/73 on it.

**And then counting them found a fourth, which is why counting is worth doing.** The commit that
added the watcher's said it completed "the three screens that can be waiting on a handshake"; there
are four. `PreGame` — seated, picking a deck, waiting for the others — is the one that reads worst
without it: *"Share this code"* in front of a player whose table will never hear them, above a seat
list that cannot fill because nothing is getting through. It has the sentence now too. Four screens,
one sentence, one source.

### And the four browser suites, because this touched the lobby's DOM

`e2e-table` 73, `e2e-arena` 51, `e2e-pod` 41, `e2e-solo` 28 — **193 checks clean** on the build
carrying D284 and D285. Two of them reload a browser mid-game, which means they exercise a real
seat reclaim through the new `PodJoinInput` validation rather than only the refusals the unit tests
cover: the happy path is checked by the thing that would notice if it broke.

### Left alone, and said rather than half-fixed

`joinTable`, `watchTable` and `createTable` still show `res.error.message` on a refusal, which for a
mistyped code reads *"pod BRAVE-OTTER-42 does not exist"* — relevant, and with this codebase's word
for a table in it. That is a wording problem rather than a silence, it needs sentences for a
different set of cases (a player who never had a seat is not a player who lost one), and writing one
function for both would have made one of the two wrong. Noted here instead of guessed at.

## D286 — The clock's third shape, built because the arithmetic turned against the divisor

`clockRate` divides `exposedPower` by the opponents the table started with. D276 added that as a
units fix for a reading that was three times too large at four seats, and **most of that largeness
was a bug** — `exposedPower` pooled one set of blockers across the whole table until #264. What is
left is not an error: a pod seat really is attacked three times before its own next turn, so the
undivided sum is the honest damage per cycle.

And **damage per cycle is what lethality depends on**, which is the arithmetic that settles it. At
ten life:

| | their turns | dead on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| one opponent, 9 unanswerable | −9 → 1 life, then −9 | their second attack, a full cycle later |
| three opponents, 3 each | −3 → 7, −3 → 4, −3 → 1, then −3 | the first of their turns in the next cycle |

**Both die on the same turn.** Nine a cycle is nine either way, so the sum was the right object all
along — the same conclusion D282 reached from the rules side — and dividing by three reads a third of
the real pressure.

### So the divisor is wrong, and it is still there

`clockCycle` is `clockRate` without it: `exposedPower * startingLife / life`, undivided. **In a duel
the two are identical** (one opponent, divisor one), which is exactly why this went unnoticed for as
long as it did: every duel measurement in the project reads the same for both, and the divisor only
exists at four seats.

It is a **fourth weight** rather than a flag on `clockRate` for one concrete reason: a 1040-pod win
rate for `{clockRate:1}` **with the divisor** was running as this was written (#268), and changing
what that arm means mid-flight would have thrown away two hours of measurement. Once that reading is
in, the same question can be asked of this arm against the same seeds.

### Four tests, and it ships at zero

The identity with D264's linear term at full life in a duel; the doubling at half life; the pod
reading of **4 against `clockRate`'s 4/3**, which is the whole of the difference; and the guard that
fails if the default moves. Plus a `term-leverage` arm, with a note that the row is only worth taking
at four seats because in a duel it *is* `clockRate`.

**Zero, and the reason is a discipline rather than a doubt.** The arithmetic favouring a shape is
precisely what `exposed` had in D264 and what `clockRate` had in D275, and both were then measured
and left off. A term whose shape is right and whose win rate is unknown is still a term with an
unknown win rate.

## D287 — CR 704.5q: the two kinds of counter never sat on the same card, and nothing noticed

`stateBasedActions` enforced eight of CR 704.5 and not **704.5q**: a permanent with both `+1/+1` and
`-1/-1` counters loses that many of each. The engine let them pile up side by side.

**The size was never wrong, which is exactly why it survived.** `characteristicsOf` reads both kinds
and subtracts, so three plus and two minus has always *measured* as one plus — a 3/3 like that is a
4/4 either way, and nothing about power or toughness gives the gap away. What was wrong is every
card that counts the counters themselves, and this pool has four kinds:

 - **Hangarback Walker** makes a Thopter per `+1/+1` counter as it dies. Three plus and two minus
   made three Thopters where the rules give one.
 - **Persist** asks whether the creature had a `-1/-1` counter and **undying** whether it had a
   `+1/+1`. A persisted Murderous Redcap that then gains a plus counter is supposed to end with
   neither and come back **again**; without the cancelling it keeps both and persist is switched off
   for good. That is the interaction the rule is famous for.
 - **Modular** moves the pluses off a dying Arcbound creature, and **Walking Ballista** spends one to
   ping. Both read a count this was inflating.

**Reachable in this pool rather than theoretical.** `-1/-1` counters arrive here from **infect**
(CR 702.90b — `dealDamage` puts them on instead of marking damage), so any Blight Vector creature
connecting with a Hangarback, a Ballista, an Arcbound creature or an undying body is the board the
rule is about, which a four-seat pod reaches the second time those decks meet.

### The fix, and where it goes

First in the per-permanent pass of `stateBasedActions`, before the branches that `continue`, so
every count a death trigger raised in that same pass reads the corrected number. Four tests: the
cancelling itself; that **the size is unchanged** while it happens (a 3/3 with three plus and two
minus is a 4/4 before and after — a test reading only power and toughness would pass on the broken
engine, which is why the counts are what the first test reads); that five against five cancels in
one pass rather than five; and that a creature the counters kill is still dead afterwards, since the
cancelling is not a save.

### Two tests had been describing illegal boards

**`proliferate`'s two failed, and they were right to.** They set a `+1/+1` on a Chasm Skulker and
then let Contagion Clasp's arrival put a `-1/-1` on it, which under 704.5q leaves the Skulker with no
counters at all — so it drops out of the candidate list and out of the kinds to proliferate. One of
them said in a comment that this made the Skulker *"the one permanent here carrying two kinds of
counter, which is the half of 'one of each kind already there' that a single-counter permanent cannot
show"*. It cannot show it because the board cannot exist. Both now give the Skulker two pluses, so
the Clasp's minus leaves one, and "each kind" is shown across the three objects answered at once —
a `+1/+1` and a poison. Nothing in those two decks carries two kinds legally: `lore`, `loyalty`,
`ice` and `vanishing` all live on cards in other ones.

**`mana.test.ts`'s "nets +1/+1 against -1/-1" is kept and now says why.** It writes both kinds onto
an instance by hand, which a played game cannot reach — and the layer that computes power is a
different thing from the one that keeps the board legal. The cancelling happens between actions and
`characteristicsOf` is called inside them, so it still has to net them.

### The shape, again

Third time today. A rule the engine states in a comment, enforces for eight cases out of nine, and
nobody checked the ninth — because the only consequence visible on screen was identical either way.
D282's blocker bug hid behind a plausible sentence; this hid behind a correct power and toughness.
**What a test asserts decides what a bug can hide behind**, and the one that catches this reads the
counters rather than the creature.

## D288 — The legend rule was not enforced at all, and this pool reaches it inside one deck

`stateBasedActions` did not implement **CR 704.5j**. Two legendary permanents with the same name sat
happily under one controller: a `deckSpecs` board with two Kalitas on one battlefield stayed at two,
with an empty graveyard.

**Found by auditing CR 704.5 against the engine after D287**, which is the method that found D287 as
well: list the cases the code cites, and check the ones it does not against what the pool can
produce. Eight cases plus `714.4` and `702.95b` were there; `704.5q` was missing and is now in
(D287); this is the second.

### Three routes, two of them inside a single deck

 - **Forge Alliance.** It runs **Blade of Selves**, whose myriad makes token copies of the attacking
   creature, and its commander **Balan** *pulls every Equipment onto himself*. So a Balan carrying
   the Blade attacks a pod and makes two more Balans — a board the rules forbid, and one where each
   of them was dealing commander damage towards the twenty-one that eliminates a player.
 - **Tidal Mind.** It runs **Clone**, which can copy its own commander.
 - **A pasted list.** Deck legality is deliberately not checked anywhere (see the header of
   `cards.ts`), so two of one legend is a list a player can hand the table — and `deckSpecs`, which
   the tests use, is the same path.

### Which one survives is a deviation, and it is stated

The rule says the controller **chooses**. This keeps the one earliest in that seat's battlefield
order, which is the one that arrived first. Asking would mean `stateBasedActions` being able to stop
and ask: it is a pure `state -> state` function called inside `settle`, and making it able to block is
a larger change than this rule is worth today. The automatic answer is also the one a player almost
always gives — of a real Balan and two token copies of him, the real one is the keeper.

Grouped by the **characteristics'** name rather than the card's, so a Clone that copied a legend
counts as that legend (CR 707.2 gives the copy the copied name). That is the whole of the Clone
route, and it would have been missed by grouping on `defKey`.

### Four tests

The rule itself; that **two players may each control one** (the half that makes a commander mirror
legal); that a non-legendary card is untouched, which keeps this from becoming a rule about names;
and that three copies lose two in one pass rather than one a pass.

### The player documentation had been promising this rule all along

`claude/play-realm-setup.md`, listing what a regeneration shield does *not* beat, ends with
*"**state-based legend and commander rules**"*. The commander half is real (`engine.ts` eliminates a
seat on 21). The legend half was a sentence about something the engine did not do — so the fix makes
an existing promise true rather than needing a doc change, and that is the worse kind of
documentation error: not stale, **never true**. It is the exact failure `mechanic-coverage.mjs` was
built to catch one level down — *"a capability the engine has, the docs describe, and no card reaches
is a claim that cannot fail"* — and nothing watches the prose for it.

### And the question it raised, now checked rather than left open

A token copy of a commander is not the commander, so it should not add to commander damage. The
first version of this entry said that was a separate question and did not answer it. It took one
read: `dealDamage` attributes commander damage with `from?.isCommander === true`, and a token has no
such flag — so the copies never counted towards the twenty-one, and the only thing wrong with three
Balans attacking was that there were three of them. **The engine was already right about the half
that would have been worse**, which is worth recording so nobody goes looking for it.

## D289 — An instrument that loses everything on interruption, and the pod reading's real price

The 1040-pod reading (#268) was killed by a **container restart at 83 minutes of CPU** and produced
**nothing**. Every number lived in three local variables until one `console.log` at the end, so an
interrupted run was worth zero pods rather than the eight hundred it had played.

`pod-duel.mjs` now prints a **checkpoint per pass** — a complete, quotable result over the pods
finished so far, on whole passes so it is never a half-rotated table. The final line is the last
checkpoint with the whole sample in it. Anything that interrupts the run now leaves a reading
standing, which is the difference between losing an hour and losing an hour's *answer*.

### And the price of a pod reading was wrong by a factor of two

One pass — 52 pods, every deck, all four rotations — takes **503 seconds** measured rather than
guessed. So `SEEDS=20` is **about two hours and fifty minutes**, not the ninety minutes this file's
docblock has claimed since D281. The two runs that were killed had reached roughly 500 pods each,
not "nearly done" as the session notes said at the time.

That matters for how the question gets asked. Three disjoint sets at 1040 pods is **eight and a half
hours of compute**, or about three in parallel on four cores. With checkpoints it is no longer
all-or-nothing: the run can be read at any pass and stopped when the sample is enough, and
*"620 pods, 310-310"* is an honest answer where a truncated run used to be no answer at all.


## D290 — Two CR 704.5 rows the audit missed, and one of them cannot be written

D288 put a table into `stateBasedActions` claiming to be the whole of CR 704.5 "audited against the
rules rather than grown one card at a time". It had thirteen rows and the rule has fifteen cases.
The two it skipped are the two that are not enforced *here*, which is exactly how a list goes wrong
— the audit found the cases that needed code and stopped at the edge of the file.

**CR 704.5p**, a creature attached to something becoming unattached, is handled: the pool's only
attached creature is a bestowed one, and the Aura branch above already turns it back into a creature
instead of binning it (`inst.bestowed === true`, which is bestow's own CR 702.103c). One row, no
code.

**CR 704.5e**, a copy of a spell outside the stack ceasing to exist, is the interesting one, because
it has no check anywhere and adding one would be writing an unreachable branch. A copy of a spell is
a stack object with no instance under its id, so there is no card to put in a graveyard and no path
that could try. `counterSpell` looks the instance up by the *stack object's* id, finds nothing, and
stops — which is the rule, arrived at by construction rather than by enforcement.

**The part worth recording is how nearly I wrote a test that proved nothing.** The obvious assertion
for 704.5e is a graveyard count: counter the Twincast copy, then check there is one Lightning Bolt
and not two. I wrote it, it passed, and then — on the D287 habit of breaking the code to see the
test fail — I made `counterSpell` fall back to `instances[object.source]`, which on a copy is the
*original's* instance, and ran it again. **It still passed.** The original Bolt resolves and reaches
the graveyard either way, so the count reads the same whether the rule holds or not. The assertion
that actually pins the rule is the one the test already had before I touched it:
`expect(s.instances[copy]).toBeUndefined()`. The shape of the state is the rule.

So: two rows added, no code, and the reverted experiment written into the docblock so the next person
who thinks a graveyard count would be a good test for this reads why it is not. Third time in this
session that what a test asserts decided what a bug could hide behind (D282, D287), and the first
time the answer was that the test I was about to add was the weaker one.

## D291 — The doc told players the opponent cannot hold mana up, 130 decisions after it learned to

The player doc describes the computer opponent twice: once in *You can play on your own* near the top
and once in *What is not done* at the bottom. Both said it "will not hold a creature back to block or
keep mana up for the counterspell in its hand".

**The second half has been false since #60**, which built `reserveForAnswers` — the filter that
keeps back the mana the cheapest answer in hand needs, on that seat's own turn, only when the play
would make the answer unpayable. #148 found why it still was not working, #149 checked the judgement
half, #152 narrowed it to answers with something to point at, and #218 corrected it for foretell.
Five tasks. The doc never moved.

**And the document contradicted itself**, which is what makes this worse than a stale line: Tidal
Mind's entry under *Thirteen starter decks* carries the measured windows for exactly this rule —
44% cast against 41% could-not-pay, where they read 7% and 87% before the fix — and names
`reserveForAnswers: false` as the switch that puts the old version back. A reader meeting the
summary first would conclude the opponent taps out; a reader meeting the deck entry first would
conclude it does not. Nothing in the file said which was current.

**The other two claims are true, and were being sold wrong.** It really does not hold a creature
back to block and really does not search your reply — but neither is an undone feature. Both were
built and measured and taken out: D110 for the reply, and for blockers a scoring bonus for an
untapped creature that moved nothing at one point, **cost 26 games in 400 at two points**, and made
the bot worse at four. In this pool attacking is right. "Not done" and "done, measured, and reverted
because it lost games" are different facts about a program, and only one of them invites somebody to
go and fix it.

**The pace figures matched no measurement.** The doc said "under a millisecond a decision in a duel
and about five in a four-seat pod". The recorded soak is D96: 200 unsteered four-seat pods, 89,188
decisions, **2ms at the median, 7.6ms mean, p99 65ms**, and one decision in ninety thousand over two
seconds. Not far out in magnitude, and not a number anybody had measured. Both paragraphs now carry
the measured ones and say where they come from, and the tail is named rather than averaged away.

No guard for this one. #265's guard works because deck names and counts are structured data a script
can parse out of `starterDecks.ts`; "does the bot hold mana up" is a default on an options interface
that prose has to describe in a sentence, and a guard that pattern-matched the sentence would fail
the first time somebody rephrased it. What the paragraph carries instead is the symbol name
(`reserveForAnswers`), the file, and the decision numbers — so the next person to change the default
has a string to grep for.

## D292 — A drawn game: written twice, reachable by one card, asserted nowhere

The engine has always been able to end a game with nobody winning. `engine.ts` finishes when
`alive.length <= 1`, and when the last two players die together `alive[0]` is undefined, so
`winnerSeat` is null. `rematch` knows about it too: it reads a null winner as "a draw, or a game
nobody finished" and hands the first turn back to `activeSeat` instead of to the seat after the
winner. Two branches, both deliberate, neither with a test.

**Why it had none is the interesting part.** A draw cannot be built out of the actions a test
usually reaches for. `life:adjust` takes one seat at a time, so the first adjustment to nought
finishes the game before the second one lands; conceding every seat does not work either, because
the last concede arrives at a game that is already over and is refused. The only way into the state
is **one effect that kills both players at once** — and in this pool that is Hurricane, which deals
X damage to each creature with flying *and each player*. The card has been in three decks since it
was written and its symmetry was tested; what was never tested is the symmetry going all the way.

So: two tests, off a shared `drawnByHurricane()`. Both seats to 3 life, Hurricane for X=3.

**`[0, 0]` is the assertion that makes it a simultaneous loss rather than merely a fatal one.** If
the seats had died one after the other, the second would still be sitting on 3 when the game ended
and every other line in the test would read exactly the same — `finished`, `eliminated` on both,
`winnerSeat` null. That is the same trap as D290's graveyard count, caught this time before the test
was written rather than after.

**The rematch half was proved by breaking it.** Replacing the branch with
`((winnerSeat ?? 0) + 1) % seats` — the obvious wrong implementation, which treats a draw as a win
for seat zero — makes the test fail with "expected 1 to be +0". So this one discriminates, which is
worth saying out loud two decisions after one that did not.

Nothing in the engine changed. Both rules were already right; what was missing was anything that
would notice if they stopped being.

## D293 — The laptop pair was post-game, and the mid-game answer is the same one

D266 refuted #249's premise with two readings at 1440x800: a duel is **1.16 screens** and its two
creature rows sit inside **229px of the 800px viewport**, so both boards are on the screen together
with room to spare. The pod answered the same way at 1.41 screens and 331px for four rows. Those
numbers have guarded the question since.

**They are all taken post-game**, after the last creature has died, and the question is a mid-game
one. The gap went unnoticed for the reason comfortable numbers always hide things: 229px of 800 is
so far inside the viewport that nobody asked whether a board with cards on it still fits. The
e2e-solo comment says in as many words that a mid-game board is taller — it quotes 2.88-3.21 screens
for a mid-game pod against a 2.35 post-game budget — so the height half was known. The **creature-row
span** half, which that same comment calls "the actual question", had no mid-game reading at all.

Measured out of band, three times, on real solo duels driven to mid-game at 1440x900:

| | run 1 | run 2 | run 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| page height | 1.59 screens | 1.33 | 1.59 |
| both creature rows | 568px | 331px | 568px |
| rows *plus* the hand | 1019px | 782px | 1019px |

**Both boards fit mid-game, every time**, inside a 900px viewport with 332-569px to spare. So
D266's conclusion holds where it actually matters, and this is a confirmation rather than a
correction. Runs 1 and 3 agree to the pixel and run 2 is a shorter game, which is the spread a
board-dependent reading should have.

Two things worth separating, because I nearly conflated them and that is how #249 went wrong in the
first place. The span of the **creature rows** is D266's question and it fits. The span of the rows
*plus your hand* is a different and weaker question — it fails in two of the three runs at 1019px
of 900 — and nothing has ever claimed it fits. Reading the second number as though it answered the
first is exactly the move that produced #249's confident false premise from a screenshot, and I made
it for about a minute before checking what D266 had actually measured.

**Nothing shipped but the readings.** No budget was added: the comment in `e2e-solo.mjs` already
rules that mid-game budgets wait on somebody deciding the mid-game table is too tall, that two more
budgets buy a guard against a regression in something nobody has called wrong, and that the existing
1.3 and 2.35 must not be raised to accommodate a mid-game number. All of that still holds. What
changes is that the decision now has figures under it instead of none.

**The instrument is in the tree** as `scripts/measure/table-fold.mjs`, because a reading nobody
can reproduce is not a measurement. It needs `node scripts/play.mjs` running, which makes it the
first browser-driven file in `scripts/measure/` — it belongs there rather than beside the `e2e-*`
suites because it asserts nothing and sets no budget; it reports. Run from its repo path it gave a
fourth reading consistent with the three above: **1.60 screens, both creature rows 568px of 900,
rows plus the hand 992px.**

**And the screenshots the suites take cannot answer this.** `shot()` captures `fullPage: true`,
which renders the sticky control bar at the viewport's bottom edge with the rest of the page
stitched below it — so a full-page capture shows the bar floating in the middle of the image with
content underneath, which is not what a player sees. That is harmless, because every geometry claim
in these suites is measured in the DOM with `getBoundingClientRect` against `innerHeight` rather
than read off a picture. It is worth knowing before anybody tries to settle a layout question by
looking at `e2e-shots/`.

## D294 — The clock's pod win rate at the planned sample: +4.2 points, and 1.35 sigma

#268 was scoped at 1040 pods an arm, chosen against D281's floor. That sample is now spent, in nine
disjoint chunks accumulated across three container restarts, and the answer is **542-498 of 1040
pods — +4.2 points at 1.35 sigma**, which does not clear a 2 sigma bar.

| seeds | margin | pods |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3300-3325 | −8 | 104 |
| 7700-7725 | +20 | 104 |
| 11100-11112 | +4 | 52 |
| 3326-3351 | −12 | 104 |
| 7726-7751 | +8 | 104 |
| 11113-11138 | +8 | 104 |
| 3352-3390 | +4 | 156 |
| 7752-7790 | −4 | 156 |
| 11139-11177 | +24 | 156 |
| **total** | **+44** | **1040** |

Six chunks positive, three negative. The running point margin was +4.8 at 572 pods, +4.5 at 884,
+4.7 at 936, +4.0 at 988 and +4.2 at 1040 — **stable to within a point across the last four hundred
pods**, which is what a small real effect looks like rather than a margin wandering towards zero.

**The sample was sized against the floor, not against the effect, and that is the finding.** D281's
floor says a 104-pod reading carries about ±16 pods, and 1040 was picked so the floor would narrow
to roughly ±5 points. It does — but an effect of +4.2 points sits just *inside* ±5, so the planned
sample could never have resolved it either way. The arithmetic, which is worth having written down
before the next long reading is planned:

| pods | null SD | what +4.2 points reads as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1040 | 3.10 pts | 1.35 sigma |
| 1500 | 2.58 pts | 1.63 sigma |
| 2000 | 2.24 pts | 1.88 sigma |
| **2267** | **2.10 pts** | **2.00 sigma** |

So resolving the sign at 2 sigma needs about **2267 pods an arm**, 2.2x what was planned. Plan a
sample against the effect you expect, not against the floor of the instrument: the floor tells you
what you can *disbelieve*, and the effect size tells you what you need to *detect*.

**Nothing changes about what ships.** `clockRate` stays at 0, exactly as D281 left it, and now for
a reason with a number under it rather than for want of one: its pod effect is small, leans
positive, and is not resolved. That is a materially better position than D258's retracted −3.8 and
D281's "unmeasured", and it is not the same thing as "the term helps".

The run is continuing past the planned sample while the machine is free, so this entry records the
reading **at 1040** specifically. Anything further is an extension of it, and the pods actually
played are quoted either way (D281).

## D295 — D294 corrected: the clock's pod effect regressed to zero, and the planned sample would have lied

D294, committed about half an hour ago, reported the clock's pod win rate at the planned 1040-pod
sample as **+4.2 points at 1.35 sigma** and described it as "small, leans positive". **That
description is withdrawn.** The run continued past the planned sample and the margin collapsed:

| pods | 572 | 884 | 1040 | 1144 | 1248 | 1352 | 1508 | 1664 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| points | +4.8 | +4.5 | **+4.2** | +4.5 | +4.2 | +3.3 | +2.7 | **+0.7** |
| sigma | 1.00 | 1.35 | **1.35** | 1.54 | 1.47 | 1.20 | 1.03 | **0.29** |

838-826 of 1664 pods. Sigma peaked at 1.54 around 1144 and has fallen since. **That is the shape of
a null, and it is distinguishable from a real effect by exactly this test:** a true +4 point effect
makes sigma climb monotonically with the square root of the sample, because the margin holds while
the floor narrows. A null makes the point margin decay as 1/sqrt(N) while sigma wanders without
trend. The second is what happened.

**The planned sample would have produced a misleading answer, and this is the finding worth
keeping.** 1040 pods was not merely *inconclusive* — stopping there would have reported a positive
lean that four hundred more pods erased. D294 is the artefact of that: an entry written in good
faith, with correct arithmetic, off a sample that had not yet regressed. It is left in the log
rather than edited, because the pair is the lesson.

**And I compounded it twice before the data corrected me.** I called the margin "stable to within a
point across the last four hundred pods" when it had been drifting down, and then observed that a
confirmed positive would mean *turning the term on* rather than leaving it off — which was true as
a conditional and wrong as an emphasis, since the premise was a 1.47 sigma reading. That is the
error D258 was retracted for, made again, in the same session that wrote D281's floor into the
README. Reading a direction off a sub-2-sigma number is apparently not a lesson one learns once.

**What this settles.** `clockRate` stays at 0 — the same decision D281 made, now resting on a
measurement rather than on an absence of one. The term is +1.5 points in a duel (D275/D276, never
retracted) and **indistinguishable from zero in a pod across 1664 paired pods**. The pod and duel
answers differ, which is the thing D280's mechanism predicted, though "no pod effect" is a weaker
claim than "negative pod effect" and nothing here supports the latter.

The run continued to about 2267 pods, the sample at which a +4.2 point effect would have read
2 sigma, so that the null could be quoted as a **bound** rather than as an absence.

### The answer, at the pre-stated sample: 1140-1140

**Dead even. 2280 decided pods, a margin of zero, 0.00 sigma.** Seventeen disjoint chunks:

| pods | 572 | 1040 | 1352 | 1664 | 1818 | 1974 | 2130 | **2280** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| points | +4.8 | +4.2 | +3.3 | +0.7 | +0.6 | −0.1 | +1.0 | **0.00** |
| sigma | 1.00 | 1.35 | 1.20 | 0.29 | 0.23 | −0.05 | 0.48 | **0.00** |

So the result is not "too small to see". It is **zero, to the pod, across 2280 paired pods**, with a
2 sigma bound of **±4.2 points**: whatever the clock does at four seats, it is smaller than that,
and the best estimate of it is nothing at all.

**`clockRate` stays at 0, and the question opened at D258 is closed.** The term is +1.5 points in a
duel (D275/D276) and exactly nothing in a pod. D280's mechanism — that caution pays at two seats
and not at four — survives as the explanation for *why* the duel and pod answers differ, but the
pod half of it is "no effect" rather than "a penalty": D258's −3.8 was retracted at D281 and
nothing since has supported a negative sign either.

**Two methodological findings, which outlast the number.**

The first is the one D294 and this entry exist as a pair to show: **a sample sized against the
instrument's floor is not sized against the effect.** 1040 pods was chosen so the floor would narrow
to ±5 points, and it did — but it reported +4.2 and a positive lean that 1240 more pods erased
completely. The floor tells you what you may disbelieve; only an effect-size target tells you what
you can detect. Every long reading planned from here gets a target.

The second is a test worth reusing: **watch sigma, not the margin.** A real effect holds its point
margin while the floor narrows, so sigma climbs monotonically with the square root of the sample.
A null decays as 1/sqrt(N) while sigma wanders. Sigma here peaked at 1.54 around 1144 pods and fell
away, which identified the null about six hundred pods before the margin reached zero — and would
have identified it even if the run had been stopped early, had anyone been reading that column.

One further chunk (seeds 7869+) was still running when this was written and is recorded in the
ledger afterwards; at a margin of zero over 2280 pods it cannot change the conclusion, and 2280 is
quoted because that is the sample the target named.

**It landed at 76-78, and did not:** eighteen chunks, **1216-1218 of 2434 decided pods, −0.08
points, −0.04 sigma, bound ±4.1 points.** The pre-registered figure and the everything-we-ran
figure agree to within a tenth of a point, which is the last thing a null needs to say for itself.

**And the calibration still reads the way D241 and D244 left it**, re-run on the current engine
after the `exposedPower` fix and the `castable` term: 62% sign accuracy at turns 5-8 (D244 recorded
61%), hand at 44% there and 38% at turns 9-12 (D241 recorded 42-46% mid-game). So nothing about the
clock measurement moved the function's shape, and the diagnosis that the next gain is *a term that
sees something new* rather than a weight stands untouched. Two things in that table are worth a
future reader's attention and neither is acted on here: turns 1-4 read **51% with 574 of 1248
samples exactly tied**, which may be honest — a turn-three board often genuinely is undetermined —
and `hand` is still the one component that points the wrong way while being inert (D243), which is
the pair that produced `castable` and may yet produce its mirror.

## D296 — Neither leverage nor calibration names the next term, and each has now produced a counterexample

#274 asked for the next evaluation term to be **chosen from leverage and calibration rather than
guessed**, which was the whole point of building the two instruments. Both halves are now run on the
current engine, and the honest answer is that the premise does not hold.

**The leverage field, measured:** 312 duels, two passes over the field, 34,262 decisions, 1763s.

| term | changed | of all | ships at |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `creature` | 2195 | 6.4% | its own weight |
| `life` | 794 | 2.3% | its own weight |
| `clockCycle` | 731 | 2.1% | zero |
| `clockRate` | 731 | 2.1% | zero |
| `exposed` | 519 | 1.5% | zero |
| `castable` | 353 | 1.0% | 1 |
| `permanent` | 326 | 1.0% | its own weight |
| `hand` | 304 | 0.9% | its own weight |
| `clockTurns` | 219 | 0.6% | zero |
| `library` | 85 | 0.2% | its own weight |
| `land` | 30 | 0.1% | its own weight |
| (control: no override) | 0 | 0.0% | — |

The control held at exactly zero, which is what makes the rest of the column terms rather than
plumbing. `clockCycle` and `clockRate` read the **same 731, to the decision** — the divisor is
`/ opponents` and a duel has one — so that pair is the arm's own positive control, and also the
table's one blind spot. More on that below.

**The two counterexamples, one from each instrument.**

- **`castable` has the weakest calibration of any shipped term and earned games anyway.** Over 1248
  samples it reads 51 / 52 / 53 / 54 / 54 / 48 across the six turn bands, against `life` and `board`
  at 51-70. It still earned **+1.35 points** over three disjoint seed sets, which is why it ships at
  1 (D271).
- **`clockRate` has the third-highest leverage of the eleven terms and earned nothing.** 2.1% of all
  decisions, 13.0% of blocks — and **0.00 sigma over 2434 decided pods** (D294/D295), with a 2 sigma
  bound of ±4.1 points.

So a high leverage reading is not evidence a term would earn games, and a weak calibration is not
evidence it would not. The reason is D243's, now visible from both ends: **leverage says a term can
move a decision and says nothing about whether the decision it moves is the better one; calibration
ranks the players and a search never asks it to.**

**What that does and does not mean for the instruments.** Both stay, and both stay worth running:
leverage is how `hand` was found to be inert while looking mispriced (D243), and the pair of them is
how `castable` was identified as the right *shape* for the question `hand` was asking the wrong way
(D271). What changes is what a reading licenses. **A reading from either is a reason to spend a win
rate on a term, never a substitute for having spent one.** Four terms have been deleted after
measurement (D116) and two of the three readings since have disagreed with their own instrument;
the only thing that has ever predicted a win rate in this engine is a win rate.

**So #274 closes with no term named**, which is the result rather than a failure to produce one. The
standing diagnosis from D241 and D295 is unchanged: the next gain is a term that **sees something
new**, and no ranking of the terms that already exist can point at one that does not.

**One thing is still open, and it is the thing this table cannot see.** `clockCycle` differs from
`clockRate` only where there is more than one opponent, and `term-leverage` plays duels — the 731
above is a divisor of one, not the term. A pod arm for that instrument is the cheap screen to run
before another two thousand pods go on the clock family, and it does not exist: `PLAYERS` in that
file is two seats. Recorded rather than built, because the clock family has had its win rate spent
and nothing is waiting on the answer.

## D297 — A player who left the game kept their whole board, and in a pod that was every game

The engine did not enforce CR 800.4a at all. A seat eliminated on turn nine left everything it
owned on the table: creatures on the battlefield, cards in hand, a library, a graveyard. Three
seats are eliminated in every pod that reaches a winner, so **every pod this engine has ever played
finished with up to three abandoned boards still in play.**

**Found by probe, not by a test, and that is the point.** Nothing in the suite asked the question.
What found it was building a four-seat pod, killing a seat with a creature on the battlefield, and
reading the zones back:

    seat 1 eliminated: true life
    battlefield still holds the creature: true   hand: 7 (was 7)   library: 52 (was 52)

and then asking what a live player could point at: a Lightning Bolt in seat 0's hand listed the
dead seat's creature among its legal targets. That is a play the table offers and the rules do not.

**Half the rule was already holding, by accident.** A dead seat's *abilities* never fire, because
`raise` collects its watchers through `apnapSeats`, which filters eliminated seats. Verified both
ways: a dead player's Chalice of the Void counters nothing, and the same board with its controller
alive counters the spell. So the visible half — a dead player's permanents still *doing* things —
has been correct for as long as `apnapSeats` has existed, and what was left behind was the objects
themselves. **A rule can be half-enforced by a function written for something else, and the half
that holds is the half you would have noticed.**

**What `leaveTheGame` does.** Objects the seat *owns* leave the game wherever they are; a permanent
it controlled without owning is exiled to its owner, which is the rule's own last clause and is
reachable only through `card:control` on a manual table. Spells and abilities it controlled come off
the stack. Its continuous effects and delayed triggers go with it. Live cards that were attached or
paired to a departed one stop pointing at it. Anything it was holding in exile "until this leaves
the battlefield" is handed back first, while `exiledBy` still has something to look up — otherwise a
live player's creature taken by a departing Journey to Nowhere would sit in exile for the rest of
the game with the permanent that could return it deleted.

**Two corrections during the work, both from tests rather than from thinking harder.**

The first: `playout.test.ts` died inside a minute with *"that ability is no longer on the stack"*. A
trigger of the departing player's was on the stack with its controller being asked for targets, and
removing the stack object left `pendingChoice` pointing at an id that no longer existed. **The state
that references an object is part of what has to go with it**, and only a real game found the
reference. Each pending question is now cleared on its own referent rather than on the seat, because
a live player can be mid-answer on their own ability — that stack object stays, so the question does.
