The second is a scope correction, and it came from the decking test: **the rule must not apply once
the game is over.** CR 800.4 is a multiplayer rule; it exists because the game continues after
somebody loses. A two-player game ends the moment one player loses (CR 104.2a), so there is no game
left for anything to leave — and emptying the loser's zones there deletes the final board the table
is still showing, which D252 decided stays up. The same holds for the last elimination in a pod. So
the departure is gated on more than one seat surviving, and a player who decks out in a duel still
has their ten milled cards in the graveyard for the test, and the player, to look at.

**The cost, stated rather than discovered later: every pod figure in `scripts/measure/` predates
this.** D294/D295's 2434 pods included. It retracts nothing — a null measured on a different engine
is still a null about that engine — but a number from before this commit and a number from after it
are not the same measurement, and a comparison spanning it is not a paired one. Both `pod-duel.mjs`
and `pod-unfinished.mjs` now say so in their docblocks, because the next person to compare across it
will not have read this entry.

## D298 — The eight undecided pods were ten, six of them are one engine throw, and four cannot be replayed

`pod-duel` ends its move loop with five distinct causes collapsed into one silent `break`, reported
only as `(N unfinished)`. #268 spent 2444 pods on the clock and ten of them ended that way.
`pod-unfinished.mjs` replays those exact seeds, arms and seating and names each cause, with a
non-zero exit if any is a throw — because a throw is the engine refusing an action the bot built out
of its own `legalActions`, which is an invariant `playout.test.ts` asserts never breaks.

**First, a correction to my own arithmetic.** I said eight undecided pods of 2442. The ledger's three
annotated chunks are 2, 6 and 2, so it is **ten undecided of 2444 played**. The decided total is
2434 either way, which is the figure D295 quotes and computes on, so nothing in that conclusion
moves; the number I got wrong was the one I stated in passing rather than the one I measured.

**Six of the ten reproduce, and every one of them is the same throw.**

| chunk | ledger | replayed | cause |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7830-7868 | 2 | **2** | `pact:offer: seat 2 has been eliminated` — seed 7830, shifts 1 and 3, turn 29 |
| 11217-11255 | 6 | **4** | `pact:offer: seat 1 has been eliminated` — seed 11253, all four shifts, turn 26 |
| 7869-7907 | 2 | **0** | — |

Not the move cap, not a seat with nothing to do: **the engine refusing a deal the bot offered on
behalf of a player who had left the game.** Isolated by probe (#277): `seatsToAct` returns
`[state.pendingX.seat]` for all six pending questions with no elimination check, so a question
outstanding on a seat that is then eliminated makes the engine name a dead seat as the one it is
waiting on. Driving the bot for that seat produces a refused action in three of five cases —
`pendingChoice` to `auto:choose`, `pendingPayment` to `auto:pay`, and `pendingOfferedCast` to
`pact:offer`, which is the one the pods hit. The pact falls out because a dead seat's life is 0, so
`openPower(foe) < life` is false for every foe and `offerPact` always finds one.

**The conclusion it was asked to protect survives.** The throws *removed* games rather than
mis-scoring any: all ten were excluded from the denominator, so the margin was never computed on
them. What a throw can do is end a game that would have been decided, and that is bounded by
10 of 2444 — **0.4 percentage points**, against a 2 sigma bound of ±4.1. D295 stands.

**Four cannot be replayed, and that is the finding worth keeping.** Two of chunk 11217's six and
both of chunk 7869's do not reproduce on the current build. The candidates are an engine difference
between when those chunks ran and now, or an `ALWAYS=` setting on those runs that seated a deck the
replay does not — and **neither is checkable, because the ledger records seeds and margins and
nothing else.** A chunk row carries no arms, no build, no environment. So a long accumulated
measurement has rows in it that cannot be audited, which is the same class of problem as a harness
that swallows a throw: the number survives and the thing that would let you check it does not.
What the ledger needs, before the next long run, is the arm JSON, the commit, and the full command
per row. Recorded rather than retrofitted — the rows that exist cannot be given a provenance they
were never asked for.

**And a replay is only a replay of the build the figures came from.** These six were reproduced on an
engine that did not yet enforce CR 800.4a (D297); that commit changes the back half of every pod, so
the same seeds now play different games. `pod-unfinished.mjs` says so in its docblock, and the result
above is quoted with the build it was taken at rather than as a standing fact.

## D299 — The engine was waiting on players who had left, and a harness found it before a test did

D298 traced six of #268's ten undecided pods to one throw: `pact:offer: seat N has been eliminated`,
the engine refusing an action the bot had built out of its own rules. This is the fix, and the
mechanism is more general than the card that surfaced it.

**`seatsToAct` reads a seat off whichever question is outstanding, and none of its six branches
asked whether that seat was still in the game.** `pendingDecision`, `pendingChoice`,
`pendingPayment`, `pendingDredge`, `pendingOfferedCast`, `pendingDiscard` — each returns
`[state.pendingX.seat]`. So a question standing on a seat that was then eliminated made the engine
report a dead player as the one it was waiting on, and any caller that drives bots acted for them.

**Three of the five produce an action the engine refuses, and two produce one it accepts**, which is
the worse half. Measured by probe, one pending at a time on a departed seat:

| outstanding | the bot's move | the engine |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pendingChoice` | `auto:choose` | refuses: "that ability is no longer on the stack" |
| `pendingPayment` | `auto:pay` | refuses: "cannot pay {2}" |
| `pendingOfferedCast` | `pact:offer` | refuses: "seat 2 has been eliminated" |
| `pendingDecision` | `auto:decide` | **accepts** |
| `pendingDredge` | `auto:dredge` | **accepts** |

`offerPact` was where it surfaced rather than the cause. A departed seat's life is 0, so
`openPower(foe) < life` is false for every opponent and the rule always finds somebody to ask peace
of — which means **any** fall-through for a dead seat produced an offer. The two rows the engine
accepts are the reason this is not simply "fix `offerPact`": a dead player answering a dredge is
silent, and a silent wrong answer is what a throw at least had the decency not to be.

**Both halves of the fix, and why both.**

`resolveStateBasedActions` **withdraws** a question whose seat has left. A decision is *resumed*
rather than dropped, because the rest of its plan belongs to other players — "each player sacrifices
a creature" has to carry on round the table — and `answerDecision` with an empty answer is exactly
what `askOrFinish` already does for a seat eliminated *between* two questions. The other five carry
no continuation, so withdrawing them is the whole of it, and the pass that hands priority back
whenever nothing is blocking the game turns the withdrawal into a table that moves.

`seatsToAct` and `botAction` **guard** anyway: nothing names a departed seat, and nothing acts for
one. In a correct engine neither guard ever fires. They are there because **the two failure modes
are not equivalent.** A question that slips past the withdrawal becomes a table with nobody to act —
which every harness in `scripts/measure/` reports and `playout.test.ts` asserts against. Unfiltered,
the same question becomes the engine refusing an action it offered: a throw that 35 harnesses
swallow in silence (D282). One of those is findable and the other is not, so the guard converts the
unfindable fault into the findable one.

**The lesson is about where the bug was found.** This is the first engine bug a *measuring* harness
caught before a test did, and it only caught it because #275 built the thing that reads the silence —
`pod-duel` had been printing `(N unfinished)` over it for 2444 pods. The counterpart is that the
regression test cannot be written from the seeds that found it: two specific pods out of 2444, and
D297 changed the back half of every pod, so those seeds no longer reproduce. So the test puts each of
the six questions on a departed seat directly and asserts both halves — the engine does not name the
seat, and the next action withdraws the question. **A test built from the seed that found a bug would
have asserted nothing by the following commit; a test built from the mechanism asserts it for good.**

## D300 — The instrument prints its own provenance, because the instruction to write it down got skipped

D298 found four pod rows in the clock ledger that could not be replayed and could not be explained:
the candidates were an engine difference between those runs and now, or an `ALWAYS=` setting on
them, and **neither was checkable, because a row recorded seeds and a margin and nothing else.**
Recording that gap in a decision entry is not a fix. This is the fix.

`pod-duel` and `pod-unfinished` now print one line before the first pod:

    [bb02069 clean, dist built 2026-11-03T05:55:24Z] SEED0=3300 SEEDS=3 ALWAYS= MOVES=8000 TESTED={"weights":{"clockRate":1}} CONTROL={}

Four things, each there because leaving it out loses something:

- **The arms, as JSON** — what the margin is *about*, and the easiest thing to lose. A margin with
  no arm beside it is a number with no question.
- **Every input that changes which games are played** — `SEED0`, `SEEDS`, `ALWAYS`, `MOVES`. Named
  by the caller rather than swept out of `process.env`, so a renamed variable shows up as a changed
  line instead of being silently dropped.
- **The commit, and whether the tree was dirty.** A hash pins the build only when the tree is
  clean, and `DIRTY` says outright that it does not — a more useful thing to read six weeks later
  than a hash that quietly means less than it looks like it means.
- **When `dist` was built.** These harnesses import the built engine, not the source, so a stale
  `dist` is a run of code the commit does not describe. The mtime is the only thing that catches it.

**The point is where the line comes from.** `pod-duel`'s docblock has carried an instruction to
quote the floor beside any number from it since D281, and the lesson recorded there — *"a
precondition stated as homework gets skipped; a number in the docblock does not"* — is exactly what
happened again one level up: the ledger's header explains the denominator rule carefully and says
nothing about arms or builds, so nobody wrote them down. **A line the instrument prints is a line
the ledger cannot omit.** The same reasoning that moved the floor from an instruction into the
docblock moves the provenance from a convention into stdout.

Printed *first*, before the pods, so a run killed halfway still says what it was — the same reason
the per-pass checkpoint exists (D289). And the helper lives in `scripts/lib/` rather than
`scripts/measure/`, because the README lists that directory as the instruments and a helper sitting
in it reads as one.

**Not retrofitted.** The eighteen rows that already exist cannot be given a provenance they were
never asked for, and D298 says so. What changes is that the next long run has one.

## D301 — An Overrun was pumping creatures cast after it resolved (CR 611.2c)

The rules audit that produced #269, #270, #272, #276 and #277 kept going, and the next CR area the
engine had never been checked against was **611 — continuous effects**, which is cited nowhere in
the source. The gap it found is one of the oldest cards in the pool doing the wrong thing.

Overrun — "creatures you control get +3/+3 and gain trample until end of turn" — resolved with a
single 2/2 on the board, which correctly read 5/5. A **Centaur Courser put onto the battlefield
afterwards read 6/6**, off a printed 3/3, with trample. CR 611.2c: a continuous effect created by a
resolved spell or ability applies only to the permanents that were on the battlefield when the
effect was created, and does not pick up permanents that arrive later. Only an effect from a
**static** ability (CR 611.3) is dynamic.

**The cause is the shape of the fix, not a missing check.** `pumpTeam` and `pumpAll` pushed
`scope: { kind: 'controller-creatures' }` and `{ kind: 'all-creatures' }`, and a scope in this engine
is **re-read on every characteristics lookup** — which is exactly right for Glorious Anthem and
exactly wrong for a spell that has already resolved. There was no branch to add; the scope was being
asked a question it answers the same way for two cases the rules distinguish.

**`duration` is the discriminator, and it is honest rather than convenient.** `'permanent'` is the
duration `staticEffect` uses and the only one a static ability has; every other duration — end of
turn, end of combat, until your next turn — exists *because something resolved to create it*. So a
permanent duration keeps the dynamic scope and anything else resolves to an id list at creation,
through `pump`, which has carried `{ kind: 'cards' }` since it was written. **Reading the scope was
the wrong place to look for this, which is why it survived: the two cases were never distinguishable
from the scope.**

**The sweeps are where it changed games rather than numbers.** After a Toxic Deluge — "all creatures
get −X/−X until end of turn" — a player is entitled to rebuild that turn. With a dynamic scope every
creature they cast afterwards arrived already shrunk, and a 1/1 entering under a −2/−2 is a dead
creature on arrival. That is a different card, not a different figure, and it has been the pool's
behaviour since `pumpAll` was written.

**The test's second half is the one that makes it a test of the rule.** An implementation that simply
locked every scope would pass "Overrun does not reach the later creature" and quietly break Glorious
Anthem, so the anthem case is asserted beside it: nothing on the board when the enchantment arrives,
a creature cast afterwards, pumped anyway. Same lesson as D290 — the assertion has to be able to
fail for the wrong fix as well as the right one.

**One thing this does not fix, inherited from `pump` rather than introduced here:** a creature that
dies and comes back is a new object (CR 400.7) and should be outside the locked set, but `relocate`
keeps its instance id, so an id list still reaches it. That has been true of every "target creature
gets +3/+3" in the pool from the beginning. It wants an object identity the engine does not have, and
pretending an id is one would be the kind of silent wrongness this entry is about.

**The fix broke one existing test, and which way round matters.** `scripts.test.ts`'s "carries every
option through every builder" built its four effects from a card in the **library** — so once
`pumpTeam` and `pumpAll` lock to the creatures actually on the battlefield, two of the four correctly
produced nothing and the test's `effects.length === 1` failed. **The setup was wrong, not the
assertion**: what that test is for is that every option survives each builder, and two of the
builders now need a board to have anything to apply to. So a creature went onto the battlefield, and
the fact the failure exposed became its own test beside it — an empty board builds no effect at all,
rather than one waiting to catch whatever is cast next, and a static ability still builds one. A
failing test after a rules fix is a question about which of the two is wrong, and answering it the
lazy way round is how a fix becomes a regression.

**And it is the second engine change this session that moves every pod figure.** D297 changed what a
dead player leaves behind; this changes what a sweep reaches. A pod number taken before either is not
comparable with one taken after, and `pod-duel.mjs` now names both.

## D302 — "197 checks clean" was never a number, and the suites now say so themselves

Two engine changes landed in one session that both move mid-game state — CR 800.4a (D297) and
CR 611.2c (D301) — so the four Playwright suites were re-run, because #245 established that they sit
outside every automated gate and they are the only checks that answer the question the Play Realm
exists for: can two people sit down and play a whole game through the real UI.

**All four pass.** `e2e-table` 73/73, `e2e-solo` 27/27, `e2e-pod` 41/41, `e2e-arena` 55/55, every
check green, all four exit 0.

**That totals 196, and #260's title says 197.** The interesting part is what the one is.

Three consecutive `e2e-arena` runs on the same build read **55, 53 and 55**. The suite is unchanged
since well before #260 and nothing failed in any of them: it has a dozen checks gated on whether the
game it drives actually produced the mechanic — a ward, a flashback, a block, an {X} spell, a
dividing spell — and each already printed a careful parenthetical saying so. **The total is a
property of the game that happened, not of the suite.** So 196 and 197 were never comparable, and
#260 recorded a denominator that does not exist.

**This is the third time the same mistake has been found in this project wearing different clothes.**
D281: a floor quoted in pods read as though it were a floor in points. D298: a ledger row with a
margin and no provenance, four of which turned out to be unreplayable. Now a check total read as a
constant. Each time a number that moves was written down as though it were fixed, and each time the
cost was paid by a later reader rather than the person who wrote it.

**The fix is the same shape as #278's, and it was almost free, because the suites were already
honest — they just were not counted.** Every one of those parentheticals is now a `skip(why)` that
goes into a list, and `summarize` prints the pair:

    54/54 checks passed, 4 skipped. Screenshots in e2e-shots/arena/

    Not exercised this run — the game did not produce it:
      - no ward came up in this game — scripts.test.ts asserts all three of its outcomes deterministically
      - no X spell came up in this game — scripts.test.ts covers that path on a fixed board
      …

Eleven sites in `e2e-arena`, nine in `e2e-pod`, four in `e2e-solo`. **A total with its skips beside
it can be compared; a bare total cannot.** And the count is now informative in the other direction
too: 54 passed with 4 skipped says the suite attempted 58, so the run that read 53 skipped five, and
the question "is the number down because something broke" is answered by the output instead of by an
investigation.

A skip is deliberately not a failure and does not touch the exit code. What it is for is the ten
seconds in which somebody decides whether a dropped number matters.

## D303 — The player doc now carries the two rules that changed under it

#271 is the reason this is a task rather than an afterthought: that entry found the player
documentation telling players the opponent *cannot* hold mana up for a counterspell, 130 decisions
after it learned to, and the document contradicted itself in a way a reader had no way to catch.
Two rules changed in the engine today, both visible from a chair at the table, so the doc gets them
before it drifts again.

**CR 611.2c, in the Toxic Deluge row.** A sweeper's −X/−X reaches the creatures that were on the
battlefield when it resolved and nothing that arrives later, so a 1/1 cast into a −2/−2 board is a
live 1/1. That is a play decision, not a technicality — it is what makes rebuilding on the same turn
an option — and the row now says so, with the contrast that makes it memorable: a static effect like
a Glorious Anthem *does* reach whatever turns up next.

**CR 800.4a, as a new row about a seat being knocked out of a pod.** Their whole side goes with them:
battlefield, hand, library, graveyard, and any spell of theirs still on the stack. Two consequences
worth a player's attention — a permanent of theirs that was doing something to *you* stops (their
Chalice stops countering your one-drops), and a creature of yours they were holding with a Journey
to Nowhere comes back, because the thing holding it has left. Nothing hits a graveyard on the way
out, so nothing triggers. And in a duel none of it applies, because one player losing ends the game
and the final board stays up.

**Every claim in both rows is something implemented and tested in this branch rather than inferred
from the rules.** The spell-off-the-stack, the returned creature and the duel case each have a test;
the Chalice and the anthem follow from the permanent being gone. That distinction is the whole point
of writing the doc from the engine rather than from the CR: the rules say what *should* happen, and a
player at this table needs to know what *does*.

## D304 — A pump survived a blink, and D301 was wrong about what the fix needed

D301 closed the CR 611.2c fix with a limitation stated and deliberately not acted on: a creature that
dies and comes back is a new object (CR 400.7), but `relocate` keeps its instance id, so an effect
locked to `{ kind: 'cards', ids }` finds it again — and that entry said the problem "wants an object
identity the engine does not have". **That was the wrong diagnosis, and probing it took five
minutes.**

**It is reachable with two cards in one deck.** Verdant Guard runs Giant Growth and Cloudshift. Pump
a Grizzly Bears to 5/5, blink it, and it came back **still 5/5**. Cloudshift is a card players reach
for *as a trick*, so the engine was making it strictly better than printed: keep the pump, dodge the
removal, re-trigger the entry. The same hole applied to goad, to an Overrun, and to anything else
scoped by id.

**And it did not need object identity.** What a continuous effect needs is to stop applying when the
object it was locked onto stops existing, and the engine already knows exactly when that happens: it
is the moment a permanent gets a `vanished` snapshot. So a departing permanent's id is taken out of
every `cards` scope, and the effect is dropped only when its **last** subject has gone — because one
creature leaving an Overrun must not un-pump the other two, which is the second test and the one
that makes this a test of the rule rather than of a deletion.

**Where it sits is the interesting part, and the honest version of it is smaller than the first draft
I wrote.** The strip runs beside the `vanished` clear in `settle`, not in `relocate`, and my first
docblock justified that by saying a leave-the-battlefield trigger reading the dying creature's
*power* would otherwise get the unpumped number (CR 608.2h). That reasoning is right and the reader
does not exist: the only script in the pool that reads a `vanished` instance is unearth's
leave-replacement, and it reads a **counter**, which lives on the snapshot and never went through
`effects`. So both placements give identical answers today. The docblock now says that — the
placement is where it cannot go wrong later, which is a different and weaker claim than the one I
first made, and the weaker claim is the true one.

**What is actually left.** The id is still reused across a zone change, so this is a fix to the
*consequence* rather than to the representation. Everything else that keys on an instance across a
zone change is already cleared by `relocate` — counters, damage, `attachedTo`, `pairedWith`,
`castAs`, `enteredTurn` — so the hole had exactly one occupant and now has none. The thing to
remember is the shape: **a new register keyed by instance id will inherit this bug, and nothing in
the types will say so.**

**The lesson is about the first entry rather than the second.** D301 named the limitation, estimated
it as expensive, and moved on — and the estimate was wrong by two orders of magnitude. Naming a
known gap is worth much less than spending five minutes finding out whether the pool can reach it.

## D305 — An Aura stayed on a land that had stopped being a creature (CR 704.5m)

The state-based action for Auras checked two things: attached to nothing, and attached to something
that has left the battlefield. CR 704.5m names a third — attached to an **illegal object** — and the
two the engine had are both zone changes, which is why they were the two it had. **The missing half
is the one where nothing moves:** the Aura stays, the host stays, and what changes is whether the
host is still the kind of thing the Aura's text allows.

**Two cards reach it, and both are plays somebody would make.** A Mutavault is a land until somebody
pays {1} and a 2/2 creature until end of turn, so an Aura cast on the 2/2 is on a land by the next
upkeep. An Etched Champion has protection from every colour while its controller has three artifacts,
and playing the third artifact is how you shed an Aura — which the card's own docblock has claimed
since it was written ("cannot be blocked by, targeted by, dealt damage by, **enchanted by**") while
the engine enforced three of those four.

**The consequences ran both ways, which is what makes it worth a fix rather than a note.** A Pacifism
answered a Mutavault for the rest of the game instead of for one turn — strictly better than printed,
the same shape as D304's blink. And a bestowed Boon Satyr was *worse* than printed: it should stop
being an Aura and stand up as the 4/2 (CR 702.103c), and instead it stayed a non-creature Aura
handing a **land** +4/+2. The probe read `vault p/t: 4 2` on a permanent that is not a creature,
which is the kind of state nothing else in the engine would ever have printed.

**The fix asks the Aura's own text, not a hardcoded question.** `script.aura.target` is the spec the
spell was cast with and `BESTOW_TARGET` is the one a bestowed permanent was, so the check is "is the
host still something this may enchant" rather than "is the host still a creature" — the difference
being that a card added later with a narrower `enchant` line gets the rule for free. The Equipment
branch twelve lines below had been asking `characteristicsOf(host).isCreature` the whole time, and
that asymmetry between two branches written together is what made this worth looking at at all.

**The shape of the predicate is the decision, and it is two keywords wide.** An attachment is not a
target, so `isLegalTarget` is the wrong question: hexproof and shroud restrict *targeting* and say
nothing about an Aura already attached, while protection is explicitly also an attachment rule
(CR 702.16e). So `isLegalAttachment` is `isLegalTarget` minus exactly those two checks, and the test
that pins it is the one where a Blossoming Defense gives your own enchanted creature hexproof and the
Pacifism **stays**. Verified by flipping the flag on purpose: three of the four tests pass either way
and that one fails, which is the only reason it is in the file.

**And the effect had to go with the Aura.** `relocate` clears `attachedTo` and leaves `effects`
alone, which is invisible while the only way an Aura leaves is its host leaving first — an effect
scoped to a card that is gone applies to nothing. Binned off a *living* illegal host, a Pacifism
would have sat in the graveyard and gone on pacifying. That is the same latent leak the bestow and
Equipment branches each call out in their own comments; this is the first case that could feel it.

## D306 — The second register keyed on an instance id, and #283 said it would be there

D304 closed the CR 400.7 work with a sentence about what was left: "a new register keyed by
instance id will inherit this bug, and nothing in the types will say so." There was already one.
`scheduleDelayed` stores its `subject` as a bare id and `fireDelayed` hands it to the ability, and
`relocate` gives a card back its own id — so a delayed ability finds the replacement of the object
it was about.

**Thicket Basilisk is the reachable case and it is a play, not a board.** The Basilisk attacks, you
block, and you Cloudshift your own blocker. The blink takes it out of combat so no damage is dealt,
and the creature that comes back is a new object the delayed "destroy the creature it fought" can no
longer find. The engine destroyed it. Two seats, two decks, one combat — more reachable than the
pump bug that prompted the search for it.

**The script's own comment was true of the wrong thing.** "No `destroy` of a creature that has left:
`destroy` reads the instance and does nothing for a card that is not on the battlefield, which is
the rule rather than a guard." That holds for a card that left and stayed gone, which is the only
case anybody had in mind when it was written. A comment claiming a rule is worth no more than a test
asserting it, and this one had outlived its truth by a zone change.

**The ability still fires.** CR 603.7d: the trigger has happened, so the entry is spent and the
ability goes on the stack; what it has lost is its subject. The test asserts that on the stack
rather than inferring it from an empty `delayed` list, because "dropped before it fired" and "fired
at nothing" leave the same board and only one of them is the rule.

**Three users of `subject`, and checking the other two was not a formality.** Flickerwisp broke
within a minute of the fix landing, because it scheduled the return *before* exiling the card: a
zone change makes a new object, so the pinned seq was the permanent's and the card that arrived in
exile did not match it. The order is now exile-then-schedule and the comment that used to say the
order was "only so the log reads in the order a player saw it" says why it is load-bearing. Unearth
needed nothing: its subject is itself, and the "or if it would leave the battlefield" replacement
means it cannot be blinked at all.

**The general shape, since this is twice now.** An instance id is not an identity across a zone
change, and the engine has exactly one thing that *is* — `objectSeq`, which combat has used since it
was written. Every place that remembers "this object" across time has to carry it: continuous
effects do now (D304), delayed abilities do now, and combat always did. The next one will not
announce itself either.

## D307 — The same blink one priority window earlier, and the window a player would use

D306 pinned the delayed entry's subject and left the window in front of it. The Basilisk's block
trigger sits **on the stack**, where both players can see it, so the obvious moment to Cloudshift is
in response to *that* — and then the trigger resolves after the blink and schedules its delayed
ability about the creature that came back, pinned to the new object, which of course matches itself.
The creature died anyway.

**The fix D306 shipped was correct and covered the later of two windows.** That is worth writing
down as its own entry rather than folding into the last one, because the failure mode is specific:
a fix aimed at the place the bug was *found* can leave the place the bug is *used*. The probe for
D306 cast the blink after the trigger resolved because that was the simplest script to write, and
the simplest script to write is not the play.

`StackObject.subject` and `.blocked` now carry `aboutSeqs`, the same pinning `targetSeqs` has done
for targets since it was written. A sibling field rather than entries in that map, because the
fizzle rule reads `targetSeqs` and these two are not targets: a trigger does not fizzle for having
lost its subject, it resolves and finds nothing (CR 603.3d).

**Blanked only when the object is there and different.** An id with no instance behind it already
does nothing wherever it is read, and leaving it alone keeps the one path that reads a card the
engine no longer holds — a token's own death trigger, raised after the token stopped existing —
exactly as it was. Nothing is pinned for such an id either, so there is no check to get wrong.

**What the test asserts is the difference between two boards that look alike.** After the blink the
trigger resolves and schedules *nothing*: `delayed` is empty. "Scheduled and then missed" and
"never scheduled" leave the same creature alive, and only the second is what the rules describe —
so the test asserts the empty list and the empty stack, not just the survivor.

**Three places read the ids and one place pins them**, which is the only reason this was a small
change: `resolveTop`'s condition re-ask, `beforeDecisions`, and `completeResolution` all take
`aboutNow(state, object)` now. A script that had to remember this would eventually forget, the same
argument that keeps hexproof in `targeting.ts` rather than in each card.

## D308 — An instrument for the rules a comment claims and no test writes down, and its precision

Three of the four bugs found this morning were found the same way: **a comment claimed a rule the
code did not have.** Etched Champion's docblock listed all four clauses of protection — "cannot be
blocked by, targeted by, dealt damage by, **enchanted by**" — while the state-based action enforced
three (D305). Thicket Basilisk's said "no `destroy` of a creature that has left … which is the rule
rather than a guard", true only of a card that left and *stayed* gone, and a blink made it false
twice over (D306, D307). D306 ended with the sentence, so `cr-claims.mjs` goes looking for its
shape: every `CR <number>` in the engine's sources, every one in its tests, and the rules on the
first list only.

**90 of 245 cited rules are claimed by a comment and written down by no test**, ranked by how many
places claim them.

**And the precision is low, which is recorded rather than glossed.** Three rows read:

- **CR 704.5p** is a false positive: the rule is tested by #284's bestowed-creature tests, which do
  not write the number down.
- **CR 104.2a** is the same — it is what #277's gate turns on, and the decking test covers it.
- **CR 720.6** is a real question and it is **blocked**. `becomeMonarch` says the crown is cleared
  when its holder leaves the game and `engine.ts` does clear it; whether the rule says *cleared* or
  *passed to the next player* cannot be settled from this container, because `magic.wizards.com`
  does not resolve here — the same wall the fifteen card-text mechanics are behind. Guessing a rule
  is the same mistake as guessing a card's text (D259), so it stays a question.

Two in three rows were rules tested without being cited. **The honest claim for this file is that
it is a reading list, not a defect count**, and the number that matters about it is that one — a
reader who treats 90 as a bug count will spend a day confirming tests that already exist. What it
is good for is the thing the three bugs had in common: it puts every claim somebody wrote down in
one place, with its file and line, so they can be read on purpose rather than stumbled on.

**And it names a second thing the proxy costs us.** The fifteen thin mechanics wait on
`api.scryfall.com` for card text; this waits on the Comprehensive Rules for rule text. Both are one
allowed host away, and until then "the engine says X and I cannot check X" is the honest state of a
row rather than a reason to change the code.

## D309 — Half of CR 704.5a cannot be tested, and finding that out is the result

`cr-claims.mjs` (D308) said CR 704.5a was claimed in two comments and written down by no test, and
this one was not a false positive: the regeneration block's four tests cover a destroy spell, lethal
combat damage, the whole board at once and a shield expiring — every way a shield *works* and no way
it does not. The rule is that a creature with toughness 0 or less is **put into its graveyard**
rather than destroyed, so neither a regeneration shield nor indestructible has anything to replace.

The engine has had it right since the shield was written: both saves are guarded on
`ch.toughness > 0`.

**And only one of the two halves is testable, which is the part worth recording.** Take the guard
off the *regeneration* branch and the shield is spent, the creature is tapped, and the next
state-based pass kills it anyway for the same zero toughness — the graveyard reads the same either
way. I found that out the way the engine's own CR 704.5e note says to: by breaking it on purpose and
watching the new test pass. Take the guard off *indestructible* and the engine `continue`s past the
creature, so a 2/1 at -1 toughness sits on the battlefield for the rest of the game — a difference
a player would notice and a test can see.

So the pair that shipped is deliberately asymmetric. The regeneration test asserts the board a
player sees and says in its own docblock that it cannot distinguish the two implementations. The
indestructible test is the one that pins the rule, and it is placed with the other indestructible
tests rather than with the regeneration ones because that is where the discriminating guard is.

**The general point, which is the third time this thread has come round** (D282, D302, and CR
704.5e's note): a test that asserts the board can read identically whether the rule holds or not,
and the only way to know which kind you have written is to break the engine on purpose. Doing that
takes a minute and is the difference between a test and a comment with an `expect` in it.

Both tests go through **Toxic Deluge**, which is not the pool's only way to shrink a creature —
Golgari Charm's first mode, Night of Souls' Betrayal and Darkblast are all `-1/-1` — but is the only
one whose amount the caster *chooses*, so it is the one that can zero any toughness rather than only
a one-toughness body. Both assert the range the card computed (`{ min: 0, max: 1 }`) instead of
hardcoding the answer: a creature added to either deck with two toughness would change that number,
and the assertion says so rather than quietly testing something else.

## D310 — The doc priced a hybrid card as if it needed both colours

The player doc quotes a card's mana cost in one shape — `**Name** ({cost} …)` — eighty-three times.
Eighty-two of them match the card. **Murderous Redcap's `{2}{B/R}{B/R}` was written `{2}{B}{R}`.**

That is the one of the eighty-three that costs a player something. Both coloured symbols are
hybrid, so the Redcap casts off four Swamps or four Mountains; `{2}{B}{R}` says they need one of
each, in a document that teaches hybrid mana two sections away (#167). A player with four Swamps reads the doc and does not try the card.

**Found by asking the question in bulk rather than by reading.** Ten lines of node, 83 matches, one
disagreement — which is the same method as `cr-claims.mjs` the hour before and a much better
precision, because the shape being matched is narrow: only a bolded name followed by a parenthesis
that *starts* with mana symbols counts as a quoted cost, so prose that merely mentions a card is
left alone and the trailing words inside the parenthesis are ignored.

**So it is a guard rather than a one-off.** `checkPlayerDocQuotesEveryManaCost` sits beside the
deck-name guard #265 added, runs in the gate, reads the card definitions out of `starterDecks.ts`
*source* (guards run before anything is built) and parses commanders too, since the doc prices four
of them and a commander is not in any deck's `cards`. Verified by changing a cost in the doc on
purpose and watching it fail.

Two things it also checks, both because a guard that silently checks nothing is worse than no
guard: that the parse found some card definitions at all, and that the doc still contains at least
one quoted cost. Either coming back empty is reported as a broken guard rather than a pass.

**The standing lesson, third time now** (#265 on deck counts, #271 on the counterspell line, this on
a cost): the player doc is the one artefact in this repo that a human reads and nothing executes, so
every class of claim in it that *can* be checked mechanically should be, and the classes that
cannot — "the table feels fast", "this deck wants to attack" — are the ones worth a human's reading
time.

## D311 — Three more claims in the same parenthesis, and all three understated the card

D310's guard read one of the three things the player doc puts inside that parenthesis. The other two
were worth the same bulk pass, and it found three more errors in 117 claims:

- **Monastery Swiftspear** was a 1/1 in the doc and is a **1/2**.
- **Stormchaser Mage** was a 1/2 and is a **1/3**.
- **Thorn of the Black Rose** was "in Tidal Mind and Ashen Rite" and is only in **Tidal Mind**.

All three errors point the same way, which is the part worth noticing: two understate a creature's
body and the third sends a player to a deck that does not have the card. Reading "1/1 haste" you do
not attack into a 1/2; reading "in Ashen Rite" you go looking and come back thinking the doc lies
about everything else too.

**The guard now checks all three classes**, and the shape of the parenthesis is what makes that
possible: cost, then `power/toughness`, then `in <Deck>`. A power that is not a plain number is
skipped rather than compared, because a `*` is a fact about the board and the doc cannot quote a
number for it either. The deck check needs both directions of the identifier map — `CardDef` consts
by name, and the `{ card: IDENT }` rows in each `DeckSpec` — so it also covers commanders, which no
deck lists under `cards`. Parsed from source: 338 card definitions, 13 decks, 477 membership rows.
Verified by breaking one claim of each kind on purpose.

**Four doc errors in one afternoon from two bulk passes, and none of them would have been found by
reading.** That is the argument for the whole method: a human reading this doc checks the *prose*,
which is where the thinking is, and skims the numbers in brackets — which is exactly where a
machine is better than a human and where being wrong costs a player a combat.


## D312 — Correction to D310: the pool has two hybrid cards, not one

D310 and the guard's docblock both called Murderous Redcap "the pool's only hybrid card". It is one
of **two**: Verdant Guard's **Kitchen Finks** is `{1}{G/W}{G/W}`, and the doc prices it correctly.

The entry is better for it rather than worse — a wrong cost on one of two hybrid cards, with the
other one right, is what a one-off typo looks like, and "the only one" was quietly making it sound
like a systematic misunderstanding of the symbol. Both files now say two.

Worth noticing *how* it got written: I checked the thing I was fixing (83 quoted costs, every one
compared against the card) and then wrote a sentence about the pool from memory, in the same
paragraph. The checked claim was right and the remembered one was wrong, and nothing about the
prose distinguished them — which is the argument for the guards in D310 and D311 pointed at my own
writing as much as at the player doc's.

## D313 — An instrument for self-consistent state, three rejected invariants, and one real leak

The throw hunts (#244, #275) ask whether a game *stops* wrongly. `state-invariants.mjs` asks the
quieter question: whether the state the engine hands back after every action is one its own rules
could describe. The two bugs it was written for were both invisible to a winner — an effect still
naming a card that had gone (D305), and an id outliving the object it named (D304, D306, D307).

**Three of the nine invariants I wrote were wrong, and each was wrong in a way worth keeping a note
of**, because an invariant that merely happens to hold today fails on the next correct card and gets
switched off:

- *"every instance is in exactly one zone list"* reported **43 violations in 52 games**, every one a
  card on the stack: it rebuilt the zone key as `${seat}:${zone}` and the stack is a single shared
  zone keyed `stack`. **An invariant that reimplements the thing it checks tests the
  reimplementation.** It imports the engine's own `zoneKey` now.
- *"no card is lost"* read **123 of 122** the first time anything made a Soldier, and then **183 of
  244** in a pod — one 60-card deck and a commander, leaving the game with an eliminated seat
  (CR 800.4a). It is per living seat and by **owner** now, which is stronger than the total it
  replaced: it would catch *my* cards disappearing when somebody else leaves.
- *"a delayed trigger names a card the game still has"* was written, run and **deleted**. A pod
  produced `delayed dl34 is about t2_245, which is gone`, and a token that has ceased to exist is
  exactly the case CR 603.7d covers: the ability fires and finds nothing. Three more candidates were
  rejected before they were written, and all six reasons are in the file.

**And the survivors found something on the first clean pod pass:** `an effect from c0_60 scopes
c2_183, which is gone`. A seat had been knocked out, its cards had left the game with it, and a
living seat's pump was still naming one of them — `leaveTheGame` filtered effects by controller and
by source and not by **scope**.

Nothing a player can see comes of it: a scope id with no instance applies to nothing. It is fixed
anyway, and the reason is the shape rather than the symptom — an id outliving its object was the
*whole* of D304, D306 and D307, and the two places that prune a `cards` scope should prune it the
same way. Both now drop the effect when its last subject has gone.

**One id per scope is all this pool can produce**, because every multi-card pump here is scoped to
its caster's own creatures and those leave with the seat that controlled the effect. So the test is
the single-id case plus a control — a living seat's own pump, untouched — and the control is the half
that matters: a filter wide enough to drop the first effect would drop the second, and the board
looks the same until somebody counts the power.

**78 games bought three rejected invariants and one fix.** That ratio is the argument for the file:
the invariants I got wrong were cheaper to find than the bug they were looking for, and writing them
down is what stops the next person rediscovering them.

## D314 — A long game and a stuck table read the same, and one of them cost an hour

`LIST=extort` spent moves 135 to 630 of one run printing nothing but `primary: Pass`, and the log
could not say which of two very different things that was: a control mirror grinding through turn
after turn with nothing to cast, or a table deadlocked on one priority. Both print the same line.
I stopped the twenty-deck sequence to find out, which cost the eleven lists queued behind it.

A re-run of the same list finished in about sixty moves, 28 of 28 checks with one named skip — and
**that does not settle what the first run was doing**, which is worth being exact about. A re-run
is a different shuffle. It proves the list can finish; the five-hundred-Pass game was already gone,
and nothing was recorded about it that could say whether its turns were advancing. The honest
answer to #294 is that the question is unanswerable for that run, and the fix is that it will not
be unanswerable again.

**The finding is not about extort.** It is that the solo suite's periodic line carried the move
number and nothing else, so the one fact that separates the two cases was the one fact it did not
print. It prints the turn now: a run that is only slow climbs, a run that is stuck does not, and
the difference is visible in the first screenful instead of after the move budget runs out.

**And the first stall it caught was real, within the hour.** A solo pod reached turn 20 by move 75
and was still on turn 20 at move 570 — five hundred moves of the driver pressing Pass into a table
that was not going anywhere, and that run died at the harness's own time limit with the game checks
never reached. So the suite no longer only prints the turn: a turn that eats more than two hundred
moves is now a named failure (`the table kept moving`) that stops the loop, because a whole pod
game is about a hundred and eighty moves across forty-odd turn changes. How often that happens is
being measured; what is already certain is that it happens, and that it was invisible before.

That is the same lesson as #277 and the `nobody to act` invariant (D313) one level up. The engine
learned to say "a table with nobody to act and nothing finished is a violation with a name"; the
harness that drives a *browser* was still answering "what is happening?" with a number that goes
up either way.

## D315 — The spectacle row is a 30% shuffle, and the two fixes I built for it were both wrong

`LIST=earned` requires two rows: a Skewer the Critics cast for its spectacle cost, and a Mizzium
Mortars overloaded. One run failed with spectacle unpressed across all five deals. The suite's own
docblock sets the bar — *"a required check that fails one run in four is not a check"* — so this
needed fixing, and what it needed first was a number.

**The first explanation was wrong, and measuring is what said so.** The driver aims a targeted
spell at a lit card before it aims at a player, and Tidal Mind nearly always holds a creature — so
every Lightning Bolt and every Skewer goes at the creature, the opponent never loses life, and the
row that only exists on a turn an opponent has lost life is never on the sheet. That reads as a
complete account of the failure. Three baseline re-runs **refuted** it: all three reached the row,
on deals 1, 3 and 4. The condition is also earned in combat, and the combat route was open the
whole time.

**The second was wrong too, and this one I built before I measured it.** `atTheFace`, an option on
the shared driver reversing those two branches for this list only, on the reasoning that a mono-red
burn deck aims at the face anyway. Three runs with it: one failure with the row unpressed across
five deals, two passes. No better than the baseline, and the likely reason is the first refutation
read backwards — burn aimed at the face leaves the blockers alive, which closes the *combat* route
to the same condition. It is reverted. An option nothing uses is worse than no option.

What is left is arithmetic rather than a theory. The deals the row was first pressed on — 1, 3, 4,
and more than 5 — put it near **p = 0.3 a shuffle**. Five deals miss `0.7^5` = 17% of the time,
which is the one-run-in-four that was actually observed; twelve deals miss 1.4%, about one run in
seventy. So `LIST=earned` gets a budget of twelve, and the reason that is not simply buying a green
check with patience is that **the budget costs nothing except on the run that would have been red**:
a run that finds the row on deal one still plays one game.

**Both wrong guesses are in the file**, next to the budget they argued against, because the next
person to look at a flaky required check will have the same first idea I did.

## D316 — Two replacement effects for one event, which this pool can produce exactly once

`cr-claims.mjs` (D308) ranks rules a comment claims and no test writes down, and its docblock is
explicit that a row is a reading list rather than a defect count. Three rows read this pass, and
the results are three different kinds of answer:

- **CR 702.21b** (ward triggers off an ability) and **CR 601.2b** (a modal spell's modes are
  announced as it is cast) are already tested, by an Icy Manipulator aimed at a warded creature and
  by three tests on modal plays. Only the titles changed. 88 uncited becomes 86, and the two that
  came off are off because somebody read them, which is the only way a row on that list should
  clear.
- **CR 616.1** — the choice between several applicable replacements belongs to the affected
  object's controller — turned out to be partly untestable for the reason `automation.ts` already
  says out loud: *"Nothing in this pool can produce two."* That is nearly true, and the exception is
  the test: an **unearthed Dregscape Zombie** sacrificed under an opposing **Kalitas**. Its own "if
  it would leave the battlefield, exile it instead" and Kalitas's "if a creature an opponent
  controls would die, exile it instead and create a Zombie" both want the same event.

One event is replaced once (CR 614.1), so `replaceZoneChange` asks the widest wording first and the
*leave* is replaced before the *death* is ever considered — Kalitas never sees a death and gets no
token. That is always the choice seat 1 would make if it were asked, which is why making it for
them is a simplification rather than a wrong answer; it is still one of two legal orders, and a
card whose own replacement is worse for it than an opponent's would turn the simplification into a
bug.

**Exile proves nothing in that test** — both replacements exile, and so does unearth's own end-step
trigger — so the Zombie token is the only thing on the board that says which one won, and the
control (the same outlet eating a Tormented Soul, which does hand Kalitas its token) is half the
test. Verified discriminating the way D282 and D309 ask for: dropping the `!leaving.replaced` filter
from the death pass makes it fail, and restoring it makes it pass.

## D317 — Three pod checks were reading evidence the engine had correctly destroyed

`SOLO_POD` came back **26 of 29** on the shipping engine, and the three failures were one
assumption rather than three bugs. D297 taught the engine CR 800.4a — a player who leaves the game
takes their cards with them — and three checks were reading a seat's battlefield and graveyard
**after** the game to decide whether that seat had played:

- *the computer played a real game*, off seat 1's zones;
- *all three of them played*, which reported `[0,29,22]` for three bots that had all played a full
  pod;
- *tapping a card over a finished game opens nothing*, which had nothing to tap at all, because the
  human seat lost that pod and was stripped with the rest.

**Checked headlessly instead of reasoned about**, which is the only reason this is a one-line
diagnosis: three pods print `peak=[19,12,12,13]` against `after=[18,0,12,0]`. Every seat played;
the seats eliminated before the game ended read zero; the seats eliminated *as* it ended keep their
cards, because the game finishes before they are stripped. That asymmetry is why the symptom looked
like a bot sitting still.

So each seat's high-water mark is sampled as the game runs and the checks read that — one
`evaluate` for four seats every fifth move, because a card that arrives is there for many moves.
The post-game counts stay in the failure detail: when this does fail, those two numbers are the
first thing worth seeing. The tap falls back to any **face-up** card on the table, the winner's
board being there by definition, with the hand still excluded as the one place a card can be face
down. 29 of 29 after, and the plain solo run unchanged at 27.

This is #273's mistake again — *every "can you see both boards" reading was taken post-game* — and
it is worth naming the general shape, because it has now cost two findings: **when the engine
learns a rule about cards leaving the game, every harness that reads a zone at the end is suspect.**
The engine change was right both times. The check was reading a fact that the rule had deleted.

**And the second half of this entry is the stall the turn number caught.** D314 added the turn to
the solo suite's log line so a slow game could be told from a stuck one. Within the hour a
`SOLO_POD` run reached turn 20 by move 75 and was still on turn 20 at **move 570** — five hundred
moves of the driver pressing Pass into a table that was not advancing — and died at the harness's
own time limit with no game check reached. Printing the turn was not enough: a turn that eats more
than two hundred moves is now a named failure (`the table kept moving`) that breaks the loop, so
the remaining checks run and report the board as it actually stands. Two hundred is far outside
anything real here, a whole pod game being about a hundred and eighty moves across forty-odd turn
changes, and the first run with the check in place came back 29 of 29 with no stall line. Whether
the stall is the #70 and #277 class — a table waiting on a seat that cannot move — is #297.

## D318 — The table did not answer because the write took seventeen seconds

Three browser runs failed *"the engine never refused anything the table offered"* with `Pass: the
table did not answer`, `Block: …` and `Order: …`. That sentence is not the engine's. It is the
**client's own eight-second ack timeout** (`emit`, in `apps/web/src/lib/table.ts`): the move was
sent, the server did not answer inside eight seconds, and the page gave up — on a move it may well
have applied.

**One check was reporting two faults that want opposite fixes.** An engine refusal means the bar
offered something the rules do not allow. A timeout means the write took longer than a person is
asked to wait. The suite asks them separately now, and that is the same correction as D314: two
states that read identically are one state as far as anybody debugging is concerned.

Then the server was taught to say when a write is slow, because nothing did, and the numbers came
back immediately. Sixteen `SOLO_POD` runs, two slow writes:

```
auto:cast by seat 0 at turn 22 draw             took 17130ms and 431 server moves
auto:pass by seat 0 at turn 31 declare-attackers took  4415ms and 167 server moves
```

**Seventeen seconds and four hundred and thirty-one bot moves in one write**, against a client that
waits eight. That is not a mystery, it is the design working as written: `runBots` plays every bot
move it is owed inside the mutation the human's action provoked — deliberately, so that a bot's
whole reply lands in one pod version and one broadcast — so a player with nothing to do for a few
turns pays for *all* of those turns at once. The docblock already said "five hundred moves that end
with the person on the clock is simply a long write". It did not say how long, and seventeen seconds
is long enough that the page stops believing in the table.

**The fix is not chosen yet, and two samples are not a distribution** (#298). Raising the client's
timeout makes the error go away and leaves a seventeen-second frozen board. Bounding the moves per
write needs a continuation, or the table stops with bots still owed a move — and the continuation is
a real change to the write model, which wants its own test. Making a pod's bots think less is a
third answer with its own cost, already measured elsewhere (D275 and the clock work).

**And it is not the stall.** Run twelve of the sixteen stalled — turn 28, upkeep, stack empty,
socket connected, nobody eliminated — with the slow-write count unchanged at two and no inert move
reported. So slow writes join the engine, the bots, the rate limiter and a dropped socket on the
list of things #297 is not. The useful shape of that list is that every entry on it was removed by
an instrument rather than by an argument.

One gap closed in passing: the first stall dump to carry the pod code printed an empty string,
because `table-code` lives in the pre-game header that is gone once the game is dealt. The control
bar's code has its own testid now, so a stalled table can still be found in Redis.

## D319 — The driver reported two hundred and one passes it never sent

`press` in `scripts/lib/table-driver.mjs` returns a boolean. `makeMove` discarded it:

```js
await press(page, 'primary-move');
return `primary: ${label}`;
```

So a press Playwright refused was reported to the log, and to every check downstream, as a press
that landed. On a stalled table that happened **201 times in one run** — the driver saying "primary:
Pass" over and over while nothing was ever sent to the server.

This is why every suspect for #297 came back innocent, and the list was long: the engine (52
headless pods, every one to a winner), the pod bots, the rate limiter, a dropped socket, inert human
moves, slow writes. Each was ruled out by an instrument, correctly, because none of them was ever
involved. `podwatch` caught the state to prove it — `stuck-SLIVER-SPIRE-50.json`, turn 24, upkeep,
activeSeat 0, priority 0, `passed: []`, stack empty, nothing pending, nobody eliminated, and
`stateVersion` frozen at 193. A pod whose version never moves, with zero server errors, is a pod
that was never asked to do anything.

**The failure was in the instrument, and it was the kind that manufactures evidence rather than
losing it.** A driver that silently drops a move makes the server look broken, and every hour spent
on the server was spent on a fiction. It is the same shape as D314 and D318 one more time: a press
that landed and a press that did not read identically, so they were one state.

### The reason has to be captured where it happens

The first diagnostic for this read the DOM after the failure: `elementFromPoint` at the button's
centre, plus a list of full-width `fixed` overlays. It gave the same three readings sixteen times —
`enabled, visible, pointer-events: auto` — which rules out disabled, hidden and pointer-opted-out
and leaves the two answers that matter unseparated.

Then, before spending another twenty-four pods on it, the obvious flaw: **`press` makes two attempts
at a two-second timeout, so that read happens up to four seconds after the click was refused.** An
overlay that closed in the meantime reads as a perfectly clear button — the answer that sends the
hunt in the wrong direction, produced confidently.

Playwright had already written the answer and `press` was throwing it away in a bare `catch {}`. Its
call log names the element that "intercepts pointer events", quoted from the real markup, and says
whether the button was ever "visible, enabled and stable" — written at the moment of the failure.
`pressOrWhy` returns it; `press` keeps its boolean for the twenty-three call sites that do not care.
The DOM read stays as corroboration, which is now its honest job: whether the obstruction is *still*
there separates an overlay nobody closes from one that flickers.

Checked against a button under a `fixed inset-0 z-50` veil and the same button uncovered — the exact
three readings the stalled table gave. The covered one names `log-panel` by testid. **The check cost
five seconds and the hunt it protects costs two hours**, which is the whole argument for running it.

## D320 — A slow write's move count cannot say which fault it is

D318 taught the server to report a slow write with its duration and its bot-move count, and said two
samples are not a distribution. A census of ten pods — `SLOW_WRITE_MS=150`, every write above the
noise floor — gave the distribution: 51 writes over 150ms, median 366ms, p90 1476ms, max 7814ms, ten
at or above a second, one at or above four, none at eight.

The worst five say something the count was never going to:

```
215 server moves  3831ms
111 server moves  7814ms
```

**Duration does not track move count.** Per-decision cost dominates, and a write of many cheap
searches and a write of a few expensive ones are the two faults — with opposite fixes. Bounding the
moves per write fixes the first and cannot touch the second; if one search is over budget on its
own, no bound on how many of them run will bring the write under eight seconds.

So the report carries where the time went: how much of the write was spent inside `botAction`, and
what the single worst decision cost. That separates four outcomes where the count separated two —
many cheap searches, one search over budget alone, a cost that is not the bots at all (the engine
clones a whole game state per move), and a human action slow by itself with no bot seats to blame.

Timed with `performance.now()` rather than `Date.now()`: four hundred sub-millisecond decisions each
rounded down to zero would report a write that spent all its time thinking as one that spent none,
which is the measurement reading the opposite of the truth rather than merely imprecisely.

**The fix for #298 is still unchosen, and deliberately so.** Choosing between three answers on two
samples is what D315 is a record of going wrong.

## D321 — Correction to D320: the per-decision ceiling is 163ms, so bounding the moves does work

D320 said the move count could not diagnose a slow write, because duration does not track count, and
concluded that bounding the moves per write "fixes the first and cannot touch the second". The
conditional was right and I picked the wrong branch. The instrument it motivated settles it.

A census of 22 writes above a 150ms threshold, with the new breakdown:

```
   took  moves   think  think%  worst  ms/move
   2841     65    2245     79%    116       44
   2279     73    1701     74%    141       31
   1305     38    1125     86%     94       34
    ...
    183      9      48     26%     44       20
```

- **Deciding is 72% of the write (median).** The cost is the bots' search, not the engine's clone.
- **The worst single `botAction` across all of them is 163ms**, against a client that gives up at
  8000. That is a factor of 49.

So per-decision cost dominates the *variance* — which is why duration cannot be predicted from the
count, exactly as D320 said — but the count still **bounds** duration, because the per-decision cost
has a ceiling. D320's error was treating "cannot predict" as "cannot bound". The progress doc's
"weakens the bounding option" was premature in the same way, and is corrected there.

`BOT_MOVES_PER_WRITE = 25` follows from the measurement: 8000 over 163 is 49 moves, halved for a
decision worse than any yet seen. At the observed 45ms a move that is nearer 1.1s.

The other half is `continueBots`: a write that stops on its budget with a server seat still owed a
move has handed back a table nobody is on the clock for, which is a dead table. The socket handler
calls it until a batch does no work — **termination on progress, not on "nothing owed"**, because a
bot that cannot move leaves "owed" true for ever and spinning on exactly the broken tables would be
the worst possible choice. It is not undoable, so the step the human's own action saved survives
every continuation on top of it and an undo still removes the whole answer.

What the player sees changes: a seventeen-second frozen board becomes one that arrives in pieces.

## D322 — Two of the realtime suite's strongest assertions could never fail

`createRealtime` built its store like this:

```ts
const store = new PodStore(redis, {
  ...opts.store,
  onBotStall: ({ code, reason }) => log.warn(…),
  onNoProgress: ({ code, reason }) => log.warn(…),
  onSlowWrite: ({ code, reason }) => log.warn(…),
});
```

The spread comes first and the three assignments overwrite it. **A caller's version of all three was
silently discarded.** And the realtime suite passes exactly those three in, collects them into
arrays, and ends the whole-game test with:

```ts
expect(stalls, JSON.stringify(stalls)).toEqual([]);
expect(noProgress, JSON.stringify(noProgress)).toEqual([]);
```

Those arrays could never hold anything. The suite's own comment calls an empty list "the claim worth
making"; the claim was unmakeable. Same shape as the driver discarding `press`'s boolean (D319) and
`tap`'s (#300), and the same lesson: **a report that cannot arrive is worse than no report, because
the silence is read as good news.** Three instruments in two days, all of which answered "nothing
wrong" by construction.

Found by accident, trying to add a *fourth* callback for the per-write budget and getting
`MAX MOVES IN ONE WRITE: 0` from a counter that fires on every write.

Fixed by composing: `report(event, onward?)` logs and then calls the caller's handler, because both
readers want it — the log is how a defect is found on a running table, the callback is how a test
refuses to pass with one.

### And the assertion, once live, fails about one run in nine

Which is the point of it. With the callbacks wired and **no other change**, the whole-game solo test
failed once in nine runs and then passed eight times in a row. So there is a real bot stall or inert
human move in roughly a tenth of games, and it has been invisible for as long as the assertion has
existed.

**Not pushed yet.** A real assertion that fails one run in nine makes CI intermittently red, which is
worse than the vacuous one it replaces until the defect underneath it is found. The honest order is:
catch the failure message, fix what it names, then ship both together.

## D323 — My own gate was not gating: a pipe swallowed the exit code

The gate I have been running before every push all session:

```bash
node scripts/guards.js && pnpm v2:typecheck … && pnpm v2:test 2>&1 | tail -12 \
  && echo "gate ended" && git push -u origin …
```

`pnpm v2:test 2>&1 | tail -12` exits with **tail's** status, not the test run's. So that stage
succeeded whatever the tests did, the `&&` chain carried on, and **the push would have fired on a
red test run.** It did not bite only because CI was doing the real gating and the pushed commits
happened to be sound.

Proved by the run that found it: `Tasks: 16 successful, 17 total` with
`Tests 1 failed | 42 passed (43)` and `[exited with code 0]` on the same screen.

The gate pattern from here is a file and an explicit check, never a pipe:

```bash
pnpm v2:test > "$S/gate.txt" 2>&1; ec=$?; tail -20 "$S/gate.txt"; [ "$ec" -eq 0 ] || exit 1
```

### And the same run covered 8 of 43 tests while reading green

`apps/realtime/src/realtime.test.ts` guards its socket suite with `describe.skipIf(!REDIS_URL)`.
My gate command never set that variable, so **35 of 43 tests skipped in every local gate run this
session** and the output read `Test Files 1 passed (1) / Tests 8 passed | 35 skipped (43)`.

CI is not affected — `.github/workflows/ci.yml:52` sets `REDIS_URL`, and `turbo.json` lists it in
the test task's `env`, so the cache key differs and the suite genuinely re-runs. The defect was
entirely in my invocation, and the cost was that I reported a stronger check than I had run, several
times.

Filed as #303: a test that always runs and fails when `REDIS_URL` is unset, naming the count it
would otherwise skip. Same argument as D302 — a total without its skips beside it cannot be
compared, and "43 passed" and "8 passed, 35 skipped" must not both print `1 passed` and exit 0.

### Six in two days, and four of them mine

`press` discarding its boolean (D319), `tap` across 27 call sites (#300), `createRealtime`
overwriting three store callbacks (D322), a budget assertion of mine that passed with the budget
raised sixteen-fold, `skipIf` hiding 35 tests, and this pipe. Every one reported success it had not
earned, and the silence read as good news each time.

The two that were caught before they cost anything were caught the same way: **deliberately break
the check and confirm it goes red.** A veil over a button until the press had to be refused; the bot
budget raised until the assertion had to fire. It costs seconds. Treating that step as optional is
what produced the other four.

## D324 — #298 ships; the thing that looked like its cost was my own test harness

The bound and the continuation are right, and three arms of six runs each say so. What looked like
a latency regression was the test I wrote to prove the bound.

### The hypothesis, and its refutation

Bounding the bot moves per write made two *other* realtime tests fail intermittently on a
five-second wait for a `pod:state` broadcast. The obvious reading was that the continuation's extra
writes and broadcasts were delaying the first broadcast after an action — a cost a player would feel,
and so not a test constant to raise and walk away from.

Reading the handler weakened it: the ack and the first broadcast both happen **before** any
continuation, so a continuation cannot delay its own broadcast. At most it could delay the *next*
action, if socket.io holds a socket's handler before processing that socket's next event.

Then the measurement killed it. `BOT_MOVES_PER_WRITE` is read from the environment, so the suite
A/Bs itself without a code change:

```
these two tests present, budget  25 -> 3/6 runs failed, 3 broadcast timeouts
these two tests present, budget 500 -> 5/6 runs failed, 8 broadcast timeouts
these two tests skipped, budget  25 -> 0/6 runs failed, 0 broadcast timeouts
```

**The middle arm is the opposite of the hypothesis**: with the budget at 500 the continuation barely
fires, writes go back to being long, and the timeouts get *worse*. Bigger writes delay broadcasts.
That is evidence for the bound.

**And the third arm names the real cause.** Each of my two tests stands up a second
`createRealtime` so it can have its own budget, and that instance's Redis clients, cluster adapter
and HTTP server are not fully released by `close()`. The pressure starves the five-second waits in
whatever runs next. With them skipped and the source changes present: six clean runs, no timeouts.

### What this retires

- **#302 is closed as not a defect.** It was never `onBotStall` — those assertions pass — and it was
  never a broadcast regression. The two reproductions I could inspect were contention: once from
  three jobs sharing four cores, once from my own tests. The single original failure under
  `io.ts` alone stays recorded as **one unreproduced event** against 31 clean runs plus a clean CI
  draw; the message was never captured, so it is not promoted to a cause.
- **Three wrong attributions of mine, in one thread.** A dead table, then a protocol regression,
  then a broadcast regression. Each was stated before the deciding measurement existed, and each was
  refuted by the measurement I then built. The pattern is not that the guesses were unreasonable —
  it is that I said them in the register of findings rather than hypotheses.

### What ships, and what it owes

The source changes ship: `BOT_MOVES_PER_WRITE = 25`, `continueBots`, `reportBotStall` for the
condition the bound displaced, and an injectable round cap so that report is provable.

The two tests are **skipped, not deleted, and not because the claim is unproven** — both passed,
45/45, and between them showed no write exceeding its budget with no seat left owed, and the cap
report firing. The rewrite is to drop the sockets and drive `applyAction` and `continueBots` against
a `PodStore` built in the test. Both are store-level concerns; neither needs a second server.

## D325 — The rewritten budget tests, and the hole the first version could not see (#298)

The rewrite D324 prescribed: drop the sockets, drive `applyAction` and `continueBots` against a
`PodStore` the test builds from its own Redis client. No HTTP server, no socket.io adapter, nothing
`close()` fails to release. Both tests run in about 700ms.

Getting them to a state worth trusting took four corrections, and all four were mine.

**The budget starved its own fixture.** At `botMovesPerWrite: 1` the three server seats cannot
settle their own opening hands inside the write `auto:keep` provokes, so the game had not begun and
the first move came back `FORBIDDEN: you do not have priority`. The fixture now drives the
continuation to a standstill after every setup step, exactly as the handler does after it acks.

**The second test's premise was wrong.** It passed once, then asserted the cap report. But the one
move that write spends hands priority straight back to the person, so `continueBots` returns with
nothing owed and no report is made. It failed printing `after 0 round(s)` — proof only that I had
guessed where the condition lived. A seat is owed real work when the **turn** has gone to the
server's seats, so the test now plays the person's turn out until a capped chain actually hits its
cap, and fails naming why if it never does.

**An `onBotStall` assertion that could not fail.** I wrote `expect(stalled).toEqual([])` into the
budget test. `runBots` reports "ran out with a seat still owed" only when its **guard** is spent,
and a budget below the guard makes that unreachable — so the assertion was green whatever the budget
did. The seventh such check this session, and the fourth of mine. Removed, with the reason left in
the test; the stranding property is now carried by things that can fail: the `hasPriority` break,
a `settle` that throws rather than shrugging, and a turn counter that has to move.

**Half the budget was unobservable.** `onSlowWrite` fired only in `applyAction`. Both writes call
`runBots` with the same bound, but only one said what it had spent — so a bound applied correctly
in `applyAction` and wrongly in `continueBots` would have read as a clean table. `continueBots` now
reports on the same terms, which is also the right thing for a player: those writes run while the
page is already waiting.

### What the tests assert, and the proof they discriminate

`toBe(1)`, not `toBeLessThanOrEqual(1)`. Equality carries the bound **and** the proof it was
reached — a write that wanted more and was cut to one. A `<=` passes on a table that never asked for
a second move, which is the vacuous shape above.

Three deliberate breaks, one per claim:

```
applyAction  passes BOT_MOVE_GUARD -> writes [0,0,3,0,0,0,14,2,0,3,38,...]  expected 38 to be 1   FAIL
continueBots passes BOT_MOVE_GUARD -> writes [0,0,1,4,0,0,0,1,6,0,0,0,1,8]  expected 8 to be 1    FAIL
reportBotStall swallows its report -> "expected the cap report, got []"                            FAIL
```

The second is the bug this guards and the one I nearly shipped: it fails **only** because of the
continuation reporting added above. Break A fails the cap test too — an unbounded write never leaves
work over.

### Stability, which is what the rewrite was for

D324 measured the old pair at 3 of 6 full-suite runs failing with broadcast timeouts, and 0 of 6
with them skipped. The store-level pair: **40 consecutive clean full-suite runs (46 passed each)** —
10 taken while the rewrite settled, then a 30-run hunt with full failure output armed and nothing to
record — plus 14 consecutive clean runs of the cap test alone.

One earlier run of six, before the orphaned docblock came out, failed on the cap test with its
message uncaptured. It is not called a flake and it was not left alone: the hunt existed to catch
it and did not, so it stays recorded as **one unreproduced event against 44 clean runs**, cause
unknown, rather than attributed to anything. Note what the arithmetic does not support: at the rate
that one failure implied, 30 runs had a better-than-four-in-five chance of reproducing it, so the
most likely reading is that whatever it was is gone — but "most likely" is not "shown", and the
event keeps its line.

## D326 — The in-flight marker does appear, and three of my own instruments said otherwise first (#299)

#299 shipped a marker reading "opponents deciding" while a move is with the server. `table.test.ts`
pins the *decision* — `waitingNote`, and the reducer's `waiting` flag — but nothing pinned the
**moment**: whether it shows on a real page, during a real write, and stops when the answer lands.
A marker that renders correctly and never shows is, to a player, no marker at all.

**It works.** `scripts/check-in-flight.mjs`, two arms, against the shipping client:

```
ARM=slow   every socket frame held 600ms each way   36 moves, 6 appearances, 5 departures   9/9 checks
ARM=quick  the same game, unthrottled               36 moves, 0 appearances                 6/6 checks
```

It appears, it says "opponents deciding" (the bot branch of `waitingNote`), and it goes away. The
quick arm is half the measurement: on its own, `slow` would pass on a marker stuck permanently on
screen.

### Four wrong readings, each from my own instrument, before any of that

1. **The wrong button.** It waited on `start-game`, which this lobby does not offer; the game starts
   on `start-engine`. Fifteen seconds of timeout, no reading.
2. **An observer that never attached.** `observe(document.documentElement)` throws in an init
   script, because there is no `<html>` yet. It reported **0 appearances across 18 moves** — a
