   confident zero from a watcher that was never watching. Only the page-error check caught it. The
   script now plants a marker in front of its own watcher and requires it to be seen, and says
   plainly that nothing below that check means anything if it fails.
3. **The arm itself was the wrong theory.** `BOT_MOVES_PER_WRITE=500` was supposed to make writes
   long. Measured with `SLOW_WRITE_MS=0`: **18 writes, slowest 167ms, none over 400ms**, the
   greediest wanting 9 bot moves. #298's 431-move write came from a *deep* pod game; no budget makes
   turn three slow. So the premise, not the marker, was what produced the zero — the same shape as
   D320, where the duel's writes wanted three moves and a sixteen-fold budget left the suite green.
4. **A check that called a working arm broken, twice.** "The latency actually reached the table",
   measured as the median time of a driver move: 79ms, while every frame was being held 600ms each
   way. A click returns when the button is pressed, not when the ack lands, and many driver moves
   are local taps that emit nothing. Only sampling the routed frames — real `pod:action` payloads
   and their acks going through the delay — showed the arm had been working the whole time. It now
   measures frames held, which is the thing it is actually claiming.

Chrome's `Network.emulateNetworkConditions` is also recorded as **not sufficient**: at 1200ms the
median move was 335ms and only the occasional one crossed 400ms, because it does not apply to
frames on an already-open WebSocket. `page.routeWebSocket` with a promise chain per direction does,
and keeps socket.io's ordering intact.

The tally for this session's theme is now **eleven** instruments found reporting something they had
not earned, of which **eight** were mine.

## D327 — Correction: a stuck server seat *is* reported, and I deleted the assertion that proves it

D325 removed `expect(stalled).toEqual([])` from the budget test, filed #304 against
`continueBots` for ending a dead table in silence, and "corrected" a comment in `handlers.ts` to
say so. All three came from one true observation generalised wrongly, and all three are now undone.

**What is true.** `runBots`' "ran out with a seat still owed" report is guarded by
`stopAt >= BOT_MOVE_GUARD`, so at a budget of 25 against a guard of 500 it cannot fire. That is
why the shipping budget displaced it and why `reportBotStall` exists.

**What I inferred, wrongly.** That a server seat which is owed a move and cannot make one therefore
ends the chain in silence. It does not. `runBots` calls its stall in three more places, all inside
the loop and none conditioned on the budget:

```
seat N is owed a move at turn T step and botAction offered none
<action> by seat N at turn T step changed nothing
<action> by seat N at turn T step was refused: <why>
```

Those are exactly the "a bot cannot move" cases. `continueBots` then returns null, the handler
stops, and the report has already gone out through `onBotStall` — which, since D322 wired the
caller's callbacks back up, reaches the caller.

**The cost.** `expect(stalled).toEqual([])` was not vacuous, and deleting it dropped real coverage
of the property the test is named for. Restored, and this time proved to discriminate rather than
argued about: a one-shot synthetic stall at turn 2, which the table then recovers from, fails it
and nothing else —

```
["synthetic one-shot stuck seat 1 at turn 2 upkeep"]: expected [ Array(1) ] to deeply equal []
```

A blunter break (every bot move stuck from turn 3) fails the `hasPriority` assertion first, so the
one-shot was needed to show this assertion earns its place on its own.

**#304 is closed as not a defect**, with its filing kept as the record of the error. Two notes
worth keeping. First, the general lesson: "this *particular* report cannot fire" is not "this
condition is unreported", and the way to tell is to read every call site of the callback rather
than the one the change touched. Second, the thing that made it cheap to find was writing the claim
down in a task and a comment where I would read it again.

That makes three corrections of my own reasoning in this stretch — D321 (the count does bound the
duration), D326 (the arm, not the marker, produced the zero), and this one — against which the
measurements that settled them all existed only because the claims were written down somewhere they
could be checked.

## D328 — The surface audit, and the five wrong guesses covering four controls cost (#305)

`scripts/surface-coverage.mjs` asks the question 225 passing browser checks cannot: which rendered
controls does no check ever press? First reading: **100 controls, 10 that no check even names.**

`scripts/check-table-controls.mjs` now covers eight of them — the d6, handing a tabletop game to
the rules engine, "Move by hand", conceding, starting over, leaving, and both of the watcher's
lobby doors — at **23/23**. The audit reads **3 unnamed, down from 10**.

**Its own script, not a block in `e2e-table.mjs`.** Two of these controls change what the table is,
and the first attempt put them at the end of that suite, where they aborted the run and would have
left its other 70-odd checks reading a different game.

### What the five guesses were, because each one is a fact about the product

1. **The d6 is not in the feed.** `TableFeed` is a transient overlay of notable lines that renders
   nothing at all when there are none, so the first check waited 30s for an element absent by
   design and reported it as the d6 not working. A roll lives in the **log**.
2. **The engine will not start on a finished game.** `startAutomation` throws `NOT_STARTED`
   ("deal the table first"), and the first attempt pressed `hand-to-engine` after the tabletop
   suite had played to a winner. A control only reachable mid-game has to be checked mid-game.
3. **"New game" only exists after a game ends.** It sits in the post-game block beside "Play
   again"; pressing it on a live table waited 30s for a button that was not there.
4. **A reset clears the decks, not just the board.** `game:reset` empties `cardDefs` and
   `instances`, so `start-game` comes back **disabled** rather than absent — which is exactly what
   the button's own comment promises ("what you want when somebody is changing decks"), and what
   the check now asserts.
5. **Concede arms on the first press and concedes on the second** — "Concede", then "really?",
   because conceding is irreversible and a phone misclick would end somebody's game. A single click
   sent nothing, and the failure said so only because the check had been taught to read the log:
   *"no concede in the log, so the click did not land"*. That message is the difference between a
   five-minute fix and an afternoon.

Three of those five were found only because a check was written to report **what it found** rather
than that it did not find what it wanted. That is the cheapest habit in this file.

### What is left, and why

Six controls remain unnamed by any check, and they are not one kind of thing:

- **`confirm-targets` is unreachable** with the present pool (D327's neighbour finding, recorded at
  the button): a fixed-target spell is sent as its last target is chosen, so the Cast button only
  appears for an "up to N" spell, and every optional spec in the pool is also `divided`, which the
  bar declines to draw it for. It stays for the first non-dividing "destroy up to two target
  creatures".
- **`ward-decline` and `pact-decline`** are the *declining* halves of two prompts whose accepting
  halves are covered. Each needs a specific board to reach; the engine's own suite covers both
  outcomes, so what is missing is only that the button sends what it says.
- **`toggle-manual`** ("Move by hand") was the escape hatch inside an automated game and is now
  covered, with a guard that the manual moves are **absent until it is pressed** — otherwise the
  check would pass on a sheet that offers them always.
- **`watch-open-*` and `stop-watching`** are covered now, and getting there turned up two facts and
  one thing that needed fixing.

  **The Watch button beside an open table only exists before the table is dealt.** `listPublic`
  lists a pod while its status is `lobby`, and *readying deals the table*, so the listing drops it
  one step earlier than I assumed twice over — not at "start game" but at "ready". Watching a game
  **in progress** is the code box's job (`watch-table`, which `e2e-arena` covers). Whether a game in
  progress should be findable from the lobby at all is a product question, left as one: listing
  in-progress tables changes what the lobby advertises, and that is a call about the product rather
  than a defect to fix in a test.

  **What that press lands on is good behaviour, and a check looking for the wrong element read it as
  a blank page.** The spectator gets *"Watching — Waiting for the table to deal. Nothing is being
  hidden from you that the players can see."* My check waited for `watching-code`, which is the
  dealt-table header, and reported "landed on: (no known screen)". Printing the page's own text in
  the failure message is what settled it in one run.

  **And that screen had no testid, nor did its Stop button** — which is why the audit never listed
  either and no check could reach them. An element with no testid is invisible to the instrument as
  well as to the suites, so the audit's own count was an undercount. Both have one now
  (`watching-waiting`, and the same `stop-watching` as its twin on the dealt-table header: same
  label, same action, never on screen together). The audit now reads 196 testids rather than 195,
  which is the honest direction for a number like this to move.

Named rather than left as a number, which is the point of the instrument.

### The instrument's second category was half false alarm, and fixing it found two more

"Looked at but never pressed" read 23 controls, and the list was wrong about about half of them:
the driver's usual shape is `const lit = page.locator('[data-testid^="card-"]')` on one line and
`await tap(lit.first())` a line or two later, so a selector by itself says nothing about which it
was. Sampled nine families by hand: **five were being tapped, four were not.** Reading six lines
past each selector moved the counts from 64 pressed / 23 unpressed to **78 pressed / 12**, and what
was left standing was the point:

- **`life-up-*` had never been pressed.** `e2e-table` presses `life-down-0`; nothing had ever
  pressed the other direction — the control a player uses for every lifelink hit and every "undo
  that". Covered now, both ways, read from the other player's screen, because a life total that
  moves only locally is the oldest bug a tracker has. **25/25.**
- **`cmd-dmg-*` is covered now**, and the script's table is **Commander** rather than Modern to
  reach it — which is also the format this project is built around, so it is the likelier table for
  two people anyway. The counter is a button only when the format is Commander, the row is somebody
  else's, and the table is tracked by hand; on your own row the same testid renders as a read-only
  span, which is part of why the control/passive split found it confusing.

  The sixth wrong guess in this file lives here: there are **two** elements, and the check read the
  wrong one. `cmd-dmg-<seat>` on an opponent's row is what you *record*; `cmd-taken-<seat>` on your
  own row is what you *read* — the worst single commander's damage and whose it is, because
  "cmd 7/0/14" tells a player nothing actionable when CR 903.10 is per-commander. The host presses
  the first, the guest reads the second, and the second renders only once there is damage to show,
  which makes it a good assertion rather than a vacuous one. **26/26, twice.**

Five of the twelve that remain (`chat-messages`, `list-note`, `attach-hint`, `token-sheet`,
`table-error`) are containers and labels that the control/passive split gets wrong — they sit
inside something clickable, so the JSX around them looks like a button. That is the heuristic's own
error rate, stated rather than quietly carried.

---

## D329 — The card fields a rules engine needs, and an importer that had never written half of them (#306)

Nick asked how close the Play Realm is to all Commander-legal cards being scripted, and then which
import would serve best. The measured answer to the first was **348 unique scripted cards across 13
decks, about 1% of the roughly 30,000 cards legal in Commander** — and the blocker is not the
scripting API, which handles 60-odd mechanics. It is that the project has no card data to script
against.

The answer to the second came out of the code rather than a comparison. `scryfallService.js`
already fetches Scryfall's `oracle_cards` bulk file — one row per unique card, not per printing, so
a tenth the bytes of `default_cards` and no less rules information. MTGJSON's `AtomicCards` gives
pre-split `types`/`subtypes` and a `leadershipSkills.commander` flag, which is genuinely more
convenient, at the price of a second schema and a second source of truth for the same facts. The
file this project already downloads wins on that alone.

What was actually wrong was narrower and worse than the choice of file.

**`scryfall_cards` had 22 columns and the importer wrote 13 of them.** The nine it skipped included
every one a rules engine would need to do anything with a card it has no script for:
`color_identity` (the rule that decides what may go in a Commander deck), `legalities` (how the
deck is checked at all), `keywords`, `card_faces` and `edhrec_rank` — all five present in the
baseline schema since 0001, all five left NULL by every sync that has ever run. And six more had no
column at all: `power`, `toughness`, `loyalty`, `layout`, `oracle_id`, `produced_mana`.

So: **migration 0015** adds those six, and the importer's Postgres upsert goes from 13 parameters
to 26, refreshing all of them on conflict.

Four things in that are decisions rather than mechanics:

- **`power`, `toughness` and `loyalty` are TEXT.** A creature can be printed `*`, `1+*` or `?`, and
  a planeswalker can be printed `X`. An `integer` column does not merely store those badly — it
  rejects the row, so the cards whose size *is* a rule are exactly the cards that would go missing.
  This is asserted, and the assertion was proved by typing the column `integer` and watching
  `invalid input syntax for type integer: "*"` fail two tests.
- **`oracle_id` is indexed but not unique.** It is the card's identity across printings, which is
  what a decklist means by a card name and what a script attaches to; the table's primary key `id`
  is a *printing*. `oracle_cards` holds one row per oracle id, but this table has been written by
  other paths over the years, so a unique index would make the migration fail on existing data
  rather than on anything a sync does.
- **`card_faces` is trimmed on the way in.** Scryfall's faces carry `image_uris`, `artist`,
  `illustration_id`, `flavor_text` and more; each face now keeps the eight fields that are rules
  plus one image. Storing the raw blob would make the largest column in the table the one nothing
  queries.
- **The SQLite statement is deliberately untouched**, and the file says why. The live SQLite table
  is `card_name`-keyed with a different column set, this container's `grimore.db` has no
  `scryfall_cards` table at all (checked by PRAGMA), and widening a dialect nothing here can
  execute is precisely how the `scryfall_id` bug shipped in the first place.

`SCRYFALL_BULK_FILE` points the import at a file already on disk. That is not a test convenience:
`api.scryfall.com` is unreachable from this environment, and the loop was previously unrunnable
without a several-hundred-megabyte download from a host an egress allowlist may refuse. Download
`oracle_cards` anywhere, copy the JSON across, point the variable at it — the file is the same
artifact the downloader would have produced.

### What the dry run showed, and the counter it exposed

Run against a scratch Postgres from a seven-card fixture built to carry the awkward shapes: 28
columns after migrations, six rows written, `*`/`1+*` and `X` intact, the modal-DFC's trimmed faces
intact, `produced_mana` on the land, `commander=banned` preserved, and `no_identity /
no_legalities / no_oracle_id` all zero.

And a line that read **"Wrote 7 cards"** over six rows.

`insertCard` returns early for a token, an emblem, an art-series card, a silver border, a digital
printing, or anything legal in no format — and the loop incremented `cardCount` whenever it
returned without throwing, which a filtered card does exactly as a written one does. On the fixture
that is one row of overstatement. On the real dump it is every token in it.

The wrong number is the smaller half. **The guard meant to catch a broken import tested
`cardCount === 0`, and with filtered cards counted as written it could not fire.** A sync that
filtered all 30,000 rows and wrote nothing would have reported 30,000 written, 0 rejected, and
raised nothing at all — the eleventh instrument this session that reported success it had not
earned, and the ninth of those that was mine. The two outcomes are counted apart now, the tally
prints both, and the second guard — wrote nothing, nothing rejected — is reachable for the first
time. Both its arms were fired on purpose: a file of nothing but tokens, and a file of nothing
parseable.

### The test

`apps/api/src/card-sync-schema.test.ts` runs the statement against a migrated scratch database — no
download, no network — and now covers the widened half. Three things in it are worth naming:

- `expect(named.length).toBeGreaterThan(10)` is gone. It passed just as well on the statement that
  wrote 13 columns as on the one that writes 28, so it could never have said the importer was
  leaving `legalities` empty. It is an equality now: **28 columns, 26 parameters, 26 in the row
  builder.** The first draft asserted 26 columns and failed at 28 — `name` and `card_name` are two
  columns fed by one `$2`, and `last_updated` is CURRENT_TIMESTAMP — so both counts are stated.
- A **structural** check that every inserted column appears in the `DO UPDATE SET` list. Forgetting
  half of a widening is the thing that actually goes wrong here; the old conflict clause refreshed
  six of thirteen, so a re-sync wrote new oracle text into a row that kept its old rarity.
- The three breaks, run rather than reasoned about: withdraw migration 0015 → seven of eight tests
  fail; drop `power = EXCLUDED.power` → the structural check names `power` and the round-trip check
  fails; type `power` as `integer` → the `*` row is refused by Postgres.

Gate green afterwards: 2138 tests across 17 packages.

**Still Nick's call, and untouched here:** running the import on the VM, and whether the Scryfall
host is reachable from it. Nothing in this entry touches live data; the migration adds nullable
columns and an index, and the importer only runs when something calls it.

## D330 — A check that printed 26/26 and exited 1 (#307)

The background full-suite run came back with `check-table-controls.mjs` reporting **"26/26 checks
passed"** and **`exit=1`** on the same two lines.

`summarize()` in `scripts/lib/table-driver.mjs` sets `process.exitCode` on failure and returns
nothing. Two callers — `check-table-controls.mjs` and `check-in-flight.mjs` — end with
`process.exit(summarize() ? 0 : 1)`, so `undefined` sent both to 1 on every run, including every
run where nothing failed.

This is the same defect as a check that cannot pass, and it is the mirror of the one this session
has found ten times over: the printed tally and the exit code disagreed, and which one you believed
depended on whether a human was reading or a script was. I read the tally, twice, and called the
file done. The background runner read the exit code.

`summarize()` returns a verdict now, and a press or tap that never landed counts against it — those
are checks that did not really run, which is why they are printed above the tally rather than below
it. Both directions were exercised directly: `true` with only a passing check, `false` once one
fails. `check-table-controls.mjs` now exits 0 on its 26/26.

---

## D331 — The probe that moved the whole problem: it was never the creatures (#308)

The data path from D329 is only worth building if something can use the data. So before writing any
of this, a throwaway probe asked what the engine actually does today with a card nobody has written
a script for. Three readings, and two of them meant the plan I had was wrong.

1. **An unscripted vanilla creature already works.** A 2/2 with no script, no registry entry and no
   change anywhere: cast, resolved, on the battlefield, attacking the next turn.
2. **An unscripted creature whose text is `Flying, vigilance` already has both keywords.**
   `characteristicsOf` read `flying` and `vigilance` off it. `printedKeywords` was written for
   exactly this — its own docblock says "so an **unscripted** card still behaves" — and it works.
3. **An unscripted land produces no mana whatsoever.** `manaSources` returned `[]` and the potential
   pool was all zeros, with `{T}: Add {G}.` printed on the card and visible in the UI. The engine
   reads mana abilities off the script and nowhere else.

So the shortfall was never the creature side. I had been about to build a general card generator;
what the engine actually needs is **one** thing generated, and it is the thing printed data states
most exactly. A deck of data-derived cards was not failing because its creatures were blank. It was
failing because its lands did nothing, so it could not cast anything at all.

A fourth reading settled a rejection rule: a `*`/`*` creature cast with no script went **straight to
the graveyard**. That is correct Magic — its size comes from a characteristic-defining ability
nobody read, so it is a 0/0 and dies to CR 704.5f — and it is the reason `fromCardData` refuses a
non-numeric power or toughness. A card that reliably dies on arrival is strictly worse than a card
you move by hand.

### What shipped

`packages/rules-engine/src/fromCardData.ts`: a row in, either a `CardDef` (plus a script where one
is needed) or a refusal with a reason. Five accepted shapes — basic land, readable mana source,
vanilla creature, keyword-only creature, blank noncreature permanent — and a long list of refusals,
each carrying text rather than a count, because a count of rejections cannot tell anyone what to
script next and a list of reasons is exactly that input.

Four decisions in it are the file:

- **Parse the text; `produced_mana` is the cross-check, not the source.** That field says *which*
  colours a permanent makes and nothing about how many. A Sol Ring produces `["C"]` and taps for
  **two**. A derivation that read the field and ignored the text would ship a Sol Ring that taps for
  one — wrong in the direction that loses games. So the ability comes from the printed line, matched
  against two deliberately narrow shapes, and Scryfall's answer is then compared against the parse.
  A disagreement in either direction is a rejection: a missing colour means an ability went
  unparsed, an extra one means the parse invented mana.
- **A basic land's ability comes from its subtype** (CR 305.6). A Forest's oracle text is
  `({T}: Add {G}.)` — brackets, because it is a reminder — so reminder text is dropped and the green
  comes from the type line, which is where the rule actually lives.
- **One tap ability per colour**, not one ability producing several. The same shape the hand-written
  Guildgates use and for the same reason: `manaSources` collapses several free tap-for-mana
  abilities into one source making *one of* its colours, so a single two-colour ability would be two
  mana off one land and the engine would start offering two-drops that cannot be paid for.
- **A `WeakMap` keyed by the definition, not a registry keyed by name.** A name-keyed cache would be
  global mutable state shared by every game in the process, and two games holding different data
  under one name — one from a card sync, one from a fixture — would silently get whichever derived
  first.

### The wiring, and the one line that mattered most

`scriptForCard(def)` consults `scriptFor(def.name)` **first**, so all 348 pool cards read exactly as
they did before and derivation only ever reaches a card nobody has written. That claim is not an
argument, it is the 1364 pre-existing engine tests still passing unchanged.

Five call sites now pass the definition instead of the name: `manaSources`, `potentialMana`, the
ability-offering loop in `legalActions`, the arrival hook that reads `entersTapped`, and —
the important one — `scriptOf` in `automation.ts`, the chokepoint every activation goes through.
Without that last one a derived land would have been *offered* in `legalActions` and then refused on
activation, which is the "an option offered and then refused is worse than an option that was never
there" failure this codebase has two decision entries about already.

### Honest limits, stated in the code

`scriptForCard` derives from a `CardDef`, and a `CardDef` has no `produced_mana` — so **the
cross-check cannot run on that path.** It has the printed text and the type line and nothing else.
A caller holding the database row should hand that row to `cardFromData` directly and keep what it
returns; this is written into the function rather than left for someone to discover.

Three breaks, run rather than reasoned about, each failing exactly the tests that depend on it:
unwire `manaSources` → the mana test fails alone; unwire `scriptOf` → the three tests that cast or
play fail; unwire the arrival hook → only the enters-tapped test fails.

28 tests, gate green at 2166 across 17 packages (1392 in the engine, up from 1364).

### What this is not

It is not "the engine now knows thirty thousand cards". It is the slice of a Commander deck whose
rules its data already is — and in particular a mana base, which is the half of a list that has to
work before any of the rest can. Everything whose text is a paragraph of English still becomes
cardboard, which is the right answer for it. The next question is a measured one rather than a
guess: run `tallyDerivations` over a real `oracle_cards` file and read what share of it comes
through, and which refusal reasons are the common ones. That needs the import from D329 to have been
run, which is Nick's call on a machine that can reach Scryfall.

## D332 — Measured: lands 61%, creatures 14%, everything else 0% (#308)

`customDeck` now resolves a pasted name three ways instead of two — the pool, then any card rows the
caller supplied, then cardboard — and `scripts/measure/derivable.mjs` answers the question that
decides how much that is worth.

The instrument's default arm reads the engine's **own 348 cards** back as data rows. Those are real
cards with real printed text, so this is a measurement rather than an estimate; it is also thirteen
decks assembled by hand to exercise sixty mechanics, so it is far heavier in paragraph-text cards
than a list anybody plays. The share it reports is therefore a **floor**, and the script prints that
caveat itself rather than leaving it in a header nobody reads.

| | built | of | share |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Lands** | 17 | 28 | **60.7%** |
| Creatures | 24 | 173 | 13.9% |
| Instants | 0 | 69 | 0% |
| Sorceries | 0 | 50 | 0% |
| Artifacts | 0 | 18 | 0% |
| Enchantments | 0 | 17 | 0% |
| Planeswalkers | 0 | 5 | 0% |
| **Overall** | **41** | **360** | **11.4%** |

**The by-type row is the reading that transfers**, and it is why the script prints it. The aggregate
is a fact about whatever set was measured; the rate *within a type* can be applied to a deck whose
type mix you know. A Commander deck is about 37 lands and 30 creatures, and a real mana base is
basics and simple duals rather than the pool's Mutavaults and cycling lands — so somewhere around a
third of a hundred-card list should come through, almost all of it the mana base.

Which is the same answer the probe in D331 gave from the other direction. The derivation's value is
concentrated in lands; lands are the single largest block of a Commander deck; and the mana base is
the part that has to work before any of the rest of the deck can do anything at all. That is a
coherent result rather than a consolation one.

The refusal shapes, grouped and counted, are the work queue:

- **189 (52.5%) "cannot read the line"** — one unhandled line of text. The example is Mutavault:
  `{1}: Mutavault becomes a 2/2 creature until end of turn.`
- **114 (31.7%) instants and sorceries**, which are nothing but their text and always will be.
- **9 split and modal cards, 5 planeswalkers, 2 with a `*` in their power.**

**Correction to the paragraph above, which was wrong when first committed.** It claimed the grouping
made the unreadable bucket mineable — "twenty common line shapes is a list of things to teach the
reader". It was not. The top-level grouping flattens every quoted line to `"…"`, so all 189 landed
in **one** bucket with **one** example, and what the script actually printed was a number and an
anecdote. Calling that a work queue is the same species of overclaim this session has been finding
all day, committed by me within the hour of writing about it.

Fixed by grouping the unreadable lines by what they *open with*: the card's own name replaced by `~`
(every trigger says its own name, and leaving it in gives one bucket per card), numbers and mana
symbols flattened, first six words kept. Now it is a queue, and the first thing it says was not
visible before:

```
    8  When ~ enters the battlefield you        e.g. Kitchen Finks: "...you gain 2 life."
    6  When ~ enters the battlefield exile      e.g. Banisher Priest
    5  Cycling {M}                              e.g. Tranquil Thicket: "Cycling {2}"
    4  Morph {M}{M}                             e.g. Ainok Survivalist: "Morph {1}{G}"
    4  Enchant creature                         e.g. Robe of Mirrors
    4  ~ enters the battlefield with X          e.g. Chalice of the Void
    3  Soulbond / Convoke                       e.g. Trusted Forcemage / Siege Wurm
    2  Echo {M}{M}                              e.g. Mogg War Marshal: "Echo {1}{R}"
```

**Cycling, morph, echo, soulbond and convoke are mechanics the engine fully implements.** They are
refused here for one reason: `printedKeywords` recognises a keyword as a bare word, and these print
with a cost attached, so `Cycling {2}` reads as a line with rules in it rather than as a keyword.
That is about seventeen cards of 360 — 11.4% would become roughly 16% — and it is a well-bounded
change of exactly the same shape as the mana ability: a mechanic that exists, parameterised by a
number the data states. It is the next increment here, and it was invisible until the grouping was
fixed.

### Two things worth recording as decisions rather than code

**`unknown` changed meaning, and the field is renamed in its docblock rather than in its name.** It
used to be "the names the pool does not have"; it is now "the names nothing could make playable".
All three readers in `apps/realtime` report it to players as the cannot-read count, which was always
the second question — and a table told the first number would refuse to deal an Arena game it could
have dealt. A new `fromData` reports what the card table bought, separately, because "can this be
played" and "how much of that is the import rather than the 348 hand-written cards" are different
questions and only the second can tell a card sync that worked from one that silently wrote nothing.

**The realtime integration is not done, and it needs a decision that is Nick's.** `apps/realtime`
has no database access at all — only Redis — and all three `customDeck` calls sit inside a
synchronous compare-and-set write where no query can happen. So passing real rows means one of:

1. give `apps/realtime` a Postgres pool (a new dependency on a service that currently has none);
2. have it ask `apps/api` over HTTP for the rows;
3. have `apps/api` resolve the list and park the rows in Redis for realtime to read.

What it must **not** be is the client sending the rows with the paste, which is the one option that
needs no new plumbing and is also a cheating vector: a player could hand over a row claiming a
100/100 vanilla creature. Noting that explicitly because it is the option that looks easiest.

Proved to discriminate, as usual: consult the data before the pool → the "prefers the pool" test
fails alone (asserted with a row that is wrong on purpose, a Forest typed as an Island, because a
row agreeing with the pool would pass either way); remove the data lookup → five of the seven new
tests fail.

Gate green: 2173 tests across 17 packages, 1399 in the engine.

---

## D333 — Morph and echo derived, which bought two cards, and the line that stops there (#308)

The queue D332 produced named this family first among the things that are fixable: `Morph {1}{G}`,
`Megamorph {2}{W}`, `Echo {1}{R}`. All three are mechanics the engine **fully implements**, and all
three were refused for one reason — `printedKeywords` reads a keyword as a bare word, so a keyword
printed with a cost reads as a line with rules in it.

So `fromCardData` now parses them into the script fields the engine already has: `morph: { cost: {
mana } , mega? }` and `echo: { cost }`. A new kind, `costed-keyword-creature`, reports them.

**It bought two cards of 360.** 11.4% → 11.9%. That is the measured number and it is small, for a
reason the measurement could have told me before I wrote the code and I did not ask it: six of the
pool's morph creatures have text *besides* the morph line, because a turned-face-up trigger is the
whole reason most morph cards get printed. Only a body-plus-morph-line card derives, and the pool
has two. That limit is now a test of its own rather than a surprise for the next reader.

Whether it is larger on real Magic I do not know and have not claimed anywhere as a number: most
printed morph creatures *are* a body plus a morph line, which argues it is, but this pool cannot
check that and the `--file` arm is the thing that would.

### Where the line is, and why it is a rule rather than a backlog item

The next buckets are "When ~ enters the battlefield, you gain 2 life" and its twenty-odd siblings,
and plain `Cycling {2}`. **Neither is being done, and that is a decision.**

A morph cost is **data**. The engine already knows what morph does; the card supplies a number;
nothing is inferred, so nothing can be inferred wrongly — a misparse is a refusal, and both
directions are tested (`Morph — Pay 3 life.`, which is in this pool, is refused rather than guessed
at; so is a card printing the keyword twice).

"You gain 2 life" is **English**. Turning English into an effect is the direction in which a card
silently does less than it reads: no error, no failing test, and a player loses a game to the engine
rather than to their own misreading — which `measure/card-promises.mjs` exists because of. This
project already has the rule written down for card *text* — *inventing the text of a real card is
worse than leaving the mechanic out* (D259) — and this is its sibling: **inventing the effect of a
real card is worse than leaving it cardboard.**

Cycling sits just on the far side and is the interesting case: its effect is always "draw a card",
so almost nothing is being inferred. What stops it is different — it needs an ability with an
`effect` function rather than a data field, which means this module reaching into `effects.js`, and
a derived ability that *runs code* is a different commitment from one that states a cost. Left out
deliberately, named in the code so the next reader knows it was a choice and not an oversight.

Gate green: 2177 tests across 17 packages, 1403 in the engine.

---

## D334 — Running the instrument's unrun arm found two defects in it (#308)

`derivable.mjs` shipped with two arms and only one had ever been run. The `--file` arm — the one
that matters, since it is what turns the pool's floor into the real figure once the import has been
run — had never been executed at all. Pointing it at the seven-card fixture took one command and
found two things wrong with the instrument.

**A token was refused for having faces it does not have.** `token`, `double_faced_token`, `emblem`,
`art_series` and `memorabilia` fell through to the multi-face check and came back as
*"layout token has more than one face"*. A token has exactly one. The message was simply false —
and `oracle_cards` lists tokens as their own entries, so on a real file it would have been false
thousands of times and sent the next reader hunting a multi-face bug that does not exist. They now
refuse as *"a token is not a card"*, with a test that asserts both the new wording and the absence
of the old one.

**The denominator counted rows the importer would never write.** The first run reported 4 of 7
refused where the honest answer is 3 of 6, because one of the seven was that token. `scryfallService.js`
filters a long list on the way in — tokens, emblems, art series, memorabilia, silver and gold
borders, digital-only printings, and anything legal in no format — so counting them inflates the
refusal rate with rows that were never candidates. The `--file` arm now applies the same filter
before anything is counted and **prints how many it dropped**, so the two can be compared rather
than trusted.

That comparison is now a cross-check worth having: the script keeps 6 of the fixture's 7 rows, and
the importer's own dry run wrote exactly 6 of 7. Two independently written filters agreeing on the
same file is a better reason to believe either of them than the fact that both looked right.

The general lesson is one this session keeps paying for in a new place each time. An unrun code path
is not "probably fine"; it is a claim nobody has tested, and in an *instrument* it is worse than
that, because the output of a broken instrument looks exactly like a finding. Two arms, one run,
and the unrun one was wrong in both halves.

Gate green, 2178 tests.

---

## D335 — All six browser suites on the mana-path change, and what three runs' skips say (#308)

The derivation wired `scriptForCard` into `manaSources`, `potentialMana`, the ability-offering loop,
the arrival hook and `scriptOf` — the engine's core mana and activation paths. 1404 unit tests
passing is necessary and not sufficient for that, so the full browser set ran on the HEAD:

| | |
|---|---|
| `e2e-table` | **73/73** |
| `e2e-arena` | **54/54**, 4 skipped |
| `e2e-pod` | **41/41**, 1 skipped |
| `e2e-solo` | **28/28**, 1 skipped |
| `SOLO_POD=1 e2e-solo` | **30/30**, 1 skipped |
| `check-table-controls` | **26/26**, **exit 0** |

252 checks, 7 named skips, every suite exit 0. The last row is the D330 fix confirmed by the thing
that found the bug: this is the same background runner that reported "26/26 checks passed" beside
"exit=1", and it now reports exit 0.

One scare along the way, recorded because the reasoning was the useful part. The pod suite ran past
**1475 moves** of a 2400 cap, almost all of them passes, which is the exact shape of #297 — a solo
pod that stalled on turn 20 for 500 moves. Before treating it as a stall I read what the moves
actually were, and at moves 1225 and 1325 Cleo cast a Lhurgoyf and a Strionic Resonator. A table
still casting spells is playing a long game, not stuck. It finished 41/41. The slowness was mine:
I ran two full gates (17 packages of vitest) alongside it on a four-core box, which is the same
contention D250 warned about, and the earlier run of the same suite in this session finished
quickly.

### The skips vary by shuffle, which retires an audit I was about to build

I started enumerating the ten prompt kinds the engine can raise (`mustPay`, `mustChoose`,
`mustDecide`, `mustDredge`, `mustCastOffered`, `mustOrder`, `mustDeclare`, `mustDiscard`,
`mustSettleHand`, `mustAttack`) to ask which a browser has ever *answered* — the prompt-axis twin of
`surface-coverage.mjs`. Two things stopped it, both worth keeping.

**First, my own first reading was wrong.** Grepping the two table components reported `mustChoose`,
`mustDecide`, `mustOrder` and `mustAttack` as "NOT RENDERED". They are all handled — in
`apps/web/src/lib/arena.ts`, the interaction reducer, which routes them into sheets rather than
inline rows in the bar. A two-file grep would have reported a four-prompt gap that does not exist,
which is `surface-coverage`'s own 67%-precision lesson arriving in a new place.

**Second, the suites already report this**, and three runs of them answer the question the audit was
for. The skips are named (D302), and across the three full passes in this session they are a
different handful each time:

| skipped | run 1 | run 2 | run 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| nothing searched a library | yes | yes | — |
| no flashback | yes | — | — |
| no X spell | yes | — | — |
| no card asked for a type or colour | yes | — | — |
| no ward | yes | — | yes |
| no modal spell | yes | — | yes |
| no dividing spell | yes | — | yes |
| no card stopped to ask a question | — | — | yes |

**Every gated check has run in at least one of the three.** So no prompt kind is systematically
unexercised in a browser; a single run's skip list is a fact about that shuffle, not about coverage,
and only the union across runs is evidence. That is a negative result, and the right place for it is
here rather than in a new instrument — which is the same call D247 made about thirty clean runs.

---

## D336 — Closed as a negative: no other measure script has an unrun arm (#308)

D334 cost an hour because `derivable.mjs` shipped with two arms and only one had ever been run, and
the unrun one was wrong in both halves. The obvious follow-up is whether any of the other fifty
measure scripts is in the same state. Asked, and the answer is no.

Fifty-one scripts, env-gated flags extracted, the parameters every run uses (`SEED`, `SEEDS`,
`BOT`, `MOVES`, `VERBOSE`, `SUBJECT`) set aside, and five flags left with no recorded run anywhere
in the decision log or the measure README: `PROBE_DECISIONS`, `EXPOSED`, `ALL`, `AGAINST`, `DRAWS`.

**All five are parameters with defaults, not alternative arms.** `PROBE_DECISIONS=3000`,
`AGAINST='ember-rush'` and `DRAWS=3` are defaults every run already uses; `EXPOSED=1` is the weight
that shipped, and the flag exists so a different one needs no edit; `ALL=1` widens
`mechanic-coverage`'s output from the thin rows to every row, which is a different view of data the
default already computes. Not one of them is a branch nothing has executed.

Which makes `derivable.mjs --file` the exception rather than an example of a pattern, and names what
was actually special about it: **the pool arm's own output points at the other arm for the real
answer.** An unrun parameter value is an untried setting. An unrun arm that a recorded conclusion
defers to is a hole in the conclusion.

One note on the instrument, since it is the same lesson a third time. My proxy for "has this been
run" was "does a doc mention the flag with a value", which measures *"never set to a non-default"* —
not *"never executed"*. It happened to surface the right five names, and it would have missed an arm
somebody ran once without writing down, and it flagged three parameters that run constantly. Stated
rather than quietly relied on, which is the whole of `surface-coverage.mjs`'s precision note and
`cr-claims.mjs`'s before it.

---

## D337 — Twelve of twelve clean on the two-person paths, and no vacuous check in the suites

### The evidence Nick's question actually wants

*"Confident that me and a friend can functionally play an entire game"* is a reliability claim, and
one clean run is not evidence for it. So the two suites that drive **two human browsers at one
table** — `e2e-table` and `check-table-controls` — ran six times each, back to back, on the HEAD
that changed the engine's mana paths.

**12 of 12 clean. 73/73 and 26/26 every time, exit 0 every time, not one `FAIL` line in the whole
log.** This is the same shape of evidence D247 recorded for the engine before `scriptForCard` went
into `manaSources`, `potentialMana`, `scriptOf` and the arrival hook, which is why it was worth
re-spending.

One methodological note, since it cost an hour earlier today: the first pass of these suites ran
while two full gates were running beside it on a four-core box, and the pod suite's pace fell from
D250's measured 253ms a move to something like 1.6s. The repeat ran with nothing else on the
machine. **Timings from a contended run are not timings**, which D250 said and I had to be reminded
of by a pod that looked stalled and was not.

### And an audit that found nothing, which is the useful kind to record

The session's recurring find is a check that cannot fail. So: are there any in the browser suites?
`grep "check([^,]*, *true)"` finds **18 checks whose condition is the literal `true`**, which looks
exactly like the shape.

It is not. All 18 are sound, in two different ways:

- **14 sit inside an `if (seen.X)` guard with a paired `skip()` in the `else`.** The `if` is the
  assertion — `seen.ward` is set by the driver only when a ward actually resolved — and the skip is
  counted and named when it does not fire. That is precisely D302's design, and reading
  `check('a ward stops a spell …', true)` out of context inverts it.
- **4 are labels on a preceding `waitFor`**, which throws on timeout. `await waitFor(nick,
  'deck-ember-rush')` *is* the test; the `check(…, true)` on the next line is what puts a positive
  statement in the log for a reader.

So nothing to fix, and the audit's own precision is the thing worth stating: a grep for `, true)`
has 18 hits and 0 findings, because it matches the *syntax* of a vacuous check rather than its
meaning. The same lesson as `surface-coverage.mjs`'s 67% first pass, arriving by grep this time.

One honest observation that falls out rather than a defect: the four `waitFor`-backed ones mean a
**setup** failure aborts the suite with a Playwright timeout instead of printing a named failed
check and carrying on. That is defensible and is the reasoning `check-table-controls`'s own header
gives for being a separate file — if the table never deals, the seventy checks after it are reading
a different game, so continuing would produce seventy misleading results rather than one clear
one. Left as it is, deliberately, and written down so the next reader does not have to re-derive it.

---

## D338 — Cycling, the reasoning I used to exclude it, and the lookup that was missed (#308)

D333 left cycling out and gave a reason. The reason was weaker than it sounded, and re-reading it
is what produced this entry.

The objection was: cycling needs an ability carrying an `effect` **function** rather than a data
field, so `fromCardData` would have to reach into `effects.js`, and *"a derived ability that runs
code is a different commitment from one that states a cost"*.

That conflates two different things. What is worth being afraid of is **inferring an effect from a
card's English**, because a card that silently does less than it reads throws nothing and fails no
test. Cycling is not that: **CR 702.29a defines the keyword as "Discard this card: Draw a card"**,
so the effect comes from the rules and the only card-specific parameter is the cost — exactly as
with morph. Whether the engine implements a mechanic as a script field or as an ability holding a
function is a fact about the engine, not a measure of how much is being guessed.

It is also where the value was. **Five of the eleven lands the pool refused were cycling lands.**

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Lands | 17 of 28 — 60.7% | **22 of 28 — 78.6%** |
| Overall | 43 of 360 — 11.9% | 48 of 360 — 13.3% |

Lands are where the measured share lives (D332), so this is the largest single step the derivation
has taken — five cards against morph-and-echo's two, and in the half of a deck that has to work
before the rest of it can do anything.

Typed cycling is refused: `Swampcycling {2}` and its relatives **search a library** rather than
drawing, which is a different ability with a different prompt, and CR 702.29a defines only the
typeless version. The line D333 drew still holds: "When this enters, you gain 2 life" is English,
and no keyword defines it.

### The lookup that was missed, and why only driving it could find that

The end-to-end test earned its keep immediately. The derived cycling ability was **offered
correctly** — `abilityIndex: 1`, `fromHand: true`, cost `{2}` — the cost was paid, the card went to
the graveyard, the ability went on the stack, and it **resolved doing nothing**. No error, no
refusal, no draw. A card that silently did half of what it reads, which is exactly the failure this
module's whole design exists to avoid, arriving by a route the design did not cover.

The cause: D331 wired five call sites and all five are **battlefield** lookups — `manaSources`,
`potentialMana`, the ability-offering loop, the arrival hook, and `scriptOf`. It did not wire
**`scriptOnStack`**, which is how a resolving spell or ability finds its `effect`. That one still
read the hand-written registry by name, which has no entry for a derived card.

Two things make it worth writing down rather than only fixing:

- **An ability on the stack is the one lookup that can reach a card no longer in play.** A cycling
  cost discards the card as the ability is activated, so by the time resolution runs the instance is
  in the graveyard and the only thing left is `cardDefs[object.cardKey]` — which is precisely what
  `scriptForCard` takes. The shape of this mechanic is what exposed the gap; a mana ability never
  leaves the battlefield and would never have found it.
- **Inspecting the derived script would not have caught it.** A unit test asserting that
  `abilities[1].effect` is a function passes either way — the script was always right. What was
  wrong was the engine's path to it, and only resolving the ability could say.

Proved by break: revert `scriptOnStack` to `scriptFor` and the cycling test fails alone while the
other 35 pass.

Gate green: 2181 tests across 17 packages, 1407 in the engine.

---

## D339 — Correction to D332: realtime should not get a database pool, and a prior decision says why

D332 listed three ways to get card rows to `apps/realtime` and called it Nick's decision. I was
leaning towards the first — give realtime a Postgres pool — and had talked myself into thinking the
only objection was availability, which an *optional* pool with graceful fallback to pool-only
resolution would answer completely: no new failure mode, the Play Realm still runs without the card
database, pasted lists just stay as they are today.

Then I read `packages/shared/src/env.ts`. The reason `realtimeEnvSchema` exists is a decision
already taken, with its reason written down:

> It had been calling `parseEnv()`, the whole-platform schema, so it refused to boot without
> `DATABASE_URL` and `SESSION_SECRET` — neither of which it ever reads. That is worse than
> inconvenient: **a process that demands a database URL it never opens invites someone to put the
> production one into its environment**, and it makes "the table will not start" look like a
> database problem when there is no database involved.

That is not an availability argument, which is why my optional-pool design does not answer it. It is
about **where a production credential ends up**. Giving realtime a pool means handing the socket
server a database credential it would use for one optional feature — exactly the thing that change
was made to prevent, and exactly the kind of decision somebody should not quietly reverse six
months later because it was the shortest path to a feature.

So the ordering changes. **Option 2 — realtime asks `apps/api` for the rows over HTTP — is now the
leading candidate**, because it keeps the credential in the service that already holds it and adds
no new place for it to live. Its costs are real and smaller: a network hop on the paste path, and
realtime needing to know the API's address.

Two things worth keeping from this:

- The decision is still Nick's, but it is a **different** decision than I described. Not "which
  plumbing is tidiest" but "should the socket server hold a database credential" — and the
  codebase's own answer to that is already no.
- I nearly reversed a recorded decision by not reading the file that holds it. The `env.ts` docblock
  did its job; I only had to look. The general version: before choosing between options, check
  whether one of them has already been decided against, because a stated reason in the code outranks
  a fresh preference formed without it.

## D340 — What actually bounds the wire payload, and the extrapolation that got it right by luck (#308)

My own work made a question live that nothing covered. Now that a pasted decklist can be *played*
rather than just loaded (D331-D338), a singleton Commander list is a real shape the wire has to
carry, and the existing size test in `packages/rules-engine/src/automation.test.ts` does not reach
it. That test measures a **starter** deck — twenty-four basics and a handful of four-ofs, so roughly
fifty definitions for sixty cards — and then extrapolates in a comment:

> a 100-card Commander library is roughly twice this one

The extrapolation is on **card count**. Its own next line concedes the part that makes that
suspect: *"dedup saves nothing on a singleton"*. A hundred different names is a hundred definitions,
not fifty, so "roughly twice" is doing two jobs at once and only one of them is card count.

So I measured the uncovered shape with a scratch probe, then turned the probe into a test beside the
existing one rather than leaving the answer in a scratchpad.

**Measured**, 99 singleton names plus a commander, drawn from all 348 pool names, in `edh` at turn 6:

| what | bytes | share of `WIRE_CAP` (131,072) |
|---|---|---|
| seat 0's view, empty board | 6,504 | 5.0% |
| seat 0's view, busy board (14 creatures, 7 in hand, 8 in graveyard) | 27,145 | 20.7% |
| the full server state at that same moment | 84,961 | 64.8% |

102 definitions are in `state.cardDefs`, which the test asserts (`> 99`) so it cannot quietly become
a deck that deduped away.

**The structural finding, which is the point of the entry.** `viewFor` inlines a card definition
only onto cards the seat may actually see; a library travels as face-down counts. So **what bounds
the payload is how many cards are visible, and the board bounds that — not how many different cards
the deck holds.** The old comment reached a true conclusion ("a Commander deck fits") by a route
that does not support it. Had definitions travelled as a dictionary, "roughly twice" would have been
right about the mechanism and the test would still have passed; it passes because the mechanism is
different from the one it names.

**Why the threshold is `WIRE_CAP / 2` and not the cap.** The 84,961-byte figure is the one that
chose it. That is the same position with every definition carried, and it is *inside* `WIRE_CAP` —
so an assertion at the cap would pass on the exact regression this test exists to catch, something
starting to inline a whole library. At half the cap, 84,961 fails and 27,145 passes. A bound that
cannot fail on the failure it is written for is the session's recurring defect (D330, D334, D337);
this one discriminates, and the number that proves it is in the comment so the next person does not
have to re-derive it.

Not pinned to 27,145 exactly: that number moves whenever a card in the pool gains text, and an
assertion that breaks on a deck edit is noise.

Verification: the full gate before the push — `node scripts/guards.js`, `pnpm v2:typecheck`,
`pnpm v2:typecheck:tests`, `pnpm v2:test` — with `@grimore/rules-engine: 1408 tests` and
`Tasks: 17 successful, 17 total`.

## D341 — Mana that is not a land, derived, and a refusal of my own I had over-read (#309)

`derivable.mjs` groups the lines the derivation cannot read by what they open with, and one bucket
in that list was not English at all:

```
      2  {M} Add {M}
         e.g. Llanowar Elves: "{T}: Add {G}."
```

A Llanowar Elves prints the same line as a Hagra Broodpit. The land derived; the dork did not — and
a Sol Ring, whose entire card is `{T}: Add {C}{C}.`, did not either. Both were refused by
`fromCardData.ts`, which read mana abilities in the land branch only and refused a nonland permanent
with any text whatsoever.

### Why this family and not the one above it in the list

The bucket above it is twenty-odd cards opening `When ~ enters the battlefield, …`, and that is the
larger number. It stays refused, because `fromCardData.ts` wrote down where its line is and the
reason holds: an ETB effect is **English**, and turning English into an effect is how a card comes
to silently do less than it reads. The module's own words — *"inventing the effect of a real card is
worse than leaving it cardboard"* — and I am not crossing that in the same session it was drawn,
without new evidence, which is the D339 lesson.

A mana ability is on the other side of the same line, for the reason cycling was: nothing is
inferred. The text states the cost, the colour and the quantity; the parse either matches the whole
line or refuses it.

### The over-reading I had to correct, which was mine

The first draft refused every line adding more than one mana, and justified it by naming *"the Sol
Ring case named in this file's header"*. Reading the header back, that is not what it says. Its
argument is against deriving an ability from **`produced_mana`** — the field says *which* colours a
permanent makes and nothing about how many, so `["C"]` would have produced a Sol Ring that taps for
one. The Sol Ring is the header's example **because the field is insufficient**.

`parseManaLine` does not read the field for quantity. It reads `{T}: Add {C}{C}.`, which states two.
So the refusal was a good rule applied to a case it was not about, and the shape of that mistake is
worth naming: **a stated reason can be cited for a conclusion it does not support, and the citation
makes the conclusion look already-argued.** The fix was to re-read the paragraph I was citing.

### What is in

`ManaLine` now carries a mode, which is the distinction the engine has always drawn and this parse
had flattened:

| printed | read as | built as |
|---|---|---|
| `{T}: Add {G}.` | choice of one | one ability |
| `{T}: Add {G} or {W}.` | choice | one ability per colour |
| `{T}: Add one mana of any color.` | choice of five | five abilities |
| `{T}: Add {C}{C}.` | **sum** | one ability, `produces: ['C','C']` |

`manaSources` collapses several free tap-for-mana abilities into a single source that makes *one of*
their colours, so a choice must be several abilities and a sum must be one — a five-colour bird
built as one ability would make five mana off a 0/1. A **mixture** (`Add {G}{G} or {W}`) is refused,
and so is a sum beside a second mana line, because the merge rule those would need is the kind that
is wrong in one direction with nothing to notice.

Three branches now read it — land, creature (`mana-creature`), and artifact/enchantment — and all
three run the `produced_mana` cross-check, which only the land branch did before.

### The verification that is not mine

The three cards this is about are **already in the pool, hand-written from the printed card before
this module existed**. So the tests do not assert that the derivation matches what I think a Sol Ring
does; they build a row out of the pool's own `CardDef` — its real type line, mana cost and oracle
text — and compare the derived script against `scriptFor(name)`:

- **Sol Ring** → `mana-source`, abilities equal to the hand-written ones, one ability, `['C','C']`.
- **Birds of Paradise** → `mana-creature`, five abilities equal to the hand-written five.
- **Llanowar Elves** → `mana-creature`, equal to the hand-written one.

And the negatives from the same pool, which are what keep those honest: **Mind Stone** stays refused
(its second ability sacrifices it for a card — half of that card is not the card), **Mana
Confluence** stays refused (its mana costs a life), and a Sol Ring row whose `produced_mana` says
green is refused by the cross-check.

At a table, with the assertions a parse cannot pass by accident: a derived rock puts **two**
colourless in the pool from one permanent; a three-drop is cast off two derived rocks with **no land
on the board at all**; and a derived dork is **not** a mana source the turn it arrives (CR 302.6) and
is one two turns later, asserted as green going 0 → 2 so the forest cannot be what is counted.

Proved to discriminate: reading a sum as a choice — the Sol-Ring-taps-for-one bug — fails four of
them.

### Measured

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| pool, built from data alone | 48 / 360 (13.3%) | **51 / 360 (14.2%)** |
| creatures | 26 / 173 | 28 / 173 |
| artifacts | 0 / 18 | 1 / 18 |

Three cards, which is a small number and an **unrepresentative** one. This pool holds one rock and
two dorks because it was built to exercise sixty mechanics, not to play Commander; a real list runs
five to fifteen. This is the one family so far where the pool proxy understates the real figure for
a structural reason rather than as a general caveat, and it is the reason to prefer it over a bucket
with twenty cards in it.

Gate: guards, typecheck, typecheck:tests, test — 1418 rules-engine tests, 17/17 packages.

## D342 — The measurement that could not see the change, which is the eleventh of these and the second I caught on myself

Straight after the change above, `derivable.mjs` printed **48 of 360, 13.3%** — the figure from
before it, to a tenth of a percent.

Nothing was wrong with the number. The instrument imports
`packages/rules-engine/dist/index.js`, `dist` had not been rebuilt, and it was an honest measurement
of the previous build. **That is the most misleading thing a measurement can be**, and it is worse
than a broken one: a broken instrument says so.

`scripts/lib/provenance.mjs` already prints when `dist` was built, and its docblock says the mtime
*"is the only thing that catches it"*. Reading that again after being caught by it: the mtime is the
only thing that **could** catch it. Catching it was left to a reader noticing that one timestamp
precedes another, and in the one case anybody has run this, the reader was me and I did not notice.

So the comparison happens in the instrument now. `provenanceLine` walks the engine's sources,
takes the newest mtime, and appends `STALE(src <time>)` when the build is behind it. Test files are
excluded on purpose — editing one does not change what `dist` holds, and an instrument that cried
stale after every test edit would be ignored inside a day.

Proved in all three directions, because a staleness check that always fires and one that never fires
read identically on a clean tree:

- fresh build → `[3163669 DIRTY, dist built 2026-11-03T21:55:45Z] …`
- `touch src/fromCardData.ts` → `… dist built 21:55:45Z STALE(src 21:56:44Z) …`
- rebuild, then `touch src/fromCardData.test.ts` → no `STALE`

`derivable.mjs` now prints that line, which it did not before. **Five of the fifty-two scripts that
import `dist` print provenance**; the rest are left, deliberately, as a known gap rather than a
fifty-file sweep made at the end of a long session — and this is the one that had actually misled
somebody.

## D343 — A mana cost beyond tapping, and the land branch's honest ceiling (#310)

D341 read mana abilities whose whole cost is `{T}`. Three cards in this pool print one clause more,
and each clause is a field the engine already has:

| printed | engine field | hand-written twin in the pool |
|---|---|---|
| `{T}, Pay 1 life: Add one mana of any colour.` | `cost.life` | Mana Confluence |
| `{T}, Sacrifice Lotus Petal: Add one mana of any color.` | `cost.sacrificeSelf` | Lotus Petal |
| `Morph {2}` on a **land** | `script.morph` | Zoetic Cavern |

All three are now read, and each is compared against the hand-written script rather than against my
expectation of it — the same verification as D341, for the same reason: somebody built those three
from the printed card before this module existed.

### The printed cost text is carried, not rebuilt

`ManaLine` carries the cost prefix **exactly as printed** — `{T}`, `{T}, Pay 1 life`,
`{T}, Sacrifice Lotus Petal` — and the derived ability's `description` is that string plus
`: Add {W}.`

That started as a convenience and turned out to be the thing that makes the twin comparison exact.
A rebuilt label would have had to choose between the card's **name** and `this artifact`, and both
are printed — on different printings of the same card. Carrying the text sidesteps a choice that has
no right answer, and the tests then compare descriptions as well as costs, which is the half that
could silently drift.

### Three refusals that are one word from an acceptance

- `{T}, Sacrifice a creature: Add {B}.` — refused. That is a *choice* of which creature, made when
  the ability is activated, and nothing in this parse models a choice. One word from a Lotus Petal.
- `{T}, Pay 1 life, Sacrifice Painful Petal: Add {W}.` — refused. Two clauses; only one is read,
  because a cost this parse half-reads is worse than one it refuses outright.
- A permanent whose mana abilities **cost different things** (`{T}: Add {W}.` and
  `{T}, Pay 1 life: Add {U}.`) — refused. `foldManaLines` builds one source from several lines, so
  it would have to flatten two costs into one, and flattening either way prices the card wrong:
  free when it is not, or painful when it need not be. The same rule refuses a printed costed
  ability folded in with a basic land type's free intrinsic one.

Proved to discriminate by reading a pain land's life cost as free: three tests fail, including the
one at a table.

### At a table

Two spires pay for a two-drop and the life total reads **18** — the engine collects the cost, so
what the test checks is that the derivation put it there. A derived Petal pays for a Bear and is
**gone from the battlefield**, in the graveyard, and still gone two untap steps later, which is what
a consumed source means.

### Measured, and the ceiling this reaches

| | D341 | now |
|---|---|---|
| pool, built from data alone | 51 / 360 (14.2%) | **54 / 360 (15.0%)** |
| lands | 22 / 28 (78.6%) | **24 / 28 (85.7%)** |
| artifacts | 1 / 18 | 2 / 18 |

The four lands still refused were checked one by one, and **every one of them is a land that does
something**:

- Mutavault — `{1}: … becomes a 2/2 creature until end of turn.`
- Maze of Ith — untaps an attacker and prevents its damage
- City of Brass — `Whenever City of Brass becomes tapped, it deals 1 damage to you.`
- Aether Hub — enters with an energy counter

So the land branch is at its honest ceiling for this pool: what is left is not unparsed mana, it is
four different effects, and each needs the thing this module refuses to invent. That is a better
stopping point than a percentage, because it says *why* the next land is not coming.

### One side effect worth writing down

Adding the two new cards to the test deck dropped its forests from 36 to 20, and the multi-turn
playout test — which plays a land whenever it has one and checks that a land reached the battlefield
by turn eight — **failed**. Nothing was wrong with the derivation; I had diluted the mana base of a
deck another test measures through. The counts are back near where they started and the reason is in
a comment beside them. A shared fixture is a shared assumption, and changing its shape changes tests
that never mention it.

Gate: guards, typecheck, typecheck:tests, test — 1425 rules-engine tests, 17/17 packages.

## D344 — The schema drift nobody had looked for: what local SQLite does not have (#311)

CLAUDE.md says to verify every change by running `python execution/verify_master_suite_orchestrator.py`,
the project's own 14-suite master test. **Nothing in this entire effort had ever run it.** I ran it.

With no server up, 13 of 13 suites failed on `Connection refused`, which says nothing. With
`node server.js` running against the local SQLite store, **8 of 13 passed**, and three of the five
failures named a cause worth chasing:

```
Error in /api/decks/discover: SqliteError: no such column: d.is_public
                              SqliteError: no such column: ds.season_id
Profile API error: HTTP 500   (no such column: profile_theme)
```

### The direction nobody had audited

This project has a thorough record of schema divergence — `claude/postgres-schema-gap-2026-09-27.md`
and `scripts/audit-postgres-schema-gap.js` — and the existing parity test's docblock says outright:
*"Duplicated security logic plus good intentions is how the schema divergence in this repository
started."*

Every one of those looks the **same way round**: what does **Postgres** not have that `server.js`
writes. That is the production direction, and it is the one that got the attention.

The other direction had never been looked at: **what does local SQLite not have.** `db.js` builds a
different table set per dialect, and its Postgres branch carries a block of two dozen
`ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` statements titled "Column migrations for Postgres". The
SQLite branch has the four `players` ones and **nothing else**.

So on a freshly created local database:

- `/api/decks/discover` — the home feed, which this project's own product rules call a primary
  surface — answered **500**.
- The metagame endpoint answered **500**.
- `GET /api/players/:id/profile` answered **500**.
- `INSERT INTO decks (... is_public, format)` names columns that did not exist, so **creating a deck
  could not work at all**.

And this is the direction that matters most for how the project says to work, because CLAUDE.md's
first rule of the deployment workflow is *"Test Locally First: always implement, run, and verify
changes on local server (http://localhost:3000)"*. **Local was the broken one.** The instruction and
the environment it names had been pointing in different directions for as long as the drift existed.

### Measured against the project's own statement of the schema

One 500 at a time is whack-a-mole, so the gap was enumerated instead: every
`ALTER TABLE x ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS y` in `packages/db/migrations/` — which is this project's
statement of what the schema **is** — compared against a freshly created local database.

**Twenty-one columns missing, across four tables.** Fifteen are now added, and the six left out are
left out on purpose:

| table | columns | status |
|---|---|---|
| `decks` | `budget_limit`, `include_basic_lands_in_price`, `created_at`, `updated_at` | added |
| `players` | `profile_theme`, `featured_deck_id`, `discord_handle`, `moxfield_username`, `email_verified_at`, `sessions_valid_from` | added |
| `seasons` | `allowed_colors`, `allowed_rarities`, `banlist`, `budget_limit`, `max_rares` | added |
| `scryfall_cards` | `power`, `toughness`, `loyalty`, `layout`, `oracle_id`, `produced_mana` | **not** added |

Plus eleven more from `db.js`'s own Postgres ALTER block (`decks.is_public` and seven siblings,
`deck_stats.total_matches` and `season_id`, `seasons.schedule_mode`).

The `scryfall_cards` six are migration 0015, from #306 three hours ago, and `CARD_UPSERT_SQLITE` was
deliberately left at thirteen columns there. Adding columns nothing writes would be the opposite of
closing a gap, so they stay out with the reason beside them.

### Read-then-add, not try-then-ignore

The blocks already in that file wrap each `ALTER` in a `catch` that swallows everything, because
SQLite has no `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS`. That cannot tell "the column is already there" from a
typo, a missing table or a locked database — **a real error reads as a successful migration**, which
is the same defect shape this session has found eleven times now in instruments.

So the new block reads `PRAGMA table_info` first and adds only what is missing, logging each one.
That is also how the twenty-one were counted: the log says exactly what it repaired.

Two deliberate divergences, stated in the code: `TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()` has no SQLite
equivalent — SQLite refuses a non-constant default on an added column — so the four timestamp
columns are added **nullable with no default**. Safe because the code already reads them that way:
`server.js` guards `sessions_valid_from` with `row ? new Date(...) : null`, and null reads as "no
cutoff", which is the right answer for a row that predates the column.

### What it bought, measured

| | suites passing |
|---|---|
| no server running | 0 of 13 |
| server up, before the fix | 8 of 13 |
| after the schema repair | 10 of 13 |
| after the guest-auth step (D345) | **11 of 13** |

The two that still fail both time out against an external AI advisor service this environment
cannot reach, which is the blocked-service class already recorded for Scryfall and the rest. They
are left failing rather than made to pass.

Verified by endpoint, not by inference: `/api/decks/discover` and `/api/players/1/profile` both went
500 → **200**. Legacy unit tests 40/40. And the legacy Postgres write-path suite, which skips
silently without `POSTGRES_TEST_URL` (the same shape as D303's Redis finding), run deliberately
against a scratch database: **28 of 28**, so the Postgres branch is verified untouched rather than
assumed untouched. The v2 gate is green.

## D345 — A suite that could not pass in any environment, and the four audits behind it

`verify_full_ui_button_and_modal_suite.py` — one of the fourteen CLAUDE.md names — failed at its
first of five steps:

```
[1/5] Auditing 1-Click Guest Auth (/api/auth/guest)...
[FAIL] Guest auth error: HTTP Error 404: Not Found
```

Not a 500, not a timeout: a **404**. So I went looking for the route. `/api/auth/guest` does not
exist in `server.js`, which registers eleven other `/api/auth/*` routes. It does not exist anywhere
in the repository. The only mention of that path in the whole codebase was **the test that audits
it**.

What did exist is the reason it is gone: `passwordPolicy.js` blocklists `guestpass123`, and the
parity test beside it says *"The shared guest account's password, retired in migration 0012."* The
feature was removed on purpose.

So this suite has failed in every environment, forever, and because the step is the first of five it
`sys.exit(1)`s before the other four have run. **The orchestrator CLAUDE.md names as the verification
step could therefore never report success** — which makes it worse than no suite at all, because a
standing failure is indistinguishable from a real regression. This is the session's recurring defect
in its purest form: not a check that cannot fail, but its mirror, a check that cannot pass.

The step now asserts the endpoint is **gone**, and says why in the file. That is not a weakened
check — it is a better one: a shared guest login with a publicly known password quietly coming back
is exactly the regression worth catching, and nothing was watching for it.

**And the four steps behind it ran for the first time. All four pass:**

- five section endpoints (`/api/cards/recommendations`, `/api/decks/public`,
  `/api/cards/autocomplete`, `/api/leaderboards/season`, `/api/sandbox/ai-meta-decks`)
- TCGplayer affiliate attribution — the literal `xJoE0d` from this project's own rules, across the
  cart exports
- the A2UI core renderer and its component schemas
- the login form in `public/index.html`

Four audits of rules this project states explicitly, that had been written, committed, listed in
CLAUDE.md, and never once executed.

The general version, which is new: **when a check has never passed, the thing to ask is not "why is
it failing" but "has it ever passed".** A failure that predates everyone's memory of the code gets
read as environmental, and the five minutes it takes to grep for the endpoint is the whole
difference between that and finding four unrun audits.

## D346 — The sibling audit nobody had written, and six false positives from a one-line detector

D344 found the drift by chasing 500s one at a time, then enumerating against
`packages/db/migrations/`. That closes the columns the migrations name. It does not answer the
general question, which is the one `scripts/audit-postgres-schema-gap.js` answers in the other
direction: **what does `server.js` write that the local store does not have.**

So `scripts/audit-sqlite-schema-gap.js` now exists, as the mirror of the script that has been there
since September. Same method — `INSERT INTO <table> (<columns>)` out of `server.js`, compared against
the live catalog after `initDb()` — and the same reason for using INSERTs rather than every
reference: a SELECT of a missing column fails too, but an INSERT is where the two schemas were
written apart and it names its columns explicitly.

### The detector, and why its first version was worse than nothing

`server.js` writes dialect-specific SQL as a ternary:

```js
const SQL_UPSERT_COLLECTION_CARD = db.isPostgres
  ? `INSERT INTO collection_cards (..., foil, ...)`
  : `INSERT INTO collection_cards (..., is_foil, ...)`
```

The Postgres audit skips the SQLite branch; this one has to skip the **Postgres** branch. My first
detector tested for `isPostgres ?` on the same line as the match — which misses the multi-line form
above, the only form the file actually uses. It reported **seven** missing columns.

**Six were false positives**, and each one was the Postgres spelling of a column SQLite has under
another name:

| reported | SQLite actually has |
|---|---|
| `collection_cards.foil` | `is_foil` |
| `collection_cards.created_at` | `added_at` |
| `card_price_cache.cached_at` | `last_updated` |
| `scryfall_cards.id` | `scryfall_id` |
| `scryfall_cards.name` | `card_name` |

Every one of those pairs is in `claude/postgres-schema-gap-2026-09-27.md` as a divergence **already
fixed**, so acting on that output would have argued for changes that reintroduce a closed bug. The
existing script's own comment warns about exactly this and says why it tests a line's first
character rather than using a proximity window: *"a proximity window is not good enough"*. I wrote a
worse version of a detector whose correct version was ten lines above the function I was mirroring.

Corrected to the exact mirror — a line whose first non-space character is `?` — the output is
**one** column: `deck_cards.custom_tag`, which is a real gap and which **no schema anywhere
creates**. `server.js` inserts it on the deck-save path and selects `dc.custom_tag` in the deck
queries; it is in neither branch of `db.js` and in no migration. Added to SQLite; recorded for
Postgres in that document rather than fixed with a migration from here, because the migration list
is a cutover artifact and the cutover is Nick's.

### Nine tables, and seven of them are the same seven

```
account_events  active_roster  direct_messages  email_verifications  friend_requests
password_resets  pod_results  pods  wishlist_cards
```

Seven of those nine — `active_roster`, `pods`, `pod_results`, `wishlist_cards`, `friend_requests`,
`direct_messages`, `password_resets` — are on the Postgres document's list too. League check-in,
pods, results, wishlist, friend requests, DMs and password reset are dead in **both** halves of a
dual-mode setup.

That sharpens the existing argument rather than adding a new one. The document says the v2 migrations
are, right now, the fix for seven broken features in the app serving users. The other direction adds
the reason nobody noticed: **there is no environment in which those features work**, so nobody has
