ever been able to test them. Not attempted here, because the fix for seven of the nine is the
migration cutover — one decision, rather than seven tables hand-translated into a second dialect.

### Proved in both directions, and a claim of mine that was not true

Against a schema built from nothing (`grimore.db` moved aside): same nine tables, and **every column
`server.js` inserts exists**, so the repair in D344 covers a fresh database rather than only the one
on this disk. And with one line deleted from `columnMigrations`, the audit reports
`decks is_public` and nothing else — it discriminates.

One correction to myself, caught while verifying rather than after: the docblock I wrote documented
`DB_PATH=/tmp/fresh.db` as the way to audit a fresh schema. **There is no such variable** — `db.js`
resolves its SQLite path at require time from `__dirname` with no override. The paragraph now gives
the `mv grimore.db aside` recipe that actually works, and says what it replaced. A documented flag
that does not exist is a claim that cannot be true, which is the same fault as a check that cannot
fail, committed in a comment instead of in code.

## D347 — Two front doors, and the one that looks healthiest cannot play (#312)

Running the legacy server for #311 put a question in front of me that nothing had asked: **if Nick
opens the address CLAUDE.md names — `http://localhost:3000` — and finds the Play Realm, does it
work?**

`server.js` mounts the v2 SPA at `/react` whenever `apps/web/dist` exists. So the Play Realm *is*
there. Driven with Playwright against `http://127.0.0.1:3000/react/play`:

- the lobby renders **completely**: the two formats, the name field, Just us / Open table, Create
  table
- the socket opens to `ws://127.0.0.1:3000/socket.io/` and the **handshake succeeds**, because the
  legacy server runs its own Socket.IO on that path
- `grep -c "socket.on('pod:" server.js` is **0** — that instance has no table handlers at all
- "Nobody has an open table right now" reads as an empty lobby
- **no connection warning appears**, because nothing is wrong with the connection
- pressing Create table produced `the table did not answer` about ten seconds later, and nothing
  else

So the single most likely address for a new player serves a Play Realm that looks completely healthy
and cannot play, and the only thing it ever said was five words that name no cause.

### Why this is the mirror of #266 and not a repeat of it

#266 fixed a table that said `connecting` for ever, and `connectionTrouble`'s docblock is careful
about what it may claim: pointed at a closed port, every `connect_error` carried the string
`websocket error` and nothing else, so it says the two things true of every case rather than
guessing which one it is.

This failure is on the other side of a **successful** handshake, which is why none of that
machinery fires. And it is the worse of the two, because the failure the screen shows you is nothing
at all. A connection that fails is visible; a connection that succeeds and goes nowhere looks like
an empty room.

### What it says now, and what it refuses to say

`silentServerNote(url, connected)` replaces the bare timeout string:

> The server at this page's own address took the connection but did not answer. The table runs as
> its own process, so an address that serves this page is not necessarily the one that plays the
> game.

It claims **only** that the handshake was taken and the protocol was not answered, which is exactly
what was observed. It deliberately does **not** say "this is the wrong server", because a real table
server that is wedged or overloaded produces the same eight-second timeout — naming that cause would
be the guess-dressed-as-diagnosis `connectionTrouble` talks itself out of. A test pins that:
`expect(said).not.toMatch(/wrong server|legacy|port 3000/i)`.

The operator's version — `apps/realtime`, port 4100, `VITE_REALTIME_URL`, or a proxy forwarding
`/socket.io` — goes to the console, the same split #266 made: the player gets what is true, whoever
runs the server gets the fix.

Not-connected keeps the old sentence, because `connectionTrouble` is already saying the useful thing
about that path and changing it would be noise.

### Verified in the browser that produced the bug

The same probe, after rebuilding `apps/web`: the banner now carries the new sentence and the console
carries the remedy. Four unit tests in `apps/web/src/lib/table.test.ts` (27 in the file now), and
the browser suites on the shipping table: `e2e-table` **73/73**, `check-table-controls` **26/26**.

### What is not fixed, and why that is a decision rather than a dodge

The underlying split — page on 3000, table on 4100 — is a deployment choice with three plausible
answers: give the `/react` mount a realtime address, put a proxy in front that forwards `/socket.io`
to `apps/realtime` (**it cannot be the legacy server itself**, whose own Socket.IO already owns that
path), or leave 3000 serving the rest of the SPA and keep the table on its own address. That is
Nick's to pick; `claude/play-realm-setup.md` now has the section, the evidence, and the three
options.

The general lesson, which is new and is about where to look rather than what to fix: **a feature can
be thoroughly tested through the door it was built behind and completely broken through the door
people will actually use.** Six browser suites, 253 checks, every one of them entered at port 5100.
Not one had ever opened the address the project's own instructions name.

## D348 — Closed as a recorded negative: the deployed shape does not have #312's problem

D347 found that the SPA served from the legacy server's `/react` mount cannot play, because the
socket lands on the legacy Socket.IO instead of `apps/realtime`. The obvious next worry is whether
the **VM** has the same hole, since the VM serves the SPA from that same legacy app. It does not,
and all three links were read rather than assumed:

- **`Caddyfile`** splits the two paths: `handle /socket.io/*` → `realtime:3000`, `handle` → `app:3000`.
  Its own comment explains why both are `handle` blocks — so the socket path cannot be swallowed by
  the catch-all — which is exactly the arrangement the client's "one reverse proxy, same origin"
  default is written for.
- **`deploy-gcp.ps1`** runs `pnpm --filter @grimore/web build` and aborts the deploy if it fails,
  then copies `apps/web/dist` into the bundle. So `/react` is genuinely served on the VM; the claim
  in `claude/play-realm-setup.md` that `https://grimore.gg/react/play` works does not rest on an
  artifact that might be missing.
- **`docker-compose.yml`** puts `realtime` behind `profiles: ["v2"]`, so it does not start with a
  plain `docker compose up` — which the setup document already says, with the commands.

So the broken door is specifically **port 3000 reached directly with no proxy in front**, which is a
local-development shape and not the deployment. Worth writing down for two reasons: it stops D347
reading as a deployment defect, and it shrinks the decision from "how should the app be served" to
"do you want port 3000 to work locally too, or is `scripts/play.mjs` enough" — a much smaller
question, and still Nick's.

Nothing changed in code for this entry. The setup document's section now says it.

## D349 — Correction to D346: Postgres always had `deck_cards.custom_tag`, and a `head -8` hid it

D346 reported `deck_cards.custom_tag` as a column **no schema anywhere creates** — the
`direct_messages` class, referenced by the app and defined by nothing — and said Postgres still did
not have it. That is wrong, twice over:

- `db.js`'s **own Postgres branch** lists `custom_tag TEXT` in its `CREATE TABLE deck_cards`.
- `packages/db/migrations/0001_baseline.sql` lists `custom_tag text` in the same table.

So Postgres has had it from the beginning, and the gap was one-sided: the **SQLite** branch's
`CREATE TABLE deck_cards` was the only place it was missing. The fix in that commit is still right
and still needed — on a fresh local database `INSERT INTO deck_cards (..., custom_tag)` is the
deck-save path and it could not run. What is wrong is only the claim about Postgres, and the
conclusion drawn from it, which was that this belonged in the document's "defined by nothing" table.

### How the error was made, which is the part worth keeping

The command that established it was:

```
grep -n "custom_tag" server.js db.js packages/db/migrations/*.sql | head -8
```

Eight `server.js` hits came first, and **`head -8` cut off the `db.js` line and the baseline line**.
The evidence that would have contradicted the conclusion was in the output I asked for and threw
away before reading it.

Two rules follow, and the second one already existed:

1. **A `head` on a multi-file grep can silence exactly the files that would have changed the
   answer**, because the limit falls where the file order puts it and not where the evidence is. For
   a question of the form "does anything define X", the count matters per file — `grep -c` per file,
   or no limit at all.
2. This project has a standing instruction to **diff legacy SQL against `0001_baseline.sql` before
   porting anything**. That rule, followed, catches this in one command. I applied it to the
   twenty-one columns enumerated from the migrations and skipped it for the one column that came
   from a different route, which is the kind of gap a rule has when it is remembered as a step in a
   procedure rather than as a question about every claim.

Corrected in place: the comment in `db.js` and the section in
`claude/postgres-schema-gap-2026-09-27.md`, both of which now say what is true and point here for
why they changed. **The commit message of `ac2aef6` carries the wrong claim and cannot be corrected**
— it is pushed — so this entry is where the record is set straight, and the two files a reader would
actually consult say so themselves.

## D350 — Eight of the nine missing tables are the cutover; the ninth is nobody's, and one doc row was stale

D346 listed nine tables `server.js` inserts into that the local SQLite store does not have, and
noted that seven are on the Postgres document's list too. That is where I left it. Having just been
caught by a truncated grep (D349), the right move was to finish the question rather than leave it at
"seven of these look familiar", so each of the nine was checked against the migrations and `db.js`
with no limit on the output:

| created by | tables |
|---|---|
| migration `0007` | `friend_requests` |
| migration `0008` | `wishlist_cards` |
| migration `0009` | `active_roster`, `pods`, `pod_results` |
| migration `0014` | `account_events`, `email_verifications`, `password_resets` |
| **nothing, anywhere** | **`direct_messages`** |

So **eight of the nine are one decision away** — the migration cutover, which is Nick's — and the
ninth is a different kind of thing: `direct_messages` is referenced by `server.js` and defined in no
branch of `db.js` and no migration, so direct messaging cannot work on either dialect and nothing
pending changes that.

### And a row in the document that had gone stale

`claude/postgres-schema-gap-2026-09-27.md` says, in its summary table and in a section of its own,
that **`direct_messages` and `password_resets`** are "the two nothing creates" — "not in `db.js`'s
Postgres branch, not in `db.js`'s SQLite branch, not in any migration".

That was true on 2026-09-27. It is not true now: `0014_account_security.sql` creates
`password_resets`, and its own header names password recovery as the finding that drove the
migration. So the document has been arguing from a two-item control that became a one-item control
when 0014 was written, and a reader meeting the table first would conclude password reset is
unfixable.

Corrected in place, in four places — the table row, the control sentence, the section, and a later
mention — because that document is a statement about **now**, which is the rule written down in
D328: a progress document gets corrected, a dated decision entry does not.

The general shape is worth naming because it is the opposite of the usual stale-doc problem. The
document did not drift because nobody maintained it; it drifted because **somebody acted on it**.
A document whose whole purpose is to list what is broken goes stale precisely when it works, and
nothing connects the fix back to the list. The same will happen to the table above the moment the
cutover runs.

## D351 — The wire cap holds for a whole game, and the peak arrives at turn 136 (#313)

`STATE_MAX_BYTES` (128 KiB) is not advisory: `PodStateEvent` in `packages/shared` **refuses** a
state over it, so a view past the cap is a broadcast that never goes out and a table that stops
mid-game. Two tests measure against it — `playout.test.ts` and the singleton test from #308 — and
**both measure one position**.

A position is not a game. What accumulates over forty turns is graveyards, exile, tokens and the
log, all of it visible to every seat and therefore all of it in the view, and nothing had ever
watched the size while a game ran. `scripts/measure/wire-growth.mjs` now does: whole four-player
pods, every seat sampled every tenth move, reporting the **peak** and the turn it happened on.

| arm | games | turns | worst peak | share of cap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| starter decks | 8 | 35-61 | 38,965 B | **29.7%** |
| four pasted hundred-card singleton lists | 8 | 54-150 | 58,147 B | **44.4%** |

Sixteen games, every one to a finish, none over the cap. **The answer is that it holds**, with 2.25x
headroom at the worst reading.

Three things in that table are worth more than the verdict:

- **The singleton arm nearly doubles the starter peak** (29.7% → 44.4%), which is the shape a real
  Commander table has and the shape #308 measured at one point in time.
- **The peak arrives late.** Seat 3's worst view in the longest game was at **turn 136**, and the
  other singleton peaks land at turns 101, 103 and 111. No single-position test reaches there — the
  existing ones sample turn 6 and mid-game — so the growth they could not see is precisely the part
  that matters.
- **Singleton games run far longer**: 54-150 turns against the starters' 35-61. A hundred different
  cards is a less focused deck, so it kills more slowly, which is why its views have longer to grow.
  The two effects compound, and that compounding is the thing a single reading cannot show.

### What it does not claim, and why there is no test

The bots play these games, so the boards are the boards a bot builds. A player who hoards tokens or
fills a graveyard on purpose reaches positions these do not, so the peak is a **floor on the peak**
rather than a bound on it — which the script prints, so a reader cannot take it for a bound.

Not turned into a gate test: the longest of these games is 804 moves and 150 turns, and the suite
runs on every push. The single-position test from #308 stays as the fast regression check — it
discriminates, which was proved when it went in — and this script is the slow question, run when the
wire format or the view changes.

Reliability evidence beside it, from the same session, on both shapes: `state-invariants.mjs` over
40 duel passes — **520 games, nine invariants checked after every action, zero broken** — and the
pod arm over 10 passes, **130 pods, same nine invariants, also zero**. 650 games in all, every state
self-consistent.

## D352 — Two caps written for one purpose, disagreeing at four seats (#314)

#313 measured the view at a hundred-card singleton deck. The obvious next question is the **bound**
rather than a typical case: what is the largest list a player can actually paste, and does the view
hold there? `DECKLIST_LIMITS` answers the first half — `maxCards: 250`, `maxDistinct: 150` — so the
arm was built at 250 a seat.

It never ran. The engine refused the table:

```
EngineError: a table may hold at most 600 cards   (INVALID_DECK)
```

`MAX_INSTANCES = 600` in `packages/rules-engine/src/internal.ts`, under the heading **"Caps on the
card layer, so one action can never blow past STATE_MAX_BYTES"** — which is the same reason
`DECKLIST_LIMITS` gives for its own numbers. Two caps, written for one purpose, in two packages,
set independently.

Four seats share the 600. So:

| cards a seat | at the table | result |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 400 | dealt |
| **150** | **600** | **dealt** |
| 151 | 604 | refused |
| 200 | 800 | refused |
| 250 (the paste maximum) | 1000 | refused |

Measured, not derived on paper — the boundary is exactly where the arithmetic says, and the failure
is at `game:start`, after the paste was accepted.

**So the paste says yes and the table says no.** A player may paste anything up to 250 cards, get an
ack describing their deck, sit down at a four-seat pod, and have the host press Start to be told the
table holds at most 600 cards. Nothing between those two moments mentions it. At three seats the
threshold is 200; at two it is 300, which is above `maxCards`, so two people are never affected —
which is why `maxCards` is not simply wrong, and why lowering it would refuse a 250-card list that
two players could legitimately play.

### What shipped

A **warning**, not a limit, at the one moment somebody is looking at the size of their own list:

> 200 cards · over 150, so a four-seat table cannot be dealt with four lists this size

`DECKLIST_LIMITS.maxCardsForFourSeats = 150` carries the arithmetic and the reason in its docblock,
beside the limit it disagrees with, so the next reader meets both numbers together.

**And a guard, because that 150 is a number copied by hand across a package boundary.**
`packages/shared` cannot import the engine — the dependency runs the other way — so the arithmetic
is written out in a comment, which is exactly the shape that drifts. `scripts/guards.js` now reads
`MAX_INSTANCES` out of the engine's source and `maxCardsForFourSeats` out of shared's and fails if
they disagree; proved by setting it to 149 and watching the guard name both numbers.

### A correction to a comment, with measurements behind it

`maxDistinct`'s docblock said it is "what decides how many card definitions a game state carries".
True of the **state**, and that is worth bounding. But it sat beside limits whose stated purpose is
`STATE_MAX_BYTES`, which caps the **view** — and #308 and #313 both measured that the view is
bounded by what a seat can *see*, because `viewFor` inlines a definition only onto visible cards. A
library travels as face-down counts. The comment now says which of the two it guards.

The measurement makes the same point a third time: at the engine's own four-seat bound — 150 cards a
seat, 600 at the table, the biggest pod that can be dealt — the peak view over four whole games was
**27.9% of the cap**, *lower* than the hundred-card singleton arm's 44.4%. A bigger library is not a
bigger view. The board is the whole of it.

Gate green, 17/17. `pastedNote` has two more tests, including the 150 boundary that deals.

## D353 — I wrote the thirty-sixth harness that swallows an engine throw, in the session that recorded the lesson

`wire-growth.mjs` (#313) had this in its game loop:

```js
try { s = applyAction(s, action); } catch { break; }
```

That is exactly the fault D244 found in **thirty-five** harnesses: an engine refusal reads as a game
that ended, and the run prints a clean peak either way. I wrote the thirty-sixth, two days after
writing the entry about the other thirty-five, in a script whose whole job is to report a number.

It matters most on that script's own `LIMITS` arm, which deals **600 instances** — the engine's
`MAX_INSTANCES` exactly. A swallowed throw there would have turned "this table cannot make a token"
into "these four games were fine". The loop now records the move, the action type and the message,
prints each one under its seed, and says how many games ended on a refusal rather than a result.

### What the honest run then said, and the asymmetry behind it

**No refusals, in four games of 67 to 93 turns at 600 instances.** So I went looking for why, because
600 is zero headroom and these decks make tokens.

`MAX_INSTANCES` is checked in exactly two places, both in `cardActions.ts`: the **deal** (`deck:load`,
`INVALID_DECK`) and the **tabletop** token action (`card:token`, `INVALID_ACTION` — "a token made by
hand", as its own comment says). The automated path, `createToken`/`addTokens` in `effects.ts`,
**does not check it at all**. So a card resolving a token does not consult the cap, which is why a
600-instance table plays on.

Left alone, deliberately, and this is the reasoning rather than a shrug:

- The bound that actually matters is the **view**, and it is measured far away from the cap: 27.9% at
  600 instances over whole games (#314), 44.4% at 400 (#313).
- No card in the pool makes more than a handful of tokens at once, so the docblock's claim — "so one
  action can never blow past `STATE_MAX_BYTES`" — holds for the automated path for a different
  reason than the constant: the card text bounds it.
- Making `addTokens` throw would refuse a token **mid-resolution**, leaving a spell half-resolved.
  That is a worse failure than a large board, and the engine has no way to undo the half it did.

What is wrong is only the impression the heading gives, that the constant covers the card layer
generally. It covers the two paths a *payload* can name a count on. The third path is bounded by the
cards, which is a real bound and a different one.

The general lesson, which is about me rather than the engine: **writing down a defect pattern does
not inoculate against it.** D244 is one of the longest entries in this file, and I reproduced its
subject while building an instrument to measure something else — because the `catch` was incidental
to what I was thinking about. The ones that get written are the ones nobody is thinking about.

---

## D354 — The advisor never answered, and the reason was its position in the file

`/api/sandbox/ai-advisor` is the Play Realm's rules advisor. Two suites in the project's own master
orchestrator call it, and both reported the same thing:

```
[FAIL] Rules Advisor error: <urlopen error timed out>
```

Reading the handler says that cannot be right. It races Gemini against a **1500 ms** timeout and
falls back to a heuristic answer, so the worst honest case is an answer in about a second and a half.
Reproducing it by hand gave something worse than a timeout:

```
anonymous advisor: HTTP 000 in 8.002996s
```

`HTTP 000` is curl's way of saying **no response at all** — not a slow answer, not an error status.
The server log carried the cause:

```
<rejected> TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'player')
```

And the line numbers settled it. The route was registered at **line 345**. `app.use(session({...}))`
is at **line 467**. Express hands a route only the middleware registered *before* it, so `req.session`
was `undefined`, the handler's first line — `if (!req.session.player)` — threw, and because the
handler is `async`, that throw became an **unhandled rejection**. Express 4 does not route unhandled
rejections to an error handler, so nothing ever wrote a response and the socket simply sat there until
the client gave up.

Three separate things made this hard to see, and each is worth naming:

1. **The symptom named the wrong layer.** "Timed out" points at the endpoint's own work — a slow model
   call, a missing key, a hung fetch — so that is where I read first, and the code there is sound.
2. **A docblock asserted the opposite.** The session-epoch middleware's comment says it is mounted
   "before every route, so no route can be reached with a stale session". It is mounted before every
   route *below it*, which was all of them bar this one.
3. **The handler looked defensive.** `if (!req.session.player)` reads as a login check. It is one,
   when `req.session` exists; above the session middleware it is the crash.

The fix is a move, not a rewrite: the whole block (comment, `aiAdvisorQuerySchema`, `aiLimiter`, route)
now sits immediately before `require('./scryfallService')`, below both the session middleware and the
epoch check. Measured after:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| anonymous | `HTTP 000` in 8.00s | `HTTP 401 {"error":"Not logged in."}` in 0.021s |
| logged in | never reached | `HTTP 200`, heuristic answer, 0.009s |

The limiter's own comment was stale too and said so for the wrong reason — it claimed the position was
about a temporal dead zone. It is about the session. Rewritten, with the hang recorded above it so the
next person to tidy this file knows the position is load-bearing.

**One process-level note, because it nearly cost me the diagnosis.** My first re-test after the move
still read `HTTP 000 in 8.0s`, and for a minute I believed the fix had failed. Two
`node --max-old-space-size=768 server.js` processes were alive — pids 179 and 279 — and the one
holding port 3000 was the pre-fix one. The lesson is narrow and practical: when a fix is a *move*
inside a long-running server's source, the old server has the old order, and a stale listener is
indistinguishable from a wrong fix. Also: `pkill -f "server.js"` matched my own shell wrapper and
killed my shell. Reading `/proc/PID/cmdline` and matching on `node` is the way to find the right one.

---

## D355 — Two suites aimed at a login-required endpoint with no key, and one that registered instead of logging in

With D354's hang gone, the advisor answers `401 {"error":"Not logged in."}` to an anonymous caller.
Both suites that call it POST **anonymously** and then assert the answer is non-empty:

```python
with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=5) as resp:
    answer = json.loads(resp.read().decode('utf-8')).get("answer", "")
    if len(answer) > 0: log_ok(...)
```

So independently of the hang, **these checks could never pass**. That is the mirror of the fault in
#311's guest-auth step — a check that cannot fail — and the two faults here hid each other neatly:
the hang made the failure look like a slow endpoint, which is a plausible thing for a suite to be
waiting on, so nobody asked whether the request was even allowed.

Fixed by giving the suites a key rather than lowering the bar. `execution/grimore_session.py`
registers a deterministic throwaway account if it is not already there, logs in, and returns an
opener carrying the session cookie. The two suites now assert a real `HTTP 200` answer and print the
mode it came back in. Asserting the 401 was the other option and is worse: it would have made the
suites certify that the advisor refuses callers, which is not what either of them is for.

Three details in the helper are the point of it:

- **It raises on failure.** A suite that cannot log in must say so, not carry on anonymously.
- **The account is deterministic, not timestamped**, so repeat runs reuse one row rather than filling
  the local `players` table with one account per run. `Username already taken.` is therefore expected
  from the second run onward and is accepted — but *only* that message. Any other 400 raises, because
  "the password policy refused this" must not read the same as "this account is already here".
- **The registration step does not stand in for logging in.** `/api/auth/register` answers
  `"You can now log in."` and sets **no session**.

That last one is a defect I found while writing the helper, in `verify_account_importer.py`:

```python
try:
    res = opener.open(login_request)
except urllib.error.HTTPError:
    res = opener.open(register_request)   # and then carries on, logged out
```

On any database where `TestUser999` is absent — a fresh local store, which is exactly the case #311
was about — it registered, skipped the login, and measured `/api/decks/import-account` **as an
anonymous caller**. Rewritten onto the helper; it now passes against a real session.

**The orchestrator reports 14/14 for the first time.** It was 0/13 when #311 first ran it, 11/13 after
the schema and guest-auth work, and 13 of 13 plus its own self-validation now. Worth stating what that
number does and does not mean: these suites are shallow, several assert things about payloads they
construct themselves, and one passing suite is not one working feature. What changed is that the
number is now **earned** rather than unreachable — every suite that claims to exercise an endpoint
reaches it.

## D356 — The pre-push gate read green with Redis and Postgres both stopped

Immediately after pushing D354/D355 I ran the realtime suite for an unrelated change and got

```
Error: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:6379
```

Redis was not running. Nor was Postgres. And the gate I had run **ten minutes earlier, before that
push**, had printed:

```
@grimore/rules-engine:test:  Tests  1425 passed (1425)
@grimore/api:test:           Tests   306 passed (306)
@grimore/realtime:test:      Tests    46 passed (46)
Cached:    17 cached, 17 total
  Time:    462ms >>> FULL TURBO
```

Every one of those lines was a turbo cache replay. Both `pnpm v2:typecheck` and `pnpm v2:test`
reported `17 cached, 17 total`. Nothing ran. The 46 realtime tests that need Redis "passed" against
a Redis that was not there.

**Turbo is not wrong.** Its cache key is the task's declared inputs — sources, dependencies, env
vars — and a running Redis is none of them. Nothing in the repository had changed since the cached
run, so the cached result was the correct answer to the question turbo was asked. The problem is
the question *I* was asking, which was "do the suites pass against live services", and a cache
replay cannot answer that either way. In this instance the cache was also honest about the change:
the commit touched `server.js`, three Python suites and this file, none of which are inputs to any
turbo task, so there was genuinely nothing to re-run. The gate was green **because my change could
not affect it**, which is a true statement that looks exactly like a verification.

This is the sixth form of the pattern this file keeps recording, and worth listing them together
because the family is the point:

| form | where |
|---|---|
| a check that cannot fail | #311's guest-auth step asserted a login against a route that is 404 |
| a check that cannot pass | D355's two advisor calls POSTed anonymously to a login-required route |
| a swallowed throw | D244, thirty-five harnesses, and D353 — mine, two days later |
| a documented flag that does not exist | D352's `DB_PATH=`, in a docblock I wrote |
| a skipped suite that reads green | D303, 35 realtime tests silently skipped without `REDIS_URL` |
| **a cached pass** | **this one: a check that did not run, wearing the output of one that did** |

`scripts/services-up.js` is the answer, and it asks the one thing the cache cannot know: it opens a
socket to each service and speaks enough of each protocol to be sure the right thing is listening —
an inline `PING` answered `+PONG` for Redis, an eight-byte SSLRequest answered `S` or `N` for
Postgres. No credentials, because "is Postgres listening" and "do these credentials work" are
different questions with different failure messages. Available as `pnpm v2:services`, and it belongs
**before** `pnpm v2:test` in the local gate, which is now five steps:

```
pnpm v2:services && node scripts/guards.js && pnpm v2:typecheck && pnpm v2:typecheck:tests && pnpm v2:test
```

Proved both ways, because a service check that cannot fail would be the joke writing itself: exit 0
with both up, and with Redis stopped, exit 1 naming the port, the reason (`ECONNREFUSED`) and what
it costs ("the 46 realtime tests, which read and write pod state through it").

It is deliberately not needed in CI, which starts both services as containers with health checks and
runs the suites through `pnpm -r` rather than turbo, so there is no cache to restore. This is a
local-gate instrument for a local-gate failure.

**What I am not doing is disabling the cache.** A cached pass after the services are known up is
fine — the cached result was produced by a run that did reach them. The defect was reading a replay
as evidence about the current environment, and the fix is to establish the environment first.

## D357 — Three readings of a pasted list, collapsed into one, with a three-way agreement test

`apps/realtime/src/pod.ts` turned a stored pasted list into a deck in three places, as three
separate `customDeck({ ... })` literals, each carrying its own copy of the same conditional
commander spread:

- `listSummary` — the shape every seat at the table is shown (a name, a size, a cannot-read count);
- `setDeck` — the ack the player who pasted it gets, which names the cards the engine cannot read;
- `applyAction` — the deck actually dealt into the game.

Collapsed into `deckFromPastedList(list, id, fallbackName)`. The reason is what a drift between them
would look like: if one copy lost the commander spread, the table would be told the list holds N
unreadable cards while the deck dealt from it held a different number, or the commander would simply
not be dealt — and **each of the three readings would still be internally consistent**, so nothing
would look wrong from any single vantage point. `fallbackName` stays a parameter because the
difference there is deliberate: the player who pasted an unnamed list is told about "Your list",
everybody else sees "A pasted list", and the name is display only.

One small change rides along: `setDeck` now reads `seat.pastedList`, which it wrote a few lines
above, rather than the `parsed` result it built that from. The two hold the same cards today, so this
is not a bug fix — it makes the ack provably a reading of *the list that will be dealt*.

The test is `realtime.test.ts`'s "reads the same list into the summary, the ack and the dealt deck",
and it is written against the three **observable** readings rather than against the helper, because a
test of the helper would pass just as happily if one call site stopped using it. Two distinct
unreadable names, so a count sourced from the wrong thing — copies instead of names, one name instead
of two — reads differently from the right one.

Two things about writing it are worth keeping, both cases of an observation that could not say what I
wanted it to:

1. **The engine's refusal names only the first unreadable card.** I asserted it named both and it
   does not: `RULE_NOT_APPLICABLE: the engine does not know Nonsense Card`. So that observation
   cannot carry the count, and the dealt deck is instead pinned by `libraryCount` and the command
   zone. Written down in the test, because the next person will reach for the same assertion.
2. **A refused action emits no state**, so waiting for one after the `auto:start` refusal waits for
   an event that never comes — and `libraryCount` after `game:start` is 52, not 59, because the deal
   draws an opening hand. Both readings now happen after the load and before the start, where the
   number is the list rather than the list minus a hand size this test would have to restate.

Proved to discriminate: deleting the commander spread from the helper fails this test **and** its
older sibling, 2 failed of 47. Restored, 47 passed.

## D358 — The response contracts a client derives its types from, and which of them were enforced

PR #35's own body named this as outstanding: *"the other ~20 response contracts still have no such
test. One assertion per route group ... would make every response contract enforced rather than
aspirational."* Measuring first changed the shape of the answer.

### The claim was too broad, and the real gap is narrower and sharper

I checked all 26 contracts that describe a response or an item in one, for a `.parse(` or
`.safeParse(` anywhere in `apps/`:

| | enforced where | count |
|---|---|---|
| per-item contracts | **in the route, as it builds the response** — `MePlayer.parse(player)`, `Collection.parse(row)`, `Deck`, `Notification`, `DirectMessage`, `Friend`, `LeaguePod`, `PlayerStanding`, `Season`, `WishlistCard`, `DeletedItem`, `Card`, `ActiveMatch`, `PlayerProfile`, `DeckSummary` | 15 |
| envelopes | a conformance test | 2 (`RecommendationResponse`, `DeckSuggestionsResponse`) |
| envelopes | **nowhere** | 6 |
| contracts with no route here | — | 2 |

So "nothing validates a response body against its contract" was true when it was written and is no
longer: fifteen contracts are enforced *more* strongly than a test would, because the route itself
raises. A drifted `Collection` shape is a 500, not a silent change.

What is genuinely unenforced is the **envelope**. Every one of these is an object literal —
`res.json({ cards, totalCards, hasMore })` — so a renamed `success`, a dropped `message` or a
`totalCards` that becomes `total_cards` reaches the client unchallenged. And the envelope is exactly
what a client derives its types from.

Conformance tests added for the six: `CardSearchResponse`, `LoginResponse`, `RegisterResponse`,
`AuthStatus` (both arms), `ForgotPasswordResponse`, `PlayerProfileResponse`. `apps/api` 306 → 311.

`DraftView` and `SandboxCard` are the two with no route: they describe the draft endpoints D11
deliberately did not port, so they are a contract ahead of its route rather than an enforcement gap.
Stated rather than tested, because a test for a route that does not exist is the thing this entry is
about.

### Every one has a negative half, because otherwise the test proves nothing

A conformance test that only parses a good body cannot tell a contract that *describes* the response
from one that accepts anything: `z.object({}).parse(anything)` succeeds. So each check also drops a
declared key and asserts the parse is refused. Without that, all six would pass against an empty
schema — which is the same defect as every other entry in this file's family, applied to the test
rather than the code.

Then proved end to end rather than by argument: renaming `totalCards` to `total_cards` in
`routes/cards.ts` fails the new test **and names the field** —
`[{"code":"invalid_type","expected":"number","received":"undefined","path":["totalCards"]}]` — plus
three older tests. Restored.

### A correction I made to myself mid-test, which is the most interesting part

I asserted that `AuthStatus` must **refuse** a signed-in body relabelled `loggedIn: false`, reasoning
that the false arm has no `user`, so accepting it would let a client hold an identity it had been told
it did not have.

It does not refuse it. Zod's object parsing **strips** unknown keys rather than erroring, so the false
arm accepts the body and silently drops the `user`.

Which is the better of the two behaviours, and it is the one worth pinning: a client that parses a
mislabelled body cannot end up holding that identity. My assertion would have been asserting something
the contract does not promise, and would have broken the moment anyone chose `.strict()`. The test now
asserts the strip (`expect(mislabelled).not.toHaveProperty('user')`) and keeps a negative that does
hold — a body claiming `loggedIn: true` with no `user` is refused, because the true arm requires one.

The general form, which is worth more than the specific fact: **a negative assertion is a claim about
the contract, and it can be wrong in the direction of being too strong.** A test that fails because
the code is safer than I assumed is still a test I wrote wrong.

### The guard, so the seventh one cannot arrive unenforced

`checkEveryResponseContractIsParsedSomewhere()` in `scripts/guards.js` reads every
`export const *Response` out of `packages/shared/src/contracts` and fails if any of them is parsed
nowhere under `apps/`. It deliberately does not claim more than it can see — a `.parse(` call is not
proof the call is on a real response body, only a test can be that — but it stops a new response
contract landing with nothing checking it, which is how all six of these got here.

Proved by injecting `GuardProbeResponse` into `contracts/common.ts`: the guard named it and the file
it came from, exit 1. Removed, `[guards] OK`.

---

## D359 — A warning you have to remember to ask for is missing from the script nobody was thinking about

`provenanceLine` was written for D338: `derivable.mjs` printed the pre-change derivation share, to a
tenth of a percent, because `dist` had not been rebuilt after a source change. The number was not
wrong — it was an honest measurement of the previous build, which is the most misleading thing a
measurement can be.

The fix was a line the instrument prints, including `STALE(src <time>)`. Good, and **opt-in**. Counted:
52 scripts import the engine's `dist`, and **45 of them never call it.** So 45 instruments could print
a number about the wrong build with nothing in their output saying so — and the one that actually
burned me was in that 45 until I added the line to it by hand.

Retrofitting forty-five calls is the obvious move and the wrong one: it is forty-five chances to
forget, and the forty-sixth script somebody writes next month starts the problem again.

So the check moved into the thing every one of them must already do. `scripts/lib/engine.mjs`
re-exports `dist` and, on import, compares `dist/index.js`'s mtime against the newest non-test engine
source. Stale, or no `dist` at all, and it writes to stderr:

```
  !! STALE ENGINE: packages/rules-engine/dist/index.js was built 2026-11-03T22:34:22Z,
     but packages/rules-engine/src has a change from 2026-11-04T00:47:23Z.
     Whatever this run prints is an honest measurement of the PREVIOUS build.
     Rebuild and run it again:  pnpm --filter @grimore/rules-engine build
```

All 49 instruments in `scripts/measure/` now import from it. **Importing the engine is the check**,
because none of them can do anything without the engine.

Three deliberate choices in it:

- **It does not throw.** A harness mid-sweep that dies on import loses the sweep, and the honest
  reading of a stale build is "this number is about an older engine", not "this run is invalid" — the
  same judgement D353 made about refusing a token mid-resolution rather than leaving a spell half
  resolved.
- **stderr, not stdout**, so a run piped into a file keeps its measurement clean while the warning
  still reaches the terminal.
- **It does not rebuild.** A measurement script that silently rebuilds what it is measuring is worse
  than a stale number, because then nobody knows which build produced which row.

`distStaleness` was extracted out of `provenance.mjs` so the printed line and the stderr warning
cannot disagree about what counts as stale — including the tie case, where a build finishing in the
same millisecond as the last source write is **not** stale, because an instrument that cried wolf
after every save would be ignored within a day.

And a guard, because the import path is the whole mechanism: `checkScriptsImportTheEngineWrapper()`
fails if any script under `scripts/` or `scripts/measure/` imports `dist` directly. It matches an
import specifier rather than the path anywhere, because a docblock saying "reads
packages/rules-engine/dist, so build first" is correct and common. Proved both import shapes: a plain
`from '...'` in `poison.mjs` and the `new URL('...', import.meta.url)` in `e2e-table.mjs`, each named,
each exit 1. Restored, `[guards] OK`.

### Two corrections to this entry, both made after writing it

**The guard over-reported, and the reason is worth more than the fix.** The first version was one
regex over the whole file:

```js
/(?:from|import\s*\()\s*[^;\n]{0,80}?['"][^'"]*rules-engine\/dist[^'"]*['"]/
```

It named two instruments that are perfectly clean. `[^'"]*` **matches newlines**, so starting from a
stray `"` in a docblock — `a figure from "40 and 38"` — it walked across three lines to reach the path
in a later sentence and called that an import. Bounding the gap with `{0,80}` did nothing, because the
crossing happened *inside* the quotes rather than before them. It is now matched one line at a time,
with `[^'"\n]*` inside the quotes and the path required to follow `from`, `import(` or `URL(` on that
same line.

I only noticed because I happened to know those two files were clean. **A guard that cries wolf is a
guard somebody switches off**, which arrives at the same place as one that cannot fail — and it is the
less obvious of the two failures, because its output looks like diligence.

**The two browser drivers are covered after all, and my reason for exempting them was wrong.** I wrote
that `e2e-table.mjs` and `e2e-solo.mjs` could keep importing `dist` directly because "they assert
behaviour rather than printing a number, so a stale build fails them loudly instead of producing a
plausible figure". Checking rather than asserting: they *do* fail, but the claim about loudly is the
part that does not hold, and the setup is worse than I had it. **The server they drive runs from
`src`** — through tsx and Vite — **while the driver reads `dist`.** So a stale build means the driver's
expectations come from an older engine than the one actually playing. `e2e-table` picks a card out of a
stale `tidal-mind` and reports that the browser does not show it; `e2e-solo` pastes a list naming a
card the live engine cannot read. Both read as a product bug in the thing under test. A misleading
failure is cheaper than a misleading success and still worth one line of warning, so both now import
through `engine.mjs` and the guard covers `scripts/` as well as `scripts/measure/`.

Four instruments re-run afterwards to check the indirection changed nothing: `derivable` (360 cards),
`wire-growth` (25.5% and 28.6% of the cap on the first two seeds), `mechanic-coverage` (81 mechanics,
81 counted), `card-promises` (0 gaps, with its own control reporting 1 for a planted card).

`provenanceLine` stays per-script rather than universal, and the README now says why: the commit, the
dirty flag and the arms matter for a number headed into a ledger somebody will re-run later (D300).
The staleness warning is the part that applies to every one of them, which is why that is the part
that moved into the import.

(The paragraph that stood here claimed the two browser drivers were safe to leave alone. It was
wrong on the facts and is corrected above rather than deleted, because the reasoning in it — "this
one fails loudly, so it does not need the warning" — is the kind I will reach for again.)

---

## D360 — The browser suites are in CI, because they turned out to cost 40 seconds rather than ten minutes

#245 found the four browser suites were outside every gate. D302 made them count their own skips. But
they still ran **only when somebody remembered to run them**, and what they check is the one thing the
Play Realm is for: two real browsers playing a game through the actual UI. Neither `pnpm v2:test` nor
CI touches that path.

I had been carrying an assumption that putting them in CI was a Nick-sized decision about CI cost — a
browser download on every push, ten minutes of wall clock. So I measured instead of continuing to
assume:

| | |
|---|---|
| `e2e-table.mjs` (73 checks, two browsers, whole game) | **29s** |
| `check-table-controls.mjs` (26 checks, every control pressed) | **11s** |

Forty seconds. The Chromium download is most of the job, not the tests. That is not a decision, it is
an obvious yes, and I had been about to write it up as a question.

The new `browser` job: Redis as a service, pnpm install, playwright pinned at 1.56.1 installed **into
`/tmp/pw` rather than the repository** (an `npm i` in a pnpm workspace root writes into a
`node_modules` pnpm owns and lays out differently, which is a good way to break the install the rest
of the job depends on), `pnpm -r --filter './packages/*' run build` so `dist` exists, then
`scripts/play.mjs` in the background behind a readiness loop that polls
`curl -sf http://127.0.0.1:5100/react/play` for up to 60s and **prints the Play Realm's log and fails**
if it never answers. On failure it uploads `e2e-shots/`, because a browser failure is diagnosed from
the screenshots and there is no browser to hand in CI.

Playwright stays out of `package.json` deliberately, which is the drivers' existing stance: it is a
test tool that ships a ~130MB browser, and making it a workspace dependency puts that download in
front of every `pnpm install` anybody runs. `PLAYWRIGHT_PATH` points at the `/tmp/pw` install, and a
wrong value there is harmless rather than fatal — `loadPlaywright` try/catches each candidate and
falls through to a bare `playwright` specifier.

**Only the two fast suites.** `e2e-arena` and `e2e-pod` drive more browsers for longer, and `e2e-solo`
has twenty `LIST=*` arms. Those stay manual until this job has proved stable over a few pushes,
because a browser job that flakes gets ignored and then deleted, and I would rather have two suites
that are trusted than five that are muted.

Also added: `pnpm play`, `pnpm play:e2e`, `play:e2e:controls`, `play:e2e:arena`, `play:e2e:pod`,
`play:e2e:solo`. Before this the only way to run any of them was to know the script's filename — they
were not in `package.json` at all, which is a smaller version of the same problem as not being in CI.

**What I could not verify from here:** GitHub Actions is not reproducible in this container, so the
first push was the first test of the job. I wrote that the parts most likely to be wrong were the
Chromium install and the readiness loop, and that both fail loudly rather than passing vacuously.

### The first run failed, at exactly the predicted place, and said why

```
BEWARE: your OS is not officially supported by Playwright; installing dependencies for
ubuntu26.04-x64 as a fallback.
Cannot install dependencies for ubuntu26.04-x64 with Playwright 1.56.1!
Error: ERROR: Playwright does not support chromium on ubuntu26.04-x64
```

`ubuntu-latest` is now **Ubuntu 26.04**, and Playwright 1.56.1 refuses it outright. The runner is now
pinned to `ubuntu-24.04` — the only job here that pins one — because the runner and the Playwright
version are a **matched pair**, and having one of them float while the other is pinned is what broke
it. Bumping either means bumping both and watching the install step.

A second, smaller fault in the same run, and it is one I have written about twice today in other
forms: the failure step `cat /tmp/play.log` **failed on its own**, printing
`cat: /tmp/play.log: No such file or directory` and exiting 1 *underneath* the error that actually
mattered. A diagnostic that reports its own absence as a failure adds noise to the one moment somebody
is reading carefully. It is `cat /tmp/play.log || true` now.

The readiness loop was still untested at that point, because the job never reached it.

### The second run is green, and here is what it actually cost

| step | |
|---|---|
| install playwright + Chromium | 23s |
| build packages | 6s |
| **start the Play Realm (the readiness loop)** | **9s** |
| `e2e-table.mjs` | 14s |
| `check-table-controls.mjs` | 5s |
| whole job, queue to finish | **83s** |

So the readiness loop works, and 99 browser checks across two real Chromium contexts cost **83
seconds** — against the `v2` job's 185s, which is the longest in this workflow. My estimate of the
shape was right (the Chromium download is the single biggest step) and wrong about the scale: 23s of
83, not most of a ten-minute job. The suites run faster in CI than on this hardware — 14s against 29s
for `e2e-table`.

That is cheap enough that the reasoning for holding `e2e-arena`, `e2e-pod` and `e2e-solo` back is now
only about flake risk and not about cost. Left as it is for a few pushes anyway, because "it is cheap"
was the argument that got the first version of this job wrong.

## D361 — All five browser suites, and the one thing #314 shipped that no browser had ever shown

Ran every browser suite on this tree, which is the check that actually answers "can two people play a
whole game":

| | |
|---|---|
| `e2e-table` (two browsers, whole game, phone widths) | 73/73, then **75/75** with the two added below |
| `check-table-controls` (every control pressed) | 26/26 |
| `e2e-arena` | 52/52, 6 named skips |
| `e2e-pod` (four browsers) | 41/41, 1 named skip |
| `e2e-solo` | 28/28, 1 named skip |

Then `surface-coverage.mjs` named `list-note` under "controls looked at but never pressed". That one is
a false alarm in the obvious reading — it is a `<p>`, so "never pressed" is correct and uninteresting,
and `e2e-table` and `e2e-solo` both *read* it. But the useful question behind it is whether anything
reads it **in the state that matters**, and there the answer was no: #314's over-150 warning had unit
coverage in `table.test.ts` and no browser coverage at all, because every paste in the suite is 60
cards — comfortably under the boundary.

So the warning that exists to stop a player pasting a list a four-seat table cannot be dealt had never
been shown on a screen. Added, as a **pair**: 150 cards, asserting the note says `150 cards` and does
**not** say `over 150`; then 151, asserting it does. One assertion on a large list could not tell a
warning about the boundary from a warning about any big deck.

Two things the writing of it taught me, both from the check failing on its author:

1. **`151 Forest` is refused before the warning can be reached.** `DECKLIST_LIMITS.maxPerLine` is 40,
   "because '999 Forest' is a typo at best", so a single line of 151 never gets as far as a size
   warning. The list is four lines now. I had reasoned about `maxCards` (250) and `maxDistinct` (150)
   and simply not read the limit that applied.
2. **The paste order matters to a later check.** `e2e-table` reloads the browser further down and
   asserts the saved-list box refills *the last list pasted*, naming two of its cards. Inserting a
   paste after that one would have broken a passing check for a reason that has nothing to do with it,
   so the new pastes go in before it.

## D362 — Hybrid automation: the engine plays the deck it can, and you move the rest by hand

Nick's goal for this project is now explicit: script **every** competitively-legal Magic card —
roughly 27,000 of them — so that any deck he or a friend uploads plays like Arena, with the rules
enforced. Tabletop stays available for people who want it; the automated table is the draw.

That goal makes one existing decision wrong, and it is the first thing to change because everything
else is gated behind it.

### What was wrong

`auto:start` refused any deck containing a card the engine could not read:

```
the engine does not know Black Lotus: a pasted list plays on the tabletop, not with the rules engine
```

Correct for a 348-card hand-scripted pool, where a deck either is in the pool or is not. Wrong for a
pool drawn from every card ever printed, where a hundred-card Commander deck will contain one or two
unreadable cards for a long time yet — and refusing automation for those one or two costs the other
ninety-eight their turn structure, priority, combat, triggers and state-based actions. Asked
directly, Nick chose hybrid: automate what can be automated, and let the rest be moved by hand.

### The change was one `throw`, and that is the interesting part

The engine was already built for this and I did not expect it to be. `card:move`, `card:tap` and the
other tabletop actions work while `automated` is true, and they do more than work — they record the
zone changes, so a creature somebody moves to the graveyard by hand still raises the death event that
other cards trigger on. The two halves were designed to coexist; `startAutomation`'s `throw` was the
only thing between them.

Evidence: removing the refusal broke **one test of 1425** — the test that asserted the refusal. If
the architecture had been fighting this, it would have broken dozens.

### What shipped

- `coverage.ts`: `manualCards(state)` — the cards the engine is not playing, by name, deduplicated
  and sorted — and `manualNote` for the log line.
- `startAutomation` reports instead of refusing, and the note goes on the **same** log message as
  "the rules engine takes over", because "the engine takes over" and "except for these cards" are one
  fact and a player who scrolls past the second has been misled by the first.
- `GameView.manual`, present only while automated (on a tabletop table the answer is "every card",
  and a badge on all of them is noise). Unredacted on purpose: it is a fact about the engine's
  coverage, not about anybody's hand, and redacting it per seat would mean a player could not be told
  why their own card does nothing.
- `cardBadges` badges them **in every zone**, above the battlefield-only guard, because the zone that
  matters is the hand — that is where somebody discovers their card has no "Cast" on its sheet.
- The lobby's engine button is no longer disabled; the note says what the engine will and will not do
  and lets the host decide.

### Two things this is careful not to claim

**It detects one of the two ways a card can fail to be automated.** "No printed data" is certain —
`customDeck` fell through to cardboard and the type line is empty. "Printed data, unimplemented text"
is not detected at all: a card with a real type line is dealt, cast and attacks with, and its oracle
text silently does not happen. The reason code `text-not-automated` exists in the type and nothing
emits it, which is stated in the module rather than glossed. The oracle-text compiler (#317) is what
will be able to answer it, and when it can, nothing else has to change shape.

So a game this reports as fully automated may still contain a card whose text is not running. Saying
"every card is automated" would be a claim the code cannot support, and the UI wording follows from
that: it names what it found and promises nothing about the rest.

**`deckIsAutomatable` survives as a report rather than a gate**, with its docblock corrected to say
so. "Is this deck fully automated" is still a real question; it is just no longer a veto.

### Three things found while testing it, each by a check failing on its author

1. **A `GameView` fixture in `apps/web` had an `as GameView` cast**, so adding a required field to
   `GameView` did not fail the typecheck — it failed eight `cardBadges` tests at *runtime*, on
   `view.manual.some(...)`. The cast is removed, so the next field added fails where a fixture should
   fail. **A cast is a claim the compiler stops checking**, which is this file's recurring subject
   wearing a type system.
2. **My own engine test passed `seat` to `auto:keep`**, which has no such field. It ran fine — the
   extra key was ignored — and `pnpm v2:typecheck:tests` caught it, which is the step that exists
   because nothing used to run it (D263).
3. **`cardBadges` now guards `view.manual ?? []`**, because that view arrives over a socket and a
   client talking to a server that predates the field would have thrown and taken the whole table
   render down — a blank screen instead of a game, for one badge.

### And one test got better rather than worse

`realtime.test.ts`'s three-way agreement check (D357) read the dealt deck's unreadable cards out of
the engine's **refusal**, which named only the first one it found — a limit I had recorded in its
comment. The refusal is gone and `view.manual` names all of them, so the third reading now carries
the count it always wanted.

Verified: engine 1429 passed (+4), gate 17/17 with services up, `e2e-table` **76/76** including the
lobby now offering the engine on a deck it cannot fully read.

## D363 — The badge that was in one zone, and the browser check that read the shuffle instead of the build

D362 added "move by hand" to `cardBadges`, above the battlefield-only guard, with a comment saying
it was placed there deliberately so the badge would show in **every** zone — and naming the hand as
the zone that mattered most, because the hand is where a player discovers their card has no "Cast"
on its sheet.

It was in exactly one zone: the battlefield.

`PlayTable` has nine `badgesOf` call sites. Four of them — the hand, the graveyard, the exile pile
and the command zone — did not call `cardBadges` at all. Each passed a lambda of its own:

```tsx
badgesOf={(card) => (automated && playsForCard(view, card.id).length > 0 ? ["playable"] : [])}
```

Four hand-written copies of one rule, which between them could produce exactly one word. So every
badge `cardBadges` has ever grown was invisible in those four zones, and the newest one was
invisible in the zone its own comment called the most important.

### Why nothing caught it, which is the part worth keeping

- **The unit tests passed**, all eight of them, because `cardBadges` was correct. The defect was not
  in the function; it was in *which function four call sites chose*. No test of a function can see
  that.
- **The typecheck passed**, because a `badgesOf` is a `(c: VisibleCard) => readonly string[]` no
  matter what it computes. The type says the shape of the answer and nothing about the question.
- **The browser check passed, most of the time.** `check-hybrid.mjs` asserted the badge on a deck of
  `24 Mountain / 20 Forest / 15 Grizzly Bears / 1 Nonsense Card`, and a badge renders only on a card
  the page is drawing. One copy in sixty is in the library about seven times in eight, and a library
  draws nothing. So the check read **green on a broken build** seven runs in eight, and its one
  failure looked like a flake.

I had written the shuffle dependence down in that check's own comment — *"which zone the one copy is
in on turn one is a fact about the shuffle rather than about the badge"* — and then written a check
that depended on it anyway. A check whose result is a fact about the shuffle is the twelfth member
of this file's family, and the first one whose failure mode is **a true failure that reads as
noise**: the others read as good news.

### The fix is one function, not five

`playable` moved above the battlefield guard, and the four zone-local lambdas were deleted in favour
of the shared `badgesOf`. The zone rows had a laxer rule than the battlefield's —
`playsForCard(...).length > 0` against `.some((p) => !p.isManaAbility)` — because in a hand or a
pile there is nothing to tap; keeping the stricter one is right in every zone, and the web suite's
246 tests agree.

Two regression tests, both proved to discriminate by reverting the move and watching them fail:
`cardBadges` says "playable" for a castable card in hand, and badges an unreadable card in the hand
as well as on the battlefield.

### And a guard, because the next badge will be added by somebody who does not know this

`checkBadgesAllComeFromCardBadges` in `scripts/guards.js` requires every `badgesOf=` prop in
`PlayTable.tsx` to pass the shared `badgesOf` or name `cardBadges` on the same line. Proved to
discriminate: reinstating one of the deleted lambdas fails it with the file and line.

A test cannot catch this and a type cannot either. A grep can, because the defect has a shape.

### The browser check now proves it by construction

`check-hybrid.mjs` runs **two** tables, because neither deck can carry both claims:

- `24 Mountain / 20 Forest / 15 Grizzly Bears / 1 Nonsense Card` — the engine starts, the log names
  the card, and **the engine really plays the other fifty-nine sixtieths**, checked by asking it for
  four moves and making them. A deck of nothing but unreadable cards would prove only that the
  engine starts.
- `30 Mystery Alpha / 30 Mystery Beta` — nothing in it is readable, so all seven cards dealt to that
  hand are unreadable and the badge **cannot** be missed by a build that has it, or produced by one
  that does not. This also exercises the plural half of the lobby copy, which nothing had read.

Verified: web 246 passed (+2), guards OK and proved to discriminate, `check-hybrid` **11/11**,
`e2e-table` 76/76, `check-table-controls` 26/26, `e2e-arena` 52/52 with 6 named skips. Added to CI's
`browser` job and to `package.json` as `play:e2e:hybrid`.

## D364 — The oracle-text compiler: lines, not cards, and a vocabulary copied from the hand-written scripts

The goal Nick set is every competitively-legal card playable with Arena-style automation. `fromCardData.ts`
answers a narrower question — *is this card's text nothing but its data?* — and on the engine's own
pool the answer is yes for **15%**. The other 85% looked like a wall.

It is not a wall, and the reason is worth stating as the thesis of this whole piece of work: a
Murderous Redcap is persist plus one sentence; a Basilica Screecher is flying plus extort; a Mystic
Remora is cumulative upkeep plus one triggered ability. For almost every card, *some* of the text is
machinery this engine already has. So the unit of measurement is the **printed line**, not the card,
and the question is "how much, and what is left".

Hybrid automation (D362) is what makes a partial answer worth having at all. Before it, a card the
engine only partly read dropped the whole table out of automation, so 60% of a card was worth
nothing. Now it is dealt, flagged, and the rest of the game runs.

### What shipped

- **`printedDef` and `printedRulesLines`**, split out of `cardFromData`. The four refusals kept at
  the top are the ones meaning *this row is not a single-face card at all*, where there is no
  `CardDef` to hand back. Everything past them is the narrow question and stays with it.
- **`compile.ts`**, a new module above both `fromCardData.ts` and `scripts.ts` — it needs printed
  data from one and builders from the other, and `scripts.ts` already imports `fromCardData.ts`, so
  living in either would have made that a cycle. `compileCard(row)` returns the def, whatever script
  it could build, the lines it compiled, and **the lines it could not, each with a reason**.
- **`keywordScriptFor`** in `scripts.ts`: the first stage, ten keywords.
- **`scripts/measure/compilable.mjs`**, the instrument, with the unread lines grouped and counted.

### Why the compiler can exist at all

The hand-written scripts were already factored into parameterised builders, so **for a keyword the
printed line is the argument**. `Modular 1` is `modularTrigger(1)`. `Ward {1}` is `ward(name, '{1}')`.
`Undying` takes no argument. Nothing is invented: every rule emitted comes from a builder a card in
the pool already uses, with arguments read off the line (D259).

### The unit of compilation is a partial `CardScript`, and three keywords prove it

My first instinct was keyword → trigger. That is wrong, and reading Calciderm is what showed it.
`vanishingTrigger(4)` takes a time counter off and sacrifices the permanent when the last one goes —
but the counters come from `entersWith`, and the declaration lives in `vanishing`. Emit the trigger
alone and you get **a Calciderm that never dies**: a creature whose clock is conditioned on a counter
it never had. That is strictly worse than a card left to be moved by hand. Modular and fading have
the same three-part shape.

So a fragment carries *every* field the hand-written twin sets, and `compile.test.ts` asserts the
counters explicitly as numbers rather than "is defined".

### Three keywords deliberately left out, each because the line does not determine the rule

- **Soulbond.** Its line is the word alone; the pair's bonus is on the *next* line. A
  `soulbond: { effect: { power: 1, toughness: 1 } }` guessed from the keyword is a number this module
  made up.
- **Level up.** `levelUpAbility(cost)` is readable, but a leveler's `levelBands` are three blocks of
  printed text below it, and a level-up ability with no bands to reach costs mana and does nothing.
- **Morph and echo.** Already read by `keywordWithCost`. Two readers of one line is two places for
  them to disagree.

### The test that makes it trustworthy

Not "does the compiler produce a plausible script" — **does it produce the one a person wrote by
reading the same card?** Ten keywords, ten pool cards, deep equality on the fields that keyword owns,
plus triggers compared by their `on` and `description` (the two fields that come from the builder
rather than the card, since closures cannot be compared). A compiler calling a different builder, or
the same one with a different argument, fails.

Two further cases worth keeping: a keyword line the engine reads straight off the `CardDef`
(`characteristicsOf` calls `printedKeywords(def.oracleText)` with no script involved) counts as
compiled and emits **nothing**, because restating it would be a second source for one fact; and two
lines fighting over one script field are reported as `field-conflict` rather than letting the last
one win, because a half-applied fragment is a creature with the wrong number of counters and the log
never explains it. No real card prints both vanishing and fading, which is exactly why the merge has
to be safe for a card nobody has thought about yet.

### Measured, on the pool

| | |
| --- | --- |
| whole-card (`cardFromData` read all of it) | 51 — 15.0% |
| **keywords (this compiler read some lines)** | **21 — 6.2%** |
| printed-only (it read none) | 267 — 78.8% |
| not a single-face card | 9 |
| **Lines compiled** | **142 of 538 — 26.4%** |

21 cards gained partial automation that previously had none. The headline is the line-level 26.4%,
because that is the number that moves.

One correction found by a failing test of my own: I expected the pool's Mountain to derive as
`basic-land` and it reads `mana-source`. The difference is the **row**, not the card — Scryfall sends
a basic land with empty `oracle_text` and its mana comes from the type (CR 305.6), while the pool's
Mountain spells `{T}: Add {R}.` out. The test now asserts what it is and says why.

### The work queue, which is the output that matters most

245 distinct openings, 185 printed by a single card. The ten biggest:

```
  36  When ~ enters the battlefield        19  ~ deals N damage to
   7  Draw a card                           6  Whenever you cast an instant
   5  Equip {M}                              5  Enchant creature
   4  When ~ is turned face                  4  As long as ~ is
   4  ~ enters the battlefield with          4  Whenever ~ deals combat damage
```

This is the pool, which is thirteen decks built to exercise sixty mechanics and so far heavier in
paragraph cards than a list somebody plays — a **floor**. The real distribution needs the Scryfall
bulk file, and `api.scryfall.com` is still refused by this environment's egress proxy, so #318 lands
source-agnostic.

Next stage is the top bucket: `When ~ enters the battlefield, <effect>`, which is one trigger shape
and a growing vocabulary of effects.

## D365 — The gate printed GATE FAILED and exited zero, and it had done so for weeks

The pre-push gate is the five checks between a red tree and `git push`: services up, guards,
typecheck, typecheck:tests, test. It was a shell script in a session-local temp directory, written
earlier in this session to close two holes of exactly this kind — D323's pager exit code and D356's
cached green.

Running it on the compiler work, it printed, in full:

```
GATE FAILED at: node scripts/guards.js (rc=0)
[guards] 1 violation(s)
```

and exited **0**.

```bash
if ! $step >> "$log" 2>&1; then
  rc=$?                       # 0, always
  echo "GATE FAILED at: $step (rc=$rc)"
  exit "$rc"                  # exits 0
fi
```

`!` inverts the status; the `if` therefore *succeeds*; and `$?` read inside the branch is the status
of that successful test, not of the failed command. The `(rc=0)` was printed right there in the
message every time and I had never read it, because the words before it said what I expected.

This is the thirteenth member of this file's family and the second whose failure is not silent:
**a check that reports failure and returns success.** It is worse than a check that cannot fail,
because it looks like the thing working. Any `gate.sh && git push` would have pushed a red tree
while printing the reason not to.

### What changed

- **The gate is in the repository**, as `scripts/gate.sh` with `pnpm v2:gate`. That move matters as
  much as the fix: the one script standing between a red tree and a push lived in a temp folder
  where nobody could review it, nothing could test it, and the next session would not have it.
- **Run, then capture, then test** — `$step; rc=$?; if [ "$rc" -ne 0 ]`. Never `$?` inside `if !`.
- **`scripts/check-gate.sh`** (`pnpm v2:gate:check`) runs the gate against a step that cannot pass
  and fails if it reports success, in its words or in its status. The gate's own exit code had never
  been asked for by anything; now something asks.

### And the check immediately found a second one, pointing the other way

`check-gate.sh` failed on its *passing* case. The gate's last line is a summary:

```bash
grep -E "Tests  |Test Files|Tasks:" "$log" | tail -20
```

With `set -o pipefail` and a log holding no matching line, `grep` exits 1 — so the gate exited **1
after passing every step**. A gate that cries wolf is a gate somebody stops running, which ends in
the same place as one that cannot fail. Now `|| true` and an explicit `exit 0`: the summary is
diagnostics and its status is not the gate's.

Two bugs in a twenty-line script whose entire job is to report a status correctly, both found by
asking it for its status once. That is the whole lesson: **the gate needs a gate.**

## D366 — The compiler's second stage: one trigger shape, seven untargeted clauses, compared by behaviour

D364 read keywords, whose fragments are **data**. This reads the first *sentence* shape, whose
fragment is a **closure** — which changes both what can be compiled and how it can be checked.

### What it reads

One trigger shape, `When ~ enters the battlefield, <clause>`, because it is the largest single
bucket in `compilable.mjs`'s work queue by a factor of two. The shape and the effect are separate
functions on purpose: `untargetedEffect` is shared with every trigger shape added after this one —
"When ~ dies", "Whenever ~ attacks" — and with the instants and sorceries that `cardFromData`
refuses outright, which is the 114-card bucket and the largest prize in the queue.

Seven clauses: gain life, lose life, draw, become the monarch, scry, get energy, each opponent
discards at random.

### The rule for what counts as readable here

**The clause has to determine the effect completely, with nothing chosen by anybody.** So the
untargeted half only. "It deals 4 damage to target creature" needs a target spec, and a target spec
is its own sub-vocabulary — "target creature", "target creature an opponent controls", "another
target nonland permanent", "any target" — with its own failure modes. Reading those *badly* would
aim real removal at the wrong thing, which is worse than not reading them at all. Next increment.

### Two questions I could not answer by guessing, both settled from the engine's own comments

1. **`draw` or `drawLater`?** The pool uses both for "draw a card", which is a behavioural
   difference, not a style one. `drawLater`'s docblock states the constraint — *"only for a draw
   that is the last thing the card does"* — and then says *"the compiler cannot tell the two apart"*.
   That is true of a compiler reading a sentence; it is not true of one that matches a clause **only
   when the clause is the draw and nothing else**. A clause that is exactly "draw two cards" cannot
   read what it drew, so the deferral is safe by construction — and it is the better primitive,
   because only a deferred draw can be replaced by a dredge (CR 702.52a).
2. **`{ kind: 'etb' }` or `{ kind: 'etb', who: 'self' }`?** Both appear in the pool.
   `automation.ts` settles it: *"`self` is the default … a trigger that says nothing about `who`
   watches only its own permanent."* They are the same trigger. The compiler writes `who: 'self'`
   out, because a generated script is read by people.

### The test had to change shape, and that is the interesting part

A keyword's fragment can be compared field by field. A trigger's cannot: closures are not
comparable. The obvious fallback — compare `description` strings — would have been **wrong**, and
the pool shows why: Kitchen Finks stores the clause (`'you gain 2 life'`) while Aether Hub stores
the whole printed line including the "When ~ enters the battlefield" that `on` already carries. A
cosmetic inconsistency, so a string comparison would fail a compiler that was right.

So the check is **behavioural**: hand both effects the same game state and assert the resulting
states are identical. That is the actual claim — *does the compiler build the same rules a person
did* — rather than a proxy for it.

Two things that made it honest rather than merely green:

- **A comparison between two no-ops is not evidence.** The first version used a bare `arena()`,
  whose hands are empty, so Ravenous Rats' "each opponent discards a card at random" discarded
  nothing, both effects returned the state unchanged, and `toEqual` passed on two functions that had
  done nothing. The non-vacuity assertion (`expect(mine).not.toEqual(base)`) is what caught it; the
  fixture now deals seat 1 a card so the effect has something to do. This is the same family as
  D363's shuffle-dependent browser check, found one increment later and by a deliberate guard
  rather than by luck.
- **`drawsOwed` is a flat list of seat indices, one entry per card owed** — not a count per seat. I
  asserted `drawsOwed[0] === 1`, which compares the *seat* owed the first card against a count, and
  the `?? 0` I had written beside it would have hidden the error behind a plausible-looking compare.
  Corrected to filter by seat and count.

Proved to discriminate: changing the compiled `gainLife` by one point fails Kitchen Finks.

### The `as EffectContext` cast, and why it is sound here

D362's lesson is that a cast is a claim the compiler stops checking, so this one is argued rather
than hoped. Both effects receive **the same object**, so a field the fixture omits is a field
neither effect can read, and the comparison stays a comparison. It would be unsound if the two
effects were given different contexts, or if the assertion were about the context rather than the
output.

### Measured

| | D364 | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| whole-card | 51 (15.0%) | 51 (15.0%) |
| **cards with compiled rules** | 21 (6.2%) | **34 (10.0%)** |
| printed-only | 267 | 254 |
| **lines compiled** | **142 of 538 (26.4%)** | **156 of 538 (29.0%)** |
| the ETB bucket | 36 | 22 |

`source: 'keywords'` is renamed `'lines'`, since it is no longer only keywords.

The remaining 22 ETB lines are almost all targeted — "exile target creature until ~ leaves the
battlefield" (4), "it deals N damage to target creature", "return target creature to its owner's
hand", "put a -1/-1 counter on target creature" — which is the next increment's bucket, and the one
that also unlocks removal and bounce on instants.

## D367 — Targets, spells, and a new path that replaced the old one instead of extending it

Two things at once, because they share a prerequisite. Targeted clauses need a **target spec**, and
instants and sorceries need a **resolution path** — and both want the same effect vocabulary D366
built, which is the architecture claim that file made and this one tests.

### Target specs, and the flag that cannot be read off the phrase

`targetSpecFrom(phrase, friendly)` reads `any target` and `target creature`, which between them are
47 of the ~95 target phrases printed in the pool. The long tail is 28 further phrasings, 1-2 cards
each.

`friendly` is the interesting parameter, because **it is not in the phrase**. "Target creature" is
the same two words on a Doom Blade and on a Giant Growth. It is a fact about the *effect*, so the
caller supplies it — and D252 added the flag in the first place because the bot's default is "the
enemy and the enemy's creatures". A pump that forgets it is not illegal: it is a bot that buffs the
