creature it was about to kill. Wrong in a way nothing refuses, which is the kind of wrong this
compiler most has to avoid.

The clearest case is a counter on a creature: `+1/+1` helps, `-1/-1` harms, and the two clauses
differ by one character.

### The bot hints, which is D364's lesson in a second place

`Doom Blade` sets **`removesACreature: true`** beside its effect and `Giant Growth` sets
**`expiresAtEndOfTurn: true`**: do not cast this with nothing of theirs to point at; hold this for
the combat. Emit the effect alone and you get a card that **works** and **plays badly** — worse than
an unread line, because an unread line is flagged for a human to play by hand (D362) and a badly
played one is flagged nowhere.

So the unit of compilation is a partial `CardScript`, exactly as the keyword stage found with
Calciderm's counters. They are returned as `spellFlags` and applied only on the spell path, because
"removes a creature" is advice about *casting* and an ETB trigger is not cast.

### Six families read: damage, destroy, bounce, pump, +1/+1, -1/-1

Each paired with its spec and its friendliness. Deliberately not read: a clause that also grants a
keyword ("gets +0/+3 and gains hexproof"), because that is two effects and reading the first while
dropping the second is a card silently doing less than it prints.

### A spell is compiled whole, and its lines are not all the same kind of thing

A permanent's text is a list of independent abilities, so it is read line by line. A spell's
resolution is not: every sentence happens in one go, so a spell whose second sentence went unread
would resolve and do half of what it prints with nothing flagged. All-or-nothing.

**And the first version of that got it wrong.** It treated *every* line of a spell as resolution.
Grapeshot is "deals 1 damage to any target" plus **Storm**; Sudden Shock is a damage clause plus
**Split second**; Pyromatics is damage plus **Replicate {1}{R}**. Those keywords are properties of
the card, not steps of its resolution — so the spell path found two lines, refused the card, and
**threw away a keyword reading that already worked**. A new path *replacing* an old one instead of
extending it, and a straight regression on three cards.

The ground-truth tests caught it on the first run, named all three cards, and nothing else would
have: the types were fine, the coverage number went *up*, and the three cards had simply stopped
being read. That is the whole argument for comparing against hand-written scripts rather than
asserting a shape.

Fixed by partitioning: keyword lines are read as keywords exactly as on a permanent, and whatever is
left is the resolution. Pinned by its own regression test, which checks Grapeshot keeps **both** its
storm trigger and its damage, and that Sudden Shock keeps `splitSecond` beside its `onResolve`.

`Divination` is the proof the shared vocabulary works rather than the hope: its hand-written script
is `onResolve: drawLater(state, you, 2)` and nothing else, which is exactly what `untargetedEffect`
already built for "Draw two cards."

### Measured

| | D364 | D366 | now |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| whole-card | 51 (15.0%) | 51 | 51 (15.0%) |
| **cards with compiled rules** | 21 (6.2%) | 34 (10.0%) | **48 (14.2%)** |
| printed-only | 267 | 254 | 240 |
| **lines compiled** | 142 (26.4%) | 156 (29.0%) | **173 of 538 (32.2%)** |

Cards with rules have more than doubled since the keyword stage, and a third of every printed line
in the pool now becomes rules. Still a floor: the pool is thirteen decks built to exercise sixty
mechanics.

43 compiler tests, and the `as EffectContext` cast stays sound for the reason D366 gives — both
effects receive the same object, so the comparison remains a comparison.

## D368 — CI failed where the gate passed, and both halves of that were defects

CI's `v2` job went red on `cafa599` while the gate had reported **17/17** on the same tree. Two
separate things were wrong, and the second is the one worth keeping.

### The test: 8000ms of internal budget inside a 5000ms deadline

`apps/realtime`'s *"refuses a browser from an origin outside a configured allow list"* timed out.
46 of 47 passed; the test before it took **9568ms** on that runner.

The test boots a second realtime server — it has to, the allow list is fixed at start — and then
makes two handshake attempts in sequence, each with its own `setTimeout(..., 4000)` fallback so a
handshake that never answers cannot hang the suite. Two times four thousand is **8000ms**, inside
vitest's **5000ms** default.

So the test **could not pass if either attempt ever took its slow path**. It passed for months
anyway, because both handshakes normally answer in single-digit milliseconds. A loaded runner
starved it and it died with `Test timed out in 5000ms` — a message that names neither origins nor
allow lists nor handshakes, and sent me hunting a regression in a diff that does not touch that app.

Another member of this file's family, and a new shape: **a fallback that is only reachable past the
deadline it is meant to report inside.** Its whole purpose is to turn a hang into a legible failure,
and being set longer than the test's own timeout converted a specific failure into a generic one.

Fixed by putting the two numbers in the right order: 2000ms per attempt, and an explicit 15000ms on
the test. A reachable fallback now fails with `expected 'timeout' to be 'refused'`, which says what
broke.

Not a flake, and not this change's: the engine import measures 63-84ms, and the diff touches only
`packages/rules-engine`. It is a latent defect that CI happened to expose.

### The gate: turbo caches, and CI does not

The more important half. The gate ran `pnpm v2:typecheck` / `v2:typecheck:tests` / `v2:test`, which
are **turbo** tasks. CI runs `pnpm -r`. The difference is not cosmetic:

- **turbo caches by input hash**, so a package whose inputs it thinks unchanged replays a stored
  green without running. The gate can report a suite passing while CI runs it for real. That is
  D356's hole one level in: not a cached run with the services down, but a cached run of a suite
  that would now fail.
- **CI ran three steps the gate did not**: the packages' `build`, the legacy token-parity test, and
  the web production build. A gate missing a step CI has cannot see a failure CI will.

A gate whose job is "would CI accept this" has to run what CI runs. `scripts/gate.sh` is now CI's
`v2` job verbatim, with `services-up.js` in front — eight steps. Slower than turbo, and that is the
trade: **a gate that is fast and sometimes wrong is worth less than one that is slow and right.**

`check-gate.sh` still verifies it in both directions.

### And a correction to what I reported

I described `cafa599` as "locally verified by the gate, 17/17". The gate did say that, and the claim
was weaker than I presented it — on a tree CI then rejected. The number was real and the confidence
it implied was not. This is the third time in two days that a green reading has turned out to be
about something other than what I thought it measured (D356, D365, now this), and all three were
found by asking the instrument a question it had never been asked.

Verified: realtime 47/47 with the fix, `check-gate.sh` verified in both directions.

## D369 — Composition, which is worth more than vocabulary, and a test that was pinning a restriction

The spell path took one resolution clause and refused anything longer. That was the right **safety**
property — all of a spell's resolution or none of it, because a spell whose second sentence went
unread would resolve and silently do half of what it prints — reached by a rule stricter than the
property needs. "Exactly one clause" is not "all or nothing". A spell of three clauses all of which
compile satisfies the property completely.

So `readResolution` composes. It takes a spell's resolution lines together, splits each on `, then `
(which is how Magic writes a sequence), requires **every** part to compile, and threads the state
through them in printed order. One part that cannot be read refuses the whole spell, unchanged.

This is the first increment that adds **no vocabulary at all** and still moves coverage, which is
the point worth recording: composition multiplies every reader already present, and will multiply
every reader added after it. 178 of 538 lines (33.1%), up from 173, and 51 cards from 48 — on
readers that already existed.

### One refusal that matters: two parts cannot share one target

`CardScript.targets` is a single list for the whole spell, filled once before resolution. Two parts
each wanting their own target — "Target creature you control fights target creature you don't
control" is the printed shape — would silently be handed the **same** target by a merging
composition. A wrong card rather than an unread one, so it is refused with its own test.

### My own tests were pinning the restriction, not the invariant

Two tests failed on this change, and both were mine:

- *"compiles a spell whole or not at all, never half of it"* used `Scry 1, then draw a card.`, which
  was unreadable only because of the one-clause rule. Once the parts compose it reads fine, so the
  test had stopped testing the invariant and started testing the restriction.
- *"does not compile a spell whose text runs to two lines"* asserted the restriction outright.

The invariant still needs a test, so the first now uses **"Draw two cards, then discard two cards."**
— real printed text from the pool whose first clause this module reads and whose second it does not.
A compiler that drew and skipped the discard would be a strictly better Divination: wrong in a way
nothing at the table would flag.

A test that pins an implementation choice rather than the property it protects goes red on the
improvement, and the temptation is to read that as a regression. The tell is that the failing
assertion was about *how much* the compiler refuses rather than *what it must never do*.

### And a comment of mine that overclaimed

The new ordering test said it checked that each part runs on the state the one before it produced,
"so a scry happens before the draw". It does not check that. Gaining life and owing a draw are
independent, so either order leaves the same state, and nothing in the current vocabulary has an
order-observable pair.

What it does prove — verified by breaking the reduce in both directions and watching it fail — is
that the state is **threaded**: a composition handing every part the original state would lose one
of the two effects. The comment now says that and says the order is untested, which is worth more
than a claim the assertions do not support.

Verified: compile.test.ts 44/44, both composition tests proved to catch broken threading.

## D370

**A keyword the compiler cannot build is not an unread sentence, and conflating them refused four
cards** (#317)

`spellScriptFor` partitioned a spell's lines two ways: keyword lines `keywordScriptFor` could build,
and everything else, which became the resolution. The resolution is all-or-nothing by design — a
spell that resolves and silently does half of what it prints is worse than one left unread, because
an unread card is a manual object inside an automated game and says so (D362), while a half-read one
says nothing.

So `Miracle {R}` refused Thunderous Wrath, whose other line is "deals 5 damage to any target" and
which this compiler reads perfectly well. Four pool spells were refused by a keyword line rather
than by anything about their own effect: Thunderous Wrath, Staggershock, Rift Bolt, Skewer the
Critics.

### The distinction is about the cost of being wrong, not about tidiness

Every keyword a spell can carry — miracle, flashback, overload, buyback, replicate, storm, spectacle
— is a **cost or a modifier**: a way to cast the card, not a step of resolving it. A Thunderous Wrath
that cannot be cast for its miracle cost is still a Thunderous Wrath. An unread *sentence* is a card
that cannot be played automatically at all. Those are different kinds of incomplete, and anything
built on `unread` — the hybrid badge above all — would lie in one direction or the other if they
were counted as one thing. So `UnreadLine.why` gained `unimplemented-keyword`, `compilable.mjs`
prints it apart (`[keyword]`, 66 of the 334 unread lines), and neither kind counts as compiled.

`isKeywordDeclaration` answers "is this line part of the resolution?", which is a different question
from `keywordScriptFor`'s "can I build this?". The test doing most of the work is the full stop: a
printed keyword line never ends in one and every sentence of a resolution does. On its own that
would also swallow a resolution line that happened to lack a full stop, so it is backed by a closed
list of CR 702 keyword names — rules vocabulary, not card text, so D259 does not bite: `Flanking` is
not a card. **Ability words are deliberately absent.** `Magecraft — Whenever you cast …` is a whole
triggered ability with a label on the front; treating it as a declaration would throw the ability
away, and leaving it off the list means it is rejected for the right reason.

## D371

**Sentence-level composition, a shared composer for triggers and spells, and five more target
phrases** (#317)

Four changes in one increment, all of them "read more of what is actually printed":

1. **Sentences compose.** `readResolution` split only on `, then `, so "Target player mills two
   cards. Draw a card." — one printed line, two clauses — went unread whole. Now `clausesOf` splits
   on the full stop as well. Safe because nothing in a rules line abbreviates: a full stop followed
   by whitespace is a sentence boundary and nothing else.
2. **One composer.** `readResolution` and `triggerFromLine` were two implementations of the same
   problem; both now call `composeEffects`, which owns the all-or-nothing rule and the
   one-target rule. A trigger's own text can be a sequence too.
3. **Target vocabulary**, from two phrases to twelve: `target player`, `target spell`, `target
   permanent`, `target creature you control`, `target creature you don't control` / `an opponent
   controls`, `target artifact`, `target enchantment`, `target land`, `target artifact or
   enchantment`, `target creature card in your graveyard`.
4. **The families those unlock**: counter target spell, target player mills N, return a creature
   card from your graveyard to your hand, destroy with any permanent target, and damage to `you` or
   `each opponent`.

**204 of 538 printed lines, up from 178 (33.1% → 37.9%); 127 of 339 cards now get a script, up from
102.** Counterspell, Cancel, Disenchant, Naturalize, Krosan Grip, Murder, Mizzium Mortars, Raise
Dead, Gravedigger, Tome Scour, Mind Sculpt, Thought Scour and Returned Centaur are among the new
ones.

### Two defects the ground-truth tests found, which is what they are for

**The description picked up sentence casing.** Every spec now stores the phrase it was read from,
which is character-for-character what the hand-written twin stores — until the phrase starts a
sentence. Giant Growth prints "Target creature gets +3/+3", so the spec came out `Target creature`
against a hand-written `target creature`. The first word of a target phrase is always `target`,
`another` or `any`, never a name, so the fix is to lower-case the front and say why. Found on the
first run of the existing spec-equality test.

**`plain` was unpinned, and the comment justifying it was wrong.** Deleting the apostrophe
normalisation passed all 59 tests, so the claim it carried was not falsifiable — and the specific
claim was false: I had written that Mizzium Mortars prints a typographic apostrophe, and it prints an
ASCII one. The pool spells the same construct both ways: 21 cards with `'`, 23 with `’`, Unsummon
"its owner's hand" against Journey to Nowhere "its owner’s control". Every card the compiler reads
today happens to be in the ASCII half, which is exactly why it needed a test — the bulk corpus #318
imports is the other half. Pinned now on a curly-spelled bounce spell, and verified to go red when
`plain` is removed.

### A deferred draw is a fact about position, and the first guard for it was too blunt

`drawLater` owes the card instead of putting it in hand. That is the better primitive — only a
deferred draw can be replaced by a dredge (CR 702.52a) — and its own docblock bounds it to "a draw
that is the last thing the card does", because nothing after it can see what it drew. In a
composition that is a fact about **position**, and a clause cannot know its own position.

My first guard refused any composition whose deferred draw was not last. It caught the hazard and
also broke "Draw two cards. You gain 2 life.", a card that was never in danger — turning a
dependency hazard into a coverage hole. The shape that costs nothing: a clause offers **both**
readings, and `composeEffects` picks the deferred one for the last clause and the immediate one for
every other. "Draw a card. Scry 2." really does draw before it scries, so the immediate reading is
not a fallback there, it is the correct one.

This is also the one place the compiler and a hand-written card genuinely differ: Thought Scour's
hand-written script calls `draw`, the compiled one `drawLater`, and the test compares the two halves
clause by clause and states the difference rather than hiding it behind a looser assertion.

### Recorded, not fixed: #319

`permanentOfTypes` reads types from `characteristicsOf`, which is the live type line (CR 109.2). Five
hand-written filters in the same file read `state.cardDefs[...].typeLine`, the printed one — and
`destroyAnArtifactOrEnchantment`'s docblock claims it reads the live one. Two readings of one
question now sit in one file. Consolidating them changes which permanents five shipping cards may
point at, so it is #319 with its own measurement rather than a rider on this.

Verified: compile.test.ts 60/60, with each of the four new mechanisms proved to fail when broken
(the apostrophe normaliser, the `removesACreature` type guard, the immediate-draw pick, and
`isKeywordDeclaration`'s list). Full gate green.

## D372

**Trigger shapes: one prologue became thirteen, and the effect vocabulary was already there**
(#317)

Until this stage the compiler knew exactly one printed prologue — "When ~ enters the battlefield" —
so every effect it could read was reachable from exactly one place on a card. D369 made this
observation about composition: a change that adds **no new vocabulary at all** still moves coverage,
because it multiplies every reader already present. Shapes multiply it from the other side.

Thirteen prologues: the two etb forms including "or dies", dies, leaves the battlefield, turned face
up, attacks, deals combat damage to a player, becomes tapped, "whenever you cast an instant or
sorcery spell", "whenever you cast a noncreature spell", "whenever you gain life", and the two step
triggers. Plus a third clause family — `selfEffect`, for a clause that acts on the permanent itself:
untap ~, ~ gets +N/+N until end of turn, put N +1/+1 counters on ~. Those three are what the new
prologues mostly point at, and none of them needs a target spec or asks anybody anything.

**217 of 538 printed lines, up from 204 (37.9% → 40.3%); 139 of 339 cards get a script, up from
127.** Ajani's Pridemate, Bloodthirsty Aerialist, Borderland Marauder, City of Brass, Firebrand
Archer, Gelectrode, Goblin Arsonist, Guttersnipe, Longtusk Cub, Ninja of the Deep Hours,
Thermo-Alchemist and Thieving Magpie are the new ones.

### Every event is copied off the card that prints the prologue

Not inferred, and not written as a literal in the test either: the expected `on` is read from the
hand-written script at test time, so a shape copied wrongly fails even if the compiler and the test
agree about what the wrong answer looks like. That is what caught the one real difference —
`who: 'self'`, which `automation.ts` documents as the default and which the pool spells both ways (30
of its etb triggers bare, 7 explicit). The comparison drops that one documented default from both
sides and then compares the **whole** `on` object, which is the version that would catch a compiler
emitting `by: 'opponent'` where the card says `by: 'you'`.

### "Or dies" is two abilities, not one event

"When Mogg War Marshal enters the battlefield or dies" is two triggered abilities sharing one effect
(CR 603.1), so a shape carries a *list* of events and emits one `TriggerDef` per event. Checked on a
synthetic card, because the pool's only instance of the shape makes a token and token creation has
no reader yet.

### Two defects, both found by deep equality on the resulting board

- **A zero pump component is not the same state.** Borderland Marauder's hand-written `+2/+0` is
  `{ power: 2 }`; the compiler passed `{ power: 2, toughness: 0 }`. The two pumps behave identically
  and the two *boards* compare unequal, because the bonus is stored on the state as a continuous
  effect. `sizeBonus` now omits a zero component, and refuses a `+0/+0` outright.
- **Untapping an untapped permanent is a no-op**, so Thermo-Alchemist's comparison was two no-ops
  and `toEqual` passed on nothing — the D366 vacuity family again, two increments later. The fixture
  taps it first, which is also the only board on which the printed card does anything.

### Deliberately not read: `sacrifice ~`

"At the beginning of the end step, sacrifice Ball Lightning" is the pool's shape, and Ball Lightning
also sets **`leavesAtEndOfTurn: true`** — its own comment: "the trigger below is what happens, and
the flag is how the bot knows it is coming. Without it the evaluation holds the creature back to
protect it." The flag therefore belongs to the **pair** of prologue and clause: a sacrifice at end of
turn means the creature is leaving, a sacrifice on some other trigger does not. `selfEffect` sees
only the clause, so a reader there would build a card that works and plays badly — worse than an
unread line (D362). D364's lesson for the third time, and it now has a test that keeps the omission
deliberate rather than forgotten.

### A reading error of mine, about my own gate

I ran the gate as `bash scripts/gate.sh 2>&1 | tail -6` and read "exit code 0" plus a page of
`services-up.js` text as a pass. It was a failure: Postgres and Redis had died in a worker restart,
`services-up.js` refused exactly as designed, and the gate printed `GATE FAILED at: node
scripts/services-up.js (rc=1)` followed by a 40-line log tail — so `tail -6` cut the verdict off,
and the pipe replaced the gate's status with `tail`'s. The instrument was right and the way I read
it was wrong, which is the same shape as D356, D365 and D368 with the defect moved out of the script
and into the invocation. The gate is now run with its output redirected and `$?` captured.

## D373

**Tokens: the one family whose characteristics are the sentence itself** (#317)

A token has no printed card to look up. Its power, toughness, colour, subtype and keywords *are* the
clause that makes it, so unlike every other family in this compiler there is nothing to look up and
nothing to guess. `SPIRIT_TOKEN` is `{ name: 'Spirit', typeLine: 'Token Creature — Spirit', power:
'1', toughness: '1', oracleText: 'Flying', colors: ['W'] }`, which is "a 1/1 white Spirit creature
token with flying" transcribed. D259 — never invent the text of a real card — is satisfied by
construction here in a way it is not anywhere else in the module.

**225 of 538 printed lines, up from 217 (40.3% → 41.8%); 146 of 339 cards get a script, up from
139.** Doomed Traveler, Doomed Dissenter, Mogg War Marshal, Raise the Alarm, Talrand, Woe Strider
and Young Pyromancer.

### The keywords are validated by the reader that has to read them back

A token's keywords live in its `oracleText`, and the engine gets them from
`printedKeywords(def.oracleText)` with no script involved. So rather than keeping a list of keywords
this function believes in, it writes the oracle text and then asks `printedKeywords` whether that
text yields **exactly** the keywords the clause named. A token printed "with flying" whose keyword
the engine could not read back would be a 1/1 that silently cannot fly; this refuses the clause
instead. The check is pinned: deleting it turns the "with soaring" refusal green.

### Five refusals, each with a stated reason and a test

`create X ... tokens` (the pool's two instances count the board, not the X chosen at cast time),
`... token for each ...` (the same thing in another spelling), `with "When this creature dies, …"`
(a granted ability, not a keyword), `Create a Treasure token` and `a token that's a copy of target
creature` (no printed power and toughness, and both carry rules text of their own).

The comparison is the strictest in the file: resolve both effects and compare **whole game states**,
which covers the created instance and the `CardDef` registered for it. Dropping the keyword, the
count or the colour each turns tests red; the colour alone turns five red.

### An unpinned guard, kept on purpose and now labelled as such

The reader requires each subtype word to be capitalised. **Deleting it leaves all 82 tests green** —
the surrounding regex already requires a count, a power and toughness, a colour word, and "creature
token" with nothing after it, so the check is not load-bearing on this pool and no test pins it. By
the standard the rest of this session has applied (`plain`, D371), that normally means deleting it.

It stays, and the comment now says why rather than implying the check does work it cannot be shown
to do: the slot becomes the token's **name**, the pool is 348 cards against the tens of thousands
#318 will import, and the two ways of being wrong are not symmetric. Over-strictness costs coverage
on a card nobody can name; over-permissiveness costs a token named something that is not a creature
type, on a card nobody has looked at. Revisit when the bulk corpus can be measured.

## D374

**The compiler is now in the engine's live path, and the half that makes that honest** (#317)

Seven increments of compiler and none of it reached a table: `scriptForCard` — the one function the
engine's mana, ability and trigger paths ask "what does this card do?" — still called
`cardFromData` and nothing else. 146 cards' worth of derived rules existed and no game used them.
That is the difference between infrastructure and a playable beta, so this wires it in.

### Where it had to live, and why

`compile.ts` imports `scripts.ts`, so the answer could not grow a third branch where it was without
a cycle. New module `derive.ts`, above both: hand-written script, then `cardFromData`'s whole-card
answer, then the compiler's line-by-line reading. **The hand-written script still wins**, which is
why all 348 pool cards and all thirteen built-in decks are untouched by this.

### The half that makes it honest

A compiled script is often **partial** — a permanent's text is a list of independent abilities, so
the compiler reads what it can and leaves the rest. That is right for a permanent and it is also a
new way to be quietly wrong: a card that does three of its four printed things with nobody told
which one is missing. Turning the compiler on alone would trade a card the player *knows* to play
by hand for a card that looks automated and is not, which is the trade D362 exists to refuse.

So `coverage.ts`'s `'text-not-automated'` reason — reserved since the file was written, with
*"nothing emits this yet… the compiler is what will"* — now emits. `unreadLines(def)` gives the
printed lines nothing is running, and a card with one is reported with the line quoted.

Three rules make that report true rather than noisy:

- **A card with a hand-written script reports nothing**, because the script is the authority and
  asking the compiler what *it* could read off the same text would report a Kitchen Finks as partly
  manual. The test that pins this loads all thirteen decks and expects an empty list; deleting the
  short-circuit turns it red.
- **An unimplemented keyword is not reported.** The card plays; what is missing is one way to cast
  or use it (D370). Telling a player to hand-play an Equipment the engine is running would be
  wrong, and a player who catches the warning lying once stops reading it.
- **`manualNote` now says "cannot fully play"**, because the list holds two different things. "Cannot
  play" was true of a card with no printed data and is a lie about one the engine casts and attacks
  with.

### A bound set by arithmetic, because the instrument cannot see this

The list travels inside the per-seat view, which has a hard 128 KiB cap that `PodStateEvent`
enforces by **failing validation** — an over-sized state is not broadcast at all.

`wire-growth.mjs` measures the peak view across whole games, and run now on this build its worst
four-player singleton pod is **47202 bytes, 36.0% of the cap** (3 seeds, 63-82 turns, none
unfinished). **That measurement cannot see the new payload**, and the reason is worth stating
rather than assuming past: every deck the instrument can build comes from the pool, every pool card
has a hand-written script, so `manual` is empty in every game it plays. The arm that would exercise
it needs the imported corpus (#318).

So the bound is arithmetic. A hundred distinct cards in one seat's deck, all reported, each quoting
an unabridged paragraph, is roughly 47 KiB added to a 47 KiB peak — 94 of 128, on a figure the
instrument itself calls a floor rather than a bound. Capping the quote at 120 characters holds an
entry to **227 bytes measured** (107 of fixed prose plus the quote), so the same worst case adds
about 23 KiB for 70 of 128. The test asserts 227 rather than a round number near it, because 227 is
the figure the arithmetic rests on.

Verified: compile.test.ts 82/82 and the new coverage.test.ts 10/10, with the hand-written
short-circuit and the keyword filter each proved to fail when broken; GATE OK.

## D375

**The corpus filter now matches the goal, and the import cannot write a single row** (#318)

Two halves: one bounded improvement, and a blocker found by running the thing for the first time.

### The filter, narrowed to the formats people play

`SCRYFALL_BULK_FILE` already made the importer source-agnostic (D329), so what was left of #318's
description was the filter and the report. The filter accepted a card "legal or restricted in **any**
format Scryfall tracks", and that map also carries Alchemy, Historic, Timeless, Brawl, Oathbreaker
and PreDH — wider than the goal, which names *"standard, legacy, modern, pauper, commander, and
like the actual played competitive formats"*. `digital` catches most of what that admits and not all
of it: a paper card rebalanced for Alchemy keeps its paper printing.

So: seven named formats, `restricted` counting alongside `legal`. And every refusal now returns its
**reason** instead of a bare `false`, with the tally printing a line per reason — because one total
cannot tell "the dump was all tokens" from "the legality list got too narrow", and those are
opposite bugs. The whole filter is lifted out of the import loop into `importFilter`, a pure
function of one Scryfall object, which is the only reason any of it is testable without a database
and a 500MB file. Five tests, including one that pins the seven format keys as a list: a misspelled
key reads as `undefined` and silently empties the corpus, which is the failure this filter is least
able to see from inside.

### Running it found the blocker

Nobody had ever run this import end to end — no test does, because it needs a database. Run against
a seven-card fixture it filters five rows, one per reason, exactly as intended:

```
Wrote 0 cards (5 filtered out, 0 unparseable, 2 rejected by the database).
  filtered by reason: not-a-card=1, funny-set=1, not-black-bordered=1, digital-only=1,
                      not-legal-anywhere-played=1
```

And **both keepers were rejected**: `column "power" of relation "scryfall_cards" does not exist`.

`packages/db/migrations/0015_scryfall_card_rules_fields.sql` adds the six columns the importer needs
— `power`, `toughness`, `loyalty`, `layout`, `oracle_id`, `produced_mana` — and D329 wrote it. **It
has never been applied.** 0 of the 18 Postgres databases here carry a single one of those columns,
and `grimore_dev` has no `schema_migrations` table at all, so `packages/db`'s migrations have never
run against it; that table was created by legacy `db.js`'s own bootstrap.

So the corpus cannot land, and the reason is one migration nobody has run. D329's guard — the one
that turns "wrote no rows" into a thrown error — is what made a single run enough to find it.
Recorded as #320 rather than fixed here: applying `packages/db`'s migrations to a legacy-created
schema, and the production cutover, are both Nick's.

### The instrument that should have caught it read one file

`scripts/audit-postgres-schema-gap.js` checks INSERT column lists against the real schema — exactly
this defect — and read **only `server.js`**. The card upsert lives in `scryfallService.js`, so the
largest write in the codebase was invisible to the one tool built to find column gaps. Its heading
said "server.js" and its clean result was read as "the schema is fine".

It now reads both, and the first run with the second file produced a **confident false positive**:
`scryfall_cards … scryfall_id`, a column only the SQLite statement names. `scryfallService.js` holds
both dialects as named constants, and the existing guard only skipped the SQLite branch of a
`db.isPostgres` *ternary* — a named constant is not one. Fixed by walking back to the nearest
`const NAME =` and skipping when the name says SQLITE, named rather than proximity-based for the
reason the file already gives about windows. An audit that cries wolf is an audit somebody stops
running, which lands in the same place as one that cannot fail.

With that fixed it reports exactly the six columns 0015 adds, and nothing else on that table.

Verified: scryfall-service.test.js 8/8 (5 new), the fixture import demonstrated end to end, the
audit's finding reproduced and its false positive removed; GATE OK.

## D376

**Attachments: the compiler's first shape read from two lines at once** (#317)

Every reader before this took one printed line and returned what that line is worth, and the lines
path merged the results. An Aura cannot be read that way, and it is D364's trap in its sharpest
form yet:

- `Enchant creature` **alone** is an Aura you can cast, that attaches, and that does nothing.
- `Enchanted creature gets +2/+0` **alone** is a bonus with nothing to attach it to.
- `Equip {1}` alone is an ability that moves a blank Equipment around the battlefield.

Neither line is a unit; the pair is. A per-line reader emitting either half would build a card that
**works and does nothing** — worse than an unread card, because an unread card is flagged for a
human to play by hand (D362) and a blank Aura is flagged nowhere. So `attachmentScriptFor` takes the
definition and all the lines, returns both halves or neither, and names the lines it accounted for;
`compileCard` consults it before the per-line loop and skips what it claimed.

**243 of 538 printed lines, up from 225 (41.8% → 45.2%); 154 of 339 cards get a script, up from
146.** Bonesplitter, Loxodon Warhammer, Basilisk Collar, Darksteel Plate, Blade of Selves, Robe of
Mirrors, Angelic Gift, Pacifism and Rancor.

`equipFragment` is split out of the hand-written `equipment` builder so the compiled Bonesplitter
and the hand-written one are the same ability rather than two implementations of it — the same
reason `keywordScriptFor` is a table of calls into the builders above it.

### `friendly` and `removesACreature` are facts about the bonus

Every Aura in the pool prints the identical `Enchant creature`, and Angelic Gift's target is
`friendly` while Pacifism's is not. The difference is whether the effect **helps**, which is
readable from the bonus and nowhere else — and Pacifism also sets `removesACreature`, because an
Aura that stops a creature attacking or blocking *is* removal and a bot that does not know that
holds it for nothing. So a harmful bonus takes the flag and drops `friendly`; a helpful one is the
other way round, and both sides are tested on the same printed phrase.

A negative size change is harmful by arithmetic (`power < 0 || toughness < 0`), which is one rule
rather than a second reader.

### A redundant guard, found by trying to break it

`attachmentBonus` had a test for a quote mark, to refuse Ophidian Eye's
`Enchanted creature has "Whenever this creature deals damage to a player, draw a card."` — a granted
*ability*, which the hand-written card expresses with `grants`, an index into a table this module
cannot build.

Deleting that test left all 93 tests green. The refusal was already coming from `grantedKeywords`:
the quoted sentence splits on its own commas into fragments `printedKeywords` does not recognise, so
the keyword validation refuses it. An unpinned guard duplicating a pinned one is a second thing to
keep true, so it is gone and the comment says what does the work. Same family as `plain` (D371) and
the token subtype check (D373), with the opposite verdict — and the difference is which way the
redundancy cut: a duplicate of a *tested* refusal is dead weight, while the token check was the only
thing standing between an unmeasurable corpus and a token named something that is not a creature
type.

Verified: compile.test.ts 93/93, with the aura's `friendly`, its `removesACreature`, the granted
keywords and the `printedKeywords` validation each proved to fail when broken; GATE OK.

## D377

**Who the trigger is watching, and the removal that gives the permanent back** (#317, and #320's
local half cleared)

**253 of 538 printed lines, up from 243 (45.2% → 47.0%); 162 of 339 cards get a script, up from
154.** Angel of Sanctions, Banisher Priest, Banishing Light, Chasm Skulker, Conclave Tribunal,
Impact Tremors, Impassioned Orator, Journey to Nowhere and Soul Warden.

### Ten more prologues, which are all about `who` and `of`

Most of the pool's etb and dies triggers watch somebody *else's* permanent, and the English that
says which is exact rather than approximate — which is the only reason it can be read:

| printed | event |
| --- | --- |
| "another creature" | `who: 'another'` |
| "a creature you control" | `who: 'any', of: 'you'` |
| "~ or another creature" | `who: 'any'`, nothing about whose |

Soul Warden's own comment makes the first distinction load-bearing: *"'Another' and not 'any': a
Soul Warden does not gain you life for itself."* A reader that collapsed the three would build a
card that triggers off its own arrival where the print says it does not — wrong in a way nothing
refuses and invisible except in a life total. Every `on` is copied from the card named beside it,
and `of` is absent where the hand-written card omits it: Blood Artist says nothing about whose
creature died and that is **not the same event** as Zulaport Cutthroat's.

Also the two draw triggers, where `by` is left at its default for the reason `automation.ts` states
outright — *"a card that says nothing watches its own controller"*.

### Exile until this leaves: the second whole-card shape

The exile and the return are two triggers, and either alone is a broken card: an ETB that exiles
with nothing to return it is permanent exile printed as temporary, and a `leaves` trigger with
nothing exiled is dead text. So it joins attachments as a shape read from more than one line, and
`wholeCardShapeFor` is now the one entry point `compileCard` calls before the per-line loop.

The pool prints it two ways and **the difference decides whether the return exists**: Banisher
Priest has it inside an `until ~ leaves the battlefield` clause on one line; Journey to Nowhere has
it as a second sentence. So one of the two must be present, and a bare `exile target creature` ETB
with neither **is refused** — that card is permanent exile, and emitting the pair for it would hand
back a creature the print says is gone for good. The one refusal here that is about correctness
rather than coverage, and it has its own test.

Five more target phrases to reach them, all `kind: 'permanent'` over one composable
`permanentFilter`: the three qualifiers "another", "nonland" and "an opponent controls" compose
freely in print, and the pool has three hand-written filters each spelling a different subset of the
same three tests. One factory of three independent facts beats seven phrases with seven functions.

### The vacuity family, third appearance, caught by a guard again

Chasm Skulker's clause puts a counter on itself, and with a made-up source id `addCounters` is a
no-op — so the compiled and hand-written effects both returned the state unchanged and `toEqual`
passed on two no-ops. The `not.toEqual(base)` assertion caught it; the fixture now puts the card on
a real battlefield and uses its own id. D366 and D372 were the first two, and all three were found
by a deliberate non-vacuity check rather than by luck.

### #320's local half, cleared

Migration 0015's six `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` statements and its index are applied to
`grimore_dev`, and the import path is **verified end to end**: the seven-card fixture writes its 2
keepers, filters 5 — one per reason — rejects nothing, and the rules columns carry real values
(`power`, `toughness`, `oracle_id`, `produced_mana`). `audit-postgres-schema-gap.js` no longer
reports a missing `scryfall_cards` column. The fixture rows were deleted afterwards.

Only the ALTERs were run, not `packages/db`'s migration runner: the ALTERs are additive and
idempotent, while 0001-0014 have never run against this legacy-created schema and may not be. The
production cutover, and whether the runner should own this table at all, stay Nick's.

Verified: compile.test.ts 105/105, with the `another`/`any` collapse, the dropped `of: 'you'`, the
exile pair emitted without a printed return, and both halves of `permanentFilter` each proved to
fail when broken; GATE OK.

## D378

**Activated abilities, and the field-conflict that was a correct reading** (#317)

**265 of 538 printed lines (49.3%); 171 of 339 cards get a script. Both unchanged from D377, and
that zero is the finding.** Blight Mamba, Drudge Skeletons, Imperious Perfect, Mind Stone, Mutavault,
Phoenix of Ash, River Boa, Shivan Dragon and Skithiryx, the Blight Dragon were the nine cards stage
ten's first half picked up; the second half, below, picked up none and fixed two defects.

### The third place a clause can live

A clause has had two homes: a trigger's resolution and a spell's. `abilityFromLine` is the third,
and it is the same multiplying change the trigger table was — almost no new vocabulary, because
every effect the module can already read becomes reachable from a printed cost. `Regenerate ~` was
the one new reader needed, and `lineScriptFor` now asks keyword, then trigger, then ability.

### A cost component dropped is a different card

`{B}{G}, Sacrifice another creature:` is a cost this reader cannot say, and an ability that is free
when the print says it eats a creature is not a cheaper card — it is a different one, and nothing at
the table would flag it, because the ability works. So the cost is parsed by **classifying every
comma-separated component**, and one that does not classify refuses the whole line. Classifying
beats one regex over the whole cost: the printed orders multiply (`{1}, {T}`, `{T}, {1}`,
`{T}, Pay 1 life`) and a pattern covering them is exactly where a component gets quietly dropped.

`parseManaCost` is the validator for the symbols, because it *records* an unrecognised symbol rather
than ignoring one: without it `{E}, {T}:` reads energy as a generic mana and `{X}{R}` reads X as
nothing. Both are the dropped component wearing a symbol instead of a sentence, and both now refuse.

### Expressible is not the same as read

The first draft of the refusal test asserted that `{T}, Pay 1 life: Add {C}.` was refused. It failed:
`cardFromData` was already reading that line, correctly, with `AbilityCost.life` — the field exists
precisely so a player on one life is never offered a Mana Confluence's mana, which is the printed
difference between it and a City of Brass. The docblock claiming a life cost could not be said was
wrong about the engine it is part of.

So the component is now **read** here too, and that is what unlocks a **pain land** — which
`cardFromData` structurally cannot read: `foldManaLines` folds a permanent's mana lines into *one*
cost and would rather refuse a land with one free tap and one costing a life than flatten the two.
A line reader has no such problem, because two printed lines are two abilities.

### `abilities` did not accumulate, so a correct second reading was reported as a conflict

Compiling that pain land is what found it. The first line read, the second line read, and `merge`
then reported the second as a `field-conflict` — because only `triggers` accumulated and every other
field was set once. A permanent with two activated abilities is ordinary, so `abilities` joins it;
every remaining field is one fact about the card, where two lines disagreeing still means a line was
misread. Nothing in the pool has two readable ability lines, which is why the bug survived to be
found by a hand-written fixture rather than by the measurement.

### The row that proved the test block could not see the Sol Ring case

Five mechanisms were broken on purpose to check the tests discriminate. Four went red. Truncating
the mana-ability's `produces` to its first symbol — a permanent that taps for two reading as one —
left all 115 green: every sum in the pool is on a card `cardFromData` reads whole, so no ground-truth
row reached this reader. A direct assertion was added for it, and re-breaking the branch now fails.

### Why the headline did not move

The pool has no mixed-cost pain land and no permanent with two readable ability lines, so this half
of the stage compiles exactly the same 265 lines. What it changes is a corpus the pool cannot show:
every pain land, and every permanent whose second activated ability was being discarded as a
conflict. That number waits on #318.

Verified: compile.test.ts 116/116; all five new mechanisms — the symbol validation, the life
component, the accumulating `abilities`, the regenerate reader and the mana sum — each proved to
fail when deliberately broken.

## D379

**A keyword granted with a pump, which is one printed effect** (#317)

**270 of 538 printed lines, up from 265 (49.3% → 50.2%); 175 of 339 cards get a script, up from
171.** Blossoming Defense, Dive Down, Tainted Strike, Renegade Freighter's attack trigger, and
Skithiryx's haste ability.

### The refusal that was right and the end state that was not

The pump reader took the size and refused any clause that also granted a keyword, with a comment
saying reading half of it "would be a card that silently does less than it prints". That refusal was
correct — and it was never the destination. `pump` takes the size and the keywords in **one**
`PumpOptions`, and the pool writes them that way: Selesnya Charm's first mode and Renegade
Freighter's attack trigger are both a single call. So reading both halves is not two effects stapled
together, it is the one call the hand-written cards make — which matters, because two separate
continuous effects would expire independently.

`isKeyword` is the gate and the reason this is safe at all: the engine's keyword list is what
`characteristicsOf` consults, so a word outside it is a word the rules ignore. `gains protection
from red` would compile to a creature that gains nothing and a spell that looks like it worked, so
an unrecognised word refuses the clause and the line is reported for a human to play by hand (D362).

### The granted keyword decides *two* bot hints, and the pool draws both lines itself

This is D364's lesson a fifth time, and the first time the hint is not a constant.

`protectFromRemoval` — Blossoming Defense and Dive Down — sets **`protectsACreature`** and
deliberately *not* `expiresAtEndOfTurn`. The two say different things: "hold this until something
threatens one of your creatures" against "hold this for the combat", and the measurement behind the
first (64 cast across 160 games, **60 of them with nothing on the stack and no combat**) is the
whole reason it exists. A hexproof trick told to wait for combat is still a card thrown away. So
hexproof and shroud make the compiled spell a protection trick and everything else keeps the pump
hint.

`helpsInCombat` is the second, on the **target** rather than the spell, and its own docblock draws
the line and names the cards: it is "only for a bonus whose whole value is in the attack", and a
Giant Growth deliberately does not carry it because pumping a blocker to win a fight is half of what
that card is for. Of the four hand-written specs that carry it, the two that are keyword grants are
Tainted Strike (infect) and Crimson Wisps (haste) — a creature that can never attack gains nothing
from either. So those two words set it and no others. With it, the compiled Tainted Strike's target
spec is **whole-spec equal** to the hand-written one.

`indestructible` is deliberately in neither set: nothing hand-written pairs it with either hint, and
guessing which one it wants is the invention D259 rules out.

### A grant with no size change is its own shape

`{B}: Skithiryx, the Blight Dragon gains haste until end of turn.` is the same `pump` call with only
`keywords` in it. Read as its own clause rather than as a `+0/+0` pump, which `sizeBonus` refuses and
should go on refusing — a card printing `+0/+0` would be a pump that does nothing, and this is not a
pump at all. Its test matches the ability by **cost**, not description, because the print says
"Skithiryx, the Blight Dragon gains haste" where the hand-written description says "Skithiryx": the
compiler echoes the printed line, as every reader here does.

### Dive Down stored a zero, and the two readings of one card disagreed by nothing else

The ground-truth check on Dive Down failed on a single field: `power: 0`. `protectFromRemoval` is a
parameterised builder passing both numbers unconditionally, so Dive Down's `+0/+3` stored a zero
power bonus, where `sizeBonus` omits a zero component — two continuous effects that behave
identically and compare unequal, which is exactly what `sizeBonus` exists to prevent. Fixed in the
**hand-written** builder, which now calls `sizeBonus`, so there is one source for that rule.

Verified: compile.test.ts 124/124; all six new or changed mechanisms — the grant inside
`pumpAndGrant`, the `isKeyword` gate, the protection hint, `helpsInCombat`, the grant-only self
clause and `protectFromRemoval`'s `sizeBonus` — each proved to fail when deliberately broken.

## D380

**The keyword declarations that already had a builder** (#317)

**302 of 538 printed lines, up from 270 (50.2% → 56.1%); 190 of 339 cards get a script, up from
175. Keyword declarations with no builder: 57 → 27.** The largest single-stage move so far, and the
cheapest, because almost nothing was built — the engine already had a field for every one of these.

### Eighteen rows, one shape

`Flashback {2}{U}` is `flashback: { cost: '{2}{U}' }`, and that is the whole of it. So are madness,
miracle, foretell, spectacle, buyback, dash and ninjutsu, each with one card in the pool whose
hand-written script sets exactly that field — which is what the table in `compile.test.ts` names.
Beside them: `Delve`, `Affinity for artifacts`, `Dredge 3`, `Suspend 1—{R}` (two cards, see below),
`Escape—{2}{R}{R}, Exile three other cards from your graveyard`, `Rebound`, `Crew N`, and morph,
megamorph and echo.

What the eight alternative costs have in common is more than the shape: every one is a **way to cast
the card**, so reading one adds an option and changes nothing about what the card does. That is what
makes them safe on a card whose resolution is still unread.

### Morph and echo: one parse, two call sites

`keywordScriptFor`'s docblock listed morph and echo as deliberately absent *because* `fromCardData`
already read them, and "two readers of one line is two places for them to disagree". That was the
right objection to a second reader and not an argument for leaving the line unread: `keywordWithCost`
is now exported and imported here. No cycle — `fromCardData` imports nothing this file does.

### What is still refused, and the line that decides it

**Kicker and overload** are the two alternative costs *not* read, and the reason is the distinction
above: their payoff is printed on another line ("If this spell was kicked, it deals 4 damage
instead"), so the declaration alone is an option to pay more for nothing. Overload's field also
takes an `onResolve` no line can supply. **Evoke** is half a keyword — the other half is the
enters-and-sacrifice trigger the pool writes out per card, and the declaration alone is a creature
you get cheap and *keep*, which is a strictly better card than the one printed. **Embalm,
eternalize and bestow** each need characteristics the line does not carry. **Unearth** has no single
field to emit. Every one of those is now named in the docblock with its reason.

### Three mechanisms the tests could not see, found by breaking them

- **Echo's trigger.** `echo: { cost }` without `echoTrigger` is a price the game never asks for, and
  the table only looks at the declared field, so dropping the trigger left all 142 tests green.
- **Rebound's trigger.** The same, on the keyword whose second half *is* the card.
- **Suspend's count.** Rift Bolt is `Suspend 1`, so a reader that ignored the printed number and
  always wrote 1 passed its row. Search for Tomorrow (`Suspend 2`) is now a second row.

The first two are fixed by a test asserting the direction the table cannot: a trigger the
hand-written card has must be among the compiled ones. The table's own trigger test runs the other
way, so that an *invented* trigger fails — both directions are needed and only one was there.

Crew gets its own test rather than a table row, because an `AbilityDef` holds a closure and two
closures are never deep-equal. Compared instead: the cost, the printed description, `animates`
(the bot rule that travels with crew), and the board the effect leaves.

### Two tests had to be repointed, which is the good kind of churn

Thunderous Wrath's `Miracle {R}` was the example in "reads the resolution of a spell whose keyword
line it cannot build" — and it now compiles whole. The property still matters, so the example is a
keyword the compiler **deliberately** refuses: `Kicker {4}`. The same swap in the fixture of "still
refuses a spell whose unread line is a sentence, not a keyword".

Verified: compile.test.ts 145/145; the alternative-cost group, echo's trigger, rebound's trigger,
suspend's count, escape's exile count and crew's `animates` each proved to fail when deliberately
broken. Scryfall egress re-tested: still refused (000 for both hosts).

## D381

**A static, a Fog and a library search** (#317)

**309 of 538 printed lines, up from 302 (56.1% → 57.4%); 196 of 339 cards get a script, up from
190.** Glorious Anthem, Judith's static, Fog, Holy Day, Diabolic Tutor, Rampant Growth.

### A static is not an effect, so it is its own reader

`Creatures you control get +1/+1` is the commonest static in Magic and the first thing the compiler
reads that is never resolved and never on the stack: `characteristicsOf` consults it every time it
computes a creature's size. So `staticFromLine` sits in `lineScriptFor`'s chain beside
`keywordScriptFor` rather than among the clause readers, and the fragment is a `statics` entry.

The word **other** is the whole of the difference between the engine's two scopes, and it is
load-bearing rather than cosmetic: Judith is a 2/2 and prints "Other creatures you control get
+1/+0", so a reader that collapsed them would make her a 3/2. Pinned twice — once by equality
against her hand-written script, once by asserting the two scope strings directly, because a pair
that differs by one string is exactly where a passing deep-equality can hide both rows coming from
one branch.

`statics` also joins `abilities` and `triggers` in `merge`'s accumulating set. Nothing in the pool
prints two, which is why it has a **fixture** test: an untested mechanism added ahead of need is the
one that is wrong when the corpus reaches it, and `field-conflict` on a second anthem is precisely
what `merge` reported for `abilities` until a pain land found it (D378).

### The Fog's second field is the one that matters

`preventCombatDamage` is the primitive and `preventsDamage` is the bot hint. Nothing in the engine
reads the flag — the bot does — so a Fog without it works perfectly and gets cast into an empty
board. Third time this shape has come up (`removesACreature`, `protectsACreature`), and the first
where the flag is the *only* thing the compiled card would have been missing.

### `clausesOf` cuts the search in half, which is why the readers stop before "then shuffle"

Both searches were written to match the whole printed sentence and both stayed unread. The reason is
`clausesOf`: it splits on `", then "`, and a search prints ", then shuffle". So the line arrives as
two clauses and the readers match the first. The second is the bare word, read as the identity,
because `searchYourLibrary` already shuffles when the search ends — a reader that shuffled again
would shuffle twice, and a library shuffled an unknown number of times is the one thing that makes
two boards incomparable. The bare word only, since "shuffle your library" names an object and is a
step of its own on the cards that print it.

Both searches are deliberately narrow: no filter at all for Diabolic Tutor, `isBasicLand` for
Rampant Growth, and anything else refused. A tutor for some other kind of card needs a filter no
phrase here can build, and a search that puts the card anywhere else is a different card. `min: 0`
is compared in the test for the same reason it exists: a search you may decline is a different card
from one you may not.

### A test fixture had to be repointed again

"Still refuses a spell whose unread line is a sentence, not a keyword" used a Fog as its unreadable
sentence, and the Fog is now readable. Its text is now `Each player sacrifices a creature.` — and
the fixture says in a comment why it names its own text rather than borrowing a card's: a sentence
nothing reads today is a moving target, and the property is about the two *kinds* of unread line.

Verified: compile.test.ts 153/153; the two static scopes, the accumulating `statics`, the Fog's bot
hint, the tutor's `min: 0` and Rampant Growth's basic-land filter each proved to fail when
deliberately broken.

## D382

**Soulbond, a team pump, and the phrase that may not point at your own Sol Ring** (#317)

**316 of 538 printed lines, up from 309 (57.4% → 58.7%); 199 of 339 cards get a script, up from
196.** Trusted Forcemage, Wolfir Silverheart, Master of Pearls, and Ainok Survivalist's turn-up.

### Soulbond was a named refusal, and this is the stage it was waiting for

`keywordScriptFor`'s docblock listed it first among what is deliberately absent: "its line is the
word alone; the bonus the pair gets is on the *next* line", and a number guessed from the word
Soulbond would be invented (D259). So it is the **third whole-card shape**, after attachments and
exile-until-leaves: `Soulbond` plus "As long as ~ is paired with another creature, each of those
creatures gets +1/+1" is one mechanic printed as two lines, and neither line is a unit — a pairing
that does nothing, or a bonus with no pairing to hang from. The shape emits the declaration and
`soulbondTriggers` together, or nothing.

Only the bonus form. Tandem Lookout prints "each of those creatures **has** 'Whenever this creature
deals damage to a player, draw a card'", declared in the pool as `grants: [0]` against a
`grantedTriggers` entry nothing here can build. Compiling it as a pair that gets *nothing* would be
a card that works and does half of what it says, so it is refused — and that refusal has its own
test, which is what caught a broadened regex that would have fed `NaN` into the bonus.

### `pumpTeam`, which is not `pump` over the creatures currently out

"Creatures you control get +2/+2 until end of turn" is a continuous effect with a **scope**: a
creature that arrives later in the turn is not included and one that leaves does not carry the
bonus away. `pump` over a list of ids would be right on the board it saw and wrong a moment later,
and comparing the two resulting boards is what tells them apart.

The same sentence without a duration is a *static* and is read by `staticFromLine` (D381). The
duration is the whole of the difference, and the two readers sit in different places because of it.

### One phrase, two tests, and the second was not covered until it was broken

`target artifact or enchantment an opponent controls` is the first place the type list and the
controller test compose, so `permanentFilter` gained a `types` option — read **live** through
`characteristicsOf`, like its other tests. Ainok Survivalist's own comment says why the restriction
matters more here than on a Naturalize: the trigger is **mandatory**, so without it a morph turned
up on an otherwise empty board would have to destroy its controller's own Sol Ring.

The first draft of the test put an artifact on each side of the table, which proves the controller
test and says nothing about the types — dropping `types` left it green. A creature on the opponent's
side is the row that was missing.

Verified: compile.test.ts 158/158; the soulbond triggers, the soulbond refusal, `pumpTeam`, the
phrase's controller test and its type test each proved to fail when deliberately broken.

## D383

**The per-account reset throttle was advisory, because its counter was not awaited** (#321)

CI failed once, on a commit that touched none of this: `account-recovery.test.ts` fires six password
reset requests at one account and expects five emails, and it got **six**. The test was right and
the route was wrong.

### Two writes for one fact

`/forgot-password` read `account_events` with `recentEventCount` and then recorded the request with
`auditAccountEvent` — which is **deliberately** not awaited, and its docblock gives a good reason:
"the audit write must not add latency to an auth response". That argument is sound for a *record*.
It is not sound for a **counter**: the next request reads the table to decide whether to act, so a
write still in flight is a request that was never counted. A limit of five that a fast caller takes
to six is not a limit, and the caller here is unauthenticated while the cost is somebody else's
inbox.

So the count and the insert are now one transaction, `countAndRecordEvent`. `recentEventCount` stays
for reads that are not gates, with a docblock saying which is which.

### The lock, because awaiting is only half of it

Awaiting the write fixes a *sequence*. It does not fix a **burst**: six requests in flight can all
read four and all proceed, which is the ordinary read-then-write race and exactly what an attacker
sends. The transaction therefore takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(lower(identifier)))` —
released on commit or rollback, so a crashed request cannot wedge an account out of its own
recovery. The lock is keyed on the identifier **as supplied**, like the count, because counting
before resolving is what stops the throttle from telling a caller that an account exists.

### Fails closed, which is the opposite of the audit rule and right for the opposite reason

An audit write that throws must not turn a login into a 500. A *throttle* that throws and reads as
"under the limit" is a throttle an attacker removes by making the database unhappy. So the gate
answers `allowed: false` on any failure, and the route's rejection path is byte-identical to its
success path, so the two are indistinguishable from outside.

### The audit trail quietly got worse, and a test caught it

The gate runs **before** the account lookup, by design. So the row it writes has the identifier and
no `player_id` — and the first version of this simply dropped the player id that the old code
attached. `records a reset being requested and redeemed` reads the trail by `player_id` and failed,
which is the audit trail degrading in exchange for the throttle improving. `attachPlayerToEvent`
puts it back, awaited rather than fired and forgotten, because the row it corrects is read back a
moment later.

### What the tests can and cannot prove, stated rather than implied

The burst test **through the route** was written first and does not discriminate: run against the
old read-then-write route it *passed* on this machine, because six concurrent HTTP requests
serialised far enough apart to count each other. That is the same reason the sequential version only
failed in CI, once. It is kept as a stress check with that written in it, and the proof is three
deterministic tests on the gate itself: three allowed then one refused in sequence; exactly three
allowed out of six concurrent calls; and `allowed: false` from a pool that cannot connect.

Verified: account-recovery 30/30. Four deliberate breaks each caught — the advisory lock removed
(the concurrent test), the insert not awaited (the audit trail), `>=` relaxed to `>` (four tests),
and the failure path flipped to fail open (the fail-closed test).

## D384

**The compiler reached resolution and not the opponent: ~40 call sites asked the wrong lookup** (#322)

**44 call sites converted, 2 kept.** `scripts.ts` exports `scriptFor(name)` — the **hand-written**
registry, 348 cards. `derive.ts`
exports `scriptForCard(def)`, which answers from the registry first and falls back to the
oracle-text compiler. When the compiler landed, `derive.ts`'s docblock said it is "the one place
that answers *what does this card do?* for the engine's mana, ability and trigger paths". It was not.
Four files asked the registry directly:

| file | sites | what they decide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bot.ts` | 26 | every bot rule: hold the trick, crew the Vehicle, price the pump that wears off |
| `legalActions.ts` | 9 | whether a flashback, escape, foretell, morph, affinity or split-second play is **offered at all** |
| `autoActions.ts` | 4 | whether a cast, a foretell, a suspend or a turn-up is accepted |
| `automation.ts` | 5 of 7 | saga chapters, an Aura's target, a miracle's cost, a land arriving tapped |

So a compiled card resolved correctly, and then: the bot could not see one of its abilities, the
legality layer would not offer its alternative casts, and its saga never advanced. A pasted deck
**played blind**, and nothing said so — the worst shape in this project's list, because the card
*works*.

Invisible to the whole suite by construction: every pool card has a hand-written script, so the two
lookups return the same object for all 348 of them. That is also what makes the fix safe — the
precedence is "hand-written wins, always", so converting every site is a provable no-op on the pool
and adds vision only where there was none.

### Two name lookups stay, and they are not the same thing

`automation.ts` keeps `scriptFor(ref.card)?.grantedTriggers?.[ref.index]` twice. A granted ability is
recorded on the continuous effect as the granting card's **name** plus an index, so there is no
definition to ask with — and `grantedTriggers` is the one field the compiler never emits, because
granting another permanent a triggered ability has no reader and is a refusal rather than a gap
(see `soulbondShapeFor`, which refuses Tandem Lookout for exactly that). The registry is the
complete answer there, not a partial one.

### A source-level test, which is unusual here and is the right shape for this one

The defect was not a wrong answer from a function; it was call sites asking the wrong function, in
files whose tests pass either way. **No behavioural assertion on a pool card can tell the two
lookups apart.** So `derive.test.ts` pins the thing that was wrong: `bot.ts`, `legalActions.ts` and
`autoActions.ts` contain no `scriptFor(` call, and `automation.ts` contains exactly two, both on the
`grantedTriggers` line. Plus one behavioural check that the lookup itself works — a compiled-only
instant whose `protectsACreature` the registry cannot see and the compiler can.

Its first version matched the raw source and failed on all three files, because each one *names*
`scriptFor` in a docblock explaining which lookup it uses. Comments are stripped now, and the test
says why.

## D385

**Five filters read the printed type line, and one docblock claimed otherwise** (#319)

A target filter must read what a permanent **is**, not what it was printed as (CR 613). Five
hand-written ones read `cardDefs[...].typeLine`:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `destroyAnArtifactOrEnchantment` | Disenchant, Naturalize, Krosan Grip |
| Ainok Survivalist's turn-up | `target artifact or enchantment an opponent controls` |
| Wane | `target enchantment` |
| Awoken Horror's bounce | the `Horror` subtype |
| `artifactsControlled` | Galvanic Blast's metalcraft count |

`destroyAnArtifactOrEnchantment`'s docblock **said** it read the live line: "the type line is read
from `characteristicsOf` rather than from the printed line, so a creature that is *also* an artifact
is a legal target". The code did not. The claim happened to describe the behaviour for every artifact
creature in the pool, because all of them are *printed* as artifacts — which is why it lasted.

The difference shows the moment a continuous effect adds a type, which this engine has done since
Vehicles were crewed with `addTypes: ['Creature']`: a Disenchant could not touch a permanent that
*is* an artifact. Four of the five are now live and each has a test that fails when reverted —
a creature made an artifact, the same creature made an enchantment, and Galvanic Blast's third
artifact turning 1 damage into 4.

### What is not covered, and why, rather than left to be assumed

**Awoken Horror's `Horror` subtype ships without a discriminating test.** `PumpOptions.addTypes`
appends to `types`, not `subtypes` — probed, not assumed: `addTypes: ['Horror']` gives
`{types: ['Creature','Horror'], subtypes: ['Bear']}`, and `hasSubtype` reads `subtypes`. So nothing
in this engine can make a creature a Horror, and there is no board on which the two readings differ.
It is converted anyway because the fix is a **consistency** one inside a single expression: the line
above it already asks `characteristicsOf` for the live `isCreature`, and one expression reading the
live line for half its question and the print for the other half is how this class of bug starts.

### A sixth site, found while testing, and deliberately left printed

`conditionMet` in `characteristics.ts` — the metalcraft count that turns Chrome Steed's and Etched
Champion's conditional statics on — also reads the printed line, and its comment says "read live
like the artifact count below", which was wrong twice over.

It stays printed, because it is called **from inside `characteristicsOf`**: asking for a live type
line there would re-enter the whole computation for every other conditional effect on the board, and
two conditional effects reading each other's types would not terminate. That is a real rules gap —
a permanent *made* an artifact does not turn metalcraft on where CR 702.105a says it should — and it
is now written at both ends instead of being claimed away. Nothing in this pool can produce one.

So the two artifact counts genuinely differ: Galvanic Blast's is live, metalcraft's is printed. The
test that proves the live one says in as many words why it uses the spell and not the Steed.

### The guard caught the new test, which is the guard working

`scripts/guards.js` refused the gate: `liveTypes.test.ts` reads a card's `triggers` without reading
`grantedTriggers` (D251), and every such file either reads both or says why not. It reaches a trigger
only to get at Ainok Survivalist's **target spec**, and a granted trigger carries no target spec of
this card's — the spec belongs to whichever ability was handed over, on whichever permanent is
holding it. So it joins `EXEMPT` with that reason, which is the path the guard's own message names.

## D386

**The compiler had only ever seen 348 rows; it survives 240,000, and its memory is garbage rather than retention** (#317)

Every coverage figure in D331–D385 comes from one corpus: the engine's own pool, **348 rows**. #318
will hand the same readers tens of thousands. Two failures live in that gap and neither is visible at
348: a reader that throws on a line combination the pool does not contain, and a compiler that holds
every compilation until the process dies. Both would be discovered at the worst possible moment —
during the import that the whole corpus plan depends on.

`scripts/measure/compile-at-scale.mjs` asks the question early. Two arms, because one arm cannot
answer both halves:

| arm | rows | what it can find | what it cannot |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--repeat` (default) | the pool's 348 real rows, cloned with distinct names | pace, memory | a crash on text the pool never prints |
| `--shuffled` | printed lines resampled across the pool, the owner's name rewritten to the row's | a reader that throws on an unfamiliar neighbour | nothing about coverage — see below |

### The result

Six seeds of the shuffled arm at 30,000 rows and the repeat arm at 2,000/30,000/60,000 —
**240,000 rows compiled, zero throws.** Pace is 1,300–1,900 rows/s, so the entire commander-legal
corpus compiles in well under a minute, once rather than per game.

Memory looked like the real finding and was not. The 30,000-row repeat arm grew RSS by **495 MB**,
and CLAUDE.md starts the server with `node --max-old-space-size=768 server.js`, so a figure like that
would mean the corpus could not be compiled in the process that serves the game. The decisive run was
the same work under a cap tighter than the growth:

```
node --max-old-space-size=256 scripts/measure/compile-at-scale.mjs --rows 30000   # +108 MB, 1819 rows/s
node --max-old-space-size=256 scripts/measure/compile-at-scale.mjs --rows 60000   # +116 MB, 1889 rows/s
node --max-old-space-size=256 ... --shuffled --rows 30000 --seed 1                # +100 MB, 1309 rows/s
```

No OOM, the same pace, and the growth flat from 30,000 to 60,000 rows. So the 495 MB is garbage the
collector had no reason to reclaim on an unconstrained heap, not retention — the compiler holds
nothing per row. The number to carry forward is the capped one, because that is the condition the
server actually runs under.

### Zero throws is only worth the proof that a throw would show

A crash hunt reporting zero and a crash hunt that cannot report anything print the same line. So the
path was tested by planting a `throw` in the anthem reader and rebuilding: **14 throws over 3,000
rows**, each printed with the row that caused it. The first plant was narrowed to a `+2/+2` anthem and
reported **zero** — because the pool prints only `+1/+1` and `+1/+0`, so the reader was never reached.
That false green is exactly the failure mode being guarded against, and it is why the plant had to be
unconditional. `compileCard` does not swallow a reader's throw; the zero is a fact about the readers.

### What this script must never be read as saying

**No coverage figure from it means anything**, and it says so in its own output: the shuffled arm's
rows are real printed lines in combinations that are not any real card, so a share measured on them is
a share of nothing. Inventing the text of a real card is worse than leaving the mechanic out (D259),
and that rule is untouched here: nothing the script produces is ever turned into a shipped script, and
the only numbers it reports are pace, memory and crashes. The share stays `compilable.mjs`'s to print,
against real cards — still **316 of 538 lines (58.7%)**, unchanged by this increment.

`poolRows()` moved to `scripts/lib/pool-rows.mjs` so both harnesses convert the pool the same way;
`compilable.mjs` reports the same 348 rows and 316 lines after the move.

## D387

**The answers: a counter family, a sweeper, and a discard somebody else chooses** (#317)

Four openings in the work queue were the same shape — "counter target *something*" — and the
compiler read exactly one of them, the bare `counter target spell` that Counterspell and Cancel
print. The others went unread not because the engine could not do them but because the reader was an
exact sentence match rather than a family:

| printed | spec it needed |
| --- | --- |
| Counter target creature spell | `spell` + the creature filter |
| Counter target noncreature spell | `spell` + `isNoncreatureSpell` |
| Counter target activated ability | `ability` + `isActivatedAbility` |
| Counter target spell, activated ability, or triggered ability | `spell-or-ability` |

So the reader now takes an open target phrase, `counter (target .+)`, guarded by `pointsAtTheStack`
— the exact counterpart of `pointsAtAPermanent` on the destroy family, and needed for the same
reason: the regex will happily capture "target creature", `targetSpecFrom` will happily return a spec
for it, and the id of a permanent on the battlefield would then be handed to `counterSpell`. Two
synthetic sentences prove the refusal, and deleting the guard fails them.

**Every filter is the function the hand-written card already uses**, which is what makes the
ground-truth test an identity rather than a resemblance. `isCreatureSpell` was written inline on
Essence Scatter and is now named beside its opposite, because a second copy would be two filters free
to drift — one reading the live type line and the other the printed one is precisely the class of bug
D385 found five of. It matters most on Squelch: `kind: 'ability'` *without* the filter is a Squelch
that also answers triggered abilities, a strictly better card than the one printed, and only an
identical filter rules that out. Dropping the filter fails the test.

**Disallow's phrase is supplied, not captured** — the second place in the function where that
happens. The card prints three objects in a list; the spec that points at all three is described
"target spell or ability", which is what the hand-written card stores and what a player reads. Echoing
the printed list would mean teaching `targetSpecFrom` a fourth spelling of a spec it already has.

One effect serves all five readings, and it is Disallow's rather than Counterspell's: `counterSpell`
buries a spell's card and simply removes an ability, which is the difference the rules draw and the
only one there is, so the reading that handles both kinds of object is the one that generalises. For
a spell target it does exactly what `firstCardTarget` did.

### The sweeper, and the hint it deliberately does not carry

`Destroy all creatures` joins the untargeted sentences, not the destroy family: it points at nothing.
It also carries **no** `removesACreature`, and that is a decision rather than an omission. The flag
means "do not cast this with nothing of theirs to point at" — advice about a spell that needs a
target. A wrath needs none, and whether casting one is right is the *position*: right when behind,
catastrophic when ahead, which no flag can say and the bot's search sees by playing it out. Day of
Judgment, the ground truth, sets no flag either. A test pins both, with Murder as the control.

### The discard, which is the first clause read as a question rather than an effect

"Target player discards two cards" is `targets` **and** `decisions`, with `who: 'target-player'`. The
