tempting shortcut was `discardAtRandom`, which exists and is simpler — and would have built Ravenous
Rats and called it Mind Rot. `CardsDecisionSpec.who` names this card in its own docblock for exactly
that reason. The chooser is pinned by name as well as by equality with the hand-written card, because
an equality alone would follow the hand-written card if it ever changed too; switching it to
`controller` fails two tests.

The prompt echoes the printed count and its noun — "Discard two cards", "Discard a card" — rather
than being built from the number, which would say "Discard 1 cards". The pool pins the plural and a
synthetic row pins the singular.

### Measured

**316 → 323 of 538 printed lines (58.7% → 60.0%)**, and **199 → 205 of 339 cards** get a script:
Essence Scatter, Negate, Squelch (both its sentences, so the card compiles whole), Disallow, Day of
Judgment and Mind Rot. Each of the four new mechanisms was deliberately broken and each break fails a
test — the guard, the ability filter, the chooser, and the sweep. Two further 30,000-row shuffled runs
of `compile-at-scale.mjs` (D386) found no throw on the new readers.

**Psychic Strike is the near miss worth recording:** "Counter target spell. Its controller mills two
cards." Its first clause reads now; the second needs "its controller", which means the controller of
the object this spell is pointed at, and nothing in the clause vocabulary can say that yet. All or
nothing, so the card stays printed-only.

## D388

**Modal spells: a shape that is one sentence spread over several lines** (#317)

A charm's text is a header and a bullet per mode, and **no line of it means anything alone**: a
bullet without its header is a sentence the spell does not have, and a header without its bullets is
a question with no answers. So `modalScriptFor` is a whole-card shape read before `readResolution`
sees the lines — which it had to be, since the resolution reader would hand "Choose one —" to
`readEffect` as a clause, get null, and refuse the card without ever looking at the bullets.

Nothing here arranges the rules point; putting the reading in `modal` is what gets it. Modes are
chosen as the spell is **cast** (CR 601.2b), before targets, where an opponent can see the choice and
respond — reading a charm as a mid-resolution decision would let somebody counter it without knowing
what it was going to do.

### Whole or not at all, and the three cards that prove it

Selesnya Charm exiles a creature by power, Golgari Charm regenerates a team, Healing Salve prevents
damage: one bullet each that this module cannot read. All three are refused **entirely**, header and
all. Shipping the readable bullets as the card's modes would be a strictly different and better
spell, because `legalActions` offers one play per legal combination of modes — a charm missing its
third mode is a charm whose third mode nobody can choose, with nothing at the table to say so. The
refusal leaves every line flagged for a human to play by hand (D362), which is the whole point of
counting unread lines.

### Two headers, and the rest refused rather than guessed

"Choose one —" and "Choose one or both —" are what the pool prints and the only two read. "Choose
two", "choose the same mode more than once", entwine and escalate are each a different `min`/`max`,
and a header read as the wrong one is a card that takes the wrong number of modes. "Choose one"
leaves both off, which is what they default to and what Selesnya Charm stores; "one or both" is
`min: 1, max: 2` and is refused over anything but two modes.

### The one hint dropped, and the rest refused

`ModeDef` holds `expiresAtEndOfTurn` and `preventsDamage` and nothing else — the same shape a person
writing the card by hand has. Both travel from the bullet's reading onto that bullet's mode, which
matters: merging a pump's wear-off onto the *card* would tell the bot to hold a whole charm for the
combat when the rest of it is not a combat trick, and `ModeDef.expiresAtEndOfTurn` exists naming
Selesnya Charm for exactly that reason.

`removesACreature` is **dropped**, and the argument is structural rather than a judgement call:
`ModalDef` offers one play per legal combination of modes, and "a combination whose targets cannot be
filled is not offered at all", so a destroy mode is already unavailable on an empty board — which is
the whole of what that flag buys. Any **other** flag refuses the card, because no such argument
exists for it: `protectsACreature` is advice about *timing*, which no combination enforces, and a
silently dropped hint is a card that plays badly with nothing to flag it.

### Three filters that were four copies

`isCreatureSpell` had an inline copy on Essence Scatter (D387) and a second on Soul Manipulation;
Grim Discovery carried an inline graveyard-land spec. Both are now one shared function each, beside
`yourGraveyardCreature` — which is what makes the ground-truth test compare the real object rather
than a lookalike, and removes two more places where one copy could start reading the printed type
line while the other reads the live one (D385).

The graveyard return also became a two-type family, `return target (creature|land) card from your
graveyard to your hand`, with the type lower-cased into the supplied phrase. That is what lets Grim
Discovery compile at all.

### Measured

**323 → 329 of 538 printed lines (60.0% → 61.2%)**, and **205 → 207 of 339 cards**: Soul
Manipulation and Grim Discovery, mode for mode against the hand-written cards. Three deliberate
breaks — a loose header, skipping an unreadable bullet instead of refusing, and dropping the leftover
flag rule — each fail tests. A further 30,000-row shuffled run found no throw.

## D389

**Two burn spells could not point at a planeswalker, which their printed text allows** (#323)

Lava Spike prints "Lava Spike deals 3 damage to target player or planeswalker" and was scripted with
`TARGET_PLAYER`. So was Lava Axe. Neither could be aimed at a planeswalker at all, and this pool has
four of them — a player facing a Garruk could not Lava Axe it, which the card plainly permits.

The phrase is **`any target` with the creatures taken out** (CR 115.4 names the three; this phrase
names two), and the omission is the card rather than a detail: a one-mana three-damage spell is
printable precisely because it cannot kill a creature, and a five-mana five-damage one is playable
only to the face. So neither existing kind will do — `player` loses the planeswalker half, `any`
gains a creature the card may not touch — and the fix is a new `TargetSpec.kind`,
`player-or-planeswalker`, rather than a filter on an existing one.

It is three lines of `targeting.ts`: the player candidate is admitted, a battlefield candidate must
be a planeswalker, and `legalTargets` lists the seats as well as the permanents. Both cards now point
at the shared spec and resolve through `damageFirstTarget`, which hands the target straight to
`dealDamage` — the one path that turns damage on a planeswalker into lost loyalty (CR 120.3c). A
seat-shaped resolution could never reach it.

### The test, and both directions of it

A board with Jace Beleren on one side and a Monastery Swiftspear on the other: the creature is
refused ("that is not target player or planeswalker") and three damage to three loyalty puts Jace in
the graveyard (CR 704.5i). Reverting the card to `TARGET_PLAYER` fails the second half; deleting the
planeswalker-only line in `targeting.ts` fails the first, and also fails the older "Lava Spike deals
3 to a player only" test, which had been pinning half of this all along.

**Found while probing: the Swiftspear's prowess goes on the stack above the Spike**, so one round of
priority resolves the trigger and leaves the burn spell sitting there. The test uses `drain` and says
why, because the stack depth read 2 and a single `passBoth` would have made the test fail for a
reason that has nothing to do with targeting.

### And the compiler reads the phrase

`targetSpecFrom` gained the case, so `damageEffect` reads both cards straight off their printed line:
**329 → 331 of 538 lines (61.2% → 61.5%)**, 207 → 209 of 339 cards. The compiled spec is compared for
identity against the hand-written one, and a second test keeps "any target" and "target player or
planeswalker" distinct — which is the whole difference between a Lightning Bolt and a Lava Spike. A
30,000-row shuffled run found no throw.

## D390

**The drain and the edict: one effect joined by "and", and a question asked of everybody** (#317)

Two clause families, four pool cards, and both turn on a distinction the text makes in one word.

### The drain is one effect, not two clauses

"Each opponent loses 1 life and you gain 1 life" is joined by **and**, and `clausesOf` deliberately
does not split on that word — "gets +2/+2 and gains trample" is one effect too, and a splitter that
broke on "and" would cut that in half. So the drain is read whole and in printed order: lost first,
gained second, which is what all three hand-written drains do (Zulaport Cutthroat, Cruel Celebrant,
Blood Artist, plus Healing Salve's heal for the pointed form).

**The two numbers are read separately rather than assumed equal.** Every drain in this pool prints
the same number twice, so reading one of them twice would have passed every ground-truth test while
asserting a symmetry the text does not promise. A synthetic "loses 3 life and you gain 1 life" pins
it, and collapsing the two fails that test and nothing else — which is exactly why it had to be
written.

The tail is optional: "each opponent loses 2 life" with no gain is the same clause without its
second half, with its own test that nothing is gained.

The pointed form carries `friendly` on the heal and not on the drain, which is the clearest case in
this family for why the flag cannot be read off the target phrase: "target player" is the same two
words on both, and the bot's default is the enemy — so a heal without the flag is a Healing Salve
cast on the opponent.

### The edict is a question, and its `who` is the card

"Each player sacrifices a creature" is `decisions`, not an effect: `who: 'each-player'` expands into
one question each, asked in turn order from the active player (CR 101.4), which is sometimes the
whole card — the second player to sacrifice has seen what the first gave up. That ordering is why it
cannot be a reduce over seats inside the effect.

**"Each player" includes you and "each opponent" does not**, which is one word of the reader and a
completely different card — Fleshbag Marauder against an Eldest Reborn chapter. The two spellings are
captured rather than conflated, and forcing them both to `each-player` fails a test.

The filter is what decides *what* may be given up; without it a player answers an edict with a land.
It is compared against the hand-written filter on the same board, so both answers come from the same
objects, and deleting it fails.

### Measured, and one fixture moved

**331 → 335 of 538 printed lines (61.5% → 62.3%)**, and **209 → 213 of 339 cards**: Blood Artist,
Zulaport Cutthroat, Cruel Celebrant and Fleshbag Marauder. Four deliberate breaks, four failing
tests. A 30,000-row shuffled run found no throw.

The keyword-and-a-sentence test used "Each player sacrifices a creature." as its example of an
unreadable sentence, which this stage made readable — the second time that fixture has had to move
(it was a Fog before). Its comment now says so, and names the reason it owns its own text rather
than borrowing a card's: a sentence nothing reads *today* is a moving target, and the property being
tested is about the two kinds of unread line, not about any particular one. It is now "Exchange
control of two target creatures."

**Kambal stays unread, and the reason is worth keeping:** it prints "**that player** loses 2 life and
you gain 2 life", where "that player" is the opponent who cast the spell that triggered it
(`c.actor`). The subject is supplied by the *event*, not by the clause, and "that player" means
something different under a different trigger — so reading it here would be the compiler guessing
which event it is inside.

## D391

**The shrinking sweep, the combat filter, the untapper — and a sixth printed type line** (#317, #319)

Four readers, three cards, and one more instance of D385's class found by giving a mode a reading.

### Golgari Charm, which this file called "the card that was not scriptable"

Its own comment says so: "a modal card with one unscriptable mode is an unscriptable card, and the
mode was *regenerate each creature you control*." All three modes read now — a sweep that shrinks, a
typed destroy, and regenerating the team — so the compiler reads the card whole.

`All creatures get -1/-1 until end of turn` is **`pumpAll`, not `pumpTeam`**: "all creatures"
includes the caster's own, which is exactly what makes that mode a decision rather than a free sweep
and what the hand-written mode says. The sign is read off the print rather than assumed negative —
the same sentence with a plus is a mass anthem, `sizeBonus` handles either, and it still refuses
`+0/+0`. Hardcoding the minus fails a synthetic test and nothing else, which is why that test exists.

### The one filter that reads the combat

`target attacking or blocking creature` is Divine Verdict's phrase and the only filter in this module
that reads `state.combat` rather than the board. It was inline on the card; it is `attackingOrBlocking`
now, shared, so the compiled spec is the hand-written spec — function included — and the test is an
identity rather than a resemblance. A second test shows it refusing the only creature on a board where
nothing is attacking, so the phrase is narrow rather than decorative.

### The untapper, and the hint whose absence is a hang

`{T}: Untap another target permanent` reads, and it carries **`untapsOnly: true`**. That is not a
nicety: an ability whose whole effect is an untap can put the board back exactly where it found it, so
a bot that does not know can tap and untap for ever — the loop #124 was opened for. Dropping it is a
hang, not a missing hint.

`untapsOnly` lives on `AbilityDef` and nowhere else, so it cannot travel in `spellFlags`, whose type
is `Partial<CardScript>`. `ReadEffect` gained **`abilityFlags`** for it: a field belonging to one of
the three homes a clause has, declared for that home, and dropped by the other two exactly as
`spellFlags` already is. `friendly` rides on the spec, because untapping an opponent's land is a card
thrown away and the bot's default aim is the enemy's board — Kiora's Follower's own comment says that.

`pointsAtAPermanent` guards the open target phrase, as it does for destroy and bounce: "untap target
player" is refused rather than compiled into an untap pointed at a seat.

### The sixth printed type line (#319)

Golgari Charm's enchantment mode read `parseTypeLine(cardDefs[...].typeLine)` inline, so a permanent
*made* an enchantment was not a legal target for it. D385 found five of these and this is the sixth,
found the same way: by needing the compiled reading to match the hand-written one. It uses the shared
`permanentOfTypes` now, which also moved up the file — a module-level card builds its `targets` array
as the file is evaluated, so a filter it calls has to exist by then.

`liveTypes.test.ts` gained the case: a creature made an enchantment is a legal target for that mode
and is not one before. Reverting the filter fails it.

### Measured

**335 → 341 of 538 printed lines (62.3% → 63.4%)**, and **213 → 216 of 339 cards**: Golgari Charm,
Divine Verdict and Kiora's Follower. Five deliberate breaks, five failing tests — the dropped
`untapsOnly`, the ignored sign, regenerating the whole board, the dropped untap guard, and the
reverted type line. A 30,000-row shuffled run found no throw.

Golgari Charm also **left the modal refusal list**, where it was one of three cards proving "whole or
not at all" (D388). Two remain, and the test now says what to do if a later stage reads those too:
replace them with a synthetic bullet, for the reason the keyword-and-a-sentence fixture already owns
its own text.

**Icy Manipulator stays unread**, and it is the near miss: `{1}, {T}: Tap target artifact, creature,
or land.` Its phrase is a three-type union that `targetSpecFrom` does not have, and its filter also
refuses an already-tapped permanent and the Manipulator itself — none of which the printed phrase
says. Reading "tap target …" without that filter would offer the ability with nothing useful to point
at.

## D392

**Counts read off the board, and a correction: the landwalk "defect" was my probe** (#317, #324)

`tokenEffect`'s docblock named the gap: "`create X … tokens` — `countFrom` has no reading for `X`,
and the pool's two instances are a count read off the board, not the X chosen at cast time". Several
printed grammars want that same number, so `boardCount` reads it once and the grammars share it —
the same multiplying shape the trigger table and `composeEffects` were, with no new effect
vocabulary.

Five readings, each a function a hand-written card already used: lands you control, artifacts you
control, creature cards in your graveyard, +1/+1 counters on this, and creatures of a subtype.
`creaturesOfSubtype` was Krenko's `goblinCount` until this needed it, which is what keeps the ground
truth exact rather than approximate.

Wired into two grammars: `create X … tokens, where X is <count>` (the tail is stripped **before** the
token is read, because `with (.+)` is greedy and would swallow it) and `deals damage equal to <count
| its power>`.

**The counters read the snapshot first.** Chasm Skulker and Hangarback Walker count the counters they
had as they *died*, and by the time a death trigger resolves the card is in a graveyard with none
(CR 608.2h) — so `subjectCounters` wins where there is one and the live instance answers everywhere
else. Ignoring the snapshot fails two tests.

**The zero guard is the cards' own.** Krenko and Chasm Skulker both return the state untouched rather
than asking for no tokens, and Murderous Redcap deals nothing at power 0 — which for the body persist
returns is the normal case, since this pool's Redcap is a **1/1** and a −1/−1 counter makes it a 0/0.
A damage event of zero is a different thing from no event, so the guard is the card rather than
defensive programming.

**The plural is the one place this could be wrong rather than incomplete.** "Goblins" has to become
"Goblin" and "Elves" "Elf": `-ves → -f`, otherwise drop a trailing `s`, and **refuse anything that
does not end in `s`**. That gate is what keeps Fungi, Homunculi and Efreeti out — each would give a
subtype no creature has, and a count of zero is a card that resolves and does nothing, which is worse
than an unread line because an unread line is flagged for a human (D362). Both halves are tested.

### The correction: I reported a defect that was not one

I probed the Squid token with a hand-made state and read `landwalk: []`, and wrote it up as a
shipping defect: Chasm Skulker's Squids blockable by anyone with an Island. **That was wrong.** The
token has a `CardScript` found by its name carrying `statics: [{ scope: 'self', effect: { landwalk:
['Island'] } }]`, `scripts.test.ts:13264` pins it, and the comment above that script explains the
mechanism. My probe built a state with no scripts installed, so it was measuring a board that cannot
occur.

What the probe did find, once read correctly, is a real gap one level down: `KEYWORDS` has no
`islandwalk`, so `printedKeywords` can never return one, and before this `landwalk` was set **only**
by a continuous effect. A card with a script can declare one; a card that arrives from printed data
cannot, and the corpus #318 imports is unscripted by definition. So `printedLandwalk` now reads it
off the text with `printedKeywords`' own whole-line rule, the two scripted cards are redundant rather
than wrong and stay as they are, and the token reader's read-back check counts landwalk beside
keywords — which is what lets Chasm Skulker's Squid clause compile with the islandwalk it prints.

The lesson is the one this log keeps relearning from the other side: a probe that bypasses the path
under test measures something that cannot happen. A hand-made state with no scripts is exactly that.

### Measured

**341 → 344 of 538 printed lines (63.4% → 63.9%)**, and **216 → 217 of 339 cards**: Krenko, Chasm
Skulker and Murderous Redcap now read whole. Four deliberate breaks, four failing tests — the ignored
snapshot, a tribe count that counted every creature, the accepted irregular plural, and unread
printed landwalk. The whole engine suite is 1671 green, and a 30,000-row shuffled run found no throw.

One stale refusal row left `tokenEffect`'s list: "Create X … where X is …" is read now, and the "for
each" spelling of the same count remains, since that grammar puts the count after the token rather
than in a `where X is` tail.

## D393

**Loyalty abilities, and a number word nobody had printed before** (#317)

A planeswalker's line is an activated ability with a cost that is a **number** rather than a list of
components: `+1`, `0`, `−3`. So the cost parse takes it before the component loop, which has no
`{T}` and no mana to classify on such a line, and `AbilityCost.loyalty` is a field rather than a
component because it carries its own restrictions — sorcery speed, once a turn, controller only.

**The minus is U+2212, not a hyphen.** A real card prints the typographic minus, and reading it as a
plus would make a planeswalker that gains loyalty for its ultimate instead of paying it. Both
spellings are read; the pool prints only the typographic one, so the hyphen is pinned by a synthetic
card, and collapsing the sign fails two tests.

Two clause readers came with it, because the pool's planeswalkers are mostly made of clauses the
compiler already had:

- `each player draws N cards` — symmetrical, the opponent included, eliminated seats skipped. That
  *is* Jace Beleren's +2: a reader that drew only for the controller would be a strictly better
  Divination, and the test asserts both hands.
- `you draw a card`, which is the same sentence as `draw a card` spelled the long way.

### The word that was missing

`WORD_NUMBERS` stopped at ten, and Jace Beleren's `−10: Target player mills twenty cards` went
unread for want of one row while the two lines around it compiled. Eleven through twenty's round
numbers are added — and nothing beyond, because a word nobody prints is a row nobody can test. The
mill test asserts **twenty**, since ten would pass a reader that stopped at the word it knew.

### Measured

**344 → 353 of 538 printed lines (63.9% → 65.6%)**, and **217 → 222 of 339 cards**. Jace, Memory
Adept and Jace Beleren now compile **whole** — the first planeswalkers the compiler reads end to
end.

Garruk Wildspeaker is the test for the hybrid this exists to produce: his `−1` reads, his `+1`
(untap two target lands) and his `−4` (a team pump with a keyword grant) do not, so one ability is
automated and the two unread lines are reported for a human to play by hand (D362). Nissa and Ajani
are the same shape, each one line short.

Three deliberate breaks, three failing tests. The whole engine suite is 1678 green and a 30,000-row
shuffled run found no throw.

## D394

**The grant family widened — and the hint the team pump had been dropping** (#317)

Three readings, four cards, and one defect found by needing the compiled card to match the written
one.

### The defect: a compiled Inspired Charge was never held for the combat

`expiresAtEndOfTurn` means "hold this for the combat", and both hand-written cards of this shape set
it — Inspired Charge and Overrun. The compiled team pump **did not**, so a compiled Inspired Charge
was a card that works and gets cast in a main phase with nothing to attack with. That is D364's trap
in the one clause family whose *targeted* twin already carried the flag, and no rules test could see
it: nothing in the engine reads it, the bot does.

### Two keywords, as one continuous effect

`grantedKeywordList` reads "gains trample" and "gains flying and double strike" alike, one or two
words joined by "and", each gated by `isKeyword` — the engine's keyword list is what
`characteristicsOf` consults, so a word outside it compiles to a creature that gains nothing and a
spell that looks like it worked. "Soaring" (made up), "protection from red" (a real ability this
engine stores in another field) and a list of three are each refused and reported unread.

Both halves travel in one `PumpOptions`, which is how Ajani's ultimate is written by hand and why it
matters: two continuous effects would expire independently.

### A grant with no size is its own sentence

"Target creature gains flying and double strike until end of turn" gets its own branch rather than
an optional size on the pump, because `sizeBonus` refuses `+0/+0` and should go on refusing it — a
clause that pumped by nothing would be a continuous effect doing nothing. The two bot hints are
decided by exactly the rule the sized branch uses (hexproof/shroud make it a protection trick,
infect/haste make it an attacker's bonus), and the branches sit adjacent so that stays one rule
rather than two.

### Measured

**353 → 356 of 538 printed lines (65.6% → 66.2%)**, and **222 → 225 of 339 cards**: Overrun,
Inspired Charge and Ajani, Caller of the Pride now compile whole — Ajani being the third planeswalker
read end to end. Garruk Wildspeaker is one line short: `+1: Untap two target lands`, a count on a
target phrase this module cannot read.

Three deliberate breaks, three failing tests. The whole engine suite is 1686 green and a 30,000-row
shuffled run found no throw.

Garruk's `−4` left the loyalty stage's refusal test one increment after joining it, which is the
churn that kind of test is for: the property is "a line with no reader is reported and its neighbours
still compile", not any particular line, and the test now says so.

## D395

**Every planeswalker in the pool, read end to end — and a seventh printed type line** (#317, #319)

Three readings, and with them all five planeswalkers compile whole. That is worth saying as its own
result because a planeswalker is the shape most likely to compile *partly*: three or four
independent abilities, so a card three quarters read is the hybrid D362 describes rather than a
finished reading.

- **A counted target.** "Untap two target lands" is the pool's only `TargetSpec.count`, and the
  engine fills the list before resolution — so the effect reduces over `cardTargets` rather than
  taking the first, and the description stays the singular phrase, because that is what a player is
  asked for each time and what the hand-written spec stores. Dropping the count untaps one land and
  is a worse card.
- **Counters on the team**, which is Nissa's `−2` and emphatically not an Overrun: her own comment
  says why — counters stay, they stack with the next activation, and a sweeper that kills everything
  else leaves the survivor bigger. So `addCounters` per creature, nothing added to `effects`, and
  only the controller's creatures. The compiled reader and the hand-written effect came out as
  byte-identical code, which is how a break attempt found its anchor matched twice.
- **A count announced in the clause's own tail**: "You gain X life and draw X cards, where X is the
  number of lands you control" — the one place in the pool where the same announced count is spent
  twice in one sentence. Gain before draw, which is the printed order and matters on an empty
  library: a player who gains the life and then cannot draw has still gained the life.

### The seventh site (#319)

Garruk's `+1` filter read `parseTypeLine(cardDefs[...].typeLine)`, so a Mutavault animated into a
creature — still a land (CR 613) — was not a legal target for it. Found exactly as the sixth was: by
giving the line a compiler reading and needing the two specs to agree. It uses the shared
`permanentOfTypes('land')` now, with its own case in `liveTypes.test.ts` that fails when reverted.

### The refusal test moved to a synthetic, and this time for good

That test was written against Garruk, listing his `−4` as unread; the next increment read it, and
this one read his `+1`, leaving no pool planeswalker with an unread line. The property it pins is
"**a loyalty line with no reader is reported and its neighbours still compile**" — not any
particular card — so it now owns its text: a synthetic walker whose first ability is a sentence this
module has no reader for, with the other two still read in printed order. Same reasoning as the
keyword-and-a-sentence fixture, which has now moved twice for the same reason.

### Measured

**356 → 359 of 538 printed lines (66.2% → 66.7%)**; cards with a script unchanged at **225 of 339**,
because Garruk and Nissa were already partly read — what changed is that they are now read *whole*,
which the share of lines is the honest instrument for and the share of cards is not.

Four deliberate breaks, four failing tests. The whole engine suite is 1696 green and a 30,000-row
shuffled run found no throw.

## D396 — The same count, written the other way round: "for each", in the singular

Magic writes one count in two grammars, and until now the compiler read one of them:

- `, where X is the number of <things>` — the count is announced in a tail and the sentence's own
  number is the letter X. Krenko and Chasm Skulker print this; D392 read it.
- ` for each <thing>` — the count is a multiplier and the sentence's own number is "a", one per
  thing. Izoni and Lotleth Giant print this, and **the noun is singular**.

`tokenEffect`'s docblock listed those as two separate missing bullets. They are one gap: the count,
not the sentence. So `boardCount` split into `boardCount` (the announced tail) and `forEachCount`
(the per-thing one) over a shared `countOfThing(thing, name, 'plural' | 'singular')`, and every row
of the vocabulary now accepts either spelling — "lands you control" and "land you control" are the
same set.

### Why the grammatical number is a parameter and not a guess

Exactly one row reads differently in the two grammars: a **creature subtype**.

- The plural ("the number of Goblins you control") has to derive the singular the engine spells:
  `-ves` → `-f`, otherwise drop the trailing `s`, and **refuse a word that does not end in `s`** —
  which is what keeps Fungi, Homunculi and Efreeti out. A derived "Fungu" is a subtype no creature
  has, so the card would resolve and count zero.
- The singular ("for each Goblin you control") takes the word **as printed** and derives nothing.
  Stripping a letter here would turn "Homunculus" into "Homunculu", with the same result.

So each grammar takes only the spelling it actually prints, and the pair is tested together: the
pool's one Homunculus (Aeromunculus) makes the singular reading's answer **one** where the plural
rule's answer would be none, and `the number of Homunculi you control` is still refused outright.
The refusal and the acceptance sit in adjacent tests so neither can quietly become the other.

### The drain, read before the flat one

`Each opponent loses 1 life for each creature card in your graveyard` — Lotleth Giant, whose whole
card is that line — had to be read **before** the flat `each opponent loses N life`, because the flat
form is its prefix. A reader in the other order would drain one life per opponent and ignore the
graveyard: a card that works and is wrong, which is this file's commonest failure shape and the one
hybrid automation cannot flag, because nothing is unread.

No zero guard, deliberately: `loseLife` refuses a non-positive amount and returns the state it was
handed, so an empty graveyard already drains nothing, and a guard would be a branch no test could
tell from its absence. The hand-written Giant has no guard either, so the two read identically at
zero — which is asserted rather than assumed.

The printed amount is multiplied by the count. The pool cannot tell `each * counted` from `counted`
because Lotleth Giant's amount is 1, so a synthetic "loses 2 life for each" is what makes the
multiplication the thing under test.

### What a per-thing token clause may not say

`Create **two** 1/1 tokens for each creature card` is a real sentence with a real meaning this
reader does not implement, so the printed count is required to be `a`/`an`/`one` (and `x` for the
announced grammar) and anything else is refused. An unread line is dealt to a human (D362); a halved
one is not.

### Measured, and a drift in the log corrected

**359 → 361 of 538 printed lines (66.7% → 67.1%)**, and **223 → 225 of 339 cards**: Lotleth Giant is
read whole, Izoni's ETB line is read with her activated ability left for a human.

The card figure needs a correction. D395 recorded "unchanged at 225 of 339"; re-measured on the
clean commit it was **223**, so the running count in the log had drifted two ahead of the
instrument. The figures above are from `compilable.mjs` on `ce7b254` clean and on the same tree
dirty, and the per-card verbose output of the two was diffed: Izoni and Lotleth Giant are the only
two cards that moved, so nothing regressed to pay for them.

Eight deliberate breaks, eight failing tests — the plural rule applied to the singular grammar and
each way round, the dropped multiplier, the drain read after the flat form, the token tail not
stripped, the printed count widened to accept "two", and the creature-card row narrowed to the
plural. 11,000 rows at scale (two shuffled, one repeat) found no throw. The engine suite is green,
and all four browser suites pass on this engine: table 76/76, arena 53/53 with 7 named skips, pod
41/41 with 1, solo 28/28 with 1.

## D397 — Counters a permanent arrives with, and the one word that narrows a death trigger

Two readers, both for fields the engine has had all along.

### The arrival sentence

`entersWith` existed and three keywords already built it — modular, vanishing and fading each declare
a count — but the **printed sentence** went unread. So Endless One, whose whole card is
"Endless One enters the battlefield with X +1/+1 counters on it", was a `printed-only` card for a
field that was already there and already tested.

It is its own reader in `lineScriptFor`'s chain rather than a clause: a permanent entering with
counters is a replacement effect applied as it arrives (CR 614.1c), never resolved and never on the
stack. The count is `X` (which `entersWith` spells `'x'`, resolving to zero for a permanent that
arrived any other way), a number, or a number-word.

**The counter kinds are an allow-list — `+1/+1`, `charge`, `ice` — and that is the one refusal here
about correctness rather than coverage.** A kind is a key in a plain record, so an unknown one would
be stored and read by nothing; for those three that is the printed card, because +1/+1 counters are
read by `characteristicsOf` and the charge and ice counters are read by another line of the same
card, which is read or unread on its own merits. `time` and `fade` are refused: their behaviour does
not live in the counters at all but in the trigger vanishing and fading put on the card, so a
sentence read on its own would lay a countdown on a permanent with nothing counting it down — a
creature that should leave the battlefield and never does, which is strictly better than the print.
D364's rule again: the unit of compilation is both halves or neither.

### The nontoken death

`Whenever a nontoken creature you control dies` — Judith, the Scourge Diva — and the sentence turns
on two words that a copied shape gets wrong in opposite directions:

- `who: 'any'`, **not** `'another'`: Judith is a nontoken creature you control, so she triggers on
  her own death. Her hand-written script says so in as many words.
- `nontoken: true`: without it every token her own deck makes would ping something on the way out.

Both are asserted as fields as well as compared against the hand-written trigger, because a pair
differing by one string is where a passing deep-equality hides two rows coming from one branch —
the same reasoning as D381's two static scopes.

Judith now compiles **whole**: her anthem was already read (D381) and this was her other line, which
is why the test asserts the merged script carries both rather than trusting the unread count.

### A fixture defect found on the way, and deliberately left (#325)

Chalice of the Void, Walking Ballista and Hangarback Walker each keep their **whole card on one
`oracleText` line**, abilities separated by ". " where the printed card uses newlines. So all three
arrive as a single line and every ability goes unread — including two sentences this increment can
now read. The real Scryfall text for all three uses newlines, so this is a transcription defect in
the pool's fixtures rather than a compiler gap, and the corpus will not have it.

Not fixed in this pass on purpose: inserting newlines changes what `printedRulesLines` and
`printedKeywords` see for cards that also have hand-written scripts, so it needs its own
verification run; and it would move the coverage share, which would conflate "the compiler reads
more" with "the fixtures were corrected". Two numbers worth keeping separable. Filed as #325 with
the rejected alternative written down — splitting a permanent's line on sentence boundaries — since
a sentence is not an ability ("When ~ dies, create a token. Then draw a card." is one) and the
corpus never needs it.

### Measured

**361 → 363 of 538 printed lines (67.1% → 67.5%)**, and **225 → 226 of 339 cards**: Endless One and
Judith both whole. The per-card output was diffed against the previous run, and those two are the
only cards that moved.

Six deliberate breaks, six failing tests: the reader out of the chain, the allow-list widened to
admit fade and time, every count read as X, word numbers not read, the nontoken death read as
`another`, and the `nontoken` flag dropped. 4,000 more rows at scale, no throw. compile.test.ts
257/257, gate green.

## D398 — A clause joined by "and", and an invariant that cannot be observed from outside

`clausesOf` splits a printed line on the full stop and on `, then `, deliberately **not** on "and"
(D387), because "and" is most often *inside* one clause rather than between two: "target creature
gets +2/+2 **and** gains trample" is a single `pump` with a keyword in it, and "you gain X life
**and** draw X cards" is one announced count spent twice. Splitting those would make two continuous
effects that expire independently, and two counts where the card prints one.

So the conjunction is read as a **fallback**: `conjoinedEffect` sits last in `readEffect`'s chain and
sees only clauses all four readers have already refused. What is left over is the genuine sequence —
"you draw a card and you lose 1 life", Phyrexian Arena, whose whole card is that line — and
`composeEffects` already has the right invariants for it: all or nothing, and at most one half may
point at something.

### The guard that could not be written, which is the finding

The ordering protects an invariant worth stating: *a conjunction an earlier reader understands as one
clause keeps that reading*. The obvious guard is a sweep over every printed clause with an "and" in
it, asking whether both readings can read it. **That sweep cannot be written from outside the
compiler**, because `compileCard` does not say which reader read a clause: once the fallback exists,
"reads whole" includes the fallback, so every split-readable clause is also whole-readable and the
sweep reduces to "the fallback exists".

Three versions of it were written before that was clear, each one wrong in its own way and each one
found by planting a reader and watching the sweep stay green:

1. The first compiled every clause under a **stand-in card name**, so any clause naming its own
   source ("Judith, the Scourge Diva deals 1 damage to any target") could not be read at all. A
   sweep that found nothing, and would have gone on finding nothing for ever.
2. The second kept the **trigger's prologue**, so it was asking whether an instant could be read
   from "At the beginning of your upkeep, you draw a card and you lose 1 life" — always no, for a
   reason with nothing to do with the conjunction.
3. The third was correct about both and still tautological, for the reason above.

That is the third time in this file a check has turned out unable to fail (D386's planted throw,
D394's dropped hint), and the first time the right answer was to **delete it and say so** rather
than to fix it.

### What is observable, and so what is tested

The sweep's one useful output was its list. The pool prints exactly **four** conjunctions both
readings can reach: Zulaport Cutthroat and Cruel Celebrant ("each opponent loses 1 life and you gain
1 life"), Phyrexian Arena, and Tatyova ("draw a card and you gain 1 life", behind a prologue nothing
reads yet). For the ones with a hand-written script to compare against, **the two readings agree** —
which is the real reason the ordering is safe on this pool rather than merely argued, and the reason
no test can tell them apart. That agreement is asserted against the hand-written card.

The hazard the ordering guards is therefore a *future* single reader that disagrees with the split on
the same sentence. Nothing in the suite would catch that, and the test says so in as many words,
which is better than a test that looks like it would.

### Measured

**363 → 364 of 538 printed lines (67.5% → 67.7%)**, and **226 → 227 of 339 cards**: Phyrexian Arena,
whose one line this reads. The full verbose output was diffed against the previous run and exactly
one line changed — which is the structural claim as well as the measurement, since the fallback can
only fire where every other reader returned null.

Five deliberate breaks, five failing tests (compose only the first half, allow two targeting halves,
the drain reader dropping its gain half, the fallback removed, and the planted single reader that
proved the discarded sweep could not fail). 4,000 more rows at scale, no throw. compile.test.ts
264/264.

## D399 — The X a spell was cast for, as a spell shape rather than a clause

Three cards whose whole resolution is a sentence spending X: **Fireball** ("deals X damage to any
target"), **Savage Twister** ("deals X damage to each creature") and **Mind Spring** ("Draw X
cards"). All three have hand-written scripts, so all three are ground truth rather than guesses.

### Why this is not a row in the clause vocabulary

X is chosen as the spell is cast and paid for then (CR 601.2b), so by the time the effect runs `c.x`
is a settled number — **on a spell**. On anything else it is zero: a triggered or activated ability's
stack object carries no X, and `automation.ts` fills the context with `object.x ?? 0`.

So a clause reader that understood bare `X` would quietly produce a card that **works and does
nothing** the first time the same sentence appeared in a trigger. That is the failure this module is
most careful about, because nothing is left unread for a human to notice (D362). Keeping the reading
in `readResolution`, above `composeEffects`, makes it impossible by construction rather than by a
rule somebody has to remember — the same argument that keeps `spellFlags` on the spell path.

It is tested the only way that counts: a synthetic creature printing "When ~ enters the battlefield,
draw X cards" is **refused**, and planting the same reading in the clause vocabulary turns that test
red.

### One clause, deliberately

Every X card in the pool whose resolution is readable is a single sentence, and the multi-clause case
is refused rather than half read. Exsanguinate is why: "Each opponent loses X life. **You gain life
equal to the life lost this way**" — the second sentence does not spend X at all, it reads the life
actually lost, which at a pod is X times the number of opponents. A reader that took the first
sentence and stopped would be a drain with its lifegain silently dropped.

Named as still unread so the next pass has somewhere to start: `Create X … tokens` (Secure the
Wastes), which belongs with `tokenEffect`'s count rather than here, and that second drain sentence.

### Three small readings taken from the hand-written cards rather than invented

- **No zero guard on the targeted burn.** `dealDamage` refuses a non-positive amount, so a Fireball
  cast for zero deals nothing without a branch saying so — and the hand-written Fireball has no
  guard either. The sweep *does* guard, because its own hand-written script does: a Twister cast for
  zero is no event rather than a damage event of zero to every creature.
- **The sweep is every creature, the caster's own included**, which is the card and the reason it is
  not a target.
- **`drawLater`, not `draw`**, which is Mind Spring's hand-written reading: cards the controller is
  *owed* arrive as moves they make, so a player drawing their last cards can act between them.

### Measured

**364 → 367 of 538 printed lines (67.7% → 68.2%)**, and **227 → 230 of 339 cards**: the three cards
above, confirmed by the per-card diff as the only ones that moved.

Five deliberate breaks, five failing tests: X read as one, the sweep narrowed to the caster's
creatures, the X draw taken instead of owed, the one-clause rule dropped, and the planted clause
reader that proved the spell-path restriction is tested. 5,000 more rows at scale, no throw.
compile.test.ts 270/270.

The live game is untouched by all of this: a hand-written script wins over a compiled one, so every
card in the pool still plays exactly as it did. What changes is what the compiler can do with a card
nobody has written a script for, which is the corpus.

## D400 — X tokens, and one parser for the token a clause names

Secure the Wastes: "Create X 1/1 white Warrior creature tokens", an instant, which is the X card
D399 named as still unread and said belonged with `tokenEffect`'s count rather than with the burn.

It belongs with **both**, which is why this is a refactor and not a fourth regex. The token's
*definition* — "1/1 white Warrior creature token", or "1/1 colorless Thopter artifact creature token
with flying" — is the same parse wherever the count comes from, and that parse is not small: colour
words taken from the front, the optional "artifact", a capitalised subtype, and the keyword
read-back that asks `printedKeywords` whether the engine can read back the text about to be written
down. A second copy of it would be a second place for the same sentence to be read differently.

So `tokenFrom(body)` returns `{ token, printed }` — the definition, and **the count word unread** —
and the two callers make sense of the word:

- `tokenEffect` accepts a number or a number-word; `X` with a `where X is` tail is a board count
  (D392), and `a … for each` is the per-thing count (D396).
- `xSpellResolution` accepts `X` alone, which is the cast's X, and only on the spell path for the
  reason D399 sets out: a trigger's stack object carries no X.

The refactor was made first and verified to change nothing — 270 tests green before the new reading
was added — so the coverage move is attributable to the reading and not to the shuffle.

The zero guard is Secure the Wastes' own hand-written one, and the equality test against that script
compares the **whole token definition**, so a compiled Warrior of the wrong colour or size fails
there rather than in a count.

### Measured

**367 → 368 of 538 printed lines (68.2% → 68.4%)**, and **230 → 231 of 339 cards**: Secure the
Wastes, the only card the per-card diff shows moving.

Three deliberate breaks, three failing tests: the X count read as one, the zero guard dropped, and
the printed-`X` requirement dropped (which would hand the cast's X to a token clause that printed a
number). 4,000 more rows at scale, no throw. compile.test.ts 273/273.

## D401 — Statics that come and go, and the ability word in front of them

Four cards, and the thing they have in common is a word that means nothing.

### The conditional static

`PumpOptions.while` has exactly two kinds, and this reads the English of both:

- **"as long as you control three or more artifacts"** → `controller-artifacts`, which is
  metalcraft. The pool prints it on a size (Chrome Steed, "gets +2/+2") and on a grant (Etched
  Champion, "has protection from all colors").
- **"as long as ~ is monstrous"** → `source-has-counter`, because being monstrous *is* a +1/+1
  counter on the creature itself in this engine (D182). That is the modelling the hand-written
  Fleecemane Lion uses, not a reading invented here — which matters, because compiling a condition
  to an approximation nobody had chosen would be exactly the kind of quiet wrongness D259 is about.

"Protection from all colors" is the five-colour list and not a special case: protection is already a
list (D83), so all five is what the card says and every rule protection has applies with nothing
new. The hand-written Etched Champion stores the same five.

Refused, each for a stated reason: **any threshold but three** (every metalcraft card printed says
"three or more", so a different number is a different card and reading it as metalcraft would turn a
static on at the wrong time); **a keyword `isKeyword` cannot read** (a creature that looks protected
and is not); and **a conditional protection from one colour**, which is coverage rather than
correctness — `protectionFrom` is a list so it is expressible, but no card in the pool prints it, and
a reader with no card behind it is a reader nothing has ever run (D57).

### The ability word

"Metalcraft —" and "Battalion —" are **flavour with no rules meaning** (CR 207.2c): the word names a
pattern for players and the sentence after the dash is the whole ability. So `withoutAbilityWord`
drops it, and both `staticFromLine` and `triggerFromLine` call it before reading what is left.

It is a **named list** — `metalcraft`, `battalion` — and not a general "capitalised word then a
dash". The general form would also eat a saga's chapter markers and anything else printed with an em
dash, and a line mis-split is a line read *wrongly* rather than refused. The list grows with the
cards that need it, and a test pins the decision: the same sentence behind an unknown ability word is
refused, while the bare sentence and the known word read identically.

With the word off the front, **Firemane Avenger** compiles whole: `{ kind: 'attacks', withAtLeast: 3 }`
is "this and at least two other creatures", which the hand-written card spells the same way, and its
body — "deals 3 damage to any target **and** you gain 3 life" — is read by D398's conjunction reader
inside a trigger. Two increments meeting on one card, which is the first time that has happened.

### Measured

**368 → 372 of 538 printed lines (68.4% → 69.1%)**, and **231 → 235 of 339 cards**. Chrome Steed,
Etched Champion and Firemane Avenger whole; Fleecemane Lion a hybrid, its monstrosity ability still
unread. The per-card diff shows those four and nothing else.

Seven deliberate breaks, seven failing tests: the threshold read as two, the condition dropped from
the size static, protection read as one colour, monstrous read as a board count, the ability-word
list opened up, battalion counting two attackers, and the ability word left on the trigger. 4,000
more rows at scale, no throw. compile.test.ts 282/282.

## D402 — A size that is a count, and the creature that sacrifices itself

Two readers, four cards, and one of them is the sharpest case of D364's rule the file has.

### The characteristic-defining ability (CR 604.3)

`definesSize` has exactly two counts and the pool prints exactly two cards: Lhurgoyf's power is the
creature cards in *all* graveyards with its toughness one higher, and Enigma Drake's power is the
instants and sorceries in *your* graveyard with its toughness printed. The counts are **named** in
`definesSize` rather than written as a vocabulary (D57), so the reader takes the two phrases the pool
prints and refuses the rest: "the number of cards in your hand" is a real Magic card and not a count
the engine can take, and compiling it as one of the two it does have would be a creature of the wrong
size every turn with nothing flagged.

The two shapes are one sentence with an optional tail. "and its toughness is equal to that number
plus N" present → the count defines **both** (`applies` left at its default) with `toughnessPlus`;
absent → the **power** only. Those are precisely the two hand-written scripts, and the test reads the
live creature as well as comparing the data: a Lhurgoyf with two creature cards in a graveyard is a
2/3, which a reader with the wrong count or no count could not produce.

### The end-step sacrifice, which is one line and two halves

"At the beginning of the end step, sacrifice ~" — Ball Lightning and Hellspark Elemental — is read
as a **whole-line shape**, not a prologue plus a clause, and the reason is the flag:
`leavesAtEndOfTurn`. Both hand-written cards carry it with the same comment — *the trigger below is
what happens, and the flag is how the bot knows it is coming; without it the evaluation holds the
creature back to protect it.* The trigger alone is a correct rules implementation and a badly played
card, which is the failure hybrid automation cannot flag because nothing is unread.

It cannot be a clause reader either, and that is the other half of the argument: "sacrifice ~" behind
a different prologue does not mean the permanent leaves at *end of turn*. So the pair is read
together and "Whenever ~ attacks, sacrifice ~" is refused — a sibling test keeps that true.

`of: 'any'` and not `of: 'you'`: "the end step" is every player's, which is what kills a Ball
Lightning cast on somebody else's turn.

### A refusal test that became an acceptance

`compile.test.ts` already had a test named *does not read "sacrifice ~", because the flag belongs to
the shape and not the clause* — written by the increment that deliberately left this unread. The
property it pinned has not changed; what changed is how it is expressed, from "the line is left
unread" to "the line is read and emits both halves". So it was rewritten rather than deleted, with
the churn and the reasoning in it, which is the fourth test in this file to move for that reason.

### Measured

**372 → 376 of 538 printed lines (69.1% → 69.9%)**, and **235 → 239 of 339 cards**. Lhurgoyf, Enigma
Drake and Ball Lightning whole; Hellspark Elemental a hybrid with its unearth still unread. The
per-card diff shows those four and nothing else.

Six deliberate breaks, six failing tests: the flag dropped, the end step read as the controller's
own, "your end step" accepted as well, the CDA toughness bonus dropped, the power-only case read as
both, and an unknown count defaulted instead of refused. 4,000 more rows at scale, no throw.
compile.test.ts 291/291.

## D403 — A word that stands for a sentence, mana out of a trigger, and damage divided

Three readers, five cards, and a dropped bot hint the coverage diff caught.

### Investigate

One word standing for text the card does not print: create a colourless Clue artifact token with
"{2}, Sacrifice this artifact: Draw a card" (CR 701.33a). The reading is a **call** to the engine's
own `CLUE_TOKEN`, a definition D243 wrote and tested, rather than a transcription — which is the only
safe way to read a word like that, because writing the token's text here would be inventing the text
of a real card (D259).

### Mana out of a trigger

"Add {R}{G}" — Burning-Tree Emissary's whole ability — and "Add {B}{B}{B}", which is Dark Ritual.

The **regex is the validation**: it admits only the six symbols `addToPool` takes, so `{E}` is not
read as mana and `{2}` — generic mana, which a *cost* has and a pool does not hold — refuses the
clause. An earlier draft also ran `parseManaCost` over the matched string, which could not fail; it
was deleted, because this file has caught itself writing that three times already (D386, D394, D398).

### The dropped hint, found by the diff rather than by a test

Dark Ritual started compiling as a **side effect** of the add-mana clause — it was not in the
increment's plan — and it arrived without `makesMana`, the bot hint whose absence makes the search
cast a Ritual into nothing (#63). A card that works and plays badly, for the third time (D364, D394),
and the per-card coverage diff is what surfaced it: five cards moved where three were expected.

The fix is `spellFlags: { makesMana: true }`, and the carrier is the whole answer. `spellFlags` reach
the spell path only, so one reader gets both cards right: Dark Ritual's resolution applies the flag,
and Burning-Tree Emissary's ETB trigger drops it — which is that card's own rule, with its own
measurement in its own comment (46% of copies cast with the flag against 101% without, because a 2/2
for two is worth casting on its own).

And one more rule, in `composeEffects`: `makesMana` **does not survive composition**. The field is
for a spell whose *whole* effect is mana; one that adds mana and draws a card has a visible effect, so
the hint would hold it back for a follow-up it does not need. Nothing in the pool prints that pair,
so the deletion is there for the first card that does.

### Damage divided as you choose (#119)

"Arc Lightning deals 3 damage divided as you choose among one, two, or three targets" — **two numbers
out of one sentence, and they are not the same number.** `divided` is the damage to share out;
`count` is how many targets may be chosen, which the card spells as a list of counts. Pyromatics is
what proves they are read separately: "1 damage divided as you choose among one or two targets" is
`divided: 1, count: 2`.

Every word in that list has to be a number, and that check needed its own test row. Dropping it still
refuses "among any number of targets" — nothing there is a number, so the maximum is zero and a
separate guard refuses it — but it quietly accepts "among **two or many** targets", reading a card
whose list it did not understand. The row that catches it was added after a break run passed.

`optional: true` because the lower numbers in the list are real choices, and the effect is
`dividedAmong`, which is one `dealDamage` per target with its own share: each is a separate dealing
of damage from the same source (CR 601.2d), so protection, prevention and deathtouch are each asked
about separately. Both hand-written cards are written that way, and the test asserts two and one
rather than three and three.

### Measured

**376 → 381 of 538 printed lines (69.9% → 70.8%)**, and **239 → 243 of 339 cards** — past seventy per
cent. Thraben Inspector, Burning-Tree Emissary, Arc Lightning and Dark Ritual whole, Pyromatics too
(its replicate was already read). The per-card diff named all five, which is how the Dark Ritual
defect was found.

Seven deliberate breaks, seven failing tests: investigate making a Treasure, only the first mana
symbol added, the mana regex admitting generic, the divided count read off the damage, the division
ignored so each target takes the whole amount, the `makesMana` hint dropped, and the composition
keeping it. 9,000 more rows at scale, no throw. compile.test.ts 301/301.

## D404 — A target chosen by power, read live, and the exile that is not a destruction

Two cards, and the increment is mostly about **when** a filter asks its question.

### The threshold, and the number read off the card

Selesnya Charm's second mode exiles a creature with power **5** or greater; Hidden Dragonslayer's
turned-face-up trigger destroys one an opponent controls with power **4** or greater. A reader that
fixed either number would make one of the two point at creatures its own print excludes, so the
number is read from the phrase — and that needed a test the first draft did not have. Two is below
both thresholds and six is above both, so the obvious board cannot tell four from five; a break run
that pinned the threshold at four passed. The row that catches it is a creature at **exactly four**,
refused by the charm's five.

### Live power, which is #319 in a new place

`permanentFilter` gained `powerAtLeast`, and it asks `characteristicsOf` rather than the printed
line. Both hand-written filters say why in a comment: *a 2/2 pumped past five is a legal target and a
6/6 shrunk below it is not, which is the whole reason characteristics are computed on demand.* The
test grows a Grizzly Bears with +1/+1 counters and watches the same creature change from an illegal
target to a legal one.

"An opponent controls" is the other half of the Dragonslayer's phrase and is load-bearing on its own:
a morph turned face up that could kill its own team is a different card. It reuses `opponents: true`,
and a break that drops it fails.

### The exile

`exile (target …)` reads as `exileCard`, which is destroy's sibling and differs where it matters: it
is **not** a destruction, so indestructible and regeneration do not answer it (CR 701.19a). It
carries `removesACreature` exactly when the target is a creature, which is the rule the destroy
reader already follows — an exile aimed at any permanent would have the bot holding it for a board it
cannot answer.

**Selesnya Charm now compiles whole**, all three modes: the pump with trample, this exile, and the
Knight token.

### Three refusal tests that became acceptances

All three were written by earlier increments against examples this one reads, and all three keep
their property while changing how it is expressed:

1. *"leaves a clause it cannot read alone"* used `exile target creature` as its unreadable example;
   it now uses Rest in Peace's graveyard sweep, which has no reader and no near miss.
2. *"refuses a bare exile with no return"* — D377's one correctness refusal. The property is **no
   invented return**, and it was expressed by leaving the line unread. Now the sentence is read as
   what it says, so the test asserts the emitted triggers instead: one `etb`, and no `leaves`.
3. *"refuses Selesnya Charm whole, because one bullet has no reader"* — the test had already written
   down what to do when this happened ("this test needs a synthetic bullet rather than a card"), so
   Healing Salve is the last real card holding the property and a synthetic charm now owns it.

### Measured

**381 → 386 of 538 printed lines (70.8% → 71.7%)**, and **243 → 244 of 339 cards**. Hidden
Dragonslayer and Selesnya Charm, which the per-card diff names and nothing else.

Five deliberate breaks, five failing tests: the power read off the printed line, the threshold fixed
at four, the opponent half of the Dragonslayer's filter dropped, exile reading as destroy, and the
removal hint on every exile. 5,000 more rows at scale, no throw. compile.test.ts 306/306.

### The live game, re-checked end to end

Nine compiler commits is a lot of engine change to leave unexercised, so the four browser suites were
run on a freshly built stack: **table 76/76, arena 52/52 with 6 named skips, solo 28/28 with 1, pod
40/40 with 1.** Clean. The counts move by a check or two between runs because a check the game did not
produce is skipped and named rather than failed (D302) — `play-realm-setup.md` now says so, instead of
printing one run's numbers as though they were the suite's size.

## D405 — An additional cost, which is paid as the spell is cast

"As an additional cost to cast this spell, sacrifice a creature" — Bone Splinters and Village Rites,
and both compile **whole**, because the sentences after it ("Destroy target creature", "Draw two
cards") already read.

It needs a reader of its own rather than a clause, and the reason is the difference between casting
and resolving. A spell's sentences all happen when it resolves; this one happens as it is **cast**
(CR 601.2h), so it cannot be responded to and the creature cannot be saved in reply. Handing it to
`composeEffects` would either refuse the card or — worse — run the sacrifice on resolution, which is
a different card. So `spellScriptFor` reads it beside the keywords, where the lines that are not part
of the resolution come out before `readResolution` sees them, and `lineScriptFor` reads it too, for
the permanent spells that print the same line.

`additionalCost` holds a **sacrifice and nothing else**, so that is all this reads. "Discard a card",
"pay 3 life" and "exile a creature card from your graveyard" are real printed costs this engine
cannot express, and a reader that dropped one would make the spell **cheaper than the card** — the
clearest kind of card that works and is wrong, and the one a player would notice last. They are
refused, and the line is reported, so the card is dealt as a hybrid rather than cast for less.

The engine already honours the field: a spell whose additional cost cannot be paid is **not offered**
rather than offered and refused, so Bone Splinters with an empty board is not a legal play.

### Measured

**386 → 390 of 538 printed lines (71.7% → 72.5%)**, and **244 → 246 of 339 cards**: Bone Splinters
and Village Rites, which the per-card diff names and nothing else.

Three deliberate breaks, three failing tests: any additional cost accepted as a sacrifice, "another"
read as the plain sacrifice, and the cost line left in the resolution (which fails four tests,
because leaving it there refuses both cards). 4,000 more rows at scale, no throw. compile.test.ts
313/313.

## D406 — A clause that points at a player, and a duplicate reader a break run found

Sign in Blood: "Target player draws two cards and loses 2 life", which compiles whole and is the
pool's only card whose **two halves aim at the same player**.

That is why it is one reader and not two. `composeEffects` refuses two targeting parts — `targets` is
one list per script, so two would silently be handed the same object, which is the rule that keeps
"target creature fights target creature you don't control" honest. D398's conjunction fallback would
hit exactly that refusal here, so the sentence is read whole instead.

Drawing before the loss is the printed order, and the hand-written card's comment says why it
matters: a player taken to 0 by the life loss still drew the cards, and a player with no cards left to
draw has already lost either way.

### The duplicate, and the break run that found it

This increment also added a reader for "target player gains N life" — Healing Salve's first bullet —
and it was **dead code**. The drain-and-heal family (D390) already read that phrase, and the branch
sat below it. Nothing failed, nothing was wrong at the table, and the measurement did not move; what
found it was a deliberate break: turning `friendly` off in the new branch changed no test, because no
test could reach it.

So the lesson is about the method rather than the card. A break run is normally a check that a
mechanism *works*; here it was a check that the mechanism **exists at all**, and a reader with no
caller is exactly as invisible as a check that cannot fail (D386, D394, D398, D403). The duplicate is
deleted, the test stays pointed at the reader that does the work, and the near miss is written into
the test so the next person adding a phrase looks for it first.

### Measured

**390 → 391 of 538 printed lines (72.5% → 72.7%)**, and **246 → 247 of 339 cards**: Sign in Blood,
the only card the per-card diff shows moving.

Three deliberate breaks, three failing tests: the draw and the loss aimed at the caster instead of
the target, the life loss dropped, and a missing target guessed as the caster (CR 800.4a — a player
who has left the game is not a target this spell has). The fourth break is the one above, which
failed to fail and found the duplicate. 4,000 more rows at scale, no throw. compile.test.ts 317/317.

## D407 — Fate Unraveler drained where its text says it deals damage

The card prints "Whenever an opponent draws a card, **Fate Unraveler deals 1 damage to that
player**." The script called `loseLife`.

Damage and life loss are not the same thing at a table, and the differences are the kind a player
notices and cannot explain:

- a **prevention shield** absorbs damage and does nothing at all to a loss of life (CR 120.3, CR 615);
- damage can be **redirected** (CR 615.9), and a loss of life cannot;
- "whenever a source deals damage" sees one and not the other, and infect replaces damage rather
  than life loss.

### Why nothing caught it

The one test on the card read the **life total**, and both readings move it by the same amount. That
is the shape this project keeps finding: a check that cannot fail, here by measuring the one quantity
the two implementations agree on. `card-promises.mjs` (#215) could not see it either — it reads the
text for *structure* (keywords, a trigger, an ability, protection, landwalk) and asks whether the
script carries each, so "a trigger whose effect does the wrong thing" is invisible to it by design.

It was found by reading the card beside its printed text while looking for a compiler reading of
"that player" — which is the same mechanism as every other defect the compiler has turned up (#319,
#322, #323, D394, D403): writing a second reading of the same sentence and requiring the two to
agree.

### The fix, and a fallback that was worse than nothing

`dealDamage` to the actor as a player, with the controller and source, so prevention and redirection
apply. The guard also changed: the old effect was `loseLife(c.state, c.actor ?? c.controller, 1)`,
and that `?? c.controller` would have drained **the controller** on an event with no actor — the
opposite of what the card says. `by: 'opponent'` means that cannot happen today; a card whose wrong
case is its own controller is one bad event away from a very confusing game, so it now does nothing
instead.

### Verified

A **prevention shield** is the discriminating test: one point of shielding up, two cards drawn, and
the printed card costs one life where the drained version costs two. It fails when the effect is put
back to `loseLife`, which is the whole point of writing it that way. The engine's own suite is
883/883.

### Still open, and filed rather than built

The general instrument this wants is a measure that resolves **the compiled reading and the
hand-written script on the same fixture, for every card both can read, and reports the
disagreements** — which is what compile.test.ts does by hand, card by card. Filed as #326 with the
design; it is the instrument that would have found this one without anybody reading the card.

## D408 — "That player", which only a trigger has

Kambal, Consul of Allocation and Fate Unraveler: two cards whose effect is about **the player the
event was about**, and both compile whole.

- "Whenever an opponent casts a noncreature spell, that player loses 2 life and you gain 2 life"
- "Whenever an opponent draws a card, ~ deals 1 damage to that player"

### Trigger-only, by construction

"That player" is `c.actor` — the seat whose action raised the event — and a stack object that is not
a triggered ability carries no actor at all. A *spell* printing the same sentence would read
`undefined` and silently do nothing, with no line left unread for a human to notice (D362).

That is D399's X hazard in reverse, and it is answered the same way: the reading lives on the path
where the word means something, so the other path cannot reach it. `eventRelativeEffect` sits inside
`triggerFromLine`, above the shared `composeEffects`, and a sorcery printing the clause is refused —
asserted as a card, and a break that moves the reader into the shared vocabulary fails four tests.

### The guard, which is the cards' own

An event with no actor, or one whose actor is the controller, does **nothing**. Fate Unraveler's
script had `?? c.controller` there until D407, which would have drained **the caster** — the opposite
of the card, and the kind of wrongness that only shows up in a game nobody can reconstruct. Both
compiled clauses carry the guard and a test asserts both halves of it.

### Both halves of the printed event

`by: 'opponent'` and `spell: 'noncreature'` are printed and load-bearing: the same event without them
fires on every spell anybody casts, the controller's own included, which is a very different card. A
break that widens it fails two tests.

### Measured

**391 → 393 of 538 printed lines (72.7% → 73.0%)**, and **247 → 249 of 339 cards**: Kambal and Fate
Unraveler, the only two the per-card diff shows moving.

Four deliberate breaks, four failing tests. 4,000 more rows at scale, no throw. compile.test.ts
322/322.

This is also the increment that found D407: writing the damage clause meant reading Fate Unraveler's
script beside its text, which is where the drain-for-damage substitution turned up.

## D409 — The attack a trigger was about, and a guard copied from the wrong card

Hellrider and Ichor Wellspring, the two cards this increment moves, and they are about the two
different ways a trigger refers to something outside its own text.

- "Whenever a creature you control attacks, ~ deals 1 damage to the player or planeswalker it's attacking"
- "When ~ enters the battlefield or is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, draw a card"

### The attack travels on the stack object

`c.attacked` is what *that* attack was declared against, and it has to travel with the ability
rather than be looked up on resolution: by then the attacker may be dead and combat may no longer
say what it was aimed at. In a pod three creatures can attack three different players and this card
has to hit each of them once, which is why the whole attack travels and not just a seat.

A planeswalker that was attacked takes the damage **instead of** its controller — that is why the
clause names both — so the reader hits `{ kind: 'card', id: c.attacked.planeswalker }` when one was
attacked and `{ kind: 'player', seat: c.attacked.defender }` otherwise. A break that always takes
the defender fails the planeswalker test.

### Trigger-only, for D408's reason

Like "that player", "it's attacking" is a word that only means something on a trigger: a spell
carries no attack, so a sorcery printing the clause would read `undefined` and quietly do nothing,
with no unread line for a human to see (D362). The reading therefore lives in
`eventRelativeEffect`, inside `triggerFromLine`, and an absent attack answers with the state
unchanged — asserted directly.

### "Dies" is a word artifacts cannot use

`dies` is defined for creatures (CR 700.4), so Ichor Wellspring — an artifact — prints "or is put
into a graveyard from the battlefield" for the shape Lotleth Giant spells "or dies". One prologue
row for the long spelling, one effect for both events, the pair the hand-written card already uses.
A break that drops the row fails two tests.

### A guard copied from the wrong card

Writing that row meant reading Ichor Wellspring's script beside its printed text, and the graveyard
half was guarded on the card still being in a graveyard — copied from Rancor, whose comment the
guard's own comment cited.

The two cards are not the same shape. **Rancor returns itself**, so a Rancor that was moved on
before its trigger resolved is a card there is nothing to return; the guard is the rule there.
"Draw a card" asks nothing about the source. A triggered ability on the stack exists independently
of the permanent that made it (CR 603.2, CR 608.2), so an Ichor Wellspring exiled from the
graveyard before the trigger resolved still draws — and the guarded version silently did less than
the card says, which is the failure shape this engine can least afford.

Corrected, with the test that resolves the trigger after moving the card to exile and asserts the
draw on **both** the compiled reading and the hand-written script. Restoring the guard fails it.

This is the second defect in two increments found the same way — by reading a hand-written script
beside its printed text while writing the reader for it (D407 was the first) — which is the
argument for #326, the measure that would find them without a person in the loop.

### Measured

**393 → 395 of 538 printed lines (73.0% → 73.4%)**, and **249 → 251 of 339 cards**: Hellrider and
Ichor Wellspring, the only two the per-card diff shows moving.

Three deliberate breaks, three failing tests. compile.test.ts 327/327.

## D410 — The gate's four middle steps ran nothing, and pnpm exited 0 saying so

Found while typechecking the test files by hand: `tsc -p tsconfig.test.json` in `packages/rules-engine`
exits 2 on four real errors in `compile.test.ts` — and the gate, run minutes earlier on the same
tree, had printed **GATE OK**.

### What the gate was running

Nothing, for four of its eight steps. The steps are strings run as `$step`, unquoted, so the shell
does both halves of its job: word splitting, which is wanted, and **pathname expansion**, which is
not. CI writes the filter quoted:

```
pnpm -r --filter './packages/*' --filter './apps/*' run typecheck:tests
```

and inside a `$step` string the quotes are characters rather than quoting, so the shell expanded
`./packages/*` into the six real directories. What pnpm received was

```
pnpm -r --filter ./packages/db ./packages/rules-engine … run typecheck:tests
```

where only the first path is a filter and the rest are positional arguments — making `./packages/db`
the script name. pnpm answered

```
None of the selected packages has a "./packages/db" script
```

and **exited 0**. Four steps did that: the packages' `build`, `typecheck`, `typecheck:tests` and
`test`. The gate's whole middle. For several days "gate green" meant `services-up.js`, `guards.js`,
one legacy node test and the web build.

### Why nothing caught it

`check-gate.sh` exists because of D365 and asks exactly one question: does the gate fail when a step
fails? It does, and it always did. **A step that runs nothing really does succeed**, so no amount of
exit-code checking could see this. It is D365 one level out: not a check that cannot fail, but a
check that never ran.

The gate's own log said so in plain English on every run, once per step. Nobody read it, because the
last line said GATE OK — which is the recurring lesson of this file, and this time the evidence was
sitting in the file the script prints the path of.

### The fix, and the check that goes with it

`set -f` for the loop: pathname expansion off, word splitting on, so the glob reaches pnpm to match
itself exactly as CI does. Quoting inside the step strings cannot do it.

Then the fix carries a check, because an exit code cannot express this one. After each step the gate
reads **only the lines that step appended** and fails on either of pnpm's two ways of selecting
nothing — `No projects matched the filters` (no package matched) and `None of the selected packages
has a … script` (packages matched, none has the script). The real bug printed the second, and only
because the mangled command line turned a package path into a script name; a gate watching for one
phrasing would miss the other spelling of the same hole.

`GATE_STEPS` is now split on **newlines** rather than whitespace, which is what lets `check-gate.sh`
inject a real `pnpm -r --filter … run …` step. Split on whitespace, that step became six one-word
steps beginning with a bare `pnpm`, and the probe tested nothing. Both probes are in
`check-gate.sh` now and both fail the gate: `bash scripts/check-gate.sh` reads

```
ok    the gate exits non-zero on a failing step (rc=1)
ok    and it names the step that failed
ok    the gate fails a step that ran nothing (rc=1): pnpm -r --filter ./nothing-here/* run build
ok    the gate fails a step that ran nothing (rc=1): pnpm -r --filter ./packages/db run no-such-script
ok    and it passes when every step passes
gate verified
```

### What the hidden steps were hiding
