One defect, and only one: four `entersWith(...).script ?? {}` call sites in `compile.test.ts`, where
`compileCard` returns a union whose `ok: false` arm has no `script`. vitest transpiles without
checking types, so the tests passed throughout. Fixed by narrowing once in a sibling helper,
`entersWithScript`, and leaving `entersWith` whole for the refusal rows that assert on `ok` and
`unread`.

Everything else was already green. The repaired gate runs **2,577 tests** across every package and
app — rules-engine 1,786, apps/api 315, apps/web 246, shared 118, realtime 47, auto-tagger 26,
recommender 15, mailer 10, db 7, theme 7 — plus four typecheck passes, the packages' build, the
legacy token-parity test and the web production build. That is the number the gate should have been
reporting all along.

A note for the next reader: the figures in checkpoints between D368 and this entry were measured by
running the suites directly rather than through the gate, so they stand. What does not stand is
"gate green" as a claim about those commits — it meant less than it said.

## D411 — A token the card names instead of describing

Pirate's Prize: "Draw two cards. Create a Treasure token." Both clauses now read, so the card
compiles whole.

### Look it up, do not write it out

Magic names a predefined token rather than describing it, and the bracketed reminder after it is not
rules text (CR 207.2). So a Treasure's characteristics are **nowhere in the sentence** the compiler
sees — the only way to describe one would be to transcribe the reminder as rules, which is D259's
rule exactly: inventing the text of a real card is worse than leaving the mechanic out.

So the reading is a lookup. `TREASURE_TOKEN` and `CLUE_TOKEN` are the engine's own definitions,
written and tested by D243, and the compiled Treasure is the same object the hand-written card
makes. That matters beyond the name: the Treasure's sacrifice-for-mana ability is what makes the
mana solver count it, so a token that merely looked like one would be a spell that appears to ramp
and does not.

This is `investigate`'s argument (D403) generalised from one word to a table.

### The table is the validation

Two names, because there are two definitions. Food, Blood, Map and Powerstone are as real as
Treasure and this engine has never needed one, so reading them would mean inventing their text.
They are refused, and the refusal is asserted for three of them. The table grows when a definition
does, not when a card does.

Clue is in the table with **no pool card behind it** — Thraben Inspector prints "investigate"
instead — and that is said rather than left to be noticed. It is there because the table's rule is
"a token the engine has a definition for", and leaving it out would be an exception with no reason.
A synthetic card pins it against `CLUE_TOKEN`'s own text and type line, so the entry is falsifiable:
a break that describes a Clue from memory fails it.

### The count was already solved

`namedTokenFrom` returns the token and the **printed count word**, unread, exactly as `tokenFrom`
does — so "two Treasure tokens" and a `for each` tail go through `tokenEffect`'s existing count
machinery and needed nothing new. A break that hard-codes one fails the count test.

### One refusal became an acceptance

"Create a Treasure token." was a row in the token refusal table, for having no printed power and
toughness and carrying rules text of its own. Both facts are still true and are the reason
describing it is forbidden; the reading that replaced the refusal does not describe it. The reason
is written where the row was rather than deleted with it.

### Measured

**395 → 396 of 538 printed lines (73.4% → 73.6%)**, and **251 → 252 of 339 cards**: Pirate's Prize,
the only card the per-card diff shows moving.

Three deliberate breaks, three failing tests. compile.test.ts 330/330, 4,000 shuffled rows with no
throw — and the first increment in this series verified by a gate that actually runs CI's steps
(D410).

## D412 — A colour change in the same pump, and a bot hint two cards were right to omit

Crimson Wisps: "Target creature gains haste until end of turn and becomes red. / Draw a card." Both
lines now read, so the card compiles whole — and reading it found a defect in the reader written two
increments ago, plus a difference between the compiled and hand-written scripts that was the
hand-written one's to fix.

### One printed effect, one `PumpOptions`

The colour rides in the same object as the keyword, which is `pumpAndGrant`'s rule applied once
more: `pump` takes both and the hand-written card passes
`{ keywords: ['haste'], setColors: ['R'] }` in a single call. Two continuous effects where the print
is one would expire independently — and this pair especially, because layer 5 **replaces** the
printed colours (CR 105.3) rather than adding to them, so a colour change that outlived its keyword
would leave a creature whose colours came from a spell that has finished.

The word list is `TOKEN_COLOURS`, shared with the token reader so a colour word is spelled in one
place. `colorless` is in it as `null` and is **refused** here: `setColors: []` says "has no colours",
which is a different claim from the absence of the effect, and nothing in the pool prints it. Red,
not purple; a word that is not a colour refuses the clause. Both refusals are asserted.

### The hint neither hand-written twin carries

The grant readers set `protectsACreature` for hexproof and shroud and `expiresAtEndOfTurn` for
everything else — so a **haste or infect** grant carried "hold this for the combat". Both
hand-written twins, Crimson Wisps and Tainted Strike, carry no spell flag at all.

The flag is wrong there rather than merely extra. Its own docblock says what it does to an instant:
"an instant can wait for blockers". A haste grant waited out is a card that never did its job,
because the creature it was cast to let attack has not attacked; an infect grant is the same. The
hint this family needs is on the **target spec** — `helpsInCombat`, aim it at something that can
attack — and the two together would say hold it *and* aim it at an attacker.

So the split is three ways now: protection keeps `protectsACreature`, a bonus whose whole value is
in the attack carries nothing, and a size bonus keeps `expiresAtEndOfTurn`. Both call sites changed,
the grant-only branch and the sized one.

A test asserted the wrong value. "Carries the protection hint on a hexproof trick" ended with
`expect(Tainted Strike's expiresAtEndOfTurn).toBe(true)` — written from the reader rather than from
the card, because that row never compared against the hand-written script. That is the third time in
this series a check has encoded the implementation it was meant to judge, and the fix is the same
one every time: compare against the card.

### And one correction the other way

The compiled reading and the hand-written Crimson Wisps differed by one field after resolving:
`drawsOwed: [0]` against a card already in hand. `composeEffects` picks `drawLater` for a clause
that is last and `draw` for one that is not, and this draw is last.

`drawLater` is right, and its own docblock says why: only a deferred draw can be replaced by a dredge
(CR 702.52a), and it is "for a draw that is the last thing the card does". So the hand-written card
now calls it too — one rule with one source, the same resolution the Dive Down `sizeBonus` case took
(D-series). The card's own test drains owed draws before counting the hand, so it passes unchanged,
and so do the other 1,789.

### Measured

**396 → 398 of 538 printed lines (73.6% → 74.0%)**, and **252 → 253 of 339 cards**: Crimson Wisps,
the only card the per-card diff shows moving. Two lines for one card, because its colour clause and
its draw were both unread while the card as a whole was refused.

Four deliberate breaks, four failing tests: the colour group dropped, `colorless` let through, the
hold-for-combat hint restored, and the attacker hint dropped. compile.test.ts 334/334, engine suite
1,790/1,790, 4,000 shuffled rows with no throw.

## D413 — A draw that has to happen before the question

Faithless Looting: "Draw two cards, then discard two cards." The first card in this series whose
reading is about **order** rather than effect, and the first to need a field of `CardScript` the
compiler had never written.

### The composition is right and the card is wrong

`clausesOf` splits on ", then ", so the sentence arrives as two clauses — "Draw two cards" and
"discard two cards" — which `composeEffects` runs in printed order. That is the correct order for
two *effects* and it produces the wrong card, because the discard is a **question**: questions are
planned before the resolution runs, so the player would be choosing which two cards to pitch out of
the hand they held **before** drawing.

The hand-written card says it in one line, `beforeDecisions: (c) => draw(c.state, c.controller, 2)`,
and its docblock is explicit: "the cards it offers to discard are the ones it has not seen yet".

So `lootResolution` is a **spell-shape** reader, like `xSpellResolution`, and sits *before*
`composeEffects` in `readResolution` rather than after it. A fallback consulted only on failure
could never correct this, because the composition does not fail — it succeeds and is wrong. That is
a new failure mode for this module and worth naming: every refusal so far has been a clause nothing
could read, and this is a clause everything could read and nobody should.

### `draw`, not `drawLater`

The one place in the compiler where the immediate primitive is right. A card that is *owed* is not a
card you can be asked to discard, so a deferred draw here reproduces the exact bug the reader exists
to avoid. `drawLater`'s own docblock bounds it to "a draw that is the last thing the card does", and
this draw is the first. A break that swaps them fails the test.

### `beforeDecisions` is spell-shape only, by construction

`ReadEffect` gained the field and `spellScriptFor` writes it, but **`composeEffects` deliberately
does not propagate it**. A clause cannot know whether a question comes after it, so a
`beforeDecisions` surviving a composition would be an effect moved in front of somebody else's
question by accident. Keeping it to readers that see the whole resolution makes that impossible
rather than forbidden — the same argument that keeps X on the spell path (D399) and "that player" on
the trigger path (D408).

For the same reason the reader refuses a loot sentence sharing a resolution with anything else:
`beforeDecisions` runs before *every* question the spell asks, so the whole resolution or none of it.

### The two counts are read separately

"Draw two cards, then discard a card" is Thrill of Possibility. Nothing requires the numbers to
match, so nothing assumes it, and the prompt echoes the printed count and its noun rather than being
built from the number — which keeps "Discard a card" singular and matches the hand-written prompt. A
break that reuses the draw count fails a synthetic row.

### One test had to move

"Compiles a spell whole or not at all, never half of it" used Faithless Looting's text as its example
of a half-readable spell, and that gap has closed. Its example is now "Draw two cards, then put a
card from your hand on top of your library" — the same shape with a second clause nothing here can
read. The invariant is unchanged and the churn reasoning is in the test, which is the second time
this particular row has been repointed for the same happy reason.

### Measured

**398 → 399 of 538 printed lines (74.0% → 74.2%)**, and **253 → 254 of 339 cards**: Faithless
Looting, the only card the per-card diff shows moving.

Four deliberate breaks, four failing tests: `drawLater` for `draw`, the draw count reused for the
discard, a longer resolution admitted, and `beforeDecisions` dropped from the assembly.
compile.test.ts 339/339, 4,000 shuffled rows with no throw.

## D414 — A blink: two clauses about one object

Cloudshift: "Exile target creature you control, then return that card to the battlefield under your
control." Whole now, and the third spell-shape reader, arrived at from the other side of D413's
argument.

### Why a clause cannot do it

`clausesOf` splits on ", then ", so the sentence arrives as "Exile target creature you control" and
"return that card to the battlefield under your control" — and the second clause is about **the first
clause's object**. "That card" is neither a target nor the source; it is whatever the exile just
moved, and a clause reader is handed a context and a target list and nothing at all about what the
clause before it did.

Reading the first half alone would be **worse than refusing both**, and this is the strongest version
of that argument so far: the exile clause already has a reader (D404), so a compiler that took it and
stopped would turn a blink into unconditional removal of your own creature — a card that works,
plays, and does the opposite of what it prints. Nothing at the table would flag it.

So `blinkResolution` joins `xSpellResolution` and `lootResolution` ahead of `composeEffects`, and
refuses a loot-style longer resolution for the same reason they do.

### `blinks` is the point of the spec

`TargetSpec.blinks` is not a restriction and its docblock is long about why: a blink is a help *or* a
hit depending on whose permanent it lands on, because what the permanent loses by leaving is what
decides — a token ceases to exist (CR 111.7), and counters, Auras and marked damage all go. The bot
cannot read any of that off a candidate list, so the flag is how it is told, and a compiled blink
without it is a card the bot plays blind (#322's shape). Cloudshift's hand-written spec carries it;
so does this one, and a break that drops it fails.

### Only "under your control"

Flickerwisp returns the permanent **under its owner's control** and at the beginning of the next end
step — a different card twice over. Read as this shape it would be a blink of somebody else's
creature handed straight back to you, so the phrase is matched as printed and the other wording stays
unread (D362). A break that widens the regex to any controller fails.

"Another" is admitted in the regex and dropped for the spec, deliberately: the word excludes the
source, and a **spell** is never on the battlefield to be excluded. Keeping it in the pattern means
the sentence is matched as printed rather than approximately.

### Still hand-written

The trigger form of the same pair — Soulherder's end step — needs `triggerFromLine` to gain a
clause-pair path of its own. That is its own change, and said here rather than left for someone to
discover the reader does not fire on it.

### Measured

**399 → 400 of 538 printed lines (74.2% → 74.3%)**, and **254 → 255 of 339 cards**: Cloudshift, the
only card the per-card diff shows moving.

Four deliberate breaks, four failing tests: the return dropped, the `blinks` hint dropped, the
controller wording widened, and a longer resolution admitted. compile.test.ts 343/343, 4,000 shuffled
rows with no throw.

## D415 — A characteristic read before the permanent leaves, and two guards that could not fail

Swords to Plowshares: "Exile target creature. Its controller gains life equal to its power." Whole
now, and the increment where the break runs earned their keep twice.

### The dependency

The fourth spell-shape reader and the third kind of internal dependency. `lootResolution`'s was an
**order** (draw before the question); `blinkResolution`'s was an **identity** ("that card" is the
object the clause before moved). This one is a **reading**: "its power" is a characteristic of the
creature the sentence before exiled, and no clause reader is handed the object another clause moved.

Whose life matters and is asserted: "its controller" is the seat the creature is under, so aiming
this at your own creature pays **you**. `removesACreature` is carried, because the flag is the bot's
only way to know this spell wants somebody's creature to point at (#322's failure).

### Two breaks that passed, and what they settled

Four deliberate breaks; **two of them passed every test**, which is the point of running them.

**The order could not be told from its absence.** Reading the power *after* `exileCard` instead of
before gave the same answer, so the test said nothing. The reason is a known, documented limitation:
`pump` scopes an effect to an instance id and `relocate` keeps that id across a zone change, so the
effect follows the card out of the battlefield. Probed directly — a 2/2 pumped +3/+3 then exiled
reads power **5** in the exile zone. `pumpTeam`'s docblock has had it written down all along: a
creature that changes zone is a new object (CR 400.7) and should be out of the set, and "it wants the
object identity the engine does not yet have".

So the printed order stays, because it is the card and the hand-written script and it is what will be
right once zone changes strip what they should — and the docblock now says it is **fidelity, not
correctness**, instead of defending it with a claim no test can hold. Filed as **#326** with the
probe, because it is a real hole and this is the second mechanism it has made untestable.

**The clamp could not fail either.** The hand-written card writes `Math.max(0, power)`, and
`gainLife` returns the state untouched for any amount `<= 0` on its first line — so dropping the
clamp from the compiled reading changed nothing. Deleted rather than mirrored, which is this file's
standing rule: a guard that cannot fail reads as care and is noise. The behaviour it stood for — a
creature at negative power pays nothing — is asserted, and the test says plainly that it holds
because of `gainLife` rather than because of a clamp.

Both tests were rewritten to claim only what they prove. That is the third time this series a check
has been found asserting the implementation rather than the card, and the first time a *docblock* was
the thing that overclaimed.

### Measured

**400 → 401 of 538 printed lines (74.5%)**, and **255 → 256 of 339 cards**: Swords to Plowshares, the
only card the per-card diff shows moving.

Four deliberate breaks, **two** failing tests and two that could not — both diagnosed rather than
patched over. compile.test.ts 347/347, 4,000 shuffled rows with no throw.

## D416 — A land that turns itself into a creature, and a second figure worth printing

Mutavault's animation: `{1}: Mutavault becomes a 2/2 creature until end of turn. It's still a land.`
The first **ability**-shape reader, beside the four spell-shape ones.

### The second sentence decides what the first one does

`clausesOf` splits that into two, and the second is not an effect at all. `addTypes: ['Creature']`
adds a type where `setTypes` would replace the line, and "it's still a land" is the printed reason to
add (CR 613.1c). A reader of the first sentence alone has to guess between them, and guessing wrong
makes a Mutavault that **cannot be tapped for mana for the rest of the turn** — a card that works,
plays, and is worse than the print.

So the pair is one reading, and `animateSelf` is consulted ahead of `composeEffects` in
`abilityFromLine` exactly as the spell-shape readers are ahead of it in `readResolution`. The clause
**without** the second sentence is refused rather than read as either (D259): nothing in the pool
prints it, and a non-land becoming a creature is a different family anyway (a Vehicle's crew). A
break that makes the sentence optional fails that row.

`setPower`/`setToughness` and not a pump, which is layer 7b: a 2/2 **base**, so an anthem lands on
top of it. A break that pumps instead fails, because the anthem test reads 3/3 where the pump gives
1/1 on a 0/0 land.

`animates` is carried and is load-bearing twice: it is how the bot knows not to press this without an
attack or a block to make, and pressing it spends the land as a mana source for the turn. A compiled
animation without the flag is #322's failure again.

### A second figure, and why it is new rather than a correction

This increment moves **no card** on the figure every entry since D366 has quoted — Mutavault already
had a script, because its mana ability compiled long ago. What moved is that it now has **nothing
left unread**.

Both numbers are real and they measure different things:

- **cards with a script** (`whole-card` + `lines` in the measure's source split) — the card plays,
  possibly with a line flagged for a human (D362). **256 of 339.**
- **cards with every printed line read** — nothing is left for a human at all. **228 of 339**, up
  from 227.

Every figure quoted so far has been the first, and none of them was wrong; the second was simply not
being printed. Across the eight increments measured this stretch it ran 220 → 228 while the first ran
249 → 256. Both are quoted from here on, because "it plays" and "it plays completely" are the two
questions a person about to use this would ask, and one number cannot answer both.

### Measured

**401 → 402 of 538 printed lines (74.5% → 74.7%)**; cards with a script unchanged at **256 of 339**;
cards with every line read **227 → 228 of 339**. The per-card diff shows exactly one card leaving the
incomplete list: Mutavault.

Four deliberate breaks, four failing tests: `setTypes` for `addTypes`, a pump for a base, the
`animates` hint dropped, and the land sentence made optional. compile.test.ts 351/351, 4,000 shuffled
rows with no throw.

## D417 — The compiler checked against every card the pool can check it against, mechanically

Four increments in a row found a defect the same way: **somebody read a card beside its script.**
D407 (a drain where the card said damage), D409 (a guard copied from the wrong card), D412 (a bot
hint two cards were right to omit), D415 (two guards that could not fail). Each argued that the
reading should be mechanical. `packages/rules-engine/src/compiled-vs-written.test.ts` is that.

### What it covers that `compile.test.ts` cannot

`compile.test.ts` is the better check per card and will stay: a describe block per family,
comparing closures by resolving them. But it covers something like **sixty** of the pool's 348 cards
and only the fields somebody thought to assert.

This covers **every card with both a hand-written script and a compiled reading with nothing
unread — 205 of them** — and compares the *whole* script: which fields exist, every scalar, every
target spec, every trigger's event, every ability's cost. Functions become `[fn]`, so it is
structure and data rather than behaviour; the two checks are complementary and the division is
clean. A missing field is this one's job, a wrong effect is the other's.

It matters more for #318 than for the pool. Tens of thousands of imported cards will have **no
hand-written script to check against**, so the pool is the only ground truth the compiler will ever
have — and spending all of it automatically is the difference between "the families somebody tested"
and "every card we can check".

### The result: 175 agree, 19 differ harmlessly, 11 are real

Three normalisations, each because the two spellings are the same card: **key order** (twelve cards
differed by nothing else), **`who: 'self'`** on an event (the documented default, which most
hand-written cards omit and the compiler writes), and **`description`** (prose for the log on one
side, the printed line on the other).

Nineteen cards then differ only by a `keywords: ['flying']`-style declaration the compiled reading
omits, and that is not a gap: `characteristicsOf` seeds keywords from `printedKeywords(oracleText)`
**unconditionally**, so a compiled Shivan Dragon has flying because its text says so. Checked
rather than assumed — a second test asserts every keyword those nineteen declare really is printed,
so the day one declares a keyword its text does not, the difference stops being called harmless.

The remaining **eleven** are in `DISAGREE` with what each difference is. Filed as **#327** with the
triage; the headline ones:

- **Magma Jet** — the compiled reading puts the damage in `onResolve` where the card puts it first,
  so the scry is planned **before** the damage lands. Not one card: any resolution shaped "an
  effect. a decision." has it, because `spellScriptFor` puts every clause's effect in `onResolve`
  and the engine asks decisions first. D413 one level up.
- **Flame Slash, Journey to Nowhere** — `removesACreature` missing, for two different reasons: the
  hint is set for a destroy or exile aimed at a creature but not for damage aimed at one, and the
  trigger path cannot set a card-level flag at all.
- **Capsize** — the compiled spec has no filter where the hand-written one does.
- **Garruk Wildspeaker** — the compiled `+1` adds `friendly` and `untapsOnly` to an ability whose
  text is "Untap two target lands", with no "you control" in it.

### The fingerprint, which a break run forced

The first version compared **names only**, and that was not enough: removing the `blinks` hint from
the blink reader left every test green, because Cloudshift was already on the list and the check only
asked *whether* it differed. **A known-bad card was a hole the size of its whole script.**

So every row now carries the differing field names and a digest of the compiled side of them, and
the assertion is an equality over all three. It fails in four directions: a new disagreement, a card
that stopped disagreeing, a known card differing in a new field, and a known card whose difference
changed shape. Whoever fixes one deletes its row; whoever changes one updates the digest the failure
prints.

Five deliberate breaks, five failing tests: a row deleted, the blinks hint dropped on a known card,
`removesACreature` dropped on an agreeing card, the normalisation widened to ignore `targets`, and a
hand-written card made to declare a keyword its text does not print.

A deliberate guard against the check hollowing out: one row asserts the pair count is **at least
200**, because a compiler change that refused half the pool would otherwise leave every other
assertion here green.

## D418 — A composition splits at its first question

The first finding of D417's standing check to be fixed, and it was never one card.

### The defect

The engine plans a resolution's decisions and **asks them before the resolution runs** —
`automation.ts` runs `beforeDecisions` and then plans the questions against the state it produced.
`spellScriptFor` put every clause's effect in `onResolve`, so a card shaped "an effect. a question."
asked the player about a board its earlier clauses had not changed yet.

Magma Jet is the pool's instance — "deals 2 damage to any target. Scry 2" — and the hand-written
script has had the answer from the start, with the reason in its comment: "by the time the player is
looking at the top of their library the creature is already dead … what is drawn next is a different
decision once the board has changed."

### The fix is an assembly rule, not a reader

`composeEffects` now splits: the parts before the first part that asks something become
`beforeDecisions`, the rest stay in `effect`. A question in the first clause leaves nothing before
it and nothing changes. The earlier parts run in their `immediate` reading, because something *does*
come after them — the question — which is `ReadEffect.immediate`'s own rule.

Threaded through all three assemblies, because all three ask before they run: `spellScriptFor`
already carried the field for `lootResolution`, and `abilityFromLine` (both branches) and
`triggerFromLine` now carry it too.

A composition whose **part** already has a pre-question half is refused: `conjoinedEffect` composes,
so a nested one is reachable and would be silently dropped. D364's rule.

### `appliesNothing`, so the two scripts are identical rather than equivalent

With the split, Magma Jet still differed by one field: the compiled reading had an `onResolve` where
the hand-written card has none. The scry clause's own effect is the identity — the engine applies a
scry answer itself, and the reader's comment has always said so — so the composition's remaining
effect did nothing.

`ReadEffect.appliesNothing` is how an assembly is told that. `CardScript.onResolve` and
`AbilityDef.effect` are optional, so both omit the field entirely; `TriggerDef.effect` is required,
so a trigger whose whole content is a question keeps the identity, which is said in the docblock
rather than left as a surprise. A function that cannot be told from its absence is deleted here, as
everywhere else in this file.

### Two breaks that passed, and the fixtures that fixed that

Five deliberate breaks. Three failed immediately — no split, the first half run as final, the
identity `onResolve` kept. **Two passed**, and both were a test that could not fail:

- **Slicing from *after* the asking part** changed nothing, because every composed question in the
  pool is a scry and a scry applies nothing. A question with a real effect is a different matter, so
  the fixture is now "You gain 2 life. Target player discards a card." — where throwing the asking
  part away would ask which card to discard and never move it. It fails the break and asserts the
  card really moved.
- **Deleting the nested refusal** changed nothing, because the fixture was a loot sentence in a
  conjunction and `lootResolution` matches an exact sentence, so the guard was never reached. The
  fixture is now "You gain 2 life and scry 2. Draw a card." — a conjunction whose *second* half asks,
  so the inner composition splits and the outer one sees a part carrying a half. That reaches it.

Both are the same lesson as D415's and this file keeps relearning it: a break run is the only thing
that tells a test from a decoration.

### Measured

No coverage change — **402 of 538 lines (74.7%)**, 256 of 339 with a script, 228 complete — because
this is about *what* a compiled card does rather than how much of it compiles. The number that moved
is the disagreement count: **11 → 10**, with the Magma Jet row deleted and the reason written where
it was.

compile.test.ts 356/356 (two rows added, one re-pointed with its churn reasoning), 4,000 shuffled
rows with no throw.

## D419 — Five disagreements, four about one flag and one about a word the card prints

The second batch off D417's list, and the pattern is worth naming: of five rows, **two were real
defects, one in each direction**, and three were a field written on one side and not the other.

### Garruk Wildspeaker, wrong in both readings

`+1: Untap two target lands.`

- **The compiled ability carried `untapsOnly`, which the field's own docblock forbids by name.**
  `AbilityDef.untapsOnly` says: "Garruk's +1 untaps two lands *and* puts a loyalty counter on him —
  both have a payoff the question below would miss." The flag exists for one thing, stopping the bot
  tapping and untapping for ever because the board ended where it started, and a `+N` loyalty cost
  **gains** a counter, so the board did not end where it started. The loyalty branch of
  `abilityFromLine` drops it now.
- **The hand-written spec lacked `friendly`, and here that is not cosmetic.** The card says "target
  lands" with no "you control", so the filter admits an opponent's — and untapping an opponent's
  land is a card thrown away. `friendly` is the bot's **ordering** hint (`friendlyRank` instead of
  `rank`), so without it the default aim is the enemy's board, which is the wrong half of this
  ability. The compiled reading had it right.

Two readings of one card, each missing what the other had. Neither would have been found by reading
one of them.

### Three about `friendly` beside a filter

Cloudshift, Blossoming Defense and Dive Down: the compiled spec carried `friendly: true` next to a
filter that already restricts to your own side, so the flag changes nothing —
`targetSpecFrom`'s own comment says it is moot where the phrase names a side. Written on the
hand-written cards too rather than carried on the list for ever: one rule with one source, and a
field neither reading uses is not worth a permanent exception.

### Basilica Guards: a static that restated the card's own text

It carried `statics: [{ scope: 'self', effect: { cantAttack: true } }]` — a hand-written spelling of
defender. `defender` is a printed keyword, `KEYWORDS` has it, and `characteristicsOf` sets
`cantAttack` from it unconditionally (`if (hasType(typeLine, 'creature') &&
keywords.has('defender')) cantAttack = true`). So the static said again what the text says, and the
compiled reading — which has no static — refuses the attack just as firmly.

Deleted rather than mirrored into the compiler, and **proved rather than argued**: a new row asks
`canAttack` of the Guards and of a Serra Angel on the same board, placed the same way. The Guards
are refused, the Angel is not. Deleting the keyword handling in `characteristics.ts` fails that row
and two older ones (Wall of Blossoms, Wall of Air), which is the check that the keyword is really
what does the work.

### Measured

No coverage change — **402 of 538 lines (74.7%)**, 256 of 339 with a script, 228 complete. The
number that moved is the disagreement count: **10 → 5**. What is left is Capsize's missing filter,
two `removesACreature` gaps, and the two keyword-versus-expansion questions (ninjutsu, dash).

Four deliberate breaks, four failing tests: `untapsOnly` restored, Garruk's `friendly` dropped, the
Guards' static restored, and the defender keyword handling deleted.

### And the gate caught what the per-file runs did not

Two rows in `compile.test.ts` failed in the full run while every file I had re-run was green, because
I had re-run `compiled-vs-written.test.ts` and `scripts.test.ts` and **not the file the change was
about**. Both were stale assertions, and both were the same shape as the ones this series keeps
finding:

- `carries the count and the untap-only flag on Garruk's +1` asserted `untapsOnly: true` — written
  from the untap reader rather than from the card, which is the **fourth** time a check has encoded
  the implementation it was meant to judge.
- `aims an infect grant at a creature that can attack` recorded the `friendly` difference as a known
  gap, which is now closed.

Both re-pointed with the churn reasoning in them. The lesson is not about those rows: a per-file run
is a convenience and the gate is the check, and this is the first time since D410 repaired it that it
has failed on something real.

compile.test.ts and the rest: engine suite **1,816/1,816** across 15 files.

## D420 — A hint missing from one family, and a guard the engine already had twice

Third batch off D417's list. Two rows, one in each direction, and both settled by reading what the
engine already does rather than by adding anything.

### Flame Slash: the hint was on three families and not the fourth

`removesACreature` keeps a removal spell from being cast with nothing worth hitting (#322). The
compiler set it for a **destroy** aimed at a creature and for an **exile** aimed at one, and not for
**damage** aimed at one. Flame Slash is "deals 4 damage to target creature" — creature-only by its
own spec, so there is nothing else it could ever be cast at, and the hand-written card has carried
the flag all along.

So the damage reader now applies the same rule the other two already follow, and **adding it
introduced no new disagreement** — which is the useful part of having the standing check: the rule is
not a guess about one card, it matches every hand-written card in the pool that the rule touches.

Not for "any target": Lava Spike and Magma Jet can be aimed at a face, so a board with no creature
on it is still a board they do something on, and neither hand-written card carries the flag. A rule
that set it on every damage clause would make the bot hold a burn spell it should be pointing at a
player — asserted as its own row, because without that arm the first one says only "the flag exists
somewhere".

### Capsize: a filter that could not refuse anything

It carried `filter: zone === 'battlefield'` on a `kind: 'permanent'` spec. The engine requires that
**twice**, in both places it can ever be asked:

- `legalTargets` enumerates a permanent spec's candidates out of the battlefield zone and nowhere
  else — graveyard kinds have their own branch above it, and the stack kinds return before it.
- `isLegalTarget`, which validates a target somebody *submitted* rather than one the engine offered,
  reaches `if (inst.zone !== 'battlefield') return false` before it looks at a type at all.

So the filter could not refuse anything the engine would have allowed: a guard that cannot fail,
which this file deletes rather than keeps. Proved rather than argued — a board with one creature on
the battlefield and one card in a graveyard offers exactly the first, through `legalTargets` on the
compiled spec.

### Measured

No coverage change — **402 of 538 lines (74.7%)**, 256 of 339 with a script, 228 complete.
Disagreements **5 → 3**. What is left is Journey to Nowhere (`removesACreature` on a card whose
removal is an ETB trigger, which only the spell path can currently set) and ninjutsu and dash as a
keyword field versus a hand-written expansion.

Three deliberate breaks, three failing tests: the damage hint dropped, the damage hint set on every
spec, and Capsize's filter restored.

## D421 — Two keyword fields that were labels, and the machinery that was never compiled with them

Fourth batch off D417's list, and the one where the standing check found a card that *did not work*
rather than a card that disagreed about a key.

### The question the rows asked

Ninja of the Deep Hours and Mardu Scout each differed from their hand-written twin on a list —
`abilities` on the Ninja, `triggers` on the Scout — and in both cases the compiled side was the
shorter one. The compiler read the printed `Ninjutsu {1}{U}` and `Dash {R}` lines, set the matching
script field, and stopped. The hand-written cards set the same field **and** carried an ability.

So the row was a question about the engine rather than about the compiler: is the field the
implementation, or only a label? If the engine reads the field and does the work, the hand-written
expansion is a duplicate and should go. If it does not, the compiled card is broken.

### The answer: both were labels, and both cards were broken

- **Ninjutsu.** `CardScript.ninjutsu`'s own docblock says it is "read nowhere but the card that
  declares it … it is here so the pool can be audited for the keyword". The play comes from
  `collectLegalActions`, which walks `script.abilities` for a cost with `returnsUnblockedAttacker` —
  that flag is also what tells it the ability is used **from the hand** and does not spend the card.
  A compiled Ninja had the field and no ability, so no ninjutsu play was ever offered: the keyword
  did nothing at all.
- **Dash.** Half of it *is* the engine's: `completeResolution` writes the `DASHED` counter and grants
  haste itself. The return to hand is not — it is a delayed ability (CR 603.7) scheduled by finding
  the card's one `delayed` end-step trigger, behind an `index >= 0` guard. A compiled Mardu Scout
  got haste, attacked, and **stayed on the battlefield for ever**, silently, because that guard is
  what keeps a missing trigger from being a crash.

Both are D364's unit-of-compilation rule, which `echo` in the same reader already follows: the
declaration and what it declares are one unit, and either half alone is a card that does less than
it reads. The reader's own docblock claimed all eight of its alternative-cost keywords "add an
option and change nothing about what the card does"; that was true of six.

### The fix

`keywordScriptFor` now emits the machinery with the declaration — `triggers: [dashReturn()]` for
dash, `abilities: [ninjutsuAbility(mana)]` for ninjutsu. `ninjutsuAbility` is a new factory, and the
hand-written Ninja was rewritten to call it, so the two readings share one implementation of the
keyword rather than two that are free to drift. The reader's docblock now says which two keywords
take machinery and why, naming both engine sites.

`abilities` and `triggers` are in `compile.ts`'s `ACCUMULATING` set, so a keyword line contributing
one of each merges with the card's other lines instead of conflicting with them.

### Tested as what the card can do, not as which keys match

The field matching was never in question and was never the part that mattered, so the new tests ask
the engine's questions:

- the compiled dash reading carries **exactly one** delayed end-step trigger, which is what
  `dashReturnIndex`'s `findIndex` needs — the same invariant `scripts.test.ts` holds over the
  hand-written pool, now asked of the compiled side;
- running that trigger moves a Mardu Scout from the battlefield to its owner's hand, and leaves one
  already in a graveyard where it is (CR 608.2);
- the compiled ninjutsu ability's cost is `{ mana: '{1}{U}', returnsUnblockedAttacker: true }`, read
  off the printed line rather than hard-coded;
- running it puts the card onto the battlefield **tapped and attacking** the seat the cost was aimed
  at, and does nothing at all with no attack to join.

### Measured

No coverage change — **402 of 538 lines (74.7%)**, 256 of 339 with a script, 228 complete: these two
lines were always read, they just did not do anything. Disagreements **3 → 1**, and the one left is
Journey to Nowhere's `removesACreature`, which only the spell path can currently set.

Four deliberate breaks, four failures: the dash trigger dropped from the reader (3 compile rows and
the standing check), the ninjutsu ability dropped (3 and the standing check), the factory's
`enteringAttack` guard removed (the no-attack row only — correctly *not* the standing check, since
both readings share the factory), and the reader hard-coding `{2}{U}` instead of the printed cost
(the cost row and the standing check).

## D422 — The last disagreement: a card-level flag read where the whole card is in scope

Fifth and final batch off D417's list. `compiled-vs-written.test.ts`'s `DISAGREE` table is now
**empty**: every card in the pool with both a hand-written script and a compiled reading agrees.

### Why the flag had nowhere to come from

Journey to Nowhere's removal is a *trigger* — "When ~ enters the battlefield, exile target creature"
— and `removesACreature` is a card-level field. The targeted-removal readers do produce the hint, as
`spellFlags.removesACreature`, but `triggerFromLine` drops `spellFlags` deliberately and says why in
a comment: "it is advice about casting a spell, and a triggered ability is not cast". That is right
about the ability and wrong about the card, so the flag was unreachable on the permanent path.

### Where it belongs instead

`exileUntilLeavesShapeFor` — the whole-card reader that already pairs the exile with the return, and
the only reader here that holds the `CardDef`. That matters because the flag's own docblock makes it
a fact about the whole card: *"this card's whole effect is to remove a creature"*, and *"not for a
card that is good without a creature to kill"*. A per-line reading could only guess at what the rest
of the text does.

The rule is two tests, and the pool prints a card that each one is the only thing excluding:

| card | printed | flag | which test keeps it off |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Journey to Nowhere | Enchantment, exiles a creature | yes | — |
| Banisher Priest | Creature — Human Cleric, same text | no | the host is a creature |
| Banishing Light | Enchantment, exiles a *nonland permanent* | no | the spec is not a creature |

Both are exactly the distinctions the hand-written scripts already draw, and Journey's own docblock
has stated the first one since #48: the Priest "is a 2/2 worth casting for the body alone, while
this is two mana for an enchantment that sits there doing nothing if its entry trigger finds nothing
to point at". So this is reading a judgement the pool already made off printed data, not inventing
one — and adding it produced no new disagreement anywhere.

### Measured

No coverage change — **402 of 538 lines (74.7%)**, 256 of 339 with a script, 228 complete. The flag
is a hint for the bot's waste rule, not a line of text, so nothing moved. Disagreements **1 → 0**.

Four deliberate breaks, four failures, each naming a different card: the condition always true
(Banisher Priest, Banishing Light and the standing check), the type-line test dropped (Banisher
Priest), the spec-kind test dropped (Banishing Light), and the flag never set (Journey).

### What the empty table is for

The table being empty is the state to keep it in. A new disagreement is now a row somebody has to
explain and settle, not a row to add — and the test asserts equality against the table rather than
mere membership, so a stale row fails as loudly as a missing one.

## D423 — Damage with no target, and the payoff that changes its number

First increment off the compiler's own work queue since the disagreement list closed. Three cards,
one sentence read in two halves — **where** the damage goes and **how much** of it there is — and
neither half was any use to the pool without the other.

### `sweepDestination`: a sweep is a destination, not a target

"Each creature with flying and each player" is one damage event's recipients. Nothing is chosen,
nothing can be made illegal, nothing goes on the stack for an opponent to answer by killing the
thing it points at — so it is read apart from `targetSpecFrom`, and the amount is handed in.

One function, because there were about to be two. `xSpellResolution` already spelled out the bare
"each creature" for Savage Twister, and `damageEffect` read none of this at all, so the
printed-number cards had no path. Two spellings of one phrase is #319's defect in a new place.

Three things taken from the hand-written cards rather than invented:

- **The keyword must be one the engine knows.** `isKeyword` refuses anything else, so a sweep
  filtered by a word this engine cannot test is an unread line (D362) rather than a sweep that
  quietly hits everything. D259's rule applied to a filter.
- **"And each player" is every seat, the caster's own included** — Hurricane and Breath of Darigaaz
  both loop `state.seats` and skip only the eliminated.
- **The creature list is taken once**, before any damage is dealt, as both hand-written cards do.

### `kickerSpellFor`: the declaration and its payoff, or neither

`keywordScriptFor`'s docblock had already named kicker as deliberately absent from its
alternative-cost table, with the reason: the payoff is on another line, so "the declaration alone is
an option to pay more for nothing, which is not the card". That argument is the specification, so
this is a **whole-spell** shape — the spell path's equivalent of an Aura on the permanent path — and
it runs before the keyword loop, which would otherwise report the declaration as an unimplemented
keyword and refuse the resolution line separately. Both of the pool's kicker burn spells did exactly
that.

Narrow on purpose: two printed lines, and a resolution of "deals N damage to <somewhere>" then "if
this spell was kicked, it deals M damage instead". **Agonizing Demise also has kicker and is not
this shape** — kicked, it throws the dead creature's power at that creature's controller, which is a
different effect rather than a bigger number — so it stays unread rather than being forced through a
reading about numbers.

### `damageDestination`, factored out

Both readers need the same four destinations and disagree only about the number, so the destination
table moved out of `damageEffect`: "you", "each opponent", a sweep, or a target spec, each returning
an `apply(context, amount)` plus whatever the destination decides — the targets, and the
`removesACreature` hint where the spec is creature-only (D420).

### A negative result: the zero guard cannot be told from its absence

The sweep was first written with the hand-written cards' `if (amount <= 0) return state`. A break run
deleting it failed nothing, and the reason is that `dealDamage` opens with `if (amount <= 0) return
state` itself. So the branch was a check that cannot fail — **D415's lesson, found a second time** —
and it is deleted rather than kept. What replaced it is a test that pins the equality: the compiled
Hurricane with no branch against the hand-written one with a branch, both at X=0. If `dealDamage`
ever stops refusing zero, that fails here instead of diverging quietly. `damageDestination`'s three
inherited branches are left alone and the docblock now says they are belt and braces rather than
claiming they are load-bearing.

### A test that recorded the gap as a property, for the fifth time

"Does not read a list of recipients as a sequence of clauses" asserted that Hurricane's phrase left
the card **unread**. The property worth guarding was never that — it is that the "and" is not a
clause boundary. Re-pointed onto the board: the flier takes the damage, the grounded 0/4 takes none,
and every seat loses the life. Same family as the four D419 found.

### Measured

**407 of 538 lines (75.7%)**, up from 402 — Hurricane (1 line), Burst Lightning (2) and Breath of
Darigaaz (2). Cards with a script **256 → 259 of 339**; cards with every printed line read
**228 → 231 of 339**. The three are exactly the cards that left the incomplete list; nothing else
moved. 4000 shuffled rows compile with 0 throws.

Six deliberate breaks, six failures: the sweep never reaching the players, the with/without filter
ignored, an unknown keyword accepted as a filter, the kicked amount never chosen, no `kicker` field
emitted, and `damageDestination` skipping the sweep so a printed-number sweep fell through to a
target spec.

## D424 — Printed protection, one classifier for three readers, and a figure that was wrong

Second increment off the work queue, and it ends with a correction to a number this log has been
quoting for four entries.

### The hole: an unscripted card had no protection at all

`Characteristics.protectionFrom` was set **only** by a continuous effect. So a card with no script
had no protection however plainly its text printed it — exactly the hole `printedLandwalk` closed
for landwalk in #324, and it matters for the same reason: the corpus #318 imports is unscripted by
definition, and protection is common in it.

`printedProtection` reads it. Colour words spelled out, both printings of two colours ("black and
from red" is Paladin en-Vec's, "black and red" the other), and **anything that is not a colour
refused** — *protection from everything*, *from all colors*, *from creatures*. The field is a list
of colours, and a card promising more than that is a card for a human to play (D362), not a card
given protection from nothing and reported as read.

### One classifier, because there were three whole-line rules

`printedKeywords`, `printedLandwalk` and `printedProtection` each wanted a different slice of the
same classification, and the first two each had their own copy of the whole-line rule. That is how
**Phyrexian Crusader's line ended up read by none of them**: "First strike, protection from red,
protection from white, infect" is four printed abilities in one list, so `printedKeywords` refused
the whole line because two parts were not keywords and `printedLandwalk` refused it because none
were landwalks. An unscripted creature printing exactly that had no first strike, no infect and no
protection.

`printedPart` classifies one comma-part; the three readers take their own kind out of the result.
The rule widens in the faithful direction — every part must be an ability the engine can model,
mixed freely — and keeps the half that mattered: a part it cannot model refuses the whole line, so
"target creature gains protection from red" is a sentence, not a list.

### Two cards now have no script at all, and a third lost a static

`compile.ts` counts a printed ability line compiled and emits nothing, because restating it in a
script would be a second source for one fact. That check asked `printedKeywords` alone, so three
lines were reported unread on cards the engine was already playing: River Boa's `Islandwalk`,
Paladin en-Vec's protection, Phyrexian Crusader's mixed list. It asks `isPrintedAbilityLine` now.

With the lines read, the statics restating them are the Basilica Guards case again (D419):

- **River Boa** lost its islandwalk static — found by the standing check, which failed the moment
  the compiler counted the line as read, because the compiled card had no static and the
  hand-written one did. #324 had left it in place "because the reading was added the same day"; that
  reason has expired. The Squid token's identical static went with it, and the test that pinned the
  token's islandwalk now pins the printed reading, which is what a token from printed data relies on.
- **Paladin en-Vec** and **Phyrexian Crusader** have **no scripts at all**. Everything they print is
  read off the card definition. The protection suite from #83 — damage, equipping, blocking and
  targeting, all four of CR 702.16 — therefore exercises the printed reading now, at no cost to what
  it asserts.

The deck-coverage test's `keywordsOnly` helper was the other place that re-derived this question
from `printedKeywords`, and it reported both cards as missing a script. It asks the compiler's own
predicate now: one question, one answer.

### Correction: "cards with a script" has been over-counted since D417

This log has quoted 251 → 256 → 259 "cards with a script", worked out as the measure's `whole-card +
lines` source categories. **That is not what those categories mean.** A card on the whole-card path
reports that source even when `cardFromData` decides it needs no script at all, so the sum
over-counts by every vanilla creature on it.

The real figure, measured rather than inferred, is **236 of 339**. `compilable.mjs` now counts and
prints it directly, along with cards whose every printed line is read and how many of those need no
script — so the number quoted comes from the instrument instead of from arithmetic on something
else. The *line* and *complete* series were measured directly all along and stand: 402 → 407 → 410
lines, 228 → 231 → 234 complete.

### Measured

**410 of 538 lines (76.2%)**, up from 407 — River Boa, Paladin en-Vec, Phyrexian Crusader. Cards
with every printed line read **231 → 234 of 339**, and **25** of those 234 need no script at all.
Cards with a compiled script: 236 of 339.

Five deliberate breaks, five failures: protection parts never classified (12 rows), the printed
protection not seeded into `characteristicsOf` (8), a non-colour accepted as a protection, the
whole-line rule dropped so a sentence classifies, and the compiler back to asking `printedKeywords`
alone.

## D425 — Three ability words whose whole instruction is their own reminder text

Third increment off the work queue, and the first keywords here that build a **trigger** out of a
bare word rather than setting a field.

Exalted (CR 702.90a), evolve (CR 702.100a) and battle cry (CR 702.91a) are each one printed word
with nothing else on the card for them, no number implied and no second line to miss. So the
declaration *is* the ability, which is exactly what D364 asks of a keyword before it is safe to
read: the unit of compilation is the whole thing, and here the whole thing is the word.

What makes building a trigger from a word safe is `echo`'s arrangement, and `ninjutsuAbility`'s
(D421): the trigger is written **once**, in a factory the hand-written card calls too. So there is
one implementation of each keyword rather than two spellings free to drift, and the standing check
compares them for free.

Three details that are the rule rather than the effect, each taken off the hand-written card:

- **`alone: true`** on exalted. It watches *any* creature its controller attacks with, not itself —
  a Guardians of Akrasa that stays home still pumps the attacker — and only when that creature
  attacks alone.
- **The intervening-if** on evolve, asked again on resolution through `evolvesInto`, so a creature
  killed in response evolves nothing (CR 702.100a).
- **The word "other"** in battle cry. A Goblin Wardriver attacking alone pumps nothing.

### Measured

**413 of 538 lines (76.8%)**, up from 410. Cards with a compiled script **236 → 239 of 339**; cards
with every printed line read **234 → 237**. Keyword declarations with no builder **20 → 17**. The
three cards are exactly the ones that left the incomplete list.

Five deliberate breaks, five failures, and worth noting *which* tests caught them: exalted losing
`alone: true` and battle cry pumping itself failed one row each — the existing engine tests from
#114 and #165, which now exercise the factories because the hand-written cards call them. Evolve
dropping its condition failed two, the reader emitting no trigger for exalted failed two, and the
reader passing the wrong name to the evolve factory failed one.

## D426 — The corpus, from a source this container can actually reach

#318 — "every competitive-legal card, from Scryfall bulk data" — has been blocked since it was
filed, and re-tested on every pass: `api.scryfall.com` and `data.scryfall.io` both answer 403 to
CONNECT, and so do `mtgjson.com` and `api.magicthegathering.io`. Every card-data host this project
would reach for is denied.

### What is not denied

Reading the proxy's own status (`$HTTPS_PROXY/__agentproxy/status`) rather than guessing: its
`noProxy` list carries `registry.npmjs.org`, `pypi.org`, `files.pythonhosted.org`, `index.crates.io`
and `proxy.golang.org`, and **GitHub is allowed** — `git ls-remote` over https works through the
session's git proxy and `raw.githubusercontent.com` answers 200. (`api.github.com` answers too, but
is governed per-repository and refuses anything outside this session's scope.)

So the corpus can come out of a public repository that keeps card data **in git**, and
`Card-Forge/forge` does: one plain-text file per card under `forge-gui/res/cardsfolder`, 34,134 of
them. A blobless, depth-1, sparse fetch of that one directory is 159 MB.

### What is taken, and what deliberately is not

`scripts/corpus/from-forge.mjs` reads the **printed card data** — name, mana cost, type line, power,
toughness, loyalty and the `Oracle:` text — which is exactly `CardDataRow`, which is exactly what
Scryfall's bulk file provides. So `compilable.mjs --file` and D329's importer read it unchanged.

Forge's own `A:`/`T:`/`S:` ability scripts are **not** taken. They are a different engine's DSL, and
copying their semantics would import a second implementation of the rules that nothing here could
verify — the opposite of what the compiler is for.

Two gaps stated rather than glossed:

- **Fidelity.** Forge's `Oracle:` lines are a community transcription, not the canonical Oracle
  feed, so a line can lag an errata. D259's rule applies to the source as much as to the reader, so
  this is recorded as a **second-best source**: the moment Scryfall egress opens, the same flag
  takes the real bulk file.
- **Legality is not filtered.** Forge's files carry none; it lives in Scryfall's and MTGJSON's
  `legalities`, both unreachable. `rebalanced/` and `upcoming/` are skipped by directory and the
  silver-bordered cards are kept, which makes the coverage figure **pessimistic** rather than
  flattering — the safe direction. The candidates for closing it are the Scryfall file itself or a
  package from one of the registries the proxy does not govern.

### The real numbers, for the first time

| | pool (339) | corpus (33,847) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Printed lines compiled | 413 of 538 (76.8%) | **14,472 of 60,940 (23.7%)** |
| Cards with a compiled script | 239 of 339 (70.5%) | 5,506 of 32,948 (16.7%) |
| Cards with every printed line read | 237 of 339 (69.9%) | 3,328 of 32,948 (10.1%) |
| …of those, needing no script at all | 25 | 1,064 |
| Not a single-face card at all | 9 | 899 |

The pool was always described as a floor on difficulty and a ceiling on coverage — thirteen decks
built by hand to exercise sixty mechanics. Now there is a number that is neither.

**No throws.** `compilable.mjs` calls `compileCard` with no try/catch, so compiling all 33,847 rows
and exiting 0 is the crash hunt over the whole corpus, not a sample of 4,000.

### The work queue is now the real one

13,614 distinct openings, 9,434 printed by a single card. The top buckets are not what the pool's
leftovers were, and one of them is a **systematic miss the pool could never show**:

      1168  At the beginning of your …
       578  Enchant creature  [keyword]
       476  ~ deals N damage to …
       367  When ~ enters you may …
       349  Whenever ~ deals combat damage …
       347  ~ enters tapped
       314  At the beginning of each …
       312  Choose one
       307  {T}: Add {M} or {M}
       276  Whenever a creature you control …

Four of those openings — 367 + 347 + 218 + 147 + 138 and more besides — are the **modern "enters"
templating**. Wizards retemplated "enters the battlefield" to "enters" in 2024, every reader in this
compiler was written against the old wording, and the pool's hand-written card data uses the old
wording too. So the single biggest miss in the corpus is a spelling the pool is structurally unable
to reveal, which is the clearest argument for having built this that I could have asked for.

## D427 — The templating the pool was structurally unable to reveal

The first increment off the **corpus** work queue, and the largest single change the compiler has
had: one aliasing change, **+1,286 printed lines**.

### What was wrong

Wizards shortened "enters the battlefield" to "enters" in 2024, and made "this creature" the way a
card refers back to itself. Every reader in `scripts.ts` was written against the long form and
against the card's own name — and so is the engine's own card data, because the thirteen decks were
written by hand from memory.

So the pool could never show it. D426's corpus counts the gap: of 33,847 cards, **5,898** print
"enters," and **47** still print "enters the battlefield"; about **860** say "this creature enters"
or the same of an artifact, enchantment, land or permanent.

### The change

Two constants, used everywhere the old spelling was written out:

- `ENTERS = 'enters(?: the battlefield)?'` — eight regex sites, including the three
  "another creature enters" prologues and `entersWith`.
- `selfRef(name)` — the card's name **or** "this creature / artifact / enchantment / permanent /
  land / planeswalker / battle / Vehicle / Equipment / Aura / token / card / spell", replacing
  `escapeName(name)` at all thirteen reader sites. A non-capturing group, so no capture index moves.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corpus lines compiled | 14,472 of 60,940 (23.7%) | **15,758 of 60,940 (25.9%)** |
| Corpus cards with a script | 5,506 (16.7%) | **6,630 (20.1%)** |
| Corpus cards with every line read | 3,328 (10.1%) | **3,833 (11.6%)** |
| Pool lines compiled | 413 of 538 (76.8%) | 413 of 538 (76.8%) |

The pool is unchanged, which is the point: a wider pattern still matches the old wording, and the
standing compiled-vs-written check agrees with all 236 hand-written cards exactly as before.

### The over-match, probed rather than assumed

"This creature" on a card that is not a permanent cannot mean the source — so if printed text ever
used it to mean something else, the alias would read a spell's quoted granted ability as the spell's
own trigger, which is the one outcome D362 calls worse than an unread line.

It does, inside quotes: Abnormal Endurance grants `"When this creature dies, return it to the
battlefield tapped under its owner's control."` So the risk was measured over the corpus: of the
**111** instants and sorceries whose text says "this creature" or the same of another permanent
type, **five** compile to a script at all, and all five are a bare keyword declaration —
`flashback`, `split second`, `escape` — with no trigger and no resolution. A spell's lines are its
resolution, so the prologue readers are never asked about them, and the clause readers refuse quoted
text.

### An untested claim, recorded as one

Four deliberate breaks: dropping the `enters` alias (6 rows), dropping the self-reference (2),
keeping only the short form (42 — which is the pool's own data, all of it in the long form), and
**adding "that creature" to the self-reference list, which failed nothing.**

That last one is not a hole in the test; it is the test being about something else. On a spell no
word list can matter, because the prologue readers are never consulted, so the quoted-ability row
guards the **path split** and not the list. The list's exclusion of "that" rests on a templating
argument — printed text says "this" for the object an ability is on and "that" or "it" for something
else — and **nothing in the pool or in a fixture discriminates it today**. Written down as an
untested claim rather than left looking covered, which is D415's and D423's lesson a third time: a
check that cannot fail is worse than no check, because it reads as one.

## D428 — A one-line reader that was the fourth-biggest bucket in Magic, and two steps

Second increment off the corpus queue: **+438 lines**, and the clearest demonstration yet of what
the pool was hiding.

### "~ enters tapped"

`cardFromData` has read this phrase since D331. The reason it was still the corpus's fourth-largest
bucket, 347 cards, is that the whole-card path reads it **only as part of a whole card it can
account for** — so a land printing nothing else was read, and a land printing one more line that
path could not take reported the tapped clause as unread *and lost the other line with it*, because
the whole-card path is all-or-nothing and the per-line path had no reader for the clause at all.

`entersTappedFromLine` is that reader, placed ahead of the statics because arriving tapped is a fact
about the arrival rather than a continuous effect. Both spellings of the subject through `selfRef`:
the corpus prints "Joined Up enters tapped" and "This land enters tapped" in similar numbers, and
`fromCardData`'s own check compares the rest of the string after the name, so it reads the first and
not the second.

The conditional arrival — "enters tapped **unless** you control two or more other lands" — is
refused by the anchor, and asserted: reading it as the plain field would be a land that always
arrives tapped, strictly worse than the printed card.

### The two steps a card names after the upkeep

"At the beginning of your **draw step**" and "At the beginning of **combat on your turn**" are the
same `step` trigger the upkeep and end-step prologues already build, with a different step — and the
engine has had both steps since #10. 1,168 corpus cards open "At the beginning of your …" and 258
"At the beginning of combat on your turn".

"On your turn" rather than "your" is how printed text says it for a combat step, so only the printed
spelling is read.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corpus lines compiled | 15,758 of 60,940 (25.9%) | **16,196 of 60,940 (26.6%)** |
| Corpus cards with a script | 6,630 (20.1%) | **6,860 (20.8%)** |
| Corpus cards with every line read | 3,833 (11.6%) | **3,874 (11.8%)** |
| Pool | 413 of 538 (76.8%) | unchanged |

### A test gap the breaks found, and a break that was not one

Six deliberate breaks. Three failed straight away: no enters-tapped reader (4 rows), an unanchored
pattern letting the conditional arrival through (1), and the combat prologue aimed at `end-combat`
instead of `begin-combat` (1).

Two needed fixing rather than recording:

- **Deleting the draw-step prologue row broke the file**, so vitest collected nothing and reported
  "no tests" — which is not a passing break, it is no break. Redone as an unmatchable pattern:
  2 rows fail.
- **Widening the draw-step prologue to "each opponent's" failed nothing.** The negative row
  described the *upkeep* alone, so "`of: 'you'` is the card saying your" was asserted for one
  prologue and assumed for the two new ones. The row is now a table over all three, plus the end
  step, and both widening breaks fail.

That second one is the useful kind of break: it did not find a bug in the reader, it found a claim
in the tests that was not being made.

## D429 — Cycling, and the landfall trigger the engine had a field for and no card

Third increment off the corpus queue: **+347 lines**, and two cards out of the pool's incomplete list
as well.

### Cycling (192 corpus cards)

"Cycling {2}" means "{2}, Discard this card: Draw a card" and nothing else is printed on the card for
it, so the declaration *is* the ability — D364's condition for reading a keyword, and the same shape
as ninjutsu (D421) and the three ability words (D425). `cyclingAbility(mana)` is the factory, and
Compelling Argument's hand-written script now calls it, so the two readings are one ability.

`discardSelf` is the half of the cost that is not mana, and it is what tells `collectLegalActions`
the ability is used **from the hand** and spends the card.

**Only plain cycling.** Landcycling, basic landcycling and the typed cyclings put a card of a named
kind into your hand out of your *library*, which needs a filter this reader would have to invent
(D259) — so they are reported rather than read as a draw, which is a different card. Asserted as its
own row, and a break widening the pattern to `\w*cycling` fails it.

### Landfall (184 corpus cards)

`TriggerDef`'s `what: 'land'` has existed since #163, with a docblock calling it "the landfall
templating" and noting that "until a card asked, nothing could hear it". This is the card asking.

`landfall` joins `ABILITY_WORDS`, so `withoutAbilityWord` strips it before the prologue table is
consulted and "Landfall — Whenever a land you control enters, …" and the same sentence without the
word are one row — which is what an ability word is.

### The standing check corrected a hand-written card again

**Tatyova, Benthic Druid** disagreed on `triggers` the moment the compiler could read her line. Her
script said `who: 'another'`, arguing "she is not a land and her own arrival is not one" — true of
her and not of the phrase. "A land you control" includes a land that is itself, and the corpus
prints exactly one such card: **Chocobo Camp**, a land with this trigger, for which `another` would
miss its own arrival. So the general reading wins and her script now says `who: 'any', of: 'you'`,
which for her is a change of wording rather than of behaviour.

That is the fourth hand-written card the check has corrected (after Garruk, Basilica Guards and
River Boa), and the second where the compiler's general rule was simply better than the one card's.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corpus lines compiled | 16,196 of 60,940 (26.6%) | **16,543 of 60,940 (27.1%)** |
| Corpus cards with a script | 6,860 (20.8%) | **7,145 (21.7%)** |
| Corpus keyword declarations with no builder | 3,903 | **3,636** |
| Pool lines compiled | 413 of 538 (76.8%) | **415 of 538 (77.1%)** |
| Pool cards with every line read | 237 | **239** |

The two pool cards that left the incomplete list are exactly Compelling Argument (its `Cycling {U}`)
and Tatyova.

Seven deliberate breaks, seven failures: no cycling reader, cycling without `discardSelf`, the
pattern widened to the typed cyclings, the landfall prologue made unmatchable, landfall watching any
seat's land, landfall watching creatures instead, and `landfall` removed from the ability words.

## D430 — The compiler was never asked by the one path a player's own deck takes

Nine increments of compiler work (D418-D429) had been measured against two things: the 348-card
pool, and the 33,847-card corpus as *text*. Neither of those is the goal. The goal is "no matter
what deck we upload, it enforces the rules of the game", and nothing had ever asked that question,
because nothing played a deck of arbitrary real cards.

`scripts/measure/corpus-decks.mjs` asks it. Two random 60-card decks out of the corpus — 24 basics
in the colours the spells need, 36 distinct non-lands of mana value 6 or less — resolved through
`customDeck` exactly as a pasted list is, then played bot against bot to a finish. It reads three
things a coverage percentage cannot: whether the engine **throws** (`applyAction` is deliberately
not wrapped inside the loop, for D244's reason), whether the table **stalls** (a move that does not
move `stateVersion`, or a position with nobody to act and the game unfinished), and how much of each
deck was automated at all.

The first run answered the goal question, and the answer was no:

> **34.3 of the 60 cards in each deck were cardboard** — a blank with no cost, no type line and
> nothing anybody can do with it.

Not because nothing could read those cards. Because nothing asked. `customDeck`'s `resolve` called
`cardFromData`, which answers the all-or-nothing question *is this card's text nothing but its
data?* — false for every instant, every planeswalker and every creature with a paragraph. The
oracle-text compiler, which by then read 27% of every printed line in Magic, was wired into
`derive.ts` for cards the engine already held and was **never consulted for a card a player
uploaded**. Every increment since #317 opened had been improving a reader that the upload path could
not reach.

`resolve` now calls `compileCard` and keeps `compiled.def`. The cardboard branch stays for a row
`printedDef` refuses — no type line, or more than one face — which is what cardboard now means.

| per 60-card deck of random real cards | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cardboard — nothing playable | **34.3** | **0.3** |
| playable from printed data | 1.4 | **35.3** |
| with a hand-written script | 11.1 | 11.1 |
| with at least one flagged line (D362) | 13.2 | **30.3** |

The table is the same six seeds either side, so it is the same two decks and the same shuffles.
The remaining 0.3 cardboard is D431's refusal, below. Games still reach a finish — and they finish
in 22.5 turns rather than 93.3, because a board now develops instead of two players drawing blanks
at each other for ninety turns.

Widened to 40 games (80 random decks) on the fixed engine: **40 finished, no throw and no stall**,
21.8 turns and 70 moves on average, 9.9 scripted / 35.2 from data / 31.0 with a flagged line / 0.3
cardboard per deck. That is the first time the project has been able to say anything at all about a
deck nobody built.

## D431 — Every creature the compiler dealt was a 0/0, and the state-based actions binned it

D430's measurement was 34.3 cardboard cards replaced by 34.3 playable ones, and one of its new
assertions did not agree: a compiled creature's `power` and `toughness` came back `undefined`.

`printedDef` — "the printed data as a `CardDef`, with no judgement at all" — built the def without
`power`, `toughness` or `loyalty`. It had been that way since it was split out of `cardFromData` in
#317, and it was invisible for as long as its only two callers were `cardFromData`, which adds the
size itself in its creature branch, and `derive.ts`, which takes the compiler's `script` and
`unread` and gets its def from somewhere else entirely. D430 made the compiler's own def the card a
player is dealt, and `characteristicsOf` reads a missing size as zero.

So **every one of the corpus's 18,603 creatures arrived as a 0/0**, and CR 704.5f put it in the
graveyard before anybody had priority. All 327 of its planeswalkers arrived at zero loyalty for
CR 704.5i to do the same. D430 had not turned 34 blanks into 34 playable cards; it had turned 34
blanks into 34 corpses, and the only reason the harness read it as an improvement is that a deck of
corpses still finishes a game faster than a deck of blanks.

Three pieces, and the split between them is the fix:

- **`printedDef` carries the printed size as printed** — `*` and `1+*` included, which is what
  `CardDef.power` is a string for — and omits the field when the card prints none, so a Lightning
  Bolt does not gain two blank ones.
- **`printedBody` and `printedLoyalty`** are the one place that says whether a printed size is a
  number the engine can play. `cardFromData` and `compileCard` both ask, so neither can be more
  generous than the other. This is where the two used to disagree in the worst direction: one
  refused a `*`/`*` creature outright, the other silently dealt every creature sizeless.
- **The compiler refuses what it cannot size**, rather than flagging it for a human (D362). That
  trade does not apply here: a 0/0 is gone before anybody can apply anything by hand, so there is no
  unread line left to be the player's job. Cardboard — the card played manually — is strictly
  better, which is the probe `cardFromData`'s own refusal was built on.

The refusal waits until the text has been read, which is the part worth keeping in mind. A `*`/`*`
creature *is* playable when the compiler read the characteristic-defining ability that sizes it:
Lhurgoyf is a 2/3 with two creature cards in a graveyard and is dealt. Hand Goyf's count ("cards in
your hand") is one `definesSize` does not have, so nothing sizes it and it is refused. And
`definesSize` supplies the toughness only when it does not say `applies: 'power'`, so a `*`
toughness beside a power-only count is refused too while Enigma Drake's printed `4` is kept — the
one asymmetry that a table-driven test pins rather than assumes.

233 of the corpus's 18,603 creatures and 2 of its 327 planeswalkers land in the refusal. That is the
0.3 cards per deck that are still cardboard.

## D432 — Legality was not unavailable, it was in a different part of the same repository

`from-forge.mjs` has said since D426 that format legality could not be had: "Forge's files carry no
legality: that lives in Scryfall's `legalities` object and MTGJSON's, both unreachable." The first
half is true and the second half was a conclusion drawn from it, and the conclusion was wrong. The
*card files* carry no legality. The repository does:

- `forge-gui/res/formats/Sanctioned/*.txt` — one file per sanctioned format, each with a `Sets:`
  allowlist of set codes, a `Banned:` list, and for Pauper a `Rarities:` list.
- `forge-gui/res/formats/Casual/Commander.txt` — a `Banned:` list and **no** `Sets:`, which is
  exactly what Commander is: every paper set.
- `forge-gui/res/editions/*.txt` — one file per set, with `Code=`, `Type=` and a `[cards]` block.

The checkout D426 made was sparse (`blockdata` and `cardsfolder` only), so none of it had been
looked at. Two directories and 12 MB later, `scripts/corpus/legality.mjs` emits Scryfall's own
`legalities` object for 32,591 cards.

**npm and PyPI were the other candidate and are a dead end**, which is worth recording so nobody
spends the afternoon again: every MTG package on npm is a *client* for `api.scryfall.com` or
`mtgjson.com` — `scryfall`, `scryfall-client`, `@scryfall/api-types`, `mtgjson`, `mtgjson-sdk`,
`mtgjson-promise` — and both hosts are refused by the proxy. A client for a blocked host is not a
data source.

### Three judgements, because each one excludes cards

1. **`Type=Funny` sets are legal nowhere** (25 sets) — the un-sets, which the goal excludes by name.
2. **`Type=Online` sets are legal in no paper format** (59 sets) — Alchemy and the digital-only
   products. `from-forge.mjs` already skipped `rebalanced/` for this reason; this catches the rest.
3. **A card whose printed type is not a deck card is legal nowhere** — Scheme, Plane, Phenomenon,
   Vanguard, Conspiracy, Dungeon, Emblem, Attraction, Sticker, Contraption. 384 cards.

Same second-best-source caveat as the oracle text, for the same reason (D259 applies to the source
