as much as to the reader): Forge's banned lists are a community transcription and can lag an
announcement. So the output is Scryfall's shape and Scryfall's vocabulary — `legal`, `banned`,
`restricted`, `not_legal` — and the moment Scryfall egress opens its own object replaces this with
no change to anything downstream.

### The check, and the bug it caught

`--check` asserts 13 cards whose legality is not in dispute, each a *different* way for the parse to
be wrong: a set allowlist unread (Black Lotus is not Modern-legal), a banned list unread (Ponder is
banned in Modern and legal in Legacy), Commander's own banned list (Mana Crypt), Pauper's rarity
rule in both directions (Mountain legal, Thoughtseize not), Vintage's restricted list (Black Lotus),
and the type refusal (an Archenemy scheme, a Planechase plane).

**It failed 2 of 13 on the first run, and the failure was a real defect in this script.** The two
rows read `(no such card)` — the scheme and the plane were not in the printings map at all, so the
type check I had written them down to prove was not what excluded them. The cause: I required a
plain integer collector number, and Forge's numbers are not plain integers. 345 `[cards]` lines use
a star (`1★`, which is how *every* scheme and plane is numbered), 374 a foil suffix (`123F`), 310 a
set prefix (`M-1`), 385 a half suffix (`123a`/`123b`, the halves of a split or flip card). All were
being dropped in silence, and for a card whose only printing carries one that is not cosmetic — it
vanishes from the map and every format reads `not_legal`, which is the most damaging direction a
legality bug can point. The number is now unconstrained and the **rarity letter** is what identifies
a card line; 252 cards came back and all 13 rows agree.

### Measured

`LEGAL=1` on the two measures restricts to the formats the goal names. The filter is **off by
default**, so every figure recorded before it existed is still reproducible.

| | every row | legal in a format the goal names |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cards | 33,847 | **31,654** |
| Lines compiled | 16,448 of 60,460 (27.2%) | **15,869 of 56,421 (28.1%)** |
| Cards with a script | 7,126 | 6,936 |
| Cards fully read | 3,992 | 3,915 |

Filtering **raises** coverage, which is the useful part: the cards it removes are ones the compiler
read worse than average, so the 27.2% was understating the engine against the decks anybody will
actually upload. Random legal-only decks still play: 10 of 10 games to a finish, no throw, no stall,
0.1 cardboard cards per deck.

### What it does to the work queue

The two biggest prologue buckets in the whole corpus were **"Whenever chaos ensues" (136 cards)**
and **"When you set this scheme in motion" (81)** — Planechase and Archenemy. Both are gone. That
was real reader work queued against cards nobody can put in a deck, and it would have been done
before anybody noticed.

### The measurement that redirected the queue

Also built, as a scratch instrument rather than a committed script: for every unread line shaped
like a trigger, keep its prologue and swap the body for "draw a card", then re-compile. If it reads
now, the prologue is fine and the **body** is the gap; if not, the **prologue** is. Of 12,338
distinct trigger-shaped unread lines, **10,196 fail on the prologue and 2,142 on the body**. The
work queue groups by printed opening and the body distribution groups by what follows the comma, and
neither answers the question a reader-writer actually has. Both halves are long tails — 7,060
distinct prologue shapes, 1,489 body shapes — so the next increments are families of prologues, not
single lines.

## D433 — A trigger whose subject is the permanent it is attached to, and three ways that reading was wrong

"Whenever equipped creature attacks, put a +1/+1 counter on it." The compiler had no way to say
that: every trigger it emitted was about the card printing it, and an Equipment is never the
creature the event happened to. 45 corpus cards print the combat-damage version of the prologue and
69 more print the `dies` version, so this is a family rather than a card.

The shape is one field — `who: 'attached'` on `attacks` and on `combat-damage` — resolved at the
call site in `fireTrigger`, where `attachedTo` is known, rather than inside `triggerMatches`, which
only sees the event. Armory of Iroas is the hand-written card that pins it (`{2}`, "Whenever
equipped creature attacks, put a +1/+1 counter on it. / Equip {2}", in Ember Rush), and the compiler
reads its printed text to the same script.

### The break run is the whole story of this entry

Six deliberate breaks, each meant to fail a named test. **Five failed nothing.** The cause was not
five missing tests but one structural hole: `compiled-vs-written.test.ts` skips any card with an
unread line, by design — so every break that makes a line *stop* reading removes the card from the
comparison instead of failing it. A standing check that stops looking is not a check. Four direct
assertions in `compile.test.ts` closed that half. What the remaining breaks then found is worse.

**1. The counter was going on the Equipment.** Deleting the body reader meant to own "put a +1/+1
counter on it" changed nothing: `selfEffect` runs three readers earlier, its clause accepts
`(?:<name>|it)`, and it resolved both to `c.source`. So the compiled Armory of Iroas reported
`unread: []` — fully automated — and grew the sword instead of the creature holding it. That is the
worst shape a reading can take: an unread line gets D362's badge and a human plays it by hand; a
line read *wrongly* is flagged nowhere.

The fix is to tell the two alternatives apart instead of merging them. `itMeans(named, c)`: a clause
that names the card means `c.source` however the trigger was raised; a clause that says "it" means
`c.subject ?? c.source` — the permanent the event was about, falling back to the card where there is
no event, which is every activated ability and every spell by construction. The fallback is what
makes it not a behaviour change for the rest of the pool: a self-subject trigger has
`subject === source`. All four of that reader's bare-"it" clauses were wrong the same way, so all
four are fixed, and the downstream clause is narrowed to "that creature" — the one spelling nobody
else claims — so that if the upstream clause is ever removed the line goes *unread* rather than
falling through to a second reading.

Measured: 411 legal cards print one of those bodies; **54 print it under a prologue about somebody
else**, and the compiler reads the line on **8** of them today — Armory of Iroas, Bone Sabres,
Enduring Courage, Fervent Charge, Gleam of Battle, In the Web of War, Reaper's Talisman, Sword of
Hours. Every one was putting its counter or its pump on the wrong permanent. Each of the four arms
is now pinned by a real printed card.

**2. The combat-damage arm could never be reached.** Setting `triggerMatches`' `combat-damage` case
back to `isSubject` failed nothing either, and the reason was not a missing test: `raise` kept
`combat-damage` in its *self-only* watcher set, so the event was offered to the creature that dealt
the damage and never to the Equipment printing the trigger. The field existed, the matcher had an
arm, and nothing on earth could get an event to it. 45 corpus cards would have compiled with
`unread: []` and done nothing.

Taking the name out of that set is the fix. It is safe because the matcher's default does the
narrowing instead — `who` defaults to `'self'`, which requires `isSubject`, so Thieving Magpie still
draws only for its own damage. And it had to be the **only** change: the watcher condition names the
board-watching events explicitly *and* falls through to the same list for anything unnamed, so
naming `combat-damage` in both places made two independent statements of one thing and no single
break could move it. That is recorded in the comment, because it is the second time in one increment
that redundancy hid a dead branch.

The test for it is a **compiled** card, not a hand-written one: Prying Blade's printed row through
`customDeck`, which is the route a player's own decklist takes (D430). Two goblins attack and one is
wearing the Blade; one Treasure token, not two.

**3. A comment asserting a distinction that does not exist.** `fireTrigger` read the attachment off
`next.instances[holder]` and said it did so because "a granted trigger belongs to the permanent it
was given to, so an Equipment handing a creature its ability would otherwise ask the Equipment's own
attachment". Both call sites pass the holder's *own* instance, the granted one included, so `inst`
names the same permanent and the claim was false. The lookup is kept — it re-reads from `next`
rather than from the snapshot the loop captured, which is right by construction rather than by an
argument about what the loop does not do — and the comment now says that, and says the break cannot
be made to bite.

### Also fixed on the way

A bonus-less Equipment lost its equip ability entirely: `attachmentScriptFor` required a line
beginning "Equipped creature …" and returned nothing without one, so the Armory — which prints no
static bonus — compiled with no equip at all. The static line is optional for an Equipment now and
still required for an Aura, which cannot exist without "Enchant …".

**Nine breaks, eight of which now fail a named test.** The ninth is the holder/`inst` one above, and
it is recorded as provably indistinguishable today rather than as coverage.

## D434 — Eleven of the thirteen steps raised no event, so the cards that named them did nothing

`onEnterStep` raised `{ kind: 'step' }` from inside its `upkeep` case and its `end` case. There is no
case for `begin-combat` at all, and the `draw` case returns its deferred draw without raising
anything. So for eleven of the thirteen steps, a trigger that watched the step could not fire —
not because the matcher was wrong, but because no event ever existed to match.

That was invisible for as long as the only cards asking were an upkeep card and an end-step card.
Then D426 added two prologue rows, and **"At the beginning of combat on your turn" is the third
biggest step bucket in Magic**: 262 legal corpus lines, 19 of them on cards this compiler reads
whole. Every one of those cards compiled with `unread: []`, was reported fully automated, and did
nothing whatsoever. Same for the 18 lines of "At the beginning of your draw step".

**Confirmed by probe before anything was written**, because a claim about an event that does not
exist is exactly the kind that looks obvious and is sometimes wrong: a compiled Luminarch Aspirant
on the battlefield reached declare-attackers with no counter on any creature, nothing on the stack
and nothing in the log.

### One raise, for every step

The fix is to raise it once in `advanceStep`, after the step's own turn-based action and before
`fireDelayed`, and to take the two raises out of `onEnterStep`. That is the printed order either
way — the untap, the draw, the Saga's lore counter and the monarch's card all happen as the step
begins, and what triggers on the step goes on the stack after them.

Every step, `untap` and `cleanup` included, rather than a list of the steps a card can name. A
trigger raised in a step where nobody receives priority waits for the next step that grants it,
which is the rule; and a list would be a second thing to keep in step with `TRIGGER_SHAPES`, which
is the lesson D433 paid for twice in one increment.

The break run shows how much that single line now carries: deleting it fails **37** tests, among
them Phyrexian Arena and Ball Lightning — cards that have worked since #10.

### Three prologue rows out of twelve candidates, and the count that decided it

Twelve printed spellings of "At the beginning of …" were counted in the legal corpus. The number of
*lines* is not what decides a row: a row for a card whose body stays unread changes nothing, because
the line is flagged either way (D362). So every candidate was compiled across the corpus first, and
the column that matters is the last one.

| printed | lines | cards the compiler can finish | shipped |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| each end step / the end step / each player's end step | 152 | **17** | `end`, any |
| each player's upkeep / each upkeep | 149 | **10** | `upkeep`, any |
| your first main phase | 47 | **2** | `precombat-main`, you |
| each opponent's upkeep | 31 | 0 | no |
| each combat | 27 | 0 | no |
| each player's draw step | 13 | 0 | no |
| your second main phase | 10 | 0 | no |
| each opponent's end step | 7 | 0 | no |
| combat on each opponent's turn | 5 | 0 | no |

**`of: 'opponent'` was written and then taken back out.** Three of those spellings need it — 43
printed lines — and not one of them has a body this compiler can read. The field, its matcher arm
and its three rows would have been a mechanism no card exercises, and this repository's own rule is
that an untested mechanism added ahead of need is the one that is wrong when the corpus reaches it.
The counts are recorded in `TriggerDef`'s `step` docblock and in `TRIGGER_SHAPES`' table so the
question is one command to re-ask rather than a family to rediscover.

Also refused, for reasons that are not about counts: "the upkeep of enchanted creature's
controller" (21 lines) wants an *attachment's* seat, which is D433's `who: 'attached'` one level
out rather than `of`; "each of your postcombat main phases" (8) is a turn structure this engine does
not have; "your next upkeep" (5) is a delayed trigger scheduled by an effect, not a prologue.

### A test that pinned the gap instead of the card

`compile.test.ts` asserted that "At the beginning of each end step, draw a card." stays **unread**,
under the heading *"because 'your' is the half that is the rule"*. That was true of what the
compiler did and false of Magic, and the row failed the moment the gap closed — which is the right
behaviour for a test and the wrong content for one. It is retired in place, with the reason and the
new counts written where it stood. The three `each opponent's` rows beside it stay, because those
really are still unread.

### Verified

Four runtime tests, each a **compiled** card from printed corpus text driven through `customDeck` —
the route an uploaded decklist takes (D430) — because a compile-level assertion on the trigger's
shape could not have caught any of this: the shape was already right. Luke Cage for begin-combat
(chosen over eight others in the bucket because its ability takes no target, so the Treasure is the
whole observable), Celestial Force for `of: 'any'` on the opponent's turn, Spark Elemental for "the
end step", Four Knocks for the first main phase, measured across the main phase alone so the draw
step's own card cannot carry the test.

Plus an 18-row compile table for which sentence becomes which trigger, and nine rows asserting the
refused spellings stay unread — each with a body the compiler definitely reads, so the prologue is
the only thing that can leave the line unread.

**Six breaks, six failures.** One honest gap in that: collapsing the *end* row's `of: 'any'` to
`'you'` fails only compile-level rows, because Spark Elemental dies on its own controller's end step
either way. The matcher arm itself is proved at runtime by the upkeep card; the end rows are proved
by shape.

Legal-only coverage 15,964 of 56,421 lines (28.3%), 7,018 cards with a script. The line count barely
moves, and that is the point: the 280 lines this fixes were already *counted* as compiled. They just
did not work.

## D435 — The cast family: four filters that existed, one that did not, and one branch nothing used

`spell-cast` has carried `by`, `spell`, `self` and `how` since the engine's first Guttersnipe. The
compiler could read **three** of the sentences that use them: "you cast an instant or sorcery
spell", "you cast a noncreature spell", "an opponent casts a noncreature spell". Everything else in
the family went unread, which the body/prologue split put at the top of the remaining queue — the
cast cluster is the largest coherent group of prologue gaps left after D434.

Ten candidate spellings, counted in the legal corpus and judged on **cards whose body the compiler
already reads** rather than on lines printed, which is D434's rule and the only measure that
predicts anything: a row for a card whose body stays unread changes nothing, because the line is
flagged either way (D362).

| printed | lines | cards | shipped as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| you cast a creature spell | 44 | **11** | `by: 'you', spell: 'creature'` |
| you cast an enchantment spell | 17 | **9** | `ofType: 'enchantment'` |
| you cast a spell | 49 | **8** | `by: 'you', spell: 'any'` |
| when you cast this spell | 80 | **7** | `self: true` |
| you cast an artifact spell | 21 | **7** | `ofType: 'artifact'` |
| a player casts a spell | 35 | **2** | `by: 'any'` |
| an opponent casts a spell | 27 | **1** | `by: 'opponent'` |
| you cast a historic spell | 19 | 4 | refused |
| you cast a multicolored spell | 19 | 4 | refused |
| an opponent casts a creature spell | 7 | 0 | not yet |

Seven rows, 45 cards. **The two refusals are refused on the mechanism, not the count**, and that
distinction is asserted rather than described: "historic" is artifact *or* legendary *or* Saga and
"multicolored" is a fact about the mana cost, so neither is a card type and neither is expressible
by the new field. A reading that pretended otherwise would fire the ability on the wrong spells,
which is worse than leaving the line for a human. The opponent-creature row is the other kind —
expressible today, held back only because nothing it would read has a readable body yet — and it
sits beside the other two in the test table so the two reasons cannot be confused later.

### One new field, and the shape of its docblock

`ofType` holds one lowercased card type and is compared against the `types` the engine already
raises on the event. It is **separate from `spell` rather than another value in it**, because
`spell` is answered from the engine's creature/noncreature split and this is answered from the type
line: an artifact creature spell is a creature spell *and* an artifact spell, so the two filters
have to be askable together rather than instead of each other.

### `spell: 'creature'` had no user anywhere

It was in the union and it had a comparison in `triggerMatches`, and `grep` found **zero** scripts
setting it. A branch with no user is a branch with no evidence — the same shape that hid a defect
twice in D433 and once in D434 — so it gets a runtime test of both halves rather than a shape
assertion: Beast Whisperer draws for Raging Goblin and does not draw for Lightning Bolt.

### The break run found the hole that mattered

Seven breaks. Six failed a named test immediately. The seventh —

```
if (want.ofType !== undefined && e.spell === 'creature') return false;
```

— rewriting the new filter as the creature/noncreature split it is deliberately *not*, **failed
nothing**, because both `ofType` fixtures agreed with both readings: Bonesplitter is a noncreature
artifact and Raging Goblin is a non-artifact creature. The discriminating case is the one the
docblock's whole argument rests on: an **artifact creature** spell, which is both. **Arcbound
Worker** is now the third row, and the break bites.

That is three increments in a row where a plausible, well-commented claim turned out to have no
test that could contradict it. The pattern is specific enough to name: when a field's docblock
argues that two things must be kept apart, the fixture set needs the case where they *overlap*, or
the argument is decoration.

### Verified

Six runtime tests, every fixture a compiled card from printed corpus text driven through
`customDeck` (the route an uploaded decklist takes, D430), plus a 13-row compile table for
sentence-to-trigger and three rows holding the refusals unread. The four rows whose filters already
had hand-written users — `by` and `spell: 'any'`, driven by Kambal, Chalice of the Void and every
prowess creature — are asserted at the shape level only, and that is stated where it is done.

The `self: true` test also reads the board *after a second spell*, because the failure that is
specific to a compiled permanent is not the trigger missing but the trigger firing again from the
battlefield.

Legal-only coverage 16,016 of 56,421 lines (28.4%), **7,066 cards with a script** (7,018 → 7,066),
3,953 cards with every printed line read. GATE OK, 1,942 engine tests.

## D436 — The second card drawn each turn, and why the ordinal has to travel with the event

After the cast rows, the biggest remaining prologue family by cards finished — measured the way
D434 and D435 were, by swapping a readable body onto every unread line and re-compiling:

| candidate | lines | cards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **you draw your second card each turn** | **54** | **24** |
| a creature you control dies | 27 | 10 |
| you cast your second spell each turn | 32 | 10 |
| a creature you control deals combat damage to a player | 33 | 9 |
| you attack | 87 | 8 |
| enchanted creature dies | 52 | 7 |
| equipped creature dies | 17 | 5 |
| an artifact you control enters | 26 | 5 |
| one or more creatures you control attack | 5 | 0 |
| this creature enters | 337 | 0 |

Twice the next candidate, and the one with the smallest engine change: `cardsDrawnThisTurn` is
already per-seat, and every entry in `GameState.drew` already carries `nth`, the card's place in
its seat's turn. Miracle put it there (D204).

**"this creature enters" is 337 lines and 0 cards**, which is the clearest number in the table for
why lines printed is the wrong measure. That family's prologue reads already; what is unread is 337
different bodies.

### The one thing that could go wrong

The ordinal is carried **on the event** and not looked up from `cardsDrawnThisTurn`, and that is the
whole of the engine work. The running total has already counted *both* cards of a `draw(2)` by the
time either trigger is matched — so a reading taken from the total puts two counters on an Atlantean
Cavalry that drew a Divination, every time, on a card whose entire text is about counting. Miracle
hit this first and its comment in `settle` says so in as many words; this is the second reader to
need the same distinction, so the ordinal is now a field on the event rather than a local in one
loop.

`onNth` is the question and `nth` is the engine's answer, which is the same split
`withAtLeast`/`declared` keeps for battalion and `spell`/`types` for a cast.

### Only "second" is read, and the field is general anyway

Of the 65 legal corpus lines naming an ordinal, **63 say "second"** — 54 "you", 6 "an opponent", 3
"a player" — and the remaining two are one "first" and one "fifth". Three rows shipped, one per
subject. A word-to-number map for five ordinals to gain two lines would be a parser nothing
exercises; `onNth` takes any number the day a card arrives, so the *field* is general and the
*reader* is narrow, which is the right way round.

Alandra, Sky Dreamer prints both: "second" on one line and "fifth" on the next. She is the clearest
case in the corpus for what the hybrid reading is for, and she is now a test — the second-card line
compiles and the fifth-card line is handed to a human with D363's badge, on the same card.

### Verified

Two runtime tests on a compiled Atlantean Cavalry through `customDeck` (D430): no counter from the
draw step's card, exactly **one** counter from a Divination's two, and the count starting again next
turn with the first card taking nothing and a second card taking one. Plus a seven-row compile table
and the Alandra split.

**Five breaks, five failures**, including the one this entry exists for: rewriting the filter to read
`drawnThisTurn(state, seat)` instead of the event's own ordinal fails both runtime tests.

Legal-only coverage 16,055 of 56,421 lines (28.5%), **7,097 cards with a script** (7,066 → 7,097),
3,971 cards with every printed line read. GATE OK, 1,951 engine tests.

## D437 — The death the attachment watches, and three places the board had already forgotten

Three prologue rows, measured on cards finished: "a creature you control dies" (27 legal lines, 10
cards), "enchanted creature dies" (52 lines, 7) and "equipped creature dies" (17 lines, 5). The
first is one line of code. The other two are the family D433 opened and deferred "on a question
about ordering", and that question had an answer: **a defect, in three layers.**

### A probe, before anything was written

A compiled Lead Pipe equipped onto a Raging Goblin, the Goblin killed by a Lightning Bolt: the
opponent's life was unchanged and the Equipment's `attachedTo` was already `null`. `relocate` is the
one place a card changes zone and it detaches everything pointing at the card on the way out — it
has to, or a dead creature's `+2/+0` would sit in `effects` for the rest of the game, which is the
Aura bug D21 found one card type along. So by the time a death is **announced**, nothing on the
board remembers the attachment.

### Layer one: the fact has to travel with the event

`GameState.detached` records what `detachAllFrom` cleared, `settle` drains it into the `dies` events
it raises, and `fireTrigger` prefers the event's answer over the live board:

```ts
const wasAttached = (event as { attachments?: readonly string[] }).attachments?.includes(holder);
... wasAttached ?? (attachedHost !== null && attachedHost === subject)
```

`??` is what makes the two readings one rule: the event's answer when there is one, the board's when
there is not — an attack or a hit still reads the live attachment, because for those it exists.

**This is the third increment running to need a fact the state no longer holds**, after miracle's
draw ordinal (D204, re-used by D436) and the attachment host at the moment of an attack (D433). The
rule those three suggest is now written on the field: *if a trigger has to know something about the
instant its event happened, the event carries it.*

### Layer two: the Aura is not on the battlefield either

The Equipment stays in play (CR 301.5c) and the fix above was enough for it. An Aura does not: CR
704.5m buries it, also before the death is announced, so it was not in anybody's watcher list. Two
more changes, and the first alone did nothing — `raise` splices the event's attachments into the
watcher list, *and* the zone gate that let a `dies` trigger fire from the graveyard "only for the
creature that died" now also lets through a permanent the event was about. Each half has its own
break and the splice-only break fails nothing on its own, which is why both are in the entry.

### Layer three: the Aura could not be read at all

Bequeathal is "Enchant creature / When enchanted creature dies, you draw two cards". It compiled to
a spell with **no target** that attached to nothing and did nothing, because
`attachmentScriptFor` required a bonus line for an Aura — and that requirement is wrong for the
majority of this family: of 55 legal Auras printing "enchanted creature dies", **29 have no bonus
line at all.**

The bonus is optional now, as it has been for an Equipment since D433. The first attempt dropped the
requirement outright and the existing "emits both halves or neither" test failed at once, which is
exactly what it is for: `Enchant creature` as the *whole card* is still refused. The rule is "some
other printed line", not "a bonus line" — and a second line the compiler cannot read is fine, since
the Aura attaches and the line is flagged, which is the hybrid reading working rather than failing.

`friendly` is **omitted** when there is no bonus: Bequeathal wants to be on your own creature and
Banewasp Affliction on theirs, and both print nothing but a trigger, so the bot gets no hint rather
than a wrong one.

### Verified

Four runtime tests, every fixture a compiled card from printed corpus text through `customDeck`
(D430): Original Skullclamp draws two when its own creature dies and nothing when a different
creature dies; Bequeathal — the Aura, the word "When", and the buried-watcher path — draws two;
Phyrexian Vivisector fires its own "a creature you control dies" for its own death, which is the one
word (`any`, not `another`) separating the new row from the one above it, and the only fixture that
can show it, since the other four compilable cards with that line are enchantments. Plus a nine-row
compile table and both directions of the Aura bonus.

**Seven breaks, seven failures.**

Legal-only coverage 16,262 of 56,421 lines (28.8%), **7,284 cards with a script** (7,097 → 7,284).
The jump is mostly layer three: the Aura requirement was blocking every Aura whose second line was
anything but a bonus, not just this family. GATE OK, 1,964 engine tests.

## D438 — The name a card calls itself by, when the card has a title

Oracle text names a legendary permanent in full the first time and by its **short name** after.
*Alesha, Who Laughs at Fate* prints "Whenever Alesha attacks, put a +1/+1 counter on it"; *Bilbo,
Retired Burglar* prints "Whenever Bilbo deals combat damage to a player". `selfRef` matched the full
name and the 2024 "this creature" retemplate (D426) and nothing between, so both lines were lines
nothing could read.

**924 legal cards use their own short name in their own text.** Reading it finishes 71 lines on 70
cards, 11 of which had nothing else left unread — measured by rewriting each card's short name to
its full name and re-compiling, before touching the compiler.

### Why this was worth doing before the next trigger family

The increment queued next was "whenever a creature you control deals combat damage to a player" — 33
legal lines and 9 cards. This one is a single line in `selfRef`, and `selfRef` is read by about
twenty readers: the entry trigger, the attack trigger, the tapped trigger, "enters tapped",
"enters with counters", the activated-ability object, the counter readers. One change, every reader.
It was found while measuring the combat-damage family: the probe's self-name bucket held 476 unread
lines, which is far too many for a prologue the compiler claimed to read, and the reason was the
name.

### The comma is not always a title

`shortName` takes the text before the first `", "`, and the **space is the whole guard**. Three
printed names carry a comma that is a thousands separator: *70,000 Light-Years from Home*,
*Borrowing 100,000 Arrows* and *Guan Yu's 1,000-Li March*. Two of those three have letters before
the comma, so "does it contain a letter" does not tell the two kinds of comma apart — it was in the
first version and the break run showed why it had to go: with the space guard broken, the letter
check still refused "70", so no test moved. Two statements of one rule, and no single break could
reach either (the same trap D433 named). The letter check is gone; no name in 33,847 with ", " in it
has a part before the comma without a letter, so it bought nothing.

### The imprecision that is documented rather than fixed

Every reader in the module matches case-insensitively, and JavaScript cannot switch that off for
part of a pattern — `(?-i:…)` is not in V8. So the alias also matches its own short name spelled as
an ordinary lowercase word. Scanning all 33,847 cards for an alias occurrence spelled differently
from the name found **exactly two**: *Eleven, the Mage* ("your maximum hand size is eleven") and
*Storm, Force of Nature* ("has storm"). Neither clause is one any reader matches, so neither is
misread today — and both are now pinned by a test whose job is to **fail the day the collision
becomes reachable**, which is the guard available when the language will not give the precise one.

### Verified

Three runtime tests, every fixture a printed corpus row driven through `customDeck` (D430): Alesha
takes the +1/+1 counter when Alesha attacks; *Alirios, Enraptured* arrives tapped off a line that is
nothing but its short name and three words; *Ant-Man, Scott Lang* takes a counter from "{4}: Put a
+1/+1 counter on Ant-Man", which is the activated-ability path rather than a trigger. Plus a
six-row compile table over printed rows (including `April O'Neil`, whose apostrophe is what the
escape is for), the title/thousand pair, and the two pinned collisions.

**Two breaks, two failures.**

Legal-only coverage 16,331 of 56,421 lines (28.9%), **7,344 cards with a script** (7,284 → 7,344),
3,997 with every printed line read (3,985 → 3,997). GATE OK, 1,976 engine tests.

Card-data egress re-tested this pass: `api.scryfall.com`, `data.scryfall.io` and `mtgjson.com` all
answer 000 through the proxy, so #318 still loads from the Forge-derived corpus.

## D439 — "A creature you control deals combat damage to a player", and the event that had its own rules

`combat-damage` was the one board event with its own arm in `triggerMatches`:

```ts
case 'combat-damage':
  return (want.who ?? 'self') === 'attached' ? isAttachedSubject : isSubject;
```

Two values of `who`, no `of` at all, and no way to express the commonest printed form of the line —
"whenever **a creature you control** deals combat damage to a player", which is 33 legal corpus
lines and **9** cards this compiler can finish. That sentence is "whenever a creature you control
dies" with a different verb, and the `dies` version has been writable since D437.

### One branch, not two vocabularies

`etb`, `dies`, `attacks`, `blocks`, `becomes-blocked` and `attacks-unblocked` already share a branch,
with a comment saying why: `who` and `of` have to mean the same thing on all of them, and a second
copy of the filter is a second place for them to drift. `combat-damage` is the sixth member and was
outside it, which is exactly the drift that comment predicts. It is folded in and its arm deleted.

Behaviour-preserving for everything already there, and not by inspection: `who` defaults to `'self'`
and that arm requires `isSubject`, `of` defaults to `'any'` and returns before the seat is read — so
a Thieving Magpie and an Equipment's "equipped creature deals combat damage" both read what they
read before, which the existing runtime tests for both still assert.

### Two facts the event did not carry

Folding it in was not enough, and the runtime test is what said so — the compile table was already
green on the trigger's shape:

1. **`subjectSeat`.** `of: 'you'` is answered from it, and the enrichment block that attaches it
   covered `to-graveyard`, `etb` and `dies`. `combat-damage` joins the `to-graveyard` line rather
   than the `etb`/`dies` block, because the creature that connected is still on the battlefield, so
   the live instance is the right read and the `vanished`-first block is not.
2. **`about.subject`.** "Put a +1/+1 counter on **that creature**" needs the creature the event was
   about, and the list of events that carry a subject did not include this one. It never had to:
   while the event was its own permanent's business the subject *was* the watcher, so no card had a
   "that creature" to mean. `who: 'any'` is what creates the distinction.

That is the shape named at D437 showing up again from the other side — not a fact the state has
forgotten this time, but a fact the event never bothered to carry because nothing could ask.

### The plural is refused, deliberately

"Whenever **one or more** creatures you control deal combat damage to a player" is 26 legal lines and
**8** cards — more lines than the row that shipped — and it is left unread. It is a batched trigger
that fires once however many creatures connected, and this engine raises one `combat-damage` event
per creature, so the row would pay Grim Hireling two Treasures *per attacker* instead of two per
combat. A reading that is wrong is worse than a line left unread (D362), so it waits for a batched
event. A test asserts it stays unread, so adding the prologue without the event fails rather than
ships.

### Verified

Two runtime tests, both on **Sphere Grid** — a printed enchantment, which can never be the creature
that deals the damage, so a trigger that fires at all is `who: 'any'` working and a counter that
lands on the attacker is the event's subject reaching "that creature". The pair is the `of: 'you'`
lever: the same board from the other side, an opponent's Grizzly Bears connecting with the Sphere
Grid on the receiving player's side, puts no counter on anything. Plus a five-row compile table
covering the new row, both `attached` spellings, the self-naming row and the refused plural.

**Five breaks, five failures** — the prologue row, `who: 'any'`, `of: 'you'`, the event's
`subjectSeat`, and the event's `about.subject`.

Legal-only coverage 16,340 of 56,421 lines (29.0%), **7,352 cards with a script** (7,344 → 7,352). GATE OK, 1,983 engine tests.

## D440 — "Your second spell each turn", and the count storm cannot be

47 legal corpus lines print "whenever you cast your **second** spell each turn", 17 of them on cards
this compiler can finish — the largest prologue family left after D436's draw ordinal. It is the
cast half of exactly that mechanic, and it needed a count the engine did not have.

### `spellsCastThisTurn` is the table's total, and storm needs it to stay that

Storm counts every spell cast this turn by anybody (CR 702.40a); "your second spell each turn" counts
only yours. One number cannot be both, and at a four-seat table the two differ for most of a turn —
so `GameState.spellsCastThisTurnBy` is a second, per-seat tally beside the first rather than a change
to it.

The ordinal travels on the `spell-cast` event, for the third time in this run of increments and the
same reason D436 wrote on the draw ordinal and D437 on a dying creature's attachments: a trigger that
has to know something about the instant its event happened needs the event to carry it. A Clarion
Spirit whose trigger resolves after a third spell has been cast would read three and do nothing.

### One function for two cast sites

`spellsCastThisTurn + 1` was written out twice — the ordinary cast and the face-down morph — and
adding a second count to both would have been two more statements of one rule, the trap D433 named.
`countCast` is one function returning both tallies, called from both places, so one break can move
it. A morph is a cast (CR 702.37a) and counts like any other spell.

### What shipped and what did not, on the measure

- **"second"**: 47 lines, **17** cards. Shipped.
- **"first"**: 3 lines, **1** card (*Rodeo Pyromancers*, "add {R}{R}"). Shipped.
- **"third"**: 2 lines, **0** cards. Declined — a prologue row for it would read onto two cards whose
  bodies are still unread, which changes nothing (D362) while adding a branch no test can
  discriminate (D425). `TriggerDef.onNth` takes any number the day one of those bodies reads.

### Two ability words, and a finding about the rest of them

Most of this family prints an ability word in front: "Flurry — Whenever you cast your second spell
each turn, …". `ABILITY_WORDS` is a named list of three, and neither `flurry` nor `eukrasia` was on
it, so 14 of the 47 lines were unread for a reason that had nothing to do with the trigger. Both are
on the list now — they are the ability words for *this* mechanic, which is why they arrive here.

Measuring that turned up a bigger one: **2,129 legal unread lines carry a word and an em dash, and
56 of them read once the word comes off** — `exhaust` (44 lines, 15 cards), `alliance` (24, 10),
`boast` (18, 8), `solved` (15, 2), `imprint` (28, 2) and a long tail of one-card flavour names like
"Diana — Equip {2}". That is the next increment, and it is not a list: a general "word then em dash"
rule would also eat a Saga's chapter markers, since "I", "II" and "III" are letters before an em dash
too. Recorded in `ABILITY_WORDS`' own docblock so whoever opens that list finds the number.

### Verified

Three runtime tests, all on printed Clarion Spirit through `customDeck`: a Spirit on the second spell
and none on the first; the count starting again next turn, asserted as **two** Spirits rather than
"still one", because a missing cleanup looks exactly like a trigger that never fires; and the per-seat
lever — seat 1 casts, then seat 0 casts its own first spell, which is the *table's* second, and
nothing happens. Plus a six-row compile table including both ability-word spellings, the plain cast
row that the ordinal rows must not swallow, and the declined third.

**Eight breaks, eight failures.**

Legal-only coverage 16,363 of 56,421 lines (29.0%), **7,374 cards with a script** (7,352 → 7,374),
4,013 with every printed line read (3,997 → 4,013). GATE OK, 1,992 engine tests.

The gate caught one thing the engine suite could not: a conditional spread in the new fixture made
`battlefield[1]` optional, which `tsc -p tsconfig.test.json` refuses and vitest does not typecheck
at all (D246's reason for having that step at all, earning itself again).

## D441 — The label in front of an ability, inverted from an allow list to a refusal list

`withoutAbilityWord` dropped three words: `metalcraft`, `battalion`, `landfall`. Its docblock argued
for a named list on the ground that a general "capitalised word then a dash" rule would also eat a
Saga's chapter markers. The argument is right about the hazard and wrong about the conclusion, and
the corpus is what settles it.

**Of 2,733 legal lines carrying a letters-only label and an em dash there are 540 distinct labels**,
and most of the ones whose remainder this compiler can read are named on *one card*: "Rosarius",
"Keen Senses", "Gae Bolg", "Blade of Magnus". Universes Beyond prints a flavour name where older
cards print a shared ability word, and both are the same thing — flavour with no rules meaning
(CR 207.2c). A list naming them would be a list of cards.

So the question is inverted: a label comes off **unless it has a rules meaning**. Three things do,
each measured:

1. **A keyword ability's name** — `KEYWORD_ABILITY_NAMES`, matched on the whole label *and* on its
   first word. There the em dash joins a keyword to its **cost**: "Cumulative upkeep—Put a -1/-1
   counter on Aboroth", "Escape—{2}{R}, Exile three other cards", "Flashback—{1}{G}, Pay 3 life",
   "Suspend X—{X}{3}{U}", "Splice onto Arcane—Exile four cards". Dropping "Cumulative upkeep" turns
   a price into an unconditional effect. Both checks are needed and neither is redundant: the whole
   label catches "cumulative upkeep", the first word catches "Suspend X" (whose digit sibling
   "Suspend 3" the label pattern refuses anyway).
2. **`ward` and `channel`**, two keyword abilities that list does not name — it names the keywords
   whose *declaration* this module recognises, and those two are read elsewhere. 51 legal lines
   print "Ward—<cost>" and 40 "Channel — <ability>", and a channel ability is activated from your
   **hand**.
3. **A Saga's chapter markers** (CR 714): `I`, `II`, `III`, `IV` are letters before an em dash like
   any label, and they carry **473 legal lines**.

### The judgement: three keywords whose remainder would read

`Exhaust` (43 lines, 15 readable), `Boast` (18, 8) and `Max speed` (40, 5) print
"<keyword> — <activated ability>", so stripping the label *would* finish 28 cards. They are refused
anyway, because **the keyword is the restriction on the ability**: an exhaust ability may be
activated only once, a boast ability only during your turn and only after that creature attacked.
Read the remainder on its own and the engine offers an unrestricted ability — 28 wrong readings
rather than 28 lines left unread, which is the trade D362 settles the other way.

### Six refusals, and the honest note about which can be tested

Every printed line carrying `Ward`, `Channel`, `Suspend X`, `Splice onto Arcane` or a chapter marker
has a remainder this compiler cannot read either way, so a fixture built from a real card would pass
whether the refusal were there or not — the check-that-cannot-fail shape this log keeps naming. They
are pinned on a **probe sentence** the compiler definitely reads instead, with `Keen Senses` as the
control, so each guard fails the day a reader makes its collision reachable.

### Verified

One runtime test on printed **Owlbear** through `customDeck` — "Keen Senses — When Owlbear enters,
draw a card." — which needs the label off *and* the trigger to fire. A three-row compile table on
printed rows (a one-word flavour name, a three-word one, and `Metalcraft`, so nothing the allow list
read stops reading), a four-row refusal table on printed rows (cumulative upkeep, boast, exhaust,
and a digit in the label), and the seven-row probe table above.

**Six breaks, six failures.**

### One existing test retired, in place

`compile.test.ts`'s "strips only the ability words it knows, and refuses the rest" asserted the
decision this entry reverses — that `Constellation — <static>` compiles to no script at all. The row
is rewritten rather than deleted, with the old claim and the reason it went quoted in its comment,
and what survives is the invariant that was always the valuable half: **a label changes nothing
about the reading**, now asserted for any label rather than for the three the list happened to name.

Legal-only coverage 16,400 of 56,421 lines (29.1%), **7,405 cards with a script** (7,374 → 7,405),
4,032 with every printed line read (4,013 → 4,032). GATE OK, 2,007 engine tests.

The worker restarted mid-increment and took the scratch Postgres and Redis with it, so the first
gate run stopped at `services-up.js` — which is exactly the trap that script exists for, since
turbo's cache would otherwise have printed a page of passing tests without either service running
(D303). Restarted both; the gate is green on a real Postgres 16 and Redis.

## D442 — "Whenever you attack": one event for the declaration, not one per creature

92 legal corpus lines print "Whenever you attack" and **8** of them are cards this compiler can
finish — the largest prologue family left after D440. Five more print the longer spelling of the same
sentence, "Whenever one or more creatures you control attack".

It could not be read off `attacks`, and not because of a missing filter. `attacks` is about a
*creature*, so the declaration handler raises it once per attacker; "whenever you attack" is about
the **declaration**, and fires once however many creatures were in it (CR 508.1). Any reading taken
from `attacks` would have made Adeline create a token per opponent *per attacker*, and Bard draw
three cards for a three-creature swing. That is the shape D439 refused for the plural combat-damage
line, met from the other side — and this time the fix is the event rather than the refusal.

### The new event

`{ kind: 'attack-declared' }`, raised once at the end of the declaration handler, **only when at
least one attack was declared** — "one or more" said out loud, and the engine's own log line for the
other case is "attacks with nothing". `by` defaults to `'you'` and is the only form printed; the
other two values exist so that `by` means the same three things here as everywhere else in the file.

Three details inherited rather than written:

- **Myriad raises nothing**, for the reason `myriadCopies`' own comment already gives: a myriad token
  was never declared as an attacker (CR 508.4), so it is no more part of this declaration than it is
  part of battalion's count. The new raise sits after that call and reads `attacks`, which is the
  declaration and not the board.
- **After the per-attack loop.** The two sets of triggers are simultaneous (CR 508.1) and within one
  player's batch the order on the stack is that player's own choice, so the engine picks one.
- **Every permanent sees it.** The event has no subject, so `raise` falls through to the whole
  battlefield and the `by` filter is the only thing narrowing it — which is what the opponent test
  checks.

### Five variants refused, each with its count

Every other printed shape carries a restriction this event cannot express, and reading one as the
bare declaration would be a wrong reading of a real card (D362): "with three or more creatures" (8
legal lines), "with one or more <type>" (8), "a player" (7), "with two or more creatures" (6), "with
your commander" (2), "while creatures you control have total power 8 or greater" (2). Six compile
rows assert they stay unread, so widening a prologue row to swallow one fails.

### Verified

Four runtime tests on printed **Bard, Heir of Girion** through `customDeck`. The one that matters is
a pair on one board: attack with one creature and with all three, and the draw is **one card either
way** — read off `attacks` the second row draws three. Plus the empty declaration (draws nothing) and
an opponent's declaration (draws nothing). A two-row compile table, the six refusals, and the row the
new ones must not swallow: "Whenever ~ attacks" is still `{ kind: 'attacks' }`.

**Six breaks, six failures.**

### The mechanic-coverage test needed a decision, and it has one

`deck coverage > has a card behind every mechanic it declares` failed on
`trigger attack-declared`, which is #223's check working exactly as designed: D229's rule is that a
mechanic needs a card to exist in the pool, and that test reads "a card" as "a card in one of the
thirteen starter decks".

**That reading predates the compiler.** Since D430 a `TriggerEvent` kind can have cards — printed,
real, tested — without any of them being in a built-in deck, and adding a card to a deck whose
balance has been measured since #96 to satisfy a test would be the tail wagging the dog. So the test
now carries a small `compilerOnly` exemption set, and an entry has to **name its evidence**: the
corpus count, and the runtime block that drives a compiled card through `customDeck` and asserts the
mechanic does what the card says. A second assertion keeps the exemptions honest in the other
direction — each one must *still* be an orphan in the pool, so an entry left behind after its card
arrives in a deck is reported rather than carried for ever. The control row (a mechanic nothing can
possibly carry) is untouched.

Legal-only coverage 16,408 of 56,421 lines (29.1%), **7,411 cards with a script** (7,405 → 7,411),
4,036 with every printed line read. GATE OK, 2,020 engine tests.

## D443 — The batched hit, which D439 refused and D442's answer unlocked

"Whenever **one or more** creatures you control deal combat damage to a player" is 26 legal corpus
lines and **8** cards this compiler can finish. D439 measured it, read it, and **refused to ship
it**, because `combat-damage` is raised once per creature that connected — so the row would have paid
a Grim Hireling two Treasures per *attacker* instead of two per hit. That refusal was recorded with
a test asserting the line stays unread, and the reason: a wrong reading is worse than a line left
unread (D362).

D442 built the batched event for the attack declaration. This is the same move for the damage, and
the two now sit side by side: `attacks` / `attack-declared` for the declaration, `combat-damage` /
`combat-damage-dealt` for the hit. In each pair the first is about a creature and raised per
creature, the second is about the event and raised once.

### Once per damaged player, and the templating is the evidence

The batch is keyed on a **pair** — whose creature, and who it hit — not on the combat. *Anowon, the
Ruin Thief* prints "whenever one or more Rogues you control deal combat damage to a player, **that
player** mills a card for each 1 damage dealt to them", and "that player" can only mean one. So a
swing that splits between two opponents is two hits and two triggers, which is also the only reading
that makes `defender` a single seat.

In a duel the two readings agree, so this is tested in a **pod**: two creatures, two opponents, four
Treasures. Keying the batch on the seat alone fails exactly that row and nothing else.

### Verified

Four runtime tests on printed **Grim Hireling** through `customDeck`. The pair that matters is one
board attacked with one creature and with two — **two Treasures either way**, where the per-creature
event would make four. Plus the pod row above, and an opponent's hit (nothing). The D439 compile row
that asserted the refusal is **rewritten in place**, with the old claim and why it was right at the
time quoted in its comment, and a second row keeps the singular and plural readings apart: they
differ by one word of English and by how many times they fire.

`combat-damage-dealt` joins `attack-declared` in the mechanic-coverage test's `compilerOnly` set,
with its corpus count and the name of the runtime block that drives it (D442's rule for that set).

**Five breaks, five failures.**

Legal-only coverage 16,416 of 56,421 lines (29.1%), **7,419 cards with a script** (7,411 → 7,419). GATE OK, 2,025 engine tests.

## D444 — A mana ability that is a choice of colours, which was left to a path that cannot reach it

The single biggest "one line from finished" shape in the corpus, found by asking a better question:
instead of ranking prologue families by lines printed, rank **shapes by how many cards have no other
unread line**. 17,439 legal cards are one line from finished, and the top of that list is a mana
ability:

| shape | legal lines | cards one line from finished |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `{T}: Add {B} or {R}` | 252 | 67 |
| `{T}: Add one mana of any color` | 112 | 55 |
| `{T}: Add {W}, {B}, or {G}` | 22 | — |

The branch that reads an activated ability had a comment saying a choice "is a *choice*, which
`AbilityDef` expresses with one ability per colour on the hand-written dual lands, so it is left to
`cardFromData`'s land path rather than guessed at here". The first half is right and the conclusion
does not follow: **`cardFromData` reads a whole card or nothing**, so *Akoum Refuge* — which also
enters tapped and gains its controller a life — got no script from either path. A reader that defers
to a path that cannot reach the card is not deferring, it is dropping it.

### The shape is the pool's own

`AbilityDef` has no "one of these", and it does not need one: the hand-written Guildgates and Birds
of Paradise express a choice as **one ability per colour**, and `manaSources` already collapses
several free tap-for-mana abilities on one permanent back into a single source that makes one of
their colours. So this emits two abilities for "Add {B} or {R}", three for the Oxford-comma form and
five for "any color" — nothing new in the model.

The descriptions are **per colour**, not the printed line, because the table puts one on each button
and two buttons reading "{T}: Add {B} or {R}." cannot be told apart. The cost prefix is kept
verbatim, so *An-Havva Township*'s "{2}, {T}: Add {R} or {W}." becomes "{2}, {T}: Add {R}." and
"{2}, {T}: Add {W}.".

### What stays unread, and why the anchors do the refusing

Each narrower form carries a restriction this shape cannot express: "Spend this mana only to cast a
creature spell" (37 legal lines), "Add one mana of the chosen color" (20 — there is no chosen colour
until something reads "As ~ enters, choose a color"), "Add two mana in any combination of colors"
(10), "Add {c} or one mana of the chosen color" (10), and *Adarkar Wastes*' painland sentence. None
needs a refusal list: the pattern is anchored at both ends, so a second sentence or an extra word
simply does not match.

### The break run caught a test that could not fail

The "any color" row was first written with Accomplished Alchemist's *first* line only — and the
break that disabled the branch passed. With one line, `cardFromData` reads the whole card as a mana
creature (#309) and the line reader is never reached. Both printed lines are in the fixture now, so
the whole-card path refuses and the row exercises what it claims to.

### Verified

Two runtime tests on printed **Akoum Refuge** through `customDeck`: three copies pay for a Lightning
Bolt ({R}) and then a Doom Blade ({1}{B}) off one printed line, which is the choice working in both
directions through the engine's own auto-tapper; and a fourth copy played from hand arrives tapped
and gains the life, which are the other two lines `cardFromData` used to refuse the card over. Plus
a five-row compile table on printed cards and four refusals.

**Six breaks, six failures.**

### The instrument is the deliverable

The probe that found this is now `scripts/measure/one-line-short.mjs`, with a row in the measure
README. It prints what `compilable.mjs` cannot: 16,698 legal cards are **exactly one unread line**
from a finished script, grouped by that line's shape and ranked by how many cards each shape would
finish. Its own docblock says the row is a ceiling and not a forecast, and names the row that must
*stay* unread ("Spend this mana only to cast a creature spell") so nobody reads the list as a to-do.

Legal-only coverage **16,855 of 56,421 lines (29.9%)**, **7,652 cards with a script**
(7,419 → 7,652, +233), 4,157 with every printed line read (4,036 → 4,157, +121) — the largest single
increment in this run. GATE OK, 2,035 engine tests.
